name: ABC Cave
info_ref: Corres LXXI pp.12-29A, 48; Corrected position: Objective ID: A7029708
info_origin: In the 1950's a longtime member of the New Zealand Alpine Club, Jim Gilkinson, along with other members first built a rock wall at the cave entrance to form a sleeping platform (bivvy), and at this time the feature was just referred to as 'the cave' in rock climbing circles. In the later 1960s after many years of use by the NZ Alpine Club and the Otago Tramping & Mountaineering Club, it came to be referred to as ABC cave, for the initials of Alan Smith, Bruce Clark, and Colin McKenzie, three of the more active members. In 1990/91 the accomodation at the cave was formally upgraded with the permission of the Department of Conservation and the installation of a sleeping platform and cooking bench. Part of the rationale for official recognition of the name was an incident in 1983 where three schoolboys died in a snowstorm just minutes away from the cave near The Gap to the east, who might have survived if the feature was more widely known about. While the name was added to official maps in 1987, the proposal sought further awareness through recognition as an official name.

The area was depicted as a named Māori forest clearing of about 125 hectares, one of a number in existence at the time of the original survey of nearby Greytown in 1854. In the 1874 Māori census six males and 10 females of all ages resided at Ahikōuka. Details of the original sale were relitigated before the Native Land Court in 1868, which awarded the northern and western portions to Ngātuere Tāwhao (?-1890), an eastern portion to Wi Kingi, and more controversially a southern portion of 780 acres (315 ha) to Matiaha Mokai. This allocation did not resolve the matter and Charles Heaphy, the Commissioner of Native Lands appointed independent adjudicators to settle the case. Intended to finalise the matter, an Ahikōuka Native Lands Claims Bill passed through the House of Representatives in 1870 but lapsed in the Legislative Council. Matiaha Mokai also petitioned Parliament in 1877 seeking the issue of a Certificate of Title. Much of the Ahikōuka Block eventually passed into the hands of Sir Walter Buchanan MP (1838-1924) and, known as the ‘Buchanan Block,’ was subdivided and on-sold by a later owner Arthur P Whatman (1862-1938) in 1901. Whatman also gifted some of his land for a five farm World War One soldier settlement at Ahikōuka.

name: Ahipara
info_origin: 'Northland, 16 km from Kaitaia. Lit. ahi: fi re; para: large fern, or a species of cabbage tree. Parts of both plants are edible, so literally the name could mean Fire at which para was cooked. Possibly a contraction of ahi parapara, an earth oven at which special rites are performed. Until the mid-nineteenth century the locality was known as Wharo, which can be rendered as Stretched out or At great length. The chief Tohe, wishing to know how far the tide had receded, ordered his slave to measure the distance by holding his arms out to count out the number of spans from high water level.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: This locality is at the end of Akaroa Road which was surveyed in 1892 but only created in a series of stages from 1897 to 1905 and was still only 6ft (1.8m) wide in 1900. Akaroa Road took its name from the hill overlooking it then known locally as Mount Akaroa which was marked as a permanent survey point on future Commissioner of Crown Lands, Reginald Greville’s (1862-1923) plan of Pahiatua No. 2 Farm Homestead Settlement of 1892 and opened for settlement as Lease-in-Perpetuity farms that same year. Akaroa Peak replaced Mount Akaroa from about 1913 and was used locally until at least the 1930s. On today’s topographical maps the hill is unnamed but shown as a spot height of 335m. Some observers believed that the area around Pongaroa was formerly part of a large Māori clearing and at ‘Mount Akaroa’ in pre-European times Ngāti Kahungunu had fought a decisive engagement with northern invaders. The 1957 topographical map of Pongaroa and Turnagain Survey Districts shows Akaroa positioned about three-quarters of the way along Akaroa Road. The 1976 cadastral map of Pongaroa Survey District also includes Akaroa as does the 1986 update by which time it migrates from three-quarters of the way along to the end of the road. Akaroa is a Māori name but does not appear to be an original Māori name for this locality.

name: Akaroa Marine Reserve
info_origin: The Ngāi Tahu sub-tribes Ngāi Tarewa and Ngāti Irakehu settled in the area naming the harbour “Akaroa”, meaning the long harbour. This is confirmed in the publication “Old Maori Place Names Round Akaroa Harbour” by Louis Vagioni and supplementary notes by DJC Pringle, (http://christchurchcitylibraries.com/Heritage/Publications/Akaroa/OldMaoriPlaceNames/Vangioni-1967.pdf), where it is suggested that “Akaroa” is the South Island form of Whangaroa (“Whanga” – harbour; “Roa” – long). Numerous other publications also offer this interpretation.
info_description: Located at the entrance to Akaroa Harbour.  It lies between Gateway Point and Elephant Head and between the eastern shore and Wainui Leading Lights line.  It is approximately 4 km long, and varies in width between approximately 0.4 km and 1.8 km. The marine reserve lies alongside an area known as Dan Rogers Bluff (an unofficial name and not recorded on official maps/charts), with spectacular volcanic cliffs, sea caves and sea stacks.  The underwater topography is spectacular, with the cliffs and bluffs falling vertically to the seabed.  These are colonised by marine communities in interesting zonation patterns.  Huge room-sized boulders provide spectacular underwater scenery and habitat for marine communities of Banks Peninsula.
info_note: Reviewed by the NZGB on 23 April 2014. Determined by the Minister of Conservation on 8 May 2014.
cpa_legislation: Section 4(1) of the Marine reserves Act 1971. See also Marine Reserve (Akaroa) Order 2014.

All the information has been orally provided by our kaumātua Wake Tua whom is 90 years of age, and states that he received this information from his grandfather Motukiwi Hone Tua, and ably supported by kaumātua Rawiri Timoti whose great great grandmother Maungaroa was an elder sister to Motukiwi as well as kaumātua Rawiri Henare and kaumātua Pita Pangari. info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5104718 {https://street-stories.nz/street/akura-road-ngaumutawa-road/; [Maori Meeting.1869. info_origin: An original Māori name. Ākura is named after Kura an ancestress of the people from the area. This block of land passed through the Native Land Court in 1869, although only after a rehearing of the interested parties. Much of the area remained in forest in the 1870s, but there was a large pā on cleared land. In the 1874 Māori census only five males and five females including children were residing at Ākura. An 1876 description of the pā suggests a larger population noting that the inhabitants, ‘were grouped around a small clearing on the bank of the river and were dressed in every variety of costume, bright colour being prevalent, and carried spears, tomahawks and other weapons of greenstone, etc. Most of the women were occupied smoking and working, some at needlework, and others making quilts with bright-coloured silks, and the rapidity with which these women worked was only equalled by the workmanship. In the foreground the trunk of a large tree was burning for the purpose of supplying campfires and dotted about here and there were the fires at which cooking operations were going on. The bright rugs and shawls spread over the calico tents in different places and the gay trappings of the horses lying around the trees’. A road of the same name was cut through the bush in 1876.

The Māori name is Okahukura, meaning place of rainbow or butterfly". http://www.northshorecity.govt.nz/Services/OnlineServices/Documents/nsc-suburb-map.pdf. North Shore City suburb centred around 2662150E 6494900N; 'Alexander McArthur, a resident of what was then known as Lucas Creek, named Albany after a place of the same name in Western Australia. McArthur was impressed by the township in Western Australia, which was in a successful fruit growing region, and saw similarities with the Auckland locality. The name was officially changed from Lucas Creek on 1 December 1890. Maori name: Okahukura, lit. o: place of; kahukura: rainbow, or butterfly.' name: Alb Valley
info_ref: Source: British Antarctic "Terra Nova" 1910-1913 Expedition Reports Physiography Vol.B, 1923, p.60 & Plates 56-58
info_origin: A name that arose from Arthur Helm's misunderstanding of a reference in R.E. Priestley's Physiography (Robertson Bay and Terra Nova Bay Regions), 1923. The Northern Party of the British Antarctic Expedition (Terra Nova expedition, BrAE), 1910-13 lead by Campbell, referred to the feature as Kar Terrace. Priestley in his Physiography noted that Kar Terrace was an "Alb Valley" in the sense of Shackleton's earlier memoir (E. Shackleton, British Antarctic Expedition 1907-09, Geology Vol. I).  Shackleton described "alb" valleys or terraces as one archetypal form, referring to many Antarctic valleys as being of the "alb" type, likely for the Alb Valley, St. Blasien, Germany. There is no evidence that the British Antarctic Expedition (Nimrod expedition, BAE), 1907-09 named this feature Alb Valley.
info_description: A broad valley at the eastern flanks of Mount Dickason, at the west of Priestley Glacier where it begins to descend steeply to Terra Nova Bay, Victoria Land.

name: Alexandra Courthouse Historic Reserve
info_origin: The old Courthouse in Alexandra's Centennial Avenue is one of the town's oldest stone buildings and had an important role in the life and administration of the Central Otago goldfields. Opened on 16th June 1879, it housed both the Warden's and Magistrate's Courts. The courthouse was just that for almost a century, until 1972 when the court moved to a new building. After that it housed other government departments, was a temporary library, Plunket rooms and information centre. The Alexandra Courthouse is now a Category 2 Historic Building and a DOC reserve, managed by the department. (Source: Department of Conservation)

Mount Alma and the Alma River were named by W.T.L. Travers.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Amundsen Coast
info_origin: Named by NZ-APC in 1961 for Capt. Roald Amundsen, the Norwegian explorer who led his own expedition in 1910-12 to the Antarctic. Setting up a base at Framheim at the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, he sledged southward across the shelf and discovered a route up the Axel Heiberg Glacier along this coast to reach the polar plateau. He was the first to reach the South Pole, December 14, 1911.
info_description: That portion of the coast to the S of the Ross Ice Shelf lying between Morris Peak on the E side of Liv Glacier and the W side of the Scott Glacier.

name: Amundsen Glacier

name: Amundsen Icefall

name: Anatimo
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche December 2022: Objective ID: A5139262; A5383948 {Dollimore Edward. 1952. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand: Wises.; McKay, Alexander. 1872. A Compendium of Official Documents Relative to Native Affairs in the South Island. Volume Two. New Zealand: Luckie and Collins.; [Possible Tasman Relic, Ancient Musket Barrel from Golden Bay. 1938. Press, 12 September, Page 8.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/CHP19380912.2.52); [David A. Armstrong. 'Mackay, Alexander', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1993. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2m11/mackay-alexander) (accessed 7 December 2022); Nomenclature Committee. 1908. Journal of the House of Representatives. 10 October.}
info_origin: In 1872 Alexander McKay, resident magistrate and Commissioner of Native Reserves in the South Island, in reporting on 'Native Reserves' in Nelson and Marlborough referred to a small 4 acre [1.6 ha] reserve set aside as part of the New Zealand Company purchases and known as Anatimo which had been abolished and replaced by a 26 acre [11 ha] reserve. With the arrival of European farmers, the locality became known as Wainui Bay after the adjacent Wainui Inlet. After the arrival of the telegraph in 1907 and a school in 1909, Anatimo again became the established name. The Nomenclature Committee set up in 1908 to consider 'alterations and improvements' to place naming focusing on post offices and railways stations believed Anatimo was a 'doubtful spelling'. Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen accepted the committee's view but accepted that it had come into regular use. Comparatively remote, the mail for Anatimo was sent by boat from the mid-19th century with a weekly service commencing around 1911. This was replaced by horseback delivery after WWI and continued into the 1950s. The discovery of an old musket barrel and broken sword blade at Anatimo in 1914 led to speculation that these were relics from Abel Tasman's 1642 visit, although the Dominion Museum thought they were more likely a British army flintlock. In 1928 residents petitioned the Minister of Public Works for improved access. This road was much damaged by slips after the Murchison earthquake in 1929. Later visitors were attracted by the limestone formations in the vicinity.

info_origin: A glacier named by George Edward ‘Guy’ Mannering (1862-1947) in 1889 after the wife of visiting Austrian scientist and mountaineer Dr Robert von Lendenfeld (1858-1913). Mannering, regarded by some as New Zealand’s ‘first real alpine climber’, originally rendered it as Frau von Lendenfeld Glacier but it later became known by her first name of Anna. In 1891 Mannering also named the Lendenfeld Saddle after her husband. Robert and Anna von Lendenfeld (1860-1946) came to New Zealand from Australia in 1883. Already experienced mountaineers they travelled to Aoraki/Mount Cook for three weeks. Anna twice accompanied Robert up Haast Ridge to take measurements and assisted him in his topographical survey of Haupapa/Tasman Glacier. They initially intended to attempt Mount Darwin but settled on the unclimbed Hochstetter Dome (2810m). With New Zealander Harry Dew as porter, they made their ascent on 25 March 1883, ‘the first alpine ascent to a summit in New Zealand’. A contemporary newspaper account related that, ‘Roped together they followed up the line of the glacier. Travelling was at first terribly rough work, the crevasses, walls of ice, and broken nature of the glacier causing immense labour’. Dr von Lendenfeld observed that ‘the sort of thing met with was quite beyond his experience in Switzerland’. Mrs Jessie Westland, a subscribing member of the New Zealand Alpine club, in reviewing Von Lendenfeld’s ‘A voyage to Australasia’ in the New Zealand Alpine Journal in 1893 observed that ‘we consider it a serious dereliction of duty on her husband’s part, that amid his name-giving, he has not conferred upon any of the Alpine peaks or glaciers the privilege of handing down her name to posterity.’ In 1923 William Kennedy (1865-1950) a prominent Canterbury mountaineer wrote to the Commissioner Crown Lands for Canterbury requesting the adoption of the name Anna Glacier. This was approved by the Surveyor General that same year. Anna Glacier first appeared on the map ‘Part of New Zealand alpine regions’ in 1929.

name: Anzac Bay
info_ref: Bay of Plenty Times, 6 November 1915, p. 4; 11 November 1915, p. 2; 8 January 1916, p. 2; 26 February 1916, p. 4; 12 June 1916, p. 2.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: This feature name resulted from several initiatives taken by local bodies. During a September 1915 meeting of the Katikati Domain Board, it was observed that the steep ascent from the beach at St George’s Bay closely resembled that at the bay on the Gallipoli Peninsula where Australian and New Zealand forces had landed on 25 April. The Board, therefore, proposed that St George’s Bay should be retitled Anzac Bay. The Tauranga Harbour Board then took up this suggestion. Its members resolved that renaming the Bay after the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps would be a fitting ‘commemoration of our heroic boys and their fellow soldiers’. During November 1915, local dignitary George Vesey Stewart wrote to Tauranga MP William Herries requesting that the change be granted legislative approval. In the event, it was decided not to wait for official permission. On 6 January 1916, a ceremony was held to ‘christen’ the bay and open its new jetty and shelter shed, with both the Mayor of Tauranga and the Mayor of Waihi in attendance. Given that it took place only eight months after the original landings, this renaming was one of the first measures adopted in New Zealand to commemorate those who served at Gallipoli. However, efforts at a governmental level ended in disappointment. Repeated entreaties from Stewart and Herries were turned down by the Lands Department, which refused to sanction the use of Anzac Bay on the grounds that a Māori name would be more appropriate. A further approach made to Prime Minister William Massey received a noncommittal reply.
info_description: A bay on the north side of Katikati Entrance in Tauranga Harbour between Yellow Point and Papatu Point. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BC36 635489 to 641489

name: Anzac Bay
info_ref: NZ History, ‘ANZAC Day: The Anzacs’, http://www.nzhistory.net.nz/war/anzac-day/the-anzacs; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: The name of this feature commemorates the men and women of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps. It was originally planned to call that unit the ‘Australasian Army Corps’, following the practice employed at several sporting events. However, soldiers of both nationalities were unwilling to surrender their separate identities. Although the exact origins of ‘ANZAC’ are unclear, it is widely believed that Sergeant K.M. Little, a headquarters clerk, developed the acronym after finding the full title too cumbersome to write down. The Anzacs first saw action in 1915 when they played a significant role in Allied efforts to capture the Gallipoli Peninsula from Ottoman forces. By 1917, the re-organised I ANZAC Corps and II ANZAC Corps were both serving on the Western Front, while other ANZAC units were stationed in Egypt, Palestine, and Mesopotamia. Exactly when this name came into common use is unknown with references in newspapers dating back to the early 1920's.

name: Anzac Peaks
info_ref: Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 1, pp. 38-43.; Langton, Graham, ‘Samuel Turner: Climber and Egotist Supreme’, New Zealand Wilderness, May 2002, pp. 7-9.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 1947 (90); LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: The English mountaineer Samuel Turner first scaled these two peaks on 6 February 1917. Despite achieving many notable feats during his career, including the first traverse of Aoraki/Mount Cook, Turner was a controversial figure. He was strongly disliked by many for his egotism and frequent attempts to downplay the efforts of other climbers. The name Turner bestowed on these features was the ‘Anzacs’, which had become the common shorthand for referring to the men and women of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps. It was originally planned to call that unit the ‘Australasian Army Corps’, following the practice employed at several sporting events. However, soldiers of both nationalities were unwilling to surrender their separate identities. Although the exact origins of ‘ANZAC’ are unclear, it is widely believed that Sergeant K.M. Little, a headquarters clerk, developed the acronym after finding the full title too cumbersome to write down. The Anzacs first saw action in 1915, when they played a significant role in Allied efforts to capture the Gallipoli Peninsula from Ottoman forces. By 1917, the re-organised I ANZAC Corps and II ANZAC Corps were both serving on the Western Front, while other ANZAC units were stationed in Egypt, Palestine, and Mesopotamia. Turner’s choice of the ‘Anzacs’ received initial sanction from the Ministry of Lands, but was quickly superseded by Anzac Peaks on most maps.

info_ref: File BRD-02-02-00-07; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760}
info_origin: [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={e36db1e3-3d52-e311-8212-005056970030}); [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for James Cook](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1c25/cook-james); .; 'The name Aoraki is also found in other parts of the country and the Pacific (such as the mountain Aora’i in Tahiti). Two traditions are related to the naming of this, New Zealand’s highest mountain. The first relates the wreckage of the Āraiteuru waka at Matakaea (Shag Point). After capsizing, many of the passengers went ashore to explore the land, including Kirikirikatata who carried his grandson Aoraki on his shoulders. The travellers needed to be back at the waka before daylight, but most did not make it, instead turning into many of the well-known landmarks of Te Waipounamu; Aoraki, being on his grandfather’s shoulders, was the tallest. In the second tradition Aoraki was an atua (god) who descended from the heavens with his brothers; attempting the return voyage their waka crashed into the Pacific Ocean forming what would later be known as the South Island (Te Waka-o-Aoraki). Aoraki and his brothers climbed to the highest side of the waka where they turned into the highest peaks of the Southern Alps. Despite the association of the English name with Captain James Cook, he did not actually see the peak when sailing up the west coast of the South Island in 1770. The mountain did not take an English name until 1851, when Captain John Lort Stokes of the survey ship HMS Acheron christened it after the famous explorer. The current dual name dates from the 1998 Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act, and is also the name of the national park.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Aotea Conservation Park
info_origin: Aotea is the traditional (non official) name for 'Great Barrier Island (Aotea Island)'. Locals often refer to the island as either Aotea or Great Barrier. The island was visited by the ancestral Aotea canoe and occupied by Tainui and Te Arawa sub-tribes. Captain James Cook renamed the island Great Barrier in 1769 because of the protection it gave to the Hauraki Gulf. The use of the traditional name for this CPA recognises the long connection with the island held by tangata whenua.
info_description: Public conservation land on Great Barrier Island (Aotea Island), which lies 100km northeast of Auckland in the outer Hauraki Gulf. Numerous areas formerly held under the Conservation Act 1987 as mostly stewardship areas (with various names) were reclassified under one classification and named Aotea Conservation Park.

info_origin: Arahura is the final resting place for Waitaki where Poutini (the kaitiaki of Pounamu) transformed her into pounamu. ; 'Arahura River: It is said that the name was conferred by Ngahue, the early explorer who accompanied Kupe on his epic tenth-century voyage to Aotearoa, and that it means Path discovered (by Ngahue). Another rendering of the name is Pathway of the dawn (hura meaning to begin to dawn), because the first rays of the summer sun shone through a gap in the hills. It was here that Ngahue discovered greenstone. James Cowan pointed out that Ara’ura was the classic name for Aitutaki in the Cook Islands, and that it may have been imported from there. There is another legend to the effect that Ngahue and Tamakiterangi or Tama-ahua were the discoverers.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche Janurary 2024: Objective ID: A6084106 {Census of the Maori Population. 1878. AJHR, G2.; [Maori church at Arapaoa, Kaipara. 1878. New Zealand Herald, 29 June, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH18780629.2.47); Maori Place Names [Handwritten list giving origin of name]. R21682778. Archives New Zealand, Wellington. Digitisied; NZGB XXIII/262-3 1948}
info_origin: An original Māori name associated with Arapaoa River. From 1911 the New Zealand Post Office maintained a register of its offices with Māori names. By 1933 they believed that their use of Arapoa was a misspelling, that Arapaoa was correct and literally translated as ‘the spray way’, which they considered meant the river marked by its spray. Kaipara Resident Magistrate John Symonds (1816-83) recorded 37 people at Arapaoa for the 1878 Māori census, including 13 males and 5 females over 15 years old, and 11 males and 8 females under 15 years of age. That same year saw the completion of a Māori church. An Arapaoa Native School was opened by 1902. In 1948 the Post Office wrote to the New Zealand Geographic Board about possible confusion over Arapawa and Arapaoa noting ‘from this Department’s point of view it rather resembles Arapaoa’. The Board’s Secretary sought the opinion of members Sir Apirana Ngata (1874-1950), Pei Te Hurinui Jones (1898-1976), a licensed interpreter, and ethnologist Johannes Andersen (1873-1962), with the subsequent discussion focusing largely on the correctness of Arapawa and with Arapaoa left untouched.

name: Arapaoa Island
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Te Atiawa and Ngati Tama note that this island is the location of traditions of Kupe but highly significant to Te Atiawa. Kupe finally dispatched whekenui with a massive Arapaoa (downwards blow) to its head, spiritual home of Te Atiawa, many Kaimoana sites, many papakaianga, fortified Pa sites, whaling sites, cultivation sites, waka landing, building waka, repairs, and Arapawa is a spelling error. Ngati Kuia Tribunal evidence notes that Ara means ‘to rise’ and ‘paoa’ is to strike with a weapon. The Island was named after Kupe’s rising stroke which killed the octopus Te Wheke o Muturangi. It features in waiata and stories of the iwi.

name: Arawhatawhito
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche April 2024: Objective ID: A6258696 {Andersen, J. C. (Compiler) (1934). Place-names of New Zealand. Rules of Nomenclature and list of Names Approved or Changed or Expunged. Wellington: Polynesian Society Reprint No. 4.; Further Papers relevant to Military Operations against the Rebel Natives. 1870. AJHR A8B.; Hill, Henry Thomas, 1849-1933: [Map of Kaingaroa tableland [ms map]. H. Hill, 1926-1927. MapColl-832.18gdw/1926-27/Acc.5836](https://natlib.govt.nz/records/23095569); National-endowment Land set apart as a Permanent State Forest. 1927. New Zealand Gazette, 59, 2692-93.; [M. P. K. Sorrenson. 'Ngata, Apirana Turupa', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1996. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3n5/ngata-apirana-turupa); [Weao Survey District S.J. Bryers, Oct. 1937.](https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE4546082); NZGB Minutes, 1941.}
info_origin: An original Māori name. School inspector and amateur geologist Henry Hill’s (1849-1933) map of the Kaingaroa Plains from 1926-27 shows ancient Māori tracks passing through Arawhatawhito. In 1870 Captain Gilbert Mair (1843-1923), commanding the Arawa Flying Column, met up with Major Roberts who was bringing supplies of food from Opepe to what Mair spelled as Te Arawhatataiwhito. In 1927 the 56508 acres (22868 ha) encompassing Arawhatawhito, previously surveyed as Run 59, was gazetted as a Permanent State Forest becoming State Forest No. 79 Kaingaroa Plantation Extension and was planted in the following years. The 1937 cadastral Map of Weao Survey District drawn by draughtsman Sperry James (Jim) Bryers (1908-?) recorded the locality as Arawhata Tawhito. In reviewing names on the new provisional topographical sheets, in 1941 Ngāti Porou leader, politician and scholar Sir Āpirana Ngata (1874-1950), an Honorary Geographic Board member (1932-50), put forward Arawhatawhito rather than Arawhatataiwhito as the correct form of the name. In joining up the name which Bryers’ broke into two parts Ngata was following the orthographic rules that the Board had published in 1934. Hyphens were avoided because cartographers were concerned that they may be mistaken for physical features on the ground. However, Ngata was mindful that satisfying cartographic conventions could obscure the story behind the name.
info_description: A locality name corrected from Arawhatataiawhito by Sir Apirana Ngata

name: Arethusa Pool
info_ref: Colledge J.J. and Barlow, Ben, Ships of the Royal Navy: The Complete Record of All Fighting Ships of the Royal Navy from the 15th Century to the Present, Newbury: Casemate, 2010.; Evening Post, 14 November 1924, p. 2.; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 11, pp. 166-170.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Correspondence, vol. 42, p. 156.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: In 1924, Sir Frederick Chapman, a former Supreme Court judge and member of the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand, suggested new names for two features on Lake Wanaka. He proposed that the body of water on ‘Pigeon Island’ should become Arethusa Pool and that the Island’s highest point should be titled Tyrwhitt Peak. When the time came to seek official approval for these changes, the Governor-General, Admiral John Jellicoe, further moved that ‘Pigeon Island’ be renamed ‘Harwich Island’. Chapman’s submission of Arethusa Pool was based on two considerations. Firstly, he noted that the feature was not stream-fed, but rather obtained water from snow that melted off the surrounding mountains and then travelled through rock fissures. To Chapman, this phenomenon recalled the site in Syracuse known to the Ancient Greeks as ‘Arethusa Spring’. The second factor concerned the light cruiser HMS Arethusa, which had served as the flagship of the Royal Navy’s Harwich Force under Commodore Reginald Tyrwhitt. Formed at the outbreak of the First World War, this squadron was given three main objectives: to protect the approaches to the English Channel; to monitor German activities in the North Sea; and to escort ships sailing between Britain and the Netherlands. The Arethusa’s wartime service proved extremely eventful. She was so badly damaged at the 1914 Battle of Heligoland Blight that she had to be towed back to port. Having been refitted, the ship then took part in the Cuxhaven Raid and the Battle of Dogger Bank, before capturing four German trawlers in September 1915. On 11 February 1916, the Arethusa struck a mine off the coast of Felixstowe and sank with the loss of six of her crew. The name Arethusa Pool was first Gazetted by the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand in 1924, and was officially confirmed by the New Zealand Geographic Board in 1948.; 'The name was suggested to Lord Jellicoe because it had the same features as the fountain in the island of Ortygia, near Syracuse. Arethusa was also the name of the warship commanded by Admiral Sir Reginald Tyrwhitt; the island was previously Harwich which was named after the admiral’s squadron. Also known as Paradise Lake. There are three small islands in the lake named Faith, Hope, and Charity. Maori name: Moutimu, which has been rendered Ebbing tide, because the level sometimes rises and falls. It has also been called Manuka.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Armistice Peak
info_ref: Corres XLVII, XLVIII, pp 191; 285, 363; File 15, pp 226; File 0775-01 v/2 f/227 9/03/1982; Langton, Graham, ‘Samuel Turner: Climber and Egotist Supreme’, New Zealand Wilderness, May 2002, pp. 7-9.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Correspondence, vol. 47, p. 285, vol. 48, p. 191.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 1985 (18).; NZAJ Vol 6, p 210; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: Samuel Turner and Edgar Williams first scaled this peak in 1918 as recorded in the NZAJ. Williams was a prolific climber whose other notable achievements included the first ascents of Mount Greenlaw and Mount Sibbald. As for Turner, he was one of the most controversial figures in New Zealand mountaineering. An Englishman who performed many daring exploits, including the first traverse of Aoraki/Mount Cook, he was intensely disliked for his perceived arrogance and tendency to belittle the efforts of his contemporaries. The significance of Turner and Williams’ climb lies in the precise date on which it took place: 11 November 1918. At 11am (Paris time) that same day, an armistice negotiated by Allied and German representatives in a railway carriage parked at the forest of Compiègne came into effect. Under its terms, the Germans agreed to withdraw from all French and Belgian territory, and to surrender most of their navy, air force, and artillery. Although technically only a suspension of hostilities, in practice the Armistice marked the end of the fighting on the Western Front that had been raging for nearly four and a half years. Many countries still mark the signing of the Armistice on 11 November, although it usually forms part of wider Remembrance Day commemorations.

name: Aroarokaehe Range
info_origin: Aroarokaehe was a passenger on the Arai-te-Uru waka, along with Aoraki and his grandfather Kirikirikatata, who both turned into a mountain (Aoraki/Mount Cook) and its associated/attached range (Kirikirikatata / Mount Cook Range). Aroarokaehe was the wife of Mauka Atua and he turned into a peak on the Ben Ōhau Range, while his wife was persuaded by Kirikirikatata to move away from her husband to the larger and closer range next to himself and Aoraki, and thus she was located on the woman’s side. This traditional heritage is core to Ngāi Tahu Whakapapa and of significant importance in terms of restoration and preservation in the public record.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={086eb1e3-3d52-e311-8212-005056970030}))

name: Arohaki Lagoon
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-06/301; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Arohaki takes its name from a description of “the taking off of the birds, one by one, circling around”. Arohaki Lagoon is a significant area for Ngāti Whare as the place where all the water birds congregate and it was carefully managed as mahinga manu. It was abundant with native trout including the kōkopu, raumahe and mārearea, which attracted bird life, including the whio and parera, which were hunted traditionally by Ngāti Whare. The fish in Arohaki also provided sustenance. Ngāti Whare consider Arohaki to be a Tohu, or sign/marker for the area, which the birdlife navigates from. An old waka was discovered at the lagoon around 1955.

info_origin: 'Hawke’s Bay, 40 km from Napier. Lit. aro: kidney fat; paoa: to bash; nui (in this case): well or thoroughly. On one occasion the pa at the mouth of the Aropaoanui River was attacked, but the raiders were overcome by the defenders. To celebrate the victory the bodies of the slain were prepared for a feast. When the umu (earth ovens) were opened up, the bodies were moving. The chief Rakai, realising it was only the kidney fat of the victims twitching, went to the open ovens and paoa nui (thoroughly bashed) the offending portions.' The name 'Arthur Pass' was approved by the Geographic Board in 1929 prior to the passing of the NZGB Act 1946, with the name then confirmed in 1948. name: Arthur's Pass
info_origin: The pass was named after Sir Arthur Dudley Dobson, who first found it in 1864. He had heard of the existence of the pass from the West Coast chief Tarapuhi. Sir Arthur's brother George was sent out by the Canterbury Provincial Government to examine every possible pass between Waimakariri River and Taramakau River to open up access to the West Coast. George reported back that Arthur's Pass was more suitable for a road than any of the others, hence the name. The Honorary Geographic Board approved Arthur Pass for the newly created National Park Board in 1929, and Arthur Pass for the pass, locality, post office and railway station in 1950, in keeping with their policy of not using possessive names. Arthur's Pass was restored for the pass and locality in 1957. The reasons given were lack of public acceptance and protest at the 1950 change, and irrespective of the decision of the Board, the name of the National Park would be changed by an amendment to the Act creating the park. The names of the railway station and the post office were left to the discretion of the respective departments running them.
info_description: Pass on the Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana between the Bealey River and Ōtira River.

name: Arthur's Pass
info_origin: The pass was named after Sir Arthur Dudley Dobson, who first traversed the pass in 1864. Sir Arthur had heard of the existence of the pass from the West Coast chief Tarapuhi. Sir Arthur's brother George was sent out by the Canterbury Provincial Government to examine every possible pass between the Waimakariri River and Taramakau River, to open up access to the West Coast. George reported back that Arthur's Pass was more suitable for a road than any of the others, hence the name. The Honorary Geographic Board approved the name Arthur Pass for the newly created National Park Board in 1929, and Arthur Pass for the pass, locality, post office and railway station in 1950, in keeping with their policy of non-use of possessive names. The name Arthur's Pass was restored for the pass and locality in 1957. The reasons given were lack of public acceptance, and protest at the 1950 change, and irrespective of the decision of the Board, the name of the National Park would be changed by an amendment to the act creating the park. The names of the railway station and the post office were left to the discretion of the respective departments running them.

name: Arthur's Pass National Park
info_origin: Arthur Pass National Park was altered to Arthur's Pass National Park by Section 6(1) and (2) of the National Parks Act 1980, in which the possesive apostrophe was reinserted into the name. The name comes from the pass, named after Arthur Dudley Dobson (later Sir) who did much exploration work between Canterbury and Westland in the early 1860's. 'After Arthur Dudley Dobson, a son of Edward Dobson, Canterbury provincial engineer, who in the company of his brother (also Edward) discovered it in 1864. During the twentieth century the name was officially changed to Arthurs Pass in conformity with the policy laid down by the Geographic Board, but the omission of the apostrophe gave rise to violent protest by local residents and many others, and the Minister of Lands reinstated it. It was not until the publication of the Official Circular of 16 September 1975 that the post office formally became Arthur’s Pass. The site of Arthur’s Pass township was referred to by Edward Dobson in 1865 as Camping Flat. Arthur’s Pass National Park was inaugurated in August 1929, becoming New Zealand’s third national park.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Ataturk Memorial
info_ref: Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 13, pp. 105-150.; Ministry for Culture and Heritage, ‘Atatürk Memorial’, http://www.mch.govt.nz/nz-identity-heritage/national-monuments-war-graves/atat%C3%BCrk-memorial LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: The construction of this memorial resulted from a series of diplomatic negotiations. In 1984, the Australian and Turkish Governments began discussions over a mutual commemoration of their First World War dead. The Turkish authorities agreed to change the name of the site where Australian and New Zealand soldiers first landed during the 1915 Dardanelles Campaign from ‘Ari Burnu’ to Anzac Cove. For their part, the Australians would open a memorial to the Turkish defenders of Gallipoli in Canberra. Dismayed at being excluded from these consultations, and pointing out that ‘ANZAC means as much to New Zealand as to Australia’, the New Zealand Government pressed for the scheme to be extended. It was subsequently resolved that another memorial to the Turkish dead would be built above Tarakena Bay on the south coast of Wellington, a site chosen for its striking likeness to the landscape of the Gallipoli Peninsula. The Wellington memorial was unveiled on 25 April 1990. In addition to a marble crescent and soil from Anzac Cove, it features a bust of Mustafa Kemal. As commander of the Ottoman 19th Division, Kemal played a pivotal role in frustrating Allied efforts to seize the Dardanelles. His units helped contain the initial landings at Anzac Cove, before retaking the crucial height of Chunuk Bair during the August Offensive. Kemal would later become the first president of modern Turkey and in 1934 was granted the honorary surname Atatürk, or ‘Father of the Turks’.

name: Ātiamuri
info_origin: 'Atiamuri, Lake: Lit. Tia who follows behind. The name may refer to the explorer Tia, who was forced to turn back on reaching the since-flooded Atiamuri Falls here. According to another tradition, Tia reached the bank of the Waikato River and was disappointed to find that the water was muddy, a sign that Ngatoro had already reached some point further upstream. Tia’s crossing place was then called Atiamuri (Place where Tia followed behind, or came last). On another account Atiamuri refers to an ancestress who was petrified, her body remaining in the river in the form of a large rock. Alternatively, it may be a contraction of the tribal name Ngati-a-Muri (Descendants of Muri). Lake Atiamuri is an artificial lake formed by the construction of the Atiamuri hydro-electric power station, commissioned in 1958. The lake covers the former location of the falls and river gorge.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Auahitōtara Kāinga
info_ref: Objective ID: A2404063. Feature shown on: NZMS260 T21 Edition 1 1982.
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: Auahitōtara was one of the permanent residences and a notable pā of the Ngāti Rangi hapu, Ngāti Rangituhia. 'Auahi' means smoke and 'Tōtara' is the native tree which still grows there today. Therefore the meaning of the name is 'Smoke of the Tōtara Tree.' Most maps show the name on a trig point, but the actual site is the next ridge over from the trig, and then encompassing the grove of trees (including tōtara) lower down from that ridge. It was occupied by the Ngāti Rangi ancestor Te Keepa Rangihiwinui and others. Auahitōtara was a Ngāti Rangi fighting pā which Ngāti Rangi used to defend their eastern flank. The pā was strategically located on a prominent summit of the ridge, sitting above a natural defense of cliffwalls, accessible only through a bottle necked entrance that was easily defendable as a pre-musket war pā. The site also provided panoramic views of the Moawhango River valley and any approaching enemy. Occupation began in the time of Tutakaroa, a descendant of Rangituhia.
info_description: A hill at 1147m approximately 8km east of Waiouru. NZTopo50-BJ35 387278.

name: Auckland
info_origin: ’The first governor of New Zealand, Captain William Hobson, named the city and province in honour of George Eden, Lord Auckland, who was governor-general of India 1836–42. Lord Auckland had given Hobson the command of HMS Rattlesnake in 1834, after a lengthy period of retirement on half pay. The family name of Lord Auckland is preserved in Mount Eden and other landmarks in the city. Queen Victoria’s approval of the name was announced in the New Zealand Government Gazette of 26 November 1842. The Māori form of the name Auckland is Akarana. Māori name: Tāmaki-makaurau: see Tāmaki.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Avoca Col
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Acland, LDG. 1946. The Early Canterbury Runs. (3rd edition) New Zealand: Whitcombe & Tombs; MacLean, Chris. 2003. John Pascoe. New Zealand: Potton; Reed, Alfred. 1975. Place Names of New Zealand, Wellington: Reed; NZGB Card Index - Canterbury; First ascents and explorations. 1931. New Zealand Alpine Journal, (4) 18, 147-172.}
info_origin: At the head of the Avoca Glacier giving access to Greenlaw Peak. This name was used informally by New Zealand Alpine Club members as early as 1930. The Canterbury Mountaineering and Tramping Club, which had its origins in the Christchurch Tramping Club founded in 1925, formally submitted Avoca Col to the Honorary New Zealand Geographic Board in 1941. Avoca Col was approved for mapping purposes in 1943 and, having initially been deferred for further investigation, became official in 1948. Avoca was used in a set of associated names being ultimately derived from the Avoca homestead on the Avoca Station (Runs 215, 214, and Class II 163). The run was initially taken up by Charles John Harper in 1857, who called it West End. It passed to Reginald Foster and Lorenzo Moore about 1864 as Avoca, and they sold it in 1873. Avoca probably took its name from a settlement in Ireland.
info_description: At head of Avoca Glacier, giving access to Greenlaw Peak.

Gisborne Standard and Cook County Gazette, Volume I, Issue 71, 24 November, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/GSCCG18871124.2.8)}
info_origin: Named for the now drained Awapuni lagoon of some 730 acres (295 ha), formerly a branch of Waikanae Creek that flowed into Waipaoa River. Awapuni was the name of several associated land blocks, sometimes referred to as 'the sand hills' which were between the northern end of the lagoon and Waikanae Creek. The Māori settlement here was named Awapuni. Ethnographer and Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen considered puni meant stopped or blocked and that punipuni could refer to fine driftwood and leaves left by a river or the tide. The Awapuni land blocks came before the Native Land Court in the 1870s with early subdivisions dating from 1876. Houses and a 'Maori church' were constructed on the block in 1882-83, which by 1884 also included 'a very handsome runanga whare of which painting is a special feature and there is also some very fine carving'. The marae was named Te Kuri a Tuatai. In 1887 members of Ngaitekete and Ngaitawhiri hapū met at Awapuni and reached the decision to oppose Te Kooti visiting Gisborne District. From the 1930s to the 1960s the lagoon was drained for land settlement and in part as the site for a golf course.

name: Awapuni
info_origin: 'Manawatu-Wanganui, 1.5 km from Palmerston North. Lit. awa: river; puni: blocked up. Originally Te Awapuni, it was an oxbow or cut-off river bend, and was thus described as a blocked-up river. In the early days the Awapuni Lagoon was a favourite spot for picnics and boating. Another meaning of Awapuni is a channel in the rocks, used as a landing place for canoes.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: In 1904 Sir Joseph Ward, the MP for Awarua and a senior minister in the Liberal government, accepted a petition from Invercargill mayor William Scandrett and others on behalf of the settlers of Seaward Moss. The petition was addressed to the Minister of Lands, TY Duncan, asking for the district to be renamed Awarua Plains. In Scottish standard English, a ‘Moss’ described an area of boggy ground or a moorland. Seaward Moss was described as an ‘an almost impassable swamp’ in 1878 when drainage and development of the peatlands first commenced. The petitioners in 1904 asserted that the ‘Moss’ part of the name was hampering attractiveness of continued settlement of the area. The Surveyor-General, JWA Marchant, consulted with the County Council which had no objection, and the name change went ahead. Awarua was borrowed from adjacent Awarua or Bluff Harbour and Awaura Bay. Awarua is a Māori name but not an original name for this wetland area. While the land was flat and can be designated a plain, from a scientific viewpoint it has been better described as a swampy bog, a class of wetland.

name: Āwhitu
info_origin: ’Lit. āwhitu: to feel regret for, or to yearn for, i.e. longing to return. Māori at the settlement near the heads of the Manukau Harbour were forced to abandon their pā on account of the depredations of the taniwha Kaiwhare, and took the title Te Rua-a-Kaiwhare (The den of the house-eater). They longed to return to the place they loved. According to another account, Hoturoa, commander of the Tainui canoe, named the bay, saying: ‘We leave Āwhitu, but some day we shall return.’ His descendants, long afterwards, besieged Ngararapapa Pā and took possession of Āwhitu.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

Journal of the New Zealand Federation of Historical Societies, 1 (6), 37-40.; [Awhitu Gathering, 1939. New Zealand Herald, 27 January, Page 12](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH19390127).; http://heritageetal.blogspot.com/2017/09/presbyterianism-on-peninsula.html; Hawken, Rachael and Walker, Lloyd. 1999. Heads, Harbours, & Hills. An Awhitu History. New Zealand; Awhitu History Book Society.; [Tenders for Inland Mail Services. 1892. Auckland Star, 16 August, Page 8.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/AS18920816.2.61.4); Walker, Lloyd. 1976. Making rough country Habitable. History of the Awhitu Highway Board (1874-1915). Auckland-Waikato Historical Journal, 28, 35-40.}
info_origin: Named with respect to the settlement of Āwhitu which was also the original Māori name for the northern portion of the larger peninsula. The Crown purchased the Kauritutahi Block in the 1850s. Āwhitu settlement migrated the name southwards and onto the eastern coast of Manukau Heads. Āwhitu Central was inland at a mid-point on the peninsula. A school was opened here in 1869, which was also used for a time for church services. An Āwhitu Central Presbyterian Church was built in 1877 on land donated by George Garland. A post office opened in 1891 and tenders for separate (thrice weekly) Āwhitu and Āwhitu Central mail services were called the following year. New school buildings opened in 1889, which by 1894 were known as Awhitu Central School. An Āwhitu Central polling station was designated in 1902. In addition, from 1897 farmers began using Āwhitu Central as an address in the Sheep Returns. The licensing option poll held in 1938 produced 23 votes for continence, 3 for State control, and 42 for prohibition.

name: Banks Peninsula
info_origin: ’When Captain James Cook sighted the peninsula on 17 February 1770, he named it Banks’s Island after Joseph Banks, the naturalist on the Endeavour. It was not until 1809 that Captain Samuel Chase of the Pegasus proved that it was a peninsula and not an island. Cook’s Banks’s Island continued in use until 1813. If, as has been claimed, a sawmill boiler was taken by water up the Heathcote River to Little River in the mid-1800s, the peninsula may have been, technically, an island at that time. Māori names: Te Pātaka-o-Rākaihautū, lit. the storehouse of the Waitaha explorer Rākaihautū; Horomaka, a name that has been applied to Banks Peninsula, but is more specifically an island in Koukourarata (Port Levy) and commemorates the arrival of the Makawhiu waka.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDIzRkI4QUYwMTBGRjg3Q0ZBNUI)
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 N36; NZTopo50-BX25 020574
info_note: Cook’s journal entry reads: ‘At 8 o’clock the Extreams of the Island bore N.76°W. and N.N.E.1/2E., and an opening that had the Appearance of a Bay or Harbour [Akaroa Harbour], lying near the South point N.28°W., distant 3 or 4 Leagues, being in 38 fathoms, a brown Sandy bottom. This Island, which I have named after Mr. Banks, lies about 5 Leagues from the coast of Tovy Poenammu [Te Wai Pounamu, the Maori name for the South Island, q.v.]

name: Barrett Lagoon
info_origin: 'Barretts Reef: Wellington, at the entrance to Port Nicholson. After Richard (Dicky) Barrett, the whaler and early trader. When the New Zealand Company’s settlement was established at Wellington, Barrett’s Hotel was a popular rendezvous. Maori name of Barrett Lagoon: Rotokaro: lit. roto: lake; karo: several meanings including a protective spell, to parry, a slave, a marauding party, or to pick out. Maori name of Barretts Reef: Te Tangihanga-o-Kupe: lit. te: the; tangihanga: lamenting; o: for; Kupe. The rocks stood like a row of people lamenting (tangi aua). According to legend they were men and women who had been turned to stone. The first name given to the reef was Te Raranga-a-Kupe (The rank or row of Kupe), but when Kupe left it was given the name Te Tangihanga-a-Kupe (The lamenting for Kupe) because his daughters were distressed at his departure. According to Place Names of the Ancestors, this was named by Kupe because of the mournful sound of the water around it.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: A small lagoon located between Barrett and Cowling Roads, approximately 5km southwest of New Plymouth city centre. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BH29 900726

name: Barrier Inlet
info_ref: Refer diagram p.72, Ernest H. Shackleton (1909), The Heart of the Antarctic Vol.II, J.B. Lippincott Company, Philadelphia
info_origin: A former inlet in the Ross Ice Shelf (aka the 'Great Ice Barrier', hence the name), where Shackleton planned to land in 1908 and establish his Winter quarters. He found the feature as described and mapped by previous explorers had disappeared leaving a wider inlet in the ice shelf. Refer pp.71-75 Heart of the Antarctic Vol.I. After an unsuccesful attempt to land on King Edward VII Land, Shackleton sailed to Ross Island and established Winter Quarters at Cape Royds.

name: Bauza Basin
info_origin: A basin named for nearby Bauza Island in Doubtful Sound. In 1793 a round-the-world Spanish expedition (then in its fourth year) spent three days carrying out a reconnaissance in Fiordland on board the Spanish Royal Navy ships Descubierta and Atrevida . The principal objective of the expedition was to obtain exact hydrographic charts of the South Pacific, but also to carry out experiments with the pendulum to calculate gravity in Dusky Sound, compare it with 45° north, and form an idea of the meridian. A hydrographic chart from the Spanish expedition to Doubtful Harbour dated 1793 was issued by the Hydrographic Office of the British Admiralty in 1840, and Spanish names in Doubtful Sound / Patea also appear on Wyld’s map of New Zealand dated 1841. McNab records that Don Filipe Bauza was the official director of charts and conducted the astronomical observations on the Spanish expedition. He was also captain of the armed boat which surveyed Bauza Island at the entrance to Doubtful Sound / Patea, made observations on latitudes, longitudes and winds, and named a number of features. Te Ara Encyclopaedia (ibid.) notes that ‘in his charting of Doubtful Sound in 1851, Captain Stokes of the Acheron changed many of Bauza’s names, but they have since been reinstated.’ According to Hall-Jones, Bauza and his crew were the first Europeans to enter and explore Doubtful Sound / Patea in 1793.
info_description: Located north-west of Bauza Island in Doubtful Sound / Patea, Fiordland. Maximum depth 218m. NZTopo50 CD05-Dagg Sound, Chart NZ7625, Doubtful Sound NW Chart© Irwin & Main 1981D.

name: Bay of Islands
info_origin: ’On 27 November 1769 Captain James Cook sighted ‘a large and pretty deep Bay lying in S.W. by W., in which there appear’d to be several small Islands’, and so he recorded it as the Bay of Islands. On 4 May 1772 the expedition commanded by Marion du Fresne entered the bay, which they named Port Marion in honour of their commander. Ipipiri is the original name for the Bay of Islands, meaning ‘to raft up’ or ‘bring together’; it was reported by early French explorers and used by Murphy Shortland on his map of traditional place names. Another Māori name for the Bay of Islands district derives from the saying ‘Ka kata ngā puriri o Taiamai’: lit. The puriri trees of Taiamai are laughing. There is a locality called Taiamai between Ohaeawai and Waimate North. The name Taiamai has at times been extended to include the Bay of Islands, but appears strictly to apply only to a rock in the bay on which a kūkupa or wood pigeon alighted before melting into the rock. In this context Taiamai means ‘borne or wafted hither from the sea’. The bay itself was known as Tokerau: lit. northern, although the name may have been Tokirau or Tokarau: lit. hundred rocks. A contemporary Māori name for the Bay of Islands is the transliteration Pēwhairangi.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEQ3MkJBMDk0QzEwNDE2RTlDOEM)

name: Bay of Seals
info_origin: Discovered and named by Prestrud, leader of Amundsen's Eastern Party in 1911, who killed seals there and left a food depot for their return journey. Appears to have been named prior to Okuma Bay, but Okuma Bay gained currency on subsequent expeditions. During the first Byrd Expedition the feature was briefly named Hal Flood Bay, before corrected to Okuma Bay on published charts.
info_description: A former bay described as 'about 3 miles wide and about 4 miles long'. The feature was formed where the Ross Ice Shelf pushed out beyond a curve of King Edward VII Land's coast. The original bay no longer exists due to movement in the Ross Ice Shelf and the calving of Iceberg B-9 in 1986. However, as the Ross Ice Shelf continues to push forward the bay may reform in this area.
info_note: Considered to be the same feature as Okuma Bay based on the published descriptions. The feature also no longer exists due to changes in the iceshelf, particularly the calving of Iceberg B-9 in 1987.

name: Bay of Whales
info_origin: The feature was so named by Ernest Shackleton in the Nimrod, 24 January 1908, because of the large number of whales seen in it. The original Bay of Whales served as the base site for Amundsen's successful dash to the South Pole, 1911, the Byrd Antarctic Expeditions of 1928-30 and 1933-35, and for the West Base of U.S. Antarctic Service, 1939-41. A survey by the Byrd expedition in 1934 determined that the feature lay at the junction of two separate ice systems, the movements of which are influenced by the presence of Roosevelt Island. Commander Glen Jacobsen, United States Navy (USN), who visited in the Atka in January 1955, found that calving of the ice shelf rendered the iceport temporarily unusable.
info_description: An iceport indenting the front of Ross Ice Shelf just northward of Roosevelt Island. Due to the flows of ice around Roosevelt Island, there is typically a bay in this area, though its configuration is always changing. The position of the bay has moved back and forth across 30km as the front of the Ross Ice Shelf calves.

info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche Janurary 2024: Objective ID: A6084106 {[Bedford, H.D. 1913. From the Rees to the Dart. info_origin: On early survey maps the stream in what became Bedford Valley in 1938 was shown as Cascade Creek. Harry Dodgshun Bedford (1877-1918), in company with noted Otago mountaineers Hugh Francis Wright (1866-1938) and John Robertson (1870-1946), descended along this valley from East Peak in 1913. Bedford noted how ‘reaching the outlet of the valley, the stream took a precipitous leap, and a detour had to be made’ which is consistent with the descriptive name of Cascade Creek. While the valley was named Bedford Valley by the Honorary Geographic Board in 1938 (having been initiated in 1931), the Otago section of the New Zealand Alpine Club did not seek to rename the stream. This was done for the NZMS1 topographical series in 1943 seemingly to avoid confusion with two Cascade Streams and three Cascade Creeks in the wider area. In 1980 the New Zealand Geographic Board rejected a proposal to restore Cascade Creek because of confusion arising from the name being duplicated.

The first ascent of Pluto peak and an unclimbed Peak on the Forbes Range now called Mt Sir William. New Zealand Alpine Journal, 4 (18), 191-204.}
info_origin: ‘Jock’ [John Anderson] Sim (1895-1967), a Dunedin solicitor and a committee member of the Otago Branch of the New Zealand Alpine Club, proposed Bedford Valley to the Honorary Geographic Board in 1931. The Board sought further information from Sim in 1932, and the name wasn’t formally approved until 1938. Bedford Valley had been informally used by members of the Otago Branch of the New Zealand Alpine club prior to 1931. It was one of a batch of names put forward relating to climbs by Hugh Francis Wright (1866-1938) along with John Robertson (1870-1946) and Harry Dodgshun Bedford (1877-1918) in 1912-13 on the western flanks of Mount Earnslaw/Pikirakatahi. Wright gave Sim approval for proposing Bedford Valley after the deceased member of his climbing team, HD Bedford. As leader, Wright was a technically competent climber, a member of the Alpine Club and New Zealand Alpine Club president, 1934-36. Robertson, an Inspector of Schools for Otago and friend of Wright was a ‘rangy, athletic and nimble witted’ climber who complemented the ‘short, fiery and dynamic’ Bedford. A Dunedin solicitor, Bedford was a former MP, university lecturer, and subsequently Professor of Economics and History at the University of Otago. In descending from East Peak, Bedford described the valley that would later bear his name as offering a ‘practicable route down into the Dart Valley’ and being ‘very beautiful, having its upper end adorned by a full and unencumbered view of the great peak of Earnslaw, which had just been ascended, and having its slopes richly carpeted with mountain lilies. It was the most extensive field of Ranunculus Lyallii’. Their climbs were notable at the time for being undertaken without guides.

name: Beeby Peak
info_origin: Named by NZGB (2000) after Chris Beeby. Chris Beeby (1935-2000) was a leading New Zealand diplomat and negotiator on Antarctic matters for over 30 years. As Deputy Secretary of Foreign Affairs and Trade, he chaired the international negotiations to establish an Antarctic Minerals regime during the 1980s. A convention was designed to establish clear rules about any minerals related activity which might in the future be proposed for Antarctica, together with strict environmental  protection measures, which was eventually superseded by the Protocol on environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty. Chris Beeby hosted an international seminar on this work on the Beardmore Glacier in 1982/83, at which NZ's most southerly game of cricket also took place.
info_description: A peak at 1511m and 4.3km east-northeast of the summit of Mount Bird in northwest Ross Island. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME14
info_note: Feature # 8 in ACAN minutes of 19/06/2000. Name included with proposals # 4, 6 and 7 for "prominent statesmen and administrators." The feature was requested to be named by the US on 12/01/2000. A new name was recommended by the NZ Antarctic Place Names Committee at its meeting of 31/03/2000 which was ratified by the NZGB at its meeting of 20/02/2001 and Antarctica NZ were consulted on 23/03/2001. Shown on US 250000 Topographic Reconnaissance Maps - Ross Island, Franklin Island.

Gordon Bell of Bellevue, Richmond. The bellbird also used to be plentiful in the district, owing to the native Bush, until the mid-twentieth century. Batt, Roger (2015), The way we were, p. 10: The Morrison family, who settled in this area, named their property “The Grove”. name: Belmont
info_origin: Named possibly in 1880 after the home of Mr and Mrs Bull ‘Belmont Heim’ meaning ‘beautiful mountain home’ or after a building named ‘Belmont’ built by a local builder which was used as a church, school and meeting house. Belmont being his old home in England. North Shore City Suburb centred around NZMG coordinate 2670000E 6487000N. http://www.northshorecity.govt.nz/Services/OnlineServices/Documents/nsc-suburb-map.pdf; 'Auckland, North Shore. On one account, named after the Belmont Heim farm at Takapuna purchased in 1880 by Mr and Mrs James Bull. Mrs Bull’s sister, Frances Urry, then governess to one of the Hapsburg families in Austria, wrote suggesting the name, which means Beautiful mountain home. Another account is that the name derives from the home of a Presbyterian minister, the Rev. Robert J. Roberts. A daughter-in-law of Roberts has stated that the house had originally been built as a racing stable, named after the American stable Belmont Park. When the church was built in Lake Road in 1910, the name Belmont was applied to it and to the primary school which was held in the church building from 1912.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Bendigo
info_origin: 'A name transplanted from the Victorian to the New Zealand goldfields. It originated indirectly from the English prizefighter William ‘Abednego’ Thompson, popularly known as Bendigo; a local boxer at Ravenswood in Victoria was nicknamed after his British counterpart, and the name stuck for the area.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. 'It is generally agreed that ‘Bendigo’ is an altered form of the biblical ‘Abednego~Abednigo’, /əˈbɛdnəgoʊ/ ‘servant of Nego’ (< abed ‘to serve’), a Babylonian name given to Azariah, one of the three captive princes of Judah who were Daniel’s companions at the court of Nebuchadnezzar II, the king of Babylon (Daniel 1:7). The name ‘Abednego’ was at its peak in Britain between 1720 and 1785, spiking in 1741 (Geneanet). It is not too difficult, if you’re a phonetician, to track the shift from ‘Abednego’ to ‘Bendigo’.' Source: Newsletter of the Australian National Placenames Survey #100, September 2026, article by Jan Tent CC BY 4.0 https://placenames.org.au.

name: Benson Glacier
info_origin: Surveyed in October by the Northern Survey Party of the NZTAE, 1956-58, and named by them after the late Professor W N Benson, formerly Professor of Geology at the University of Otago, whose publications included at major contribution to the petrology of Victoria Land.
info_description: A glacier approximately 25km long between the Fry and Mackay Glaciers, reaching the coast on the north side of Granite Harbour. It flows from ice dropping off Flight Deck Névé to its terminus at Granite Harbour. The initial broad flow drops north of Black Pudding Peak and narrows south of Mount Perseverance, also losing a large distributary, the Hunt Glacier. On the northwest of Red Buttress Peak the Benson Glacier descends steeply into a narrow valley, turns south at Tiger Island and reaches sea level where it forms a floating tongue that merges near Lion Island with the distributary Hunt Glacier. Originally considered to be a significantly greater feature, a 1989-90 NZARP field party determined the upper section was a separate glacier (Midship Glacier) abutting Benson Glacier at Jetsam Moraine. name: Beuzenberg Peak
info_origin: This peak was named after Erica Beuzenberg’s achievements and contribution to mountaineering. She was a local mountain guide, having lived in Fairlie for 15 years, and had a reputation both nationally and internationally of some distinction. At the age of 41, she tragically lost her life in 2005 while guiding two other climbers. The feature chosen is in an area where she would have climbed more often than anyone else and the submitter described that she had a spiritual connection with this area. Erica Beuzenberg's mountaineering career began in 1989 when she climbed 29 of New Zealand’s 3000m peaks in a single winter, receiving the accolade of ‘Mountaineer of the Year’ from the Canterbury Mountaineering Club. She went on to conquer a number of firsts as a woman mountaineer.

info_origin: 'Auckland, 13 km from Silverdale. Named by G. Laurence Taylor and Bill Brown of Auckland, who subdivided the area in 1923, and were struck by the resemblance of this place to Manly in Sydney. Big Manly and Little Manly are separated by Tarihunga Point. At one time it was called Polkinghornes Beach after a family of this name that owned an isolated farm and house.' name: Birdwood Range
info_ref: First World War.com, ‘Who’s Who – Sir William Birdwood’, http://www.firstworldwar.com/bio/birdwood.htm; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 1, p. 50; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: At the height of the First World War, the Ministry of Lands drew up a scheme to replace New Zealand feature names that were considered too ‘alien’, i.e. German or Austro-Hungarian, with others deemed more appropriately ‘British’. Along with a number of statesmen, explorers, and admirals, one of the substitute names mooted was ‘Birdwood’. However, it was quickly discovered that ‘Birdwood’ had already been allocated to a mountain range at the head of the Wilberforce River. Lieutenant-General William Birdwood was the first commander of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC). He led that unit during the landings at Anzac Cove on 25 April 1915, as part of an attempt to force the straits of the Dardanelles and eventually capture Constantinople. Eight months later, it fell to Birdwood to coordinate the Allied evacuation of Gallipoli, which many historians describe as the only successful part of the whole operation. Birdwood subsequently commanded I ANZAC Corps on the Western Front in France and Belgium, followed by the Australian Corps. He ended the War as a full General leading the British Fifth Army during the successful Hundred Days Campaign.

Birkdale is a suburb of Southport, Lancashire in England. Most of Birkdale was originally known as Parkview.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Birkenhead

North Shore City Suburb centred around NZMG coordinate 2664150E 6486900N. http://www.northshorecity.govt.nz/Services/OnlineServices/Documents/nsc-suburb-map.pdf. Birkenhead was constituted as a Borough in 1888 and became a city in 1978, then in 1989 was amalgamated into North Shore City.; 'First known by Europeans as Woodside. The name was registered on 23 June 1863 by land agent Samuel Cochrane; it reminded him of his home town ‘being across the water’ from Auckland as Birkenhead in England is from Liverpool. But the name has also been said to originate with the artist and surveyor Charles Heaphy, for the same reason as Cochrane. See also Highbury.' info_description: A wedge-shaped island approximately 22km long from Cape Hodgson in the north to Cape Beck in the south, and 16km wide from Row Nunataks in the west to Cape Spirit in the east, projecting through the ice shelf between Brown and White Islands. It forms a contrast to White Island, which is almost hidden by snow, because it is kept almost entirely snow-free due to its being sheltered from the prevailing wind by Minna Bluff. Its chief characteristic is the large extent of low land surrounding the group of old craters which rise to a height of 1041m at Mount Aurora

name: Bligh Sound
info_ref: Feature shown on: NZMS260 B41 C41 PtC40. LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-18/639
info_origin: Named prior to 1838 after Governor Bligh by Capt. John Grono, whose first command was the ‘Governor Bligh’, which visited Fiordland for the first time in 1809.; 'Named after Captain (and later Governor) William Bligh by Captain John Grono, who owned a farm next to Bligh’s on the Hawkesbury River in New South Wales. Maori name Hawea, or Te Ana-Hawea: lit. te: the; ana: cave; hawea: Hawea iwi. Smoke was seen coming from the cave in 1842, but the members of the ‘Lost Tribe’, as the Hawea were known by early Europeans, had fled by the time contact was attempted. The surrounding region was known as Te Whenua-o-Kati-Hawea: lit. te: the; whenua: land; o: of; Kati (South Island form of ngati): a tribal prefix; Hawea. The name therefore could be rendered as The Land of Hawea.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: The hill of 310m is located by the junction of the Sherry River and Wangapeka River. Geologist Ferdinand Hochstetter travelling through this area in 1859 described the hills as comprising ‘tertiary strata, marl, sandstone, and limestone’. Gold mining in the Sherry River commenced in 1861 and continued for most of the decade. A prominent feature, the hill was presumably named by the miners for the colour of the rock. The first ‘depasturing licences’ in the vicinity were granted in 1865. A lease agreement in 1885 defined the area in question as extending to ‘Blue Rock Bluff’.

name: Bluff
info_origin: ’The name comes from the high bluff that dominates the town and the harbour, although it was not officially recognised until 1917. Early whalers referred to the locale as Old Man Bluff, or Old Man’s Bluff; another early name was Cape Bernadin, given by Royal Navy Lieutenant Thomas McDonnell in the 1830s, from San Bernadino in the Philippines, where his son had been born. For many years it was known as Port Macquarie after Lachlan Macquarie, an early governor of New South Wales. When the township was surveyed it became Campbelltown, after the maiden name of the wife of Colonel Sir Thomas Gore Browne, governor of New Zealand. Awarua, meaning ‘twin channels’, is the traditional Māori name for Bluff Harbour and the wider Bluff region. A name for Bluff peninsula was Motupōhue, Island of convolvulus (pōhue or Calystegia sepium). It is now officially The Bluff / Motupōhue following the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Bluff Harbour
info_origin: 'Named after the bluff that dominates the town and harbour. The harbour had been christened Bloomfield Harbour by Captain Edward Cattlin, after William and Richard Bloomfield, who were his partners in attempting a large land purchase in 1840. It was first named Port Macquarie after the governor of New South Wales, either by the Sydney shipowner Robert Jones or by Robert Murray, master of the Perseverance, who came here in 1813. Maori name: Awarua: awa: river; rua: two; the two rivers, could refer to either the two channels at the entrance, or more likely, the two main channels within the harbour. Nowadays the name is confined to the eastern limb of the harbour — Awarua Bay, q.v.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Borchgrevink Coast
info_origin: Named for Carstens Egeberg Borchgrevink who accompanied H J Bull's Expedition to the Antarctic 1894-95. During this expedition the first landing on the Antarctic Continent was made at Cape Adare, and at Possession Island Borchgrevink discovered a lichen growing on the rocks, the first evidence of plant life obtained within the Antarctic Circle. In 1898 Sir George Newnes sponsored the first British Antarctic Expedition, 1898-1900, which was led by Borchgrevink. The vessel used was the "Southern Cross". The party of 10 men left at Cape Adare was the first to spend a winter on the Antarctic Continent. Being restricted in movement through failure to penetrate inland, and because of the ice conditions along the coast, only local exploration and naming was accomplished before the return of the ship. The coast was followed to Cape Washington, and a landing was made on Coulman Island and at the foot of Mt Melbourne. Wood Bay was found to run much further inland than Ross had supposed, and the large feature of the Lady Newnes Ice Shelf was discovered and named. Some thick reindeer moss was found near Mt Melbourne. Landing were made at Franklin Island and at Cape Crozier, and the Ross Ice Shelf was found to have receded some 30 miles since Ross discovered it in 1841. A landing was made on the Ross Ice Shelf, and Borchegrevink an Colbeck skied south to latitude 78°50', a record at that time or southern travel. Borchgrevink was born in Norway, but was partly English in ancestry, and at the time of Bull's expedition he was living in Australia.
info_description: That part of the coast of Victoria Land lying between Cape Adare in the north to Cape Washington in the south.

name: Borchgrevink Glacier

The vessel was tied to sea-ice on the south side of Mt Lubbock, observations were made, and a dog-sledge was taken across the sea-ice to the westward for a few miles, probably to the floating face of the Borchegrevink Glacier. Named by the NZ Geological Survey Antarctic Expedition 1957-58.
info_description: A large glacier flowing from the south-east end of the Victory Mountains to pass between Mt Phillips and Mt Lubbock, and thence projecting into the sea for several miles as a floating ice tongue which forms the northernmost part of the Lady Newnes Ice Shelf.

name: Borchgrevink's Bight
info_ref: Refer pp.278-279, Carstens Egeburg Borchgrevink, (1901), First on the Antarctic Continent, George Newnes Limited: London and pp.72-74 Ernest H. Shackleton (1909), The Heart of the Antarctic Vol.II, J.B. Lippincott Company, Philadelphia
info_origin: Originally named after Carstens Egeburg Borchgrevink, a Norwegian, who was one of the first men to set foot on the Antarctic Continent when he accompanied Christensen to Victoria Land in 1894-95. He returned to Cape Adare in 1898 in charge of the BAE, 1898-1900, and with a small party spent the winter of 1899 there, the first group to winter on the Antarctic Continent. Later they sailed in their ship the Southern Cross along the Ross Ice Shelf, and landed in a bay where the barrier was low, Borchgrevink giving a position of 78°34'S, 195°50'E. Borchgrevink and Colbeck skied as far south as 78°51'S, establishing a new farthest south record. In 1908 Shackleton in search for Barrier Inlet AKA Balloon Bight and found large sections of the Ross Ice Shelf had calved off, merging the inlet into the broad bay he identified as "Borchgrevink's Bight". The new wider feature was named the Bay of Whales.
info_description: Formerly a bight in the Ross Ice Shelf, later merged into the Bay of Whales.

info_origin: The peak is named after Gottlieb Braun-Elwert (1949 – 2008) who passed away in August 2008 during a ski trip in the Mackenzie country with a party of seven, including the then Prime Minister, Helen Clark, and her husband, Peter Davis, as well as senior Cabinet Ministers David Parker and Damien O'Connor. Gottlieb Braun-Elwert was a well-known mountain guide who operated his Alpine Recreation business from Tekapo since the 1980s. He emigrated to New Zealand from Germany in the late 1970s. He was not only an internationally qualified mountain and ski guide, but also as an academic with a Master's degree in physics from the University of Munich. On his arrival, he immediately began work with the New Zealand Mountain Guides Association on building international recognition of New Zealand's alpine recreational opportunities. During his lifetime he gained significant respect as a distinguished mountain climber. He was also a keen photographer and conservationist.
