info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA325625; fA417315; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5111558 {[Untitled. 1902. Evening Post, 18 December, Page 5.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19021218.2.41); [Our Beautiful City. 1924. New Zealand Times, 18 December, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZTIM19241219.2.121.3); [In Breaker Bay. Evening Post, 2 February 1924, Page 10.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19240202.2.107); Adkin, Leslie. 1959. Great Harbour of Tara. New Zealand: Whitcombe and Tombs}
info_origin: A suburb of Wellington on the southeast coast of Te Motu Kairangi / Miramar Peninsula named after the bay of the same name. Archaeologist and ethnologist, Leslie Adkin, considered that a kainga or village named Whitikai, of which no signs now remain, may have been located here. The suburb includes the smaller Eve Bay, Flax Bay, Reef Bay and Palmer Bay. The latter is likely associated with George Palmer MP, a director of the New Zealand Company. Breaker Bay is exposed to southerly gales and its name’s aptness attracts ongoing comment. An early newspaper reference dates from 1902 when the YMCA planned a picnic in the bay. A road linking the bay to the city was formed in 1923 and 93 sea front facing sections, notable in that they extended to the high tidemark, were advertised for sale by the Branda Estate in 1923 and 1924. The Pass of Branda was the name given to the road cutting linking Seatoun to Breaker Bay. The Breakers Bay Progressive Association lobbied the Wellington City Council for improved sealed roads in 1926. Breakers Bay co-existed as a form of the name into the 1960s.

name: Browning Pass/Noti Raureka
info_ref: File BRD-02-02-00-07; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760}
info_origin: 'Browning, Lake/Whakarewa: Browning Range: The pass, from the head of the Arahura River to the head of the Wilberforce River, was discovered by John S. name: Brown Island
info_origin: Original description: An island about 10 miles long and 4 miles wide, protruding through the Ross Ice Shelf northward of Mt. Discovery, to which it is connected by a low isthmus. The highest point is 2812 ft. Discovered in 1901 by the NAE, 1901-04 and named beacuse of its colour, which is caused by weathered volcanic ash and lava. The island is comprosed chiefly of basaltic lavas, and is bare of permanent snow. It was visited by a party from this expedition, who climbed to the highest point at the southern end where they found a large crater. Off the northern end of the island there is a small island which may be entirely morainic . Not Broune Inseln (German) or Brun Oya (Norwegian)
info_description: A mostly ice free peninsula extending north from Dreary Isthmus which connects it to Mount Discovery, for approximately 20km, where Bratina Island sits at the tip, separated by a system of small ponds on the McMurdo Ice Shelf. The feature is kept ice free by Mount Discovery, sheltering it from the prevailing winds. Rises to 816m at Mount Wise.

name: Burleigh
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Scholefield, GH. 1940. Dictionary of New Zealand Biography. New Zealand: Department of Internal Affairs; [Obituary Thomas Carter. 1900. Marlborough Express, 1 March, Page 3](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/MEX19000301.2.33); [Auction Sales. 1918. Marlborough Express, 4 February, Page 4](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/MEX19180204.2.23.3); [Obituary Thomas Redwood. 1918. Marlborough Express, 13 May, Page 2](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/MEX19180513.2.12); McIntosh, AD. 1940. Marlborough A Provincial History. New Zealand: Marlborough Provincial Committee.}
info_origin: Burleigh was named for the Burleigh sheep run taken up by James Balfour Wemyss. From Fife, Wemyss had originally come to Canterbury in 1852 and shifted to Marlborough, sheep farming in the Wairau valley in 1854. He represented Wairau in the Nelson Provincial Council (1857-59) and after the cleaving of Marlborough from Nelson to form a separate province, Wairau Valley in the Marlborough Provincial Council (1865-69). He was also Provincial Commissioner of Crown lands 1868-71 and Provincial Secretary from 1868-71. Wemyss returned to Scotland in 1871. Burleigh was next purchased by Thomas Redwood, an experienced run manager of Vernon and Bank House Station and a member of the Marlborough Provincial Council (1865-68), who retained the property until about 1894. Burleigh, then of some 4000-5000 acres (1618-2023 ha) next passed to Thomas Carter (1827-1900). British born Carter arrived in Nelson via the Californian and Australian gold fields in 1855. His significant landed interests in Marlborough, included Stronvar, Wantwood, Hillersden, the Wither, Glenfield, Te Arowhenua, Richmond Dale, the Clarence, as well as Burleigh runs. At the time of his death, he was considered the largest land holder and richest man in the province. He was the third Superintendent of Marlborough Province (1862-64) and a member of numerous local boards and committees. He gifted the site and endowed a scholarship for the newly formed Marlborough High School. By 1918 Blenheim had expanded sufficiently that Carter’s trustees, in inviting tenders for the lease of the homestead and 26 acres (10.5 ha) of surrounding gardens, plantations and orchards could describe it as situated in ‘close proximity to the Borough of Blenheim’.

info_origin: Probably named after the Rev. John Butler, the first ordained minister to work among Maori. But it may have been named after Captain William Butler, master of the whaling barque Nimrod, who settled opposite the Mangonui wharf in 1840. Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; Named after Captain William Butler (1814-75), master of the whaling barque Nimrod, who settled opposite Mangonui wharf in 1840. A pā named Moehuri was earlier located on Butler Point, linked to Moehuri captain of the waka Raukaramea who, guided by a large shark, landed in Mangōnui Harbour. Butler established a flax and timber trading station at what was known as Waikeke, a peninsula close to deep water anchorages. Here he provisioned vessels from the American Pacific whaling fleet. Thomas Ryan claimed five land purchases made from 1836-1838 for 2280 acres (923 ha) for £128 in goods (including oil, blankets, tobacco, soap and muskets) for land stretching from Rangitoto Point to Waitetoki Stream. From Ryan, William Butler (1814-75) purchased small areas at Butler Point – then known as Ryan’s Point, for his trading station. His establishment became known as Captain Butler’s Point by the 1860s. Butler was MP for Monganui from 1861-66. Butler’s Point is named on the 1927 Mangonui cadastral map NZMS 013 NAK12 drawn by William Bardsley in 1921. It was not included on the initial 1:63360 provisional topographical sheets in 1943 and ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1874-1962), in reviewing the sheets for the 1943 map, was determined to apply Green Point to the point. The Honorary Board agreed, and the name was gazetted in 1948. However, when printed the 1943 map sheet showed neither Butler Point nor Green Point. Correspondence between the Chief Surveyor for Auckland and the New Zealand Geographic Board failed to identify detailed evidence and both names were omitted from the new topographical series in 1958. Butler Point was reinstated on the 1964 topographical map.

name: Camp Bay
info_origin: NZGB Correspondence Volume 53, p.63 - Notes on D'Urville Island place names: The land bordering this bay was the site of a large bush felling camp in pioneering days. On the north side of this bay is a high spur of land which is a lovely place to sit to observe beautiful sunsets and quietly philosophize. At this time too seagulls gently hover between the beach and the top of the spur so observers can study their grace and precision of wing movements. As soon as dusk sets in the shadows become uncanny as though ghosts are about. Then the observer jumps up and hurries back to the warmth and cheer of the camp fire. A well-known Maori Elder said that as a young man he two had sat on this spur in the evening philosophising and watching the sunsets and then at dusk felt the presence of ghosts.

name: Cannibal Gorge
info_origin: A letter dated 10 February 2015 from a Tumatakokiri iwi spokesperson advises that the original Māori name for the gorge (and hut) is Maruia - the same name given to the river which flows through the gorge. Tumatakokiri and Ngāi Tahu iwi battled here after Werata Tainui stole a wife, Kokore, and because Tau of Ngāi Tahu killed Kehu's father at Koriri (Arnold River). This information is apparently recorded in documents relating to a declined depasturage licence by James MacKay in 1859, where records describe MacKay secretly buying land belonging to Tumatakokiri iwi. A Treaty of Waitangi settlement claim more fully describes the history. This information has not been verified.; 'A literal translation of the Maori name: Kopi-o-kaitangata, lit. kopi: gorge; o: of; kai: food; tangata: man. Cannibalism was common among Maori seeking greenstone on the West Coast travelling across the Amuri or Ahaura Pass. One Maori informant spoke of a raid on a village at Ahaura in the Grey valley, after which the fugitives were pursued up the gorge, where all were killed or captured. An alternative name was Ka-pai-o-kaitangata: lit. How good is a feed of human flesh!' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Canterbury Region
info_origin: The region that is administered by the Canterbury Regional Council (Environment Canterbury). Constituted by Local Government (Canterbury Region) Reorganisation Order 1989, Gazette 1989, p2296 Shown on SO 18043.; ’The name was decided at the first meeting of the Canterbury Association of which Dr John Bird Sumner, archbishop of Canterbury, was elected president. The minutes of the Association meeting record that it was decided ‘to call it Canterbury, after Canterbury, our ecclesiastical mother’. The streets of Christchurch are named after Anglican dioceses throughout the world. Māori name of the Canterbury Plains: Kā Pākihi Whakatekateka-o-Waitaha, lit. kā (Ngāi Tahu dialect for ngā): the; pākihi: open grass country; whakatekateka: to walk with pride; o: of; Waitaha iwi. The Waitaha ancestor Rākaihautū, who with his travelling party had traversed much of the South Island, met up with his son Rakihouia in South Canterbury and they marched on happily together. Māori name of the South Canterbury coast: Kā Poupou-o-Te-Rakihouia, lit. kā (ngā): the; poupou: posts; o: of; te: the; Rakihouia; he had built a number of eel weirs, the posts of which gave rise to the name.’' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Discovered by the NAE, 1901-04, at the end of January 1902. Named by Scott for Lieutenant (later Captain) William Colbeck, RNR, who had been a member of the BAE, 1898-1900. With Borchgrevink, Colbeck went on skis to 78°51' S, the farthest south reached at that time. Later, in 1903 and 1904, he commanded the relief ship Morning sent to replenish the NAE, 1901-04.
info_description: The western cape of King Edward VII Land.

name: Cape Constance
info_origin: Named by Borchgrevink after his wife, Constance Prior Borchgrevink (nee Standen). Later found to be the same feature named Cape Jones by Ross. Transferred to the next cape west by the New Zealand Antarctic Place Names Committee in 1959.
info_description: A broad cape abutting Borchgrevink Glacier Tongue, and west of Cape Jones, Victoria Land

name: Cape Cornely
info_origin: Mapped by United State Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and U.S Navy aerial photographs, 1957-61. Named by United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Joseph R. Cornely, U.S. Navy, radioman with the wintering parties at Little America V, South Pole Station, and McMurdo Station in three years, 1958, 1961 and 1963.
info_description: A cape on Scott Coast, Victoria Land 5.7km north of Cape Day. The cape is marked by a rock exposure and is situated at the south side of the terminus of Mawson Glacier, where it becomes the Nordenskjöld Ice Tongue.

name: Cape Cornish
info_origin: The cape was named by personnel of the RRS Discovery II in 1938 for Allan William Cornish, meteorologist with the Australian Central Bureau, who was an observer aboard Discovery II during 1937-38.
info_description: A cape forming the northern extremity of Buckle Island, in the Balleny Islands.

name: Cape Cotter
info_description: A line of spectacular bare rock cliffs rising 1,500 m above the Ross Sea and forming the seaward (east) face of Hallett Peninsula, in Victoria Land.

name: Cape Crossfire
info_origin: The name alludes to the converging flow of ice at this feature from different directions, and was given by New Zealand Antarctic Place Names Committee (NZ-APNC) in 1966. Originally suggested in a group of names put forward by the surveyor Malcolm Ford and cartographer Denys Breffny McCandless Rainey.
info_description: A promontory at the southeast extremity of a ridge extending east from Malta Plateau, marking the point of convergence of the Mariner Glacier from the west and Borchgrevink Glacier from the north, in Victoria Land.

name: Cape Crozier
info_origin: Discovered and named in 1841 by Ross for his second in command, Commander Francis R M Crozier, captain of the Terror. Crozier was later second in command of the ill-fated Franklin Artic Expedition. Near Cape Crozier is the largest area of bare land surface on Ross Island. The cape itself consists of bluff cliff, varying between 200 and 400 ft high, vertical and even overhanging in places, extending for some 3 miles from the junction with Ross Ice Shelf towards the large penguin rookery. This cape has been frequently visited by various expeditions, and was the goal of the Winter Journey Party, led by Dr Wilson, of the BAE, 1910-13, in 1911, to obtain information about the breeding habits of the Emperor Penguin.
info_description: The eastern extremity of Ross Island. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME16

name: Cape Daniell
info_origin: Named by Ross on 15 February 1841 for Professor Daniell, chemist of King's College and Foreign Secretary of the Royal Society.

name: Cape Davydov

name: Cape Day

name: Cape Dayman
info_origin: Named by Ross in 1841 for Joseph Dayman, mate of the Erebus, one of the expedition's vessels.

name: Cape Douglas
info_origin: Discovered by the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, in December 1902, and named for Admiral Sir Archibald Douglas, Lord of the Admiralty, who had persuaded the Admiralty to assign navel seamen to this expedition.
info_description: A headland projecting out on the south of Mattherson Inlet on the western edge of the Ross Ice Shelf.

name: Cape Downshire
info_description: A line of precipitous basalt cliffs rising to 2000m above the Ross Sea and forming most of the east side of Adare Peninsula, extending over 60km along the coast of Victoria Land.

name: Cape Dunlop
info_origin: First chartered by the BAE, 1907-09, which named this feature Rocky Point. It has since taken its name from Dunlop Island, situated just off this point, and named for H J L Dunlop, chief engineer of the Nimrod, the expedition ship. Not Dunlop Point or Rocky Point.
info_description: A rocky headland, approximately 24km south-southeast of Cape Roberts, along the Wilson Piedmont Glacier of Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MD10

name: Cape Edwardson
info_origin: Replaced by East Cape 13/01/1966 1:18 'Southland, Stewart Island/ Rakiura. See also East Cape, Edwardson Sound. After Captain William Edwardson, of whom Alexander and Neil Begg have written: ‘ . . . though he made only a single short visit to New Zealand, [he] helped to transform its southern part from a scene of vicious fighting and racial hatred to one where peaceful development could, and did, take place’.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Cape Egmont
info_origin: See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDVFREI0QzkyRDEwMDdBRENBQ0I) 'Egmont is the European name of the mountain known to Maori as Taranaki, as well as of the cape, national park (33,534 ha, created in 1900), Egmont Road, a railway station 10 km from New Plymouth, and Egmont Village, 5 km from Inglewood. Both Tasman and Cook sailed past the cape. Tasman did not actually see the mountain, but he named the cape Cabo Pieter Boerel and, as Professor J.C. Beaglehole says, ‘deduced’ the mountain. On 11 January 1770 Captain Cook wrote: ‘saw a very high Mountain, and made very much like the Peak, Teneriffe’. He named it in honour of the second Earl of Egmont, then first lord of the Admiralty at the time. Two days later Cook briefly saw it: ‘It is of Prodidgeous height and its Top is cover’d with Everlasting Snow.’; Joseph Banks called it ’the noblest hill I have ever seen’. On 25 March 1772 it was sighted by the French navigator Marion du Fresne, who named it Le Pic de Mascarin after his vessel the Mascarin; but Cook was the first European to sight it, his name took precedence. Maori name: Taranaki, q.v.; an even earlier name was Pukehaupapa, lit. puke: hill; haupapa: ice or frost. See also Tama-ahua.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDVFREI0QzkyRDEwMDdBRENBQ0I)

name: Cape Ellsworth
info_origin: Named by the personnel of the Discovery II in 1936. After this vessel had rescued Lincoln Ellsworth, a running survey of the northern end of the Balleny Islands was made on the way back to Australia. Ellsworth led an Arctic submarine expedition with Wilkins in 1931, and accompanied Amundsen to the North Pole by dirigible in 1926. He made four visits to the Antarctic: in 1933 to the Ross Sea, in 1934-35 and 1935-36 to the Weddell Sea, including a flight from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea in the latter year and to Princess Elizabeth Land in 1938-39.
info_description: A rocky bluff, about 290m high, forming the northern extremity of Young Island, in the Balleny Islands.

name: Cape Ermak
info_description: A point on the west of Rennick Bay where Pryor Glacier merges with Kooperatsiya Ice Piedmont, approximately 31.5km southeast of Belousov Point.

name: Cape Evans
info_origin: Discovered by the NAE, 1901-04, which named it the Skuary. The BAE, 1910-13, built its headquarters here, and before doing so, Scott, in 1911, renamed it Cape Evans in honour of his second in command, Lieutenant Edward R G R Evans, RN, later Admiral Lord Mountevans. The cape is the termination of a comparatively low peninsula which projects about 1 1/2 miles into McMurdo Sound. The Ross Sea Party of the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, 1914-17, also wintered here.
info_description: A low promontory on the west coast of Ross Island forming the northern entrance to Erebus Bay. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MF13

name: Cape Farewell
info_origin: See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDNCRTYyQTgzMDBGRjg3ODIzNDE). 'Captain James Cook named the cape at the north-west point of the South Island on 31 March 1770, as he left New Zealand at the conclusion of his first visit. Abel Tasman was the first European to see it, on 18 December 1642. He called it Visschers Hoeck (Visscher’s Point) after Franz Jacobszoon Visscher, a pilot, surveyor and navigator who drew the outline map of the west coast of New Zealand showing Tasman’s discoveries. Māori names: Onetāhua, a descriptive name meaning Heaped up sand, referring to the sand dunes on Farewell Spit; or Taumauka: lit. Dry hill ridge. Te Hiku o te Matau (fish hook) is another name for Farewell Spit.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Cape Foulwind
info_origin: ’The first European to see the cape was Abel Tasman, who sighted it on 15 December 1642, and named it Clijppijgen Hoeck (Rocky Point). On reaching here on 20 March 1770 Captain James Cook encountered ‘rain, and Squall,’ and the next day ‘a fresh Gale’ — ample reason to name the cape, which had been dimly discerned through the mist, where there was a ‘prodigious swell rowling in upon the Shore’. Māori name: Te Kara o Tamatea. The bay just south of the cape is called Tauranga.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Cape Geology

'Marlborough, between Port Gore and Queen Charlotte Sound. Named by Captain James Cook on 29 March 1770, after Sir George Jackson, one of the Admiralty secretaries. Maori name: Taonui-a-Kupe, lit. tao: spear; nui: large; a: of; Kupe. According to legend Kupe left a fishing net here, giving rise to the name Te Kupenga-a-Kupe, lit. kupenga: net; a: of; Kupe; i.e. The fishing net of Kupe, which is on a rock formation near the cape. See also Stephens Island.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Cape Kidnappers
info_origin: [Information relating to Captain Cook's voyage](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEVEMjhEOTk4MzBGRjg4QTdGMEU); 'Hawke’s Bay, the southernmost point of Hawke Bay. Captain James Cook named the cape after a tense situation on 15 October 1769, when an armed boat carrying twenty-two men seized Tiata, Tupaea’s servant. Sailors from the Endeavour fired on the boat, giving Tiata the chance to jump overboard and return to the ship. Maori name: Te Matau-a-Maui, lit. te: the; matau: fishhook; a: of; Maui. According to legend this was the hook by which the Fish of Maui, the North Island of New Zealand, was taken by the demigod. See also Hawke Bay. The small island at the end of the cape was Te Iho-o-Te Rei, lit. te: the; iho: heart, umbilical cord, or lock of hair; o: of Te Rei.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Cape Kidnappers / Te Kauwae-a-Māui
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA221999; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Heretaunga Tamatea history: ‘The first contact of Heretaunga Tamatea people with the Crown was on October 15, 1769. It was at sea just out from the outcrop of steep white cliffs and rock formations presently known as Cape Kidnappers. It was not an amicable contact. Spotting a young Polynesian boy in the hands of strange creatures on a strange vessel, local Māori mistook Captain James Cook and his crew for kidnappers of children. When they attempted to free Tiata, the nephew of Tahitian navigator Tupaia, from a small dingy, Cook fired upon them and two Māori were killed. Ironically, Cook called the local people ‘kidnappers’ and the outcrop of steep white cliffs and rock formations has borne the name Cape Kidnappers ever since. Te Kauwae-a-Māui (the jawbone belonging to Māui) is the ancient Māori name of the jaw bone shaped coastal geographical phenomena at the distal end of the peninsula that stretches from the Black Reef in an easterly fashion to the outcrop of steep white cliffs and rock formations that extend into the ocean presently known as Cape Kidnappers. We believe the cartographical understanding of Cape Kidnappers to be the steep white cliff/rock formation outcrop. Modern usage, however, in a heavily tourist oriented Hawke’s Bay, has the rise of a widespread use of Cape Kidnappers" to apply to the whole peninsula area from Clifton, in the north, across to just south of Rangaika, in the south. To recognise our dual history and the widening parlance of modern usage we wish the proposed place name change to apply to the whole peninsula/headland area whose southern boundary reaches from Clifton across the peninsula to just south of Rangaika. This obviously includes both Cook’s Cape Kidnappers and the ancient area known to Māori as Te Kauwae-a-Māui.’ See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEVEMjhEOTk4MzBGRjg4QTdGMEU)"
info_description: A cape approximately 20km southeast of Napier, which protrudes into the South Pacific Ocean at the southernmost point of Hawke Bay. NZTopo50-BK40ptBK39 463035 to 486995
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "the jawbone of Māui"

name: Cape L'Eveque
info_origin: In 1838 a French Corvette l'Héroïne under Captain Cécille was dispatched to investigate the killing of the crew of the 'Jean Bart', accompanied by two whaling vessels. In charting the coast the original French name ‘le Bonnet d’Évêque’ – the Bishop’s hat, was applied by Captain Cécille to what is now Te Whakahewa / The Horns, also descriptive of its shape. In 1840 Charles Heaphy charted the anchorages and produced a new chart of the Chatham Islands for the New Zealand Company, instead recording Mount Wakaiwa for Te Whakahewa / The Horns and applying Cape Young to the Cape. When the Admiralty compiled a chart for publication from Fournier and Heaphy’s charts in 1842, it retained ‘Eveque’, albeit moving the name to the cape, (Cape Young moving to the opposite side of the island), and named the southeasternmost cape, Cape Fournier.

name: Cape Palliser
info_origin: See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDdFOEZBRkVENDBGRUE1QzlGNTc); 'Named by Captain James Cook after his mentor Captain Pallisser, afterwards Sir Hugh, comptroller of the British navy. Until 1773 he signed his name Pallisser. Jules Dumont d’Urville named it Useless Bay in 1827, when he was unable to go ashore on account of heavy seas, despite the comments he made at the time: ‘Instead of the names Tera-Witi and Palliser given by Cook, they [the Māori] gave me Poli-Wero and Kawa-Kawa, which on our map I restored to the capes which should bear them, convinced that it would be absurd not to designate these points by the names used, for centuries perhaps, by tribes as numerous and intelligent as those of New Zealand.’ Māori name: Te Kawakawa: lit. te: the; kawakawa: a shrub (Macropiper excelsum). Kupe went ashore near Cape Palliser and named it Te Kawakawa because it was here that one of his daughters wove a headband of kawakawa leaves. Cape Palliser / Mātakitaki-a-Kupe also recalls Kupe’s stay here. Standing on a rock, Kupe recited karakia to attract fish such as hāpuku, and in the distance observed snow-covered Tapuae-o-Uenuku. He explained this to his daughter Hine-a-uira, who bestowed the name meaning ‘The outlook of Kupe’.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: A cape at the southernmost point of Te Ika-a-Māui. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BR33 894908

name: Cape Reinga
info_origin: 'Northland, at the far north of the Northland peninsula. Maori name: Te Reinga, lit. te: the; reinga: leaping place. This is the famous Leaping place of spirits, a name also used for the underworld of the wairua, the souls or spirits of the departed who travelled northwards and leapt from the overhanging branches of an ancient pohutukawa tree into the surging waters that covered the entrance to the underworld — or the commencement of the long journey to Hawaiki. It was also known as Te Rerenga Wairua, lit. The leaping place of spirits. See also Three Kings Islands.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Cape Reinga / Te Rerenga Wairua
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/1017; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Te Hiku history: Te Rerenga Wairua is part of the spiritual pathway, of which Te Aupouri are kaitiaki. Stokes notes that Kupe declared Te Rerenga Wairua to be the departure point for the spiritual return to Hawaiki. Stokes recounted the following ancient whakatauaki: "Papaki e nga I te Rerenga Wairua, Te tutakinga o Rehua, o Whitirea, He ara wairua i te Rerenga Wairua; Hear the resounding tides at Te Rerenga Wairua, It is the meeting place of Rehua, of Whitirea, The flight path of the spirits." (Stokes, A review of the Evidence in the Muriwhenua Lands Claims, pp. 19-22. This is drawn from evidence of Waerete Norman, Wai 45, Document C19, p. 24). Miraka Szaszy started her evidence to the Waitangi Tribunal by stating that “on behalf of Ngāti-Kuri and Te Aupouri tribes, I stand to claim guardianship rights to the Mauri of Te Rerenga Wairua.” Szaszy noted that “the classical poetical description Te Rerenga Wairua has been used by our Maatua Tipuna from long ago. She also stated that “at the time of his departure, Kupe dedicated the promontory at Te Reinga as the place from where the spirits of the dead may take their departure from the Spirit World. He named if Te Rerenga Wairua. Henceforth our people have regarded this territory as a very tapu place to which we are all spiritually linked. This becomes more poignant during the loss of loved ones. Therefore, we lay claim to the guardianship of it for all these reasons” (evidence of Miraka Szaszy, Wai 45, Document A6, December 1987, p. 1 and 4). Waerete Norman cites the following (wai 45, Doc C19, pp. 29-30): "Te Aupouri Ngāti Kuri, Nga Kia Tiaki O, Te Rerenga Wairua, I te Hiku O te Ika; Te Aupouri Ngāti Kuri, the guardians of, the Spirit Trail, the tail of the fish." Te Rangihiroa (Sir Peter Buck) wrote in The coming of the Maori (Wellington, 1952, p. 439) “thus the path of the Māori spirit led north to Te Rerengawairua (the spirit’s leap), a rocky promontory near the North Cape”.
info_description: A coastal feature 7km northeast of Cape Maria van Diemen. Feature shown on: NZMS260 M02 N02; Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-AT24 706912
info_note: Ngāti Kuri, Te Aupouri, NgāiTakoto and Te Rarawa are four of the iwi which make up Te Hiku Forum. These four iwi have shared Treaty settlement redress including this geographic name. Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "departing place of the spirits"

This occasion’d our calling the Point of land off which this happen’d, Cape Runaway.’’ Māori name: Tihirau, meaning Many prominent peaks.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEJCQkIzOTJCMjBGRjg2RjIwNjM)

name: Cape Scoresby
info_origin: The cape was charted by the Discovery II, which made running surveys of the northern portion of the Balleny Islands in 1936-38. Named for the William Scoresby, a companion research ship of Discovery II in carrying out oceanographic work in Antarctic waters at that time.
info_description: A high cape marking the northern end of Borradaile Island in the Balleny Islands.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Cape Scott
info_origin: Discovered and named in 1841 by Ross for Peter A Scott, mate on the Terror.
info_description: A cape lying about 6 miles east-south-east of Cape Oakeley, with an ice tongue extending about 15 miles northward, in Victoria Land.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Cape Selborne
info_origin: Discovered and name by the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, in December 1902 for William Waldegrave Palmer Selborne, Second Earl Selborne, who entered the Cabinet as First Lord of the Admiralty in 1900. Not Cape Selbourne.

info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Cape Sibbald
info_origin: Named in February 1841 by Ross for the Senior Lieutenant (later Commander) of the Erebus, John Sibbald.
info_description: A bare sheer cliff, 600m high, at the southern margin of Lady Newnes Ice Shelf, in Victoria Land.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Cape Smith
info_description: Cape formed by the northern end of the Lillie Range where it terminates at the Ross Ice Shelf.

name: Cape Smyth
info_origin: Ross, in 1841, viewing Sturge Island from a considerable distance, thought it to be a group of three islands, and named the supposed southernmost one Smyth Island after his friend, Captain William Henry Smyth, RN, President of the Royal Astronomical Society. The error was discovered by the NAE, 1901-04. Scott applied the name Cape Smyth to the southernmost point on Sturge Island.
info_description: The southern extremity of Sturge Island, in the Balleny Islands.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Cape Soucis
info_origin: 'Croisilles Harbour. The name appears on d’Urville’s chart, and means anxiety. D’Urville and the crew of the Astrolabe found themselves in rough seas from which they could not escape for a night as they waited, fearing they would be wrecked on the coast. Maori name: Raetihi, lit. rae: cape; tihi: summit.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Cape on the western tip of the entrance to Croisilles Harbour, north eastof Nelson. Feature shown on: NZMS260 O26 P25 Pt P26

name: Cape Spencer-Smith
info_origin: Named by the New Zealand Geological and Survey Antarctic Expedition (NZGSAE), 1958-59, for the Rev Arnold Patrick Spencer-Smith, BA of Queen's College Cambridge, England, padre with the Ross Sea Party of the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, 1914-17, who died on 9 March 1916 on the return journey after laying the depots to Mount Hope for Shackleton's party. He had suffered from scurvy and had been carried for 40 days on a sledge by his companions prior to his death.
info_description: The northern cape of White Island, approximately 24km southeast of Scott Base at Pram Point, Ross Island.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Cape Spirit
info_origin: Visited by the New Zealand Geological and Survey Antarctic Expedition (NZGSAE), 1958-59, and named by them because of the almost constant and "spirited" winds blowing through the strait between Black and White Islands.

name: Cape Teall

info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Cape Terāwhiti
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}; Orthographic standardisation: Objective ID: A6575726
info_origin: 'On either side of the Cook Strait are two headlands with apparently Māori names, but it is possible that neither is correct. Both were recorded by Captain James Cook, but neither have the spelling that he applied. Cook recorded the name for the southwest headland of the North Island, which he obtained from a Māori informant, Topea, as Cape Teerawhitte. The present name is probably a corruption of Tarawhiti: ‘near sunrise’, or ‘disturbed crossing’. The components may be interpreted Tarawhiti: ta: near to; rawhiti: sunrise; or ta: disturbed or unsettled; whiti: crossing. Other meanings of Terāwhiti are hoop or ring and, as a verb, to encircle.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDg5RUE5NDVBQzBGRjg0NTRFM0Q)
info_description: Point on the west coast, due west of Wellington city and northwest of Oteranga Bay. Feature shown on: NZMS260 R27 R28 PtQ27; NZTopo50-BQ31 351284
info_note: Meaning of Tarawhiti "to encircle" Sourced from Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995 Correct spelling argurd to be Tarawhiti, but Terāwhiti adopted. Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): ""that is the east", the answer Cook received from Topea at Motuara, having asked for the name of the headland across Te Raukawa-o-Moana"

name: Cape Turnagain
info_origin: ‘Named by Captain James Cook: ‘The Bluff head or high point of land we were abreast off at Noon I have called Cape Turnagain because here we returned.’ The ancestral name for Cape Turnagain, on the Wairarapa coastline, is Te Aho-a-Māui, lit. Māui’s fishing line, part of the story of Māui and his brothers fishing up the North Island. Further north, Te Matau-a-Māui, sometimes referred to as Te Kauwae-a-Māui (Cape Kidnappers), is the hook used by Māui, and the coastline running south is his line. The bend in the line at Cape Turnagain represents where the line was held.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDkyODg0RjlDQjEwMDgwREUzRDE)
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 V24; NZTopo50-BN38 066116
info_note: Cook's journal recorded ‘no likelyhood of meeting with a Harbour, and the face of the Country Visibly altering for the worse, I thought that the standing farther to the S. would not be attended with any Valuable discovery . With this View, at 1 p.m. I Tack’d and stood to the Northward . . . The Bluff head or high point of land we were abreast off at Noon I have called Cape Turnagain because here we returned.’

info_origin: 'The locality is Castlepoint; the cape is Castle Point. This prominent feature was seen by Captain James Cook on 11 February 1770, who described it as a ‘remarkable hillock’. Joseph Banks made the following record: ‘We passed two points of land to which we gave the names of Castle Point and Flat Point.’ The tiny harbour at Castle Point was called Deliverance Cove by William Colenso, after the mission schooner Columbine found refuge here after from a severe gale in Cook Strait in 1843. Maori name: Rangiwhakaoma, lit. rangi: day; whakaoma: to hasten. This referred to the day when the pioneer explorer Kupe hastened after the giant wheke (octopus) which he chased down the coast, across Cook Strait, and into Tory Channel, where he succeeded in killing it at Whekenui (lit. wheke: octopus; nui: large).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: The name was known prior to 1838, possibly named after a royal naval officer, or could commemorate Jim Caswell who swam to procure a boat for sealers. Also possibly named by Capt. Grono after the Caswells who were living at Tanilba Station in Victoria.; 'For many years the sound was believed to be named after Jim Caswell, a local Maori who reputedly swam and hiked to Deas Cove to procure a boat for sealers. However, E.S. Dollimore suggests it was named after Captain George W. Caswell, RN, who was reportedly in charge of a naval survey at Caswell Sound in the late 1830s. The name of the family home of the Caswells in England was Tanilba, and a Mt Tanilba rises above the north head of the entrance to Caswell Sound. Possibly named by Captain Grono or his son-in-law Alexander Books after Lieutenant William Caswell (owner of Tanilba station in New South Wales). The presence of Mt Tanilba in Caswell Sound would seem to add probability to the origin. Maori name: Taitimu, lit. tai: tide; timu: to ebb. name: Cecil Peak
info_origin: 'Named after Cecil Walter Rees, eldest son of W.G. Rees, and so named by early surveyors. See also Walter Peak. Maori name of Cecil and Walter peaks: Ko-kamo-a-Hakitekura: lit. ko: a particle drawing attention to what follows; kamo: to wink or to twinkle; a: of; Hakitekura. Also Nga-kamo-a-Hakitekura: lit. The winking of Hakitekura. Hakitekura lived on the present site of Queenstown. From the slopes of Ben Lomond she saw young women playing at the foot of the twin peaks, and longed to join them. After lengthy training she swam the 3 km across the lake, guided by the dawn light winking or twinkling off the peaks that later bore her name. An alternative name for the peaks was Te Taumata-a-Hakitekura, lit. Hakitekura’s brow of the hill.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

When Tamatea-pokai-whenua arrived at the sound, his salt-impregnated garments were spread out on two flat rocks to dry. These rocks were named Te Horatanga-a-te-kakahu-o-Tamatea (The spreading out of Tamatea’s cloak), a name later abbreviated and given to the whole sound.' name: Charleston
info_origin: 'West Coast, 29 km from Westport. The Maori village on the point near Charleston was called Waitakere; see also Nile River. The old goldmining township began as Charlie’s Town, gradually changing to Charles Town and finally to Charleston. The consensus of opinion is that it was named after Captain Charles Bonner of the ketch Constant (and possibly the Woodpecker), which traded regularly to Constant Bay with supplies for the settlement. According to other authorities, Captain Beveridge was master of the Constant; having been born at Charleston on the Firth of Forth in Scotland, he gave this name to the settlement. Maori name: Tauhinu Pakihi. There was a time when the place was called Bright Town, and then Brighton; at first it had been known simply as The Pakihi, the Maori term for open grass country, or Waite’s Pakihi, after Reuben Waite.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_ref: Objective ID: A4309409; A4343787; A4329952. Refer Plates CVI and CVII from National Antarctic Expedition 1901-1904 Album of Photographs and Sketches with a Portfolio of Panoramic Views, (1908), London: Royal Society.
info_origin: Discovered and named by the Southern Polar Party of the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE) 1901-04. The chasm blocked the southern party's advance on the mountains, requiring them to follow it in parallel as it tapered out. One day they found they had accidentally crossed it over a dangerous snow bridge. Due to the shear effect of the flow of Byrd Glacier into Ross Ice Shelf, there will always be chasms in the area, though the exact configuration will change over time. The original 'Chasm' as famously photographed by the NAE would no longer exist.
info_description: A chasm parallel to the land, and tapering off to the south out from off Cape Selborne, originally described as '100ft deep, three-quarter miles wide' and with 'five-six miles of flat surface to the land on the other side’.

name: Chatham Island
info_origin: ’The first European here was Lieutenant William Broughton, commander of the armed tender Chatham, on 29 November 1791. Broughton named the islands after William Pitt, the Earl of Chatham. Māori names: Wharekauri: lit. whare: house; kauri: native tree (Agathis australis); Rēkohu: lit. rē: see; kohu: mist, or ‘misty sun’ according to Moriori. One version says that when a party of Ngāti Mutunga came from New Zealand in the Lord Rodney in 1835, they assumed that Wharekauri was the name the resident Moriori used for Chatham Island, whereas it was only that of the village where they landed. However, since kauri don’t grow on the islands, it appears more probable that Wharekauri was transferred from northern Taranaki, where it was the name of a tupuna (ancestor) and an ancient pā.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; A further account notes the name Wharekauri was already in use for the Moriori kāinga at the north of the island prior to 1834. Michael King in Moriori discussed the presence of Māori crew during the whaling and sealing period, writing 'It was likely these latter Māori who named the small kainga on the northern coast, allegedly after a house there built from salvaged kauri timber. Subsequently, Māori used this name to refer to the whole island, because, as Alexander Shand wrote, ‘they could pronounce [it] more easily than the Moriori one of Rekohu’.
info_description: Largest island in Chatham Islands group, east of New Zealand. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-CI04 006353

Both may be true, but the fact that the smaller of the islands was named Pitt supports the latter supposition.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: The Chatham Islands group, being Chatham Island, Pitt Island (Rangiauria), Mangere Island, South East Island (Rangatira), The Pyramid (Tarakoikoia), The Castle (Rangiwheau), Little Mangere Island (Tapuaenuku) The Fort, The Sisters, and other smaller islands, rocks, reefs. They are composed of three main islands, Young, Buckle and Sturge Islands, and several smaller islets that form a northwest-southeast island archipelago about 160 kilometres between 66° 15'S to 67° 10'S and 162° 15'E and 164° 45'E. The island was named Chinstrap because (together with Sabrina Island) it was the first place on this side of the Antarctica where a colony of Chinstrap penguins (Pygoscelis antarctica) were found to be breeding. The island has the only colony of Chinstrap penguins in the Ross Sea region. The next closest colony is at Peter I Øy (island) 4000km away. Originally proposed as 'Islet' but approved as Island by NZ-APNC and US-ACAN in 1975.
info_description: A small low lying island approximately 2 km south-southeast of Buckle Island, 0.3 km north-northeast of Sabrina Island, in the Balleny Islands. Included within Antarctic Specially Protected Area 104 Sabrina Island.

name: Chinstrap Islet

name: Christchurch
info_origin: ’The name was chosen on 27 March 1848 at the first meeting of the Canterbury Association on the suggestion of John Robert Godley, whose college at Oxford, England, was Christ Church. In a letter to his father some three years later Godley wrote: ‘I hope that my old College is grateful to me for naming the future capital after it.’ Māori name: Ōtautahi: lit. Place of Tautahi. Although Ōtautahi is nowadays the general Māori name for the city, it specifically refers to a kāinga nohoanga and kāinga mahinga kai (settlement and food-gathering location) on the banks of the Ōtākaro (Avon River). Tautahi, son of the Ngāi Tahu rangatira Huikai, established the settlement.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

Also includes some material on Churton Park; John Dick Walker d.1981 aged 54 cremated- Karori cemetery records}
info_origin: The suburb was designed and developed from the 1970s by Churton Park Ltd on what was previously farmland. The company was headed by John 'Dick' Walker (1926-81), who had been responsible for design work and house construction in other Wellington suburbs. A Churton Park school designed on what at the time were novel 'open plan' principles opened in 1975. In 1981, on Walker's death responsibility for completion of the work passed to a subsidiary company Middleton Developments. In 1983 the original developer was recognised by Wellington City Council through the naming of the suburb's recreation reserve as the John Walker Park and Play Area. Churton is a village in Cheshire in the UK but has no obvious link to Churton Park. Another possible connection is via Reverend John Frederick Churton (1798-1853) a chaplain to the New Zealand Company who arrived in Wellington on the Bolton in 1840 residing in Thorndon but shortly thereafter he shifted to Auckland.

name: Clinton
info_origin: 'Given by James McKerrow from the family name of the Duke of Newcastle, secretary for the colonies from 1852 to 1854, and colonial secretary from 1859 to 1864. The name was at one time rejected by Parliament as a replacement for Invercargill, which carried the stigma of being named after Captain William Cargill, the leader of the unpopular Otago Provincial Council. Subsequently the post office of Poupoutunoa, q.v., was renamed Clinton, around November 1873. Maori name: Poupoutunoa: this was the name of a post set up to mark the boundary of Ngati Mamoe and Ngai Tahu, says Murdoch Riley. The area may also have been known to Maori as Te Kohakapouakai: lit. The nest of the moa.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Clyde
info_origin: ’The name commemorates Lord Clyde (Sir Colin Campbell), one of the heroes of the Crimea and of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. J.T. Thomson, who named several places after personalities and battles connected with the Indian Rebellion, probably bestowed the name. It was first known as The Dunstan, or the Dunstan and Hartley Township (recognising the well-known prospector Horatio Hartley), then Hartley and Reilly’s Town (after Horatio Hartley and Christopher Reilly discovered gold there), and later Dunstan. The post office name was changed from Dunstan to Clyde on 22 May 1865. At one time it was also known as Upper Township, Lower Township being Alexandra.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. info_origin: The proposer advises that despite the long association of Ngāi Tahu with the island, the name is not original. The name Whenua Hou translates to 'new land' and commemorates a time in Ngāi Tahu history that relates to the occassion when the rangatira Honekai, declared the island as the place where European sealers and their Māori wives could stay under his protection. This was to remove sealers from Stewart Island / Rakiura and mainland villages where they were annoying the Kai Tahu women, hence the 'new land' Whenua Hou became the first European settlement in the south. Within the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998, the Crown acknowledges the Ngāi Tahu cultural, spiritual, historic and traditional association to Whenua Hou in the following pepeha: Ko Whenua Hou te motu, Ko Waikoropupu te whaka, Ko Waituna te awa, Ko Te Ara a Kiwa te moana, Ko Kāi Tahu, Kāti Mamoe, Waitaha kā iwi, Kei Kāi Tahu Whānui, Te ihi, te wehi, te mana, te tapu, Tihei Mauri ora. Whenua Hou is an extremely important tūrangawaewae for Ngāi Tahu Whānui. It is an important 'stopping off' point for birders converging on the Titi / Muttonbird Island in their waka and waka hunua (double hulled canoe).; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={29b8af31-97e1-e311-973a-0050569755f4})

info_origin: Mr Joseph Studholme advises that the name, ‘Coldstream’ was given to the sheep station, which was settled by William Scott and Ernest Gray in 1855 adjacent to the stream. This may account for the name ‘Gray Brook’, just north-east of this proposal, which is depicted on early historical maps and the NZMS13, S103 dated 1948, but is currently not named. Reed records that “Gray and Scott concocted ‘Coldstream’ as a punning name for the Coldstream Guards, who were composed of Scots Greys (a Scottish cavalry regiment of the British army, who rode grey horses), although it may also refer to the cold streams in the vicinity”. Acland records that, ‘Coldstream was bounded by the Hinds and Rangitata rivers, the sea coast and Maronan’ and further, ‘Scott and Gray named Coldstream in punning allusion to their names – Scots Greys – Coldstream Guards. In 1867 Scot and Gray sold Coldstream to the Studholme brothers.’ . Assigning a new name for a feature not named.

Initially approved as Commonwealth Creek by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN), the name was modified to Commonwealth Stream by NZ Antarctic Place Names Committee. The feature to be named was confirmed on a marked copy of Southern Victoria Land, and then applied on the published map NZMS 166 ST58-61/5 (1961). However, this feature has since been determined to be two streams, one flowing to the coast the other to Lake Fryxell. A second stream flowing from the northeast side of Commonwealth Glacier, named New Harbour Stream in scientific publications since the 1960s, was named Commonwealth Stream on the United States Geological Survey 1:50k topographic map (1977). In the early 1990s when New Zealand and US hydrologists studied the area intensively, the name Commonwealth Stream came into established use for this feature instead of New Harbour Stream. In 1997 US-ACAN amended its record for Commonwealth Stream to reflect this common use.

info_origin: This feature was named by John Dobrée Pascoe (1908-72) who along with Roger ‘Boney’ Rosser Chester (1906-74), Allan Hedley Willis (1911-2001) and Dr Bryan T Wyn Irwin (1905-42) climbed in the area in 1930-31, with Pascoe and Chester traversing the peak. The Honorary Geographic Board approved Comyns Peak in 1931. Alfred Comyns (1852-1920) along with William Gerard Junior and JG Richards had crossed over the nearby Mathias Pass in the 1870s and in the 1880s Comyns took 2000 sheep across the pass to open country on the West Coast side. Comyns was a long-time manager of William Gerard’s run at Double Hill. Pascoe had strong and nationalistic views on naming: ‘I oppose with all vigour any perpetuation of the old timers’ deplorable habit of naming features after themselves, their maiden aunt, their companions. The ugly plaster of English surnames that is the bequest of these parties is often the only ludicrous part of a majestic landscape’. From 1955 until his death in 1972 Pascoe was the Federated Mountain Clubs representative on the New Zealand Geographic Board.

info_origin: This place next to a bend in Wairau River was named after Thomas Conder (1842-1918). In 1880 Conder, a Yorkshire born millwright, migrated to New Zealand with his wife Mary and two children arriving in Auckland on the 25 years old City of Quebec, one of the first iron sailing ships. The name Conder in northern England is possibly a variant of Connor. Condor farmed in Taranaki, Whanganui and Wairarapa before settling near Renwick. Here in 1891, he leased 468 acres (189 ha) and another 147 acres (59 ha) of reserve land near what became known as Conders Bend. He built a house and remained farming there until Mary’s death in 1913 when he shifted into Blenheim. The lease then passed to his son William. Conders Bend was, from the early 1900s, of particular concern to the Lower Wairau River Board this being the point at which the Wairau River in flood would overtop its banks and flood Blenheim. Protective stop banks were constructed in the 1920s.

info_origin: On 20th October 1769 HMS Endeavour captained by Lieutenant James Cook sailed into Anaura Bay. Māori canoes came out to the Endeavour and gifts of linen and nails were made to two chiefs who were invited on board with Tahitian high priest and navigator Tupaia (1724-70) acting as translator. High seas thwarted the first attempt to land but this was successfully accomplished by evening. Two streams were located for refilling the ship’s water casks. This work was carried out the next day under Lieutenant John Gore (1730-90) although little water was obtained, while botanist Joseph Banks (1743-1829) and naturalist Daniel Solander (1733-82) ranged about the bay collecting plants and bird specimens. Cook’s instructions were to ‘carefully observe the Nature of the soil and Products thereof’ – and to bring back ‘the seeds of the trees, fruits and grains as you may be able to collect’. Banks and Solander were particularly impressed by gardens of kūmara, yams and taro of up to 4 hectares in extent, totalling 60-80 hectares. The National Historical Committee, planning for the New Zealand centennial 1939-40, desired to erect metal plaques at places where Cook landed. Accordingly, the Department of Lands and Survey was asked to investigate these sites, which if not alienated, were to be protected under the Scenery Preservation Act and other legislation. The Commissioner of Crown Lands for Gisborne established that the site was on Māori land vested in trust to the Tairawhiti Māori Land Board and furthermore that the area ‘required for a memorial would absorb part of the limited area available for cultivation’. As this would involve hardship for the owners, Joseph Heenan (1888-1951), Secretary of the Department of Internal Affairs who oversaw the centennial, suggested instead a small cairn on the roadside reserve. It was not until 1958 that the Historic Places Trust, established by the Historic Places Act, 1954, unveiled here its first cairn marking Cook’s visit. The plaque read ‘In this bay Captain James Cook anchored and watered his ship H.M.S. Endeavour, 20-22 October 1769’. A re-enactment of the landing was staged by children from Anaura Bay School adjacent to one of the streams where the casks were refilled. The ceremony was attended by the Mayor of Gisborne and other local dignitaries as well as incoming Historic Places Trust chair Ormond Wilson (1907-88) and historian John Cawte Beaglehole (1901-71), a world authority on James Cook. In planning for the 1969 anniversary, a New Zealand Historic Places Cook Bicentennial Steering Committee proposed only a special commemoration service at the site as part of the Cook bicentenary.

info_origin: HMS Endeavour commanded by Lieutenant James Cook (1728-79) arrived at Tolaga Bay on 23rd October 1769 and departed on the 29th. Anaura Bay Māori had informed Cook of suitable sources of water for replenishing the ships casks in the bay. Cook went ashore accompanied by botanist Joseph Banks (1743-1829) and naturalist Dr Daniel Solander (1733-82) and ‘found the water good and the place pretty convenient and plenty of wood close to the high-water mark’. Lieutenant John Gore (1730-90) oversaw the work with 12 tons of water and two to three boat loads of wood being loaded ‘a good day’s work’ Cook observed. With astronomer Charles Green (1734-71), Cook took sun and moon readings to correct an error in the observations of the transit of Venus, while Banks and Solander collected many plants and bird specimens. Local Māori traded fish for cloth and beads. In 1924 the area where Cook landed was earmarked for designation as a scenic reserve, a type that included historic reserves. This was Māori land vested in the East Coast Commissioner that had been leased for 21 years in 1925, but the plan lapsed. The National Historical Committee tasked with planning the 1939-40 New Zealand Centennial anticipated ‘inscribed metal plaques’ being placed at Cook’s landing places including Tolaga Bay. Conditions in the lease allowed for 200 acres (81 ha) to be set aside as a reserve but in 1939 the Department of Lands and Survey considered that this would create hardship for local land holders and favoured a small cairn accessible from the beach. Ultimately, in 1964 the Historic Places Trust erected a plaque ‘overlooking the cove’ with entry limited to ‘bona fide sightseers’. In 1966 the Historic Places Trust ‘National and Local commemoration Sub-committee’, planning for the Cook bicentenary in 1969, noted that ‘qualified access’ over Māori land was guaranteed but recommended the government create a reserve over the larger cove where this did not interfere with farming operations. A proposal to reserve an area under Section 439 of the Maori Affairs Act 1953 was considered in 1967 but set aside after the Director General of Lands endorsed the concerns of Māori landowners regarding road access. A subsequent meeting of interested government agencies confirmed that the owners neither wished to sell land nor did they approve of a proposal for new road access on the grounds of disturbing stock and interference with farming operations.

info_origin: Lieutenant James Cook (1728-79), captain of HMS Endeavour, landed here on 9th October 1769 after sighting land the previous day. Cook’s instructions from the Admiralty were to make observations of the transit of Venus in Tahiti and search for ‘a Continent or Land of great extent’. Cook came ashore accompanied by botanist Joseph Banks (1743-1829), naturalist Dr Daniel Solander (1733-82) and some crew. Their first encounter with Māori went tragically wrong with one man being killed by a musket shot. Returning on 10th October with high priest and navigator Tupaia (1724-70), who had joined the Endeavour in Tahiti, and some marines, this second encounter also ended in mutual misunderstanding and four more Māori deaths, with ultimately another five Ngāti Oneone dying of wounds. In 1888 Archdeacon (William) Leonard Williams (1829-1916) relocated the exact landing site by ‘careful examination of the ground, and close attention to every hint contained in the narrative which may serve as a clue to the identification of the actual site’. In 1902 his son Rev. Herbert Williams (1860-1937), a foundation member of the Honorary Geographic Board (1924-37), and William Alfred Barton (1853-1946) a Stipendiary Magistrate, as Honorary Treasurers of the Cook Memorial Fund Committee in Gisborne began soliciting donations for a commemorative monument to be placed ‘in the locality where’ he first landed. By this time the extension of the harbour breakwater and construction of the Gisborne Freezing Company works in 1896 had considerably changed the landscape. In 1904 the Committee accepted Auckland’s Messrs McNab and Mason’s design featuring a 42 ft (12.8m) concrete base and granite plinth topped by a statue of Cook. But the actual memorial dedicated in 1906 took the form of an obelisk. The Centennial celebrations of 1939-40 included ‘the re-enactment of Captain Cook’s first landing in New Zealand, on the spot now marked by the Cook Memorial’, Eurocentrically described as the ‘district’s strongest claim to historical recognition’. The Government intended to mark Cook’s landing places as ‘national historical spots’ but this was delayed by World War II. By the time of the Cook bicentenary in 1969, harbour works had encroached upon the one acre (0.4ha) reserve and memorial site. The Historic Places Trust advocated protecting this and other Cook landing sites as Historic Reserves. The Trust also recommended that further Harbour Board developments should not block the view to the sea nor to Young Nicks Head / Te Kurī. The 1969 ‘Cook bicentenary celebrations’ commenced in Gisborne on 9 October at 9am with a naval ‘ceremony of commemoration at the Cook monument’. In 2018 Tūranganui-a-Kiwa was restored as part of a dual name alongside Cook’s Poverty Bay. In 2019 ‘Tuia – Encounters 250’ marked two and a half centuries ‘since the first onshore meetings between Māori – the tangata whenua of Aotearoa New Zealand – and Pākehā in 1769–70’ and celebrated ‘the voyaging that led to its initial settlement’ with various vessels representing pacific oceangoing craft and a replica of the Endeavour sequentially arriving at the landing site.

info_origin: ’First seen by a European when Captain James Cook viewed it from a hill on 23 January 1770, and first traversed by him on 7 February of that year. Kupe, the Polynesian explorer who pre-dated Cook by many centuries in passing through the strait, bestowed a number of names on its natural features.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. The original Coromandel is a long stretch of coast on the Bay of Bengal in southeastern India; the name derives from Cholamandalam, the ancient kingdom of the Chola. Māori name: Te Tara-o-Te-Ika-a-Māui: lit. the barb of the fish of Māui. In Hauraki tradition, the peninsula is the barb on Te Ika-a-Māui (the North Island). Wai-au and Wai-aua are original Māori names for Coromandel Harbour; the literal translations are ‘swirling current’ and ‘waters containing yellow-eyed mullet’ (Aldrichetta forsteri). Māori name for Coromandel township: Kapanga: lit. the act of throwing or casting out. It is said that the chief Kahumatamomoe was trapped on one of the islands of the Wai-au by stormy weather and a hostile taniwha. To placate the seas and the taniwha he cast his feather plume into the sea and was allowed to return safely to the mainland.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Corry Glacier
info_ref: Objective reference: A4855497; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche July 2023: Objective ID: A5490634 {C1 AJHR 1939 p .24; [Among the Peaks. 1932. Hokitika Guardian, 25 January, Page 4.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/HOG19320125.2.28); Cory, Ida. 1933. Climbs at the head of the Franz-Joseph. New Zealand Alpine Journal, 5, 207-217.; [Fine Alpine Feat. 1933. Taranaki Daily News, 9 February, Page 13.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/TDN19330209.2.141); Jeffery, Robert. 1942. In Memoria. Robert Corry 1866-1941. Alpine Journal 53, 158-159.; [Mount Cook. 1932. Hokitika Guardian, 27 January, Page 4.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/HOG19320127.2.26); NZGB Minutes 1938, 7 July meeting; Pascoe, John. 1937. Relief Expeditions in the Mountains – Alpine Rescue Parties in New Zealand. New Zealand Railways Magazine, 12(2), 39-43.; Wiren, S.A. 1932. First ascents and Explorations. New Zealand Alpine Journal, 5, 3-6.; [Virgin Peak Climbed. 1932. Evening Post, 19 January, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19320119.2.39)}; Corres XIV f.191-194
info_origin: In 1938 New Zealand Alpine Club member Denis Carty (1903-75) successfully proposed the name Corry Glacier to the Honorary Geographic Board in recognition of Ida Corry’s efforts in rescuing guide Mark Lysons on Mount Gold Smith in 1933. Ida Millicent Corry (1907-97), daughter of a British shipping owner, climbed in New Zealand in 1932 and 1933 prior to marrying Patrick Robinson in the UK in 1936. Her father Robert Corry, an accomplished climber, introduced her to mountaineering and they climbed together on the Continent into his late 60s. A member of the Ladies Alpine Club, in January 1932 with guides she climbed Lendenfeld Peak (3194m) and Mount Haast (3114m) from the West Coat side, crossed Pioneer Pass, and with Australian Jack Sharp ascended Big Mac (2565m). On 22 January she climbed Aoraki/Mount Cook accompanied by two guides. Another party of four ascended the peak at that same time. She was known to Hermitage guides as ‘Wren’. In 1933 she returned and in rapid succession on 18 January completely traversed Mount Jervois (2630m), Meteor Peak (2624m) and Mount Aurora (2663m). On 22 January she traversed Mount Matenga (2665m) and Aiguille Rouge (1767m), the following day climbing Mount Conway (2889m) and Turner Peak (2338m). On 24 January, with guide Mark Lysons, she ascended Mount Gold Smith (2909m). On the descent Lysons fractured his leg. Corry ‘cut with her axe a ledge on which Lysons could sit. Then she would descend to the full length of the rope, cutting large steps. At the end of the rope she would cut another ledge for Lysons, after which she would climb back to the injured guide and hold him on the rope, while he hopped down on one leg, on which he wore a crampon’. The 16km 1525m descent to Almer Hut took 20 hours. The New Zealand Alpine Journal praised her ‘coolness, resource, careful climbing, and endurance’.

In April 1945, the Nelson Ski Club wrote that Mount Cotterell be officially recognised and shown on future maps. Two later attempts to have the name changed from Cotterell Peak to Mount Cotterell were unsuccessful.; 'Named after Sylvanus John Cotterell, an assistant surveyor and the pioneer explorer of the Wairau Valley. He climbed the mountain that bears his name while in search of land to the south of Nelson in 1843, but the name was not gazetted until 31 March 1949, as a result of representations made by the Nelson Ski Club.' name: Cradock Channel
info_ref: Auckland Star, 10 July 1934, p. 9; 14 November 1934, p. 6; 27 May 1935, p. 4.; Heathcote, Tony, The British Admirals of the Fleet, 1734-1995: A Biographical Dictionary, Barnsley: Leo Cooper, 2002.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: In 1934, the members of the Auckland Harbour Board moved that the channels connecting the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana to the Pacific Ocean be given names. They suggested that the three approach passages should each honour a popular Governor-General, with five more titles being assigned to the channels inside the Gulf. This proposal underwent some modification. The hydrographer to the Admiralty asserted that allocating so many names to a relatively small area would hinder the direction of shipping. In response, the Harbour Board reduced the number of suggested titles down to three: Bledisloe, Cradock, and Jellicoe, with each applying to a greater expanse of water than had originally been envisaged. These changes proved acceptable to the Marine Department, which adopted the scheme during 1935. Named after British Rear-Admiral Christopher Cradock who commanded the Royal Navy’s 4th Cruiser Squadron in the early stages of the First World War. Cradock has gone down in history as a brave, but reckless, leader. His squadron was made up of obsolete and under-armed vessels, crewed by inexperienced sailors. Nevertheless, on 1 November 1914, he chose to engage a vastly superior German force commanded by Vice-Admiral Maximilian von Spee off the coast of Chile. The resulting Battle of Coronel was a disaster for the British. They lost the armoured cruisers HMS Good Hope and HMS Monmouth, in addition to Cradock and over 1,500 of his men. For their part, the Germans had a total of three sailors wounded.

name: Crary Ice Rise
info_origin: The feature was investigated by the US Antarctic Research Program (USARP) Ross Ice Shelf Project in the 1970s. The name came into use among US Antarctic Research Program (USARP) workers and honours Albert Paddock Crary (1911-87), American geophysicist. Deputy Leader of the U.S. Scientific Program and Scientific Leader at Little America V during the IGY, 1957. Leader of the U.S. seismic traverse of Ross Ice Shelf, 1957-58. Leader, geophysical traverse W from Little America V, up Skelton Glacier to the Victoria Land plateau and W along the 78 parallel to c. 131°30'E, 1958-59. Leader, geophysical traverse from McMurdo Station via Skelton Glacier to the South Pole, 1960-61. Chief Scientist, Office of Antarctic Programs, NSF, 1959-65, Deputy Director, Division of Environmental Sciences, NSF 1965-69 (Director, 1970-75), Director, Division of Earth Sciences, 1975-76, member of ACAN, 1961-76 (Chairman, 1974-76).

name: Darwin Glacier

info_description: A large glacier flowing from the Darwin Névé on the Polar Plateau in Australian territory for approximately 113km to the Ross Ice Shelf, north of MacDonald Point. info_origin: Named for a dead pony that froze into the ice during Shackleton's BAE 1907-09, that was still there when Scott's Terra Nova Expedition 1910-12 visited Cape Royds. 'Another small indentation in the shore by the penguinry had been named Dead Horse Bay because one of Shackleton's ponies had died there. Strange to relate the body of that pony was still there on our arrival — coated with ice and floating amongst the rocks. Stranger still when the day after I discovered it I went down to make a snapshot of that pony's body lapped by the waves to my amazement it had disappeared! For three years it had remained. Not even the wild storms of this tempest-tossed arm of the sea had carried it away yet the night of our arrival the corpse departed!'’ - The Great White South (1921) p.99

Dennistoun emigrated to England in April 1915 and joined the North Irish Horse as a 2nd Lieutenant. He worked as an intelligence officer on the Western Front and was then attached to the Royal Flying Corps. Dennistoun was severely wounded in an attack on the biplane he was an observer in while returning from a bombing expedition in Biache (France). After several operations, he died in a German hospital at Ohrdruf on 9 August 1916.

Antarctica NZ were not sure about this name because George Denton is already commemorated by Denton Glacier, which while not geographically grouped with Denton Hills, is not too far away, and an element of confusion may arise. After further consideration on 12/11/1999, the reservations about this name were still of concern to the Board, however, given that the name has already been published on a satellite image map, the Board decided to accept it.
info_origin: Discovered and roughly mapped by the BRNAE, 1901-04, under R.F. Scott. The hills were mapped in detail by USARP and NZARP personnel in the years following the IGY, 1957-58. Named by US-ACAN (1999) after Prof George H. Denton (Denton Glacier, q.v.) of the Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Quaternary Studies, University of Maine, Osomo, who conducted geological research in the Transantarctic Mountains and Victoria Land (including work in these hills), 1958-99, making more than 25 visits to Antarctica.
info_description: A group of rugged foothills, 46km long southwest to northeast, and 10-20km wide, to the east of Royal Society Range on Scott Coast, Victoria Land. The feature comprises a series of east-trending ridges and valleys circumscribed by Howchin Glacier, Armitage Saddle, Blue Glacier, the coast and Walcott Bay. The highest summits, Mount Kowalczyk (1703m) and Goat Mountain (1634m) rise from Hobbs Ridge in the north part of the foothills. Elevations decrease southward as in Kahiwi Maihao Ridge (1075m) near the centre of the group and Xanadu Hills (826m) at the south end. The principal glaciers (Hobbs, Blackwelder, Salmon, Garwood, Joyce, Rivard, Miers, Adams, Ward) flow east but have receded, leaving several dry valleys. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MG10

During topographic mapping in the 1960's 'Descent Pass' became used for what is more of the saddle between Ferrar Glacier and Blue Glacier.

North Shore City Suburb centred around NZMG coordinate 2671000E 6484550N. http://www.northshorecity.govt.nz/Services/OnlineServices/Documents/nsc-suburb-map.pdf; 'Originally known as North Shore and renamed after the British Naval Base with the establishment of the village in 1859. Devonport is a borough of Plymouth in Devonshire, England. The village on the western side of the hill was known as Flagstaff from 1854. Māori names: A sandspit near the shore was called Te Ranga-o-Taikehu: lit. te: the; ranga: sandspit; o: of; Taikehu. Taikehu was one of the crew of the Tainui canoe, and swam ashore here. The spot where he actually landed was Te Kauanga-o-Taikehu: lit. te: the; kauanga: act of swimming; o: of; Taikehu, while the beach itself was Te Tāhuna-o-Taikehu: lit. te: the; tāhuna: sandhill; o: of, Taikehu. F.L. Phillips gives the name for Devonport as Te Kurae-a-Tura.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Māori were aware that the upper Wairau Gorge provided access to Canterbury. In March 1855, at the request of the Superintendent of Nelson Province, Frederick Weld and Charles Clifford were sent to explore this country. On their return Weld reported it was 'perfectly practicable' and some 150 miles (241 km) shorter than the established route from Nelson to Christchurch. William TL Travers, with Robert Strange and Māori guides including one named as Napera on a follow up journey in May 1855, described the area as 'The river Wairau, from the entrance of the bush above the Top House flat to its junction with the Kopiowenuku (today's Rainbow River), at the base of Turk Mountain, has level banks on both sides, extending in some places upwards of a quarter of a mile (400m) to the foot of the mountain ranges through which it flows. These banks are old boulder bars, above the reach of floods, and afford very good travelling. They are mostly covered with grass, wild Irishman, and scrub, although in some few places they are swampy, and in others the bush extends to the very edge of the river'. In 1846 John Cooper and Nathanial Morse brought across sheep from Nelson and took up land in the upper Wairau Valley. The highly contagious 'sheep scab', which caused sheep to lose both wool and condition, had spread among Marlborough flocks by 1848. Triggered by the mange mite (Psotoptes communis ovis), it was treated by dipping the stock in various solutions, initially tobacco based, to kill the parasite. Dip Flat was the site of a sheep dip. By the 1850s thanks to Weld, Clifford and Travers, Wairau Valley was on the stock route to Canterbury. After World War II the Royal New Zealand Air Force established a field training facility at Dip Flat. The wider locality also served as a mountain flying training area.

name: Disaster Burn
info_origin: Named for the 'Disaster' of Professor Mainwaring Brown's disappearance. Brown's party were exploring the ranges west of Lake Manapouri, looking for a passage through to Deep Cove. On 6 December 1888 Brown left his party's camp at the feature to explore upstream, however did not return before terrible weather set in for several days. The remaining party members Major Goring and John White after searching for the Professor unsuccessfully, erected a cairn with a wooden cross at their campsite and interred a message in a bottle in the cairn. Further search parties were organised over the following years but were also unsuccessful.; 'A name that preserves the memory of Mainwaring Brown, professor of English literature and political economy at Otago University, who disappeared without a trace on 5 December 1888 during an expedition to discover a route from Lake Manapouri to Doubtful Sound/Patea.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Doubtful Island
info_ref: See map of Victoria Land in contents pages of Captain Sir James Clark Ross, R.N., (1847), Voyage of Discovery and Research in the Southern and Antarctic Regions During the Years 1839-1843, London: John Murray
info_origin: An island between Capes Adare and Cape Downshire was reported by Ross in 1841 as being either an island or a large berg with mud and rocks upon it. The ship, Southern Cross, on 9 February 1900, and the Discovery, in January 1902, passed close to its charted position but saw no sign of it. Shackleton's map in "The Heart of the Antarctic", published in 1909, shows the island. The ship, Terra Nova, in 1911-12, passed several times close to the assigned position and saw no evidence of an island, and the Star II in January 1924 did likewise. The island has not turned up in the 100 years since and the existence of the island is therefore extremely doubtful.

name: Doubtless Bay
info_origin: See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDhFNzQ0OUYwMTBGRUE2NjcyM0U); 'Captain James Cook recorded on 9 December 1769: ‘This Bay I have named Doubtless Bay; the wind not permitting us to look into this Bay we steer’d for the Westernmost land we had in sight.’ Nine days later Jean François Marie de Surville arrived and, unaware that Cook had preceded him, he named it Lauriston Bay after Jean Law de Lauriston, governor-general of Pondicherry, the French enclave in India. Surville’s name did not last. Even fellow Frenchman Jules Sébastien César Dumont d’Urville did not use it on his map of 1831; he wrote ‘Baie Oudou-Oudou’, although he kept Point Surville for the southern head of the bay. ‘Oudou-Oudou’ may be a transliteration of ‘Ōruru’, a possible Māori name for the bay. Other recorded Māori names are Tokerau, which now applies to the long beach along one side of the bay; Taipā, although this was likely limited to the small bay that has that name in the south of the larger bay; Ōpoe: lit. ō: place of; Poe.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
