name: Dreyers Rock
info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Petersen, George. 1956. Forest Homes. New Zealand: Reed.}
info_origin: A camp site east of Mauriceville that was occupied by Scandinavian migrants in the 1870s. Named after Alexander Svend Dreyer (c.1820-1905) who was a government agent and storekeeper at the large Scandinavian Camp established on the edges of Seventy Mile Bush and south of Mauriceville, where initially the mainly Danish settlers resided until they moved onto their bush sections. Dreyer was unpopular amongst the Danish settlers who considered him to be a German speaker from Slesvig which, along with Holstein, were lands lost to Denmark after the war with Prussia in 1863. Dreyer resigned in 1873. Prior to becoming the government agent, Dreyer was naturalized in 1865 while living in Nelson (giving his birthplace as Holstein). For a time, he was a merchant and later sheep farmer in Marlborough before becoming bankrupt in 1869. His attempt to lease agricultural land in the Wangapeka goldfields in 1870 was unsuccessful, leading him to petition Parliament for compensation in 1871 with only limited only success. From 1880 he resided in Masterton, styling himself as a ‘Danish Interpreter’, until his death in 1905. Opening of the Dreyers Rock land block for settlement commenced in 1884 and resumed in 1894. The area was heavily forest covered, the principal trees being tawa, rimu, hīnau, rātā and kahikatea, with some tōtara on hilly and undulating land. It was considered suitable mainly for pastoral farming. A limestone cave was discovered on local farmer Mr A Grey’s farm 1898. The Dreyers Rock school opened in 1897, but falling rolls caused its closure in about 1930.

At the spot now known as Drybread they struck fine alluvial gold, but when they went to celebrate they found the goat had run dry, and they were forced to eat dry bread. Another version of the origin is that a Russian gold miner was unsuccessful with his claim and complained that he was forced to eat dry bread without butter.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. info_origin: 'After Freda Du Faur, the first woman to climb Aoraki/Mt Cook, on 3 December 1910.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. ; Emmeline Freda du Faur (1882-1935), known as Freda, ascended and traversed Du Faur Peak (2330m) with guide Peter Graham on 25 February 1912. Some suggestions are that the feature had been known as Madonna, but these were allayed. Du Faur climbed in New Zealand from 1908-13 ascending Aoraki/Mount Cook (3724m) with guides Alec and Peter Graham on 3 December 1910 and made many other ascents and traverses. These included Mount Sealy (2627m) with Peter Graham in December 1909, Mount Annette (2235m) with Peter Graham on 14 November 1910, Mount Darby (2531m) with Peter Graham on 21 November 1910, Silberhorn (3300m) with Peter and Alec Graham in December 1910, and Mount Chudleigh (2966m) with Hugh Chambers and guide Jim Murphy on 11 January 1911. On 12 March 1912, with Peter and Alec Graham she ascended a peak she named Nazomi (2925m), a Japanese word meaning she thought, ‘heart’s desire’, but which may better be translated as 'wish, desire or hope’. She also ascended the challenging Mount Tasman with Alec and Peter Graham on 24 March 1912, quickly followed by an ascent of Mount Dampier (3440m) with Peter Graham and Charlie Milne on 31 March 1912 and an ascent of Lendenfeld Peak (3194m) again guided by Peter Graham and C Milne on 2 April 1912. The following season, on 11 December 1912 guided by Peter Graham she ascended and traversed Pibrac (2514m), which she named after her grandparent’s house in Australia and the ancestral home of the du Faur’s in France. There followed ascents of Aoraki/Mount Cook with Peter Graham and Darby Thomson and a traverse from Hooker Glacier to Haupapa/Tasman Glacier on 3 January 1913. Next followed an ascent and traverse of Mount Sefton with guides Peter Graham and Darby Thomson on 9 February 1913. She climbed Cadogan Peak (2449m), named after her partner Muriel Cadogan, with Peter Graham on 6 March 1913. Her season ended on 21 March 1913 with an ascent and traverse of Aiguilles Rouges (2950m) with Peter Graham.

name: Dunedin
info_origin: ’The name originally intended for Otago’s future capital was New Edinburgh, but at the suggestion of William Chambers — then provost of Edinburgh, and one of the founders of the Edinburgh publishing house of W. & R. Chambers — it was named Dunedin, which is the old Celtic form of the name of the capital of Scotland. The Rev. Thomas Burns wrote to Captain William Cargill on 14 February 1845, ‘Let the settlement be called Otago — the town Dunedin, the River Matou and not Molyneux ...’ The renaming of the ‘Matou’ river appears to have settled the issue. As the name Dunedin celebrated old Edinburgh, so the name Clutha, ancient name for the Clyde, complimented old Glasgow. Alfred H. Duncan wrote in The Wakatipians: ‘In the year 1860 Dunedin was but a small place of a few hundred inhabitants, and the streets were more like muddy swamps than anything else, and to that the city owed the name of Mud-Edin by which we were wont to call it in these days.’ Ōtepoti, the name of the waka landing site in Dunedin’s upper harbour, is the Māori name commonly used for the city.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Dun Mountain
info_origin: Reed - Dun Mountain: Nelson/Marlborough, Bryant Range. Probably named because of the colour of the rock; ‘dun’ also happens to be the Irish word for mountain. Encyclopaedia of New Zealand (vol. 1, p. 502): 'Dun Mountain is conspicuous because of its lack of forest, and because of the reddish soil on the summit and upper slopes. The mountain was named by early residents of Nelson for its dun colour. In 1859 the Austrian geologist Ferdinand von Hochstetter discovered that the mountain was made of dense igneous rock, composed chiefly of two minerals — olivine (magnesium-iron silicate) and chromite (chromium-iron oxide). This unusual rock he named dunite, a name since applied to rocks of this type throughout the world. Because of the peculiar rock composition, the soils lack plant nutrients, and so are devoid of vegetation, apart from stunted shurbs and grass.' ; 'Probably named because of the colour of the rock; ‘dun’ also happens to be the Irish word for mountain. info_origin: Originally named 'duskey Bay' by Lt. James Cook in 1770 when he saw a sound that was a potential anchorage. Uncertain that he could reach it by nightfall he named it 'duskey Bay' and contined on. ; 'On 14 March 1770 Captain James Cook passed the sound without entering, apparently as dusk was approaching: At 1/2 past 3 double reeft the Topsails and hauld in for a Bay … but after standing in an hour, we found the distance too great to run before dark, and it blow’d too hard to attempt it in the night, or even to keep to Windward; for these reasons we gave it up, and bore away along shore. This bay I have named Dusky Bay. The name is now officially Dusky Sound. Maori name: Tamatea. In tracing the journey northwards from Te Waewae beach in search of his wives, the much-travelled chief Tamatea came to Dusky Sound, which was named after him. Small islands near the heads were also named Tamatea after six members of his crew, all of whom bore the same name.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Eketāhuna
info_origin: ’When the area was settled by Scandinavians in the mid-nineteenth century the little settlement was named Mellemskov, perhaps after a village in the Zealand region of Denmark (not to be confused with Zeeland in the Netherlands, the origin of the name New Zealand). Mellemskov means ‘between woods’, although it is also a general forestry term meaning ‘vegetation of overgrowth and undergrowth’. Mellemskov appears on maps in the 1870s, but by the end of that decade the name had reverted to the original, Eketāhuna: lit. eke: to land or run aground; tāhuna: sandbank. The name was probably given because this was as far as the Mākākahi River could be navigated by canoe.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: An original Māori name for this feature was reported in the Marlborough Express of 1903 as being ‘Pana-rua-white’. James Cook of the Endeavour named the inlet West Bay, only for this to be renamed Endeavour Inlet in 1849 by John Lort Stokes, captain of the Acheron on a coastal survey of New Zealand. Endeavour Inlet as a location appeared in the issuing of ‘depasturing licenses’ for stock grazing on Crown Land in 1857 and in land sales in the mid-1860s. The Endeavour Inlet school was set up in 1887 and an Endeavour Inlet post office was established in 1890. ; 'Queen Charlotte Sound. Named West Bay by Captain James Cook, the inlet was renamed after his vessel HMS Endeavour by Captain John Lort Stokes of HMS Acheron. Māori name: Panaruawhiti, lit. pana: to cause to come forth; rua: pit; whiti: to shine; possibly a reference to the emerging of the sun.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Endeavour Massif
info_origin: This feature was originally named Mount Endeavour by the N.Z. Northern Survey Party of CTAE in Oct. 1957, but on subsequent N.Z. and U.S. maps the name was identified as an 1714m summit 4.5km northwest of Mount Creak. Following additional mapping by USGS in 1999 and consultation between US-ACAN and NZGB, the name of the S block of Kirkwood Range was amended to Endeavour Massif to provide terminology better suited to the complex nature of the feature. For the sake of historical continuity, the name Mount Endeavour (q.v.) has been retained for the summit NW of Mount Creak. Both features are named after HMNZS Endeavour (formerly John Biscoe), supply ship to the 1957 N.Z. Northern Survey Party.
info_description: A huge, flat-topped massif on the Scott Coast of Victoria Land rising to c.1772m. The massif extends south from Pātiotio Gap to Fry Glacier and forms the south block of the Kirkwood Range (Robertson Massif forms the north block). Shoulder Mountain, Mount Belgrave and Mount Creak rise from the south part of the massif. Steep coastal cliffs and projecting ridges mark the east margin, but there is a gentle slope west from the massif's broad, plateau like snow summit. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MB08

The higherst peak on the spur is 2750m with the deepest peak being 4250m. The peaks in the spur deepen as the spur extends off the Subantarctic Slope towards the south. The deep ocean plain around the spur is generally ~5000m deep.

The Enderby shipowners and merchants sent the first vessel, the Amelia, to the whale fisheries of the South Pacific. Charles Enderby was the lieutenant-governor of the ill-fated colony established on the Aucklands.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Enderby Settlement
info_ref: NZMS 220 Auckland Island; http://www.doc.govt.nz/parks-and-recreation/places-to-go/southland/places/subantarctic-islands/auckland-islands/heritage-sites/enderby-settlement/ (accessed 3 May 2018); Objective ID: A4525551
info_origin: Historic site of the failed Enderby or 'Hardwicke' settlement. Established in 1849 by the Enderby Whaling Company, intended to be a permanent settlement and base for whaling in the South Pacific. Settlers arrived in December 1849 on the ships "Samuel Enderby", "Brisk" and "Fancy". Ngāti Mutunga Māori and Moriori were found already in residence (having arrived from the Chatham Islands in 1842). 18 prefabricated buildings were erected including a church and a residence for Charles Enderby as Lieutenant Govenor. The settlement grew to 300 people, including Māori and Moriori. Abandoned in 1852 due to impossible conditions for agriculture, an inhospitable climate, a lack of whales, and a breakdown of the social order.

name: Enid Peak
info_origin: Name on early (1885) maps Aeneid, then on others as Enid. First climbed 26th January 1948, by Maurice Boyd, Mary Boyd, and John Pascoe, who suggested the original spelling Aeneid as being more appropriate than the modern corruption of Enid. This was approved (121/48) as Aeneid. There was an objection lodged by L W Field of the Nelson Ski Club pointing out that Enid was a character in Tennyson's Idylls of the King, based on the legend of King Arthur, as were names from Spenser's poems, thus the names were associated. Aeneid was a poem by Virgil, and did not appear to be associated with other names in the Spenser Range. Enid was approved in 1949.

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412; A5139248 {Denton, Ralph. 1982. The Early sheep runs of Marlborough (continued) Run no 4. Journal of the Nelson and Marlborough Historical Societies, 1 (1), 4-9; Johnston, M.R. 1985. The Enner Glynn Coalmining Company Ltd. Journal of the Nelson Historical Society 1(5), 12-17; [The Enner Glynn Coal Area. 1901. Colonist, 21 May Page 1 (Supplement)](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/TC19010521.2.28.12); Wilson, John. 2011. Thematic historical overview of Nelson City}
info_origin: Newport born Arthur George Jenkins (1813-90) arrived in Nelson in 1842. He had various business interests including a flour mill and later took over Run No. 4 from Sir William Congreve (1820-60?). Jenkins acquired 2000 acres (809 ha) of land to the south of Nelson. He named this Enner Glynn after his home in Wales, albeit changing it from the original ‘Ener Glyn’. In 1859, Jenkins was involved in mining coal on the property supplying Nelson township and surrounding areas. He also served for a time as secretary of the Nelson College Board of Governors. A later Enner Glynn Coal Company operated for a time from 1901 and in 1922 was succeeded by the New Enner Glynn Coal Mining Company. The bulk of the estate, now close to the town was subdivided and sold for residential purposes in 1906. Enner Glynn became part of Nelson city in 1958.

After meeting in secret, a baby was born, and Erangi decided to reach her lover by the only way possible, swimming. Tying her baby to her back, she waded into the sea from the point that now bears her name. For further stages on her journey see O’Neills Beach, Te Waharoa Point and Te Hiki-o-Erangi.' name: Eureka
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 S14
cpa_legislation: 'Waikato, 15 km from Hamilton. The famous exclamation of Archimedes means ‘I’ve found it!’, but as explained in Plough of the Pakeha, the Waikato place owes its name to Elizabeth Steele. At a lunch hosted by Captain Wiliam Steele, director of the Piako Swamp Company, it was decided to choose a name for the locality. Elizabeth Steele suggested Eureka, which contained the initial letters of all the ladies present, and no further discussion was needed.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

Maori name: Kokotahi-te-taniwha, rendered Monster or monstrous seabird (presumably Kokotahi was its name, taniwha its description). The taniwha attempted to escape from the lake that is now part of the harbour.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Evans Cove
info_origin: First charted by the British Antarctic Expedition (Nimrod Expedition, BAE), 1907-09. Probably named by Shackleton for Captain Frederick Price Evans (1874-1959), master of the Koonya, which towed the expedition ship Nimrod south in 1907, and later captain of the Nimrod during the last year of the expedition. It was here that the South Magnetic Pole Party under Tannatt William Edgeworth David, embarked on the Nimrod, and here the Northern Party, led by Victor Lindsay Arbuthnot Campbell, of the British Antarctic (Terra Nova) Expedition, 1910-13, spent a winter under very bad conditions. Not Evans Coves.
info_description: A cove approximately 4.3km wide at its entrance between Smitch Point at Inexpressible Island to the west and Cape Russell to the east, at Terra Nova Bay, on the coast of Victoria Land. Bounded on the north by Hells Gate ice shelf.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

As the pass was named by officers of the Acheron it seems likely that the name has the same origin as that of Mt Evans, q.v., being named after its master, F.J. Evans. His recommendation of this route to the surveyor, Captain Joseph Thomas, was accepted by the Canterbury Association. See also Evans, Mount.' Abel Tasman was the first European to see it, on 18 December 1642. He called it Visschers Hoeck (Visscher’s Point) after Franz Jacobszoon Visscher, a pilot, surveyor and navigator who drew the outline map of the west coast of New Zealand showing Tasman’s discoveries. Māori names: Onetāhua, a descriptive name meaning Heaped up sand, referring to the sand dunes on Farewell Spit; or Taumauka: lit. Dry hill ridge. Te Hiku o te Matau (fish hook) is another name for Farewell Spit.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Fastier Hill
info_origin: Named for Alastair (Al) Fastier recognising his 18 years’ service as Conservation Programme Manager of the Antarctic Heritage, being responsible for the implementation of the Ross Sea Heritage Restoration Project (RSHRP) which conserved the four historic huts on Ross Island and their thousands of artefacts, Fastier spending more than 2000 days in Antarctica. From Fastier Hill, Scott's 'Discovery' Hut is just 3.4km west-southwest at Discovery Point and ‘Hut A’ (The IGY/TAE Hut AKA Hillary’s Hut) 3.5km east-southeast at Pram Point. To the northwest the sites of Shackleton's 'Nimrod' Hut at Cape Royds and Scott's 'Terra Nova' Hut at Cape Evans are also visible from the feature. Fastier was responsible for more than 80 international conservation specialists and his efforts firmly positioned New Zealand as an expert in cold-climate heritage conservation. In 2024 Fastier received the New Zealand Antarctic Medal (NZAM) for services to Antarctic heritage and conservation.

info_origin: (James) Henry St Hill (1806-66) arrived in Wellington in 1840 and occupied a number of administrative and political positions in the New Zealand Company and for Wellington Province, including being Resident Magistrate. St Hill was one of the illegal squatters on the Ahuriri Plains. In the mid-1850s he was presented with a kiwi feathered cloak by Rawinia Ngāwaka Tukeke, a wahine rangatira (female chief) of Ngāti Kere, Ngāti Hinetewai and Ngāti Pihere of Porangahau. In 1860 St Hill obtained a Crown grant for 2300 acres (931 ha) to establish his Fernside Estate. At this time, this part of the Wairarapa was covered in fern, grass, and scrub. In 1866 he sold the estate to Wellington politician Henry Bunny (1823-91). In 1876 Bunny sold 1134 acres (459 ha) of the Fernside Block to Richard Barton (1844-79), who had previously owned the Pirinoa Station, for £15,000. With the extension of the railway into the Wairarapa, two new railway stations were opened between Featherston and Greytown in 1880, one nearby the estate bearing the name Fernside.

name: Ferrar Glacier
info_origin: Discovered by the Western Journey Party, led by Armitage, of the NAE, 1901-04. Named for Hartley T Ferrar, geologist with this expedition. Ferrar Glacier was originally applied both to the part of this glacier below its right turn and to the Taylor Glacier, while the upper part above Knobhead was called South Arm. Taylor, of the BAE, 1910-13, found evidence that there are not two parts of a single glacier but two glaciers apposed. With this discovery Scott gave the names Ferrar Glacier and Taylor Glacier essentially as now applied. Later, on the map included in the scientific reports of the expedition, the names Lower Ferrar Glacier and Upper Ferrar Glacier were applied to these two ice streams, but this naming does not seem consistent with the evidence of the medial moraines on this map, which show that Taylor Glacier does not flow into the Ferrar Glacier. Since it is apparent from the fairly detailed maps that the main flow of the Ferrar Glacier heads in the plateau somewhere to the south-west of Knobhead, the name Ferrar Glacier is applied above as well as below the turn at Knobhead. Not East Fork, Lower Ferrar Glacier, New Harbour Glacier or South Arm.
info_description: A glacier approximately 72km long and varying from 3km to 6km wide, flowing from sources in South West Arm of Ferrar Glacier and between Colwell Massif and Wilkniss Mountains, west of the Royal Society Range to New Harbour in McMurdo Sound. The glacier flows northeast to a point opposite the east side of Knobhead where it is apposed, ie conjoined-twin fashion, to Taylor Glacier. From this point Ferrar Glacier flows east between Kukri Hills and the north end of the Royal Society Range to New Harbour. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MF08

info_origin: ’The name is loosely descriptive of the area of fiords, mountains, lakes and rivers of western Southland, and especially of the 1,212,032 ha reserved for the national park. The fiords of Lake Te Anau were probably so named by Captain Edward Mitford Hankinson, who charted the lake; he had been a member of the expedition that searched for Sir John Franklin in the Arctic, and was doubtless familiar with the fiords of the northern regions. There is a mnemonic rhyme that shows the order of the Sounds from south to north (although it excludes Sutherland Sound): Preserve your Chalk, it’s Dusky in Breaksea/And Dagg says it’s Doubtful if Thompson went round/But Nancy and Charles go to Caswell for marble/And George and Bligh to grand Milford Sound. Māori name for the area: Te Rua-o-Te-Moko: lit. te: the; rua: pit; o: of; te: the; moko: tattoo. The name commemorates the explorer Tamatea, who dug pits (rua) to get pigment for tattooing. ’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: ’The suburb bears the name of Captain Robert FitzRoy, who commanded HMS Beagle on her scientific cruise round the world. info_description: An elevated and unusually flat glacier névé between Flagship Mountain and Mount Razorback in the Convoy Range, Victoria Land. Approximately 10km east-west between Dory Nunatak and Mount Nespelen, and up to 9km north-south from Flagship Mountain to Scuppers Icefalls, where the ice feeds Benson Glacier. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MC08
info_note: This feature was originally proposed to be named Waterhouse Névé in 1977 by Dr Christopher Burgess (NZ), after Barry Waterhouse, who was one of the more experienced scientists of that time. However, ACAN did not accept Waterhouse Névé, since a Waterhouse Spur had already been named after Barry Waterhouse. Dr Trevor J Chinn (NZ) later proposed in 1992 that the feature be named The Flight Deck. The New Zealand Geographic Board finally agreed on The Flight Deck Névé. However, in exercising its preference not to use the definite article in names, but rather use the generic feature type, the NZGB and US-ACAN agreed on Flight Deck Névé in late 1994.

name: Fogg Horne Pond
info_origin: Named after two eminent biologists with Antarctic connections Professors G.E. Fogg and A. Horne, both of whom studied nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen fixing organisms have been found in abundance in Fogg Horne Pond. One of a group of ponds subject to continuous monitoring since 1989. Name first applied as 'Fogghorne Pond', a pun, by Professor S.J. de Mora (University of Auckland) during events K081, K013 in 1987. Surveyed and named on plan L&S 37/165 (1991). Modified by NZ-ANC to Fogg Horne Pond when approved in 2019.
info_description: Clear water, small shallow pond, approximately 129m², with benthic mats characterised by nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Located on McMurdo Ice Shelf and south of Bratina Island.

Fog regularly accumulated over the glacier from the Ross Ice Shelf.
info_description: A large, prominent tongue of blue ice, which plunges between Blank Peaks and Mount Rich into the centre of the Brown Hills. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MM06

name: Football Saddle

The pass is an all-snow route that can crossed with sledges, but there are two other saddles immediately to the east and west of Football Mountain that are no higher, and are more easily crossed on foot, though more difficult with sledges because they are steeper and in volve stretches of bare rock.

name: Ford Bridge
info_origin: One of several names currently in use, submitted by the Fiordland National Park Board in February 1965, to name features along the Te Anau-Milford Road. The construction of the road in the upper Cleddau valley was partly completed before World War II, and was left in this condition of being usable with care for about twelve years. The streams had temporary log bridges, but at this branch of the Cleddau the log bridges carried away at every flood. Boulders were moved to the site to create a permanent ford where vehicles could "leap from boulder to boulder across the stream".
info_description: Originally a constructed rock ford on a tributary of the Cleddau River on the Te Anau - Milford road, 1.6km travel from the western end of Homer Tunnel.

name: Forrest Hill
info_ref: Auckland Museum, ‘Hugh Alexander Forrest’, Online Cenotaph, http://www.aucklandmuseum.com/war-memorial/online-cenotaph/record/C5020; Evening Post, 24 March 1917, p. 8.; New Zealand Herald, 25 July 1916, p. 9; Mins v/11 20/04/2007 pp 15-18; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-05/866; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: The area was originally farmed but was developed in the sixties by the Becroft family and is elevated offering great views. The Auckland suburb is named after one of the more than 18,000 New Zealanders who were killed during the First World War. Hugh Alexander Forrest was born in Wellington in 1893, but moved to Auckland at a young age. He attended Auckland Grammar School and Auckland University College, passing his solicitor's examination in 1914. Forrest enlisted on 24 July 1916 and was sent to Trentham Camp for training. By virtue of his six years service in the Territorial Force, he was quickly made a Lieutenant in the New Zealand Rifle Brigade. After sailing from Wellington in February 1917, Forrest reached France four months later. Like many junior officers, Forrest’s front line service was tragically brief. On 12 October 1917, he and 844 other New Zealanders were killed in action while assaulting the German positions at Bellevue Spur. Forming part of the Passchendaele Campaign, this disaster remains the bloodiest day in New Zealand’s military history. The Takapuna Borough Council subsequently commemorated Forrest’s service. On 23 October 1919, it renamed several local roads after First World War soldiers, including changing ‘White’s Hill Road’ to Forrest Hill Road. When the area subsequently expanded during the 1960s and 70s, Forrest Hill was transformed into a suburb.

info_origin: Pioneering New Zealand mountaineer Malcom Ross (1862-1930) named the glacier after his ‘wife, who by her pluck and endurance, had conquered all the difficulties that lay between us and the enjoyment of this scene of Alpine grandeur’. The name appears on a map published in his guidebook 'Aorangi' in 1892.Mountaineer Guy Mannering (1862-1947) mistakenly believed this was named Kaufmann Glacier on some older maps. Forrestina (known as Forrest) Elizabeth Grant (1860-1934) was born in the UK and arrived in Dunedin in 1870. She trained as a teacher and attended the University of Otago, teaching until her marriage to Malcolm Ross in 1890. They honeymooned in the Tasman Valley. In April 1890 they climbed to Rev William Green’s (1847-1919) old 5th camp on Ball Glacier. Forrest then crossed Ball Glacier and Hochstetter Glacier while Malcolm went up Haupapa/Tasman Glacier to Mount De La Beche. Anticipating her later successful career in journalism she wrote about the trip for the Otago Witness. She described her climbing garb ‘clad in a scarlet guernsey, close tweed cap, heavy boots with nails, and a very short serge skirt.…. I felt shy about my ankles’. In 1892 with Malcolm and guide Harry Birrell they attempted to climb Mount Earnslaw/Pikirahatahi, which Birell had climbed the previous year. Forrest stopped short of the summit but did climb Mount Bonpland (2343m). That same year she became the 44th and first woman member of the newly formed New Zealand Alpine Club. Returning to the Hermitage in 1897, they were part of a party that reached the West Coast, via Haupapa/Tasman Glacier. They relocated to Wellington that same year, she as a parliamentary reporter and the first lady editor of the Evening Post, Malcom as parliamentary correspondent for major New Zealand and overseas newspapers. In 1898 she climbed Mount Ruapehu, Mount Tongariro and Mount Ngauruhoe with Malcolm. Without guides, in 1900 Forrest and Malcom traversed Haupapa/Tasman Glacier and ascended Hochstetter Dome (2810m). Later climbing was more restricted but included ‘a most fascinating excursion’ to Mount Holdsworth (1470m) in 1907. She also wrote about her climbing in ‘Under Canvas at Mount Cook’ (1890), ‘Housekeeping on a Glacier’ (1901) and ‘A Woman in the New Zealand Alps’ (1907).

info_origin: A descriptive name for the locality at the confluence of Mātakitaki River, Mangles River, Matiri River and Buller River. A report by provincial engineer John Blackett (1819-83) in 1863 on the inland route from Nelson to the West Coast referred to ‘the magnificent stretch of flat land at the junction of the Matakitaki, Matiri, and Buller rivers, where the land and timber appear to be of excellent quality.’ The Four Rivers Plains name was used in the newspapers and political speeches by 1863 and again in the early 1870s as part of unrealised plans for a rail link from Nelson to Greymouth. In 1867 railway promoters claimed Four Plains comprised 100000 acres (40468 ha) of flat land but more careful assessments described it as a basin rather than a plain and of only 7100 acres (2873ha), heavily covered in beech forest, and of limited agricultural potential. Some land was taken up for farming the 1880s. The Four Rivers Plains Dredge operated for a few years around the turn of the twentieth century.

name: Foveaux Strait
info_origin: ’The first Pākehā to discover the strait was the American sealer Owen Folger Smith, captain of the Favorite, in 1804, later sailing through it. He named the strait Smith’s Straits, but because sealing in these latitudes had been outlawed in 1805, his discovery went unrecognised. For many years the strait was known to sealers and shown on maps as Favorite’s Strait. Major Joseph J. Foveaux, governor of New South Wales from 1808, relaxed the ban on sealing in the region, which would help account for the naming of the strait after him. It was first referred to as Foveaux Strait in March 1809 by Captain John Grono of the Governor Bligh. An attempt to change the name to Tees Strait by Captain Kent in 1824 was unsuccessful. As Dr John Hall-Jones writes in his book Bluff Harbour: ‘When we learn that Grono named Windsor Point (near the entrance to Foveaux Strait) after the town closest to his farm and that he knew Foveaux personally — then it would seem likely that Grono was responsible for naming the Strait after the Governor.’ In 1968 there was a suggestion that Foveaux Strait be renamed Kupe Strait, which hit the headlines as ‘Kupe Strait ruffles Southlanders’. Māori name: Te Ara-a-Kiwa: lit. te: the; ara: path; a: of; Kiwa. One version of the name is that Kiwa refers to the atua (god) who called upon the whale Kewa to chew through the isthmus between Rakiura (Stewart Island) and Murihiku (Southland) to create a waterway so Kiwa could travel to and fro by waka. ‘ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=MkEKPwo9CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEQ1MzVERTE4NDEwMUUxNjFGREMgAQ);

name: Fox Glacier/Te Moeka o Tuawe
info_ref: NZMS260-H35 740410; File BRD-02-02-00-07; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760}
info_origin: 'The Māori name refers to the tears of Hinehukatere. Hinehukatere enticed her lover Wawe to join her in the mountains, but being unfamiliar with the snow and ice one day Wawe slipped and fell to his death. Hinehukatere was grief stricken: her tears flowed down the mountainside and froze to form the glacier, which is also known by the historic name Te Tai-o-Wawe: lit. The tide of Wawe. The first European at the glacier was Leonard Harper in 1857; Sir Arthur Dudley Dobson saw it in 1863, but didn’t name it as he assumed the surveyor at work on this portion of the coast would do so. It was left to Sir Julius von Haast, who (probably in 1865) christened it after the emperor of Austria-Hungary, using the form Francis Joseph, which was how the emperor spelled his own name. The current spelling follows that in other parts of the world (notably Franz Josef Land in the Arctic). In July 2024, despite a large number of Austrian and German historical sources verifying the spelling as Franz Joseph, Minister for Land Information Chris Penk rejected a proposal to change the name, commenting: ‘The community noted that having to change the spelling of the busy tourist centre would have been a further diversion from economic recovery.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Franklin District
info_origin: 'Auckland/Waikato, South Auckland. There seems little doubt that the district was named after Lady Jane Franklin, the wife of Sir John Franklin (see entry under Franklin Mountains). She crossed the Manukau Harbour in a mission schooner and was conveyed by a Maori party to Waiuku, long before there were any settlers in the area. After the Constitution Act of 1853 the area from Newmarket to Lake Taupo was known as the Southern Electorate. In 1860 the electorate was divided, that portion to the east of the Great South Road and the Waikato River being named Franklin, and that on the west Raglan.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. The district that was administered by the Franklin District Council. Constituted by Local Government (Auckland Region) Reorganisation Order 1989, Gazette 1989, p2247 Shown on SO 63493. Amalgamated with other Cities and Districts to Auckland Council in 2009
info_description: The unitary authority that is administered by the Auckland Council.

name: Franklin Flat
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670 Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle, Volume XXIII, Issue 57, 12 May 1864, Page 4; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; Objective folder ID: fA490228; A4405895
info_origin: Named after the Franklyn Brothers (James and William Norris Franklyn, spelled with a 'y'), proprietors of the Wakatu Hotel in Nelson. A Franklyn Street named after one of the brothers is still located off Waimea Road. The brothers set up accomodation on the flat at the halfway point for prosepctors travelling from Nelson to the new Wakamarina gold fields in 1864. At the lodgings "PROVISIONS &c. for man or beast, could be had at reasonable prices". The flat was refered to (or described as) 'the Manuka Flat' prior to the brothers' accomodation. In 1866 four gold miners were murdered by the infamous Burgess gang nearby at what became known at Murderers Rock. The 100's of newspaper articles spelling Franklyn as Franklin may have cemented use of the mispelling.

name: Franz Josef Glacier Post Office
info_origin: The Post Office and associated township were named after the nearby glacier. The glacier was discovered by Leonard Harper in 1857, and named by Julius von Haast in 1865 after the Emperor of Austria-Hungary. The name was anglicised by von Haast in the form Francis Joseph. Some uncertainty existed over the spelling for a long time. The Emperor had been baptised Franz Josef, but his signature always appeared in the form Franz Joseph. The baptised form of the name became accepted in New Zealand as it has in other parts of the world. At a very early date the small settlement at the foot of the glacier was called Waiho Gorge, a corruption of Waiau, a common Māori name meaning swirling waters.

info_origin: Discovered on 9 February 1839 by Balleny and named by him for Captain H Freeman, who was under Balleny in command of the dandy-rigged cutter Sabrina of 54 tons. The feature was estimated to be 12,000ft high by Captain Balleny and thought to be a smoking volcano - with a corresponding illustration in the Journal of the Royal Geographical Society. It is unclear what Balleny saw as the feature bears no resemblance to the original description, being a broad gradually sloping plateau. When the Discovery II surveyed the island in 1936 they described this difference as 'remarkable', noting a lack of evidence for recent volcanic activity across the island group (eg, that the feature had cataclysmically exploded).

name: French Pass
info_origin: 'So named when the French navigator Dumont d’Urville sailed the Astrolabe through the narrow pass between D’Urville Island and the mainland in 1827. The vessel was taken from Croisilles Bay on the west to Admiralty Bay, striking the rocks twice and losing her false keel. ‘To preserve the recollection of the Astrolabe,’ d’Urville wrote, ‘I named that dangerous strait “Passe des Français”.’ Maori name: Te Aumiti: lit. te: the; au: current; miti: to lick. A reef in the pass was believed to be one of the wings of a shag that Kupe had sent from the North Island to find safe harbours and calm waters. In trying to stem the current its wings were broken and the bird was turned to stone. There is a tradition to the effect that Nukutamaroro, who left Hawaiki in pursuit of Manaia, named the pass Au-miro-o-te-kawau-a-Toru, the Swishing current of the shag of Toru.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Frying Pan Lake
info_origin: Descriptive name for the thermal hot pool. It has a flat floor mainly about six metres deep. The temperature is generally between 45-55 degrees Celsius. The area was previously a flat sediment deposit area known as Frying Pan Flat. The 1917 eruption destroyed the flat and the hollow that occupied it filled with thermal and rain water becoming known as Frying Pan Lake. Many features in the Waimangu Valley Thermal Area have been named and publicised by the local tourism industry in order to sound more attractive to the tourist. Ron Keam Assoc Professor of Physics at Auckland University, published a scientific paper on "Bathymetric Survey of the Waimangu Thermal Lakes", in 1980. Keam assisted in the research of the correct names for the area. The Frying Pan Flat that preceded the lake (c.1917 eruption) was named as the flat had shallow pools, gas and steam escaping through these pools produced the sound and appearance of a "busy frying pan."
info_description: Lake in Echo Crater, which was formed by the 1886 Tarawera eruption, it is one of the worlds largest hot pools, 38,000 square metres in area and fed by numerous acid springs.

name: Gabriel Tarn
info_origin: An unnamed mountain feature and a well known campsite for climbers of Mount Longfellow. Named after the nearby Gabriel Stream. Gabriel was a leading character in Henry Wadsworth Longfellows epic poem Evangeline. Gabriel and Evangeline fall in love but are separated by cruel circumstances. Eventually Evangeline finds him but he dies of illness in her arms. Mount Longfellow is named after the poet. Applying Gabriel to the tarn is associative with the nearby Gabriel stream, Gabriel Hut and in keeping with the theme of the poet and his characters. Assigning a new name for a feature not named.

It was mentioned in Canterbury Mountaineer, 21, p.152, and seemed to be an established name. From the original submission 'It will be remembered that one of Jesus' greatest miracles was to transfer the evil spirit haunting two of the Gadarenes men into a herd of swine, which forthwith ran down hill and drowned themselves. Any party crossing this pass will have to be clever to avoid a similar fate'. The descent from the pass to the east is to a stream called Mad Water.

name: Gallipoli Heights
info_ref: McGibbon, Ian, 'Freyberg, Bernard Cyril', The Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, Te Ara – The Encyclopedia of New Zealand; http://www.TeAra.govt.nz/en/biographies/5f14/freyberg-bernard-cyril; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 2012 (53); LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013; Objective ID: A7615016
info_origin: So named for association with Lord Freyberg and the Dardenelles campaign. Naming by the Northern Party of the NZARP, 1963-64. Gallipoli Heights stand in the Freyberg Mountains, with several of the features in this area being named after the campaigns fought by New Zealand’s most famous military leader. As a junior officer during the initial landings of the 1915 Gallipoli Campaign, Bernard Freyberg swam ashore at Bulair and lit a number of flares in an effort to distract the Ottoman forces from the real landing site. For this feat of bravery he was awarded the Distinguished Service Order. Freyberg remained in the Dardanelles for the rest of the ill-fated venture, sustaining a number of serious wounds in the process, and was finally evacuated with the rest of his division in January 1916. After transferring to the British Army, Freyberg saw extensive service on the Western Front. He was awarded the Victoria Cross for extreme bravery during the Battle of the Somme and was then promoted to Brigadier-General in April 1917. However, it was during the Second World War that Freyberg’s fame reached its zenith. He commanded the Second New Zealand Expeditionary Force for most of the conflict and particularly distinguished himself during the Desert War and the Italy Campaign.
info_description: Feature Shown on: NZ 250000 map 53. In the Freyberg Mountains.

Pascoe proposed the name but initially the NZGB did not accept it and recommended that Pascoe find another name which had reference to classical mythology rather than a biblical name. Pascoe disputed this by saying that the name ‘Garden of Eden’ was well established in the limited literature about the area and was commonly used by climbing parties who had visited the area after 1934. The Board approved the name in 1962 based on its common use.

name: Garretts Bush
info_origin: The name commemorates an historical event which took place in 1861, when Henry Garrett, with a gang of 7 others, held up a group of 15 men travelling back to Dunedin via this route from their gold diggings at Gabriels Gully. Only about £400 was taken from the victims because they had already sent their gold to Dunedin via the gold escort. The victims were tied to trees and treated well, then left with the promise that someone would return to release them. However, the victims were able to get loose and subsequently Garrett and another of the gang members were caught, tried and imprisoned in Dunedin for the crime. The area is well known for this piece of history, with the trees used to tie up the victims being able to be identified for many years after the event.

info_description: A glacier flowing from the Keble Hills between Mount Alexandra and Williams Peak, to spill out in the head of Garwood Valley, McMurdo Sound, Victoria Land. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MG10
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Garwood Valley
info_origin: Mapped and named by the British Antarctic Expedition (BrAE), 1910-13, associated with Garwood Glacier.
info_description: A mostly ice-free valley in Denton Hills, between Keble Hills and Marshall Ridge, extending from Garwood Glacier to Koettlitz Glacier north of DeMaster Point, Scott Coast. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MG11

name: Gary Peaks
info_origin: Mapped by U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and U.S. Navy air photos, 1960-65. Named by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Gary F. Martin, U.S. Navy (USN), machinery repairman at the South Pole Station in 1965.
info_description: Two peaks that form a portion of the north wall of Sheehan Glacier, 7.8km west-southwest of Mount Hager in Explorers Range, Bowers Mountains.

name: Gate Pa
info_origin: ’Ngāi Te Rangi constructed a pā on the rise, which they knew as Pukehinahina: lit. puke: hill; hinahina: the mahoe (Melicytus ramiflorus). After Archdeacon A.N. Brown purchased Te Papa promontory for the Church Missionary Society, the inland limit of the area was defined by a ditch across a narrow neck of land. A bridge over the ditch was closed by a gate, hence the name Gate Pa. The Battle of Gate Pā took place here on 29 April 1864.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 U14 Edition 1 1980

name: Gate Pa Post Office

name: Gates Harbour
info_origin: 'Fiordland National Park, near Preservation Inlet. After the vessel General Gates, commanded by the notorious Abimeleck Riggs. A sealing gang which left here in 1821 was rescued 17 months later by Captain W.L. Edwardson of the Snapper.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Gates Mountain

name: Gateway Hills
info_origin: So named by the NZ-APC in 1983 on a proposal by geologist M.G. Laird because the hills bound the southern entrance to Sledgers Glacier.
info_description: A prominent pair of hills (2,000 m) immediately west of Husky Pass at the head of Sledgers Glacier, Bowers Mountains (q.v.).
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map Not shown on Mount Soza (NZ) map, SR 57-58/15; Shown on US 250000 Mount Soza, SR 57-58/15.

name: Gateway Nunatak
info_origin: Surveyed by the Northern Survey Party of the New Zealand Trans-Antarctic Expedition, 1956-58, in November 1957, and named by them because it marks the most obvious gateway through the upper icefalls for parties travelling west up the Mackay Glacier.
info_description: A prominent nunatak in the upper Mackay Glacier, 15km west-southwest of Mount Gran and 5.6km south of Reid Rigde, at the end of a long line of icefalls extending across the glacier. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MD07

name: Gateway Point
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 N37

name: Gatlin Glacier
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Harold Oad Gatlin, US Antarctic Research Program (USARP) meteorologist at the South Pole Station, winter 1964.
info_description: A tributary glacier flowing north-northwest for approximately 17km between the Cumulus Hills and Red Raider Rampart to enter the south side of McGregor Glacier, in Queen Maud Mountains.

name: Gatson Ridge
info_origin: Named by US-ACAN after Karl W. Gatson of USGS, topographic engineer on joint 1975-76 USGS-BAS project to establish control points for Landsat mosaics of Palmer Land; also to establish geodetically tied independent survey nets in the Ellsworth Mountains and Antarctic Peninsula into a worldwide reference system using Doppler satellite control.
info_description: A jagged ridge, 4.9km long, that runs east from the south part of Bowling Green Plateau in Brown Hills, Cook Mountains. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MM06
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map Not shown on Darwin Glacier (NZ) map, ST 57-60/13; Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Carlyon Glacier (USA) map, ST 57-60/13.

name: Gaunt Creek

name: Gauntlet Ridge
info_origin: The name suggests the appearance of the feature in plan and was applied by New Zealand Antarctic Place Names Committee (NZ-APNC) in 1966. Originally suggested in a group of names put forward by the surveyor Malcolm Ford and cartographer Denys Breffny McCandless Rainey.
info_description: A flat-topped, mainly ice-covered ridge, or peninsula, which extends 13km southeastwards separating the mouths of Nascent Glacier and Ridgeway Glacier where they discharge into Lady Newnes Bay, Victoria Land.

name: Gauss Glacier
info_origin: Named by the NZGB in 1993 after German mathematician and astronomer Karl Friedrich Gauss.
info_description: A steep glacier on the north side of Datum Peak, descending west from the southwest extremity of Hobbs Ridge into Blue Glacier, in Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MG10
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map Not shown on McMurdo Sound (NZ) map, ST 57-60/6; Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Ross Island (USA) map, ST 57-60/6&7.

name: Gaussiran Glacier
info_origin: Named by US-ACAN after Lt. C.D. Gaussiran, USN, a pilot with the VXE-6 detachment at Darwin Glacier Field Camp, 1978-79.
info_description: A glacier in the east part of Britannia Range. It drains north from the saddle with Merrick Glacier to a juncture with Darwin Glacier between Cranfield Icefalls and Nebraska Peaks. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MN06
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map Not shown on Byrd Glacier (NZ) map, SU 56-60/1&2 (Pts); Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Cape Selborne (USA) map, SU 56-60/2.

name: Gavin Stream
info_description: Stream flowing into Seagull Stream west of Mt Donald McLean.

name: Gawler Stream

info_description: Left bank tributary of Limestone Creek. It rises from the peak at 813m and flows into Limestone Creek 3.1km west of Gawler Downs. Blocks XIII and XIV, Alford Survey District.

name: Gawn Ice Piedmont
info_origin: Named by the Darwin Party of the NZ Party of the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition (CTAE), 1956-58, for J E (Ted) Gawn, radio operator at Scott Base who worked closely with all the field parties and whose efforts made their work much safer and easier.
info_description: A piedmont ice and snow slope bordering on the Ross Ice Shelf between the Darwin and Byrd Glaciers. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MN07

info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map Not shown on Byrd Glacier (NZ) map, SU 56-60/1&2 (Pts); Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Cape Selborne (USA) map, SU 56-60/2.

name: Gealy Spur
info_origin: This area was first sighted by Shackleton's Southern Journey Party in December 1908. Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for William J. Gealy stratigrapher with the Ohio State University Geological Expedition of 1969-70, who worked the spur and found tetrapod fossils here.
info_description: A high rock spur on the west side of Beardmore Glacier. The spur descends northeast from Mount Marshall and terminates in Willey Point.

name: Geddes Crag

name: Geikie Inlet
info_origin: Discovered by the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, who named it for Sir Archibald Geikie (1835-1924), a geologist who gave much assistance in preparing for the expedition.
info_description: An inlet about 12.5km wide at its entrance, lying between the cliffs of Drygalski Ice Tongue on the north and Clarke Glacier and Lamplugh Island on the south in Victoria Land. The inlet has essentially been blocked since the early 1980s by a semi-calved piece of the Clarke Glacier, Davis Glacier ice shelf, wedged between Cape Irizar and Drygalski Ice Tongue.

The generic "Land" has been changed to "ridge" since it is not appropriate for so small a feature, but Borchgrevink's intent in naming the whole mass has been respected. Not Geikie Land or Geikie Point.
info_description: A massive ridge, 457m high, terminating as a divide between Murray and Dugdale Glaciers, in the Robertson Bay area of northern Victoria Land. The landward extension of this feature remains to be determined.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Gentil Stream

He tramped the Waitakeres and local mountains as a loner and with his lifetime friend Jock Butcher. Taken from Wanderlust, The official "Organ of the Auckland Tramping Club." Volume 56 No. 7 August 1986.
info_description: Tributary of Anawhata Stream near the mouth at Anawhata.

name: Gentle Annie Creek
info_origin: ’This locality near Cromwell was first known as the Annieburn. Robert Gilkison heard of ‘a gentle girl from Cromwell who fell over the cliffs into the ravine, which was called Gentle Annie after her.’ More plausible connections are to two local barmaids: on an outing with miners ‘Meg’ was voluble while crossing the Roaring Meg stream, so the diggers called the next stream Gentle Annie after Meg’s much calmer companion. But the name may be a wry reference by diggers to Annie being more abusive and loud-mouthed than Roaring Meg. Gentle Annie occurs in various other places, including several on the West Coast and one on the Napier–Taihape Road, with local variations on the Otago origin story. Māori name of Gentle Annie Creek: Te Waireika.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Gentle Glacier

name: Gentleman Smith Stream

name: Gentle Valley

A smooth lobe of blue ice from Waterhouse neve flows between Barrett Bluff and Mount Razorback down into the valley from the south east.'

name: Geodetic Glacier

info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map Not shown on McMurdo Sound (NZ) map, ST 57-60/6; Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Ross Island (USA) map, ST 57-60/6&7.

info_origin: Otago, 30 km from Oamaru. Named for George Duncan, Otago provincial treasurer. The first sections were sold on 14 October 1870. Maori name: Puna-a-Maru, lit. puna: spring; a: of; Maru.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; An original Māori name for this broader area was Te Puna-a-Maru – an eeling camp which was one of several seasonally occupied settlements along the riverbank and part of ‘a food gathering highway’. Puna-a-Maru has been translated as the Spring of Maru and Oamaru and Taki-a-Maru are associated place names. Although his identity remains uncertain, two possibilities are that he was a Ngāi Tahu hero or a war god. Te Puna-a-Maru was the home of Te Huruhuru (?-1861), an important Ngāi Tahu leader. Government administrator and linguist Edward Shortland (1812?-93) visited here in 1844 when conducting a census of South Island Māori. Walter Mantell, (1820-95), the commissioner for extinguishing Māori land titles in the South Island, laid out the 376 acres (152ha) Te Puna-a-Maru riverside reserve in 1848. A lithographer, William Spreat (1841?-93), completed a cadastral plan of Awamoko Survey District in 1868 as subdivision of leasehold runs commenced. This included an 82 acre (33 ha) water reserve which became a government town site in 1870. The town plan was the work of Otago Provincial surveyor Edgeworth Richard Ussher (1839-1916). Essentially a grid layout with 62 sections of 1 rood (1011 sq m) and 47 of 1 acre (0.4ha), the internal roads were given Scottish names, mostly from the west and northwest of Aberdeen. Canadian born Ussher arrived in New Zealand in 1861 and was employed by the Provincial Government and the Public Works Department on road, rail and hydro-electric projects. The town was named after George Duncan (1826-79) who was born in Scotland and arrived in Otago in 1849. He was a farmer, and flour mill and brewery owner prior to being elected to the Provincial Council and serving as Secretary for Public Works and Treasurer. The first sections were sold in October 1870 for £5 for those fronting main streets and £3 for back sections. Interest was limited although Georgetown was still optimistically described as a ‘nascent government town’ in 1874.

info_origin: Named by the Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Major General Anthony P. German, who was commander of the New York State Army National Guard and the New York Air National Guard. From 1989 to 2003, General German served as a navigator with the 109th Airlift Wing of the New York Air National Guard, where he flew operational missions in support of scientific research in both Antarctica and Greenland. From 2003 to 2004 he served as the Department of Defense (DOD) Liaison to the National Science Foundation (NSF), Office of Polar Programs where he served as the primary interface between NSF and all DOD support elements of USAP. From 2006 to 2010 General German was the Commander of the 109th Airlift Wing and had overall responsibility for LC-130 operations and field logistics support in Antarctica. He was instrumental in increasing the efficiency of flight operations in Antarctica, which was critical to completing the South Pole Station Modernization on schedule, while also maintaining support of deep field research and numerous other high-level projects.

info_origin: The Sisters were named by the British Antarctic Expedition, 1889-1900. Gertrude Rock was named by Victor Campbell, leader of the Northern Party of the British Antarctica Expedition (Terra Nova expedition, BrAE), 1910-13, at the suggestion of Levick, after Gertrude and Rose, two sisters mentioned in a favourite comic song of the time. In 2004 New Zealand's RV Tangaroa and its launch Pelorus discovered the feature no longer existed, with depths of 17m at the last reported position. Its sister Rose Rock still existed in a much reduced state. It was initially theorised the feature had been obliterated by Iceberg B-15A, however research found the feature had disappeared earlier, perhaps victim to an earlier iceberg or perhaps just the forces of erosion.

info_origin: Gibbstown takes its name from William Gibbs (c.1820-96) who arrived in Nelson on the Duke of Bronte in 1852 and settled in Golden Bay purchasing land between Aorere and the coast. Capitalising on the Collingwood goldrush, in 1857 he laid out a township and sold the sections. Initially called ‘Gibbs’ Town’, it was described in 1857 as located on ‘a narrow neck of land jutting out into the sea, and on the inner side of which is a harbour and jetty, at which small vessels can land goods’. The temporary courthouse was beside a small Māori pā on a reserve at the extreme end of Gibbstown. In 1861 Alfred Domett, John Poynter and Thomas Brunner, the Commissioners of Native Reserves. and Gibbs transferred 1 acre 3 roods and 32 perches (0.79 ha) of land on the southern portion of Gibbstown for a smaller 2 rood and 34 perch (0.29ha) parcel of land taken from the Māori Reserve on the tip of the peninsula. Gibbs was a member of the Provincial assembly and later MP for Golden Bay. Thereafter, he was Resident Magistrate for the Golden Bay District.

name: Girdlestone
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013; Free Lance, 26 September 1918, p.4; Evening Post, 12 March 1932, p.11; http://natlib.govt.nz/records/22718693; Maclean, C., Tararua: the story of a mountain range, Wellington : Whitcomb and Tombs, 1994
info_origin: Prior to the First World War Hubert Earle Girdlestone worked as a surveyor in the Wellington District for the Lands and Survey Department. He led topographic and survey expeditions through Tararua Range in the early 1910's, producing invaluable maps, erecting trig stations, and cutting a track from Levin to Masterton. Girdlestone also took a keen interest in exploration, organizing and guiding parties through the mountains of Tongariro National Park and Tararua Range on numerous occasions. He was made a Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society in 1914. In December 1917 Girdlestone left New Zealand with the 33rd Reinforcements. On account of his technical knowledge, Girdlestone was placed on special work with the Intelligence Department when he reached the Front. His personal qualities earned him a reputation as one of the most popular non-commissioned officers, but at the Battle of Bapaume in France, August 1918, he was killed by shell shrapnel in his sleep. After his death the Tararua Tramping Club resolved to make some commemoration of Girdlestone, renaming several features in the Tararua Range after him unofficially. It is unclear exactly when the peak became known as 'Girdlestone', but in 1928 a trig was erected on the summit by H.M. Ross bearing the name Girdlestone.
info_description: A 1546m peak immediately west of Mitre (the highest peak in the Tararua Range). The highest point of Tarn Ridge. Feature shown on: NZMS260 S25 Pt R25 Edition 2 1995, NZTopo50-BN34 061810

name: Gisborne
info_origin: ’In 1870 the township was named after William Gisborne, colonial secretary in the Fox ministry from 1869 to 1872. He had arrived in New Zealand in or about 1848, was a member of the Legislative Council in the 1860s, and in 1877 was elected a member of the House of Representatives while in London. The principal streets are named after British statesmen including Gladstone, Peel, Palmerston, Bright and Cobden. Māori name: Tūranga or Tūranganui-a-Kiwa: lit. tūranga: standing; nui: great; a: of; Kiwa; now also part of the official name for what Cook had named Poverty Bay. Kiwa was the tohunga of the Horouta canoe, but he has also been credited with the command of the Takitimu. His son was Kahutuanui. One account has it that for days Kiwa stood by the mouth of the river waiting for his son to arrive, and that from this incident came the original name. On arrival Kiwa declared ownership by planting a mauri (a symbol of the principle of vitality that provides a sacred bond between man and the land) near the site of the Turanganui Hotel.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealnd Biography for William Gisborne](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2g11/gisborne-william)

info_origin: ’The settlement near Carterton, along with a locality at Lake Hāwea near Wānaka and a suburb of Invercargill, were all named after the British colonial secretary and later prime minister, William Ewart Gladstone. Māori name of Gladstone in the Wairarapa: Tupurupuru: lit. a plant of the genus Solanum (nightshades). The Gladstone at Lake Hāwea was a paper town on maps that never physically eventuated. name: Glendhu
info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412; A5139248 {https://web.archive.org/web/20201024005912/http://ketemasterton.peoplesnetworknz.info/wairarapa_archive/images/show/104-glendhu}
info_origin: Donald Cameron (c.1784-1860) born at Ockle, Ardnamurchan, Argyll, arrived in Wellington on the Blenheim in 1841. After several journeys to the Wairarapa, Cameron leased land off Māori to establish the Pahaoa sheep station in 1846. After the Crown purchased the land Cameron in 1854 freeholded the homestead block while placing the remainder of the leasehold in the names of his five sons Dugald, Alexander, Donald, John, and Duncan. The Pahaua block was divided between the brothers in 1882, with John taking the 11671 acre (4723 ha) homestead station of Pahaua, Duncan taking 5993 acres (2425 ha) renamed as Glendhu (sometimes rendered as Glen Dhu), with the inland Kaikuri block of 2553 acres (1033 ha) sold to a partnership of other family members. Glen in a Scottish setting might be translated as a narrow valley and Dhu as black, but Duncan Cameron’s exact motivation in choosing the name is unclear.

The wetland was known as “Glendhu” in the early 1900s. It was known locally as “Scaifes lagoon” from the 1940s – 1970s as it was part of Glendhu Station farmed by Arthur Scaife until 1969. The station was subdivided and the part of the station the wetland lies in became part of Alpha Burn Station. As the Scaife family is no longer associated with this property, reverting to the original name is considered appropriate. For the name Glendhu, Reed records ‘Lit. black glen. After Glendhu on the Northumberland side of the Cheviot Hills, England.’

name: Gneiss Point
info_origin: First charted by the British Antarctic Expedition (Terra Nova expedition, BrAE), 1910-13, and so named because of the gneissic granite found there. We were doubtful as to whether this, or the previous headland, was David's "Marble Cape" ; in fact, as some one said, it was a "nice point." At any rate this pun led to the name Gneiss Point by which we knew it'. [Griffith Taylor (1916), With Scott: the silver lining, London: Smith, Elder & Co, p.242]

name: Golden Bay
info_origin: 'Tasman, to the west of Tasman Bay. So named because of the accidental discovery of gold by pighunters at the Aorere River in 1857. See also Lightbands Gully. Tasman named it Mordenaers’ (Murderers’) Bay on account of the conflict with local Maori in which four of his crew were killed. In 1770 Cook included it as part of Blind Bay; Dumont d’Urville changed it to Massacre Bay in 1835; in 1842 the discovery of coal at Takaka caused a change to Coal Bay. Maori name: Te Tai-o- Aorere, q.v; also Te Taitapu, lit. te: the; tai: coast; tapu: sacred.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Golden Bay / Mohua
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Mohua is a site of significance for Te Ātiawa which is shared with Ngāti Tama, and Ngāti Rārua. Many pā and kāinga are located in the Bay belonging to these iwi. The mohua (yellowhead) was once one of the South Island's more abundant native forest birds, but there has been a dramatic decline in its population over the last 30 years. Ngāti Rārua history: Mohua is the name used by iwi for the entire area known as Golden Bay. It is also the Maori name for the Yellow Head or Bush Canary. However, this particular species of bird is no longer found in this area. An early record of the use of the name derives from a tri partite runanga made up of Ngāti Rārua, Ngāti Tama and Te Ātiawa known as Te Runanga o Mohua. The name is further entrenched in the current day Resource Management Group formed by these same three iwi called Manawhenua ki Mohua. ; 'So named because of the accidental discovery of gold by pig hunters at the Aorere River in 1857. Mohua (yellowhead, Mohoua ochrocephala), which was once one of the South Island’s more abundant native forest birds, is the name applied by iwi to the bay. Abel Tasman named it Mordenaers’ Baij (Murderers’ Bay) on account of the conflict with Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri in which four of his crew were killed. In 1770 Cook included it as part of Blind Bay; Dumont d’Urville changed it to Massacre Bay in 1835; in 1842 the discovery of coal at Tākaka caused a change to Coal Bay.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Gordonton
info_origin: 'The name was given to honour Aberdeen-born John Gordon, who was appointed in 1886 to manage the New Zealand Land Association’s Waikato peatlands. He did much for the district, then known as Hukanui, and when a post office was established and a name change was needed to avoid confusion with Hukanui in Wellington, local residents (both Maori and Pakeha) agreed to preserve his memory. The Maori name Hukanui originates from the Maori practice of hunting bush rats and keeping them alive in pits in preparation for a feast. One frosty morning the white breath rising from the rat pit was noticed by a chief, who exclaimed ‘Hukanui! Hukanui!’, lit. huka: frost; nui: great.' info_origin: ’In the beginning the site was simply ‘where the Waikaka joined the Mataura’. The first name in common usage was the Long Ford (or Longford) over the Mataura River, possibly bestowed by Alex McNab, whose run occupied both sides of the river. After the site of the township was surveyed, Dr J.A.R. Menzies, provincial superintendent of Southland, conferred on it the name of his friend, Colonel Thomas Gore Browne (governor of New Zealand 1855–61), and ‘Gore’ was placed on the provincial maps. Residents persisted in using Long Ford until the railway line reached the township when this four-letter name appeared on the station signboard. For a time the name ‘Gordon’ was used for East Gore. Māori name: Māruawai is the name of the valley where Gore is located: lit. mārua: valley; wai: water.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Thomas Robert Gore](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1b39/browne-thomas-robert-gore)

info_origin: 'On 24 November 1769 Captain James Cook described the Hauraki Gulf as ‘being defended from the Sea by a Chain of Large Islands which I have named Barrier Isles.’ Over time the names Great Barrier and Little Barrier were applied to the two largest islands. Aotea is translated as ‘The island enveloped in white clouds’ and is also linked to the ancestral waka of that name, which visited the island. Cook and crew recorded the name ‘Waootaia’ for the island.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEEyMUVFODhBQzEwMjFBQUI5QUQ)

name: Great Mercury Island (Ahuahu)
info_origin: 'So named for its vicinity to Mercury Bay. The largest island in the Mercury Islands, q.v. Maori name: Ahuahu. On the final leg of its voyage the Takitimu canoe landed on the island. Used to the heat of the tropics, the crew were suffering from the cold, for the marangai was blowing from the east. Finding that the sand dunes were warm, they lay down and heaped sand over their bodies, thus giving the name Ahuahu (Heaped up) to the island. The same incident has also been ascribed to Paikea. However, F.L. Phillips translates the name as A place of cultivation, so called because the warm microclimate here made it an ideal base for the propagation of kumara. According to Judge J.A. Wilson, the name was bestowed when the crews of Mataatua, Aotea, Te Ririno and Kurahaupo made rendezvous at the island and the leaders agreed on plans for settlement. He believed the name Ahuahu meant To shape a course. The island is also said to have been named after a locality in Hawaiki, the Maori homeland.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: The largest island in the Mercury Islands group, located approximately 8km north of Opito Bay, off the east coast of Coromandel Peninsula. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BA35 507436

name: Green Range
info_origin: Named for Allan Green, Professor Emeritus at the University of Waikato in New Zealand. He has over 35 years of research experience in the Ross Sea Region, as well as the maritime Antarctic and the adjacent Tierra del Fuego. He is recognised for his research achievements in Antarctic and lichen ecophysiology. He facilitated the first visit of a biological team to the Beardmore Glacier Region in over 50 years as well as the first comprehensive biological survey of the area. In June 2013 he was also awarded the New Zealand Antarctic Medal, as part of the Queen’s Birthday Honours List.
info_description: A distinct range including peaks, glaciers, valleys, ridges and spurs, trending generally north-south for approximately 12km. Midpoint is approximately 600m high descending to approximately 200m at its northern and southern ends. Located at the northernmost end of Queen Alexandra Range between King Glacier and The Gateway near the terminus of Beardmore Glacier as it flows into Ross Ice Shelf. Northern-most position: 83°27'30''S latitude, 170°40'E longitude; midpoint position: 83°31′S latitude, 170°43′E longitude; southern-most position: 83°34'S latitude, 170°50'E longitude. name: Grenada Village
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA417315; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche December 2022: Objective ID: A5113372 {http://grenadavillage.org.nz/naming.php; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenada_Village}
info_origin: Development of Wellington's northern suburbs in the mid-1970s included Grenada Village. This was an 881 acre (356 ha) development on the MacMillan Block initially planned by Paparangi Properties in 1975 but taken over by Grenada Estates who commenced work in 1977. Land in the vicinity was first farmed by John Drake and his wife Ceres who arrived in Wellington on the Aurora in 1840. The name Drake, as an original settler name, would have aligned with City Council's preferences, but Grenada was preferred instead. John Drake (c.1814-89) claimed a lineage back to a brother of Sir Francis Drake, who had accompanied his famous relative on an expedition to the West Indies in 1572-73 where they sacked Spanish towns, captured vessels and seized a treasure train. This was the basis of the change from Drake to Grenada in the development of the subdivision. The West Indian theme was continued in the selection of street names within the subdivision. Grenada Village was formally gazetted as a suburb name in 2020.

name: Grey River/Māwheranui
info_ref: File BRD-02-02-00-07 ; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760}
info_origin: 'Named after Sir George Grey by Thomas Brunner. Brunner named the Whakapoai River the Heaphy after his travelling companion, and Charles Heaphy wished to reciprocate by calling the Māwhera the Brunner. But Brunner declined, and proposed honouring Sir George Grey. Māori name: Māwheranui. The name refers to the atua Tūterakiwhānoa, who shaped the South Island for human habitation. The long mountain range was blocking the flow of the inland rivers to the sea, so he sat on the mountain range and moved his thighs to create the gorge through which the Grey River / Māwheranui now flows. The full name of the gorge was Te Māwherataka-o-kā-kūwhā-o-Tūterakiwhānoa: The extension made by the thighs of Tūterakiwhānoa, later shortened to Māwhera.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Grunow Peak
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-17/618; Objective ID: A6791993
info_origin: The peak was named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Anne Grunow, who worked for 12 field seasons from 1985 through 1996 in this and numerous other areas of Antarctica concentrating on all aspects of tectonic activity and related mapping activities and had continuously been part of Antarctic geological research for 32 years. She conducted her Ph.D. work in Antarctica starting in 1983 in West Antarctica and the northern Antarctic Peninsula. She was also part of three joint expeditions with the USA and the British Antarctic Survey in West Antarctica and the Pensacola Mountains, and was one of the first women to work in the deep field. In 1990, she conducted her own research expeditions to Antarctica and focused on the Transantarctic Mountains and the Antarctic Peninsula. Grunow has 34 publications concerning Antarctic geological research. In 2003, Grunow became the Curator of the Polar Rock Repository, which houses Antarctic rock samples, and makes these available to researchers around the world.

name: Haast
info_origin: The locality is named in honour of Sir Julius von Haast, a noteworthy explorer and geologist who, with Ferdinand Hochstetter, systematically described New Zealand's landforms. [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Johann Franz Julius Von Haast](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1h1/haast-johann-franz-julius-von); 'A host of features bear the name of Sir Julius von Haast — the geologist, founder of the Canterbury Museum and first European explorer of parts of the Southern Alps — who led an expedition in 1863 through what became known as Haast Pass. Māori name of Haast: Awarua: lit. awa: river; rua: two. Mount Haast was named by James Mackay, who also named Mount Haast near the Maruia Plain. The glacier and range were named by James Hector, who had just missed von Haast at Wānaka. W.S. Green named the Haast Ridge. Haast Pass had been climbed by John Holland Baker in 1861 and had in all probability been crossed by Charles Cameron, a gold prospector, in 1863; but it was not until it was crossed by von Haast and his party in the same year that it received its name. Māori name for the pass: Tioripātea. In Poutini: The Ngāi Tahu History of the West Coast, Paul Madgwick translates this as The way ahead is clear.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Haggitt Pillar
info_origin: Edward Evans, navigator on the SY Morning under Captain William R Colbeck, RNR, first sighted the feature on 25 December 1902 during a relief expedition bringing supplies for the British National Antarctic Expedition (1901-04) under Robert Falcon Scott. Colbeck initially intended to name the larger Scott Island, Markham Island, for Sir Clements Markham who organised the British National Antarctic Expedition, but his diaries and reports were silent on the naming of the pillar. In private letters with Sir Clements Markham, Colbeck discussed and confirmed the names he intended to give to the two features, with Markham replying on 20 May 1903 ‘I am glad you have given Scott’s name to your island, and Haggitt is a very good name for the small one’. According to Edward Evans who discovered the feature, Colbeck named the feature for his older brother Haggitt Colbeck. The Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Volume 12 instead states that Colbeck for his mother Martha Haggitt, citing personal communications with Colbeck's son. The longstanding misspelling 'Haggit' may have arisen due to the name being misspelled in the set of Discovery Expedition charts published by the Royal Geographic Society 1908, with the misspelling then reproduced in nautical pilots and on hydrographic charts.
info_description: A column of rock 62m high standing 200m northwest of Scott Island, approximately 583km northeast of Cape Adare, the northeastern extremity of Victoria Land on the Antarctic continent.

For a brief period it was called Sandhurst.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Heretaunga Tamatea history: ‘Hakikino is an extremely important ancient and modern pā site and kainga. It was the site of battles between the earlier Rangitāne and invading Ngāti Ira/Ngai Tahu chief Te Aomatarahi who fought alongside his cousin, Taraia, as Ngāti Kahungunu moved into the Hawke’s Bay area. The pā belonged to Rangitāne chief Kōpare and was the home of his sister Hinengātiira. It was here that Rangitāne and Ngāti Ira/Ngai Tahu made a peace marriage between Hinengātiira and Rongomaipureora, son of Te Aomatarahi. It is also known as the birthplace of their descendant and paramount chief in his time, Tūmapuhiarangi.’

name: Half Moon Bay

Elvy has recorded: the name was given to commemorate a cannibal feast which took place when Rakau-tau-wheke captured Rakautara pa. The name means a special kind of oven, where the many dead were laid out in a circle, feet to the centre, and then cooked by the steam method. The ‘joints’ were done when steam issued from the uncovered mouths.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Hamilton
info_origin: ’Named by Colonel William Moule in 1864, after Captain John Fane Hamilton, the commander of HMS Esk, one of the naval ships in New Zealand during the Waikato War. Hamilton had been killed at Gate Pā that year. The settlement was founded on 24 August 1864 by Captain William Steele on the deserted Māori village of Kirikiriroa. The postmark of the town remained Kirikiriroa until about 1906. After the Frankton to Hamilton branch railway line opened on 20 October 1879, Hamilton was renamed Hamilton Junction and a new station called Hamilton. Hamilton Junction was renamed Frankton Junction in October 1884, and then changed to Frankton in 1955. Hamilton was known as Hamilton West from 1 October 1884 to 1 March 1899. Māori name: Kirikiriroa: lit. kirikiri: gravel; roa: long; specifically a long gravel bank that was used as a pathway across swamps.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
