info_origin: Journalist-historian James Cowan (1870-1943) described Haparangi as ‘One of the most picturesque objects…a perfect type of volcanic cone, with its steeply sloping ridged and hollowed sides and its crateral summit’. Cowan’s translation was ‘crying aloud, making vociferous lamentation’, although soldier and interpreter Gilbert Mair (1843-1923), a longtime resident of the Rotorua Lakes area, preferred ‘crying to heaven’. Mair’s informant an old chief, Manihera Nihotahi, explained that the full name of the hill was Haparangi a Waiarohi after Waiarohi a noted beauty and wife of Ruamano. In the absence of Ruamano, Whaita became the lover of Waiarohi and fled to save himself on the return of Ruamano. Waiarohi was distraught and for a time suicidal, wandering the area lamenting her loss and climbing Haparangi to ‘bewail her lost lover’. Whaita did ultimately return and take Waiarohi away to his people where she perished tragically. The trig point on top of Haparangi served as a boundary for the Maketu Licensing District in 1879 and the Rotorua school district gazetted in 1886. In 1900 surveyor Edward Phillips Turner (1864-1937), later Director of Forests, was taking theodolite observations from Haparangi when he witnessed one of the first thermal eruptions of the ‘Black water geyser’ near Rotomahana. In 1927 Surveyor-General William Thomas Neill (1864-1943) approached Elsdon Best (1856-1931) as a member of the Honorary Geographic Board to check on the reliability of names, including Haparangi, that were to be shown on the new topographical survey of Rotorua County. Sir Apirana Ngata (1874-1950) as Native minister in the United government elected in 1928 instituted a Māori land development programme. In 1933 in addition to farmland development at Horohoro, unemployed Māori planted Haparangi with 444000 trees including, 30000 eucalypts, 27000 Oregon pine, 110000 Ponderosa pines, 32000 Pinus laricio, 30000 Pinus radiata, 52000 Pinus murrayana and 23000 poplars. When completed by 1935 over 1000000 trees had been planted amounting to 883 acres (357 ha). Some of the trees were planted to form ‘A.N.T.’, the initials of Ngata.

info_origin: An original Māori name given to a small terraced pā strategically located on the 117m hill between where Mangaheia River flows into Ūawa River and Waimaunu Stream joins Ūawa River. Hāparangi occupied approximately 50m of ridgeline and archaeologists estimate that it had a population of approximately 14 people. This is one of numerous pā sites in the Tolaga Bay area dating back to the 14th and 15th centuries. The pā site included three terraces and two pits but lacked any ditch and bank defences. The pā site is of cultural significance to Te Aitanga-a-Hauiti. In 1999 it was registered as a wāhi tapu area with Gisborne District Council.

info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche May 2024: Objective ID: A6324681 {NZGB minutes 1941 12 June; [Ko te Kahiti o Niu Tireni, Issue 55, 20 December 1894, Page 570](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/KNT18941220.2.6); https://www.tetumupaeroa.co.nz/land/show/a10db39f-03ec-e111-8af5-00155d027505; [M. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3n5/ngata-apirana-turupa)}
info_origin: An original Māori name. The 1200 acres (486 ha) Harongaatekahu 1A and associated land blocks came before the Native Land Court in the mid-1890s. A gazette notice from 1910 listed [Sir] Āpirana Ngata (1874-1950), Ngāti Porou leader, scholar and MP, along with extended family amongst the owners of Harongaatekahu 1A. An application for partition of the block into Harongaatekahu A, B, C, D, and E was heard by the Native Land Court in a sitting at Tikitiki in 1925. In 1941 Ngata, a member of the Honorary Geographic Board assumed responsibility for checking all the Māori place names on the new 1:63360 provisional lithographs for Gisborne Land District, which amounted to over 200 names. Ngata identified the spelling Horonga-o-te-Kaahu on the provisional map as incorrect and altered it to Haronga-a-te-Kahu. Following the cartographic conventions of the time where hyphens in names were avoided because they could be mistaken for on the ground features, the Honorary Geographic Board instead approved Harongaatekahu. Macrons were not used to signal vowel lengths at this time. The New Zealand Geographic Board formally confirmed this name in 1948 when it was published in a list of names previously approved by the Honorary Geographic Board. Variant spellings have been retained by some of the original land blocks, for example, the 108 ha Haronga-A-Te-Kaahu A2B2.

name: Haskell Strait
info_ref: Feature named for Dr. Timothy G. Haskell. Over the past 30 years Tim Haskell has led 39 scientific expeditions totalling more than 900 days “on the ice”. Tim has over 100 scientific publications, approximately half of which are concerned with the oceans of Antarctica. His contributions have related not only to the fine-scale details of understanding the physical processes of how an ice-covered ocean works, but also in developing robust operational methods for experimentation on ice-ocean interaction. Further to this he has an international reputation and has conducted ground-breaking experiments in challenging environments including the marginal ice zone and winter polar oceanography.

name: Hataitai
info_origin: ’Like other Māori names in the vicinity, this may have been imported from Hawke’s Bay; but there is also a legend of two taniwha who lived in the lake that is now Wellington Harbour. One of them, Ngake, succeeded in forcing a passage through the heads to the sea; the other, Whātaitai, failed and perished. He then changed into a bird (te keo) and flew screaming to the top of Tangi-te-keo (Mount Victoria); on this account the name should be Whātaitai. Attempts at a literal translation of Hataitai have resulted in phrases such as Lapping of the tide, and Breath of the ocean. To the Māori inhabitants, Hataitai referred more to the Miramar Peninsula than to the slopes of Tangi-te-keo.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

The island was used for a variety of functions during early settlement. Thomas Cresswell, the first settler of Nelson to die was buried on Haulashore Island. The island was used for stock sales, despite there being no water supply. The New Zealand company later supposedly built three fortifications to guard Nelson, named on a map as 'Bastia', 'Calvi', and 'Aboukir', but this might have been on paper as there is little physical evidence of the forts existence. In 1906 a channel was dug between the Boulder Bank and Haulashore Island to allow shipping access to Nelson Harbour. Nelson Historical Society's Journal Vol.2 No.4 May 1970

name: Hauparu
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2023: Objective ID: A5238764 {[Cowan, James. 1917. The Pohutukawa. New Zealand's Christmas Trees. Lyttelton Times, 28 December, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/LT19171228.2.65); Cowan, James. 1982. The New Zealand Wars. New Zealand; Government Printer. Volume 2. [first published 1922]; Howorth, Russell. 1975. New formations of Late Pleistocene Tephras from the Okataina volcanic centre, New Zealand. New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics, 18: 683-712.; New Zealand Geographic Board. 1928. Correspondence; Stafford, Don. 1996. Landmarks of Te Arawa. New Zealand: Reed. Volume 2.; Te Arawa Lakes Settlement Act, 2006.}
info_origin: An original Māori name. The site of a number of kāinga and associated cultivations. Hauparu was also the name of a land block. Historian-journalist James Cowan (1870-1934) recounted that an ancient pōhutukawa tree called Turukuruku, stood on a clifftop overlooking the lake at Hauparu. The 'manner of flowering of these trees' served to 'predict to a certainty the character of the season so far as it affects their food plantations'. Hēni Te Kiri Karamu (Hēni Pore or Jane Foley and sometimes known as Jane Russell) (1840-1933), famous for her conduct at Pukehinahina or the Battle of Gate Pā in 1864 later aligned with the Crown against Pai Mārire. Travelling with her uncle, Matenga Te Ruru, and others she was witness to the capture at Hauparu of Hori Kingi Tupaea (?-1881) of Te Whānau-a-Tauwhao hapū of Ngāti te Rangi who initially fought with the Māori King, later declared himself neutral, then joined Pai Mārire. In 1864 Tupaea and other followers of Pai Mārire endeavoured to cross Arawa territory to reach safety on the east coast. Karamū recorded Tupaea's capture in some detail: 'One morning as we were closely scanning the coast of the southern side of the lake we saw an empty canoe drifting about near the middle of the lake. The alarm was given, and soon a score of canoes were racing for it. The canoe had evidently been cast loose a very little while before. We concluded correctly that Hori and his party had crossed the lake in the early dawn and were somewhere near the shore in the bush south of us. We paddled ashore to the nearer part of the south coast, and there came on the trail. Matenga's keen eyes noticed a place where the soil had been disturbed a very little while before; it was on the cliff-side between Hauparu and Ruato Bays, and a tuft of grass with earth clinging to the roots had been dislodged from the higher parts of the steep wall. We landed and climbed the cliff, and soon we came upon the foot-tracks of a party of people leading into the forest. We followed them up rapidly into the bush south of Ruato, and we soon came upon a number of Maoris with Hori Tupaea among them'. In 1975 geologists designated one of the erupted tephra layers from the Ōkataina volcanic centre, the 'Haupara Tephra Formation'. In 1928 the Honorary Geographic Board, while examining a group of Rotorua place names, considered Hauparu over Hau Paru as the correct spelling. Under the Te Arawa Lakes Settlement Act 2006, the associated name Hauparu Bay was among those 'recognised as 'official' place names' to acknowledge their significance to Te Arawa.

name: Hauraki Gulf
info_origin: 'Hauraki Plains: Waikato. The gulf that lies between the Coromandel Peninsula and the east coast; also the extensive plain to the south of the Firth of Thames. There was a Maori proverb about Hauraki that referred to the wind that rises moaning from the sea; Taimoana Turoa translates the name as The arid north wind. An alternative explanation is that Hauraki (or Haurangi) was a personal name. Also known as Tikapamoana. The name was not used by Maori for the plains, as the area was dominated in pre-European times by the vast Piako swamp. H.D.M. Hazard, inspector of (mining) surveys at Thames, gave the name Hauraki to disassociate the area in the public mind from the swamp and the dealings of the Piako Land Company. ‘As the land was bounded on the north by the Hauraki Gulf, I suggested to the authorities the name “Hauraki Plains” and this was adopted,’ Hazard later wrote. The chain of islands across the entrance to the gulf was known as Te Kupenga-a-Taramainuku, The fishing net of Taramainuku (an ancestor). The Watchman was one of the centre posts, the Hen and Chickens Islands the floats of the net. Another name for the islands was Nga-poitu-o-te-kupenga-a-Taramainuku, The floats of Taramainuku’s net.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Hāwera
info_origin: ’Originally Te Hāwera: lit. te: the; hā: breath; wera: burnt; The breath of fire. The name recalls an attack by a taua (war party) of Ngāti Okahu, led by the chief Ngā-ngaru-tukitukiwaka, against the Tītahi people at Whareroa (near Paekākāriki). Surprising their foes at night, the taua killed all the Tītahi and razed their village. The name may, however, have been brought from Hawaiki (the main settlement on the sacred island of Ra’iātea is Avera). Pākehā adopted the name in the 1860s, when Te Hawera Redoubt was constructed near the coast, and it was then given to the town district, which in 1882 became the Borough of Hawera.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Named after Captain E.E. Hedblom, USN, Medical Officer of Task Force 43 in the Ross Sea area, Operation Deep Freeze I, 1955-56.
info_description: A glacier flowing from Mount Creak on the southwest of Endeavour Massif for approximately 10km to Tripp Ice Tongue, in the Kirkwood Range area, Victoria Land. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MB09

name: Heddon Bush
info_origin: 'The district took its name from a large estate farmed by John Tennant. It may have been named by the surveyor J.T. Thomson in 1856 after Heddon in Northumberland, England.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E45 Edition 1  1984

name: Hedgehog Island
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Hedgehope
info_origin: 'Hedgehope, Mount: Named by J.T. Thomson during his 1857 survey because the hill reminded him of the second highest mountain in the Cheviot Hills in Northumberland, England. Maori name for the locality: Waioihi; and for the hill: Rakiahua.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E46 Edition 1 1983

name: Hedgehope Stream
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E46 Edition 1 1983

name: Hedgpeth Heights
info_origin: Mapped by U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and U.S. Navy air photos, 1960-63. Named by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Joel W. Hedgpeth, U.S. Antarctic Research Program (USARP) biologist at McMurdo Station, 1967-68, and Palmer Station, 1968-69.
info_description: Mainly snow-covered heights between Barnum Glacier and Bennistoun Glacier, 27.7km long northwest to southeast, with peaks rising to c.1360 at Mount Pechell. 4km southwest of Quam Heights across Douglas Gap, in the Anare Mountains of Victoria Land.

name: Hedin Nunatak
info_origin: First roughly mapped from air photos taken in January 1947 by US Navy Operation Highjump. Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) after Alan E. Hedin, aurora researcher at Byrd Station in 1962.
info_description: A conspicuous nunatak with a flat top capped with ice and steep bare rock walls, standing 16.2km west-northwest of the summit of Mount Murphy, on Walgreen Coast, Marie Byrd Land.

name: Hedin Peak
info_description: Peak at 2135m, above Margaret Glacier and southeast of Albert Peak on Barrier Range. Feature shown on: NZMS260 E39 Edition 1 1994 Limited Revision 1996

name: Hedley Glacier
info_ref: The positions of Dun Glacier and Hedley Glacier are swapped on p.131 of With Scott, the Silver Lining, compared to Fig. 93 Map of Taylor and Ferrar Glaciers, in Physiography of the McMurdo Sound Region.
info_origin: Named by the Western Journey Party, led by Taylor, of the BAE, 1910-13.
info_description: A small glacier from Mount Coates in the Kukri Hills, flowing into the Ferrar Glacier. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MF09
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Heel Basin
info_ref: Nancy Sound Chart©, Irwin, 1974; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836; Objective folder ID: fA452842
info_origin: Named in association with Heel Cove, which describes the 'heel' of Foot Arm.
info_description: An undersea basin in Heel Cove at the south end of Foot Arm, Hinenui / Nancy Sound.

name: Heel Cove
info_origin: 'The 'heel' of Foot Arm, q.v.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 B42

name: Heemskerck Glacier
info_origin: Named after Abel Tasman’s ship, the Heemskerck, by Charles Douglas during his reconnaissance survey in 1894-5. Spelling alteration from Heemskirk Glacier. The submitter has provided a significant number of reference sources to help verify the spelling of Heemskerck. However, the origin of Tasman’s ship’s name is not provided. Possibly the ship was named after the Dutch renaissance painter, Maerten van Heemskerck (1498-1574); or the Dutch explorer, Jacob van Heemskerck (1567-1607); or the Dutch painter, Egbert van Heemskerck (1610-1680); etc.
info_description: Alpine glacier flowing northerly from the main divide into Albert Glacier, located north of Mount Tasman

name: Heemskirk Glacier
info_origin: Replaced by Heemskerck Glacier 31/05/2007 58:1514
info_description: Alpine glacier flowing northerly from the main divide into Albert Glacier, located north of Mount Tasman

name: Heenans Corner
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E45 Edition 1  1984

name: Heenans Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E44 Edition 1 1985

name: Heeney Creek
info_origin: Altered to Heaney Creek
info_description: Flowing south-easterly from the north end of Rock and Pillar Range into the Taieri River. Feature shown on Feature shown on: NZMS260 H42 Edition 1 1987; NZTopo50 CD16-Middlemarch, source: GR 755 736 to confluence: GR 818 706.

name: Heftye Island
info_origin: Named by Bull when he visited this region in the Antarctic in January 1895, for Thomas Thomassen Heftye, a Norwegian banker, whose family bank Thos. Joh. Heftye & Søn was part owner of his ship, the Antarctic.
info_description: The southernmost of the Possession Islands. Feature shown on: Chart NZ 14907
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.
ant_pn_ref: Response to US-ACAN letter 19 July 1962 (File 17/357, Archives R3950093)

name: Heidelberg
info_origin: 'Thomas Agnew, who named the area Conyerstown, sold it to German settlers Joseph and Martin Metzger. The Metzgers drained and subdivided the land, renaming it Heidelberg Hills because, says Wendy McArthur, they both had connections with the city of Heidelberg.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E47 D47 Edition 1 1983

name: Heidemann Glacier
info_origin: Named after Richard P. Heidemann, USARP glaciologist at Roosevelt Island, 1962-63.
info_description: A glacier flowing west-northwest along the north of Mount Damm for approximately 13km, to join Lowery Glacier along the north of Mount Damm, at the north of Queen Elizabeth Range.

name: Hei Hei
info_origin: 'Lit. noise, disturbance, storm, dust, or (in modern usage) fowl.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 M35 Edition 1 1984

name: Heikaretu Stream
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 W17 Edition 1 1990 Reprinted 1995

name: Heilman Glacier
info_origin: Mapped by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) from tellurometer surveys and Navy air photos, 1960-62. Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for William L. Heilman, US Antarctic Research Program (USARP) glaciologist at Roosevelt Island, 1961-62.
info_description: A glacier in the northern part of Queen Elizabeth Range, flowing northwest from Mount Sandved for approximately 11km, into Nimrod Glacier.

name: Heil Valley
info_origin: Named by United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) (2007) after Joseph J. Heil III, supervisor of the communications center at McMurdo Station for 11 austral summers from 1993. He served 18 summers and two winters in support of the U.S. Antarctic Program 1987-2007.
info_description: An ice-free valley 2.5km long that indents the northern part of V-shaped Mount Littlepage, Head Mountains, Victoria Land. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MD06

name: Heimama Stream
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 P20 Edition 1 1984

name: Heimdall Glacier
info_origin: The name, given by NZ-APC, is one in a group derived from Norse mythology, Heimdall being the warden of Asgard. Suggested by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) following unofficial use by glaciological parties.
info_description: A small glacier flowing for approximately 6km from the end of Fenrir Glacier to just east of Siegfried Peak and Siegmund Peak on the south side of Wright Valley in the Asgard Range, Victoria Land. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-ME08

name: Heim Plateau
info_description: Plateau above Lyell Glacier, between Blair Peak and Malcolm Peak in the Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana.

name: Heindemann Glacier
info_origin: Named after Richard P. Heidemann, USARP glaciologist at Roosevelt Island, 1962-63.
info_description: A glacier flowing west-northwest along the north of Mount Damm for approximately 13km, to join Lowery Glacier along the north of Mount Damm, at the north of Queen Elizabeth Range.

name: Heipipi
info_origin: 'Lit. hei: neck ornament; pipi: cockle (Chione stutchburyi etc.).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 V18 Edition 1 1987 Reprinted 1994

name: Heipipi
info_ref: Min 3, 1972; File 22 2605 3, v/6, f/84-8, 107, 118, 159, 203, 270, 281, 287; Review of Trig names - Objective folder ID: fA521377
info_origin: Name submitted by the South Auckland Chief Surveyor, October 1971, after research in connection with the drawing of NZMS1 N82. The name Hepipi was shown on the vast majority of Survey Office records, but "Tainui" by L G Kelly, page 121, states that Heipipi, after Heipipi Pa, is considered the correct form of the name. Origin and meaning unknown. Instead of "Hepipi"
info_description: Trig. Station L (Geodetic Code A8KV), 2.5km south of Awamarino (locality). Block XIII Kawhia South Survey District.

name: Heipipi
info_description: Historic pā on hill northwest of Bay View (locality). Feature shown on Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BJ39 327300
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "an ancient pā of Whatumoana and Ngāti Awa people"

name: Heipipi
info_description: Historic pā in vicinity of Masterton. Feature shown on Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BP34 253630
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "a Rangitāne pā named after the east coast pā of that name"

name: Heipipi
info_description: 203m hill approximately 6.5km east-northeast, inland from Marokopa. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BF32 571606

name: Heipipi Pa Historic Reserve
info_description: An historic reserve adjacent to State Highway 2, approximately 2km southwest of the mouth of Esk River in Hawke Bay. Centred at NZTopo50-BJ39 327300.
rev_treaty_legislation: Section 68 and 75 Ahuriri Hapū Claims Settlement Act 2021

name: Heirtzler Fracture Zone
info_origin: An undersea fracture zone named for Dr. James R. Heirtzler, a geophysicist who was a pioneer in geomagnetics studies.
info_description: Ross Dependency. An undersea fracture zone.

name: Hekeao
info_origin: [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={bc5efcfb-3d52-e311-8212-005056970030})
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 K37 Edition 1 1985; NZTopo50-BY20 746469
info_note: Published on [346-02 edition 2 (2023) – Te Waipounamu](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-waipounamu-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "kāinga mahinga kai for gathering tuna"

name: Heke Peak
info_origin: Named in 1993 by the NZGB after Randal Heke, foreman of the construction unit which built the NZ Scott Base in 1957. He remained in a supervisory role for the management of the buildings for many years until his retirement. At the time of naming the NZGB had been informed that Heke was deceased, which was not the case.
info_description: A peak, 2175m, on the ridge that forms the south wall of Mitchell Glacier near the glacier head, in the Royal Society Range, Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MG09
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map Not shown on McMurdo Sound (NZ) map,; Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Ross Island (USA) map, ST 57-60/6&7.

name: Hekepo Pa
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 R16 Edition 1 1987 Reprinted 1994

name: Hekerangi Point
info_description: Point on western coast of the Mahia Peninsula south of Otunua Stream and north of Ahuriri Point.

name: Hekerua Bay
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 S11; NZTopo50-BA33 807276

name: Held Glacier
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Lieutenant George B. Held, Civil Engineer Corps (CEC), US Navy (USN), Public Works Officer at McMurdo Station during 1964.
info_description: A tributary glacier flowing east from Anderson Heights for approximately 7.5km to enter Shackleton Glacier just south of Epidote Peak, in the Queen Maud Mountains.

name: Helena Anchorage
info_origin: Name submitted by the Marine Department in November 1963. Named after George Brassell MBE, who owned the vessel "Miss Akaroa", used in the early stages of the Manapouri power project.
info_description: Cove immediately to the east of the mouth of Lyvia River, at the southern end of Deep Cove, Doubtful Sound / Patea.

name: Helena Bay

name: Helena Bay
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 Q06 Pt R06

name: Helena Falls
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 G47 Edition 2 1995

name: Helena Falls
info_origin: 'The 1888 expedition of Sutherland, Pillans, McKinnon and Muir named the falls, but the reason for the choice is unknown.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 C43 Edition 1 1997

name: Helena Peak
info_description: Peak at 2430m on Commissioner Range just west of Mount Pollux, and above Pickelhaube Glacier and Donald Glacier, Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana. Feature shown on: NZMS260 F38 Edition 1 1995

name: Helena Peak
info_origin: 'Fiordland National Park, Princess Mountains. Named after Princess Helena, the third of Queen Victoria’s daughters, by James McKerrow.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 C45 Edition 1 1997

name: Helen Col
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I36 Edition 1 1989

name: Helen Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 H40 Edition 1 1988 Reprinted 1994

name: Helen ES Clark Seamount
info_origin: Named for Helen Elizabeth Shearburn Clark (1936-2014) in recognition of her work on marine species in the area.
info_description: An undersea seamount in the Southern Ocean.

name: Helen Glacier
info_origin: 'First climbed by Cormack and Wilson after their ascent of Mt Tyndall in December 1933, but the name’s origin is uncertain.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Tributary to the Frances Glacier at the head of the Rangitata River

name: Helen Peaks
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E43

name: Helensbrook
info_origin: 'Named by John Hardy, an early settler.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 H45 Edition 1 1981

name: Helensburgh
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I44 J44 Edition 2 1987

name: Helensville
info_origin: ’Named by John McLeod, a settler from Nova Scotia, after his wife Helen (née Alexander), either directly or through the name of their house. The settlement on the Kaipara River was first known as Helensvilla or Helen’s Villa; the name first appeared as a heading in the letterbook of Judge Rogan in January 1865. Māori name: Awaroa: lit. awa: river or valley; roa: long.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 Q10 Edition 2 1995

name: Helfferich Glacier
info_origin: Mapped by United States Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and US Navy air photos, 1960-62. Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Merritt R. Helfferich, US Antarctic Research Program (USARP) worker in the field of ionospheric physics at South Pole Station, 1967-68.
info_description: A broad glacier approximately 17km long which drains the east slopes of Pomerantz Tableland south of Armstrong Platform, in the USARP Mountains.

name: Helicopter Hill
info_origin: This hill was the first hill sown in New Zealand using the 'Sling King' bucket under a helicopter.
info_description: Hill at 1256m west of Craigieburn Cutting.

name: Helicopter Mountains
info_origin: Named by United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) (2007) in recognition of the wide use of helicopters in supporting the U.S. Antarctic Program at McMurdo Sound and McMurdo Dry Valleys. Peaks in the mountains have been named after personnel in the helicopter group.
info_description: A series of rugged mountains west of Mount Mahony, Saint Johns Range, rising to 1705m at Mount James and including also from west to east Touchstone Crag, Mick Peak and Hott Peak. The mountains form the northwest end of Saint Johns Range, Victoria Land. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MD08

name: Helicopter Rapid
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 X15 Edition 1 1983

name: Helios Ridge
info_origin: Named in association with Mount Helios.
info_description: A ridge separating Clark Glacier to the north from Wright Valley to the south, extending some 8-9km east-northeast from Mount Helios to Lake Brownworth. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-ME09
info_note: Map sheet: Denton Glacier.

name: Helix Pass
info_origin: So named by New Zealand Geological and Survey Antarctic Expedition (NZGSAE), 1967-68, because ascent of the pass required an all night trip with much zigzagging and climbing. Thus named after the genus of land snail, Helix.
info_description: A small northwest-southeast pass 7.5km east-northeast of Mount Jamroga and just southwest of Curphey Peaks in the central Bowers Mountains. The pass permits passage from the area at the head of Carryer Glacier to areas in the southern part of Bowers Mountains.

name: Helland-Hansen Shoulder
info_origin: Discovered and named in December 1911 by Amundsen on his journey to the South Pole. Named for Professor B Helland-Hansen, of the University of Oslo, Norway. Not Mt H Hassen.
info_description: A portion of the steep slopes of the snow-covered western boundary of the Mohn Basin, resembling snow-covered ridges when viewed from the east, which extend for an indefinite extent in a north-south direction on the South Polar Plateau.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Hellene Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I42 Edition 1 1984 Limited Revision 1996

name: Hellfire Beach
info_origin: Replaced by Big Hellfire Beach 13/01/1996 1:18
info_description: Beach on East coast, Stewart Island, 1.6km north of Richards Point.  Anglem Survey District.

name: Hellfire Stream
info_origin: Name submitted in July 1970 by the Nelson Chief Surveyor after research in connection with the revision of NZMS1 S33 and S40. Name supplied by DD Cummings, National Park Investigation Committee. It was a well established name by forestry employees and early settlers. The name probably originated from the gorgy terrain and turbulent water during flood time.
info_description: Right bank tributary of Wairau River. It rises in Raglan Range and flows southwestwards joining Wairau River 3.8km south of Dip Flat. Blocks VII, X and XI Rotoiti Survey District.

name: Helliwell Hills
info_origin: Named by the US-ACAN for Robert A Halliwell of Stanford University, programme director for the study of very low frequency (VLF) radio noise phenomena.
info_description: Group of hills about 34km long from Dziura Nunatak in the north-northwest to Luhrsen Nunatak in the south-southeast, located between Morozumi Range to the east and Emlen Peaks to the west.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Hells Gate
info_ref: Refer Roald Amundsen (1912) The South Pole, Vol. II, London: John Murray, p.84, and plate photo opposite p.86
info_origin: Named by Amundsen in November 1911 on his way to the South Pole in connection with Devils Glacier.
info_description: A historic ice feature at the top of Devils Glacier in the Queen Maud Range. The glacier at this point had formed a remarkable long ridge about 6m high, with a fissure about 1.8m wide as a gateway.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Hells Gate
info_origin: Name submitted by BW Woodman, GL Leov and PMK Hope of the French Pass (Anaru), Rangitoto ki te Tonga/D'Urville Island area, following a request by the Lands and Survey Department for additional names in the area.
info_description: Rocks on the northeast tip of Cape Stephens, Rangitoto ki te Tonga/D'Urville Island. D'Urville Survey District.

name: Hells Gate
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 F41 Edition 1 1991 Limited Revision 1996

name: Hells Gate
info_origin: Discovered and explored by the Northern Party, led by Campbell, of the BAE, 1910-13, who were camped near here during the winter of 1912 and gave it this expressive name.
info_description: A small area of the confluent ice of the Nansen Sheet between Inexpressible Island and the Northern Foothills, and discharging into Evans Cove along the coast of Victoria Land.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Hells Gate
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 S26 Edition 2 1993; Reprinted 1994; NZTopo50-BP33 936603

name: Hells Gate
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 N30 Edition 1 1987; NZTopo50-BS25 923436

name: Hells Gate
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 N37

name: Hells Gate Corner
info_origin: Supplied by Mr Rutherford and verified by the Ministry of Works, Christchurch.
info_description: On Waiau Uwha River along Mouse Point Road.

name: Hells Gate Rapids
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 W16 Edition 1 1990 Reprinted 1994

name: Hells Gates
info_origin: Name submitted in September 1969 by the Canterbury Chief Surveyor after research in connection with the revision of NZMS1 S72. The name was supplied by Mr AA Urquhart of Erewhon Station. Descriptive name as three streams drop into this basin, all through waterfalls, seemingly impassable.
info_description: 1km from the riverbed in the headwaters area of Lawrence River, opposite Moses Creek. Block XI Ramsay Survey District.

name: Hells Gates
info_origin: Refer 'High Endeavour' by W. Vance page 178
info_description: A steep sided approach to a rock ledge south of Devils Staircase between the Cass and head of Waterfall Creek

name: Hells Gates
info_origin: One of a series of names sourced for a new edition of the map 'Stewart Island'. The names were either taken from existing maps, charts, or publications, or supplied by Roy Traill, or other Stewart Island/Rakiura locals and confirmed by Mr Traill. Descriptive name.
info_description: Passage between small rocks off the western tip of Pearl Island in North Arm, Port Pegasus / Pikihatiti, Stewart Island/Rakiura. South Cape Survey District.

name: Helman Glacier
info_origin: Mapped by United States Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and US Navy (USN) air photos, 1960-64. Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Terry N. Helman, USN, radioman at McMurdo Station, 1967.
info_description: A small tributary glacier in the Admiralty Mountains, flowing southward for 11km between Mount Gleaton and Taylor Peak into Tucker Glacier.

name: Helmet Hill
info_origin: 'Descriptively named by James McKerrow due to its shape.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 C45 Edition 1 1997; NZTopo50-CF07 683823

name: Helmet Peak
info_origin: Name submitted in September 1969 by the Canterbury Chief Surveyor after research in connection with the revision of NZMS1 S72. Originally submitted 18/12/1952 by CG Burrows. The peak is reputed to have been first climbed by Mr Burrows and a companion in December 1952, and the name was prompted by its shape and proximity to Sword Peak and Sceptre Peak.
info_description: Peak at 2215m in the headwaters area of Havelock River, west of Cloudy Peak Range and 1.1km west-southwest of Trireme Peak. Block II Tyndall Survey District.

name: Helmet Rock
info_origin: Named by the Northern Party, led by Campbell, of the BAE, 1910-13, in September 1912, because of its shape.
info_description: A rock in front of Cape Barrow, off the coast of Victoria Land.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Helm Glacier
info_origin: Named by the Northern Party of the NZGSAE, 1961-62, for Mr A S Helm, a former Secretary of the Ross Sea Committee.
info_description: A glacier about 20 miles long on the east side of the Queen Elizabeth Range, flowing into Lowery Glacier.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Helm Point
info_origin: Two Japanese whale-chasers, apparently familiar with the site, dropped anchor there for two nights early in February 1958. Named by the NZ Geological Survey Antarctic Expedition, 1957-58, for A S Helm, Secretary, Ross Sea Committee, who gave much assistance to the expedition. It is called Helm Point and not Cape Helm because it is inside a bay, not on the outer coast.
info_description: The cape at the south-eastern point of Honeycomb Ridge, on the west side of Moubray Bay. It consists of warm-brown grandiorite and supports a relatively luxuriant vegetation of lichens and mosses, along with nests of snow petrels and Wilson's Petrel.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Helms Bluff
info_origin: Named by United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) in 1963 for Lieutenant Commander Louis L Helms, U.S. Navy, officer in charge of the Squadron VX-6 wintering-over detachment at McMurdo Station, 1961.
info_description: A prominent bluff approximately 11.5km long forming part of the northwest wall of Eady Ice Piedmont on the southeast slopes of Mount Morning, and opposite Mason Spur 6km to the south.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Helo Cliffs
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-03-10/148; A1766043; A3136102
info_origin: The name derives from a nearby USCG HH-52A helicopter (CG 1404) which lost power and crashed while enroute from McMurdo Station to Cape Bird, Jan. 9, 1971. The four crew and passengers were not injured, but the helicopter was abandoned because of its location.
info_description: Prominent cliffs at c.3400m on the north rim of the summit caldera of Mount Erebus, Ross Island. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME14

name: Helvetia
info_origin: ’The Latin name for Switzerland. In 1886 three brothers Emil, Jacob and John Schlaepfer came from Tuefen, County Apenfell, Switzerland and bought land in what became known as Swiss Settlement. In 1908 there were more than 500 ostriches on John’s farm; one of the roads in the vicinity is called Ostrich Farm Road, while about 2 ha of the original property form Schlaepfer Park.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 Q12 R12 Edition 2 1995

name: Helwan Camp
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 T20 Edition 1994

info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 N32 Edition 1 1989

name: Hemo Gorge
info_origin: 'When the sisters of Ngatoroirangi climbed a hill between lakes Tarawera and Rotorua and began to descend, one of them slipped and called the place Te Hemo: lit. the place of fainting.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 U16 Edition 1 1982

name: Hemopo
info_origin: The name 'Gordon' was submitted by New Zealand Railways for the crossing loop at the western end of the then new Kaimai Tunnel. Hemopo, the Māori interpretation of Gordon, was preferred as it would be less likely to cause confusion by duplication. Hemopo is named after the works foreman who played a heroic part after a landslide that blocked the western end of Kaimai Tunnel.
info_description: Railway crossing loop at the western end of Kaimai Tunnel. Block X, Wairere Survey District.
info_note: Hemopo was chosen as a transliteration of Gordon, due to duplication.

name: Hemphill Creek

info_origin: To tie to ones chest. Named after a feat by warrior chief Rawiri Tamanui. Previously called Areoma. info_origin: 'Herekino Harbour: Lit. here: cord; to tie, or string tied up; kino: bad. Though it cannot be vouched for, there is a story that a captive who was reserved for a cannibal feast escaped because the ropes that bound him had been carelessly tied. Florence Keene, however, says the name is connected with the chief Tohe who was travelling south searching for his daughter. When he came to this place he noticed some bird snares that had been set by a man named Taunaha, and told him, ‘These snares are badly tied’ (here kino). In early days the harbour was named False Bay, probably because HMS Osprey was wrecked here when the navigator mistook the inlet for Hokianga.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: In October 1913 at the request of Alfred Bossons (1855-1944), Frederick W Wild (1872-1951) and 24 others, the Post Office agreed to designate an area adjacent to Te Aroha township, but in Piako County, as Herriesville and to provide the necessary post boxes. Almost concurrently, the Te Aroha Chamber of Commerce complained to the Government over delays in the construction of the private railway siding for the Te Aroha A&P showgrounds in what would become Herriesville, but which was opened shortly thereafter in January 1914. Alfred Bossons was one of the oldest settlers of Te Aroha while Frederick Wild was Te Aroha Borough's Town Clerk (1903-42). The new name of Herriesville was gazetted in April 1914. The newspapers noted that it was being named after the Minister of Railways, William Herries, whose electorate it was located in. Herries (1859-1923) was born in the UK and educated at Eton and Cambridge. From 1881 he farmed near Te Aroha and by 1891 had been elected to Piako County Council, serving 9 years before becoming MP for Bay of Plenty in 1896. Herries was Minster of Railways (1912-19) and Native Affairs (1912-21) in Massey's Reform Government. He was knighted in 1920. Herriesville became part of Te Aroha Borough in 1925.

The NZ Pilot 1st edition (1856) described 'another higher and larger islet' in relation to a 'small islet', Calliope Island. Following gradual changes in each edition, 'High Island' had its own entry in the 6th edition (1891) of the NZ Pilot. The name is shown on authoritative maps and charts from 1925. Two original Māori names are recorded for the feature. 'Motu Kawau' is recorded in a Crown Purchase Deed, and probably applies to the island. 'Ngaungara' was recorded specifically for the island by the Harbourmaster William Mackenzie Fraser in 1932.

info_origin: A Māori name seemingly adopted from Hihi Stream which flows into Mangōnui Harbour 2.5km to the southeast. Old pā sites on the adjacent hills pointing to lengthy and substantial Māori occupation included Te Hihi, a kāinga and wāhi tapu, which was midway between the stream and Hihi. In the 1850s the larger locality was referred to as Waiaua, although by the 1880s this name was restricted to the land between the Waiaua Stream and Waitetoki Stream. In 1844 before Lands Commissioner Colonel Edward Godfrey, Thomas Ryan claimed five purchases made from 1836-38 totalling 2280 acres (923 ha) for £128 in goods including oil, blankets, tobacco, soap and muskets for land stretching from Rangitoto Point to Waitetoki Stream. Ryan was awarded 1542 acres (624 ha) and Gilbert Mair senior (1799-1857) received a land credit for £1500 to resolve their dual claims to some of the land. Pana-kareo, known to the Europeans as Nopera (?-1856), disputed the rights of the chief to have sold the land. In the 1920-30s Hihi, which remained linked to Hihi Stream, was described as a ‘little settlement across the harbour from the township of Mangonui’. Subdivision of the peninsula commenced in the 1970s and Hihi appears to have been informally adopted from the stream. Pickmere (1905-73) labelled the adjacent beach as Hihi Beach in his Atlas of Northland’s East Coast Harbours first published in 1974. In 1985 the Surveyor-General noted that Hihi ‘a developing seaside resort’ was proposed as a new name to appear on topographical maps, but that a New Zealand Geographic Board decision was required for this to occur. Both Hihi and Hihi Beach were approved.

name: Hikurangi Marine Reserve
info_origin: The Canyon holds a special significance to the people of Ngāti Kuri. They say that “The ocean is known as Te Tai o Marokura or the sea of Marokura. Marokura was the atua (god) who with his magical patu (war club) carved the underwater trenches and canyons, which is why we have our whales here, off our shoreline. The underwater trenches also connect us back to where we first came from. It was Paikea the whale rider who come on the back of a whale from Hawaiki along the whale route. He arrived here along the east coast of the North Island. He had two sons. One of those sons was Tahu Potiki the ancestor of Ngāi Tahu. Tahu’s people travelled down the east coast of the North Island and settled in Kaikōura where we still are today. The Hikurangi trench is what connects us to where we came from some 700 years ago.” (Kaikōura Marine Strategy 2012 page 43). The name ‘Hikurangi Marine Reserve’ was proposed by Sir Mark Solomon to reference both the geographical proximity of Hikurangi Trough and to acknowledge the relationship of Ngāti Porou and Ngāi Tahu, for whom the trough is a physical symbol.
info_description: Encompasses the undersea feature name Kaikōura Canyon which is the terminus of the south-western end of Hikurangi Trough.
info_note: There is widespread duplication of the name Hikurangi. ‘Hikurangi’ is associated with the adjacent Hikurangi Trough and with one geographic feature named Hikurangi – the East Coast mountain. This mountain is not near the proposed marine reserve. It is associated with it through the cultural history link between Ngāti Porou and Ngāi Tahu (hapu Ngāti Kuri consider that the Hikurangi Trough connects them to their path of migration 700 years ago).

info_origin: An original Māori name, Hikuwai was located on an old Māori track leading north from Tolaga Bay and along the banks of Hikuwai River. Missionary Richard Taylor (1805-73) visited the area in 1839 and found a well settled valley with numerous pā. Formation of a road along the old track began in 1894 and in 1906 Mrs O'Shea opened an accommodation house at Hikuwai. Construction of a telegraph line from Tokomaru Bay to Hikuwai was completed in 1907. Individual farmers used Hikuwai as their address in the annual sheep returns from 1909. A meeting house named Maui was relocated from Tokomaru Bay to Hikuwai in 1912 to what William Sedgewick, Bishop of Waiapu, referred to as a ‘Maori settlement’. In the 1922 elections there was a Hikuwai polling station for Easten Māori where sitting MP Āpirana Ngata (1874-1950) received 21 of 25 votes cast. Administratively, Hikuwai was one of seven ridings of Waiapu County from about 1929. The 810 acres (328 ha) Hikuwai Station was vested in the Native Trustee in 1937.

name: Hillary Ridge
info_origin: Name submitted by AJ Carruthers to commemmorate the late Sir Edmund Hillary who made the first ascent of the ridge in February 1948, along with three other members of a climbing party. Alteration from 'South Ridge'. In Sir Edmund Hillary's account in the NZ Alpine Journal Volume XII No. 35, June 1948, he and his party were the first to ascend and document their climb on the way to the summit of Aoraki / Mount Cook. Hillary traced their climb from the Hooker Hut to the Gardiner Hut up the middle of the Noeline Glacier to Nazomi. On 5 February 1948 Sir Edmund Hillary and his party set foot on the South Ridge at 6.45am, seven hours later they reached the summit. [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Edmund Percival Hillary](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/6h1/hillary-edmund-percival)

name: Hinehopu Scenic Reserve
info_origin: 'Bay of Plenty, between lakes Rotoehu and Rotoiti. The famous fighting chief Hongi Hika and an army of 1200 musketarmed warriors arrived in a fleet of canoes at the coast from the Bay of Islands in 1823. They dragged their canoes overland from one lake to the other and defeated the Maori defenders of Mokoia Island on Lake Rotorua. Maori name: Te Ara-a-Hongi, lit. te: the; ara: pathway; a: of; Hongi. The locality had an earlier name, Ko-te whakamaru-ra-o-Hinehopu, which can be interpreted as The sunshade of Hinehopu. Several hundred years ago this chieftainess planted a matai tree to mark the place where she met her husband Pikiao. See Hinehopu.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Hokianga Harbour
info_origin: ’The full name is Te Hokianga-nui-a-Kupe: lit. te: the; hokianga: the circumstance of returning; a: of; Kupe (or Te Hokianga-nui-a-Kupe: The great/permanent returning/parting of Kupe). The name refers to the moment pioneer Polynesian explorer Kupe finally left this harbour for Hawaiki, his homeland. An expanded explanation is that these were the words of farewell to his son Tuputupuwhenua, who Kupe left behind as a protector in Hokianga: ‘Hei konei rā e te puna o te ao marama, ka hoki nei tēnei, e kore anō e hoki anga nui mai’; ‘Goodbye, spring of the world of light. This one now departs permanently; there will never again be another migratory return this way!’ From this story originates a poetic name for Hokianga, Te Puna o te Ao Mārama, which refers to the glow of light Kupe saw high above the shoreline as he approached the harbour. Another name is Hokianga-whakapau-karakia: Hokianga that exhausted all incantations. This refers to a battle of incantations between Kupe’s grandson Nukutawhiti (navigator of the waka Ngātokimatawhaorua), and Ruanui (navigator of the waka Mamari). The battle began when the two leaders clashed over the opening rites for their houses of learning (whare wānanga or whare atua) on opposite sides of the Hokianga Harbour. Each used up all their incantations without succeeding in besting the other. The harbour is also known by the name Hokianga-taniwha-rau: Hokianga of the hundred guardian spirits, referring to the many taniwha offspring of Āraiteuru and Niniwa (taniwha that arrived with Nukutawhiti.) ’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Horohoro
info_origin: 'Bay of Plenty, 19 km from Rotorua. According to Don Stafford in The History and Placenames of Rotorua: ‘The original name in full is Te Horohoroinga-o-nga-ringaringao- Kahumatamomoe — the place where Kahumatamomoe (a famous explorer and chief) cleansed his hands from tapu.’' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: 'A contraction of Te Horohoroinga-o-nga-ringaringa-o-Tia, lit. te: the; horohoroinga: washing; o: of; nga: the; ringaringa: hands; o: of; Tia. This was the place where Tia, the Arawa explorer who named Lake Taupo, washed his hands ceremoniously to remove tapu caused by handling a dead body. An alternative but similar explanation is that the name was Te Horohoronga-a-Tia, which refers to Tia’s swallowing of food to remove tapu. There is another tradition that it was Kahumatamomoe who had washed his hands in a stream in a tapu-removing ceremony, a story supported by Don Stafford in The History and Placenames of Rotorua.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Horomatangi Reef
info_ref: LINZ Hydrographic Chart NZ 232 Lake Taupo (Taupomoana) and LINZ Hydrographic Chart NZ 232 Lake Taupo (Taupomoana): Horomatangi Reef
info_origin: 'One of the atua brought by Ngatoroirangi, who came to Aotearoa on the Arawa canoe, was Horomatangi. When Ngatoro’s sisters arrived from Hawaiki, the far-sighted atua recognised them at a great distance. Wishing to help them he dived into the sea at Whakaari (White Island), travelled underground to Lake Taupo, blew a huge jet of water and pumice high into the air, then dived back to the lake bed. As he dived into the tunnel he created a whirlpool, a disturbance that continued to be active four times a day, 5 km from Motutaiko Island and the Horomatangi Reef. Metamorphosing into a taniwha, he expelled his breath, which burst out of the ground at Wairakei, causing the Karapiti blowbole to erupt. The vast column of steam rose high into the air and then pointed towards Maketu, where Ngatoro’s sisters were at that time. They interpreted the signal correctly and eventually reached their brother. Horomatangi, who took the new name of Ihumataotao, then became a black rock near Motutaiko Island.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Reef in Lake Taupō. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BG36 596008

name: Hough Saddle
info_origin: Named after William Hough. Born at or near Wakefield, Yorkshire, England in 1806. Hough arrived in Nelson on the 'Olympus' in October 1842, died in Nelson 29 January 1885. Hough is thought to have worked at Baigent's Mill, Wakefield in 1843. Hough drew Lot I, Pitfure by ballot and some historians believe he was responsible for changing the name of Pitfure to Wakefield, after his hometown. He served in the mission field as a Methodist catechist, living at Patea in South Taranaki as the first Pakeha resident 1844-8. Returned to Nelson, became a storekeeper, a member of the first Nelson Provincial Council 1853-7, and remained prominant in Methodist church affairs. First visited Aorere district in January 1855 in pursuit of gold. In December 1856 together with William Lightband Jnr, Hough discovered gold deposits at 'Light-band's Gully', Massacre Bay. Subsequently, although not reqarded by any of the bonus grant, Hough was given a 'similar memorial' by public subscription. In later years doubt was cast by Arthur Dudley Dobson on the validity of Hough's claim to discovered a useful pass through the Arthur Range into the head of Karamea River. However, Hough was vindicated by two items in the Nelson Mail, in June and September 1867, and the pass continues to bear his name. One of Hough's descendants was Edgar R. Neale, wartime Mayor and National M.P. for Nelson in the 1940's. (Information from Mrs Mary Troup, 1975)

info_origin: According to Department of Agriculture Farm Advisory officer AA Duncan the area took its name from Huia – Heteralocha acutirostris and Rua – two, a reference to ‘two prominent peaks which stood above the bush in the early days’ with the ridges leading to them being ‘favourite places for huias and the locality came to be known by Maoris as “huiarua’’’. In 1874 Land Purchase Commissioner John Alexander Wilson (1829-1909) negotiated an agreement to sell Huiarua estimated at 44000 acres (17806 ha) for £2200. Native Land Court Judge John Rogan (1823-99) defined the boundaries of the Huiarua Blocks in 1876. Resident Magistrate and Land Purchase Commissioner, Samuel Locke (1836-90) concluded the purchase of Huiarua now set at 39500 acres (15985 ha) for £1281 in 1878, however the Poverty Bay Herald in 1879 referred to the ‘much disputed [ownership of] Huiarua’. By 1881 Colonel Thomas William Porter (1843-1920) had secured Huiarua No. 1 of 7750 acres (3136 ha) for £1366 and it was gazetted as Crown Wasteland that same year and surveyed by John Roddick in 1891. In 1885 ownership of Huiarau No. 2 (3682 acres – 1490 ha) and No. 3 (19456 acres – 7874 ha) was decided by Native Land Court Judge Alexander MacKay (1833-1909) with Hoani Tunuiārangi (1843/4?- –1931) as assessor. The former was in favour of Wiremu Parata and others and the latter of Pinihama Wahapeha and Mrs Herewaka Poata. Huiarua No. 3 passed to James Nelson Williams (1837-1915), son of the early missionary Henry Williams, around 1885 and to his son Heathcote Beetham (Bill) Williams (1868-1961) in 1902. Huiarua No. 2 went to Robert Moate (1849-1904) about 1895 and was taken over by Bill Williams in 1908. In 1919 Williams offered 15500 acres (6273 ha), half being in tawa bush, of his 25000 acres (10117 ha) at Huiarua to the government as a discharged soldier settlement but the sale never went ahead. In 1948 Williams again offered Huiarua for WWII rehabilitation farms for £250000 but the government valuation was £150000 and again the offer lapsed. In 1976 and 1983 the New Zealand Forest Service purchased 4159 ha for afforestation purposes. In 2022 the Overseas Investment Commission approved the purchase of sheep and beef farms Huiarua and Matanui station totalling 7100 ha by Ingka Investments, parent company of Swedish furniture company IKEA for afforestation.

info_origin: An original Māori name that the Ministry for Culture and Heritage translated as ‘large cascade’. Variations exist. Edward Dollimore suggested ‘many waterfalls’ and Wises New Zealand Index for 1946 that it was named after a commonly played Māori game Huke - ‘causing a whistling sound’. Historian-journalist James Cowan (1870-1943) more circumspect in explaining the name of the local railway station, opted for ‘great cascade’. In 1873 Civil Commissioner, Henry Tacy Kemp (1818-1901), finalised the sale of 19500 acres (7891 ha) named Hukerenui for £1512. The deed was signed by Maihi Paraone Kawiti (1807-89) and others. Thereafter the land was proclaimed ‘as waste lands of the Crown’, under The Immigration and Public Works Act, 1874. Kauri gum digging licenses were auctioned in 1876 and 1881 but this activity had largely ceased by 1912. In 1886 Albert Elliot sought village homestead land in Hukerenui Survey District on behalf of applicants, who he described as North Islanders ‘sons of bush-farmers’ or ‘farm labourers’ and all ‘first class settlers’ without the means to pay cash for land. Under the Land Act, 1885 village settlements up to 5000 acres (2023 ha) could be set aside on public reserves and Crown land for sale with village sections up to one acre (0.4 ha) and small farm allotments of 50 acres (20 ha). Officials considered much of the area too swampy for settlement, and part was needed for future railway development. Never-the-less, entrepreneur and politician John Lundon (1828?-99), described as ‘devious, enterprising and manipulative’, and not without criticism, vigorously promoted Hukerenui and other village settlements. Conditions were challenging. After two years, in 1889 the original 82 farms had been consolidated into 45 properties on which 26 original and 19 others remained on 2154 acres (872 ha), of which 187 acres (76 ha) was in cultivations and carrying 217 cattle, 59 pigs and 43 horses. A post office opened in 1887 and the railway line reached Hukerenui around 1901-2.

name: Hut Point
info_origin: Discovered and prosaically named by the NAE, 1901-04, which built their Discovery hut at this point. It was used as an advanced base by the BAE, 1907-09, by the BAE, 1910-13, and by the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, 1914-17. Nearby is the present American Base, established in 1955-56 as Williams Air Operating Facility, but known shortly thereafter as McMurdo Station.
info_description: One of the most widely known points in the Ross Dependency. It is a small promontory lying approximately 1.9km northwest of Cape Armitage at the southern end of Hut Point Peninsula on Ross Island. The feature is protected under ASPA 158, and McMurdo Station lies opposite to the east. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MF13
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Hut Point Peninsula
info_origin: The British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, built its hut on Hut Point at the south end of the peninsula. Members of the British Antarctic Expedition (Terra Nova expedition, BrAE), 1910-13, wintering on Cape Evans, came to refer to this feature as Hut Point Peninsula. Not Cape Armitage Promontory or Winter Quarters Peninsula.
info_description: A long narrow peninsula extending for approximately 28km southward from the slopes of Mount Erebus on Ross Island, and forming the south-east shore of Erebus Bay. If a line is taken from between Turks Head to Tyree Head, the feature is approximately 15km wide at the base, coming down to a point at Cape Armitage at the south. It consists of a ridge surmounted by a number of cones and volcanic stumps which much consists of volcanic scoria and compacted ice. Of these Crater Hill is the largest. Stretching towards Mount Discovery, it curiously parallels the peninsulas of Minna Bluff and Brown Island. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MF13

Maori name of the Hutt River: Heretaunga, q.v., or Awa-kairangi: lit. awa: river; kairangi: something treasured, wandering, rainbow, a variety of greenstone, or a chief of high rank. Another name, possibly of a portion of the river, was Te Wai-o-Orutu, The river of Orutu, and has the appearance of an importation from Hawke's Bay. See also Napier. Maori name of Hutt Valley: Awakairangi: lit. River of food from the sky. The name refers to the plentiful bird life once found here.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Icebreaker Glacier
info_description: A large valley glacier draining to the Lady Newnes Ice Shelf from the country between Mt Murchison and Mt Monteagle. In its upper reaches there are extensive ice falls and cascades, and a few miles above them there is an easy pass to the Aviator Glacier. It is possible that the pass is a diffluence through which some ice from the Aviator Glacier passes to the Icebreaker Glacier. Close to its mouth this glacier is joined by the Benefactor Glacier. A shorter and narrower valley glacier separates the work of the complements of the US Navy and US coastguard ice-breakers in Antarctic exploration, in supporting scientists and in aiding other shipping.

name: Icefall Lookout
info_origin: In 1935/36 JD Pascoe accompanied by AF Pearson, HA McDowall, and HM Sweeney descended from the Garden of Eden and encamped on this bluff. In the map accompanying Pascoe's Unclimbed New Zealand (1993), the feature was named 'The Icefall Lookout'. Many names from the Garden of Eden expeditions were proposed to the Honorary Geographic Board in 1939, however this was not one of them. In 1963 Alwyn Chinn proposed Icefall Lookout following his preparation of the NZ Alpine Club 'Map of the Main Divide between Arthur's Pass and Mt Cook National Parks'. However the name was disallowed at the time. In September 1969 the name was proposed again by the Canterbury Chief Surveyor in preparation for the topographic map NZMS 1 S72, but the Board advised a preference for Icefall Outlook. This may have been based on a review of the 2nd edition of Pascoe's Unclimbed New Zealand (1951) where the name was incorrectly re-transcribed: 'we crossed Angel Col and located a bivouac site on an outcrop we named the Icefall Outlook.’. While the Board gazetted Icefall Outlook in 1971, Icefall Lookout was added to NZMS 1 S72 anyway. In 1992 following an investigation the Board corrected the name to 'Lookout', however the very next year, on the first edition of the new metric map NZMS 260 I35 1993, the name was changed to 'Outlook'. Across the NZMS 1, NZMS 260, and NZTopo50 series, the name has been incorrectly positioned at a spot height 1.5km to the southeast of the intended position.

name: Iliomama Rock
info_origin: Submission by the Auckland Maritime Society, supported by several maritime organisations, the the rock off the southern coast of Rangitoto Island be renamed to Iliomama Rock. Evidence was produced that the name of the vessel wrecked there was Iliomama. The vessel had been built in the first half of the 19th century, in Baltimore, and first bore the name Greyhound. She was captured privateering, by the Peruvian government, and renamed Galga, Spanish for Greyhound bitch. She was acquired by Hawaiian owners in 1949, and registered in Honolulu under the name Iliomama, Ilio meaning dog, and mama signifying swiftness. She went up on the rock bearing her name on 25 January 1950, and spent a year under repair after the accident. The Iliomama then traded around our coasts, until being totally wrecked off East Cape on 5 July 1853.

name: Invercargill
info_origin: 'At a banquet in Dunedin on 17 January 1856, Governor Sir Thomas Gore Browne announced that it had been decided to establish a town ‘at the Bluff and suggested that it should be called Invercargill in honour of Captain William Cargill, the superintendent of the province’. The prefix ‘inver’ is a term for an estuary, particularly a meeting of waters. When Southlanders decided to separate from Otago, and Captain Cargill was unpopular in the southern town, there was a suggestion that it should be renamed Clinton, the family name of the duke of Newcastle. But the original name was allowed to stand. Captain Cargill, in reply to the governor, returned the compliment by proposing that Bluff be called Campbelltown after the governor’s wife. Māori name: Waihōpai, in reference to the Waihōpai River, which flows through Invercargill.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for William Cargill](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1c4/cargill-william)

info_note: US belatedly noted this glacier was called "Curreen Glacier" on map following page 564 in NZ Journal of Geology and Geophysics, Vol. 17, No. 3, 1974. NZGB to inform US-ACAN on the status of this name. Located in the Convoy Range area. The US comments about Curreen Glacier were noted on 4/11/1999, however there are no NZ records on Curreen. Investigation will continue in LINZ’s library records and at Antarctica NZ. No maps or gazetteers show this feature as having been named. A copy of the NZ Journal of Geology and Geophysics, Vol 17, No 3, 1974, shows Curreen Glacier. Either ‘Irving’ or ‘Curreen’ are acceptable names to the Board as at 12/11/1999. An email from the US of 2/12/1999 advised that ACAN had approved Irving Glacier.

name: Island Bay
info_origin: 'Wellington, a suburb of Wellington. Named for the island in the bay, which in Maori is Motu-tapu-a-ranga or Motu-tapute- ranga (offi cially now Taputeranga Island). It goes back to the arrival of the Mataatua canoe, which spent some months here before ending its voyage at Whakatane. The canoe sailed through Cook Strait and headed for the island. As the men prepared to beach it, it glided on to a smooth ledge of rock and was left high and dry by the retreating waves. It was a good omen. The gods had brought it to a safe landing place. The island then received its name, with the meaning Sacred island of the casting ashore. The Maori name of the Island Bay valley is Paekawakawa, a name that defi es translation, but may have some connection with pae: ridge; kawakawa: channel or depression.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Iulia Mud Volcano
info_origin: Iulia is the family name of Julius Caesar, who during the 1st century developed urban centres throughout Italy, including Tergeste. The name ‘Iulia’ is also present in the Italian regional name, Friuli Venezia Giulia and the Iulian Alps. The name Vulcano di fango Iulia, which was already used in scientific papers, was accepted by the Italian Committee for Antarctic Names in 2007, and by SCAR in its English form for inclusion in its Gazetteer in 2008. The feature's name order and generic feature type were translated to English and adopted by SCUFN in 2012.
info_description: A mud volcano with a minimum depth of 634m, maximum depth of 710m, and dimension of 2500m x 1500m. Within New Zealand’s extended continental shelf, located approximately 40 kms south-east of Drygalski Ice Tongue, and 90 kms north-west of Franklin Island, in the West Ross Sea, Antarctica. Part of OGS Explora Mounds.

name: James Ross Island
info_ref: Objective ID: A3136102 As named by Henryk Bull in January 1895 after the discoverer of Victoria Land, when on the cruise of the Antarctic. Note, Bull tentatively applied the name Svend Foyn Island to Ross' Possession Island, noting he was unsure which it was, resulting in longstanding confusion and the two names being swapped in many records, including the Provisional Gazetteer of the Ross Dependency, 1958. He named this, the middle island James Ross Island. The nomenclature of the Possession Islands was resolved in official records in correspondence between the Board and US-ACAN in 1962, with the name James Ross Island not being reapplied, noting the much more significant Ross Island to the south later named by the British National Antarctic Expedition (BrNAE) (1901-04).

info_origin: This feature is situated at the entrance to Whangaroa Harbour. It is named after Admiral John Jellicoe, who was given a tour of the area during his term as Governor-General in the early 1920s. Admiral John Jellicoe was one of the most well known figures of the First World War. Indeed, Winston Churchill called him 'the only man on either side who could lose the war in an afternoon’. He was appointed commander of the British Grand Fleet in August 1914 and led it to a strategic victory in the conflict’s largest naval battle at Jutland. After becoming First Sea Lord during November 1916, Jellicoe consistently opposed the adoption of the convoy system for merchant shipping. This was to prove his undoing and he was sacked in late 1917 when the Allies continued to suffer tremendous losses to German U-Boats. Jellicoe first travelled to New Zealand in August 1919 while undertaking a review of the Empire’s naval defences. His visit aboard the Indefatigable-Class battlecruiser HMS New Zealand proved immensely popular with the public, who came out in their thousands to view the ship and its famous passenger. Jellicoe himself was so well received that he returned to serve as Governor-General the following year.

info_origin: In 1934, the members of the Auckland Harbour Board moved that the channels connecting the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana to the Pacific Ocean be given names. They asserted that the three approach passages should each honour a popular Governor-General, with five more titles being assigned to the channels inside the Gulf. This proposal underwent some modification. The hydrographer to the Admiralty asserted that allocating so many names to a relatively small area would hinder the direction of shipping. In response, the Harbour Board reduced the number of suggested titles down to three: Bledisloe, Craddock, and Jellicoe, with each applying to a greater expanse of water than had originally been envisaged. These changes proved acceptable to the Marine Department, which adopted the scheme during 1935. Admiral John Jellicoe was one of the most well known figures of the First World War. Indeed, Winston Churchill called him 'the only man on either side who could lose the war in an afternoon’. He was appointed commander of the British Grand Fleet in August 1914 and led it to a strategic victory in the conflict’s largest naval battle at Jutland. info_origin: This feature was named by the Survey Department to commemorate the visit of HMS New Zealand in August 1919. The New Zealand was an Indefatigable-Class battlecruiser whose service included the Battles of Heligoland Blight, Dogger Bank, and Jutland. For her voyage to the Dominion, she had on board one of the most well known figures of the First World War, Admiral John Jellicoe. Winston Churchill called Admiral John Jellicoe 'the only man on either side who could lose the war in an afternoon’. He was appointed commander of the British Grand Fleet in August 1914 and led it to a strategic victory in the conflict’s largest naval battle at Jutland. After becoming First Sea Lord during November 1916, Jellicoe consistently opposed the adoption of the convoy system for merchant shipping. This was to prove his undoing and he was sacked in late 1917 when the Allies continued to suffer tremendous losses to German U-Boats. The New Zealand’s 1919 visit proved a great success, with thousands of people flocking to welcome her. Jellicoe himself was so popular that he returned to serve as Governor-General the following year. To further commemorate the tour, the Survey Department tried to assign the name ‘Beatty Peak’, after another prominent British Admiral, to the hill next to Jellicoe Peak. However, unbeknown to them, that feature had previously been named Sturdee Peak. By a remarkable coincidence, Doveton Sturdee was himself a senior naval officer during the First World War. The Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand assigned the name Jellicoe Peak in 1930, and the New Zealand Geographic Board confirmed this decision in 1948.
info_description: Peak on the Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana between Sturdee Peak and Mount Low.  Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BX15 663692

name: Judgeford
info_origin: The suburb is named after Alfred Judge, one of the earliest European settlers in the area, and that the ford across the stream by his house became known as Judge’s ford and then Judgeford. By 1883 the settlement was commonly called Judgeford, and by 1890 at 24 households in Judgeford proper, the settlement had reached its population peak. Little changed in Judgeford until the Second World War when first the New Zealand Army and then the United States Marines used Judgeford as training bases. Since their departure the land has returned to farming and is fast becoming known for the small life-style farms that are being formed around the old settlement; 'After a Mr Judge, an early settler.' name: Kahukurī
info_origin: The name Kahukurī is from oral tradition and understood to be associated with the peacemaking between Kawerau and Te Taou in this area, and the metaphor of the spotted dogskin cloak worn only by prominent rangatira to refer to their enduring obligation to protect and lead their people remembered in the ancient whakatauki: 'Ko nga kuri purepure o Tamaki, e kore e ngaro i te po' - 'Those of Tamaki who would lead in peace or in war never rest’.; 'Lit. The dogskin cloak. The name originated in a truce between Te Kawerau-a-Maki and Te Taou, a Ngati Whatua hapu, at the start of the eighteenth century. A high point on the ridge is called Rangikoroiti, lit. The little finger that extends into the sky.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: In a paper read to the Hawke's Bay Philosophical Institute in 1882 Colenso discussed this name. The correct form seems to be Kahuraanake. The name is a most expressive and peculiar term, being a sentence, including a verb, and meaning (it is) only by it revealed, shown or made known, or the only, or pre-eminent revealer. See XXIV p153. name: Kahurānaki
info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Colenso, in a paper read to the Hawke's Bay philosophical Institute in 1882, discussed this name. The correct form seems to be Kahuraanake. The name is a most expressive and peculiar term, being a sentence, including a verb, and meaning (it is) only by it revealed, , shown or made known, or the only, or, pre-eminent revealer. See XXIV p153.; 'Hawke’s Bay, 13 km from Hastings. Kahura is probably a contraction of Kahurangi. If so, the name is Kahurangi-anaki, lit. kahurangi: prized or precious treasure, or wished for; a: of; naki: peak. When a Maori party set out from Wairoa for Ahuriri in their canoes, they used the peak as a landmark; if it was obscured by clouds it was ‘wished for’. Venerated by Ngati Kahungunu, Te Hapuku, the paramount chief in the nineteenth century, identified Kahuranaki as the tribal mountain. At one time the name was further abbreviated to Kauranaki by Pakeha. There is a trig in Te Mata Survey District of the same name.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Ko Kahuroa te Maunga, Ko Te Hoiere te Awa, Ko Ruapaka te Kainga, Ko Ngati Kuia te Iwi. The name means the long cloak and comes from the mist which shrouds it. name: Kahutara Point
info_origin: 'Captain James Cook’s journal for 11 October 1769 reads: ‘This point I have named Cape Table, on account of its shape and figure . . . it is of moderate height, makes in a sharpe Angle, and appears to be quite flat at Top.’ Former Maori name: Nukutaurua, lit. nuku: wide; taurua: a canoe used in seine-net fishing; possibly named after a canoe that brought immigrants from Hawaiki. The name may have derived from the Nukutaurua rock or reef at the entrance to Mangonui Harbour. The modern Maori name applied to the cape is Kahutara, q.v.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. | See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMENENDExQTE3NDEwMEQ1QUVCMTc)

name: Kaihu
info_origin: 'Kaihu River: An abbreviation of Kai-hu-a-Ihenga: lit.kai: to eat; hu: secretly; a: of; Ihenga. Ihenga, the widely travelled grandson of Tamatekapua, took a party of men to the west coast, where they obtained a supply of toheroa (Paphies ventricosum). While his companions were out of sight, Ihenga devoured all the remaining shellfish. When they returned and discovered their loss they named the place Kai-hu-a-Ihenga. Kaihu referred to the land on the south side of the Waingarara Stream; the land on the north side was Waihu. An earlier name was Opunake: lit. o: place of; Punake,which was changed officially to Kaihu when the telephone exchange opened in 1896. But the correct version appears to be either Opanake or Opanaki, two names that appear in Maori Land Court records.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Kai Iwi
info_origin: ’Kai Iwi is also the name of a group of lakes in Northland. Two distinct interpretations can be given, lit. kai: to eat; iwi: bone; or kai: number; iwi: tribe. The former meaning is a threatening expression implying that unless the enemy withdrew, their bones would be in evidence after a cannibal feast. Two other interpretations are current, one that a woman named Hinekoatu was killed and eaten and her bones thrown into the river; the other that a woman called Kiteiwi (See the bone) was seen eating a choice morsel of food. Asked what she was eating she replied, ‘The bone of a kōkako.’ This was considered a good joke, and the place was named Kai-iwi.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
