name: Kaikaitāhuna Stream
info_origin: Ko Tiheia te maunga. Ko Kaikaitahuna me Te wai mimi a Pekehaua nga awa. Ko Tarimano te marae. Ko Tawakeheimoa te tupuna whare. Ko Te Aongahoro te tupuna kuia. Ko Rangiwewehi te iwi. Kaikaitāhuna Stream is situated within the Hamurana Springs Reserve, on an area of land situated near the eastern boundary of the Ngāti Rangiwewehi rohe at a place traditionally known as Whakarua. This area of land was widely populated by hapu of Ngāti Rangiwewehi and was where Tawakeheimoa, the father of Rangiwewehi, built his first pa on the summit at Pukehinahina. Kaikaitāhuna is the original and correct name of the stream supplied by various springs in the area now generally referred to as Hamurana. It was also the general term for the fairly extensive settlements in the immediate area occupied mainly by hapu of Ngāti Rangiwewehi – Ngāti Whakakeu, Ngāti Te Purei, Ngāti Te Okotahi, Ngāti Kereru and others. Te Puna a Hangarua is a major spring supplying Kaikaitāhuna Stream. This spring was named after the Ngāti Rangiwewehi chieftainess Hangarua and was where she raised her pet taniwha, Hinerua, a benign female taniwha. As tradition goes, Hinerua roamed and protected the waterways in the area, however, after Hangarua died, Hinerua disappeared and was never seen again. Ngāti Rangiwewehi holds strong spiritual and cultural regard for this area. Lands, rivers and fresh water springs are taonga as are the Taniwha, Pekehaua and Hinerua. These relationships are traditional ones -“Take Tupuna”- based upon concepts of best use practices and management of all natural resources according to Ngāti Rangiwewehi tikanga. To Ngāti Rangiwewehi, Kaikaitāhuna Stream is a place of special significance. It was the original home of Tawakeheimoa, the father of Rangiwewehi, and was a great place for growing and gathering food. Wildlife and birds were prolific in the area while the procuring of freshwater delicacies like the koura, toitoi, inanga, koaro and the kokopu were easy. In the late 1800s, tourists would pay our tupuna to transport them up the stream to the Puna a Hangarua where they would listen to the stories of Hinerua while watching the coins that they tossed into the puna move to and fro as they descended into the depths of the Puna a Hangarua. Therefore this place was a vital area for the spiritual, physical and economical sustenance of Ngāti Rangiwewehi.
info_description: A stream flowing for approximately 2.6km, generally south and then east through Hamurana Springs into Lake Rotorua/Te Rotorua nui ā Kahumatamomoe at Kaikaitāhuna Bay, approximately 10km north of Rotorua. info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: 'Kaikaka (also known as Kaitaka) is the point between Pukewhau Creek to the North and Te Haukono Creek to the South, jutting into the Waiuku River. Kaikaka was a large area of interconnected urupa on the peninsula. Many illustrious Ngati Tamaoho tupuna are buried here. Other parts of the headland were used as valuable fishing grounds and temporary living sites during the fishing season. There is evidence that this continued well into the 20th Century as access to traditional fishing areas became increasingly restricted. There is also evidence of cultivation on the non-urupa parts of the headland.'. Information Source - B Leonard, Ngati Tamaoho Sites of Significance, 90. D Armstrong, Ngati Tamaoho Environmental History DRAFT, 456-461.

name: Kaikōura
info_origin: ’A contraction of Te Ahi-kai-kōura-a-Tamakiteraki: lit. te: the; ahi: fire; kai: food, or to eat; kōura: crayfish; a: of; Tamakiteraki; The fire at which crayfish were cooked for Tamakiteraki. Captain James Cook named the Seaward Kaikōura Range the Snowey Mountains, and the peninsula the Lookers-On, on 15 February 1770. Fifty-seven Māori in four double canoes came out to the Endeavour ‘and would not be prevailed upon to put alongside by all that Tupia could say to them’. These were obviously the ‘Lookers-On’.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

feat_note: Parts of Kaimai Mamaku Conservation Park subject to the Conservation Act 1987 are revoked under sections 71, 72, 73, 75, 76, 77 and 78 of Ngāti Hinerangi Claims Settlement Act 2021 (‘Settlement Act 2021’). The official Crown protected area name no longer applies to those parts, in accordance with section 54 of the Settlement Act 2025. Much of the revoked land has been declared, classified and named as historic, scenic or recreation reserves through the settlement Acts, but these reserves are not Crown protected areas. name: Kaimatira
info_origin: Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui history: 'Kaimatira was a papakāinga and a fortified pā whereby waka were fashioned and a launching (test) site for waka used in the pounamu trade with Ngai Tahu. Waka were tossed over the cliff into the river. It was said, if the waka remained in one piece, it would be deemed seaworthy, and work would continue. If waka did not survive, the remains were utilised for hāngī pits or for firewood. Kaimatira also housed a cave where the Mōkai [pet], Tūtaeporoporo lived. He would emerge from his cave and attack unsuspecting travellers as they rowed past the entrance to his cave. Ngā Paerangi tupuna, Rangitauira, from Aramoho was buried at Kaimatira. Today, State Highway 4 runs right through the centre of this site. What remains can be seen above the corner of Kaimatira Road and SH4. This site was not reserved in the 1848 Purchase Deed.'
info_description: A historic site on the left bank of Whanganui River, near the junction of State Highway 4 and Kaimatira Road, approximately 5km northeast of Whanganui city centre. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BL32 788815.

info_origin: Discovered in January 1902 by the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, but not named until the Japanese Antarctic Expedition under Nobu Shirase landed there in January 1912. info_description: A former bay, once described as '1 mile wide and 8 miles long indenting the Ross Ice Shelf about 30 miles northeast of the Bay of Whales'. In 1987 a huge icebeg [Iceberg B-9] calved from the Ross Ice Shelf, taking anything left of the original Kainan Bay with it. The original position is approx 23km from the front of Ross Ice Shelf as of 2019.

name: Kaingaroa Forest
info_origin: Associated with Kaingaroa Forest (locality). 'Bay of Plenty/Waikato, Rotorua and Taupo. lit. kainga: place where food has been cooked and eaten: roa: long. The female tohunga Haungaroa, who was exploring the plain, took so long over her meal that she was teased by her companions, who called the place Te Kaingaroa-a-Haungaroa: The long meal of Haungaroa. The priestess was not amused and turned the women who made the remark into cabbage trees, which were supposed to retreat steadily before travellers on the plain. There is another explanation, that Kaingaroa means Long-enduring home. When the territory was purchased in 1880 the tangata whenua referred to it as Kaingapoto — reportedly The quickly vanishing money.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: This locality is named in association with the nearby Kaipara Harbour with ‘flats’ describing the topography. John Grant Johnson (1824-73), surveyor and licensed interpreter, as Sub-commissioner for the Purchase of Native Land, began negotiations for the acquisition of what he termed Kaipara Flats in 1854. These were completed by mid-year for 32000 acres (12950 ha) for £1200 and became known as the Ahuroa-Kourawhero Crown purchase. Johnston noted that Ahuroa, Kourawhero and Kaipara Flats ‘all being contiguous’, he had purchased them in a single transaction on ‘one deed’. Kourawhero was an alternative name for the larger area. In 1854 Johnson described Kaipara Flats as ‘an amphitheater, surrounded by hills, containing several thousand acres of the richest flats, interspersed with belts of the most valuable timber’. Johnson characterised the area as ‘much sought after by intending settlers’. In 1857 the central government transferred 5000 acres (2023 ha) of Kaipara Flats to the Auckland Provincial Government with 4900 acres (1983 ha) being immediately thrown open for selection. A postmaster was appointed in 1871 and a school opened in 1874. The extension of the railway to Kaipara Flats was first mooted in 1890 but not actually competed until 1905.

info_origin: ’Lit. kai: to eat; para: flounder. The harbour was named False Bay by Captain James Cook. Kaipara Heads is usually known as Pouto. The Māori name was Kaipara Moana. According to Te Arawa tradition, when Kahumatamomoe and his nephew Īhenga visited the area they were supplied by the wife of Taramainuku with food, amongst which was a basket of para, which Kahu had never eaten before. ‘Ho!’ said Kahu, ‘this is the food for your ancestor. It is the raho [testicle] of your ancestor Tangaroa [the sea god]. This is the first time I have tasted para. You must call this place Kaipara.’ Para may have been used as a generic name for all freshwater fish, as apart from flounder the Kaipara Harbour also abounded in mullet.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: An original Māori name. A pā and village site occupied the wooded heights southwest of the mouth of Urenui River. Ngāti Mutunga chief Whakapuke and others escaped to Kaipikari pā after they were attacked at Pohukura pā by a Waikato war party in the 1830s. During the Taranaki Wars of the 1860s the pā was the site of clashes between Māori forces supporting and opposing the colonial government in 1864 and 1865. The site was well defended with rifle pits, a row of palisades and more rifle pits in a crescent shape some 90 metres from the pā which was on a rounded knoll. The pā was burnt in 1865, destroying the whares and a considerable area of the surrounding bush. The 1874 Māori census recorded six men, five women and one child residing at Kaipikari. The Armed Constabulary had a 'bush party' of four men stationed there in 1875. In 1939 Nelson Clay, the Chief Surveyor for Taranaki, sought clarification over the spelling from the Honorary Geographic Board which considered that the 'weight of evidence' favoured Kaipikari.

name: Kaitāia
info_origin: ’Possibly a contraction of Kaitataia: lit. kai: food; tataia: arranged or set in order. The great traveller Tamatea Urehaea, the son of Rongokako, brought his wife Iwipūpū here to feast on the plentiful kererū (wood pigeons). He built a pā called Tinotinoi at Orongotea, and when Kahungunu was born Tamatea buried the baby’s pito (umbilical cord) with three whatukura (sacred pebbles) as an iho-whenua (a link with the land). The local Māori were furious with Tamatea for this and the depredations of his followers, who had taken such toll of the kererū that the name of the district was changed from Orongotea: lit. place of bright fame, to Kaitāia: lit. food in abundance — perhaps in memory of what they had lost.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Kaitangata
info_origin: 'Otago, 13 km from Balclutha. Lit. kai: to eat; tangata: man. The earliest oral account is that the locality was named for Kaitakata (Kaitangata) of the Araiteuru canoe, who found a valued type of clay, used in painted designs, near the lake. In later years a battle was fought here between two tribes over eeling rights, the chief Mokomoko being killed and eaten by the victors. Kaitangata is also the mythological son of the demigod Rupe, whose spreading blood explains the redness of the sky at sunset, but not its connection with this remote part of the South Island. The name may also refer to the disappearance of a child because of a taniwha at the lake. An 1847 map records the place as Coal Point, indicating that the first mine in the district was located here. Frederick Tuckett’s map of 1844 shows the lake as Kaitangata. It seems fairly certain that an earlier name, possibly of Waitaha origin, was Kaitiria.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Kaitaratahi
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA468340; A4635550; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche August 2024: Objective ID: A6466308 {Dollimore, E. 1952. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand, Wises.; Dollimore, E. 1963. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; R22352589 Waipoa (Kaitaratahi) Administration.; R21031370 Townships – Kaiteratahi. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; R10560294 Gisborne Borough Council’s Private Sidings Kaiteratahi. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; [Jeffrey Sissons. 'Best, Elsdon', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1993. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2b20/best-elsdon)}
info_origin: An original Māori name. In written form Kaiteratahi and Kaitaratahi were both used from the 1870s, the former being linked to road formation and most notably with Thomas Bell’s hotel at what was sometimes interchangeably referred to as Scotts Crossing. In 1902 when the Gisborne – Karaka Railway line was opened for traffic, Arthur Kempthorne (1842-1910) wrote to the Poverty Bay Herald to insist that Kaitaratahi was the correct spelling basing this on his adequate understanding of te reo Māori, having taught at the Native School at Waerengaahika and being a resident of the locality since 1865. He claimed that publican Thomas Bell (1839-1929) had engrained the misspelling through painting it on his hotel. Bell and his family relocated to the remote Kermadec Islands in 1878. Cook County in correspondence in 1902-03 with Gisborne Borough over a ballast reserve consistently used Kaitaratahi; the Borough and Railways, Kaiteratahi. A survey plan for a township of Kaitaratahi was presented in 1910 for approval under the Land Act, 1908. The Chief Surveyor noted that ‘the locality being known by the name given to the township’. An amended plan was submitted later in 1910 but with the spelling altered without comment to Kaiteratahi. Railways asked the Honorary Geographic Board to consider the station name and in 1927 it was confirmed as Kaitaratahi. Ethnologist Elsdon Best (1856-1931), a member of the Board, familiar with the area and a fluent speaker of Māori affirmed that ‘he had always heard the name as Kaitaratahi’. Notwithstanding the Board’s decision made official under the New Zealand Geographic Board Act, 1946, Edward Dollimore (1904-73), who compiled The New Zealand Guide, continued to list Kaitaratahi and Kaiteratahi as alternative names in the 1950s before settling on Kaitaratahi by 1962.

info_origin: Harry Ell, the Postmaster General on opening the new Porirua Post Office in 1912, observed that 'Kupe, the Polynesian navigator and first known discoverer of New Zealand, while circumnavigating the North Island visited the harbour, with his canoe "Mata-hou-roa" [Mātāwhaorua] and landed at Waitawa inside the entrance on the south side'. In 1908 the parliamentary Nomenclature Committee scrutinised Māori railway station and post office names for accuracy. Ell chaired the committee and 'brought up' its report in the House of Representatives. Other authorities place Kupe's landing at Green Point, where he left behind his stone anchor, Maungaroa. name: Kaiteretere
info_origin: Te Here ā Nuku Trust kōrero: 'Both iwi and cultural authorities highlight Kaiteretere as the correct traditional spelling and pronunciation. According to Pākehā sources collected in the early stages of the settlement of the region, the translation of the name comes from the following elements: kai: To eat or food, teretere: To be fast, swift, or to flow, or a company of travellers. Mr WHS Roberts, in his publication Maori Nomenclature VII The Nelson District provides context for the correct spelling and application for the name; "A pretty little bay is Kaiteretere (the food drifted, or to eat a company of travellers), not Kaiteriteri, as it is often spelt, near which is the town of Brighton, 24 miles from Nelson across Blind Bay. It was at Kaiteretere that the first surveyors under Mr Frederick Tuckett, by order of Captain Arthur Wakefield, R.N., in October, 1841, commenced to lay off a town site to be called Nelson". Additional references to the use of the name were also given during testimony to the Spain Commission in 1844. Te Iti confirmed that he had visited the Arrow at Kaiteretere on that day, accepted gifts from Wakefield, and agreed to let Europeans settle, “… but not to take all the land.” Te Iti said he did not understand the idea of reserves for Maori, and that he had in fact pointed out to Wakefield that the land he could occupy was to extend only from “Kaiteretere outwards to the ocean.” Old Tasman Bay, written by J.D. Peart, is a key source on early Tasman District life and draws extensively on Māori authorities noted in the foreword and introduction. His compilation of Māori names is extremely valuable. For instance, he uses ‘Kaiteretere’, which he describes as ‘a bay just north of Anarewa’. He explains the name as ‘As Spelt, means to eat hurriedly, Real interpretation obscure’. While the exact origin of the name remains somewhat unclear, iwi in Te Tauihu agree that the place commonly known as Kaiteriteri is more accurately referred to in te reo Māori as Kaiteretere.'

name: Kaiteriteri
info_origin: NZGB archives record: This spelling has been used on government records since 1859. Meaning 'hurried meal'. Some Māori were having a meal on the beach of an island in the bay when they heard stones rolling through the bush behind them. Fearing an attack they left in their canoes carrying their food with them and on reaching Kaiteriteri Beach returned hurriedly to their pā, eating their food as they went'. Taken from AW Reed's 'The Story of New Zealand Place Names'. The compiler of the book refers to Kaiteretere. Different spellings were: Kaiteratera by Stephens, a government surveyor in 1842, and Kaitiriteri, by Heaphy a government surveyor in 1847.; ’This spelling has been used on government records since 1859. Properly, Kaiteretere: lit. kai: to eat; teretere: to run or be spread about. The name has been rendered To eat hurriedly. A group of men were having a meal on one of the islands near the beach when they heard stones crashing through the bush. Fearing a surprise attack, they ran to their canoes, taking their food with them. On reaching the shore they returned hurriedly to their pā, eating their food as they went.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Kaiteriteri Beach
info_origin: AW Reed in 'The Story of New Zealand Place Names' records that the name for the locality was Kaiteretere, meaning hurried meal. He wrote that some Māori were having a meal on the beach of an island in the bay when they heard stones rolling down through the bush behind them. Fearing an attack, they left in their canoes carrying their food with them and on reaching Kaiteretere Beach, returned hurriedly to their pa, eating the food as they went. Kaiteriteri adopted as the form used officially over long period, since 1859.

info_origin: 'The name could be a contraction of Puhikaiti, which probably means Top of the tree. name: Kaiwharawhara
info_origin: Kai meaning food, and wharawhara is the Māori name for the edible fruit of Astelia Banksii. Although the correct name for this locality was known, several spellings and contractions were in common use, and even sanctioned by the Honorary Board in the 1930s, the most usual being Kaiwarra, or Kaiwara. Instead of Kaiwhara, Kaiwarra and Kaiwarawara. Originally official by 1939 Hon p. 12; 'In pre-Pakeha days it was Kaiwharawhara. During the 1840s Jerningham Wakefield commented that the stream was called after the ‘wharrawharra’. The name was corrupted to Kaiwarra and remained in this form for many years, until it reverted to Kaiwharawhara.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Locality on Wellington Harbour (Port Nicholson), 600m northeast of the Picton Ferry Terminal and 2.5km southwest of Ngauranga. Belmont Survey District.

name: Kakara Taramea
info_origin: Kakara Taramea is the correct name for the Karamea River, which rises in the Matiri Range of Kā Tiritiri-o-te-moana (the Southern Alps). It meanders north before flowing in a westerly direction into Te Tai-o-Rehua (the Tasman Sea), in the Buller District of Te Tai Poutini (the West Coast). Kakara Taramea means “the sweet-smelling taramea”. Kakara means sweet-smelling, and taramea is speargrass (Aciphylla squarrosa, Aciphylla colensoi), which was highly regarded as a source of perfume. Taramea once grew extensively on the flats on both sides of the river, near its entrance to the sea. The leaves of the taramea were gathered and heated to extract the resin, which was mixed with bird fat to create fragrant sachets of oil to be used as a fragrance. [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={92709345-3e52-e311-8212-005056970030})

name: Kakepuku
info_origin: 'Kakepuku was an old settlement near the foot of the mountain. Place Names of the Ancestors attributes its origin to the travels of Kahupeka, an ancestor of Tainui whose husband Uenga had just died, and left the name Te Kakepuku-o-Kahu: lit. The hill over which Kahu climbed. There are other versions, however. One is Kakipuku-o-Kahurere: lit. kaki: neck; puku: swelling; o: of; Kahurere; i.e. Swollen neck of Kahurere. The name was given hundreds of years ago by Rakataura, partly in memory of his wife, Kahurere, and partly because of the shape of the hill. Another version is that the full name is Kakipuku te aroaro-o-Kahurere: lit. kaki: neck; puku: swollen; te: the; aroaro: front; o: of; Kahurere.' name: Kanakanaia
info_ref: Objective ID: A4635550; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche April 2024: Objective ID: A6258696 {Land Purchases in Poverty Bay, 1877. AJHR G5.; [No Heading 1908. Poverty Bay Herald, 30 January, Page 4](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBH19080130.2.14); R1342052 Kanakanaia Settlement. Archives New Zealand, Auckland.; R21489302 Lands for Settlement Kanakanaia Settlement. Archives New Zealand, Auckland.; R25826030 Kanakanaia Settlement. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; [J. A. B. Crawford. 'Porter, Thomas William', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1993. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2p26/porter-thomas-william)}
info_origin: Government Land Purchase agents acquired Kanakanaia from 1875 to 1877 but almost immediately discovered there were overlapping ownership claims to the land. It was initially grazed as a 50000 acres (20234 ha) estate, eventually coming into the possession of the City of Glasgow Assets Company. In 1907 Land Purchase Commissioners bought Waingaromai No 3A Block, thought to be 5235 acres (2119 ha) from the Company for £44497/10/- or £8/10 per acre (it was actually 2138 ha). This block was subdivided into seven farms by surveyor GH Davis and opened for selection as part of the Liberal government’s closer land settlement policy in 1908, although there were only 17 applications for the leasehold sections. At the time of the purchase, Waingaromai was in wide use as the name for the locality, but the land had been known as the Kanae Kanae Estate. However, the Under Secretary of Lands, William Kensington (1845-1922), established that Kanae Kanae was not the correct spelling and that the land was balloted as the Kanakanaia Settlement. Kensington’s informant was soldier and land purchase officer Colonel Thomas William Porter (1843-1920), a te reo Māori speaker and long term Gisborne resident, who ‘explained that the correct spelling depended on, the real meaning, and on enquiry he found from the Natives that the name was taken from a "rolling eye". A sentry was posted on an eminence and instructed that he should not look only straight in any one direction to try and discover the approach of the enemy, but that he should keep a rolling eye, that is, turn his eyes about in the sockets, so that he would be more keenly watchful of an approach from any quarter,’ thus Kanakanaia was the correct spelling. In 1926 the Gisborne Chamber of Commerce regarded the settlement as a success in that the 52136 acres (21099 ha) Kanakanaia estate with 200 cattle and 700 sheep had been replaced by seven farmers with 940 cattle and 10650 sheep.

In 1927-28 the dam was repurposed for electricity generation. The present dam was built in the 1970's. Associated with the creek, reservoir, and hill of the same name. Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Waewae advise that Kapitia is their tupuna (an ancestor).

name: Kapukapuariki Rocks
info_origin: Kapukapuariki Rocks at the southern end of Paekakariki were an important source of kaimoana, particularly mussels. Paripari Pa was located on the steep slopes above Kapukapuariki Rocks, and two other pa were situated close to the reef at Whareroa Beach and Wainui. According to E.J. Wakefield, who visited in 1840, the Wainui pa was the “residence of Te Hurumutu, one of the Kawhia chiefs who had been a party to the sale at Kapiti.” Te Hurumutu had moved from Kapiti to take up permanent residence at Wainui shortly after the Battle of Haowhenua in 1835. On another occasion, prior to the battle at Waiorua, a group of Ngati Toa were ambushed by a party of Muaupoko while gathering kaimoana from the rocks. Several Ngati Toa were killed. This reef continues to be highly valued by Ngati Toa as one of the few reliable sources of kutai or mussels still used by the Iwi for customary purposes.
info_description: A reef adjacent to State Highway 1 between Pukerua Bay (bay) and Paekakariki approximately 3 km southwest of Paekakariki. NZTopo50-BP32 628594.

name: Karakatonga Stream
info_origin: Taranaki Tūpuna written and oral history: 'Karakatonga is one of the earliest known settlements associated with the Kāhui Maunga people before the arrival of Kurahaupō. The site was reoccupied after Taranaki Maunga was formed and it was from here that the deeds of Ruataranaki, Maruwhakatare, Tahurangi and others are recounted. The site of Karakatonga pā was re-situated high up in the Waiwhakaiho River valley and provided access to the pua-tahere (bird preserves), where Kākā, Kukupa, Weka, Kiwi, Koko, and other birds were plentiful. Its strategic placement meant that it was a gateway to a major source of kōkōwai, which is still used today as a pigment in painting and anointing. The name of the urupā at Karakatonga is Arakari. The marae was Tarawainuku. The wharekura (learning institution) was Kaimirumiru and the ceremonial fire was Te Ahi-a-Tahurangi. The pātaka (storehouse) was Paeāhua, named after one of the natural forces of Rongo, the provider. A takapou (ceremonial mat) named Tāpakimarae, signified a ‘forum of peace’ and became central to protocol and policy. The stream name commemorates the pā and its importance to the identity of Ngā Iwi o Taranaki, and connections to the earliest inhabitants.'
info_description: A stream that flows for approximately 4.5km from Kokowai Track on the northern slopes of Taranaki Maunga into Waiwhakaiho River. NZTopo50-BJ29 924530 to BJ29 951557.
treaty_legislation: Section 24 and 25 Te Ture Whakatupua mō Te Kāhui Tupua 2025/Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act 2025

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; Objective folder ID: fA325625
info_origin: Kakara Taramea is the correct name for the Karamea River, which rises in the Matiri Range of Kā Tiritiri-o-te-moana (the Southern Alps). It meanders north before flowing in a westerly direction into Te Tai-o-Rehua (the Tasman Sea), in the Buller District of Te Tai Poutini (the West Coast). Kakara Taramea means “the sweet-smelling taramea”. Kakara means sweet-smelling, and taramea is speargrass (Aciphylla squarrosa, Aciphylla colensoi), which was highly regarded as a source of perfume. Taramea once grew extensively on the flats on both sides of the river, near its entrance to the sea. The leaves of the taramea were gathered and heated to extract the resin, which was mixed with bird fat to create fragrant sachets of oil to be used as a fragrance.

info_origin: Ahuriri Hapū statement: The place where Karetoki lived with his wife Pania, a tipuna and ancestor to the Hapū of Ahuriri. Pania was of the sea people; a descendent of Tangaroa. She and Karetoki had a son named Moremore, the hairless one, later to become a shark and kaitiaki for this coastline. At the birth of Moremore Karetoki became concerned that he might lose his son to the sea people 'Te Iwi Ponaturi'. Karetoki consulted a tohunga in the hope of finding how to keep his son and wife with him always. The tohunga told him to place cooked food upon the mother and child while they slept and they would never again return to the sea. Evidently something went amiss; perhaps the food was not properly cooked, for Pania returned to her people, the sea people, never to return. Two places in particular on Mataruahou are associated with Pania and Karetoki. One is at Hukarere near the entrance to Coote Road, where the freshwater spring 'Tuhinapo' is located; and the other is in Sturms Gully where Pania and Karetoki lived.
info_description: An historic site above Port of Napier, on the northeast of Mataruahou. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BJ39 368227.

name: Kārewarewa
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi: Kārewarewa is a ridge westward of Ō-taha-te-kapua. To the east is the Kāramuramu ridge. Kārewarewa was a black birch bush that was referred to in Native Land Court minutes (Hinaki Te Tai, Judge Ward MB17, p127, 27/2/1893). The bush was a mahinga kai where birds, rats and other food sources were gathered. Kārewarewa itself is a ridge that Ngāti Rangi would follow to connect to Te Ara ki Paretetaitonga (the pathway to the peak, Paretetaitonga on Ruapehu) and is referred to in the waiata Kati ano au, composed by the Ngāti Rangi tupuna, Te Riaki. Kārewarewa is another word for Kārearea (bush hawk). A kārewa is a cord to which pendant bird snares are attached. Kārewa also means surface, of water.
info_description: A ridge approximately 7km long on the southern slopes of Mount Ruapehu adjacent to the lower reaches of Te Unuunu-a-Kapua-Te-Ariki Stream. NZTopo50-BJ34 186318 to NZTopo50-BJ34 202373.

name: Karitane
info_origin: ’The meaning of Karitāne, a small township and fishing port in East Otago, on the south bank of the Waikouaiti River estuary, has caused debate for many years. There remains no consensus as to its meaning, nor to whether it is a pre-European name or (as stated by the notable kaumātua Rawiri Te Maire) the transliterated name of the Wesleyan missionary Charles Creed, who succeeded the first South Island missionary James Watkin in 1844. Karitāne may simply derive from kari: to dig or scratch; tāne: men. Another story tells that when communities exchanged food in the old days, songs and chants were composed to mark the joyous occasion. But on one occasion, when a southern party arrived to barter food, no women were there, and only a few men (tāne) were available to go forward and sing an appropriate kari to welcome the food. Yet another explanation is that Karitāne specifically refers to a ditch that was dug (kari) by men (tāne) to catch tuna (eels), and which eventually widened into a lagoon.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Karl Crest
info_origin: Named by the NZGB for Brian Karl, who worked in Antarctica for 30 years including continuously between 1987 and 2016 as core member of New Zealand’s Adélie penguin programme (K122). He has also worked closely in collaboration with the US Adélie penguin programme. This feature is located near the significant Adélie penguin colonies, on the western shoreline of Mount Bird. Brian Karl’s efforts have contributed data to numerous peer-reviewed Antarctic publications (nine of which he was a co-author) and media events over the last 25 years. Over his time he supported many other personnel and events that were not part of K122 but were based at Cape Bird, including support for post-graduate students. Antarctica NZ often relied on Mr Karl’s knowledge and experience of Antarctica to support new personnel at Cape Bird.

info_origin: A descriptive name for the western extension of Karori, which became a borough in 1891 and merged with Wellington City in 1920. The New Zealand Company surveyed rural sections mostly of 100 acres (40 ha) in the forested land along the newly formed Karori Road in 1840-41. Today’s Karori West is largely on Section 43 which was drawn by ballot in 1842 by Land Order holder Dr William Butler (1815-64). Later in 1842 auctioneer John Wade sold it off as 5 acres (2 ha) sections. As late as 1870 there were only a handful of houses at Karori West. The first house in the area, Chesney Wold, dated from 1866 and was built for farmer and landowner Stephen Lancaster (1833-99). UK born Lancaster arrived in Wellington in 1857 and settled in Karori in 1859. He was later chair of Hutt County Council and the first Mayor of Karori Borough. Prominent businessman and banker Harold Beauchamp (1858-1938), father of internationally known short story writer Katherine Mansfield, leased Chesney Wold from 1893-98. By the 1920s community activities in the locality were described as taking place in Karori West. In 1932 Karori West School was opened which helped to cement the name. There were named polling booths for the 1935 elections and a Karori West Post Office dated from 1939.

info_origin: 'After Katie Gardiner, the English mountaineer who climbed many of the mountains in the Southern Alps, and on one occasion was forced to shelter from a blizzard in a crevasse for ten days.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. ; Katies Col appears in a 1934 report of a traverse and col climb by HT Douglas and WT Wilson guided by Frank Alack (1899-1991). Alack had guided for English climber Katie Gardiner on her New Zealand trips from 1928. It was described as ‘Katie Col’ in GT Mitchell’s description of his ascent of Mount Le Receveur in 1935. Kate (Katie) Gardiner (1885-1977) was born in Lancashire, the daughter of shipping owner Frederick Gardiner (1850-1919) a noted mountaineer and Vice President of the Alpine Club (1896-98). She was introduced to climbing by her father and climbed Mount Breithorn aged 10. After 1926, she climbed seriously in Asia, Africa, Japan, Europe and Australia, but particularly in Canada and New Zealand. Inspired by a photograph of Aoraki/Mount Cook she came to New Zealand in 1926 to climb in the area. She returned in 1928 to reach the summit of Aoraki/Mount Cook (3724m). Travelling to Canada, she climbed Mount Assiniboine and made other ascents with guide Walter Feuz. For the next decade she spent summers climbing in the Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana and the remainder of the year climbing in Canada and Switzerland. She ascended West Hoe (2574m) with guides Peter Graham and Frank Alack in 1929. In 1930-31 she ascended and climbed 27 peaks in all. In 1931 she wrote to the Honorary Geographic Board to propose Mount Frederick Gardiner (2680m) after her father, Mount Stephen (2546m) after guide Peter Graham’s younger son, Mount Garnier (1986m) after a friend Louie Garnier, and Moonlight Peak (2700m). Attempting Mount Tasman (3497m) in 1933, she and three companions were trapped by a storm in a crevasse on the Fox Glacier/Te Moeka o Tuawe for eight days. Later that year she successfully climbed Mount Tasman (3497m). On a later trip she climbed Mount Aspiring/Tititea (3033m) and Mount Tūtoko (2723m). The Honorary Geographic Board accepted her proposed names of Lake Agnes and Alice Peak (2155m). She ascended the latter in 1937 and named it after her mother. In 1948 she visited again and climbed Mount Taranaki or Mount Egmont (2518m) and Mount Ruapehu (2797m) before returning to live permanently in New Zealand in 1951. She made her last climb in the Minarets (3031m) at the head of Franz Josef Glacier/Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere that same year.

name: Katikati
info_origin: ’When Tamatekapua, commander of the Arawa canoe, stopped here for a meal, his men ate their food quickly, but Tama nibbled his slowly, hence Katikati-o-Tamatekapua: lit. katikati: nibbling; o: of; Tamatekapua. Another version, recorded by Captain Gilbert Mair, is that the crew of the Arawa saw mangroves in the Waiau Estuary and thought that they saw kūmara plants in the Waiau Estuary. They started to eat their stocks of kūmara, but Tama was unsure and spent a long time eating his share. After European occupation the name was applied to a large area including much of the present Waihi district. The founding of the Special Settlement of Ulstermen in the 1870s led to a change to Waterford, but since this caused confusion with Waterford in Ireland, the name reverted to Katikati on 1 October 1884.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Kauaeranga
info_origin: 'Lit. the stacked row of jawbones. The name, originally Te Kauearanga, commemorated the stranding of a pod of whales in the locality, and gave rise to the tribal saying ‘He ripanga paraoa ki Kauaeranga’ (A heap of sperm whales at Kauaeranga). The image was maintained during the wars between Ngati Huarere and Marutuahu, when a row of jawbones of Ngati Huarere warriors were set out after the battle.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Kauarapaoa Stream
info_origin: 'lit. kau: to swim; ara: path; Paoa. On this interpretation it means the route by which Paoa (or Pawa) swam across the river. Paoa was Kupe’s slave. When Kupe left his canoe some distance up the river, Paoa swam to the other side to get some korau (native turnip) for a meal but he was drowned. Another version from Kupe’s travels is that Arapawa, one of the chiefs on board the Matahourua, swam across the river to obtain food for the campers, but on his return he was caught in a whirlpool. Kupe called out three times, ‘Kau, Arapawa!’ (Swim, Arapawa!), but in vain — Arapawa disappeared from sight. The reach where he was drowned took its name from Kupe’s words, eventually corrupted to Kaurapaoa.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: An original Māori name, literally the name of a forest shrub (Macropiper excelsum). Warenga, the elder brother of the noted explorer Ihenga, eventually settled at Kawakawa. In 1815 missionary Samuel Marsden (1765-1838) visited the riverbank village the name of which he transcribed as Cowa-Cowa. Missionary Henry Williams (1792-1867) was a regular visitor and by 1834 was conducting weekly church services at Kawakawa. In the late 1850s Henry Tacey Kemp (1818-1901) the District Land Purchase Commissioner, initiated the survey and purchase of the Kawakawa land blocks. Coal was discovered at Kawakawa in 1864 and commercially mined until the turn of the 20th century, the mines being the country's largest producer in the 1880s. In 1899 the town was significantly damaged by fire and largely rebuilt on the flats. A railway station was constructed in 1911. Austrian artist and environmentalist Friedensreich (Frederick) Regentag Dunkelbunt Hundertwasser (1928-2000) settled in Kawakawa in the 1970s. He designed the town's public toilets in his distinctive architectural style, which were competed in 1999 to become a tourist attraction in their own right.

info_origin: Te Rarawa history: "Kawehītiki is bound in Te Rarawa history, particularly regarding battles and peace-making with Ngāti Korokoro, and also battles with Ngāti Whatua at te rae o Te Karaka. Kawehītiki refers to the carrying (kawe) of those killed in battle – for example, the battles at nearby Maukoro pā – to a sacred place where they could be buried. The hitiki was the carrier or mat used to carry the deceased. It was the sacred uplifting and carriage of those warriors who died in battle at that place. Kawehītiki was also important in terms of navigation between the south and north sides of the Hokianga. It is a prominent point jutting out into the harbour; locations could be judged from and by it (from Koutu on the south side of the harbour, for example): Aroha Harris, 10/02/2008

info_ref: Min 2, 97/53, 111/54; Corres XXVIII, XXIX, XXX, XXXVI pp 90-4, 130-7, 142; 124-8
info_origin: The name covers a large area on the eastern side of Tarawera River. The name is a very ancient one, belonging to an era prior to the arrival in New Zealand of Māori. It was the name of an overseas Polynesian chief from whom the inhabitants of Kawerau, a section of the Tūwharetoa tribe of Te Arawa claim their descent.; 'The first inhabitants of Kawerau were of Te Tini o Kawerau people, an iwi from Hawaiki; the land was settled shortly after the first canoes arrived, and the tini (descendants) took their name from the chief Kawerau, and also bestowed it on the district. Kawerau is hard to define in English: one possible translation, ‘countless carriers’, seemed a fitting connection with the newsprint industry that established there in the 1950s. In Māori, kawe means ‘to carry,’ and rau can mean ‘a hundred’, ‘wrapped up’ or ‘a leaf’.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: A contraction of Ka-awhia, the name given by Turi, captain of the Aotea canoe. Lit. The embracing (of Turi). Increasingly the name is being written with a macron: Kāwhia. He had a distinguished 30 year career in the Public Service, mostly with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, during which time he had a significant Antarctic focus through his work in the Legal Division and then as the Deputy Secretary responsible for Multi Lateral Affairs, which included the Legal and Antarctic Divisions. Later, as the Deputy Secretary responsible for Corporate Affairs, he retained authority for the Antarctic Policy Unit, at a time of considerable changes to the organisational structure of New Zealand Antarctic institutions from 1985 through to 1993. He provided much of the intellectual input behind New Zealand’s work leading to the adoption of the Environment Protocol.

name: Kekerengu
info_origin: Literal translation "black wood bug" common on Manuka in the summer. The place takes it's name from Ngati Ira chief Te Kekerengu, son of celebrated chieftainess Tamairangi. Kekerengu fell foul of Te Rangihaeata in the early 19th century, and fled to this area. He was later pursued and killed by Te Rangihaeata. Formerly known as Kekerangu; 'Original Maori name: Te Kotinga-o-Kekerengu:lit. The dismemberment of Kekerengu. Kekerengu was a young Ngati Ira rangatira. During the raids on the South Island in 1827–28, Te Rauparaha’s nephew Te Rangihaeata took Kekerengu’s mother Tamairangi as his wife and spared the young chief’s life, taking them to live on Kapiti Island. After Kekerengu became involved with another of his wives, Te Rangihaeata pursued mother and son down the South Island east coast to Omihi. For some time the place was misspelt Kekerangu; early settlers pronounced it Giggerigoo.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Kenepuru is an original Māori name for the sound which translates as 'sandy silt'. Ethnologist Percy Smith described 'a semi-fortified village' named Hikapu on the headland between Kenepuru Sound and Mahua Sound. Canoes were portaged from Torea over a low saddle to Kenepuru Sound. Crown Lands Ranger Joshua Rutland (1836-1915) published several papers in the Journal of the Polynesian Society in the 1890s which all pointed to the antiquity of Māori settlement in Kenepuru Sound, including middens 'near the head of the Kenepuru reach'. The Wairau purchase of some 608000 acres (246049 ha) was pushed through by Governor George Grey in 1847 and included the Marlborough Sounds except for some of Pelorous Sound / Te Hoiere and Kaituna Valley. In 1854 William Jenkins (1813-67) a Wesleyan lay preacher and official interpreter rejected the view of remaining Ngāti Toa that Rawiri Pauha (a nephew of Te Rauparaha) had excluded Kenepuru and Mahikapawa from the sale. Hakiaha ultimately secured a Crown Grant for 18 acres (7.3 ha) in Kenepuru. A detailed survey of Kenepuru by the Lands and Survey Department did not commence until 1880. The descriptive name Kenepuru Heads emerged over that decade. Extension of the telegraph to 'Kenepuru Heads' occurred in 1884. By 1896 the Lands and Survey Department referred to the 'head of Kenepuru valley' and the Beech Brothers sawmill was identified as located at 'head of Kenepuru'. A 1400 acres (567 ha) grazing run of which 210 acres (85 ha) was freehold was known as the 'Heads Farms'. The freehold portion at one time was owned by Taniora Daniel Love (1859-1937) of Te Āti Awa descent and chief at Waikawa pā. For the 1908 elections a named polling station 'Kenepuru Head' was set up.

info_origin: Southland, 10 km from Invercargill. A private subdivision that was probably named by the developers. Earlier called Puni Bush, lit. puni: company of people, blocked up. Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; An original Māori name for this area was Puni, which was attached to the stream and bush. Publisher writer Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) offered as a literal translation ‘puni, a company of people blocked up’. In 1928 the Southland Times had a more considered explanation – as a ‘noun it means “a place of encampment.” As an adjective it means “stopped up” or “filled up”.’ The former he thought more likely referred to Māori seasonal encampments occupied while harvesting food and fibre from the swamplands. William Henry Mitchell (1832-1911) took up what was then tussock covered land here naming the property Kennington Farm Park after his birthplace in the UK. Mitchell arrived in Otago in 1861 via Tasmania as part of the Gabriels Gully gold rush. Later a publican and farmer, in 1879 he subdivided and auctioned an area of his farm as a township of ¼ acre [1012 sq m] sections. Kennington was adopted as the name of the township. Kennington sold his remaining 100 acres (40 ha) in 1889. Kennington Primary School opened in 1885. The local Post Office dating from 1887 was named Kennington but the railway station was originally known as One Tree Point to avoid any confusion with the Dunedin suburb of Kensington which was on the same line. It eventually took the town’s name in 1976.

info_origin: William Henry Mitchell (1832-1911) was an original Gabriels Gully gold rush miner in 1861 and later became a publican and farmer. In 1879 he subdivided and auctioned an area as a township of ¼ acre [1012 sq m] sections which was known as Kennington after his home in the UK. The railway station which opened in 1882 was known as One Tree Point, after a nearby feature. In July 1914 New Zealand Post wrote to New Zealand Railways about changing their station name from One Tree Point to Kennington, with the acting Chief Postmaster observing that, ‘ordinarily I have given preference to the Railway name but in this case, Kennington is more euphonic and is used by the Education Board and for the public hall’. In reply Railways noted that since it’s opening the station had been called One Tree Point and dismissed any suggestion that differing station and post office names in the same town caused difficulties. They added that Kensington Station near Dunedin and Kennington could be confusing to passengers and rejected the Post Office’s request to use Kennington for the station. Late in 1914 the station was shifted a short distance further into Kennington to allow for more carriage and wagon space, but the One Tree Point Name was retained. Not until 1 October 1976 did NZ Railways rename the by now unattended ‘flag station’ meaning a flag signalled the train to stop, from One Tree Point Railway Station to Kennington Railway Station. By 1981 Paterson’s Wool Scour and the Niagara Sawmill Company were the main users of the station which closed in 1982.

name: Kerikeri
info_origin: ’Appropriately for a place of fertile soils, ‘kerikeri’ means to dig repeatedly. Jerningham Wakefield gave the verb a literal translation when he wrote, ‘I was very anxious to get to the survey-station at Keri-keri, or “Dig-dig.”’ European settlers named it Gloucester Town, but the Māori name persists. Another possible origin is from ‘kirikiri’, meaning river gravel, which was brought up from the river to be used on kūmara gardens, warming the soil and increasing crop yield. Kerikeri (often written as ‘Kidde kide’) was home to renowned northern chief Hongi Hika, particularly during the years 1819–26 when he controlled the movement of early missionaries and British settlers.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: An original Māori name for the entire Kerikeri inlet is Te-waha-o-te-Rino translatable as ‘the mouth of anger’. Some early European sources referred to the ‘head of Kerikeri inlet’ meaning present day Kerikeri or Kerikeri Inlet, meaning the narrow water passage. John Edmonds (1805-65), a stone mason and former Church Missionary Society catechist who arrived in the Bay of Islands in 1834 purchased land previously occupied by Māori on the south side of the inlet in 1838. Initially Edmonds lived at Paetai on Hauparua Inlet, the first European family to reside on the south side of the Kerikeri Inlet. Edmonds purchased several land blocks in the area later seeking title for these pre-1840 transactions from the Old Lands Claims Commissioners’. Edward Dollimore (1904-72) who compiled the New Zealand Guide noted that in 1845, during the first phase of the New Zealand wars HMS Haszard anchored at the entrance of Kerikeri Inlet and set up a forge on the opposite shore in what became known as Blacksmiths Bay. The isolated settlements along the southern side of the inlet were initially connected to Kerikeri by launch. Kerikeri Inlet was used for this locality and the inland extension of the settlement by the early 20th century. A Kerikeri Inlet primary school was established in 1909 and Kerikeri Inlet Post Office operated from 1923-41. The Public Works Department commenced work on roads linking Kerikeri Inlet and Wharau to Kerikeri in 1937. After the road was completed, further rural subdivision in 1938 cemented the name Kerikeri Inlet.

name: Kermadec Islands
info_origin: ’Known by Māori as Rangitāhua: lit. the stopping-off place. Polynesian voyagers stopped off on the Kermadec Islands around the fourteenth century or earlier. Curtis and Macauley islands were discovered by Europeans when Captain William Sever sighted them from the Lady Penrhyn on 30 June 1788. Subsequently Admiral Bruni d’Entrecasteaux discovered Raoul Island on 17 March 1793 and named it after his quartermaster on the vessel La Recherche, Joseph Raoul. The group was named after Huon Kermadec, the captain of the consort vessel L’Espérance, from which L’Esperance Rock takes its name.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: An archipelago 750-1000 km north-north-east of New Zealand which extends approximately 250 km along the western ridge of the Kermadec Trench. info_origin: An old river channel where Tutaekuri River once entered the ocean. The name derives from an incident when Tara, son of Whatonga, set out to avenge the killing of his dog at Te Whanganui-a-Ōrotu. On landing at the river mouth, he realised his pūtātara (war trumpet) had been left behind at Wairoa, whereupon Tara vented his annoyance by clicking his tongue. Alfred Reed offers a literal translation as ketekete - to click the tongue and rau – many, thus ‘many clickings of the tongue’. By the early 17th century, the channel had become blocked with shingle and by the time James Cook was offshore in 1769 the river outlet was further to the south at Petane. Keteketerau was an important traditional location for catching flounders and eels.
info_description: The original outlet of Tutaekuri River, approximately 5.5km north of Napier.

info_origin: The site of a coastal village or kāinga, the northern most settlement of Ngutu Kaka of Te Ātiawa/Taranaki Whānui. Kiakia means 'kākā beak' and could refer to either the beak of that species of bird (Nestor meridionalis) or to coloured flowers which were frequently used to decorate villages. Kiekie was sometimes an alternative spelling. Archaeologist and ethnologist Leslie Adkin, following ethnologist Elsdon Best, believed the flowers were kiekie (Freycinetia banksia). Other authorities favour the kōwhai ngutu kākā (Clianthus puniceus). Kiakia was one of the boundaries of the Port Nicholson district, a 209247 acre (84679 ha) Crown Grant to the New Zealand Company in 1848, details of which were published in the press at the request of Colonel William Wakefield (1803-48) as Principal Agent of the Company.

name: Kikowhakarere Bay
info_ref: LINZ Hydrographic Chart NZ 5328 Coromandel Harbour
info_origin: 'Lit. kiko: body; whakarere: to cast away, i.e. The abandoned flesh (of the slain). On one account, a group of Marutuahu warriors attacked a Ngati Huarere war party, which was forced back, leaving their dead on the beach. As the victorious Marutuahu were preparing the bodies for cooking, Ngati Huarere counterattacked and drove them off, forcing them to abandon their feast. F.L. Phillips says that the iwi engaged in the fighting were Ngati Tamatepo and Ngati Hei.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_description: The northwestern extremity of Marie Byrd Land, projecting into the Ross Sea between the Ross Ice Shelf to the west and Sulzberger Bay to the east.

info_origin: An original Māori name suggestive of a pā, a defensive settlement and or kainga (village) at this site. In 1843 a shore whaling station was established at Kinikini, then typically spelled Kini in the newspapers, and used interchangeably with nearby Long Point. Some 115 acres (46 ha) were set aside as the Kini Native Reserve in 1871. In 1941 the name was considered by the Honorary Geographic Board. This was part of a broader review by two of its members, Sir Āpirana Ngata and Johannes C Andersen on the application of ‘classical Maori spelling’ to place names. Ngata recommended Kinikini as the preferred form.

info_origin: This bush clearing was named after Archibald (Archie) Kirk (1888-1963) who from 1919 to about 1922 felled the forest cover for grazing land. Kirk was a fireman for the Union Steam Ship Company. He volunteered in 1917 and served as a private in the Otago Infantry Regiment on the Western Front from 1918 until his discharge in 1919 as unfit for military duties on account of wounds received in action. Along with Kenneth McDonald Doleman (1885-1973), an orchardist who also served on the Western Front as a private in the Auckland Regiment in 1918-1919, and another returned serviceman named Eddison and Archie’s son Colin, he took up the remote bush sections. Bushman Frank Anderson was contracted to help clear the forest. The area was already known as Kirk’s Clearing as early as 1919 when a party led by Ellis Fisher canoed from Mōtū Falls to the mouth of the river. By 1922 Kirk and his partners had abandoned the farm. Kirk later worked successfully as a building contractor in Gisborne.

info_origin: An original Māori name. Literally translated as a white or light-coloured kiwi and adopted as their name by Māori occupants of this part of the Oroua area. The Kiwitea Block comprising 24000 acres (9712 ha) north of the Manchester Block between Oroua River and Kiwitea Stream was surveyed and released for sale in 1876. Regarded as first-class agricultural land the area was described as consisting of ‘chiefly of level country with light open bush which can easily be cleared. The soil is, as a rule, of excellent quality, and the bulk of the land is suitable for either agricultural or pastoral purposes. No block of timbered land which has hitherto been placed in the market by the Government could be so readily cleared and laid down in grass as the one at present referred to. The timber consists chiefly of a very light kind, good for firewood, fencing, and other purposes, but not adapted for sawing. There are a few patches of totara on the Oroua and Kiwitea flats, also some rimu, matai, and kahikatea scattered through the block. A small portion of the land towards the north-west is somewhat broken, but as already said, the bulk of it is splendid level country.’ By 1877 the area was referred to as the Kiwitea Block. A township named Kiwitea was laid out in late 1877 although this never really eventuated. It was surveyed by John Barton (1823-1902) a former assistant engineer to the Wellington Provincial Council, later in private practice, and a foundation member of the New Zealand Institute of Surveyors.

name: Koettlitz Glacier
info_origin: Discovered by the NAE, 1901-04, during the summer of 1902-03. Named by Dr Reginald Koettlitz, physician and botanist of the expedition.
info_description: A large glacier lying north of Mount Discovery and Mount Morning and flowing between Brown Peninsula and the mainland to the Ross Ice Shelf at the head of McMurdo Sound. It is approximately 44km long, flowing from the Koettliz Névé at an elevation of 1500m southeast of Mount Kempe. The western half is covered with silt and raised moraine material, is deeply cut by thaw streams, and is scattered with bastions of pinnacled ice which, in the upper reaches, attain a height of 18m. The eastern side of the glacier is smoother, but contains long undulations, icefalls, ridges and gullies. There is no rock wall bordering this side of the glacier, the ice merging imperceptibly with the slopes of Brown Island, Mount Discovery and Mount Morning. About 34km southward of Cape Chocolate, the Koettlitz Glacier reaches sea level. From this point it continues as a floating sheet of stagnant ice into McMurdo Sound. This ice barrier has a height from 1.5 to 8m, but the contours and limits undergo considerable change from year to year. The extension of this glacier on the western side of McMurdo Sound is a vast field of chaotic ice. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MH10
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

info_origin: In February of 1906, the Station Master in Charge for Nelson publicly notified that the station then known as Motupiko would henceforth be renamed Kotahu. This was followed later in the same month by the Post and Telegraph Office also noting that it was changing the name of its Motupiko Railway office to Kohatu. Simultaneously, the Upper Motupiko Post Office was renamed Korere. These efforts on behalf of two government departments were intended to remove potential confusion. name: Kōhatupapā / Ranfurly Bay
info_origin: Ngatikahu ki Whangaroa statement: A known pā site of Ngati Kaitangata seasonal/kaimoana gathering kainga noho. Prior to the arrival of Lord Ranfurly to the Whangaroa Harbour, in approximately 1912, the bay and the surrounding land area was known as Kohatupapaa which was the name of the pa and seasonal kainga noho. It was at the request of the local Commissioner of the day to name the bay after Lord Ranfurly in recognition of his visit to Whangaroa. This was later followed by a request to the land owners for land to be set aside as a reservation for the peoples of NZ to which the owners agreed. But as a consequence of my research was never officially completed or surveyed. The name Ranfurly was then applied to this bay. Hence in consequence through the dealings of the Land Minister of the day and the chairman of the Whangaroa County Council the owners were to lose the whole peninsular which was set aside as a scenic reserve in 1919. (Historic research Peter McBurney AIP 2004). All the information has been orally provided by our kaumātua Wake Tua whom is 90 years of age, and states that he received this information from his grandfather Motukiwi Hone Tua, and ably supported by kaumātua Rawiri Timoti whose great great grandmother Maungaroa was an elder sister to Motukiwi as well as kaumātua Rawiri Henare, kaumātua Pita Pangari. He has in his possession minutes (papatupu books) of the Land Commissioner’s hearings in Kaeo during their investigations of land ownership during the late 1800s and early 1900s, but will not allow transcribing or copying for fear of losing this long held information. Information also provided orally by Matua Rawiri Henare kaumātua Mangatowai Marae.
info_description: A small bay near the entrance to Whangaroa Harbour at the southeast end of Kōwhairoa Peninsula. Feature shown on: NZMS260 P04 Q04 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-AV28 684259 to AV28 688259.

name: Kōhinerākau
info_origin: Heretaunga Tamatea history: ‘Mt Erin is a 490m high hill in the Kohinurākau Range. It is a mountain environment occupied/frequented by Ngāti Kurukuru of Waimārama and Ngāti Hāwea of Heretaunga and also a branch of the Ngāti Hinepare people. To the people living inland of the Tukituki River it is known as Kohinurākau – the place of the scented oil trees. To the people on the seaward side at Waimārama, Kōhinerākau celebrates the wife of the fabled chief Te Matā who died trying to eat his way through the range of hills known as Te Matā (and to some as Te Mata o Rongokako). Kohinurākau/Kōhinerākau is also the site of Papahope (the hips of Papatuānuku) one of the pillars of heaven in Ngāti Kahungunu tradition. It is more recently revered as the burial place of Pukepuke Tangiora’s mother Merihine-i-takā.’
info_description: A hill at 490m, at the northern end of Kohinurakau Range, approximately 8.5km south-southwest of Havelock North. NZTopo50 BK39 291941.
info_note: Kohinurākau and Kōhinerākau are both official names for the hill. They can be used together or separately.
treaty_legislation: Section 51 and 52 Heretaunga Tamatea Claims Settlement Act 2018

name: Kōkōariki
info_ref: Objective ID: A4635550; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche May 2024: Objective ID: A6324681 {Best, Elsdon. 1927. The Pa Maori. New Zealand: Whitcombe and Tombs; https://maungakorero.wordpress.com/2014/01/20/maungahaumi-2/kokoariki/ ; https://mangatu.co.nz/the-carvings/}
info_origin: A small pā by Waikohu River close to Mangamāhaki Stream, one of a number of fortified Ngā Potiki villages in the area. Hineteariki, a chieftainess of noble birth and her husband Tūmokonui lived at Kōkōariki. A Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki legend says that when Hineteariki died she became a taniwha and lived in Waikohu River below the pā. Ethnologist Elsdon Best (1856-1931), a foundation member of the Honorary Geographic Board, described Kōkōariki as ‘a good specimen of the fortified mound’. Best noted that mounds or alternatively ‘hillocks’ were typically fortified either by steepening the sloping sides and erecting a stockade on the top or by making an earthen wall around the sloping sides. In some cases, as with Kōkōariki, the mound was terraced.
info_description: A small pā by Waikohu River close to Mangamāhaki Stream, southwest of Pūhā. Feature shown on: NZMS260 Y17 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-BF43 205314

name: Kokorua Open Scientific Reserve
info_origin: The name ‘Kokorua’ has been used in several instances locally. It is the name given to the adjacent bay (the likely derivation of the name for its land-based use also), a nearby settlement/homestead, a local road and a defended pā site situated on a conical hill on the north side of the estuary. The Department of Conservation advised ‘Kokorua’ was chosen in reference to the nearby defended pā site. Kokorua sand spit (a locally used name, not recorded) holds important archaeological significance, being an early Māori occupation site and one of the few remaining in Tasman Bay in a comparatively intact state. Kokorua translates as ‘two bays’, referring to the two shallow bays adjacent to the reserve.
info_description: Section 1 SO 434602. A sand spit located approximately 40km northeast of Nelson at the mouth of  Whangamoa River.  The occupation site is on a low promontory on the estuary side of the sand spit, extending towards the inlet.  There are exposed middens on eroding sections of the inshore banks of the promontory and argillite flakes can be seen scattered on the shoreline.  According to the Nelson/Marlborough Conservancy Historic Places Register, the site’s significance is demonstrated by the quantity of artefactual and faunal material recovered from the site.
info_note: Reviewed and Concerred by the NZGB on 28 February 2014

name: Korokoro
info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5111558 {Adkin, Leslie. 1959. The Great Harbour of Tara. New Zealand: Whitcombe and Tombs.; Best, Elsdon. 1901. Te Whanga-nui-a-Tara. Journal of the Polynesian Society, 10(3), 107-165.; [The Korokoro Settlement. 1901. Evening Post, 9 September, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19010909.2.50); [Horokiwi Road, Korokoro to Takapu. 1937.Evening Post, 12 June, Page 10.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19370612.2.79); New Zealand Geographic Board Correspondence, 1955. vol 30 pp. 200-01}
info_origin: Korokoro Stream flows into Wellington Harbour at the western boundary of Petone. The full name of the stream is Te Korokoro-o-te Mana. Ethnologist Elsdon Best noted that because of the nature of the land there was only a single earthworks pā on a spur overlooking the stream. Ngāti Awa invaders included chief Te Poki, who took possession of the valley and delta of the Korokoro uttering ‘Ko te korokoro tenei o taku tamiti’. This literally translates as ‘This place is the throat of my child’. This was an allusion to the food supply provided by the valley with archaeologist and ethnologist Leslie Adkin surmising that Te Mana was a member of Te Poki’s family. The flat area around the mouth of the stream where it entered the harbour was known as Korokoro from the 1840s. In 1898 the Public Works Department’s estimates included a sum for roading in the hilly areas along Korokoro Stream. The following year 22 sections on 65 acres (26 ha) were thrown open by the Lands Department as the Korokoro Village Settlement. By 1901 14 houses had been constructed and 49 people were in residence and employed mainly in the nearby railway workshops and Petone. In 1955 the Koro Koro Rate Payers & Progressive Association wrote to the New Zealand Geographic Board seeking clarification over whether Koro Koro or Korokoro was the better spelling. The Board confirmed it was the latter. Accordingly, ‘Korokoro’ as a place name now ‘moved’ up the hill. Korokoro was gazetted as a suburb in 2019.

name: Koromiko
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Andrews, J. 1985. Some glimpses of history along the Tua Marina-Picton Road. Journal of the Nelson and Marlborough Historical Societies 1 (5), 23-24; Insull, HAH. 1952. Marlborough Place Names. New Zealand: Reed; [Picton and Blenheim Railway. 1875. Marlborough Press, 15 May, Page 3](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/MEX18750515.2.4.3)}
info_origin: Koromiko is a local Māori name for Veronica salicifolia, the leaves of which were chewed to help cure diarrhoea. This locality was named for the Koromiko Stream which crossed an old Māori track stretching across the Elevation Saddle to Picton, then known as Waitohi. The area was forested and totara trees suitable for large waka (canoes) grew at the spot and were dragged to the Waitohi pā at present day Picton. A road from Picton to Koromiko Stream was begun in 1857 and followed by a further extension from Koromiko Stream to the Wairau River. Forested land in the vicinity near the Koromiko Stream was purchased by James Speed (1824-74) in 1866 to supply Captain Daniell’s nearby sawmills. Early permanent residents at Koromiko included William Baillie (1827-1922), the second Superintendent of Marlborough Province (1861-63). A Koromiko Railway Station was erected in 1875.

name: Kutaroa Stream
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: The Kutaroa Stream is named after the kuta plant which was a prized resource to Ngāti Rangi for weaving. Kuta is a tall, bamboo-like rush growing to about 1 metre which spreads from a creeping rhizome and has thick hollow stems of bright green. Kuta is found throughout Aotearoa/New Zealand in swamps and on lake edges and is often partially submerged. The soft, flattened, hollow stalks (culms) of kuta are a popular resource for weavers. The long culms are harvested, placed under matting for about 3 days to flatten, then woven into soft hats, mats, and kete. Kuta dries to an attractive golden-brown shade.
info_description: A stream that flows generally southeast for approximately 2.5km from Ōpeketā Swamp to Irirangi (locality). NZTopo50-BK35 291212 to NZTopo50-BK35 307194.
info_note: Ngāti Rangi Treaty Claims Settlement

info_origin: Named by US-ACAN (2000) after Philip R Kyle, Professor of Geochemistry, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM, who worked extensively in Antarctica over 28 field seasons, 1969-2000. Completed six seasons under NZARP auspices, 1969-76. Principal investigator on numerous NSF research projects in 23 seasons of field work under USAP auspices, 1977-2000, with focus on long-term research of the volcano Mount Erebus. In charge of the Mount Erebus Volcano Observatory, 2000.
info_description: A prominent group of volcanic cones, hills, ridges, and peaks that occupy the east part of Ross Island between Mount Terror and Cape Crozier. The hills extend east-west for 16km, rising from sea level at Cape Crozier to c.2600m in Mount McIntosh at the west end of the group. Local relief of features is on the order of 200m. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME16
info_note: Feature # 64 in ACAN minutes of 19/06/2000.

Maori name: Te Moana, lit. te: the; moana: sea or lake.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Lake Alabaster
info_origin: 'Fiordland National Park. Maori name: lit. wäwähi: to break or split; waka: canoe; i.e. To split trees in two in order to make a canoe. In 1863 the cutter Aquila crossed the Hollyford bar to become the first European vessel to enter Lake McKerrow. Captains Alabaster and Duncan then rowed up the Pyke River and discovered the lake, which they named after Daniel Alabaster. In 1863 James Hector spelt this name as Wawai-i wuk. A year later the explorer A.J. Barrington arrived here without provisions and dubbed it Poverty Lake.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Lake Bennett
info_origin: A large farm dam constructed by the then occupier Mr W E Bennett - hence the name Lake Bennett. Dam has developed into an excellent wildlife and fisheries habitat with adequate shallows for wild ducks and, stocked with brown trout, it has provided good angling. Features of this size would usually be considered minor but because of its ease of observation from the adjacent road and its obvious wildlife values this dam has created an unusual amount of public interest. It is also on a regular airline route and is most conspicuous from the air.

info_origin: 'Otago. They crossed the Kawarau River to the lake, which they named after Hay. There is reason to believe that the notorious Bully Hayes inadvertently had his name fathered upon the lake, which is permanently named Lake Hayes. Maori name: Waiwhakaata, lit. wai: water; whakaata: to reflect.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Lake Ōmāpere
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche May 2023: Objective ID: A5383945 {Andersen, Johannes. 1942. Maori Place Names. New Zealand: Polynesian Society.; Buick, T. Lindsay. 1926. New Zealand's First War. New Zealand: Government Printer.; Chapman-Taylor, M. 1944. The Late Henry Matthew Stowell (“Hare Hongi”) (1859-1944). Journal of the Polynesian Society, 53, 106-110.; Lake Omapere R 3950859. Archives New Zealand, Wellington; [Political Gossip. 1888. Evening Star, 18 May, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/ESD18880518.2.18); Simpson, Tony. 1971. Te Riri Pakeha. New Zealand: Hodder and Stoughton.; White John. 1874. Te Rou or the Maori at Home. Great Britain; Sampson Low, Marston.; [Freda Rankin Kawharu. 'Heke Pōkai, Hōne Wiremu', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1990. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand]( https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1h16/heke-pokai-hone-wiremu) (accessed 4 May 2023)}
info_origin: Named from its proximity to the lake of the same name, which also distinguished it from Ōmāpere on the shores of Hokianga Harbour. One story about the formation of the lake collected by skilled interpreter John White (1826-91) says that it was the work of a taniwha named Waihou who made a hole in the land with his tail and then resided in the resultant lake. Literally translated as O - place of Mapere, a tall-plumed grass (Gahnia setifolia) colloquially known as 'cutty grass'. Publisher Alexander W. Reed (1908-79) was sceptical of an alternative advanced by Hare Hongi, the pen name of Henry Matthew Stowell (1859-1944), that linked 'pere' to 'pele' the Hawaiian volcano god. Stowell was descended from leading Ngāpuhi families and very well versed in language and lore and a skilled translator. Ethnologist Johannes Andersen (1873-1972), a member of the Honorary Geographic Board, was more sympathetic to Stowell's view declining to dismiss it out of hand particularly as the lake had volcanic origins and there were thermal springs in the area. Andersen suggested that Manawatu was an earlier name for the lake. Prior to 1915 Te Ahuahu was applied to some of this area. Hone Heke's (?-1850) pā Pukenui, also known as Te Ahuahu, was on the northeast corner of the lake, with Tamati Waka Nene's (?-1871) pā on the northwestern side. This was the heart of Ngāpuhi territory. During the 'northern war' in 1845, Heke built a new fortified pā, Puketutu. In March 1845 men of the 58th and 96th regiments under Lieutenant Colonel William Hulme (1788-1855) attacked Heke's pā with heavy losses. In hand-to-hand 'fighting with Heke and Kawhiti's men the soldiers were pushed downhill towards the lake' before rallying. By 1855 Henry Tacey Kemp (1818-1901), District Commissioner for the Purchase of Native Lands in Auckland District, had identified the 'rich country skirting lake Omapere' as an 'excellent site for an inland settlement'. A survey of 5000 acres (2023 ha) was completed in 1857 but the initial offer of £300 was rebuffed. Around 1912 a Lake Omapere Estate was established partly on the Tautahanga block by George Pitcaithly. Plans to subdivide it as dairy farms foundered for want of capital and in 1918 the land was offered to the Crown for soldier settlement.

name: Lake Puketirini
info_origin: Name proposed in December 2009 by Waikato District Council. Local iwi and hapu identified ‘Puketirini’ as the original Māori name of the area within which the lake is situated. The original lake, Lake Rotoiti, became Crown land in 1865, was subsequently drained for mining by State Coal Mines (latterly known as Solid Energy). In 1993 work began to reinstate the disused mine back into a lake. The lake has been unofficially known as Lake Weaver or Weavers Lake. Puketirini’ translates to English as ‘hills and streams’ – ‘puke’ meaning ‘hills’ and ‘tirini’ being a transliteration of ‘streams’.

name: Lake Tūtira
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-12/95; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: The land surrounding Lake Tūtira was an important area of settlement for Ngāti Tu, Ngāti Kurumokihi and Ngai Tatara. Ngai Tatara had an important settlement on the island Tauranga-koua, and although they abandoned that pa following their defeat and the death of the fighting chief Tiwaewae, they still retained rights to the land at Lake Tūtira. The chief Ngāti Tū chief Kohipipi also had settlements at Lake Tūtira. According to Guthrie-Smith one whakatauaki of Ngai Tatara was: ““Ko to ratou pa ko nga rekereke”—“their pas were in their heels””. Due to the means of their survival it was necessary for the tribe to align their settlement patterns with the seasons. Says Guthrie-Smith, “[t]he Ngai-Tatara during winter, and whilst planting of crops was in progress, dwelt chiefly about the estuaries of the local rivers. The climate of Tūtira was rather too cold and wet, the land usually too poor for the cultivation on a great scale of such exotics as the taro (Colocasia antiquorum), the hue (Lagenatia vulgaris), and the kumara (Ipomœa batatas). On the other hand, the flax (Phormium tenax)1 growing about its swamps was celebrated for strength, the shallows of the lake were paved with mussel-beds—kakahi (Diplodon lutulentus), the flavour of its eels was unsurpassed. They were speared in the lakes, they were caught in enormous numbers in eel-weirs—patunas—or in whare tunas built along the edges of streams. In the forests of the interior, pigeon (Carpophaga Novœ Zealandiœ), tui (Prosthemadera Novœ Zealandiæ), and kaka (Nestor meridionalis) abounded; they were captured by means of decoy birds, or snared by natives ambushed beneath selected trees. often a superabundance of birds preserved in their own fat was bartered for the delicacies of other hapus. Tools of wood and weapons of stone were manufactured. These relics of bygone days—pounders for the softening of flax-fibre, adzes, eel- spears, and bundles of bird-snares hidden in rocks—are still from time to time discovered.”In the later nineteenth century much of the land at Tūtira was leased to private individuals, in particular Guthrie-Smith, and then acquired by the Crown, although a small portion of Māori freehold land remains, some of which includes a part of the lake itself. Some kaumatua of MTI recall living at or utilising the resources of Tūtira. Eels were of course plentiful within the lake, on the land surrounding the lake large quantities of flax could be obtained, amongst other plant-life. one wahi tapu, according to Mrs Kuia Gray, was located where a shearing shed now[?] sits; she was taught that this was the site of a battle and following the battle was made tapu. The following, recorded by Guthrie-Smith is a waiata which makes reference to Tūtira: “e hine e tangi nei ki te makariri i a ia, Kaore nei e hine te rau o te ngahere i a taua, Pinea rawatia ki Tūtira ra; Ki te ue pata, ki te kai rakau. A ehara e hine i te roto hou; he roto tawhito tonu na matou ko o nui. Ina tonu te raro i potau atu ai e hine: Ko hine-rau- wharariki te hahanu noa nei: Ko tini o hunga ki roto kakati ai e hine. o maiden, who art weeping because of the cold, We own no garments of forest-leaves, o child. Let us gather together to Tūtira Where are eel-weirs and fruit-laden trees. The lake, my little girl, is not a new lake, But an ancient lake possessed by thy ancestral great ones. It is only just now that the food has gone: Hine- rau-wharariki is preparing the fibre: Suppressing the hunger-pangs gnawing within.”
