info_ref: Objective ID: A2658169; fA325625; fA417315; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: 'Lit. wai: water; rarapa: glistening. This was the last of the place names given by the muchtravelled tohunga Hau, a memento not only of the beauty of the lake, but of the glistening of his eyes on finding his wife Wairaka (or Hinerakahanga). A different account ascribes the naming to Tara. In Old Wairarapa, A.G. Bagnall attributes the name to Kupe who, while still at sea, looked over his shoulder, an action described by the word rarapa. On Bagnall’s account, Kupe’s daughter suggested, ‘Me waiho to moana ko te rarapatanga o ou whatu’ (Let us remain here at this lake you have descried, your anchor stone). Kupe replied, ‘E pai ana. Me waiho ko Wairarapa’ (Good. Let it remain Wairarapa). There is also a tradition that Kupe trekked overland to Wairarapa and as far as Te Matau-a-Maui. A range of hills to the east of Greytown bearing the name Nga Waka-o-Kupe (The canoes of Kupe) may be a reminder of this traverse; some of the hills are supposed to resemble a canoe.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Lake Waitaki
info_origin: 'lit. wai: river; taki (tangi): noisy, or weeping. This is the same as the North Island Waitangi, Sounding or Noisy or Weeping water, the North Island ‘ng’ being replaced by the South Island form ‘k’. The river was considered the most dangerous in the region, and the roar of boulders being swept along when the river was in flood could be heard by travellers long before it came into view. One local account is that two brothers wept for their sister who drowned at the river mouth. The brothers were turned into two hills at Lake Ohau, their tears mingling and flowing across the land. At one time it was intended to name the river the Shakespeare, and for a time it was known as the Molesworth.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Lane Plateau
info_origin: Discovered and photographed by R. Admiral Byrd on the Baselaying Flight of Nov. 18, 1929, and surveyed by A. P. Crary, 1957 - 58. Mapped by USGS from surveys, 1962 - 63, and the U.S. Navy photography taken 1958 - 63. The Plateau is named in honour of Neal Lane, Director of the National Science Foundation from 1993 to 1998. Dr Lane visited Antarctica on 3 occasions and guided the foundation through 2 high level reviews of the US Antarctic Programme. Under his leadership NSF won congressional approval for rebuilding South Pole Station as a premier international science facility set to open at the beginning of the 21st century. Lane Plateau has several nearby features which also honour people who have been instrumental in shaping US leadership in Antarctic activities including Mt Waterman, Mount Bronk, Mount Cartwright and Mount Wexler.
info_description: A flat, ice-covered plateau that rises to 3000 m between Mount Waterman, Mount Cartwright, and Mount Bronk in the central Hughes Range of the Queen Maud Mountains. The plateau trends N-S for 9 miles and is 2.5 miles wide.

info_origin: Named for Professor Patricia (Pat) Langhorne, Emerita Professor University of Otago, recognising a lifetime of contribution to the science of Antarctic sea-ice physics and ice-ocean interactions. Professor Pat Langhorne published a 'landmark' paper in 2015 describing sea ice formation in the presence of supercooled Ice Shelf Water (ISW) and its relationship to global cryosphere systems. Langhorne Rise physically plays a role in the circulation of ocean waters and the sea-ice cycle in the western Ross Sea, including the formation of ISW. Professor Langhorne was awarded the New Zealand Antarctic Medal in 2019.
info_description: An undersea feature, under the western Ross Ice Shelf approximately 320km long southwest to northeast. It rises contiguously from maximum depth -660m to a minimum depth of -473m. Between the surface of the feature and the base of the Ross Ice Shelf is a water column ~237m to ~380m deep.
feat_note: The extent of Langhorne Rise is derived mainly from the synthesis of remote/indirect measurements across different techniques: gravitational, magnetic anomaly, seismic for bed topography, satellite altimetry and radar echo sounding for ice thickness.

The mountain was named for Captain Carl Anton Larsen (1860-1924), whose explorations on the east coast of Graham Land marked the beginning of commercial whaling operations in the Antarctic.

name: Lashly Mountains

Lashly also accompanied the British Antarctic Expedition (Terra Nova expedition, BrAE), 1910-13, under Scott, during which he was a member of the Polar Party to 87º34' S, in 1912. For his part in saving the life of Lieutenant E R G R Evans (later Admiral Lord Mountevans) on the return journey from the polar plateau, Lashly was awarded the Albert Medal.

name: Le Bons Bay
info_origin: ’One account states that when a French vessel commanded by Captain Le Bas mistook the bay for Akaroa Harbour, the captain sent a boat ashore to investigate. The first sailor to set foot on the beach was called Le Bon. Another theory is that after whalers had been living here it became known as Bone Bay because of the whale skeletons littering the beach, and that the name evolved into Le Bons. A third explanation is that Le Bon was the master of a French whaling ship that put in here, buried three or four of the men up to the neck to cure them of scurvy, and returned to find the men eaten by wild pigs. A final theory is that French whalers called it Le Bon (The Good) Bay.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Lepperton
info_origin: 'After Lieutenant-Colonel Maxwell Lepper, who received a grant of land here for service in the New Zealand Wars. Maori name: Manutahi: manu: bird; tahi: one; at first this was adopted by European settlers, but Lepperton prevailed as there was another Manutahi near Hawera.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Le Receveur Peak

info_origin: Le Renard is a character in 'Le Petit Prince', one of Antoine de Saint-Exupery's most famous books. Le Renard (the fox) is the companion of the Small Prince. It symbolizes friendship.
info_description: An undersea fracture zone in the Southern Ocean, approximately 1130km northeast of Scott Island, extending from -59.5481, -169.524 to -65.3923, -148.144.

name: Lesson Creek

Lesson, a member of Dumont D'Urville's crew. M. Lesson and M. Simonet accompanied D'Urville ashore at Stilwells Bay. The area description and this event are recorded by Peart in his book on D'Urville's exploits.
info_description: Stream rising 800m East of Trig. X (Geodetic Code A73H), and flowing generally eastward into Stilwell Bay, Astrolabe Roadstead.  Block VI Kaiteriteri Survey District.

name: Lessong Monument

info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 U21 Edition 1 1983 Limited Revision 1996

name: Letitia Stream
info_origin: Name submitted by the Canterbury Chief Surveyor, August 1965, after field check for the revision of NZMS1 S66. Name suggested by the Chief Surveyor. One branch of the stream flows from Lake Letitia.
info_description: Right bank tributary of Esk River rising from and 2km North of Lake Letitia, flowing Southward and joining Esk River 1.3km upstream of Waimakariri River.  Block IV, Grasmere Survey District.

name: Lettau Bluff
info_origin: Named after Professor Heinz H. Lettau of the University of Wisconsin, an authority on Antarctic meteorology who was active in the planning and development of the meteorological program and equipment for the U.S. Plateau Station, 1966-68. He co-authored (with Paul C. Dalrymple and Sarah H. Wollaston) an analysis of the 1958 meteorological data from South Pole Station.
info_description: A rock and ice bluff that forms the central part of the west edge of Beaufort Island. It rises 200m above Ross Sea. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MD14
info_note: The New Zealand Geographic Board and Antarctica NZ accepted Lettau Bluff on 4/11/1999.

name: Lettau Peak
info_origin: Named in 1992 by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) after Bernhard Lettau, Program Manager for Polar Ocean and Climate Sciences in the Office of Polar Programs, National Science Foundation, from 1976.
info_description: A triangular peak at 2453m, 1.8km west-northwest of Fogle Peak, and 3.5km south of the prominent Camels Hump in Royal Society Range, Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MG09

name: Levels
info_origin: 'The Rhodes brothers began to develop their run at Timaru in the early 1850s, naming this part of it the Levels after their old home near Doncaster in Yorkshire, England.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 J38 Edition 1 1983

name: Levels Valley
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 J38 Edition 1 1983

name: Level Valley
info_origin: One of a group of names in the area associated with surveying applied in 1993 by NZGB. A surveyors level is an instrument designed primarily to furnish a horizontal line of sight.
info_description: A distinctive ice-free valley which descends northeastward from the Pivot Peak cirque, in Wilkniss Mountains, Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MG08
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map No available map; Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Taylor Glacier (USA) map, ST 57-60/5.

name: Leven Stream

name: Leverett Glacier
info_origin: Discovered in November 1929, by the Geological party, led by Gould, of the Byrd AE, 1928-30. Named for Frank Leverett, eminent geologist at the University of Michigan and an authority on glacial geology of the central United States.
info_description: A slow-moving glacier about 10 miles wide over 20 miles long, flowing in a west-north-west direction between the Harold Byrd and Tapley Mountains, and terminating at the head of the Ross Ice Shelf close east of the Robert Scott Glacier.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Lever Nunataks
info_origin: The name is suggested by the position and linear arrangement of the group, away from Fulcrum.
info_description: An 8km string of Nunataks extending from west of Henderson Pyramid towards the Fulcrum and Pivot Peak, at the head of Creagh Glacier in Wilkniss Mountains, Victoria Land. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MG08

name: Levin
info_origin: ’In 1889 when the Wellington-Manawatu Railway Company was formed, townships on the line were named after directors of the company, including William Hort Levin, a leading Wellington businessman. This was despite arrangements made after the purchase of the Horowhenua block, when 4000 acres (1620 ha) were made available for a township and Keepa Te Rangihiwinui stipulated it should be named Taitoko. Levin grew to encompass the adjacent settlement of Weraroa.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for William Hort Levin](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2l9/levin-william-hort)
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 S25 Pt R25

name: Levin Railway Station
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS271 Levin 1990; NZTopo50-BN33 926997

name: Levi Peak
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Gene S. Levi, meteorologist at Hallett Station, winter 1963, and 1964-65 summer season.
info_description: A rock peak rising to 2911m, approximately 6km west-northwest of Mount Stanley, at the western edge of Grindley Plateau, Queen Alexandra Range.

name: Lewandowski Point
info_origin: Mapped by U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and U.S. Navy tricamera aerial photographs, 1957-62. Named by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for John R. Lewandowski, U.S. Navy (USN), Chief Construction Electrician at McMurdo Station, 1965-66 and 1966-67.
info_description: A rugged, partially ice-free point on the Victoria Land coast, marking the south side of the mouth of Clarke Glacier.

name: Lewin Rocks
info_ref: LINZ Hydrographic Chart NZ 5124 Plans in the Bay of Islands - Waikare Inlet
info_description: Submerged rocks north of Pipiro Bay. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-AV29 15934

name: Lewis Basin
info_ref: McMurdo Sound Chart©, Pyne et al., 1985; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836
info_origin: Named in association with Lewis Bay, which the US-ACAN named in 1964 for Captain Price Lewis of the United States Navy, commanding officer of the USS Staten Island during Deep Freeze IV (1958-59), and assistant chief of staff and ship group commander, US Naval Support Force, Antarctica in 1963 and 1964.
info_description: A basin in the Ross Sea, north of Lewis Bay, Ross Island, Antarctica.

name: Lewis Bay
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Captain Price Lewis, U.S. Navy, commanding officer of the USS Staten Island during U.S. Navy (USN) Operation Deep Freeze (OpDFrz) 1959, and who in U.S. Navy (USN) Operation Deep Freeze (OpDFrz) 1963 and 1964 was assistant chief of staff and ship group commander, U.S. Naval Support Force, Antarctica.
info_description: Bay indenting the north coast of Ross Island between Mount Bird and Cape Tennyson. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-ME14
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Lewis Cliff
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Richard E. Lewis, Aviation Electronics Technician, US Navy (USN), who was injured during USN Operation Deep Freeze (OpDFrz) II, 1956-57.
info_description: An irregular cliff in the Colbert Hills, the mostly ice-free portion extending south from Mount Achernar for 20km along the west side of Walcott Névé.

name: Lewis Creek

name: Lewis Hill
info_origin: Initially named for David Henry Lewis (1917-2002), who was an expert in traditional Polynesian navigation. He is reputed to have made the first single-handed circumnavigation of Antarctica in the yacht Ice Bird. He also captained the yacht Solo on a scientific expedition to Antarctica in 1977-78. Lewis' name was reapplied to another feature.
info_description: An undersea hill in the Southern Ocean. Maximum depth: 3150m, minimum depth: 2200m, area: 10km x 10km.

name: Lewis Pass
info_origin: ’The pass was first traversed by Europeans in 1860 by the surveyors Henry Lewis and Christopher Maling, who had travelled from Nelson down Cannibal Gorge. In his own 1860 expedition Julius von Haast proposed the name; he was the brother-in-law of Lewis’ daughter. The Lewis Pass road was sometimes referred to as Burbury’s Road.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 M31 Edition 1 1989

name: Lewis Pass Scenic Reserve
info_description: National Reserve, Pt Sec 2 SQUARE 182, Was 1985 p.3172

name: Lewis Ridge
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Commander G.H. Lewis, US Navy (USN), commanding officer of the USS Burton Island during USN Operation Deep Freeze, 1964.
info_description: A rugged, ice-covered ridge, 34km long, extending eastward from the Holland Range, between Morton Glacier and Hewitt Glacier, and terminating at Richards Inlet.

name: Lewis River
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 M31 Edition 1 1989

name: Lewis River
info_origin: 'Tasman. After C. Lewis, who was one of the contractors who formed the Heaphy Track in 1886.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 L26 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-BP22 296711

name: Lewis Seamount
info_origin: Named for David Henry Lewis (1917-2002), who was an expert in traditional Polynesian navigation. He is reputed to have made the first single-handed circumnavigation of Antarctica in the yacht Ice Bird. He also captained the yacht Solo on a scientific expedition to Antarctica in 1977-78.
info_description: An undersea seamount in the Southern Ocean.

name: Lhasa Nunatak
info_origin: The central peak, bearing a striking resemblance to a Tibetan Monastery perched on the top of a hill, was surveyed and given this descriptive name by the Southern Party of the NZGSAE, 1961-62.
info_description: A long snow-free nuntak in the centre of Snakeskin Glacier.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Liberton
info_origin: 'Named after the parish and hill in Edinburgh, Scotland. The Scottish name was a corruption of Lepertown, a ghetto reserved for crusaders who had contracted the disease.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I44 J44 Edition 2 1987

name: Libretto Range
info_origin: Name submitted by the Canterbury Chief Surveyor, August 1971, after research in connection with the revision of NZMS1 maps in the area, in regard to mountain ranges. Name suggested by the Chief Surveyor, the names of the main peaks in this area have operatic associations.
info_description: Mountain range commencing at peak Trovatore [Trig. T (Geodetic Code A83T)], on the Spenser Mountains and extending southwards generally through Mount Lucia [Trig. S (Geodetic Code A840)], to peak Faust [Trig. F (Geodetic Code A83Y)].  Blocks VII, XI, and XV Boyle Survey District.

name: Lichen Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 F38 Edition 1 1995

name: Lichen Hills
info_origin: Lichens were collected at several places hence the name given by the Northern Party of the NZGSAE, 1962-63.

info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Lichen Peak
info_origin: Discovered in December 1934 by the Byrd Antarctic Expedition sledge party under Paul Siple, and so named because of the lichens and other botanical specimens obtained there.
info_description: A peak with exposed rock at 169m standing between Saunders Mountain and Swanson Mountains at the eastern edge of the Sulzberger Ice Shelf, in the Ford Ranges, Marie Byrd Land.

name: Lichen Promontory
info_description: Between Rockey Point and Morseshoe Bay, Ross Island. Dark rock exposures interspersed with snowfields. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME13

name: Lichfield
info_origin: 'From Lichfield, the cathedral town in Staffordshire, England. The settlement was promoted for settlers in 1886. It is to be noted that Bishop George Augustus Selwyn became bishop of Lichfield as well as of New Zealand, and that Lichfield in New Zealand is located in the Selwyn Block.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Locality 6.7km south-southeast of Putāruru. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BE35 473784

name: Lichfield Railway Station
info_ref: Min 2, 105/50; Corres XXV, XXVI pp 203-4, 233; 127; Discontinuation {Objective IDs: A7357523, A792255}
info_origin: The Railway Station takes its name from the locality, which in turn takes its name from Lichfield, the cathedral town in Staffordshire, England. Closed in 1978.
info_description: A former railway station on the Kinleith Branch at Lichfield, between Putāruru, and Tokoroa. Patetere North Survey District. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BE35 473782

Blocks I, II and VII Cass, Blocks IV, VIII, XI, XII, XIV and XV Cook, and Blocks I and V Godley Survey Districts.

name: Lieske Glacier
info_origin: Mapped from air photographs taken by the US Navy. Named by US-ACAN after B.J. Lieske, meteorologist, who wintered at Little America V in 1957.

name: Ligar Creek

name: Light-finger Creek

name: Lighthouse Bay

name: Lighthouse Point

name: Linden
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Joanna Barnes-Wylie, December 2024: Objective ID: A6711452; [Ken Cassells. 1988. Tawa: Enterprise and Endeavour. Wellington: Tawa Borough Council, pp.56-64, 80]; [Bruce Murray. 2014. A History of Tawa. Wellington: Tawa Historical Society, pp.78, 154, 174, 184, 188]; [Bruce Murray. 2021 (Second edition). The Streets of Tawa. Wellington: Tawa Historical Society, pp. 28-33, 37-43]; Designation of Districts: Objective folder ID: fA515085; fA417315
info_origin: The Wellington suburb of Linden took its name from [Linden Railway Station] (https://gazetteer.linz.govt.nz/place/2828) which opened in 1940. The railway station was named after ‘Linden Vale’, a local farm owned by the Duncan family who settled at the northern end of Tawa (then known as Tawa Flat) in the 1860s. Family tradition recounts that Scottish settler Charles Duncan named the farm after his favourite area of Kew Gardens in London. Duncan had trained there as a horticulturalist before emigrating to New Zealand in 1850. In the 1930s around 200 people lived in this northern part of Tawa, some in Ranui (Wellington) Limited’s newly created Tawa Downs subdivision, better known as ‘Ranui’ or ‘Ranui Heights’. Completion of the Tawa Flat rail deviation (1937) and the opening of Linden railway station in 1940 increased accessibility to the area. This improved accessibility and other factors such as post-war peace and prosperity and the finalisation of the new Johnsonville to Porirua motorway route resulted in several further housing developments in the area. In 1949 Ranui (Wellington) Ltd offered their remaining sections east of the confirmed motorway route (completed in 1950) and in the 1950s the government developed ‘Wall Block’ comprising 167 sections in north Linden. Over half of the Wall Block houses were state houses, mostly multi-dwelling units. Community facilities were built in response to the suburb’s growing population such as Linden School which opened in 1952 and the Linden shopping precinct, at its heyday during the late 1940s – 1970s. In the 1970s-1980s Linden developed further to the west of the motorway, with the gradual subdivision of the Duncan family’s Linden Vale farm. Since the 2000s there’s been ongoing development of the suburb’s eastern slopes, including numerous lifestyle blocks.

name: Linden Railway Station
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Joanna Barnes-Wylie, December 2024: Objective ID: A6711452; [Bruce Murray. 2014. A History of Tawa. Wellington: Tawa Historical Society, pp.78, 154]; [Ken Cassells. 1988. Tawa: Enterprise and Endeavour. Wellington: Tawa Borough Council, pp.60–62]; Designation of Districts: Objective folder ID: fA515085
info_origin: Named after local farm ‘Linden Vale’. By the late 1930s around 200 people lived at the northern end of the Tawa Flat valley and those who worked in Wellington City had a difficult journey to and from Tawa Flat Station. They had to walk up to a mile (1.6km) along the railway track or on unformed gravel roads. Consequently, residents requested that the New Zealand Railways Department build another station to the north of Tawa Flat Station. Their efforts were to no avail and residents decided that ‘direct action’ was their only option. It’s reported that they used to regularly pull the emergency cord on the journey home to stop the train, then ‘scuttle off into the night’. Eventually the New Zealand Railways Department agreed to stop trains at Linden on the condition that residents not push for a shelter and it invited the local community to name the station. The community held a meeting and resolved that the station should be named Linden after the Duncan family farm Linden Vale. The attendees noted that the Duncan family had farmed in the area for 80 years and ‘were a very generous and public spirited family’. Stuart Duncan had especially assisted with the campaign for a railway station in Linden. The first trains stopped at Linden Railway Station on 28 July 1940 but the lack of a shelter shed quickly proved to be an issue for commuter comfort. The New Zealand Railways Department soon relented and constructed a shelter shed which opened in April 1941.
info_description: On the North Island Main Trunk between Tawa in the south and Porirua to the north.

info_origin: Named in 1909 for either Annie Lindon (1860-1943) or her husband Leonard Harford Lindon (1859-1953). Leonard was headmaster of the prestigious Geelong Grammar School giving them the means and time to climb in New Zealand. Both were accomplished climbers and organised mountaineering holidays in New Zealand in 1906-12. In 1906, in the company of Malcom Ross, Professor Baldwin Spencer and guide Jack Clarke, they climbed Sealy Range to be rewarded with views of Aoraki/Mount Cook and Mount Sefton. In 1909 Annie Lindon climbed The Nuns Veil (2749m) and the following year crossed Graham Saddle from east to west. That same year, with her husband she ascended Mount Annette (2235m) which was named after her and climbed Glacier Dome (2424m). On a longer visit in 1912, on 12 April she made a successful ascent of Aoraki/Mount Cook (3724m) with guides Peter Graham and Darby Thompson. Returning in 1920, she made numerous other ascents. In the late 1920s various newspapers mistakenly recorded the feature as Linden Ridge and it was also misspelled on topographical maps. In 1972 this error was drawn to the New Zealand Geographic Board’s attention by the daughter of Peter Graham, who had guided the Lindons. The correct spelling was restored by a gazette notice in 1974.

name: Little Akaloa
info_origin: 'The traditional Māori name for the bay is Whakaroa: lit. whaka (Ngāi Tahu dialect for whanga): bay; roa: long. The name should of course be Little Akaroa, but reflects the southern Māori pronunciation of ‘r’. The settlement was designated ‘little’ to distinguish it from Akaroa, and was spelt Hakaroa until a Mr Hampton was appointed postmaster in 1864. When the Honorary Geographic Board considered the name in 1939 most inital comments were in favour of altering it to ‘Akaroa’. However, at its 21 September 1939 meeting, it ultimately upheld the ‘l’ spelling, although board member and Alexander Turnbull librarian Johannes Andersen dissented.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Little America
info_ref: See Plan of Little America & Map of the Bay of Whales published in Richard Byrd (1930) Little America, G.P. Putnam's Sons, New York, pp.232, 416
info_origin: Little America I was first named by Byrd on 1 January 1929. This base, used by the Byrd Antarctic Expedition, 1928-30, and Little America II, the new base built by the Byrd Antarctic Expedition, 1933-35, were established 'about 1 mile' inside Ver-Sur-Mer Inlet, Bay of Whales, about 25m above sea level on the Ross Ice Shelf, in 78º 40' S, 164º 03' W. Little America III, also known as the West Base of the United States Antarctic Service, 1939-41, was established 'about 5 miles' northeast of the east side of the Bay of Whales, in 78º 35'S, 163º 52' W. None of these features exist anymore due to changes in the configuration of the Ross Ice Shelf, particularly the calving of Iceberg B-9 in 1987. Little America IV, the base used by the Central Task Force of the US Navy "Operation Highjump", 1947-47, was established 'about 2 miles' north-northwest of the US Antarctic Services base, in about 78º33' S, 163º 56' W. The latter base was destroyed by calving of the front of the Ross Ice Shelf during the 1948-55 period and was reported non-existent by the Atka in January 1955. Little America V, the main base of US "Operation Deepfreeze", 1956-58, was established 'about 30 miles' northeast of Kainan Bay, in 78º 14' S, 161º 50' W and likewise no longer exists.
info_description: The former area and base used by four United States expeditions led by Admiral Byrd. A fifth Little America was later established northeast of Kainan Bay due to the phyiscal changes in the ice shelf at the Bay of Whales.

name: Longbush
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA417315; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5111558 {Department of Lands and Survey: Discharged Soldier Settlement Report. 1918 Appendicies to the Journals of the House of Representatives, C9; Angela Ballara. 'Mahupuku, Hāmuera Tamahau', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1993. Te Ara; Bagnall, A. Graham. 1976. Wairarapa An Historical Excursion. New Zealand: Heldey’s Bookshop; [House of Representatives. 1902. Evening Post, 15 July, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19020715.2.39) Hill, Ronald. 1963. The Vegetation of the Wairarapa in the Mid-Nineteenth Century. Tuatara. 11, 83-89.}
info_origin: Longbush was in a long ‘tongue’ of forest, which extended in the mid-19th century into the grasslands southeast of Masterton. The area was part of the much larger Ngā-waka-a-Kupe block where two members of the leading Ngāti Hikawera families, Hāmuera Tamahau Mahupuku (c.1840-1904) and his brother Wiremi (Wī) Hikawera Mahupuku successfully leased land while Tamahau Mahupuku also developed his own station. In 1903 Government Land Purchase Commissioners acquired a portion - 8500 acres (3439ha) of the Ngā-Waka-a-Kupe block from Tamahau Mahupuku for closer settlement. This land, which comprised six farms on 2241 acres (906 ha), was balloted under the name Longbush in 1903. Sawmilling commenced on Crown Land here that same year. The Longbush school opened in 1905 and in 1918 discharged soldier settlers took up farms on a portion of the land known as the Longbush Soldier Settlement.

'Heaphy, Charles', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1990. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1h14/heaphy-charles)}
info_origin: A descriptive name for the lookout at the highest point on the Heaphy Track. The routeways Aorere River-Heaphy River served as a subsidiary Māori track for distribution and exchange of greenstone or pounamu and followed a similar route to parts of the Heaphy Track. Although named after artist, surveyor, explorer and public servant Charles Heaphy (1820-81) he never actually journeyed the length of the track that bears his name as it wasn’t completed until 1888. New Zealand Geological Survey geologist Ernest John Herbert Webb (1881-1914) undertook field work in the area in 1907-08 and calculated the spot height marking the highest point of the track as 2967 feet (904m). This was incorporated into a Geological Map of Wakamarama Survey District drawn by George Edward Harris and published in 1923. Lands and Survey published a simplified map of the track for trampers in 1961, which was drawn by Clifford Holdsworth (1908-2004). Revised editions followed in 1964 and 1968. This marked Lookout Point only as the ‘highest point’ on the track which was rounded to 3000 feet (914m) but did indicate a forest clearing where the surrounding country could be viewed from. Lands and Survey’s 1984 map of the Heaphy Track labelled the highest point as Flanagans Corner, there being a bend in the track. The corner may possibly be named after the Commissioner of Crown Lands for Nelson (1906-09) Frederick William Flanagan (1856-1925) and later Valuer-General. Department of Conservation signage notes that the ‘Lookout’ is 150m from the corner.
info_description: The highest place on the Heaphy Track, on the southwest of Brown Hill, east of Gouland Downs. Feature shown on: NZMS260 M26 Edition 1 1986; NZTopo50-BP23 513717

info_origin: A descriptive name seemingly applied to distinguish it from another junction 2km upstream (later known as Upper Junction). A miners’ track ran alongside Tākaka River up to Grecian Stream. Mineral licences were issued for this area in the mid-1890s, and asbestos was discovered near the junction of Tākaka River and Grecian Stream. The New Zealand Asbestos Company established to mine these deposits in 1898 went into liquidation in 1899 although not before a track had been cut from Tākaka River to the mine site. Robert Sadd, the Nelson District Surveyor, made a trigonometrical and topographical survey of the area from Mount Arthur to the West Coast including the headwaters of Tākaka River from 1897-1902. He later noted that around 1900 he ‘went through the Flora bridle track over a low saddle and down Ghost Creek to where the old tunnel is situated, and partly explored this tunnel to see the seams of asbestos’. At this time a track existed to the saddle between Ghost Creek and Tākaka River which as a newspaper editorial noted, ‘if extended a mile would junction with the track over the Flora Saddle’. The track along Tākaka River to Upper Junction is shown as complete on Lands and Survey maps from 1944. But the place was still unnamed and indeed Lower Junction was not listed in the 1968 Gazetteer of New Zealand Place Names but was included on the metric 1977 1:50000 map series.

Wellington: Government Printer.; [Moawhango and the Awarua Block. 1894. Lyttelton Times, 16 April, Page 2](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/LT18940416.2.7); [The Timaru Settlement, 1898. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2h7/hall-jones-william) (accessed 21 December 2022); [Plan of Kawhatau improved small farms settlement, 1895.]( https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE18395918)}
info_origin: An original Māori name given to the river which formed a boundary of the 300000 acres (121405 ha) land block purchased by the Crown in the early 1890s. Kawhātau fleetingly attracted settler attention in 1869 when small quantities of gold were found in the river. The northern most extension of the main trunk railway reached what eventually became Lower Kawhātau in 1892. A Kawhatau Improved Small Farms Settlement comprising a dozen 80-90 acre (32ha-36ha) sections were surveyed by 1895. This was a new system of settlement whereby groups of aspiring farmers with little capital were employed on a co-operative basis to form access roads and fell bush and later be allocated one of the sections. Lands and Survey Head Office Assistant Draughtsman, Arthur Langdon Haycock (1860-1948), drew up the plan of the small farm settlement. This included a Tōtara Reserve intended to save valuable tōtara forest for use at a later date. A school site was also part of the original design. Many the original settlers came from Timaru and the locality was informally known as the Hall-Jones 'Timaru settlement, Kawhatua'. Timaru MP, William Hall-Jones (1851-1936), was a supporter of closer land settlement and as the Minister of Public Works was focused on completing the North Island Main Trunk railway line. In 1898 one of the original settlers wrote, 'I am very well satisfied with my farm, I have felled, burned, and sown in grass about 63 (25ha) acres of the 83 (36ha), and fenced it, which means about 78 chains (1569m) of fencing, worth 14s a chain. I have “stumped” three-quarters of an acre (0.3ha) for a garden (£7), and I have a whare, dairy, cowshed, well, etc., in all worth about £80, towards which the Government advanced £30. The rest I have had to do myself, and it has been a “hard scrap” up to the present, but I shall begin to reap the benefit of it now'. Many properties proved to be too small to be economically viable once the public works were completed. Lower Kawhātau came into use around 1902 to distinguish the settlement from the one at the head of the valley which was known from 1897 as Upper Kawhātau.

Name was obtained from Mr Allan Dick M.P., and provisionally approved in 1969. An objection was raised regarding the name, and dismissed by the Geographic Board. About 1912 two men were camped in a hut on Lucifer flat, they left the hut one morning and looked back to see the hut a mass of flames. the two men lost all their belongings, including cameras and photographic records. "Lucifer" matches were deemed to be the cause of the fire. The flat was thus named, and the stream takes its name from the flat. Name is a local one and submitted by the runholders in the region.

name: Luncheon Cove
info_origin: Name submitted by A C Begg of Dunedin in May 1963, to reinstate several Cook names. Luncheon Cove is the site of the first house built in New Zealand, by William Leith, and the first sealing gang to land in New Zealand, landed here. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDYwRjBCNkI2OTEwMEQyM0VGQzY); 'On Anchor Island, Dusky Sound. On 12 April 1773 Captain James Cook wrote: ‘I found here a very snug cove sheltered from all winds, which we called Luncheon Cove, because here we dined on crayfish, on the side of a pleasant brook, shaded by the trees from both wind and sun.’ Luncheon Cove is the site of the first European house built in New Zealand, by William Leith, and the first landing by a sealing gang. Māori name: Pīkōau: lit, pī: chicks or nestlings; kōau: shag or cormorant (Phalacrocorax varius).' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Lyttelton
info_origin: 'Lyttelton Harbour/Whakaraupō: After European settlement the township and harbour had several names bestowed on them until the final decision to honour Lord Lyttelton, a staunch supporter of the Canterbury Association. The harbour was earlier known as Port Victoria, and was called Port Cooper by Captain Wiseman, who was agent for the Sydney merchants Cooper & Levey (see also Port Levy). Maori name for the harbour: Whakaraupō: lit. whaka (South Island form of whanga): harbour or bay; raupō: native reed or bulrush (Typha orientalis). The great Ngati Kahu rangatira Te Rakiwhakaputa gave this name to the heads of Lyttelton Harbour only, as reeds grew in profusion there. See also Okete (Oketeupoko).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

Lyttle's doctor had been doubtful about Lyttle going on an expedition to Fiordland in the summer of 1908-1909, and had enquired, facetiously, if Lyttle was going to look for a farm. When the party struck this clearing on the upper Hollyford River / Whakatipu Kā Tuka in early 1909, William (Bill) Grave, Arthur Talbot and 'Charlie' Gifford jokingly named it 'Lyttle's Farm'.

name: Macaskill Lakes
info_origin: Named for Stuart Alisdair Macaskill (1931-2012) in recognition of his significant contribution to establishing this water supply feature for metropolitan Wellington. He played an instrumental political role in the creation of the lakes from 1974 through to their completion in the late 1980s. He had a keen interest in civil engineering projects and lived most of his life in nearby Akatarawa Valley. He was highly regarded by Regional Council staff, being on the Board from 1980 until his retirement in 2001, becoming Chair from 1986. He enjoyed many other achievements in local body and community affairs, including long time association with Upper Hutt and Heretaunga Rotary Clubs.

name: Mackenzie Pass/Manahuna
info_origin: 'Canterbury. Named after the notorious Scottish sheep stealer, James McKenzie (so spelt), who in January 1856 was officially pardoned for his alleged offences. The romance that surrounds this strange Inverness-shire man was heightened by his several escapes from the Lyttelton jail. As Sir Alfred Reed has said: ‘It was this Gaelic shepherd who, as the first European to encounter the Mackenzie Plains, stumbled upon a hinterland that unmasked such beautiful upland lakes as Tekapo, Pukaki, and Ohau lying at the foot of the snowy mountains.’ Maori name of Mackenzie Pass: Manahuna: this was where McKenzie was discovered with the stolen sheep. It seems to be a corruption of Manahune or Manahouna.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for James Mackenzie](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1m30/mackenzie-james)

name: Māhia
info_origin: 'Mahia Peninsula: Lit. to sound, or resound. The ancient name of the peninsula was Te Mahiamaitawhiti, lit. the murmurings of home, named by Ruawharo of the Takitimu canoe for its resemblance to a place in the homeland. Ruawharo left the canoe to deposit gravel brought from Hawaiki here, following his mother’s advice to him to settle ‘where a whale is cast ashore’. That is why he stood up and cried, ‘This is Mahia!’ when he saw a headland that resembled a whale.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Māhia is a traditional Māori name for the larger land mass known today as Māhia Peninsula, itself a contraction of a longer name brought to New Zealand via Tahiti. Shore based whaling stations developed on both sides of the peninsula in the early 1840s. Donald McLean, as general government agent, bought the peninsula as part of a wider set of Hawke’s Bay land purchases in 1864. A town was laid out by Michael Fitzgerald in 1865 at Te Mahia. Fitzgerald, a civil engineer and surveyor, had arrived in Wellington around 1845 and was in charge of road construction. By 1853 he was head of the Survey Department of Wellington and later, Chief Surveyor for Wellington Province and Hawkes Bay Province. As Surveyor of Native Lands, he laid out the towns of Te Māhia and Wairoa in 1865. On Augustus Koch’s (1834/35?-1901) 1873 map of Hawkes Bay, Te Mahia is labelled as Māhia and approximates the present-day locality of Māhia Beach with Māhia later being assigned to a settlement on the eastern side of the peninsula.

name: Mahurangi
info_origin: 'Auckland, 17 km from Warkworth. Lit. a term applied to important people, food, etc. A popular translation is Sky piercer. Another explanation is that the name honours a chieftainness in Hawaiki who designed the Tainui canoe (which later landed here). Mahurangi was originally the name for a small island off Waiwera, but was transferred by early settlers to the harbour to the north, which was originally Waihe or Kaihu. But any transfer must have been very early, since Cudlip (mate of HMS Buffalo) in 1834 shows it as ‘Maurhangi Harbour’. Also an early name for Warkworth.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Maimai
info_origin: ‘Near Reefton. The word is not Māori, although in te reo ‘maimai’ is a song or haka of welcome to a tangihanga. The name of this West Coast town owes more to duck shooting and appears to have been an import from Australian to New Zealand English via the Victorian goldfields. Australian gold-diggers prospecting in New Zealand used the term mia-mia to describe the rough shelters they erected. Eminent Australian toponymist Jan Tent writes that the word, widely in use in Victoria, has its origin as maya or maya-maya (a hut or shelter) in Nyungar, the language of the Perth-Albany region in Western Australia. Maimai was called Squaretown until the construction of the railway began in 1889.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: A small pā site - Warehou sometimes known as Mākara Pā exists on the headland. Archaeological evidence is conflicting and while the pā was occupied in the 18th century there may have been an earlier phase of occupation in the 14th century. Another pā, Ohariu pā, was recorded as being at the mouth of Mākara River in 1841. Reed offered ‘Maka’ ‘to throw’ and ‘rau’ ‘to catch in a net’ as a literal translation, while much earlier in 1918 Dominion Museum ethnologist Elsdon Best considered it was being ‘woefully mispronounced’ and that it was more accurately rendered as Makara with first and last vowels long. Best also put forward a quite different interpretation of the meaning of the name. Of the stream that flows from Mākara Hill northward to Owhariu Bay he observed that ‘in stream names mā is often an abbreviated form of manga (a stream or tributary); thus, Mangakarā may be the full name’ with kara - a stone. Settlers resided at the township of Mākara from the 1860s, with Mākara Beach some 3km away being only scantily occupied as late as the 1890s. By the 1920s it was becoming a popular seaside destination, although still remote and with minimal facilities. In 1932 it was described as ‘a barren, shingly bay, enclosed by high, rugged cliffs, about 23 miles (37km) due west of Wellington’. There was a good road to within ‘half a mile (800m) of the beach, the remainder of the journey having to be covered on foot over sparse growth on sand. It is a lonely portion of the coast seldom visited even in summer, and there are no houses within a mile of the spot. A small, turbulent stream enters the sea at the northern end of the bay, which is not more than half a mile from tip to tip’.

info_origin: An original Māori name for the associated stream. Writer-historian Alexander Wyclif Reed (1908-79) suggested as a literal translation ma: stream and karaka for the tree - Corynocarpus lavigatus - growing on its banks consistent with journalist-historian James Cowan (1870-1943) who considered ma was short for manga, the branch of a river. Edward Dollimore (1904-73) compiler of the New Zealand Guide followed suit with ‘stream of the karaka tree’. The endemic karaka has drupes with edible flesh, but the poisonous kernel requires special treatment to make it safe to eat. Karaka were planted around Māori settlements as a food crop particularly in pre-European times. Stonemason Thomas U’ren (1812-60) and family landed in Wellington in 1840 settling at Mākaraka the following year. Robert Espie (1811-68) a carpenter from NSW who arrived in Poverty Bay in 1838 as a trader also purchased 120 acres (49 ha) at Mākaraka in 1845. The Old Land Claims Commissioners disallowed Espie’s claims in 1860. The first Crown land purchase in Poverty Bay took place at Mākaraka in 1857 when 57 acres (23 ha) were acquired for £85. Resident Magistrate, Herbert Samuel Waddell (1830-1912) signed on behalf of the Crown, the sellers being Kahutia and his family and sons-in-law. Known as the Government Block it was the site of the first courthouse and Resident Magistrate’s house and later became a cemetery and domain. Rongowhakaata military leader and prophet Te Kooti (?-1893) attacked Mākaraka and other settlements in 1868. An Armed Constabulary camp at Mākaraka served as a marshalling point for a force under Lieutenant Colonel George Whitmore (1829-1903) and Major Wahawaha Rāpata (1807?-97) that captured Ngātapa Pā in January 1869. A well sunk at Mākaraka in 1877 provided both water and for several years a supply of natural gas for lighting the town’s hotel. Ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) observed that the river name had been applied by Europeans to a town. He was referring to the small 13 section township surveyed in 1908 by George Edwards under Section 16 of the Land Act, 1908. This was initially described as the Township of Glyn, but the Surveyor-General Thomas Humphries (1841-1928) overruled the district office on the grounds that the nearby railway station was already known as Makaraka and that the town should take the same name. He also considered Glyn to be a poor choice as it would be too easily confused with the existing Glen. In 1947 Makaraka Domain was the site of a temporary transit housing camp established under war time emergency regulations.

info_ref: Objective ID: A3360780; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412 {Beattie, Herries. 2001. Maori place-names of Otago (first published 1944). New Zealand: Cadsonbury Publications; Beattie, Herries. 2006. Otago Place Names (first published 1948). New Zealand: Cadsonbury Publications; Land for Settlements Act, 1894. 1899. info_origin: This is an original Māori name for the locality and was carried over onto the first survey plans for the area in the 1860s. Thereafter, the locality took the name of successive land holders being known sequentially as Hopkinson’s, Fraser’s, Wayne’s and later Kitchener’s. The locality was also known for a time as The Grange. Colonel Kitchener purchased land here in 1869 and named his estate Makareao. In 1896 AB Kitchener offered the estate to the Government which purchased it under the Lands for Settlement Act for closer land settlement. This sale was completed in two blocks of 2368 acres (958 ha) and 2536 acres (1026 ha) for £12239 and balloted that same year. In 1897 Government geologist James Hector reported rich limestone reserves in the area and kilns were constructed in 1899. The Makareao Branch Railway line was constructed from Palmerston to Inch Valley. Two European collectors of Māori place names offered rather different translations: Herries Beattie recorded an early version as Matau-kareao which he translated a fishhook and kareao supplejack, while Sherwood Roberts considered it was likely a misspelling of Makareho which he translated as ‘a bad throw’.

info_ref: Doubtful Sound SW Chart©, Irwin & Main 1981B; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836
info_origin: The University of Auckland website records that under the Spanish Crown, between 1789 and 1794 Alejandro Malaspina led a “political and scientific voyage” around the Pacific. Malaspina’s expedition, which made landfall off Doubtful Sound on 25 February 1793, was directed to describe and categorise what they saw. On his return to Spain, Malaspina became entangled in palace intrigues, and so the results of the expedition remained unpublished for many decades afterwards.
info_description: A depression in the sea floor trending north-west, south-east along the length of Malaspina Reach, descending to a maximum depth of 435m, and located approximately 2km north-west from Matai Island in Doubtful Sound / Patea, Fiordland.

name: Malaspina Reach
info_origin: Name changed in 1964 from the official Malaspina Sound, as a number of names appeared on various maps and charts over the years. The Geographic Board initiated the change and the Hydrographer, Royal New Zealand Navy suggested the extent of the reach. At the same time, the name Doubtful Sound was given to the length of the sound, from the Tasman Sea, to Deep Cove. Alessandro Malaspina was an Italian sea captain in command of a Spanish expidition that visited Doubtful Sound in 1793; 'Malaspina, Mount: Southern Alps, near Mt Dampier. After Don Alessandro Malaspina, the Spanish navigator. He led an expedition that included the Descubierta, the Atrevida, and the Sutie, which visited the West Coast Sounds in 1793. The reach was formerly called Malaspina Creek and Malaspina Sound, after Alessandro Malaspina. Earlier called Smith Sound by Captain John Lort Stokes after the second master of the Acheron, J.W. Smith.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Doubtful Sound. To be applied to that portion of the sound from Marcaciones Point (Flurry Head, Bauza Island) to Kellard Point, the eastern point at the entrance of Crooked Arm.

info_origin: Manawatāwhi is the original Māori name for this group of islands which were once occupied by Māori but are now a nature reserve. The largest was named Three Kings Island by Abel Tasman in 1643. Previously shown as Three Kings Islands on map and chart. Claudia Orange. ['Northland places - Aupōuri Peninsula', Te Ara - the Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, updated 2-Mar-09](http://www.TeAra.govt.nz/en/northland-places/1). See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDlCNjMyN0MxRTEwMEQwMjVBQUM).; 'Lit. manawa: breath; tāwhi: to hold back; Out of breath, because the original chief of the islands swam there from North Cape and arrived exhausted. Abel Tasman named the largest island Drie Coninge Eijlandt: lit. Island of the Three Kings in 1643 during the season of Epiphany, which celebrates the three magi or kings worshipping the infant Jesus. The name now applies to all the islands.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: ’Lit. manawa: heart; tū: to stand; Heart standing still, or Depressed spirit. The name was given by the tohunga Haunui-a-Nanaia while travelling down the west coast in pursuit of his wife Wairaka, who had eloped; when he reached the wide river Hau was downcast at the prospect of crossing. Māori knew the Manawatū Gorge as Te Au-rere-a-te-tonga: lit. te: the; au: current or torrent; rere: swift; a: of; te: the; tonga: south. A name for the district was Te Taperenui-o-Whatonga: lit. te: the; tapere: district; nui: large; o: of; Whatonga. The early chief Whatonga paddled up the Manawatū River and noticed how easily the tangata whenua (local people) could be defeated by invaders. A little-known alternative refers to a group of warriors who refreshed themselves in the river after a battle, and so rejuvenated, returned to claim victory, hence Manawatū: New heart.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: The story of Manawatū is recorded in an oriori (lullaby) composed for a girl named Wharaurangi by her uncle, Te Rangitakoru. The story tells of an ancestor Haunui-a-Nanaia searching for his wife who eloped with another man, naming the waterways he came across on his journey. When he came across the (Manawatū) river his heart settled (or stopped momentarily). There are a number of other stories and meanings for Manawatū, all being the compound of the words manawa (the physical heart) and tū (stop, stand). The correct meaning for the name ‘Whanganui’ is: the long wait, one meaning of ‘whanga’ being ‘to wait’. This conceptual naming is associated with the Kupe history, when he explored the interior and left a contingent at the estuary. There is also an oral history account that relates to the Ngāti Apa ancestor, Haunui, again referring to the long wait for the tide to change so that he could cross the river in pursuit of his wife. A third common but non-‘Whanganui’ version, which has gained more recent prominence, is the meaning ‘big harbour or bay’ – referring to the river’s large mouth, subject to tidal change and influence.

info_origin: The history and naming of Mandeville,  a rural locality 18 kilometres northwest of Gore, is linked to the Waimea Plains Railway. In 1878 Waimea Plains Railway Company Limited was formed under the District Railways Act 1877 for the purpose of constructing a railway from Gore to The Elbow (Lumsden). The railway was promoted as greatly improving the connection between Dunedin and the Central Otago lakes while also opening up some of New Zealand’s ‘finest agricultural land’, including the Waimea Plains. This land was owned by the newly established New Zealand Agricultural Company who had purchased several large stations. The stations included Wantwood and Caroline, co-owned by Joseph Clarke, Esq. of Tasmania and Patrick K. McCaughan, Esq, two of the directors of the Waimea Plains Railway Company Limited. By early 1879 surveys were underway for the new townships to be developed in proximity to the stations, which included Riversdale, St Patricks and Mandeville. Waimea Plains Railway Company Limited directors reportedly had naming rights for the railway stations and new settlements along the railway line. Various meanings have been provided for Mandeville, the name of the settlement established on the former Wantwood Station co-owned by McCaughan and Clarke. Some sources state that it was named for Viscount Mandeville, later Duke of Manchester. However, it’s understood that McCaughan named Mandeville after Norton Mandeville, Clarke’s Tasmanian estate. Norton Mandeville was originally established and named by Englishman John Beaumont, presumably after the ancient Essex parish of Norton Mandeville. Clarke’s fondness for the name Mandeville is also evident from the Melbourne residence he purchased in 1876 and named Mandeville Hall. The Mandeville survey plan indicates a sizeable settlement laid out with streets named after North American places (mostly states), reflecting the ambitions and optimism of the Waimea Railway Company for the town’s future. Mandeville was the first settlement to develop on the line of Waimea Plains Railway and when the railway line opened in July 1880, it comprised a railway siding, the Mandeville Hotel (later the Railway Hotel) and a store. Further growth followed, but Mandeville never became the envisaged ‘centre of some importance’. In 1900 the Otago Witness described Mandeville as a ‘little village’, with just over 100 residents.

info_origin: 'Mandeville North: Canterbury, 13 km from Kaiapoi. name: Mangakōkakotaea Stream
info_origin: Kokakotaea (arrival of the kokako) is the name given by Rereahu tupuna to a stream that commences on Pureora mountain and flows through part Maraeroa A Block thence into Maraeroa C Block where it traverses the entire width of that block prior to joining the Ongarue River just below the Wilton Falls. During the native logging operations on the Maraeroa C Block in earlier years this block was affectionately known by the native bushmen as the KK Block being a shortened version of Kokakotaea.
info_description: A stream approximately 14km in length located approximately 45km west northwest of Taupo, with its source near the summit of Pureora within Pureora Forest Park, flowing generally southwest towards Kawauariki Falls. Feature shown on: NZMS260 T17; NZTopo50-BF35 285301 to BG34 185265

Bell, Pirongia, a well known conservationist advised that Mangakotukutuku is considered to be the correct form, however Mangakotuku meaning "stream of the white heron" is also a possibility, but Kotuku visits were like a blue moon. Mr Pick can recall two visits only in 48 years.

info_origin: A descriptive name for the area nearby to where Mangamuka River was bridged, initially in the 1880s. The wider area had the original Māori name of Mangamuka, literally translated as creek and muka the sprout of nīkau palm or a brittle flax and included a marae and 'Mangamuka Maori School'. Mangamuka Bridge was in use at least by 1893 when there was local opposition to efforts to build a licensed hotel. The original bridge was destroyed in a flood in 1916 by which time the name was well established. The replacement bridge was completed in 1922. In 1934 local residents approached Hokianga County Council to have their district named Mangamuka Bridge. This was approved by the Council in November 1934. Simultaneously 50 local residents and members of the Mangamuka Valley Settlers Association also petitioned the Minister of Internal Affairs to make Mangamuka Bridge official. The Director-General of Post and Telegraph services was agreeable to renaming their Taikawhana Telephone Office and the surrounding postal area as Mangamuka Bridge. Internal Affairs forwarded the petitioners' request to the Honorary Geographic Board. Board member ethnologist Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) was concerned about the likelihood of confusion between Mangamuka and Mangamuka Bridge, particularly as it might delay mail deliveries. With the two places 3km apart another Board member, surveyor Maurice Crompton-Smith (1864-1954) did not see difficulties. Early in 1935 the Under Secretary for Internal Affairs pressed the Board for a decision. Andersen expressed his opposition to what he saw as 'duplication' of names and indicated he would vote against the proposal. The Surveyor-General also thought the proposed name 'rather cumberous' but it was officially gazetted in 1935 under the Designation of Districts Act, 1908.

info_origin: An original Māori name applied to an area at the junction of Mangaotaki River and Waitanguru Stream. Ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member, Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) believed this was a ‘commemorative name’ but was uncertain of the meaning which he thought translated to either the place of speech making – ‘a stream of oratory’ or to O Taki, a personal name. But he also considered it a ‘doubtful spelling’ following the Nomenclature Committee of 1908 which included Mangaotaki in a list of post offices with suspect Māori spelling. Andersen also recorded that the associated Mangaotaki River meant ‘beautiful rapid river’ and considered that the place name was derived from the waterway. New Zealand Geographic Board member Peehi Te Hurunui Jones (1898-1976), an accomplished translator and genealogist considered it was properly Tanga O Take and that Take or Taake was a personal name. In 1904 prospective European land settlers requested that the government provide road access to the Mangaotaki Block. Significant forest clearance followed, and 1600 acres (647 ha) was felled ‘ready for burning’ in 1906. Previously the scenery of Mangaotaki Gorge had been recognised – a deputation waiting on Deputy Prime Minister Sir Joseph Ward (1856-1930) had requested its preservation in 1903. A small 10 acres (4 ha) scenic reserve was gazetted in 1907 with a larger 121 acres (49 ha) area reserved in 1913. A named polling station was set up for the 1908 elections and a post office was opened in 1909.

However, the Williams Māori dictionary under Taipo writes: 'Goblin' states ''Note - this word is used by Maoris believing it to be English, and by Europeans believing it Maori, it being apparently neither. name: Mangapū Stream
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: ‘Ngāti Tamaoho have strong cultural, traditional and historic links with the waters of their awa. The rivers are the life-blood of their rohe. From them come the means for survival by way of lamprey, tuna and other kaimoana. They also provide the main means of travel and trade to many otherwise inaccessible parts of the rohe during ancient times. They also provided the main sources of fresh water, essential for survival. Thus, they were the connecting tissue between the many kainga, pa and cultivation throughout the rohe. Moreover, they were a source of great mana for Ngāti Tamaoho. Their use for travel, resources and kai was closely governed by complex principle of tikanga. Sometimes their use was shared and at other times it was used by other tribes on a reciprocal basis. Mangapu (Symonds Stream) drains from the foot-hills east of Drury and the Pahurehure Inlet. From here it flows west, eventually joining Outwairoa (Slippery Creek). It then meets with the Manukau Harbour near the former Opaheke kainga. Mangapu once flowed through the vast Mangapikopiko wetlands which lay stretched across the Drury lowlands. This was an especially important place for Ngāti Tamaoho who drew many resources from it. Building materials such as raupo and flax could be obtained from its shallow waters as could many important medicinal plants. The use of Mangapikopiko and of Mangapu was a source of great mana to Ngāti Tamaoho who cherished them and their mauri. Prior to deforestation of its catchment and other contributing factors, Mangapu would have been far wider, deeper and faster flowing. Traditional evidence recalls that the rivers in this area were navigable for several miles inland. Stories tell of waka from the Manukau being able to travel upstream to settlements located near the foothills. Ngāti Tamaoho often built settlements at the mouths of rivers to benefit from their great wealth of kaimoana. Tuna were harvested with nets or weirs built across strategic parts of the rivers. Ngāti Tamaoho were experts at the sustainable use of the resources of these awa. The lives of the people were closely intertwined with the quantity and quality of the freshwater that was available to them. It provide habitat and spawning grounds for native plants, bird and fish, building and weaving materials such as raupo and flax, and precious medicines and dyes. Modifications to waterways and their catchment areas have significantly altered the relationship of Ngāti Tamaoho with these resources. The protection of freshwater resources remains one of most important parts of the responsibilities of Ngāti Tamaoho as kaitiaki of the environment and their rohe. Values (both tangible and intangible) that are assigned to specific water bodies include: Ngāti Tamaoho believe that each waterway carries its own mauri. A water body with a healthy mauri will sustain healthy ecosystems, support cultural uses and mahinga kai, and be a source of pride and identity to the tangata whenua.'

info_origin: This is an original Māori name for a kāinga or village at the southern end of the inlet where geologist Julius Haast stayed in 1860 in the latter part of his topographical and geological expedition of the western parts of Nelson Province. From the coast Haast and his party crossed the 1000 to 1200 ft (300 to 365m) heavily forested limestone range and came on to the West Whanganui mudflat. Here Haast recorded 'On the east lay the broad swampy plains of the Manga-manga-rakau, bounded by the Whakamarama range, over which appeared the snowy peaks of the mountains on the eastern side of the Aorere valley'. They hugged the western shore, and late in the day at the southern end of the inlet came to what Haast described as unoccupied 'Maori huts' where they spent a comfortable night. Haast recorded 'Mangamangarakua' as the name of the waterway – todays Mangarākau River. In 1862 James Mackay, the Assistant Native Secretary, confirmed that the Mangamangarakua river also formed one of the boundaries of the 'Taitapu native reserve'. In 1897 the Mangamangarakua became part of the redefined boundary of Nelson Land District and the following year, with the same spelling, was one of a number of rivers designated for depositing of tailings under mining legislation. Further along the inlet in 1896 the Taitapu Gold Estates had established an office at a locality then called Parkeston. A postmaster was appointed in 1897 and by 1901 the place was known as 'West Wanganui mudflat (Parkeston)'. When the post office was reopened in 1904 the Chief Postmaster in Nelson specified that it would in future be known as Mangarakau, seemingly shortening the name. This was in accordance with Post Office policy of the time to prioritise the use of Māori names for new offices.

name: Mangatainoka
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412; A5139248; A5383948 {Department of Lands and Survey. 1927. Appendicies to the Journals of the House of Representatives, C1A. [Lowe’s retirement]; Andersen, Johannes C. 1942. Maori Place Names. New Zealand: Polynesian Society; [Obituary Mr. Henry James Lowe, 1937. New Zealand Herald, 20 May, Page 14](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH19370520.2.154); [Mangatainoka Village Special Settlement Map 1887 Alexander Turnbull Library](https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE26852257); Chapman-Taylor, M. 1944. The Late Henry Matthew Stowell (“Hare Hongi”) (1859-1944). Journal of the Polynesian Society, 53, 106-110; Maori Place Names R21682778, Archives NZ, Wellington [Register of NZPO names]}
info_origin: An original Māori name shared with the Mangatainoka Stream. Literally translated as the stream of Tainoka (Carmichaelia australis), a Māori name for the native broom. Also adopted by local Māori occupants of this district. The New Zealand Post Office which was trying to use correct Māori spellings for the names of its branches recorded a different meaning, manga ‘the branch of a river, a tributary’ and tai noka ‘to pull sharply away’. This matched the course of the river south of Mangatainoka Railway Station. The information had been supplied by Hone Hapi, a local authority and was confirmed by the knowledgeable and well-versed translator Henry Matthew Stowell (1859-1944) who often wrote under the pen name of Hare Hongi. In a series of land sales from 1873, the Mangatainoka lands passed into Crown ownership. Wellington Provincial Superintendent William Fitzherbert acted on the government’s behalf. Under the Native Land Purchase Act, 1877, the Mangatainoka Block of 74018 acres (29954ha) was acquired. The Mangatainoka village settlement was surveyed by Henry J. Lowe (1862-1936). Lowe was appointed to Lands and Survey in 1882. He undertook topographical work in the Remutaka Range, Tararua Range, Ruahine Range and Kaimanawa Mountains. During the 1880s he also completed surveys of settlements in the 40 Mile Bush including Mangatainoka, as well as at Pohangina, Awarua and Waimarino. Lowe later served as Chief Surveyor and Commissioner of Crown Lands in Taranaki and North Auckland. The North Island Brewery Company Limited established a brewery under the Tui brand at Mangatainoka in the early 20th century. Approximately 15 children from the Polish Children's Camp in Pahiatua attended Mangatainoka School in 1949.

name: Māngere
info_origin: ’Lit. lazy, laziness. When Īhenga journeyed northwards from the thermal regions he rested here for a while, leaving his followers to prepare a meal. They took so long that their leader was angry and commemorated the event by this name. Another version attributes the incident to Īhenga’s uncle, Kahumatamomoe. Variations of the name also occur in Rarotonga and Tahiti. During the 1840s Māori objected to the name and suggested Queen’s Town as a substitute, but no change was made. The neighbouring hill at Māngere was called Mount Elliot, after a European who witnessed the deed that ceded part of the Tāmaki Isthmus to the government.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: A descriptive name that came into use for the area once the bridge over Manukau Harbour connecting Onehunga and Mangere was completed. An Onehunga and Mangere Bridge Company was established in 1866 but was soon dissolved without completing any work. Regardless, its value was recognized: 'If a bridge were across to Mangere the whole of the lands would be soon opened up for settlement, and it required no prophet to tell them that when that boon was granted to them the property would soon rise immensely in value. In fact, the whole of that district would soon become studded with tradesmen's villas. There were 10,000 acres [4047 ha] of land that would be directly benefited by it, and…. the bridge would raise all that land in value at least £2 per acre. But the benefit would not be confined to Mangere alone'. In 1871 the Auckland Provincial Government corresponded inconclusively with the General Government about using land confiscated at Māngere during the New Zealand Wars to fund the proposed bridge. Tenders were called for by John Blackett (1818-93), Assistant Engineer in Chief of New Zealand Railways in 1873 and the bridge was completed in 1875. Almost immediately the name Māngere Bridge was used for the surrounding area. In 1874 George Vause applied unsuccessfully to the Licensing Court for a hotel licence at Māngere Bridge, a move that was opposed by a petition of 25 residents. The sale of land described as being at Māngere Bridge commenced that same year. Māngere Bridge Post Office opened in 1886. The first moves toward establishing a school at Māngere Bridge began in 1889. William Ferguson Massey (1856-1925), later Prime Minister, was elected as the school board chairperson. Tawhiao (?-1894), the second Māori king, had 11 acres (4.5 ha) at Māngere Bridge where he built a cottage around 1890 on a block returned to Māori under individualized title in 1867 having been confiscated under the New Zealand Settlement Act, 1863. After the death of Tawhiao the house was occupied by family members including children attending school in the area.

info_origin: Named descriptively with reference to its location to Māngere. A Mangere Road East existed by 1886 and Māngere East was used as a location in various death notices and property sales from the late 1890s. Efforts to secure a Māngere East school dated from 1913. In 1921 Prime Minister William Ferguson Massey (1856-1925) declined to sell some of his land at Māngere East for the school site. Deeper local identification of the area as Māngere East is found in the building of a Māngere East Hall and a successful ratepayers’ poll to raise £3500 to construct a recreation ground in 1923. Local Māngere East teams played in the ‘Outer suburban’ sports competition from 1926. In 1935 the government, after repeated representations by the Mangere East Rate Payers’ Association, agreed to establish a Mangere East Post Office, acknowledging that ‘This locality, although closely settled, has been without facilities for counter business and residents are compelled to travel fully two miles [3.2km], to either Otahuhu or Mangere Central, to transact ordinary business’. During WWII the US Army established a supply depot – Camp Euart which covered 84 acres (34 ha) in Māngere East. Edward Dollimore’s New Zealand Guide for 1951 listed Māngere East as a locality in Manukau County. Four years later in 1955 Māngere East became a Town District. In 1965 it was absorbed into Manukau City, which became part of the enlarged Auckland in 2010.

name: Mangles Valley
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412; A5139248 {Mitchell, Hillary and John. (1996). Kehu (Hone Mokehakeha): biographical notes. Nelson Historical Journal 6 (1), 3-19; [Account of an Exploring Expedition to the S.W. of Nelson. 1846. Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle, 14 March, Page 5](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NENZC18460314.2.3); [Notes of a Journey from Nelson … by James MacKay Esq. Jnr. 1860. Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle, 16 May, Page 2](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NENZC18600516.2.12); [Mr. Blackett’s report on the inland route from Nelson to the West Coast.1863. Colonist, 5 May, Page 3](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/TC18630505.2.17)}
info_origin: The valley and river were named for Ross Donnelly Mangles (1801-77). Mangles was a Director of the New Zealand Company and later chair of the East India Company. In the UK he was MP for Guildford (1841-57) and in 1842 author of a pamphlet ‘How to colonize: the interest of the country and the duty of the Government’. William Fox, Thomas Brunner, Charles Heaphy, and their guide Kehu (Hone Mokehakeha) (c.1798-1850s?), journeyed into southwest Nelson searching for open country in 1846. Fox, Brunner, and Heaphy applied the Mangles name to the river and valley. In 1860, James Mackay when travelling from Lake Rotorua to the Grey Valley muddled the Mangles Valley with the Tiraumea. Nelson provincial engineer John Blackett’s report on the Mangles Valley in 1863 corrected the situation and he observed that from ‘the second or upper portion (some open land intervening between) the country is all favourable for road making. The Upper Mangles, where the valley is narrow, will give some little trouble from the soft nature of the upper soil, which will require ditching and other works to lay it dry, and render it fit for a road; but the substratum is good, being composed of gravel, and the distance through this description of country is not great. The gradient up this valley will be easy all the way to the top of the saddle, from which to the Lake Rotoroa is a very easy decent the whole way’.

info_origin: An original Māori name, site of a pā, trig point and adjacent land blocks. In 1908 The Interim Report of the Native Land Commission, comprising Sir Robert Stout (1844-1930) and [Sir] Āpirana Ngata (1874-1950), recommended ending private alienation of the ‘large and valuable’ 9280 acres (3755 ha) Manukau Block until after title to the adjoining Ahipara Block was resolved. Ownership issues persisted and in early August 1908 Karaka Rutene and 120 others applied to the Native Land Court for a hearing to settle matters. Rutene and 29 others petitioned the Parliamentary Native Affairs Committee later that same month, claiming that kāinga and cultivations had not been excluded from land sales as agreed. In 1909 the committee reported that it had ‘no recommendation’. Meantime in 1908 the Native Land Court, investigating titles in the Ahipara Block, also considered the partition of the Manukau Block. Manukau purchasers in 1914 included Auckland architect Richard Atkinson Abbott (?-1954) and an Auckland syndicate which commenced farm development. Questions in Parliament raised concerns about the related activities of barristers and solicitors Fergus Gale Dunlop (1885-1968) and Arthur Gilbert Quartley (1882-1967) land valuations and transactions. MP Tau Henare called for further investigations and the ‘washing up bill’ for 1916 returned to the petition of Rutene. Native Land Court Judges Jackson Palmer (1867-1919) and Walter Edward Rawson (1870-1933) began their investigation in September 1916. An agreement was reached to return 105 acres (42ha), fully reimburse 100 owners who had refused to sell but had lost land, with the Native Land Board to pay £140 to the purchasing company and Quartley and Dunlop to make up any deficiency. In 1922 the Herekino Land Syndicate purchased sections 8 and 9 of the Manukau Block. The Manukau Native School was established in 1926 and shown on the original 1:63360 topographical map sheet published in 1942, even though Manukau itself was not labelled. An 83 acre (367 ha) Manukau Block half grassed, and half still forested was subdivided for Māori land settlement in 1933 – part of Sir Āpriana Ngata’s (1874-1950) land development scheme. The Northern Advocate newspaper referred to the locality as Manukau North in 1937. Edward Dollimore (1904-73), who compiled The New Zealand Guide, noted in 1962 that Manukau was also known as Manukau North.

info_origin: An original Māori name carried by a land block on the eastern bank of Waikato River. Having passed through the Native Land Court, in 1881 a 26000 acres (10522 ha) Maraetai Block was purchased by Edwin Walker (?-1898), William Williams and John Wilson for £4500. A still larger 67820 acres (27446 ha) was auctioned in 1908 as the Maraetai Block and in 1913 was reported as being in the possession of a ‘Southern syndicate.’ Subdivided into mainly 500 acres (202 ha) farms by Maraetai Farms Ltd, these properties were auctioned in 1917. New Zealand Perpetual Forests, the forerunner of New Zealand Forest Products, acquired and planted 43000 acres (17401 ha) of the fern and tutu covered ‘bush sick’ Maraetai Block from 1924-27. Waikato River, narrowing at this point, passed through what was informally known as Maraetai Gorge. Government planning for hydro-electric dam construction on Waikato River began in 1943, but was delayed by WWII. The gorge in Waikato River opposite the Maraetai Block was selected for what became the Maraetai Hydro-electric Power Station. Work commenced in 1946 and an associated Lake Maraetai of 4.4 sq km was filled in 1954. Maraetai as a name now crossed Waikato River and was listed as a locality on the west bank in Wises Index for 1946. This mobility was reinforced in 1955 when 36800 acres (14892 ha) on the southwest bank of Waikato River became known as Maraetai Farm Settlement. It was purchased by the Crown in 1946 and developed by Lands and Survey from 1949 when it was balloted to WWII ex-service personnel (84 dairy and 58 sheep farms).
