info_origin: An original Māori name for the locality and site of a kāinga or village. Of the land between Mārahau and Rākauria / Torrent Bay, in 1827 French explorer Jules Dumont' d'Urville wrote: 'A few Leptospermum (manuka) and two or three other kinds of shrubs can be seen here and there in these parts. No birds, no insects, no reptiles even; this complete absence of any living creature and the unbroken silence create a solemn, almost sinister atmosphere'. Although Dumont d'Urville saw no inhabitants, there were kāinga along the coast. These occupied areas and cultivations ought to have been excluded from the survey of 50 acre (20 ha) sections carried out by New Zealand Company surveyor Samuel Stephens in 1842 but afterwards were included in the Native Tenths Reserves instead of being in addition to them. In 1862 the three 50 acre (20ha) and one 55 acre (22ha) reserves were listed in a return of Native Reserves. In 1886 women's teams from Mārahau and Riwaka played each other at cricket, however, this was not, as is sometimes claimed, the first women's game in New Zealand. Alexander Reed offers as a translation, mara 'garden or cultivation' and hau 'wind'. Ethnologist Johannes Anderson offers the more figurative version 'wind on a garden.'

info_origin: An original Māori name applied initially to the river and literally translated as marama - month or moon and rua - two. One story about the origin of the name has a visiting Māori chief being startled on seeing the reflection of two moons in the lake (which no longer exists) and crying out 'Maramarua!'. The other tradition tells of two much loved chiefly brothers named Mara, and after their death the place was called Maramarua in their memory. Much of Maramarua River was navigable for canoes and a Māori track extended from the coast to Meremere. Canoes could also be portaged along a routeway - Te to-waka from Hauraki, at what in the 1820s was known as Pukeroro, to Maramarua River and linking to Waikato River. The missionary Henry Williams (1792-1867) described the area in 1835, 'After continuing our course for about 1/2 an hour we turned out of the main [Waikato] river and up a small branch called Maramarua, which conducted us through vast swamp on either side until we landed at noon at a place bearing the same name as the river being the nearest point to Wakatiwai'. In 1836 missionaries William Thomas Fairburn (1795-1859) and John Alexander Wilson (1809-87) travelled to Maramarua to intercede and maintain the peace between Waikato and Hauraki tribes. An anti-land selling Māori land league emerged centred on Maramarua in 1856. On 17 July 1863, marking the beginning of fighting in the Waikato, Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron's (1808-88) forces fought an engagement at Koheroa from which Māori withdrew, fighting from successive lines of defence. Cameron noted, 'as we advanced upon them they retired along the narrow crest of the hills towards the Maramarua [River], making a stand on every favourable position which the ground presented.' In August 1863 work began on the construction of the Maramarua redoubt adjacent to an old pā. Geologist Frederick Hutton (1836-1905) mapped coal fields at Maramarua in 1869 and commercial mining developed over the following decades. The first European settlers came to Maramarua around this same time and named the area Bridgewater. This name did not persist much beyond 1872. By 1886 Māori land at Maramarua numbered only ten 50 acre [20 ha] lots. A Maramarua Post and Telegraph office was established in 1895. In 1914 licensed surveyor John Dawson prepared a plan for a 7 acre (2.8 ha) 12 lot subdivision with rectangular frontages at the 'Township of Maramarua'. The plan was forwarded by the Chief Surveyor for Auckland to Surveyor-General Ernest Wilmot (1855-1952), a foundation member of the New Zealand Institute of Surveyors, who approved it under Section 3 of the Land Laws Amendment Act 1913, which imposed some conditions on private subdivisions for towns. Further town subdivisions followed in 1945 and 1947. In 2020 a Waikato District Council hearing identified 300 sites and 80 areas of Māori significance. Five were pā sites in the vicinity of Maramarua called Onoke, Opuku and Whatarua, with two unnamed.

info_origin: Located at the junction of four crossroads and accordingly named Market Cross. Around 1901 local residents petitioned the Postmaster-General, Sir Joseph Ward, for a post office. Local MP Roderick McKenzie (1852-1934) supported the petition, and a site was donated by a Mr Simpson (possibly farmer James Ryan Simpson). Mrs Jessie May Hawes (1880-1967), wife of local farmer Henry Charles Hawes, acted as 'post-mistress' from 1917 to 1941. In 1899 she had become Ōpārara School's first teacher. On retirement she was replaced in the post office by her daughter-in-law Doris Hawes. Mrs Jessie May Hawes gave 'Market Cross' as the address on all her correspondence and the Post Office in turn adopted the name.

Old Marlborough or the Story of the Province. Journal of the Nelson and Marlborough Historical Societies, 1, 41-43.}
info_origin: Samuel Bowler (1818-95), formerly a merchant at Boulder Bank, in the mid-1850s leased a sheep run at what became Marshlands Estate which he farmed in partnership with George Jackson (c.1820-81). The swampy nature of the area prompted the name Marshlands. Both Bowler and Jackson had previously captained coastal vessels. By 1870 Jackson had left to farm on his own account at Robin Hood Bay and in 1879 Bowler sold Marshlands to John Clervaux Chaytor (1836-1920). UK born, Chaytor served in the Crimean War and Indian Mutiny and after home garrison duty came to New Zealand around 1860. In Marlborough he initially acquired the Coverham Estate before purchasing Marshlands. Chaytor was a member of the Marlborough Provincial Council for Awatere (1871-74). Chaytor’s sons pursued military careers. His eldest son, Edward, served with distinction in WWI, commanding the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade and later the Australian and New Zealand Mounted Division in Palestine. He rose to the rank of Major-General and was knighted in 1918.

Renamed Massey to avoid the use of the unsatisfactory compound name. [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for William Ferguson Massey](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2m39/massey-william-ferguson); 'Named after William Ferguson Massey, prime minister from 1912 to 1925. info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Jim G. Mastro II who has a long history of deployment from 1982-1996, serving a total of 71 months in Antarctica. This included service as Winter Laboratory Manager, McMurdo Station, and Scientific Diving Coordinator in support of many marine research projects. He authored a key operations manual to guide scientific diving within the U. S. Antarctic Program (USAP). info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: ‘Matahānea was a pā and kāinga that also featured an urupā. Ngāi Hāua tūpuna, Parekahurangi Marukai, is associated with this kāinga. She was married to Tiraha Poihipi. Her whare was named Mātāpuna and was erected in about 1883. Parekahurangi died in childbirth and was buried with her child at the urupā at a nearby kāinga called Otikoke, located on a hill overlooking Matahānea. Ngāti Hāua tūpuna Makere Te Uruweherua was the aunt of Parekahurangi and an owner in the Matahānea lands. Whakapaki Hekeawai was another Ngāti Hāua tūpuna associated with Matahānea. In 1880, the gun trader William Moffatt, was killed near Matahānea after ignoring repeated warnings not to breach the aukati of the Kingitanga. When parts of the Ōhura South Māori land block were sold, those living at Matahānea were forced to move. Matahānea later became the site of a sawmill, and huge amounts of timber were extracted from the Matahānea area. Eventually, both the State Highway and railway ran over the land and through the urupā and kāinga.’

name: Matapara / Pickersgill Island
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Te Atiawa’s close association with Matapara / Pickersgill Island is through ancestry, conquest and customary occupation. This motu, like many others in Totaranui, was a strategic point for warfare, occupation and contains wāhi tapu for the iwi. The foreshore surrounding Matapara / Pickersgill Island was utilised for both offshore fishing and for preparation. Matapara / Pickersgill Island was a roosting and nesting place for the little blue penguin and the shag. It was also known for its kohekohe and tawa forest. During the turn of the century the island was used for harvesting of wheat crops, speargrass and cocksfoot. Matapara is the traditional name for the island and has been used by whanau and hapu since the conquest of Totaranui by Te Atiawa.

Matariki was earlier called Wangapeka Settlement. ; the name appears to have been determined by the Postal Department, with Matariki Post Office opening on 1 April 1911 and Harriet McCarthy appointed as postmaster (NZ Gazette 1911 (56) p.2154). In the register of Māori post office names, Matariki is stamped 'Name obtained and assigned by department' rather than 'Original Name of District or place'.

info_origin: Ahuriri Hapū statement (extract): There are considerable signs of the occupation of Ahuriri Hapū all over Mataruahou mostly in the form of shell middens. They appear in the botanical gardens, Napier cemetery, Rosalyn Road, Golding, The Terrace and Hukarere Road. Matapane Pā and Hukarere Pā on Mataruahou indicate the strategic importance of Mataruahou; significant too because it was regarded as a healing place. Mataruahou was not included in the sale of the Ahuriri block because of its strategic significance as one of the four sentinels of Te Whanganui-ā-Orotu namely Heipipi, Otatara, Kohukete and Mataruahou. There were two significant sites on Mataruahou associated with Pania. One is a freshwater spring, Tuhinapo, located at the foot of Hukarere cliff. The other is at the foot of Karetoki Whare (Sturms Gully) where Pania and her husband lived on shore. ; The hill is locally known as Scinde Island, Bluff Hill, Hospital Hill or Napier Hill. Originally an island attached to the mainland by two shingle banks. The 1931 Napier earthquake uplifted the area and resulted in the island becoming a hill.

name: Matatirohia
info_ref: File 22/2605/3 Vol. 21 pp.153-191; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche August 2023: Objective ID: A5568126 {Aeradio Committee. Report on Kermadec Islands. Plans [Photostat with additional photographs pasted in]. R18765240. Archives New Zealand, Wellington [digitized].; Gentry, Stephen. 2013. Raoul Island & the Kermadecs. Report of the Aeradio Committee, 1938 [Text & photographs]. R18765239. Archives New Zealand, Wellington [digitized].; Percy Smith, S. 1887. The Kermadec Islands, their Capabilities and Extent. New Zealand: Government Printer.; [Pierre. 1968. On things historical. The Islander – Campbell - Raoul Islander Association Newsletter, 1 np.](https://www.raoulandcampbell.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=category&id=7&Itemid=107); Stewart, P.J. 1959. Annexation of the Kermadecs and New Zealand's Policy in the Pacific. Pacific Historical Review, 28, 67-71.; Wright, A.C.S and Metson, A.J. 1959. Soils of Raoul (Sunday) Island, Kermadec Group. DSIR Soil bureau Bulletin No 10.; [Giselle M. Byrnes. 'Smith, Stephenson Percy', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1993. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2s33/smith-stephenson-percy) (accessed 13 July 2023)}
info_origin: Matatirohia was named by surveyor J Allan Henderson (1909-2001), one of some half dozen features he and JE (Jock) Anderson named on Raoul Island in 1937-38 as part of a survey prior to the establishment of a weather and radio station. Matatirohia was a trig point that with Ngaio trig formed Henderson’s base line for his topographical survey of the island. His topographical map which included Matatirohia was completed in 1939. Ngaio appears to be linked to the presence of the forest tree of that name (Myoporum laetum) but the inspiration for and meaning of Matatirohia is uncertain and it may be a created and not a transported authentic te reo Māori name. The name Matatirohia was also applied to the aeradio camp. Henderson was a licensed surveyor with the Department of Lands and Survey and deputy leader of a party to Raoul Island headed by Public Works Department engineer, Jock Anderson. Oral tradition and archaeological evidence indicate that Raoul Island was a stopover point for voyaging to and from New Zealand and the Pacific Islands being known as Rangitāhua and a landing place of the Aotea waka. Stephenson Percy Smith (1840-1922) as Chief Surveyor of Auckland Land District made a survey of the Kermadec Islands in 1887 on their annexation by New Zealand. He described what was later labelled Matatirohia as ‘a small flat east of the [Fleetwood] bluff, of about 90 acres [36ha] overgrown with Ngaio and other wood, [which] is not of much use as the [1873] eruption covered it thickly with pumice’. ACS Wright’s soil map of Raoul Island published in 1959 included Matatirohia and the name was carried over onto later earth science publications discussing volcanic eruptions.
info_description: Hill on the north coast of Raoul Island, southeast of Bells Beach, Kermadec Islands. Feature shown on: NZOITopo25-KI01

name: Mataura
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Joanna Barnes-Wylie, 8 January 2026: Objective ID: A7665390 {David Grant, Southland places – Eastern Southland, [Te Ara – the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/southland-places/page-4); [Infomap 346-02 Te Wai Pounamu Edition 1 1995](https://geodatahub.library.auckland.ac.nz/public/maps/LINZ/NZMS/NZMS_346/jpg/NZMS346_02_1995_s2.jpg); [Kā Huru Manu, the Ngāi Tahu cultural heritage atlas](https://kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas); [Mataura, Gore New Zealand](https://www.gorenz.com/our-stories/our-towns/mataura); [Mataura’s first bridge shortlived](https://www.stuff.co.nz/southland-times/news/features/109674528/matauras-first-bridge-shortlived), Stuff, 3 January 2019; [Mataura, NZ History](https://nzhistory.govt.nz/keyword/mataura); MATAURA RIVER, from [An Encyclopaedia of New Zealand[(https://teara.govt.nz/en/1966/mataura-river), edited by A. H. McLintock, originally published in 1966}
info_origin: Mataura is named for the Mataura River which flows through the town. For Ngāi Tahu, the river was a significant mahinga kai (food gathering place) renowned for its abundance of kanakana (lamprey) and an important travel route providing direct access from Southland to Lake Wakatipu, correctly Whakatipu Waimāori. Several meanings have been provided for the name Mataura. The Board’s Tangata Whenua Place Names map for Te Waipounamu (first edition, 1995) provides the meaning ‘red point’ while other sources note that it may mean ‘reddish, brown face’ or ‘glowing face’, a reference to the red glow of the river when iron-oxide rich swamp water drains into it. It could also be an ancient tupuna (ancestor’s) name, noting that Mataura was a tupuna of Ngātoro-i-rangi, the tohunga who came to Aotearoa New Zealand on the Te Arawa waka. The town of Mataura has its origins in 1859, when an accommodation house opened on the west bank of the Mataura River. The accommodation house was constructed to encourage use of the newly opened wooden truss bridge across the river at the site of the waterfall Te Au-nui-pihapiha-kanakana (Te Au-nui for short). The truss bridge, the first of several bridges built across the river in the town, was destroyed by flooding in 1861. By the late 19th century the fledgling settlement, originally known as ‘Mataura Bridge’, had transformed into a centre of significant industrial activity. The Mataura Paper Mill opened in 1876, followed by the Mataura Dairy Factory in 1887 and Mataura Freezing Works in 1893. Other early industries included opencast coal and lignite mining, flaxmilling and agricultural implement works. While the dairy factory and paper mill have both closed (in 1984 and 2000 respectively), the freezing works still operate (as at January 2026).
info_description: A locality that straddles the Mataura River on State Highway 1, approximately 12km south-southwest of Gore. Feature shown on: NZTopo50 CF12 807760.

name: Matira / Castle Rock
info_origin: The rock feature was known as Castlepoint or Castle Point adopted from the nearby location Castle Point. The feature is also known as Rangiwhakaoma by some local iwi and the NZGB Maori Oral History Atlas reads while they were at Rangiwhakaoma (Castle Point) Kupe had a fight with a giant octopus" the literal meaning according to Reed: rangi: day, whakaoma: to hasten in chase - when Kupe chase the giant octopus down across Cook Strait and into Tory Channel. The name for the whole feature is ‘Rangiwhakaoma’. Rangitāne o Wairarapa history:. The name for the whole coastal feature is ‘Rangiwhakaoma’ (lit. ‘where the sky runs’), and is possibly the name of one of the fellow voyagers of Kupe. ‘Matira’ is the head of Rangiwhakaoma whose body looks to be reclined along the length of the reef. A man’s face can be seen when approaching from the sea. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDhDMzA0MTY4MjEwMDg0N0Y3NzU)"

name: Matiu / Somes Island
info_ref: File BRD/02/01/00/13/21; Dual name standardisation: Objective IDs: A4405369, A4507521
info_origin: Matiu/Somes Island was originally named by the Polynesian explorer Kupe, who, according to Māori Tradition was the discoverer of Wellington Harbour. The island was named after one of Kupe's daughters. The name Somes is after Joseph Somes, Deputy Governor of New Zealand, from whom the crew of the Tory (who named the island Somes) purchased their ship. The name 'Somes Island' was given by Captain Edward Main Chaffers and Colonel William Wakefield whilst charting 'Port Nicholson' in the barque, Tory, over a two week period from 20 September 1839. [Reference: 'Put Him in a Longboat' by Doug Edwards (1989), page 48].; 'Named by Kupe after one of his daughters or nieces. The crew of the Tory bestowed the English name, in honour of either New Zealand Company deputy-governor Joseph Somes or his ship-building firm. The Tory had been bought from Somes in 1838.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Maunga Kākaramea
info_origin: Maunga Kākaramea (also known as Rainbow Mountain) is an iconic peak for the Ngāti Tahu-Ngāti Whaoa people and its traditional history reinforces tribal identity, solidarity, and continuity between generations. Maunga Kākaramea means “Mountain of Coloured Earth” (literal translation is maunga: mountain, kākaramea: red ochre), which is reflective of its bare brown, orange and red steaming slopes. Historically, Maunga Kākaramea was used as a place of refuge during battle for the Ngāti Tahu-Ngāti Whaoa people. Also referred to as Maunga Kara, the mountain was the main burial ground for the Ngāti Tahu-Ngāti Whaoa people. Maunga Kākaramea also provided the people with valuable food resources. Some of the foods the maunga (and its waterways) provided are fern roots, eels, freshwater crayfish, ducks and birds. The mauri of Maunga Kākaramea represents the essence that binds the physical and spiritual elements of all things together, generating and upholding all life. Mauri is a critical element of the spiritual relationship of Ngāti Tahu-Ngāti Whaoa with Maunga Kākaramea.

name: Maungakaramea
info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche September 2023: Objective ID: A5629145 {Elder, J. (ed) 1932. The Letters and Journals of Samuel Marsden. New Zealand: Coulls, Somerville, Wilkie, Ltd. and A.H. Reed for the Otago University Council.; O’Shea, Bethney. 1985. Maungakaramea Past and Present. New Zealand: Maungakaramea Reserves Board.; https://nzhistory.govt.nz/keyword/maungakaramea; https://t4wk3-website--natahliaalbert.repl.co/; [Steven Oliver. 'Te Tirarau Kūkupa', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1993. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2t31/te-tirarau-kukupa); Turton, H. Hanson 1877. Deeds of Land purchases in the North Island of New Zealand. volume I New Zealand: Didsbury.; Wises. 1946. Wises New Zealand Index. New Zealand: Wises.}
info_origin: A translation offered by Wises New Zealand Index was ‘weeping mountain’ referring to a 225m extinct volcanic cone. The Ministry of Culture and Heritage’s alternative literal translation was Maunga: mountain; karamea: red ochre or speargrass (possibly Aciphylla squarrosa). A local history acknowledging that karamea was a tree species, accepted karamea tree mountain was one possibility but considered red ochre mountain as a ‘safe’ translation. Also, speargrass species do not grow naturally further north of a line from Mount Taranaki to East Cape. From 1814 armed Ngāpuhi war parties ventured southwards to Maungakaramea in order to harass traditional enemies, Ngāti Whātua. Larger battles fought at Maungakaramea and Tangihau up until 1835 resulted in a tapu being placed on the area and the lands were no longer occupied by Māori. Missionary Samuel Marsden was the first European to travel through this area in 1820 following the old Māori track from Tangiteroria to Maungakarakmea to the Mangapai River. Maunga Karamea is used on manuscript deeds of sale in 1855 and in the press until the mid-1860s which also adopted Maunga-karamea from the late 1850s, with Maungakaramea featuring in official government papers from 1861 and only a decade later in newspapers. In 1855 Te Parawhau leader Te Tirarau Kūkupa (?-1882) was the first signatory on the two Maungakaramea Block land sales for £800 and £2000 respectively. In completing the Maunga Karamea acquisition, John Grant Johnson (1824-73) Commissioner for Purchase of Native Lands, specified ‘cultivations on [the] banks of Otaika river which are exempted’ which was later a point of contention. Twenty-three farms were advertised in the New Zealand Gazette in 1859, so called ‘40 acre farms’ promoted by the ‘constitutionalist’ faction of the Auckland Provincial Government which favoured establishing British style small yeoman farmers throughout the province, although these gum lands proved largely unsuitable for arable cultivation. In 1878 surveyor Daniel C Wilson (1841-1902) completed a plan of the Maungakaramea settlement including over 100 properties mostly over 100 acres (40 ha).

info_origin: Provided by Ngā Mana Whenua o Tāmaki Makaurau Collective: Maungakiekie / One Tree Hill is of high cultural importance to Ngāti Whātua o Ōrākei. It was the site of the Hikurangi pa occupied by the Ngāti Whātua ancestor Tuperiri in the mid 18th century. Tuperiri is also buried on the maunga. The name Maungakiekie translates as the “mountain of the Kiekie shrub” or “the mountain culminating in a pinnacle”. The name Maungakiekie has been well recorded in primary and secondary sources, including land purchase deeds, Native Land Court evidence, the New Zealand Historical Atlas and histories of pre-1840 Auckland. ; 'The name Maungakiekie translates as The mountain of the kiekie shrub (Freycinetia banksii) or The mountain culminating in a pinnacle. Sir John Logan Campbell was informed of the name by Waipeha, yet he wrote later in Poenamo that ‘as it had one large solitary tree on its crater summit we christened it “One Tree Hill”, which for ever obliterated the Māori name from Pakeha vocabulary, but the grand old tree has passed away, causing later-day arrivals to wonder why the hill bears it name.’ The tree was a tōtara, and was also acknowledged in Tōtaraiahua (ahua is a form or appearance), the name applied to the northeast peak, the southeast peak being Te Tu-po-o-te-tini: lit. te: the; tu: standing; po: night; o: of; te: the; tini: host or myriad. The hill has at times been known as Mount Prospect and Lofty Hill.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Maunganui Bay
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3951138; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche September 2023: Objective ID: A5629145 {Dollimore Edward. 1962. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand: Wises.; NZGB Minutes 102/39; NZGB Correspondence, XVI/116; XVIII/146; XXXIV/230-231; LINZ Topo File Q05; Reed, A.W. and Dowling, P. 2010. Place Names of New Zealand. New Zealand: Penguin.}
info_origin: An original Māori name. When Maunganui came before the Honorary Geographic Board in 1939 both Sir Āpirana Ngata (1874-1950) and Pei Te H Jones (1898-1976) confirmed this name over that of Deep Water Cove. The latter name was widely used in the 1920s coinciding with the expansion of big game fishing and the publicity given to it by visitors such as the American writer of westerns, Zane Grey, who camped at Maunganui. Honorary Geographic Board member and ethnologist Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) preoccupied with literal translations puzzled over whether it ought to be Manganui – a large stream or river instead of Maunganui – a large mountain. This ambivalence was carried across into successive editions of publisher-writer Alexander Wyclif Reed’s (1908-79) Place Names of New Zealand. However, Edward Dollimore (1904-73), compiler of The New Zealand Guide, instead considered Maunganui an alternative name for Deep Water Cove. In 1943, in reviewing all names on the Bay of Island topographic maps, Andersen suggested to the Chief Cartographer of Lands and Survey that Deep Water Cove be limited to the northern lobe of the bay, that Maunganui Bay be used, and that Maunganui Peninsula replace Cape Brett. For good measure and consistency, he also believed Deepwater was preferable to Deep Water. These suggestions were not adopted in full. In 1948 the New Zealand Geographic Board included Maunganui in a list of names published in the Gazette and recognised as if they were final decisions of the Board under the 1946 legislation. In 1961 Raymond Evins (1922-2018) of the Hydrographic Branch of the Royal New Zealand Navy wrote to the Chief Cartographer of Lands and Survey supporting Deep Water Cove (Maunganui) being changed on the maps to Maunganui (Deep Water Cove) following the publication of the Bay of Islands tourist map NZMS 151. The Chief Cartographer replied that they were different features in terms of local use. Unfortunately, on the subsequent edition of NZMS 151 the two names were swapped in their positions. Deep Water Cove was once again shown for the larger bay, with Maunganui Bay now shown for the cove. This error promulgated out to other topographic products such the NZMS 1 N12, then NZMS 260 Q05 topographic maps. In 1997 it was finally resolved when the Secretary of the Board reviewed the new edition of Q05, advising the names needed to be swapped.

info_origin: Provided by Ngā Mana Whenua o Tāmaki Makaurau Collective: The 11 iwi hapu members of Nga Mana Whenua o Tāmaki Makaurau have agreed this placename change reflects the historical association of manawhenua with this site. The site of a pā. Ngāti Pāoa history: How Maungarei (or Mt Wellington) got its name is one of the many Ngati Paoa stories which has been passed down through the generations. Maungarei means "the watchful mountain". Reipae and Reitu were two sisters from Waikato who both fell in love with a chieftain called Ueoneone from the north. Ueoneone and his people were hoping he would marry both sisters so he sent a large eagle down to collect them. But Reipae had second thoughts. She wanted to alight from the bird and asked it to land at Whangarei. There she met another chieftain named Tahuhupotiki who she later married. Whangarei was named after Reipae. Reitu went on to marry Ueoneonei and Maungarei makes reference to her name.

info_origin: A farming district adjacent to Mauriceville, named after George Maurice O’Rorke (1830-1916). name: Mawae
info_origin: Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui history: 'Mawae is the name of the whole land block including the Island. This particular area was named after Te Mawae. He was a TOW [Treaty of Waitangi] signatory and uncle to Major Kemp. This area was associated with the Otawe fishing Kainga, flour mill and Pihaia Pah. This is an important strategic area to the people of Putiki/Tumango. Of particular note, the renowned explorer Tamatea Pokaiwhenua, when he visited the Whanganui area in the 14th century landed on this site, desirous of dressing his hair obtained flax from the banks of the Awarua stream to present himself before the Tangata Whenua. This stream dissected both land blocks, Pungaharuru and Te Moutere and when in flood along with the Whanganui River formed the existing Island later known as Corliss Island. Traditionally and prior to 1840, this area was known as Mawae. Pungaharuru and Te Moutere were the post 1840 names given to this area. A stream ran through these two blocks, and as a result of flooding, the island was created. This area was part of the land that was taken under the Whanganui Purchase.'
info_description: A small island in Whanganui River, approximately 5km upstream of the river mouth. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BL32 739753.

info_origin: Mayfield was described as the ‘Queen suburb of Blenheim’ by its promoters, auctioneers Griffiths & Son and Land agents Messrs McLauchlan & Co. in 1911. The original subdivision comprised 65 sections of which 56 were quarter acre (1011 sq m) allotments each costing £75. Interestingly the promoters drew attention to the Liberal government’s Advances to Workers scheme as a possible source of finance. The anticipated main trunk railway line from Picton to Invercargill was a further selling point, although the Marlborough section was not finally completed until 1946. The promoters noted that the name Mayfield had been suggested by the then local Adjutant, later Field Major, Walter Home (1875-1929) of the Salvation Army.

Evening Post, 9 May, Page 20](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19250509.2.152); [Maymorn Camp](https://uhcl.recollect.co.nz/pages/ww100_Maymorn/); [Maymorn Estate](http://www.valleysignals.org.nz/maymorn/maymorn.html); [Obituary Mr Tudor Atkinson. 1928. Maymorn Estate - Akatarawa [R17274291](https://collections.archives.govt.nz/web/arena/search/#/entity/aims-archive/R17274291/), Archives New Zealand, Wellington.
info_origin: Maymorn is derived from the May Morn Estate which in turn was taken from the May Morn Trig point, now Maymorn an 851m hill, and was part of James Daniel Climie’s (1849-1928) survey of the area in 1879, according to Hutt MP Thomas Wilford, though it is possibly actually the work of his brother Henry Westcoat Climie (1857-1929).  May Morn Estates (NZ) Ltd, floated on the London Stock exchange in 1912,  purchased 18750 acres (7588ha) of land in the Akatarawa valley previously owned by the Wellington and Manawatu Railway Company in 1888 which passed it to the New Zealand Timber and Pastoral Land Company Ltd in 1911 along with 34 acres (14ha) for a sawmill site at Mangaroa, the latter acquired from Tudor Atkinson, son of former Premier Sir Harry Atkinson. The 18750 acres block became known as the May Morn Estate, although Maymorn Estate was also used in the press, and May Morn and Maymorn applied to the mill site. Here the company constructed what it claimed was the largest sawmill in New Zealand and anticipated developing a ‘garden village’ for employees. Sawmilling operations ceased in 1914, and the mill area was leased in 1915 by the Army as an overflow canvas camp site for the main Trentham military camp before it was closed in 1916. Prior to embarkation troops would march over Remutaka Hill and sleep in the open at Kaitoke and Maymorn before returning to Trentham. The May Morn Estate Company went into receivership in 1921.

info_origin: ‘This Island I have called the Mayor,’ wrote Captain Cook on 3 November 1769, ‘and a Cluster of small Islands and Rocks … we named the Court of Aldermen.’ The election of the Lord Mayor of London on 9 November may have put the thought into Cook’s mind, and it appears from Joseph Banks’ record that the officers jokingly ascribed names to each of the aldermen. The navigator Toi gave the name Tūhua during a visit after leaving Aotea (Great Barrier Island) and before taking up residence at Whakatāne. He named it after the island of Tūhua in Hawaiki (Meheti’a in the Society Islands); tūhua also means ‘obsidian’. Māori name for the Aldermen Islands is Ruamahua: lit. thrust up from the depths.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDhCNDZFQkZCQjEwMDk4NzIxQzE)

info_origin: Named by the Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Bill McAfee, who completed two decades of USAP service in support of scientific research. He managed the Computer and Information Technology Infrastructure at South Pole during his decades of service where he deployed to the South Pole 13 times (including two winter overs). During these deployments, he dramatically expanded the station's IT and communications infrastructure while providing world-class technical support to a station population of over 200 scientists and contractors. Beyond official duties, McAfee constantly sought outreach opportunities including initiating the collaboration among Google, NSF, and the Polar Geospatial Center that greatly enhanced the imagery of the south polar region.

name: McDonald Beach
info_origin: Named by the New Zealand Geological and Survey Antarctic Expedition (NZGSAE), 1958-59, for Captain Edwin S McDonald, formerly Deputy-Commander, US Naval Support Force, Antarctica, who provided extensive transport and other facilities for this NZ Expedition, and whose sympathetic support facilitated the survey of the Cape Bird district. At the time the feature was named, the fan and the beach were considered to be "sufficiently extensive for the establishment of an airfield or a comparable installation needing extensive space."
info_description: A large beach extending 3km between Keys Point to the north and Harrison Bluff to the south, approximately 12km southwest of Cape Bird. The beach consists of alternating prograded storm-wave beaches separated by shallow hollows occupied by ponds. Towards its southern end the prograded part of the beach merges with a low and extensive stream fan which in part was cut back to a low cliff edge before the present phase of progradation commenced. Behind the fan towards the southern end of the beach another cliff rises to an undulating glaciated bench, 45 to 60 metres high, on which the southernmost of the three Adelie Penguin rookeries of the Cape Bird district is situated. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-ME13

name: McMurdo Dry Valleys
info_origin: Much scientific interest has focused on this area because extensive sections of bedrock are exposed to study. Parts of the area were visited by British expeditions led by Captain Robert F. Scott (1901-04 and 1910-13), who referred to Taylor Valley, as well as Beacon Valley and Pyramid Trough (named later), as "dry valleys." In 1986, the Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) recommended the name McMurdo Dry Valleys from among several informal names which were then in use. The name is in accord with the historical use of the term "dry valleys" in this area, with the fact that the ice-free valleys are the salient characteristic of the area as a whole, and with the situation of this feature adjacent to McMurdo Sound and McMurdo Ice Shelf.
info_description: The geographic area, 200km north to south, up to 100km east to west, encompassing the largest assemblage of ice-free features in Antarctica. The area occupies the south portion of Scott Coast, Victoria Land, and is roughly defined as extending from 76°30'S to 78°30'S, between 160°00'E and 164°30'E. A variety of feature types occur within the area including mountains, ranges, glaciers, lakes, and ice-free valleys, the latter generally referred to as "dry valleys" following R.F. Scott's usage of 1907. Three concentrations of ice-free areas are notable: in the N, Alatna Valley and other ice-free valleys are associated with Convoy Range. The main central sector is bounded by Saint Johns Range, Quartermain Mountains, and Kukri Hills and includes Victoria Valley, Barwick Valley, Balham Valley, McKelvey Valley, Wright Valley, the elevated valleys of the Olympus Range and Asgard Range, the Pearse Valley, Taylor Valley, and the valleys in Quartermain Mountains. In the extreme SE, Garwood Valley, Marshall Valley, Miers Valley, Hidden Valley, Pyramid Trough, and Roaring Valley lie near the coast between Royal Society Range and Koettlitz Glacier. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME08

name: McMurdo Shear Zone
info_origin: The zone was first observed and crossed by Robert Scott’s Discovery Expedition at the beginning of the 20th Century (1901-1904). This hazardous zone was subsequently encountered and crossed by teams from Shackleton’s Nimrod Expedition (1907-1909), by Scott’s Terra Nova Expedition (1910-1913), and by the Ross Sea Party of Shackleton’s Endurance expedition (1914-1917). The zone was next encountered by teams operating in the McMurdo region during the 1950’s prior to and during the International Geophysical Year. It was crossed by operational traverses in the 1960’s in support of a broad array of science projects prior to a shift to supporting science via skied aircraft. The name first came into scientific use ~1996-1998 as the feature was more accurately described and defined using ground penetrating radar, during efforts to map a route for the South Polar Overland Traverse (SPOT). As a dynamic feature McMurdo Shear Zone continues to require active management to ensure that it can be crossed safely by SPOT and other traverses in support of science.
info_description: The dynamic boundary between the relatively fast-moving Ross Ice Shelf to the east and the slower moving McMurdo Ice Shelf to the west. An area of complex crevassing, fracturing, and folds in the ice. Averaging 9-20km wide and approximately 160km long, extending from southeast of Minna Bluff to just east of The Knoll at Cape Crozier.

name: McMurdo Sound
info_origin: Named in association with McMurdo Ice Shelf and McMurdo Dry Valleys. Discovered by Captain James Clark Ross in February 1841 and named for Lt. Archibald McMurdo of the Terror.
info_description: McMurdo Sound is the area between Ross Island and the Antarctic mainland, with the following limits: On the West: From Brown Peninsula (78°02´S - 165°32´E), on the Hillary Coast of the Antarctic mainland, northward, along the Antarctic coast, to Cape Roberts (77°00´S - 163°09´E). On the North: From Cape Roberts eastward, a line to the northern extremity of Ross Island (77°11´S - 166°50´E). On the East: From the northern extremity of Ross Island, southward, along the western coast of Ross Island. To Scott Base (77°52´S - 166°40´E), on the southern end of this island. On the South: From Scott Base southeastward, a line to the northern extremity of White Island (78°00´S - 167°30´E) and thence from this position westward, along the northern coasts of White Island and Black Island and continuing northwesterly, to Brown Peninsula (78°02´S - 165°32´E), the point of commencement."
info_note: The feature definition conforms with Chapter 10 of the draft IHO document 'Southern Ocean and its Sub-Divisions' dated 26 October 2001.

name: McMurdo Station
info_origin: Established in December 1955 and opened in 1956. The name 'Williams Air Operating Facility' was applied by its commander Admiral George Dufek. In 1957-58 the station was designated 'Naval Air Facility, McMurdo' in preparation for the International Geophysical Year. The name 'McMurdo Station' over time achieved greater currency than the official name. In 1961 the base became permanent, with the name McMurdo Station. The Williams name was reapplied to the ice airstrip. The station with around 85 buildings supports up to 1258 staff in summer, with up to 250 overwintering. The largest base in Antarctica.

name: Measly Beach
info_origin: ’Also spelt Measely Beach. At the time of the measles epidemic in 1835 Tūhawaiki was leading a raid on Te Rauparaha. The warriors took ill and were forced to land at the beach and eventually there were not enough men left to crew even one canoe out of the nine. A cautionary newspaper report from 1918 tells how the fleet of war canoes paused for a night at a small coastal settlement near Invercargill and bought blankets from a whaling trader recently returned from Sydney. The trader omitted to tell the chief that a short time before ‘a Māori girl had died of measles between those very blankets.’ The disease spread through the group over the next few days, leading to many deaths.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Mechanics Bay
info_origin: ’This was the portion of the waterfront where the ‘mechanics’, meaning labourers and workmen, were settled when the capital was transferred to Auckland from the Bay of Islands. Māori name: Te Tōangaroa: lit. The long dragging of canoes, which for Ngāti Whātua Orākei refers to the arduous task of dragging waka to the modern Beach Road on a low tide. The modern area of Te Tōangaroa is land reclaimed from the original bay/beach. Ngāti Paoa claims the name refers to an event on 17 April 1851, when a well-armed group of Ngāti Paoa, Ngāti Whanaunga, Ngāti Maru, Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki and others arrived in force by waka taua (war canoe) on the high tide to demand redress for an insult to Ngāti Paoa chief, Hoera. The colonial authorities gathered their own show of military strength, demanding that the taua leave immediately, but by the time the demand was made the tide had gone out. In the face of the threat, the party were forced to drag their heavy waka back to the water.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: A defensive line of fortifications stretching from Pukekawa to Meremere to Paparata was constructed by Māori in 1863 to defend the Waikato against imperial and colonial troops. The Meremere pā with trenches and rifle pits was on a ridgeline, flanked by swamp on one side and Waikato River on the other. The pā took its name from the hills named Meremere after an earlier fight there with meremere or small clubs. When Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron (1808-88) used river steamers to threaten their rear the Meremere pā was tactically abandoned by the defenders on 1st November 1863. The occupying troops then constructed a redoubt for 200 men at the highest point of the fortifications. The ditch and bank earthworks of the redoubt measured 40m by 45m. Unusually it was a triangular shape possibly from incorporating some of the Māori trenches. The formed redoubt served as a base for the trans-shipment of men and supplies as the military campaign moved further into the Waikato. The Daily Southern Cross newspaper stationed a correspondent at 'Camp Meremere' from February to May 1864, but there were only increasingly mundane camp activities to report on. The redoubt was abandoned a month later in June 1864 with transportation of men and materials continuing by river steamer. Construction of a coal fired power station began near the site in 1956.

info_origin: An original Māori name. On 15 May 1852 'land to the North of Aorere' was purchased from 35 Ngāti Toa, Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Rarua and Ngāti Tama owners for £550 by Nelson Provincial Superintendent Matthew Richmond (1801-87). As well as the boundaries of the block, specifically named 'parcel(s) of land or ground' including Meroiti, were listed. Signatories included Wiremu Kīngi Te Koihua, Tamiti Pirimona Marino, Tepene te Rakaherea, Rawiri Watino and Te Wirihana of Golden Bay; Rawiri Puaha, and Hohepa Tamihengia of Porirua; Hemi Kepa te Iti of Motueka; Wiremu Nga Manu of Wakapuaka, Maka Tarapiko of Kaiau. Wiremu Kīngi Te Koihua was the chief of Pākawau. He was a leader of the Tainui Taranaki alliance which had conquered Te Tau Ihu in 1828-89 and resided at West Whanganui Inlet from about 1830 before moving to Pakawau in the early 1840s. Te Koihua's name is commemorated in Billy King Stream at Te Rae. Tāmati Pirimona Marino (?-1877) was also known as Te Pua Ringahuri. His pā was at Aorere, as were his considerable land interests. He offered much needed hospitality to Heaphy and Brunner returning from their 1846 expedition, owned a sailing ship engaged in coastal trade, and survived the challenges imposed by the Collingwood gold rush of 1857. Tarapiko signed Te Tiriti at Rangitoto ki te Tonga / D'Urville Island on 11 May 1840 although there is some uncertainty over whether this is Māka Tarapiko or his father or uncle. The Aorere sale document was witnessed by Anglican Rev Thomas Lloyd Tudor (1820-1900), Wesleyan Minister Samuel Ironside (1814-97) and government translator John Tinline (1821-1907). The purchase was driven by the earlier discovery of coal at Pākawau and the desire to mine this and other minerals found in that vicinity.

info_origin: Edward Meurant was born around 1803 in London. In 1820 he migrated to Australia with his family. Meurant arrived in Kawhia in 1824. He returned to Australia but returned to New Zealand, married a niece of Te Wherowhero, Kenehuru. He became associated with the Wesleyan Mission and as he spoke Māori and negotiated with various Māori tribes in purchase of land for the mission. He also was used by various governors who entrusted him to negotiate with chiefs on Māori affairs. He died in 1851 leaving a Māori wife and children who suffered from mistrust from the Māori and lack of recognition from the Pākehā.

info_ref: H/O/M entry from Joanna Barnes-Wylie, 13 October 2025: Objective ID A7405464: {Auckland Council Heritage Unit (2014), [Papatoetoe Historic Heritage Survey: Survey Report](https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/arts-culture-heritage/heritage/heritagesurveys/papatoetoe-heritage-survey.pdf), Auckland Council; Auckland Council Heritage Unit (2016), [Māngere Bridge, Māngere East and Favona Built Heritage Survey](https://infocouncil.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/Open/2017/08/MO_20170816_AGN_7310_AT_files/MO_20170816_AGN_7310_AT_Attachment_54463_1.PDF), Auckland Council; Hayley Glover, (2022), [‘Wiri to Quay Park (W2QP): archaeological desktop assessment’](https://www.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/UnitaryPlanDocuments/appendix-i-heritage-report.pdf), report to Kiwirail; [‘History and Heritage’](https://raggc.com/club/history-and-heritage), Royal Auckland and Grange Golf Club, accessed 11 September 2025; Brian Hooker, (n.d), [Portages of early Auckland – to and from the Waitemata Harbour: the hub of an ancient communications network](https://folksong.org.nz/he_tangi_te_kiwi/portages_of_early_auckland.html); [Manukau’s Journey – Ngā Tapuwae o Manukau, Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections MJ_0054](https://kura.aucklandlibraries.govt.nz/digital/collection/manukau); [‘Meetings and Entertainments’](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH18980825.2.9), New Zealand Herald, 25 August 1898, p.3; [‘Obituary’](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH19411222.2.115), New Zealand Herald, 22 December 1941, p.7; [‘News of the Day’](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/AS19440502.2.33), Auckland Star, 2 May 1944, p.4; Board correspondence 21 June 2025 - 16 July 2025, Objective ID: A7239567}; Objective IDs: fA513856 & A5037774
info_origin: The Auckland suburb of Middlemore is located between Ōtāhuhu to the north and Papatoetoe to the south. Prior to European settlement, this area was on the route of the Waokauri / Pūkaki portage, one of several waka portages connecting Manukau Harbour with Tāmaki River to the east. The Waokauri / Pūkaki portage connected Waokauri Creek and Pukaki Creek to the Tāmaki River via Papatoetoe and Middlemore. In 1836 Anglican lay missionary Reverend William Thomas Fairburn purchased a large area of disputed land in the Papatoetoe area from several Auckland iwi. The purchased land was estimated to be 40,000 acres but subsequent surveying indicated it was over 80,000 acres. After the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840, the newly established Land Claims Commission investigated Fairburn’s purchase. The Commission found that Fairburn’s claim was problematic and in 1848 it awarded him a much smaller claim of 5,495 acres, known as Old Land Claim 269A. In 1897 George Lamberton Thomson and his uncle William Richard Middlemore Thomson purchased part of Old Claim 269A from Fairburn as tenants in common, though George Lamberton became sole owner in 1899. They named the property ‘Middlemore’ after Helen Middlemore (1763-1804), their paternal great-grandmother/grandmother, as evidenced by an August 1898 New Zealand Herald reference to ‘G. Thomson (Middlemore)’. In 1907 the Auckland Golf Club agreed to purchase part of the Middlemore property to develop a new nine-hole golf course. The club retained the name Middlemore when purchasing the property in 1909, with the golf course originally known as ‘Middlemore Links’. In 1944 the Auckland Hospital Board agreed that the new hospital being constructed immediately south of the golf course should be named Middlemore Hospital. Middlemore Station opened in 1947 (initially known as the Middlemore Hospital stop).

name: Milford Sound/Piopiotahi
info_ref: File BRD-02-02-00-07; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760}
info_origin: ’The first European name was Milford Haven. The first European to sight the sound may have been the whaling captain Peter Williams, who was born at Milford Haven in Wales. The most generally accepted theory credits the Welsh sealer Captain John Grono with the discovery and naming, and it may have been confirmed by Captain John Lort Stokes during the Acheron survey in 1851; Stokes owned an estate on the shore of Milford Haven in South Wales, and bestowed Welsh names in the sound, among them Mount Pembroke, St Annes Head, and Welsh Bay. Māori name: Piopiotahi. There are various accounts of the possible meaning: one is that Piopiotahi is a canoe that came across from Hawaiki to gather pounamu; another that after the famed explorer Māui visited Maitahi (Bruce Bay), he travelled further south along the coastline, and named Piopiotahi after a pet bird he had on board. Lit. piopio: extinct native thrush (Turnagra tanagra); tahi: single.’' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={1b38967a-3f52-e311-8212-005056970030})

info_origin: Milnthorpe on the northern side of Parapara Inlet abuts an important Māori mahinga kai or food gathering area. John W.C. Beauchamp (c.1826-82) surveyed the site in 1859 and sections were offered and then withdrawn from sale by the Provincial government. Beauchamp worked as a surveyor and architect in Nelson from 1850 to 1870. The sale of 89 town sections of 1 rood (1,011 sq m) and 102 suburban sections of 5 to 100 acres (2.02 to 40.4 ha) at Milnthorpe eventually went ahead in 1864. The township never materialized. A town plan of Milnthorpe comprising 81 sections of 1 rood [1011 sq m] or thereabouts based on Beauchamp’s survey was published by the government survey office in 1879. Milnthorpe Quay was at the waterfront, Nelson Street one back and Keswick Street formed the back boundary. These were bisected by Kendell and Wordsworth streets. Beauchamp, who arrived in Nelson in 1850, also surveyed the town site at Havelock and the Motupipi coal field. In 1903 the Post Office proposed to alter the name of the nearby Parapara Post Office to Milnthorpe or Ngarino to avoid duplication with a Parapara Post Office in North Auckland. The proposal lapsed.

The History of Taranaki. New Zealand: Edmonson and Avery.}
info_origin: Ethnologist Johannes Andersen believed Mimi was a contraction of Hamimi and was linked to Haurenui (or Urenui) and the journeys of Turi, captain of the Aotea canoe, who broke his travels to stay at Mōkau. Mimi River was one of many features named by Turi on his southward journey along the coast. Mimi was one of the places where Ngāti Mutunga sprang from. The locality takes its name from Mimi River. The river and surrounding swamps were important sources of food and were of great cultural significance to the iwi. In 1991 the Taranaki/Whanganui Conservation Board raised restoring the original name, Mimi-o-te-atua, to Mimi River with the New Zealand Geographic Board. The initiative was not carried forward, but Taranaki District Council has recognised Mimitangiatua as the full version of the river's name. Mimi marked one boundary of the New Zealand Company purchases in Taranaki in 1840. Mimi was a site of conflict during the Taranaki Wars of the 1860s.

name: Minna Bluff
info_origin: Discovered by the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, in September 1902. Originally called The Bluff, but altered before 1904 to Minna Bluff. Named after Minna (née Chichester), wife of Sir Clement Markham, the "father" of the expedition. Lady Markham befriended all the Officers of the Discovery.
info_description: A long, narrow bold peninsula 49km long from Minna Saddle in the west to the end of Minna Hook to the east and up to 7.7km wide, projecting southeast from Mount Discovery into the northwest portion of the Ross Ice Shelf. Like Brown Island, it is connected with Mount Discovery only by a low isthmus, but itself rises in many peaks over 900m high, with a highest point of c.1081m at Minna Hook. On its northern face it is very free from snow, but its southern side, which receives the full force of all the southerly weather and the pressure of the Ross Ice Shelf, is ice-covered except where the cliffs are too steep to hold the snow.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

When Kupe arrived, the peninsula was an island, hence: Motukairangi: lit. motu: island; kairangi: wonderful, chief, or wandering. A later Māori name was Whātaitai or Hataitai: lit. Murmur of the tide, which applied to the peninsula and not to the present suburb of Hataitai (see entry for Hataitai).’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Miranda
info_origin: Pūkorokoro is locally translated as “the long throated purse net”, which describes the entrance to Pukorokoro Stream and regular fishing that occurred in the area. In mid 1863 the Crown sent HMS Miranda as part of a naval blockade to suppress rebel forces. HMS Miranda tried to land soliders at the well-populated village of Pūkorokoro based on information that Kīngitanga forces might be there. Waka, whare and surrounding bush were destroyed and a large number of Ngāti Pāoa people were killed. Crown forces later constructed a redoubt which was named Miranda after the ship. This name was subsequently used for the town and surrounding area.; 'When General Cameron established his headquarters at Pokeno in 1863, HMS Esk and HMS Miranda took 900 men, with horses and equipment in other vessels, to the place eventually known as Miranda. The first redoubt was set up on the shore of the firth and named by officers after the warship. Maori name Pukorokoro: lit. long-throated purse net. The inlet here was likened to this type of net. The peak Pukorokoro or Puekekorokoro is located above the settlement, and there was a pa of the same name on its slopes.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: A populated place on the south-western shore of the Firth of Thames approximately 20km west south-west of Thames. Alteration from Miranda (recorded name). Feature shown on: NZMS260 S12 Edition 2 1994; Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BB34 054820

name: Moeraki Beach
info_origin: The area was known as Moeraki Bay before the 1920's and the Moeraki Boulders on the beach have made the name internationally known. The literal meaning for the word is 'moe': to sleep, 'raki': sky or day (south island version of rangi). The beach is notable for its small, round boulders. Legend tells that the Moeraki Boulders/Kaihinaki are food baskets, kumara, and gourds of the wrecked Arao-te-uru canoe, which can be seen in its petrified form in the reef near Shag Point/Matakaea. Kaihinaki literally means food basket. Refer "The Reed Dictionary of NZ Place Names", A W Reed.

name: Moeraki Boulders/Kaihinaki
info_origin: 'Otago, 3 km from Hampden. Lit. moe: to sleep; raki (South Island form of rangi): sky, or day. The beach is notable for its large and small spherical boulders, which legend ascribes to the gourds, food baskets and kumara of the wrecked Araiteuru canoe. The big boulders were called kaihinaki, lit. kai: food; hinaki: basket. The canoe itself in petrified form can be seen in the reef near Shag Point/Matakaea, q.v. The offi cial name of the boulders is Moeraki Boulders/Kaihinaki. The whalers called the boulders ‘The Ninepins’ and the area ‘Vulcans Foundry’.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Mōkau
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA378423; NZMS260 R18; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Maniapoto statement [extract]: Mōkau means to be basic, ordinary, unadorned. The Death of Runga-te-rangi recorded in Ngā Iwi o Tainui (pg. 234) uses double vowels, “They met up with Ngaati Tama to the south of Mookau.” Written evidence of Henare Tuwhangai speaking (July 1984) the scribe also uses double vowels “Te koorero, ko Mookau ki runga, ko Taamaki ki raro…” This justifies the use of a macron for “Mōkau”. Local historian, H Rauputu (2018) referenced an ancestor Mōkau as the origins of the place name. Mōkau who married Ruapūtahanga. Mōkau is a place of significance for Ngāti Maniapoto, particularly given its proximity to the River which, as above, provided great support for the iwi historically. Tangata whenua evidence before the Waitangi Tribunal provides further detail.

name: Mōkau
info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche October 2023: Objective ID: A5927085 {Darby, M. 2016. ‘Fallen Plumage’: A history of Puhipuhi, 1865-2015 (Wai 10-40) A# 61. New Zealand: Waitangi Tribunal.; Dollimore, Edward. 1962. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand: Wises.; Moore, P. R. 2011. The obsidian sources of Northland, New Zealand. Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand, 42 (4): 257-274.; NZGB Correspondence XXVIII/235; [Report of the Ohinemuri Miners’ rights Committee. 1875. New Zealand Times, 25 October, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZTIM18751025.2.34); https://maorimaps.com/marae/m%C5%8Dkau}
info_origin: An original Māori name, and one which occurs in several places in New Zealand. Mōkau Stream was one of the few sources of obsidian in Northland Region. Edward Brissenden (1936-1907) purchased an unspecified area of land described as Mōkau from Horomaia, Te Aru and others for 2/6d an acre in late 1874. Brissenden was a Land Purchase officer who worked on a commission of 4d per acre acquired instead of a salary and made extensive purchases of Māori land in Northland from 1874-76 before being dismissed for fraudulently issuing mining licences. In 1953 the Chief Cartographer of Lands and Survey drew the Geographic Board’s attention to the fact that Mōkau was used to name three different localities, but the status quo remained. Edward Dollimore (1904-73), who compiled The New Zealand Guide observed in the early 1960s that Mōkau Bay was used, presumably to avoid confusion with other Mōkau. Mōkau Marae, belonging to the Ngāti Wai confederation, was destroyed by fire in 2013 but had been rebuilt by 2020.

When the woman and son were found they were brought to Bluff. She was known as ‘Maggie’ and ‘Moggie’. Although there have been suggestions the island was named after her, it is more likely that she was named after the traditional Māori name for the island, Moki.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Mokoia Island
info_origin: 'Mokoia is derived from a pun on two words: ko: digging implement; and moko: facial tattoo. During inter-tribal warfare on the island a chief was stabbed by a ko in the moko pattern on his face. An earlier name was Te Motutapu-a-Tinirau: lit. te: the; motu: island; tapu: sacred; a: of; Tinirau, a name with legendary allusions across Polynesia. See also Motutapu Island. On this island is the pool known as Hinemoa’s Bath, the Maori name of which is Waikimihia: lit. wai: water; kimihia: sought for. After her long swim across the lake, directed by the flute music of her lover, Tutanekai, Hinemoa rested in the warm pool and was discovered there by Tutanekai.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Moleta Point
info_origin: NZGB Correspondence Vol. 53 p.55 - Notes on D'Urville Island place names: Molete Point: On the south side of Old Man's Head and is named in memory of the Moleta brothers who settled at Mukehanga (Waitai) in early 1890's. The Moleta brothers arrived on what is Old Mans Head with 250 sheep. The Moleta Bros. were from Italy and had first lived in Days Bays, Wgt. and fished for a living. They continued fishing at D'Urville Island and the income they made from it payed wages to local men fo bush-felling and other farm expenses. At a later date their fiances arrived from Stromboli and gradually a little Italian settlement was formed. These people were well-known for their generosity and warmth, and their singing while they returned home or head into the pass area in their boat. Son of the original Moleta Bros. still farm at Waitai.

name: Monaco
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche December 2022: Objective ID: A5113372 {[Stoke Road Board. 1923. Nelson Evening Mail, 12 May, Page 8](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NEM19230512.2.67.2); [Monaco. 1924. Nelson Evening Mail, 12 June, Page 5](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NEM19240612.2.67); [For Sale Monaco Subdivision. 1927. Nelson Evening Mail, 27 December, Page 8](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NEM19271227.2.96.5); [Waimea County. 1937. Nelson Evening Mail, 9 July, Page 6](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NEM19370709.2.90)}
info_origin: This suburb of Nelson City is on Martin Point, a spit that extends into Waimea Inlet. Council approval for road access to the point was granted in 1923 and in 1924 sections in the new beachside suburb of Monaco were advertised for sale as 'the Stoke seaside resort'. Accessibility to the city, picturesque surroundings and sandy beaches for swimming were selling points for the promoters. Additional sections were sold off in 1927 and 1930. Local surveyor Francis Ledger (1872-1939) of the firm of Ledger & Spence, undertook the design work. The popularity of the Principality of Monaco as a beach resort for the wealthy and famous attracted considerable newspaper attention in the 1920s and appears to have provided the inspiration for the name for this development.

The place has many associations with death, particularly for Te Rarawa and Te Aupouri, as in the lament ‘I te rimu e mawe ra ki Motau’ (Where the seaweed swirls at Motau). There may also be a link to an ancient carved house, which was given the name Motatau because its tatau (sliding door) was not at the front but in the side wall.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Mōtū
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2024/April 2024: Objective ID: A6197735 {[Judith Binney. 'Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Tūruki', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1990. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1t45/te-kooti-arikirangi-te-turuki); Cowan, James. 1983. The New Zealand wars, Volume II. Wellington: Government Printer [first published 1922]; Dollimore, E. S. 1952. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand: Wises.; Land Possessed by Maoris, North Island, AJHR G 15.; [Map of Motu Village 1912.](https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE26859248); Motu - Poverty Bay: [R23280926](https://collections.archives.govt.nz/web/arena/search#/entity/aims-archive/R23280926). Archives New Zealand Digital.; Oliver W.H. and Thomson J.M. 1971. Challenge and Response. New Zealand: East coast Development Research Association; [The Motu Sections. 1903. Gisborne Times, 14 April 1903, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/GIST19030414.2.22); Twiselton, D. 2007. The Motu and Beyond. New Zealand: Twiselton.}
info_origin: An original Māori name. Edward Dollimore (1904-73), who compiled The New Zealand Guide, put forward ‘an isolated place’ as a translation. At Mōtū in 1872 Te Kooti (?-1893), the Rongowhakaata religious and military leader, eluded his pursuers Captain John R (Richard) Rushton (1841-1925) and Wiremu Kingi and 50 men, and travelled into Urewera Country and ultimately the King Country. In 1876 Te Manihera and others sold the Motu Block estimated at 63391 acres (25653 ha) not including three native reserves totally 5091 acres (2060 ha) to the Crown, a transaction that was finally completed in 1880. The first tracks and roads were constructed from 1881-86. A 500 acre (202 ha) Native Reserve remained at Mōtū in 1886. Facing difficult conditions, Lands Department surveyors gradually surveyed the Mōtū area from 1889-98. A Dane, Christian Hansen (?-1910) travelling from Queensland, was one of the first to take up a 50 acre (20 ha) lease-in-perpetuity bush section at Mōtū in 1888 as well as opening an accommodation house in 1891. Mōtū was midway on the difficult route with only a bridle track from Ōpōtiki to Gisborne. A newspaper article from 1903 extolled Hansen’s pioneering spirit ‘To my mind there Is nothing nobler than the incentive that inspires and serves men to pioneer in untrodden forests and build up homes for themselves and their families’. But in 1895 the Commissioner for Crown Lands was much more circumspect about the 40000 acres (16187 ha) Motu Block which he considered ‘fit only for large holdings’ and was ‘little sought after by the general run of would-be-settler.’ A ballot for the sections surrounding Mōtū village township was held in 1903. Robert T Sadd (1856-1937) Chief Surveyor of Hawkes Bay prepared a map of Mōtū Village in 1912, which featured a school site and 15 mainly one acre (0.4 ha) sections along with 22 others of mainly of one rood (1012 sq m).

info_origin: Literal meaning is Motu - island, kokako - nz crow. Named because the Kōkako were specifically placed there so that Chiefs had their own personal supply of Kōkako feathers. Sir Piercy Brett was one of the Lords of Admiralty from whom Cook received his commission to explore the 'Southern Continent'. Name change from Piercy Island (Motukokako Island). See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMERFRjc4NDFEMzBGRUE5OTQzQkM)"

Ngāti Hei speak of huge physical nets that were strung between islands in the rohe moana and caught massive amounts of kaimoana which was then distributed between the whanau for the islands involved. name: Motu-o-Rūrū
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-12/95; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Motu o Rūrū was an important Ngāti Tū pa and kainga the origins of which may date back to the time of Tukapua I. According to Pat Parsons the name probably translates to Island of Owls because the fortress was almost entirely surrounded by water. he states that the owl, or ruru has been significant to Ngāti Tū for a long time, considered to be kaitiaki of the people and the appearance of one considered to be a good omen. Parsons relates a historical event involving Motu o Rūrū, “Documentation in Aturangi Anaru’s book confirms that it existed in the days of Kohipipi. Aturangi describes a dispute which arose in the days of Tureia. The dispute involved Te Waka and Turangiapa two chiefs from Te Putere. Tureia launched a surprise attack on them catching Te Waka without weapons. Turangiapa seized a taiaha and made his escape. He fled south to Tūtira and sought refuge at Whakairo’s pa, Te Onepu. He finally found shelter at Motu o Rūrū. Turangiapa married Kohipipi’s sister and made his home among Ngāti Tū... It is likely that Motu o Rūrū served as the fortified retreat for the kaingas on the two Richmonds.”
info_description: An historic site above cliffs on Mangaone River near the confluence with Waikinakitangata Stream. NZTopo50-BJ38 157450

info_origin: An original Māori name. Sherwood Roberts (1834-1917), an early European recorder of Māori names, offered a literal translation as 'cockleshell island' alluding to the importance of the area as a source of seafood, particularly shellfish. Motupipi was also the location of a significant pā and kāinga. Roberts described the pā as being 'surrounded by a high fence of palisades, made of round saplings with the thick end sunk in the ground, the tops lashed together, with flax'. In the 1840s there was heavy bush running up the valley with some mānuka and flax cover on the flats and rushes by the shore. The New Zealand Company surveyed the area in 1842. The 1845 Māori census recorded 24 men and 15 women, significantly down on the several hundred residents in the early 1840s. The Land Purchase Commissioner, William Spain (1803-76), paid £290 as compensation to Māori from Motupipi, Tākaka, Aorere and other parts of Golden Bay for shortcomings in the New Zealand Company land purchases. This agreement was signed at Motupipi in 1846, though disagreements continued for another decade. Four irregularly shaped 'old reserves' were initially set aside at Motupipi but through an unsuccessfully contested process of rationalisation and exchange of land these were recomposed during the 1860s into eight occupation reserves totaling 707 acres (286 ha). By the 1860s and early 1870s through the efforts of the Assistant Native Secretary, James MacKay (1831-1912), the reserves had all been partitioned and allocated to individual Māori owners. In 1860 a large hui was held at Motupipi to discuss Governor Gore Browne's justification for the war in Taranaki as presented at the well-attended Kohimarama conference in Auckland. Frederick Tuckett (1807-76), the New Zealand Company's principal civil engineer and surveyor in Nelson, had found high quality coal at Motupipi in 1842. This was being mined by 1845, and a lime kiln was in operation from 1855. In 1849 David John Kerr established a run at the head of the Motupipi valley. The first sawmill at Motupipi was started by Joseph Packard, John Perry Robinson (1809-65), C. Nicholl and James Lovell in 1855. Robinson was elected Superintendent of Nelson Province in 1856. In 1867 Provincial Engineer John Blackett (1818-93) surveyed a road line to Clifton to improve access to Motupipi. The Motupipi estuary remains a habitat of high to moderate diversity with sizable amounts of intact intertidal vegetation, although since 1943 when records began, 28 ha of salt marsh has been lost to drainage and reclamation.

info_origin: Motutere, translated by historian James Cowan as 'floating islands', was the name given to a low lying 'patch of pumice sand, with a few scrubby bushes of manuka' that had further subsided into Lake Taupō / Taupōmoana in the second half of the 19th century. A pā was built here by Tamamutu on an old track that ran around the lakeside. In 1846 Te Heu Heu Tukino II Mananui (?-1846), members of his family and 54 others perished in a landslide at Te Rapa. The event was attributed to a taniwha which afterwards fled across Lake Taupō / Taupōmoana to Motutere, then on to Waikato River and into the sea. That same year Donald McLean (1820-77), the sub protector of Aborigines, disapprovingly described the inhabitants of Motutere as 'being in a perfect state of heathenism'. In 1849-50 Governor George Grey visited Motutere as part of a longer journey from Auckland to Taranaki via Taupō / Taupōmoana. He recounted that 'On a promontory running out from the shore is the settlement of Motu-tere, a very old pa, containing now but few inhabitants. Here we arrived at half-past nine …. Preparations for a great feast for the natives were immediately commenced, whilst we partook of a lunch of preserved salmon, eaten with boiled rice off tin plates with steel forks and iron spoons'. Motutere pā was the site of an important reconciliation between Iwikau Te Heuheu Tūkino III (?-1862) and rival leader Te Herekiekie (?-1861) facilitated by missionary Thomas Samuel Grace (1815-79) in 1853. Grace's success, which was seen as ensuring peace, prompted the performance of Ka Mate, the missionary being heavily bearded was identified as the 'hairy man' of the haka. Austrian geologist Ferdinand Hochstetter (1829-84) visited Motutere in 1859 and noted 'a row of palisades of stout posts bearing carved figures'. The pā was burnt in 1869 during the New Zealand Wars. Over a decade later in one of the earlier European journeys into the King Country in 1882, James Kerry Nicholls (?-1888) observed 'At Motutere, a small, low peninsula jutting out into the lake, we found the remains of an extensive pa, with burial-places and carved palisading, which lay scattered about the ground. There was likewise the remains of a whare karakia, or church' plus old cultivations and peach trees. By the 1930s Motutere was regarded as a place for camping and fishing.

info_origin: The name Mōtūwairaka was bestowed by Haunui a Poupoto also known as Haunui a Nanaia. Following is a summarised account of our tīpuna kōrero. Haunui a Poupoto (a great grandson of Kupe) journeyed to Aotearoa concealed on the Kurahaupo waka, which landed at Nukutaurua on Mahia Penninsula. Discovered, he was cast ashore and following some escapades, he and his wife Wairaka eventually settled. Unfortunately Wairaka was kidnapped which caused Haunui a Poupoto to zealously pursue her and her kidnappers. Haunui a Poupoto, in reference to his pursuit of Wairaka and her kidnappers, bestowed many names down the west coast of the North Island and back across the Tararua range to the east coast. According to the Ngāti Kahungunu and Tūmapūhiaarangi people of this area who trace direct descent from Haunui a Poupoto , on his return journey to his dwelling place after finding Wairaka, he came to the river mouth Rongoua, Wairaka was left there and lies there in the form of a rock. Hence the name of the area Mōtūwairaka. Haunui a Poupoto named the beach at Mōtūwairaka, Te Nukutaotaoroa-a-Hau because of the extended length of the sandy beach and land.

info_origin: Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairarapa Tāmaki nui-a-Rua statement: ‘Motu Wairaka gets its name from the korero of Haunui-a-Nanaia (Hau) and Wairaka...The significance of Motu Wairaka, spelt Motuwairaka in the korero, is apparent because Wairaka accompanies Hau over to the Wairarapa from Paremata. Hau leaves her at the river mouth at Motu Wairaka, encased as rock, one side of her is stone and the other side of her is pounamu...The significance of this name to Ngati Kahungunu is also apparent in the writings which demonstrate clearly the connections between Kahungunu of the Takitimu waka and Rongomaiwahine, a descendant of Hau of the Kurahaupo waka. The descendants of Rongomaiwahine and Kahungunu form the Ngati Kahungunu iwi.’

name: Mount Albert
info_origin: ’Given in honour of Queen Victoria’s consort Prince Albert, following a petition by residents to the provincial superintendent on 22 February 1866. At a later date the city end of the suburb was known as Rocky Nook. An early name for the hill was Te Puke-o-Ruarangi: lit. te: the; puke: hill; o: of; Ruarangi. A cave in the lava on the side of the hill was Te Ara-tomo-o-Ruarangi, The cave pathway of Ruarangi. Ruarangi, the chief of the hilltop pā whose people were besieged, led them to the cave to escape through the lava-bubble caves and passages towards Western Springs. All but Ruarangi escaped; he was too large to squeeze through the passage. The better-known name, Ōwairaka, means Place of Wairaka; the daughter of Toroa, commander of the Mataatua canoe, Wairaka originated the name for Whakatāne in the Bay of Plenty; see Whakatāne. She led her people to the Tāmaki isthmus, where they established the pā on Ōwairaka.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Named for Annie Lindon who climbed it with her husband and a guide on 19 February 1910, although an ascent by Arthur Harper (1865-1955) and P Johnston dated back to 1891. Australian Annie Lindon (1860-1943) nee Hudson was married to Leonard Harford Lindon (1859-1953), headmaster of prestigious Geelong Grammer School, giving them the means and holiday time to spend climbing. Both accomplished climbers, they organised mountaineering holidays in New Zealand in 1906-12 and 1920. In 1909 she climbed The Nuns Veil (2749m) and the following year in an 18 ½ hour trip, crossed Graham Saddle from east to west. She climbed Glacier Dome (2424m) with her husband, guide Peter Graham, and B Kosti as porter on 25 February 1910. On 14 November 1910 with her husband and guide Higgins, she ascended Mount Annette (2235m) which was named after her. In 1911 she climbed Mount Sealy (2627m) which included a new traverse, the Minarets (3031m) with husband and guide Peter Graham, and De la Beche (2950m) also with husband and guide Peter Graham. On a longer visit in 1912 she climbed The Footstool (2764m) with her husband and guides Darby Thomson and Jack Lippe, and on 12 April she reached the summit of Aoraki/Mount Cook (3724m) with guides Peter Graham and Darby Thompson. She was quoted as saying having learnt at the Hermitage, ‘a native of England and a resident of Australia, she regards herself as a New Zealand climber’. Returning in 1920 with various guides, she made ascents of Mount Johnston (1241m), Anzac Peaks (2528m), Maunga Ma (2503m), Mount Darby (2531m), Mount Jeanette (2485m), Malte-Brun (3199m) and Raureka Peak (2333m).

info_origin: Named after Harcourt Richard Aubrey (1818-96) Collector of Customs and Resident Magistrate at Whangārei Heads from 1856 until his retirement in 1880, and from 1861 also postmaster. These peaks are named Pouwewe on an 1850s map accompanying Gilbert Mair (1799-1857) senior’s land claims in the area. Aubrey came to New Zealand in 1840 on the survey staff for the Plymouth Company and with Chief Surveyor Frederick Carrington (1808-1901) selected the site for New Plymouth. In 1848 Aubrey became Sub-Collector of Customs and Postmaster at Hokianga before shifting to Whangārei Heads eight years later. Mount Aubery was named on the New Zealand Geological Survey Bulletin’s Geological map of Ruakaka Survey District published in 1922. Hartley Travers Ferrar (1879-1932), who had been a geologist on Captain Scott’s first National Antarctic Expedition from 1901-04, directed the geological fieldwork. In the first decades of the 20th century the bay below Mount Aubrey was known as Aubrey Bay.
