info_origin: Journalist and Alpine Club member [Israel] Julian Grande (1874-1946) first climbed the 2800m peak with guides Peter Graham and Frank Milne on 6 March 1923 and named it after his late wife Constance Grande nee Barnicoat (1872-1922). Nelson born, she completed a BA at Canterbury College in 1895 and served as MP (Sir) Francis HD Bell’s (1851-1936) secretary before working in Britain from 1897 as a secretary/interpreter and as a newspaper reporter. In 1902 she returned to New Zealand and in 1903 with Jane Thomson, Miss Perkins and guides made up a party of women to cross Copland Pass. The guides initially doubted her fitness, but she spent a fortnight training ‘as hard as I could’ on mountains and moraines around the Hermitage: vowing ‘you shall shake your head another way before I have done with you’. Barnicoat climbed in boots, ‘a white wool “sweater”, knickers [knickerbockers] and putties to my knees’. She noted that ‘Except in some such dress the guide flatly refused the risk of taking ladies; and he was perfectly justified’. As reported in the Timaru Herald, she described the ‘trip as a very beautiful’ and spoke ‘of the scenery as very fine’ and ‘being particularly good’. She wrote an article ‘Through the Copland Pass’ for the Wide World Magazine. After travelling back to the UK, she scaled Ailefroide in France (1905) Grosser Schreckhorn in Switzerland (1911) and climbed in the Caucasus (1907). In 1910 she explored the Great Beautus Grottos in Switzerland. She travelled widely in later years including in Egypt and Palestine. She married Julian Grande in 1911 and they settled in Switzerland in 1913. During World War I she edited a multi-lingual journal and wrote critically about German war aims. Post war she closely followed the early work of the League of Nations. Mount Barnicoat first appeared on the map ‘Part of New Zealand alpine regions’ in 1929.

info_origin: Mount Beatrice (2528m) was first ascended by Miss Beatrice Holdsworth (1882-1959) accompanied by her cousin mountaineer Hugh Chambers, and guide Peter Graham on 23 January 1914. She was the daughter of John and Margaret Holdsworth. John Holdsworth was a Hawkes Bay sheep farmer with the family connections and financial resources to climb. Earlier in 1913 along with Hugh Chambers, Miss Irene [?] Chambers and accompanied by guide Charlie Milne, she climbed Mount Sealy (2627m). In March 1913 along with Irene Chambers, and Peter Graham and Jack Lippe as guides she climbed a now difficult to identify mountain that Arthur P Harper (1865-1955) described as an 8000 feet (2438m) ‘Unnamed Peak’ between The Footstool and Cadogan Peak. In February 1915, with Hugh Chambers and guide Conrad Kain she climbed Maunga Ma (2503m) and on 3 March, Glacier Dome (2424m) the latter along with Miss Irene Chambers and Mrs Muriel Graham, with Peter Graham as guide, also climbing Mount Ross. In 1920 she holidayed in Europe and in the UK married Eric Nairn (1881-1925), later settling at Omakere in Hawkes Bay. In 1937 she revisited the Hermitage where her ‘many successful pioneers ascents in the Mount Cook district’ were recalled in the Press. These included four first ascents. The 75th anniversary described her as being part of the 1910-1920 ‘golden age’ of women climbers alongside Mrs (Elizabeth) Muriel Graham (1884-1957), Margaret Lorrimer (1866-1954) and Freda du Faur (1882-1935). The name Mount Beatrice first appeared on Johannes Andersen’s ‘Sketch Map of the Mount Cook Region’ in 1916.

name: Mount Bledisloe
info_origin: The name Mount Bledisloe was proposed for this hill by Mr Vernon Reed, Secretary of the Waitangi National Trust, in 1944. The hill is named after Lord Bledisloe, Governor-General 1930-35, who gifted the Treaty House and grounds to the nation in 1932. This feature was approved as Bledisloe Hill by the Honorary Geographic Board in 1947 (3/47). Mr Reed lodged objections to the designation hill for this feature in 1948, and 1949. Both of these objections were dismissed by the Board, and the designation hill stood until 1950. In that year Mr Reed lodged a further objection, which was upheld, Mr Johannes Andersen dissenting, and the name was changed to Mount Bledisloe.
info_description: Hill, 105m, above Huia Creek, near the corner of Haruru Falls Road, Te Puke Road, and Bledisloe Road, Bay Of Islands.  Kawakawa Survey District.

name: Mount Blick
info_origin: Named after Graeme Blick, Geodetic Survey Advisor, Office of the Surveyor-General, Land Information New Zealand. From 1970 - 1995 he worked for the Institute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences (formally NZ Geological Survey) in the Earth Deformation Group as a geodetic surveyor. In the summer of 1983/84 and 1984/85 he was involved in surveys around the summit of Mount Erebus monitoring crustal deformation associated with volcanic activity of the mountain. Graeme joined Land Information New Zealand (formally Department of Survey and Land Information) in 1995 and has worked in the Office of the Surveyor General as Geodetic Survey Advisor where he has been responsible for the Department's geodetic activities in New Zealand and Antarctica. Since 1998 he has worked closely with the US Geological Survey on geodetic surveys in the Ross Sea Region and has overseen the development of the new Ross Sea Region Geodetic Datum 2000.

name: Mount Camel
info_origin: 'Northland, at the entrance to the Houhora Harbour. ‘W. by S. Leagues from this point [Knuckle Head, usually known as Cape Karikari] and about the Middle of the Bay is a high Mountain or Hill standing upon a desart [sic] shore, on which account we called it Mount Camel,’ wrote Captain James Cook on 10 December 1769. Maori name: Maungataniwha, lit. maunga: mountain; taniwha: water monster. Tamatea of the Takitimu canoe caught a whale and towed it ashore at Houhora Harbour. After providing a huge meal for the crew, most of the whale’s body remained there in the form of a mountain which was called Tohoraha (the Rarawa dialect word for whale).' name: Mount Discovery
info_origin: Discovered by the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, and named for the expedition ship Discovery. It is the most symmetrical of all the large craters and rises in a graceful dome, sheathed almost up to its summit in ice. It forms the centre of a three-armed mass of which Brown Peninsula is one extension to the north-east. Minna Bluff is a second to the south-east and the third is Mount Morning, which is really a part of the mainland. By 1950's the feature still had not been visited in spite of the fact that there are no greater obstacles than rough ice in the way. It is considered to have a most striking appearance, its bell-like dome reminding one of Mount Taranaki or Mount Egmont, in the North Island of New Zealand. On its southern side it is almost entirely covered with snow and ice, but on the north there is so much bare rock that at midsummer one could almost ascend the mountain on rock entirely, certainly up to 2400m.

info_origin: The name Mount Endeavour was given to the S block of the Kirkwood Range by the N.Z. Northern Survey Party of CTAE in Oct. 1957, but in subsequent N.Z. and U.S. maps the name was identified as the 1810m summit described above. Following additional mapping by USGS in 1999 and consultation between US-ACAN and NZGB, the name Endeavour Massif (q.v.) was approved for the S block of the Kirkwood Range. The summit and the massif are named after HMNZS Endeavour (formerly John Biscoe), supply ship to the 1957 N.Z. Northern Survey Party.

The application of these names is based on analysis of Amundsen's narrative. Not Mt Engelstat, Mt Ole Engelstad, Mt W Christophersen, or Mt Wilhelm Christophersen.

name: Mount French
info_ref: Holmes, Richard, The Little Field-Marshal: Sir John French, London: Cape, 1981.; Reed, A.W., Place Names of New Zealand, Rosedale: Penguin, 2010.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: A party comprising J.K. Inglis, E.A. Duncan, and Jack Murrell made the first ascent of this peak on 30 November 1914. By then the First World War had been underway for nearly four months. At a time when many New Zealanders retained strong emotional and practical ties to Britain, the fighting taking place on the Western Front was a matter of considerable public interest. While their fellow climbers Hugh Wright and H.E. Hodgkinson were labelling the adjacent summit Mount Joffre, after the leader of the French Army, Inglis, Duncan, and Murrell chose to name this peak for the Commander-in-Chief of the British Expeditionary Force (BEF). Field Marshal Sir John French was the logical choice to lead Britain’s forces on the continent. He had fought with distinction as a cavalry commander during the Second Boer War in South Africa, and had served as Inspector-General of the Army and Chief of the Imperial General Staff. Yet French’s time at the head of the BEF proved to be a difficult one. The Allies were initially forced into a chaotic retreat through Belgium and north-eastern France, before managing to stabilise the front at the Battle of the Marne and the First Battle of Ypres. When Trench warfare became well established during 1915, the BEF suffered dreadful casualties for little discernable gain at Neuve-Chapelle, Second Ypres, and Loos. Apparent command failures at the latter engagement saw French come under heavy criticism, with several politicians and senior officers working to undermine his position. He was eventually forced to resign in December 1915 and was replaced by Douglas Haig. French did go on to hold other senior positions. He served as Commander-in-Chief Home Forces throughout 1916 and 1917, before being appointed Lord Lieutenant of Ireland in May 1918.

Elvy maintained that it was named after the farmer ‘because it was first ascended by Mr George Fyffe, away back in the ’fifties of last century. Kaitarau is the highest peak, but I am told that this should be Manakau, and that Kaitarau refers to Mount Fyffe.’ See also Maungaroa.' name: Mount Jeanette
info_ref: Objective reference: A4855497; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche July 2023: Objective ID: A5490634 {A.J.S. 1945. In Memoriam. Mrs. Jane Thomson (1857-1944). New Zealand Alpine Journal, 11, 72-73.; Harper, A.P. 1930. First Ascents and Explorations. New Zealand Alpine Journal, 4, 100-119.; [Trish McCormack. 'Thomson, Jane', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1996. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3t34/thomson-jane) (accessed 29 May 2023); Thomson, Mrs J. 1921. A Traverse of Mount Cook. New Zealand Alpine Journal 3 (10), 14-19.; Thomson, Mrs J. 1921. Climbing in Otira. New Zealand Alpine Journal 3 (11), 100-102.}
info_origin: Named for Jane Thomson, who ascended it on 5 February 1915 with Austrian born guide Conrad Kain (1883-1934). The name was accepted by New Zealand Alpine Club climbers by 1919. Jane Thomson nee Coutts (1858-1944) was born in Canterbury. She married civil engineer John Thomson in 1879 and resided in Taranaki, Poverty Bay and Otago (1893-1909) before settling in Greymouth and after 1909 in Wellington. In 1903, with Constance Barnicoat and Miss Perkins and guides, she crossed Copland Pass. Although on this trip she wore knickerbockers and puttees under a long and tight-fitting jacket, on other climbs she favoured a knee-length skirt. Over the next 12 years she climbed mainly in the Arthur’s Pass area, writing about these in the New Zealand Alpine Journal. Over the 1915 and 1916 seasons, with guide Conrad Kain, she returned to Aoraki/Mount Cook and made a number of notable climbs. She also ascended Mount Jean (2519m) and Mount Edgar Thomson (2379m), named after her deceased only son, Maunga Ma (2503m) and Malte-Brun (3199m). Without guides, she climbed Mount Kinsey (2083m), Mount Blackburn (2409m), The Footstool (2764m) and Lendenfeld Peak (3194m). In 1916 aged 57 years, with Kain, she climbed Mount Bannie, Mount Burns, Mount Elie de Beaumont and Mount Darwin, and made the grand traverse of Aoraki/Mount Cook. She later described this climb in the New Zealand Alpine Journal. Kain described her as ‘a skilful climber and knows how to handle the rope at critical moments...we climbed more than a dozen peaks together …but she never played out or showed fear’. In 1930 she ascended the low peak of Mount Rolleston (2275m).

name: Mount Joffre
info_ref: First World War.com, ‘Who’s Who – Joseph Joffre’, http://www.firstworldwar.com/bio/joffre.htm; Reed, A.W., Place Names of New Zealand, Rosedale: Penguin, 2010; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: A party comprising Hugh Wright and H.E. Hodgkinson made the first ascent of this peak in late November 1914. By then the First World War had been underway for nearly four months. At a time when many New Zealanders retained strong emotional and practical ties to Britain, the fighting taking place on the Western Front was a matter of considerable public interest. While their fellow climbers J.K. Inglis, E.A. Duncan, and Jack Murrell were labelling the adjacent summit Mount French, after the Commander-in-Chief of the British Expeditionary Force, Wright and Hodgkinson chose to name this peak for the leader of the French Army. General Joseph Joffre was an unusual choice for such a senior position. Having been a military engineer in France’s far-flung colonies, he had no prior experience of army command or of general staff work. Nevertheless, he was appointed Chief of the French General Staff in 1911. Joffre’s record during the First World War was somewhat mixed. The first month saw the Allies forced into a chaotic retreat through Belgium and north-eastern France. However, the Germans were prevented from reaching Paris after suffering a strategic defeat at the Battle of the Marne. This engagement was Joffre’s finest hour, as his logistical brilliance and ruthless dismissal of incompetent generals played a key role in stabilising the front. When trench warfare became well established during 1915, the French Army suffered tremendous losses for little discernable gain in Artois and Champagne. A series of blunders during the Battle of Verdun then prompted criticism of Joffre’s leadership, and he was forced to step aside in favour of General Robert Nivelle during December 1916. Joffre spent the remainder of the War in administrative roles. Promoted to Marshal of France, he led the Military Missions to Romania and the United States, before sitting on the Supreme War Council during 1918.

name: Mount Kirk
info_origin: The name recognises former New Zealand Prime Minister Norman Kirk (1923-1974), particularly for his leadership through his 1973 decision to uphold the 'Save Manapouri' campaign's petition. Accepting the petition ended plans to raise the level of Lake Manapouri for hydro-electric generation, which would have connected the lake to Lake Te Anau submerging large areas of native forest and the Manapouri township. Instead, it was decided the lake would be managed within the naturally recorded variations of its level. The ‘Guardians of Lake Manapouri and Te Anau’ was created to monitor the arrangement, and remains constituted as a statutory body 'Guardians of Lakes Manapouri, Monowai and Te Anau' under Part 2B Conservation Act 1987.

name: Mount Knox
info_ref: Map sheet: Explorers Cove. Refer to NZGB minutes: 30/01/98 & 07/10/98.
info_origin: Named for Prof (Emertus) George Knox, who has been actively involved in Antarctic biology for over 30yrs. Former president of SCAR. 2007: presented with the New Zealand Antarctic Science 50th Anniversary Award. Emeritus Professor Knox, then aged 87, was born in Pleasant Point and educated at Timaru Boys High School. He was first appointed to the then National Committee for Antarctic Research in 1959 and sat on the Ross Dependency Research Committee between 1965 and 1992. He was the New Zealand delegate to the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR) from 1974 to 1986 and President of SCAR between 1978 and 1982, the only New Zealander to hold the post. Knox also sat on several other international committees, including being Secretary General and then President of the International Association for Ecology (INTECOL) from 1978 to 1982. Knox’s long-standing public service and impressive academic record in the environment and conservation sectors throughout New Zealand led to his MBE in the Queen’s Birthday honours list of 1985. Knox retired in 1984 after a distinguished academic career spanning 35 years at Canterbury University, including almost 20 years as head of the Department of Zoology. He began a long-term marine biology Antarctic research programme in 1960 and directed the team for 12 years. Incredibly, Knox participated in 13 field parties to the Antarctic and has published more than 100 scientific papers – including 25 on the Antarctic and Southern Ocean. His most recent book, the 1000-page Biology of the Southern Ocean, is the standard international reference work on the oceans surrounding Antarctica. George is also acknowledged as a key figure in Antarctic marine science.

Levick was a Staff Surgeon, Royal Navy, and was zoologist and photographer to the expedition. He was one of the Northern Party led by Victor Lindsay Arbuthnot Campbell, who spent the 1912 winter on short rations under primitive conditions at Evans Cove, '260 miles' from base. He wrote a book Antarctic Penguins about Adélie Penguins.

name: Mount Levy
info_origin: Named for Professor Richard Levy in connection to his leadership of the Friis Hills Drilling Project 2016/17, which recovered and described several drill cores, which are 'arguably the best studied and most well-dated and complete geological record…at a time of global cooling’ and have enabled a better understanding of the geological, biological, and climate history of the site and region. Professor Levy is a stratigrapher and paleoclimatologist with a long and distinguished career and more than 30 years’ experience in Antarctica, having undertaken 15 expeditions in Antarctica from the Transantarctic Mountains to the McMurdo Dry Valleys. He was a key leader in the New Zealand ANDRILL project in McMurdo Sound in the mid-2000’s, has published over 100 papers in peer-reviewed journals, and won the Sir Peter Blake Leadership Award in 2022. As of 2024 Professor Levy is leading an international drilling project at the West Antarctic Ice Sheet SWAIS2C (Sensitivity of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet under +2 degrees Celsius of global warming).

name: Mount Lucia
info_origin: Named for Lucy Mannering (née Lean), first wife of pioneer climber George Mannering. He named it on a trip with Tom Fyfe from Cass River over Rutherford Pass to Murchison River in January 1909. Possibly climbed by TN Brodrick and survey party in 1891. From January to March 1913 Lucy was at the Hermitage with her family. She climbed Mount Sealy (with Peter Graham) and Hochstetter Dome (with the whole family and Darby Thomson), and attempted Aoraki/Mount Cook with George. She drowned on 19 March 1913 at the end of that long holiday while fishing at the Aratiatia rapids in the Waikato.

info_origin: Named by Rose Moorhouse (1865?-1932) and her cousin Mabel Studholme (1869-1958) when they ascended nearby Mount Rosa in 1890. Named by 1891 on a map in GE Mannering 'With Axe & Rope'. An earlier ascent of then unnamed Mount Mabel had been made by Malcolm Ross and James Annan earlier that same year. Mabel Studholme was a daughter of Michael (1834-1886) and Iphigenia Studholme owners of the Waimate station. Mabel painted and was a member of the Canterbury Society of Arts in the mid-1890s. In 1903 she left for Durban to marry Mostyn Innes Jones (1864-1944), a former Waimate resident, and Lieutenant in the New Zealand Sixth contingent to the South African War. After the war Innes Jones was Commissioner of Lands for the Zoutspanburg district based at Pietersburg in the Transvaal. Ultimately, they returned to New Zealand and settled in Te Kūiti.

name: Mount Maunganui
info_origin: ’Lit. maunga: mountain; nui: tall or large. Mount Maunganui is often abbreviated to The Mount. The original Māori name is Mauao, which means Caught in the light of day. Mauao suffered an unrequited love for Pūwhenua, who favoured Ōtānewainuku with her charms. Heartbroken, Mauao asked the patupaiarehe (forest fairies) to take him to the ocean, but they made it only as far as the coast before daylight caused the fairies to flee.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Mount Morning
info_origin: Discovered by the British National Antarctic Expedition (Discovery Expedition, BrNAE), 1901-04, and named for the Morning, a relief ship to the expedition. It is an entirely volcanic formation. As of the 1950s no party had been nearer to it than Heald Island on Koettlitz Glacier, from which point it appears to consist of an aggregate of a large number of large cones and centres of activity rather than material from a single vent. At the time it was considered that "as it is situated right upon, or even within, the line of fracture which has given rise to the present coastline of south Victoria Land Upon its western side, if anywhere, should be found evidence of the effect of volcanic activity upon the older rocks of the mainland and possibly some arrangements of the vents showing a relationship between them and the fault line."

info_origin: This hill is named after Walter George Morrison (1877-1955). Early in 1932, realizing that some of the topography in the vicinity of Poulter River on sheet 22 of the four-inch to the mile map series was incorrect, CGS (Charles Gilmour Stead) Ellis (1897-1986), Lands and Survey Chief Draughtsman in Christchurch went into the field to make a compass survey and check the heights of peaks in the doubtful areas. In May 1932 William Stewart (1881-1957) Chief Surveyor, Christchurch, reported to Harry Walshe (1883-1948), Surveyor-General and ex-officio member of the Honorary Geographic Board, that this work was completed and forwarded a new map to Wellington. This map included a dozen new names which Walshe put before the Board for approval. The proposed new names included those of various lessees, other settlers and two New Zealand State Forest Service staff, including Walter Morrison. These Walshe recommended ‘for the favorable consideration of the Geographic Board’. He noted that ‘in the absence of local traditions or history other than the accident of residence or visits to the district I think these suggestions might be adopted failing any more imaginative or outstanding facts for perpetuation or otherwise’. Mount Morrison was confirmed at the Board meeting of 8 July 1932 and in 1948 made official under the New Zealand Geographic Board Act, 1946. Walter Morrison joined the Forests Branch of Lands and Survey in 1898 shortly after its inception. He served in the South African War with the 8th New Zealand Rough Riders and after his return was made an Assistant Forester in 1902. Transferring to the newly established State Forest Service in 1921, by 1926 he was appointed Conservator of Forests for Canterbury, the senior regional administrator, where here remained until his retirement in 1938.

name: Mount Ngauruhoe
info_origin: 'Tongariro National Park, south of Mt Tongariro. The tohunga and explorer Ngatoroirangi was nearly dead of cold when he reached the summit of the mountain, and prayed to his sisters Kuiwai and Haungaroa in faraway Hawaiki to save him. They sent the fire-demons or gods by way of Whakaari (White Island), Paeroa, Rotorua, Tarawera, Orakeikorako, and Taupo (places where thermal activity still testifies to their power). Finally they burst out of the mountain top, saving the tohunga from freezing to death. In gratitude Ngatoro slew his slave, Ngaruhoe, and cast the body into the fiery crater from which the fire gods had emerged. She left her name to the mountain. Two other versions exist. One is that Ngatoro actually sacrificed his grandson, Hoe, whose hair is seen in the plumes of smoke that escape from the mountain, hence Ngauruhoe, lit. nga: the; uru (usually huru): hair; Hoe. The other is a more literal interpretation: nga: the; uru: the act of arranging hot stones in an umu (oven); hoe: to toss out, an analogy between tossing hot stones out of an earth oven and eruptions of rock and lava.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

This is in recognition of his significant contribution to, and leadership of, New Zealand’s scientific effort in Antarctica during his ten years (1998-2008) with Antarctica New Zealand as Manager Science and Information and Science Strategy Manager. His notable achievements include: 1) developing the New Zealand Antarctic Science Strategy; 2) having significant input to the New Zealand government decision to provide new funding for International Polar Year research; 3) playing a key role in the development of the Latitudinal Gradient Project, ANDRILL and ITASE scientific projects; 4) being instrumental in the establishment of strong science collaborations with the US National Science Foundation, Australian Antarctic Division, Italy and Malaysia; and 5) acting as both Scott Base Manager and Senior Antarctica New Zealand representative in Antarctica.

Journal of the Nelson and Marlborough Historical Societies 1 (5), 23-24; [Advertisements. 1861. info_origin: John Godfrey and his wife Phyllis were early settlers in the Wairau valley. Godfrey, who was a valuer, auctioneer and commission agent, purchased land in 1860 and bestowed the name Mount Pleasant on it, presumably in part because of the nearby hill. ‘Amusement Seeker’ encountered bad weather and boggy ground when travelling through the area in 1861 and in writing to the Marlborough Press, suggested the name was applied ‘in derision I presume’. Never-the-less the name Mount Pleasant endured, being a named polling place in 1865 and having a named railway station by 1875. Godfrey (1823-91) originally migrated to Nelson before moving to Marlborough and eventually settling in Picton. He was one of the petitioners seeking the separation of Marlborough from Nelson Province and a member of the newly formed Marlborough Provincial Council from 1860-69. He was a champion of the smaller settlers who frequently involved him in political controversy.

name: Mount Rittmann
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-15/304; USGS Reconnaissance Map 1:250K SS58-60/5.
info_origin: Identified as a volcano by the 4th Italian Antarctic Expedition in the 1988/89 field season, and named by them in 1991 for the eminent volcanologist Alfred (Alfredo) Ferdinand Rittmann (1893-1980). Dr Rittmann was president of the International Association of Volcanology (IAV), later the International Association of Volcanology and Chemistry of the Earth’s Interior (IAVCEI) from 1954 to 1963. During the 6th Italian Antarctic Expedition in the 1991/92 field season, fumaroles and ground heated by geothermal activity were discovered in a small volcanic crater.
info_description: A large active volcano predominantly buried in ice, with several peaks reaching an estimated 2600m, located in Mountaineer Range, Victoria Land. Included within Antarctic Specially Protected Area 175 High Altitude Geothermal Sites of the Ross Sea Region. The mountain is covered and surrounded by glacial ice. The base of the volcano outcrops on the almost vertical cliffs of Pilot Glacier. Fumaroles and geothermally heated ground occur within a single outcrop at the summit of Mount Rittmann in a minor caldera rim at approximately 2000m above sea level.

Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. ; Named by Rose [Rosa] Moorhouse and her cousin Mabel Studholme after the former following their ascent of the 2161m peak in 1890. From the summit they also named the nearby Mount Mabel. Rose Moorhouse (1865?-1932) was the daughter of James (1832-66) and Anne Moorhouse (1846-91). From a well-connected family, she was also the niece of William Sefton Moorhouse (1825-81) a former Superintendent of Canterbury Province, MP, and Mayor of Christchurch. As early as 1880 Rose had visited Frances Glacier (named after Frances Tripp) with members of the Acland and Tripp families led by John Barton Arundel Acland (1823-1904) owner of the Mount Peel estate who had explored the head waters of Rangitata River for two decades from 1855. In 1892 Rose married Arthur Edgar Gravenor Rhodes (1859-1922), a lawyer businessman in contrast to his prominent landowning relatives. He was later an MP and Mayor of Christchurch in 1901. Her charm and style cemented their place in Christchurch social circles and considerably assisted Arthur’s political career. After Arthur’s death she lived with her son in London and died in 1932 after a fall from a window.

info_origin: In January 1913 Frank Kitchingham and Charles Ward named this peak after Rosamond Harper (1909-2005), daughter of Arthur P Harper (1865-1955) founder of the New Zealand Alpine Club. Introduced to climbing by her father as a 16-year-old, she accompanied him and Norman Blakiston in crossing Graham Saddle and Copland Pass on an eight day return journey from Waiho Gorge to the Hermitage, including scaling Saint Mildred Peak (2395m). In 1927 Arthur Harper was invited to join UK Colonial Secretary Leo Amery (1873-1955) to climb Aoraki/Mount Cook with guides Peter and Alec Graham. Amery invited Rosamond to accompany them. The route included Glacier Dome (2424m) for the views. Rosamond and her father tried skiing on Darwin Glacier. The party then crossed Graham Saddle into Westland, traversing Malte Brun Hut to Defiance Hut on 9 December 1927. The following December, along with her father S Wiren, C Turner-Williams and R Lucas, Rosamond crossed Fyfe Pass to Westland. In 1931 with Miss Barbara Crawford, she drove from Picton to Franz Josef Glacier/Waiau. Without guides they climbed Franz Josef Glacier/Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere to Almer Hut. The next day they scaled Mount Rudolf (2742m) via Graham Saddle. Bad weather then delayed them at Almer Hut before they crossed Newton Pass to the new Chancellor Hut and Glacier Hotel at Weheka. On 8 December 1934 with Betsy Blunden and Leila Davidson, Harper was part of a major all-women ascent in New Zealand, which was undertaken without guides. Describing the climb Harper explained that they originally intended to descend into the head of Twain River (now Douglas River) but instead decided to climb Mount Sefton (3151m). That year she became a member the New Zealand Alpine Club. The following year, again with Betsy Blunden, she made a winter climb of Mount Rolleston (2275m). She married Selwyn Hatfield in 1936, which ended her climbing. In 1961 she gifted her father’s mountaineering journals to the New Zealand Alpine Club.

info_ref: Ferguson, Captain David, A History of the Canterbury Regiment, N.Z.E.F., 1914-1919, Auckland: Whitcombe and Tombs, 1921.; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 9, pp. 55-57, 85.; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Minutes, 1932 (16).; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 1948 (42).; Press, 11 August 1915, p. 4.; Reed, A.W., Place Names of New Zealand, Rosedale: Penguin, 2010; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013; Corr IX f.45, 52-55 (map), 85
info_origin: Named after one of the over 100,000 New Zealanders who served overseas during the First World War. Robert Amos Row was born in 1888. He attended West Christchurch and Christchurch Boys’ High Schools, before finding work as a commercial traveller. By virtue of his extensive service in the Territorial Forces, he was given the rank of Major at the outbreak of the War. He sailed with the Main Body of the New Zealand Expeditionary Force as commander of the 1st (Canterbury) Company of the Canterbury Infantry Battalion. Row not only survived the conflict, but also served with great distinction. After undergoing extensive training, he led his unit during the ill-fated Dardanelles Campaign of 1915. There followed a period of reorganisation in Egypt, and further time spent training reinforcements in England. When the 4th New Zealand Infantry Brigade was formed during February 1917, Row was promoted to Lieutenant Colonel and placed at the head of the 3rd Canterbury Battalion. He took part in the Battle of Passchendaele, before transferring to the 1st Canterbury Battalion at the start of 1918. For his bravery in battle he was awarded the Distinguished Service Order. The name Mount Row was first assigned by the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand in 1932, and was officially confirmed by the New Zealand Geographic Board in 1948.

In 1835 Sabine presented to the British Association for the Advancement of Science Proposals for an expedition to the South Magnetic Pole. name: Mount Sheppard
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Colonel (retired) Paul Raymond Sheppard who made significant contributions to the United States Antarctic Program (USAP) during his military career. He flew over 100 resupply missions to Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station over a period of 10 years. He spearheaded development of year-round flight operations in the Ross Sea by introducing LED portable runway lighting and Night Vision Goggle (NVG) landing capabilities to McMurdo Station. He followed his military service with federal civilian service in various capacities in the Office of Polar Programs (OPP), US National Science Foundation (NSF). He was responsible for contract oversight and support for US operations throughout the continent of Antarctica. Colonel Sheppard was selected by his international peers to lead the Council of Managers of National Antarctic Programs (COMNAP) Aviation Expert Group for over 5 years. His outstanding service and contributions in Antarctica spanned 28 years.

They climbed the peak that bears Sinclair’s name. On 26 March Dr Sinclair was missed, and the following morning his body was discovered by the bank of a river. Sinclair was a former naval surgeon who had been appointed colonial secretary in 1844. His body was buried at Mesopotamia, ‘near the bank of the river,’ wrote von Haast. ‘With almost juvenile alacrity he had climbed and searched the mountain sides . . . until at last, over-rating his powers, and not sufficiently aware of the treacherous nature of alpine torrents, he fell victim to his zeal.'' name: Mount Talbot
info_origin: Named as a tribute to Arthur Talbot (1877-1917) by George Moir after he, Harry Slater, Bob Sinclair and Ken Roberts climbed the peak on 20 January 1924. Talbot was killed at Passchendaele on 12 October 1917. He and fellow mountaineer William (Bill) Grave were well known for explorations in northern Fiordland National Park. Moir's party claimed the right of first ascent to name the peak, which Talbot and Grave had named ‘Mount Lippe’ a few years earlier after the Aoraki / Mount Cook guide Jack Lippe who also worked in Fiordland. In the late 1920s, many (including Lippe himself) protested the change of name to the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand who upheld 'Mount Lippe'. Mountaineers and climbers, however, used 'Mount Talbot'. By the 1980s ‘Mount Talbot’ was in such common usage that the New Zealand Geographic Board confirmed it as the official name.

name: Mount Taranaki or Mount Egmont
info_origin: Mount Egmont was named by Captain Cook, after the Earl of Egmont, who was first lord of the Admiralty at the time. In Māori legend, Putauaki was a man mountain who originally stood at the spot now occupied by Lake Rotoaira. He played up with the woman mountain Pihanga, and her husband Tongariro, objected and took action. Putauaki, knowing his guilt tore himself up by the roots and made off to the northeast. Two other mountains were guilty and similarly made off. Tauhara to the east and Taranaki retreated toward the west coast, carving out the Whanganui River as he went. They fled while daylight lasted when night came they took root and stayed where they were. Taranaki settled at the western extremity of North Island. Refer The Reed Dictionary of New Zealand Place Names. Te Ara Encyclopaedia of New Zealand . ( http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/taranaki-region/3 ). See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDQzM0EyODFGRDBGRjg5MDdEM0E)

info_origin: The Māori name Tarawera literally means 'Burning Peak', but prior to the 1886 eruption there was no Māori tradition refering to the feature as a volcano.; 'Lit. tara: bird spears; wera: burnt. Hikawera, a chief who came from Hawke’s Bay, had a successful fowling season on the shores of the lake and the slopes of the mountain. On his departure he left his bird spears in a wharau (hut). Returning the following year, he found the wharau and its contents destroyed by fire. The northern part of the mountain was called Wahanga: lit. burst open; the middle peak Ruawahia: lit. rua: pit; wahia: broken; and the southern peak Tarawera.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Mount Teichelmann
info_origin: Named for Dr Ebeneezer Teichelmann (1859-1938) by George J. Roberts of the Westland Survey before 1910. Teichelmann emigrated from Australia in 1897 to assume the role of Surgeon-Superintendent for the Westland Hospital and soon developed a keen interest in mountaineering. Between 1899 and 1924 Teichelmann made numerous expeditions, especially up Fox Glacier / Te Moeka o Tuawe and Franz Josef Glacier / Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere. He accompanied mountaineers Alexander (Alex) Graham and Henry Newton on a number of first recorded ascents from the West Coast. During the First World War there was pressure to re-name geographic features that had ‘alien’ (ie German or Austro-Hungarian names), including Mount Teichelmann. Teichelmann's father had been a German missionary in South Australia. Teichelmann was serving as a Captain in the New Zealand Medical Corps with the 53rd Casualty Clearing Station at the time. No geographic features were actually renamed as a result of this movement.

info_origin: ’The mountain also gives its name to Tongariro National Park. Lit. tonga: south wind; riro: carried away. When Ngātoroirangi, the tohunga of the Arawa canoe, reached the summit of the mountain during his explorations, he nearly perished from the cold. In his distress he called on the gods of fire, or as some say, to his sisters in Hawaiki, to come to his rescue. ‘Kuiwai e! Haungaroa e! Ka riro au i tonga, tukuna mai te ahi!’/‘O Kuiwai! O Haungaroa! I am seized by the cold wind of the south. Send fire to me!’ The fire gods came to him by way of Whakaari / White Island and Rotorua, where they emerged briefly and left tokens of their visit for all time, finally bursting out of the mountain top. The words riro (to be carried away) and tonga (south wind) that were part of his cry were applied not only to the mountain as it is now called, but also to Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: This feature was named after Joanna Elizabeth Turnbull (1870-1955), who with Malcolm Ross (1862-1930) and the well-travelled British climber J Wontner Brown (1866-1938), ascended the 2265m peak on her 30th birthday on 10 February 1900. Immediately prior to this, in the company of Malcolm and Forrest Ross (1860-1935) and without guides, she traversed the length of Haupapa/Tasman Glacier and ascended Hochstetter Dome (2810m). Earlier women climbers to undertake the traverse were Anna von Lendenfeld (1860-1946), Tasmanian Mrs Maxwell, and Forrest Ross. Joanna Turnbull was the daughter of Walter and Alexandrina Turnbull. Walter Turnbull was a successful Wellington merchant. Her older brother, Alexander Horsburgh Turnbull (1868-1919) was the noted bibliophile. In London in late 1900 Joanna Turnbull married Sir James William Leigh-Wood (1870-1949) of the Natal Bank, Pretoria, formerly of Calcutta. Lady Leigh Wood gifted a Wedgewood medallion of James Cook, bequeathed to her by her brother Alexander, and landscape paintings by John Gully back to New Zealand in the mid-1920s. She made an extended visit to New Zealand in 1938.

name: Mount Tūwhakarōria
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-13/56. NZTopo50 CC11 Queenstown
info_origin: Proposed as part of a package proposal by Central Otago District Council and Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu. The famous tipuna, Rākaihautū, led his travel party through Te Waipounamu using his famous ko (stick) Tūwhakaroria, a Polynesian digging stick similar to a spade, and no doubt used also as an alp staff. Hence the figurative saying that with it he scooped out the basins of the lakes of Te Waipounamu, whereas it was simply with its aid that he discovered them. But to the imaginative, the picturesque appeals; whereas the unimaginative take it literally, confounding fiction with fact, and failing to see that it is fiction that gives life and immortality to fact. He started with Lakes Rotoiti and Rotoroa in Nelson and he next tackled Takapō (Lake Tekapo), Pūkaki and Ōhau. These three were more or less plain sailing, however it was more difficult when he came to scooping out Lakes Hāwea, Wānaka and Whakatipu-wai-māori. He explored this majestic country, traversed the valleys of the Greenstone and Hollyford and arrived at Whakatipu-wai-tai (Lake McKerrow) where they again came in touch with the sea. retracing their steps and again turning south they made Te Ana-au (Lake Te Anau) and Moturau (Lake Manapouri).The final resting place of the ko Tūwhakaroria culminated at Mount Bossu, Akaroa Harbour. The story relates to the first human footsteps and is highly significant for Ngāi Tahu people. To mark the conclusion of Rakaihautu's achievements, the name was ceremonially changed to Tuhiraki - the name by which it has been known ever since.

name: Mount Whewell

name: Mount Whitcombe
info_origin: 'All named after Henry Whitcombe, the mountain being named by Julius von Haast in 1866. Samuel Butler and John Holland Baker were the first Europeans to traverse the pass, in 1861, and it was crossed by Whitcombe and Jacob Lauper in 1863. Whitcombe was drowned shortly afterwards in the Taramakau River on the West Coast. Butler wrote: ‘Alas! That our having found it [the pass] should have cost poor Whitcombe his life.’ Maori name: Rurumataikau.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 J34 Edition 1 1992 Limited Revision 1996

name: Mount Whitcombe

info_description: A large mountain between the lower Fry and Benson Glaciers, 7.5km southeast of Mount Davidson, and particularly prominent from the Granite Harbour area. A high ridge runs south to Mount Perseverance. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MC09

name: Mount Wild
info_origin: Discovered and named in December 1908 by the BAE, 1907-09. For Frank Wild, one of the four men who were in the Southern Polar Party which reached "within 97 miles" of the Pole. Wild was also a member of other Antarctic expeditions.

name: Mount Wilhelm Christophersen
info_origin: Discovered by Amundsen on his journey to the South Pole in November 1911, and named by him for Wilhelm C C Christophersen, Norwegian diplomat and Minister at Buenos Aires at that time. Apparently an error in the position of Mt Wilhelm Christophersen and Mt Engelstad on the map in Amundsen's book, Sydpolen, gave rise to transposition in subsequent cartographic application of these names. The application of these names by the US Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names is based on an analysis of Amundsen's narrative. Not Mt Engelstad, or MT Engelstat, or Mt Ole Engelstad.
info_description: A mound-shaped knob, about 3389m high, rising from the edge of the South Polar Plateau at the head of the Axel Heiberg Glacier, between Mt Fridtjof Nansen and Mt Engelstad, in the Queen Maud Range.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Mount Willberg

info_description: Mountain at height 1245m, situated approximately 5km south-east of Harihari

name: Mount William

The peak was named by T D Burnett because William Grant was a firm friend of father Andrew Burnett. Name supplied by D M C Burnett of Mt Cook Station. Refer also "High Endeavour", by W Vance p 152, and "Early South Canterbury Runs", by R Pinney p 149, 150.

info_description: A large mountain massif about 4 miles wide and 10 miles long, surmounted by three sharp peaks in an east-west line, the highest of which rise to about 2700m, standing at the south side of the Albanus Glacier at the point where it joins the east side of Robert Scott Glacier in the Queen Maud Range.

name: Mou Waho
info_origin: Mou Waho is translated as "Outer Island". The word "Mou" is a corruption in the Ngaitahu dialect of "Motu" the Māori word for "island" and "waho" means "far out, or farther out". Supersedes Harwich (Gazettes 1924, page 2882, 1949, page 939) Ministerial decision to assign Mou Waho.; 'Lit. mou: island; waho: outer, open water. It has also been rendered as Te Mou-a-hou: lit te: the; mou: island; a: of; Hou. Previously named Harwich Island, probably by Sir Frederick Chapman and Lord Jellicoe, after the Harwich Naval Squadron, and Manuka Island, in reference to manuka trees.The lake on the island is Arethusa Pool, q.v.; see also Paradise Lake. ' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={437a36b9-3e52-e311-8212-005056970030})

name: Mou Waho Island (Harwich) Scenic Reserve
info_ref: Evening Post, 14 November 1924, p. 2.; Heathcote, Tony, The British Admirals of the Fleet, 1734-1995: A Biographical Dictionary, Barnsley: Leo Cooper, 2002.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Correspondence, vol. 59, pp. 169-226.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 2011 (81).; Reed, A.W., Place Names of New Zealand, Rosedale: Penguin, 2010.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: In 1924, Sir Frederick Chapman, a former Supreme Court judge and member of the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand, suggested new names for two features on Lake Wanaka. He proposed that the body of water on ‘Pigeon Island’ should become Arethusa Pool and that the Island’s highest point should be titled Tyrwhitt Peak. When the time came to seek official approval for these changes, the Governor-General, Admiral John Jellicoe, further moved that ‘Pigeon Island’ be renamed ‘Harwich Island’. The Royal Navy’s Harwich Force was established at the outbreak of the First World War. Placed under the command of Commodore Reginald Tyrwhitt, it had three main objectives: to protect the approaches to the English Channel; to monitor German activities in the North Sea; and to escort ships between Britain and the Netherlands. Each of these tasks was carried out successfully. Although it was absent from the largest naval engagement of the War at Jutland, Harwich Force played an important role at the Battles of Heligoland Blight, Texel, and Dogger Bank. It also captured or sank 24 enemy merchant vessels, and escorted 520 eastbound and 511 westbound ships between British and Dutch ports. Despite being Gazetted in 1924, ‘Harwich Island’ did not achieve common acceptance. In both 1972 and 1988, the New Zealand Geographic Board (NZGB) received numerous submissions asking for a return to the original ‘Pigeon Island’. Mindful of the legislative requirement to favour Māori names, and keen to avoid confusion with Pigeon Island on Lake Wakatipu, the NZGB put forward ‘Manuka Island’ as an alternative. However, it was forced to drop this idea after fresh objections were raised. The deadlock was finally broken by the discovery of additional evidence. Documents from the 1920s revealed that the name ‘Pigeon Island’ had actually been pre-dated by Mou Waho, or ‘outer island’. As this title offered both a new beginning and a link to the area’s Māori past, Mou Waho (for the island feature) was approved by the NZGB in 1988. A connection to the First World War was retained with the Island’s scenic reserve. In 2011, that area was officially titled Mou Waho Island (Harwich) Scenic Reserve.

name: Mullins Valley
info_origin: Named for Jerry L. Mullins, Physical Scientist, Chief, Antarctic and Arctic Program for U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and National Science Foundation Antarctic geophysical research. His was responsible for Antarctic field research in the Transantarctic Mountains, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Shackleton Mountains, Beardmore Mountains, Antarctic Peninsula, Mount Siple, Amundsen-Scott South Pole station and at deep field research locations in West Antarctica. His program conducted research in the disciplines of global positioning systems, geodesy, crustal motion, glacial geophysics, airborne geospatial systems, seismology, light detection and ranging (LIDAR), topographic mapping and he managed the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) South Pole winter-over program from 1989 to 1994. He was appointed by the National Academy of Sciences, Polar Research Board as a US delegate to the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research Geosciences Standing Scientific Group from 1995-2004 and was appointed as a member of the Advisor Committee on Antarctic Names in 1994. Mullins Valley appears in the Antarctic research literature, on the maps from the British expedition of Captain Scott and in aerial photographs from the United States expedition Operation Highjump by Admiral Byrd.
info_description: A valley approximately 4km long between Rector Ridge and Vestal Ridge, at approx. 1600m elevation, located in the McMurdo Dry Valleys. It is one the few dry valleys in the world to contains rock glaciers. US Antarctic Program (U.S. Antarctic Project (USAP)) research has dated the subsurface ice in Mullins Valley at 4 million years old making it among the oldest ice on earth. U.S. Antarctic Project (USAP) research has also shown the rock glaciers in the valley to be analogous to the Arsia Mons region on Mars. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MF07

name: Muriwai
info_ref: Objective ID: A4635550; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2024/April 2024: Objective ID: A6197735 {Dollimore, E. S. 1952. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand: Wises.; Fowler, L. 1946. Some thoughts on charcoal and the generating of fire by Percussion in old Maori Usage. Journal of the Polynesian Society, 66, 264-70.; Mackay, J. A. 1940. Historical Poverty Bay. New Zealand: Mackay.; [Muriwai. 1884. Poverty Bay Standard, 7 February, Page 2](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBS18840207.2.14)}
info_origin: A pā site associated with a lagoon where Waipaoa River entered the sea. Edward Dollimore (1904-73), who compiled The New Zealand Guide offered ‘backwater’ as a translation. In 1831 John Harris (1808-72) an employee of a firm of Sydney merchants, after negotiations with local chiefs set up a trading station at Muriwai where there was a sizable Māori population. Another trader, Peter Simpson also took up residence that same year. Thomas Halbert (1806/7? -65), a third trader arrived from Māhia in 1834. Wherowhero, the name of the adjacent lagoon, was also applied to Muriwai in the 1830s. An 1884 description of the settlement noted it presented ‘a very pretty appearance at this time of year, houses and whares of varied form and aspect, interspersed with picturesque groups of trees of indigenous and foreign origin, contributing with the background of grassy hills to form a landscape very pleasing to the vision of the beholder.’

name: Musick Point / Te Naupata
info_origin: Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki history: The original inhabitants of Te Naupata peninsula were the descendants of Huiarangi and Toi-te-huatahi. Later arrivals from Tainui waka settled on these lands around Tāmaki Heads sometime between AD 1280 and 1350. Intermarrying with the earlier tāngata whenua, they formed the iwi known as Ngāti Tai, or Ngāi Tai. Te Naupata is identified in Ngāi Tai tradition as one of the landing sites of the Tainui, and takes its name from the native shrub Coprosma lepens, known in other dialects as Taupata. Ngāi Tai remained in unbroken possession of Te Naupata from the time of the initial Tainui settlement until the Muskets Wars of the 1820s. Due to the amount of bloodshed, tapu was then enforced over the site, along with certain other wāhi tapu in the Howick and Pakuranga area. The site contains coastal urupā and many other significant heritage features, and has retained its highly tapu status to Ngāi Tai down to the present time, despite being acquired by the Crown as part of its “surplus lands” regime between the 1840s and ‘50s. The name Musick Point was given to the site in 1938 when the Government renamed the site in memory of Captain Edwin Musick. Another name sometimes applied to the site is Te Waiārohia-o-Ngāriki, or simply Te Waiārohia. This name is now believed to be erroneous, deriving from confusion with another site by that name at Hobsonville Point, Waitematā.
info_description: A coastal point at the end of an unnamed peninsula which projects into Tamaki Strait south of Browns Island (Motukorea). NZTopo50-BA32 695205.

name: Naish Peaks
info_origin: Named for Professor Timothy Naish, Director of Victoria University of Wellington's Antarctic Research Centre. The name recognises Professor Naish's highly successful Antarctic scientific career, particularly in the area of paleoclimatology. Professor Naish is well known for his leadership of the ANDRILL Project, was the 2014 recipient of the Tinker-Muse Prize for Science and Policy in Antarctica, and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand in 2015. During the 2010-11 field season, Professor Naish and his colleagues worked at 'Oliver Bluffs', an area of exposed strata and fossil deposits on the north of Dominion Range - a site overlooked by Naish Peaks.

name: Napier
info_origin: ’Originally Ahuriri. The name commemorates Sir Charles Napier, the commander-in-chief of British forces in India. Commissioner of Crown Lands Alfred Domett proposed the name on 20 March 1854 in a letter to the colonial secretary, following a settler petition to commemorate Lord Clive, former governor of Bengal. Domett chose Napier for the intended lesser ‘port town’ while reserving Clive as the name of the intended main district city, reflecting the perceived ranking of the two officials in British India. First town sections were sold in April 1855, and Napier was in common usage thereafter. The correct Māori name of the inner harbour was Te Whanganui-a-Orutū: the great harbour of Orotū, a descendant of Māhu and tupuna of the Ahuriri hapū. Another name came from the great Māori explorer Tamatea Urehaea, who called the inner harbour Te Whanga-nui-a-Rotu and the island in the middle Tapu-te-Ranga: a sacred place where rites were performed.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: National Park
info_origin: In 1908 Waimarino Railway Station was established just outside the northern boundary of the Waimarino 4 'non-sellers' block from the earlier Waimarino Crown purchases. In 1910 a 'Town of Waimarino' was surveyed around the railway station. This remained mostly a town on paper and little populated until the Marton Sash & Door sawmill opened in 1925. In 1924-1925 in response to local petitions, the Railway Department agreed to change the name of Waimarino Railway Station to 'National Park'. This change was partly a branding exercise due to the proximity to Tongariro National Park, though also for practical purposes due to misdirected mail and freight. There was ongoing confusion with Waimarino County (the administrative headquarters being in Raetihi to the south), and Waimarino Electorate (the administrative headquarters being in Taumarunui to the north-west). The newly formed Honorary Geographic Board were not consulted, and did not approve of changing the original Māori name given that the name was within its remit. The Board however accepted the change which took place in May 1926. The alteration of the name of the railway station was never formally gazetted by the Railway Department or later by the Geographic Board. Informal use of National Park for the village itself followed suit as it developed as a populated place, particularly in its role as a gateway to Tongariro National Park, with newspapers showing mixed use of either name giving way to just National Park over time. National Park was named on the official NZMS 150 map series for Tongariro National Park, although 'Waimarino (National Park)' continued to be shown on the NZMS 1 series in 1971, and it was not until the NZMS 260 series in 1985 the main series showed just 'National Park'. In 1957 the National Parks Authority wrote to the Board that it was looking to change the name of the railway station back to 'Waimarino'. Ironically, the mail and freight for other national parks around New Zealand was now arriving at 'National Park'. The proposal was shelved due to a lack of local support. The following year the Federated Mountain Clubs submitted a proposal to alter the name of the village back to Waimarino. At its 13 February 1959 meeting it declined the proposal as 'National Park' was now well established. Once more in 1967-68 the National Parks Authority informed the Board it now intended to alter the names of the railway station and village back to Waimarino. Mail and freight were still being misdirected to 'National Park', and with further national parks established in New Zealand. The residents of National Park objected, and produced a petition signed by every household, and many others in the area. The Board considered the name on 4 July 1968. Based on the strong objections the Board once again declined the change. In 1969 the Board conversely, considered a further proposal from Taumarunui County Council to alter Waimarino to National Park. This appears to have been prompted by confusion with the cadastral property parcel appellations, many remaining 'Town of Waimarino' from the 1910 survey. In 2023 Uenuku hapū/Te Korowai o Wainuiārua, an iwi collective established to represent hapū affiliated with Uenuku, Tamakana and Tamahaki for Treaty settlement negotiations, proposed altering the name back to Waimarino. The Board accepted the proposal, and public consultation between November 2023 to February 2024 drew 2,582 submissions from 2,122 individual submitters. While submissions predominately supported the proposal, they included another objecting petition signed by most of the residents of the village, along with former residents and other interested parties. The Board considered submissions in April 2024 and reported its decision to proceed with the proposal to the Minister for Land Information, who on 3 December 2024 made the final determination to alter the name back to Waimarino.

name: Nelson
info_origin: ’As Wellington had been named in honour of Britain’s most famous soldier, the New Zealand Company named the settlement across Cook Strait after her most famous sailor — Vice-Admiral The Viscount Nelson. In its early history Nelson was jocularly known as Hobson’s Choice (see Hobsonville). Māori names for the village on the site of the settlement: Wakatū: lit. waka: canoe; tū: to pile up; that is, A place where broken canoes were deposited, also rendered Sheltered harbour; or Whakatū: lit. to erect or raise up, or a formal speech. The Boulder Bank was in one version Te Tāhuna-a-Tamaiea: lit. te: the; tāhuna: shoal; a: of; Tamaiea (also spelt Te Maia). Tamaiea created the bank that gave safe anchorage for waka. An alternative name is Te Taero-a-Kereopa. A Ngāti Koata version of the naming relates it to a person who sought refuge here and was told ‘Whakatūria tou pā ki a tēnā puke’ which means ‘Set up your home on that hill’. The area became known as Whakatūria and later Whakatū.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: In 1871 the census enumerators separated Nelson township into two sub-districts divided along Trafalgar Street and named them Nelson East and Nelson West with 2917 adults in the former and 2507 in the latter. In 1880 it was proposed to cut the Nelson electorate in two as Nelson East and Nelson West. The precise description of the boundaries of Nelson East were as follows ‘bounded towards the North west and North by the sea from the Lighthouse on Boulder Bank; towards the East by the Picton Electoral District to Dun Mountain; towards the South-west by a right line to the South-western corner of Section 3, Maungatapu Survey District; thence by south-western boundary lines of Sections 3, 1, 23, 24, 27, 20, and 22, to the south-eastern corner of the Borough of Nelson; thence by southwestern boundary line of said borough to Waimea Road; again towards the North-west by said Waimea Road and Waimea Street, and by street forming the north-western boundaries of sections, 227, 229, H10, H12, H14, to the north-western corner of last mentioned section and thence by a right line across Nelson Harbour to Nelson Lighthouse, the starting point’. However, this change to the electoral boundaries did not take place. Nelson East did, particularly in the early 20th century, become a descriptor used by businesses and individuals living on the east side of Trafalgar Street. Nelson East Post office was opened in the 1930s.

name: New Windsor
info_ref: Corres LI, pp 206-209, 236; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche May 2023: Objective ID: A5325931 {Bush, G.W.A 1971. Decently and in Order. New Zealand: Collins.; [Commercial. 1882. Auckland Star, 20 March, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/AS18820320.2.4); [Cooper, Paul. n.d. John Shedden Adam (1824-1906) Presbyterian and governance philanthropist.](https://colonialgivers.com/2018/02/18/john-shedden-adam-1824-1906-presbyterian-and-governance-philanthropist); NZGB Correspondence 51, 206-09, 236; [Sale of Land at New Windsor. 1865. New Zealander, 11 May, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZ18650511.2.10); [Stone, Russell. 2001. From Tamaki-Makau-Rau to Auckland. New Zealand: Auckland University Press.]; [Township of New Windsor and Suburban farm lots. 1865. Daily Southern Cross, 28 April, Page 3.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/DSC18650428.2.4.2); [Truttman, Lisa. 2020. New Windsor: The Beginnings of a suburb.](https://www.bhb.nz/back-in-the-day/new-windsor-the-beginnings-of-a-suburb)}
info_origin: This area was part of the 12000 acres [4856 ha] Waitematā to Manukau Block purchase of 29 July 1841. Much of the land comprising today's New Windsor was sold by the Crown in the 1845-48 period. This included land purchased by John Shedden Adam (1824-1906). Another significant land purchaser in 1845 was Dr Samuel Hayward Ford (1811?-76) who had left Kororāreka for Auckland to escape from the war in the north. Adam had arrived on the Jane Clifford in 1841 to take up land in the unsuccessful Cornwallis settlement but exchanged this for Crown land in Avondale (1 acre [0.4ha] of Crown land for every 4 acres [1.6 ha] held in Cornwallis. In 1845 Adam left for Tasmania and found employment as a draughtsman in the Surveyor General's office in New South Wales. Dr Ford was a Church Missionary Society surgeon who had settled with his wife at Paihia in 1837. He returned to Bay of Islands in 1849. In 1865 auctioneers Mabin and Graham sold Adams 300 acres [121 ha] as 1 acre [0.4 ha] town and 15 acres [6 ha] farm sections at what they described as the 'Township of New Windsor'. A successful auction resulted in gross proceeds of £1300 with 'a good attendance, notwithstanding the unfavourable state of the weather, and the bidding was pretty fair'. In the 1860s Thomas Mabin and Graham operated as auctioneers and commission agents. In 1882 Messrs Cochrane and Son auctioned a further 14 farms at New Windsor. New Windsor formed part of Avondale Borough which amalgamated with Auckland city in 1927. A New Windsor school dated from 1957. However, the Post Office on New Windsor Road was established as Avondale East in 1963 and not renamed New Windsor until the early 1970s. In 1981 Auckland City Council delegated its Planning Committee to seek New Zealand Geographic Board approval for the boundaries be to be demarcated and officially named as a suburb of Auckland City, a process that was completed in 1984.
info_description: Suburb of Auckland City between Avondale and Blockhouse Bay Community Committee Areas.

name: Ngā-Hina-o-Te-Pūrewa
info_origin: Ngāti Ruapani mai Waikaremoana history: 'The name Ngā-Hina-o-Te-Pūrewa refers to the white lichen on a tree found at this place. Te Pūrewa was a prominent toa Rangatira of Tūhoe/Ruapani with a direct whakapapa from Ruapani through Tūwai. Te Pūrewa had never been defeated in combat and was responsible for negotiating several peace compacts between Tūhoe/Ruapani and other iwi including the ‘Tatau Pounamu’ set up with Te Arawa at Puke-kahu. The name obviously referred to his greying hair on his head as he aged.'

info_origin: Ngamoerangi was a coastal pā and reef located at Tangitū. It was a site used by Marangatūhetaua during a conflict between his people of Ngāti Tū and a section of a neighbouring tribe. The neighbouring tribe had been raiding the fishing grounds at Tangoio which led Marangatūhetaua to seek support from the rangatira Te Ruruku who was offered fishing rights at Arapawanui in return. Marangatūhetaua placed a number his warriors at Ngamoerangi under the leadership of Te Ruruku, who was a skilled fighting chief. Neighbouring tribe were repulsed and Te Ruruku gained rights to land within the Ngāti Tū and Ngāi Tataramoa rohe.
info_description: An historic site southwest of the mouth of Pākuratahi Stream and Te Ngarue Stream. NZTopo50-BJ39 371371 to 373373

The New Zealand Wars, Volume 2. New Zealand: Government Printer. [1st published 1922]; NZGB V/16. XXII/298, XXVI/203; [David Colquhoun. info_origin: An original Māori name that was literally translated by historian-journalist James Cowan (1870-1943) as 'the two hills' and described as a 'steep ridge covered with sparse manuka, trending parallel with the Waitaruna stream'. Cowan visited the area with Gilbert Mair (1843-1923) in 1918 writing in more detail that 'a track from the ridge to the creek descends a steep bare ridge between the two hollows mentioned, can be seen from the main road less than 200 yards (182 m) away. A short distance eastward the ridge rises to a height of about 300 ft (91 m), crowned by an ancient trenched and walled pa: this is called Kuharau. Just below it on the north two small spurs slope down and converge and enclose a kind of saucer with steep sides'. Cowan's interest in Ngapuketurua stemmed from an incident in the New Zealand Wars when (then) Militia Lieutenant Mair and a force of Arawa was engaged in a running battle with Te Kooti (?-1893) and Hauhau fighters commencing near Ohinemutu with the principal engagement taking place at Ngapuketurua on 7 February 1870. Cowan also referred to this as the 'Te Kaukaka encounter'. A rear guard action by Hauhau enabled Te Kooti's party to escape. In 1928 the Honorary Geographic Board accepted Ngapuke-turua over Nga-Puketurua as the correct orthography but by 1948 favoured Ngapuketurua.

name: Ngāroto
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/71208; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: "Statement of Association provided by Ngāti Manuhiri: Ngāroto, literally “the lakes”, is the traditional name for Lake Spectacle, Slipper Lake and Lake Tomarata which are located inland and just to the south of Te Arai Point (known to Ngāti Manuhiri as Te Ārai-o-Tāhuhu). They are the largest sand dune-impounded lakes of their type on the eastern coastline of the Auckland region. In Ngāti Manuhiri tradition these lakes and their wetland margins provided a valued source of fresh water, food and weaving materials, and were focal points for settlement until the early days of the nineteenth century. Ngāroto are located on the Wai keri ā Wera block purchased by the Crown from Ngāti Manuhiri in 1859. The place name Ngāroto is shown on the plan of the Mangawhai purchase, 1854. (H.H. Turton Maori Deeds of Land Purchases in the North Island of New Zealand, Vol. 1, Deed 98, pp. 133-136)." Ngāroto does not replace the current recorded geographic names of the three lakes.

name: Ngā Roto-o-Rangataua Scenic Reserve
info_origin: The name of this area is derived from the word ‘Rangataua’ meaning war party. Rangataua was also the name of a demi-god who lived in the clouds. He was a famous warrior and his weapons were rain, hail, snow and lightening. Te Mokai o Rangataua (a cloud formation) was his waka which would transport him. Ngāti Rangi would often call upon Rangataua to fight for the tribe. ‘Rangataua’, was also incorporated within the names of two Māori martial arts schools founded in the seventies – ‘Rangataua o Aotearoa’ and ‘Whanake Rangataua’. This site became extremely sacred after the massacre of tangata whenua in the early 1800’s by an enemy war party led by Te Whatanui of Ngāti Raukawa. While many Ngāti Rangi had already left, some still remained when Te Whatanui and his war party came upon them. The deceased bodies of the slain were subjected to cannibalistic ritual and the remnants cast into the lakes (Personal Communication, Turama Hawira, Kai Iwi, 7 January 2016). Those who survived the encounter moved to where the Ohākune township is located.
info_description: A Crown protected area approximately 3km southwest of Ohakune. Shown on Deed Plan OTS-083-014. NZTopo50-BJ34 048321.
treaty_legislation: Section 59 Ngāti Rangi Claims Settlement Act 2019

name: Ngā Roto-o-Te-Kaponga Wetlands
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: Ngā Roto-o- Te-Kaponga, meaning ‘the Lakes of Kaponga’, are now a series of wetlands on the Murimotu block within the Karioi forest. The planting of the forest and the interference with the natural flow of the waterways has significantly altered the water levels once present. What remains today are the remnants of the lakes. Ngā Roto-o-Te-Kaponga once bordered the large area called Ō-taha-te-kaupua, the old hunting and occupation site beside the Unuunuakapuateariki stream. Te Kaponga belonged to the Hioi people who descend from the Ngāti Rangi ancestor Rangiteauria. Ngā Roto-o-Te-Kaponga was a key source of food and other resources and was a place where Kaponga caught eels.
info_description: A group of wetlands within Karioi Forest on the southern slopes of Mount Ruapehu, covering approximately 172ha. NZTopo50-BJ34 242329.

name: Ngārui-o-te-Marangai Beach
info_origin: NgāiTakoto history: Korero that two tupuna, Hauraki and Tamatea were appointed the responsibilities and care of Papatuanuku and that of Tangaroa respectively. Hauraki oversaw the care of the kumara, taro etc, whereas Tamatea, the toa of the moana, ensured the seasonal observations and take of kaimoana etc. Tamatea was told by his very aged kuia, Ngarui, that she was hungry for the taste of titi (mutton bird) and she asked if he would go to Moutohora (Island) and bring her some back. This Tamatea agreed to do, knowing that it was a long swim. (Tamatea, understanding that in times of advanced age and or illness, people requested such things, as Ngarui now asked, as their literal last meal, a final taste of something to carry on their journey to the afterlife). On his return journey Tamatea heard a voice crying, he recognised that voice and as he neared the beach and land his kaumatua came forward, hugged him, and advised him that his Kuia Ngarui had passed away while awaiting his return. Saddened and hurt by the loss of his Kuia and that he was unable to fulfil her request to the point that Ngarui would taste the flavoursome Titi, Tamatea called to the people and named the onepu after his Kuia: "NGARUI O TE MARANGAI". Marangai is the easterly winds that blow into the harbour along this area, hence the slang term "East Beach". Marangai is also referred to in the Ngāi Takoto Whakatauki of the Rangunu harbour which forms the inlet harbour of East beach: he iti marangai, tu ana te Pahukahuka he iti pioke no Rangaunu he Au tona. (The marangai in this whakatauki refers to the easterly winds "marangai" that whips up the foam "pahukahuka" in the Rangaunu harbour.)
info_description: A beach in Rangaunu Bay, extending approximately 14km south-east from the entrance to Houhora Harbour to Otiaia Point. Feature shown on: NZMS260 N03; NZTopo50-AU26 141463 to 256388.

name: Ngaruroro Moko-tū-ā-raro ki Rangatira
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GEN-N15-07-22/190; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: In one account, the river takes its name from an incident in which a dog belonging to the ancient deity Māhu startled some small fish known as upokororo. As the fish dashed away they caused ngaru or ripples in the water. Extract from page 17 of the Heretaunga Tamatea Deed of Settlement Documents Schedule for the Heretaunga Tamatea statement of association and history for this name.
info_description: The original extent of Ngaruroro Moko-tū-ā-raro ki Rangatira passed south of modern Hastings to what is now Karamu Stream then looped north through the original lower channel at what is now officially Te Awa-o-Mokotūāroro, into Hawke Bay at Tukituki River's current mouth.
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "the dog of Māhu startled upokororo (the extinct New Zealand grayling) which rippled the water. Later Moko-tū-ā-raro, son of Ruawharo, was placed at the mouth of the river as a mauri to extend and protect fishing grounds"
feat_note: Extent from the vicinity of Rūnanga Lake downstream was traced approximately from Plan of the Hawke's Bay Region (1864). This is prior to the 1867 flood when it broke out east at Fernhill into the course of the former Waitio Stream, and at its mouth prior to flood control works in 1969 which diverted the last 4km through a channel northeast into Tutaekuri  River. In 1864 and earlier Tutaekuriī River turned north to Te Whanganui-a-Ōrotu, whereas the Ngaruroro shared an estuary with Tukituki River to the south.

info_origin: Original Māori name for one of The Sisters Rocks. The story is that Pani and Kereopa went on strike from food gathering and left to Picton. Kupe returned and went in search of them, Pani heard of this and they got to Nelson before Kupe. Pani sent up a karakia to the great Taniwha to save them which he did by stirring up the seas and bringing up the Boulder Bank. Pani cursed at them and as he paddled around the western side of D'Urville Island. As he went around the tip into Hells Gate area, mighty seas overturned the canoe and everyone was drowned. To commemorate this event, Kupe called the rock Nga Tamahineapani meaning "Pani's two daughters".

info_origin: Altered from Ngatoroirangi Volcano. Named after a tohunga (priest) prominent during the settling of New Zealand by Māori. One of the legends that relates to Ngātoroirangi is that springs of hot water appeared where he stamped his foot as he travelled around the Bay of Plenty and Rotorua region in the central North Island – hence the appropriateness of this name for an active volcano.

name: Ngātoroirangi Trough
info_origin: Ngātoroirangi was a tohunga (priest) prominent during the settling of New Zealand by Māori. One of the legends that relates to Ngātoroirangi is that springs of hot water appeared where he stamped his foot as he travelled around the Bay of Plenty and Rotorua region in the central North Island. In another legend Ngātoroirangi was freezing to death atop Mount Tongariro, and summoned his ancestors Pupū and Te Hōata from Hawaiiki to warm him. As they travelled south beneath the earth in the form of fire they created volcanoes and other geothermal features whenever they emerged to rest.
info_description: An elongated trough approximately 40km northeast to southeast that descends from relatively contiguous minimum depths of -3300m to maximum depth -3900m.

name: Ngongotahā
info_origin: ’Lit. ngongo: mouthpiece; tahā: calabash. On ascending the mountain, Īhenga, the early explorer and discoverer of Lake Rotorua, was offered a drink of water by a young, white-skinned, female patupaiarehe (a forest nymph), and fled to save his life. It is said by some that the mountain bears a resemblance to the funnel of a calabash. The lookout atop Mount Ngongotahā is called Parrys Lookout, after William Parry, the minister in charge of tourist and health resorts when the summit road was completed.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
