name: Ngongotahā Valley
info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2023: Objective ID: A5238764 {Cowan, James. n.d Maori Place Names of the Thermal Regions and their Meanings. New Zealand: Rotorua.; Cowan, James. 1921. The Patu-Pairhehe. Notes on the Maori Folk-Tales of the Fairy People. Journal of the Polynesian Society 30, 142-51.; [Department of Scientific and Industrial Research. 1927. Appendices to the Journals of the House of Representatives, H34.; No. 138.—Petition of Henare Werahiko. Reports of the Native Affairs Committee, 1897.]( Reports of the Native Affairs Committee, 1897); New Zealand Geographic Board Correspondence. 1927. IV/169; Shortland, Edward. 1882. Maori Religion and Mythology. New Zealand: Green and Longmans.; Tarakawa, Takaanui (translated by S. Percy Smith). 1893. The coming of Te Awara and Tainui canoes from Hawaiki to New Zealand. Journal of the Polynesian Society, 2, 231-52.; Tohunga [James Cowan]. 1935. The Wisdom of the Maori. The New Zealand Railways Magazine, 10, 49.; [Ngongotaha and district.](https://teara.govt.nz/en/volcanic-plateau-places/page-1); [Paul Tapsell. 'Tarakawa, Takaanui Hōhaia', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1996. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3t4/tarakawa-takaanui-hohaia); Cowan, James. 1925. Fairy Folk Tales of the Maori. New Zealand: Whitcombe and Tombs.}
info_origin: An original Māori name. Historian-journalist James Cowan (1870-1943) translated this as 'the carved mouthpiece of a calabash', although botanically it probably refers to a gourd. According to Cowan, Ngong also meant the act of drinking through a tube of a calabash mouthpiece. Takaanui Tarakawa (1852-1919) tohunga and historian provided ethnologist Percy Smith (1840-1922) with the story behind the name as specifically linked to Mount Ngongotahā which was named by a young Arawa chief Ihenga, as was Ngongotahā Stream, during his explorations when he was given a drink of water by one of the 'fairy women' or iwi atua (supernatural beings) who dwelled there, also because it resembled a gourd lying on its side. Tohe Te Matahaere (?-1933) separately provided Cowan with this same story of his ancestor Ihenga. Tohe Te Matahaere (?-1933) separately provided Cowan with this same story of his ancestor Ihenga. During the New Zealand Wars Gilbert Mair (1843-1923), then an ensign in the Militia, scouted on the flanks of the mount in 1867 searching for Te Kooti (?-1893) and the Waikato Hauhau in the aftermath of battle with Arawau near Rotorua. The Putaruru to Rotorua Branch railway line was opened in 1893. A Ngongotahā Railway Station operated from 1894 to 1968. In 1897 Henare Werahiko petitioned parliament in an attempt to secure compensation for land taken for the railway. Efforts to secure a named school dated from 1918 and were realized in 1921. Ngongotahā Valley was a polling station in the 1925 general election. The New Zealand Geological Survey reported on a 1.8m thick deposit of high grade white diatomite (kieselguhr), used in abrasive products, found in the valley in 1927. The same year the Honorary Geographic Board confirmed the spelling prior to the Surveyor-General finalising the publication of a new topographical survey map of Rotorua County. In 1939 springs in Ngongotahā Stream were promoted as Paradise Valley Springs.

name: Nickell Peak
info_origin: Named by United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Gregory W. Nickell, manager of the Eklund Biological Center, and of the Thiel Earth Sciences Laboratory at McMurdo Station. He died accidentally on May 15, 1974, when a truck he was driving left the road between McMurdo Station and Scott Base.
info_description: An ice free peak standing at the west side of Victoria Upper Lake, 2.3km southeast of Sponsors Peak, in Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME08
info_note:
This feature was originally named Sponsors Peak. Refer geological map naming the feature by the original proposers in Formations of the Beacon Group: A. D. Allen (1962) Geological investigations in southern Victoria Land, Antarctica, New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics, 5:2, 278-294,
DOI: 10.1080/00288306.1962.10423116. On the United States Geological Survey (USGS) 1:250k topographic map ST 57-60/5 Taylor Glacier (1965) Sponsors Peak was mispositioned, and in 1977 Nickell Peak approved for this peak. While some New Zealand publications continued to refer to Sponsors Peak in the original position, over time Sponsors Peak and Nickell Peak became set in common use for the positions as mapped. At its 27 January 2026 hui the Antarctic Names Committee reconfirmed Sponsors Peak and Nickell Peak in the positions as shown on maps since 1965.

info_origin: 'In fact the beach is only about 96 km (sixty miles) in length. The long beach of Tohe. Also known as Wharo-one-roa-a-Tohe: wharo means stretched out and is a reference to Tohe having his servant stretching out his arms to measure the tide. An alternative Maori name is Nga Tai Whakaturia e Kupe Ki Te Marowhara. See also Ahipara.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Name submitted by the Nelson Chief Surveyor, July 1970, after research in connection with the revision of NZMS1 S33 and S40. Name supplied by Lands and Survey Staff. The portion of the Saint Arnaud range between Trig. E Saint Arnaud and Mount McRae is still called the "No Catchems" by local residents and farming fraternity. This creek has its source in this area. info_origin: ’This is said not to be a Māori name, but apparently originated from the words ‘No, not I.’ The utterance has been attributed to a politician who was asked to name the railway station, and also to a latecomer to a residents’ meeting that was deadlocked over a choice of name, who was told that the first words he said would decide the matter. David Reynolds advises that the response has been attributed to both Premier Richard John Seddon and a local shearer. Reynolds also notes that Nonoti is possibly the original Māori name, as the word is defined as ‘the hollow between the summits of two mountain peaks, a mountain pass,’ in Edward Shortland’s The Southern Districts of New Zealand (1851).’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche December 2022: Objective ID: A5113372 {Cyclopedia of New Zealand [Nelson, Marlborough & Westland Provincial Districts]. 1906. Cyclopedia Company Ltd, Christchurch.; McIntosh, A.D. 1940. Marlborough, A Provincial History. Marlborough Provincial Historical Committee, Blenheim.; [Personal. 1904. Pelorus Guardian and Miners' Advocate, 14 June, Page 4.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PGAMA19040614.2.15); [Local and General. 1906. Pelorus Guardian and Miners' Advocate, 5 June, Page 4.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PGAMA19060605.2.14)}
info_origin: An original Māori name. Nōpera was sometimes referred to as Nopera Bay when the school was rebuilt in 1909. One of Nōpera's more notable residents was Arthur Beauchamp (1827-1910), who as the Marlborough Provincial Council's member for Picton, in 1865 spoke for some ten hours and 20 minutes in a stonewalling attempt to ensure that Picton and not Blenheim became the provincial capital. Beauchamp's business interests as an auctioneer and merchant took him out of the province in the late 1860s before he returned to run a sawmill at Manaroa. He then spent a decade in Christchurch returning to Nōpera about 1890 to live with his son. Nōpera was on occasions in the early 20th century misspelled as Nopere and more rarely Ngpere in local newspapers.

name: Nordenskjöld Ice Tongue
info_origin: Discovered by the British National Antarctic Expedition (NAE), 1901-04, at which time it extended about 20 miles into the Ross Sea. Scott named it for Dr Otto Nordenskjöld, the Swedish geographer who led an expedition to the Antarctic in 1901. This feature had become well established by the name Nordenskjöld Ice Tongue prior to initiation of systematic application of common specific names to a glacier and its glacier tongue. Although this feature is a glacier tongue, the generic term, ice tongue is retained in the name to reduce ambiguity.

name: North Island
land_district: North Auckland, South Auckland, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Taranaki, Wellington
info_origin: The name North Island has been in long term and common usage for over a century. The island has had another English name historically - New Ulster. Early naming of the Northern and Southern Islands was recorded by Hobson in the Proclamation of Sovereignty of 21 May 1840. Hobson had intended to use the native names as per Cook’s chart, but Colenso inserted ‘the Nothern Island’ and ‘the Middle Island’. The name for Nothern Island was later corrected by Hobson’s Proclamation of 13 May 1841 to Northern Island. The Royal Charter of 1840 was received in New Zealand in early 1841 and it named the islands New Ulster (for the North Island), New Munster (for the South Island) and New Leinster (for Stewart Island / Rakiura), with Royal sanction and the gazette notice using these names. Since Royal Charters are perpetual, the names New Ulster, New Munster and New Leinster arguably have some legal standing (but not as Geographic names under the current NZGB Act 2008). They have not been used for the island names since 1841, though they did survive as provincial names up until 1853. Assigning North Island as an alternative name made official under the NZGB Act 2008, is an action that effectively overrides the Royal Charter by bringing the name within the statutory place naming framework empowered by Parliament in the NZGB Act 2008. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDA1MDZGQUY4MjEwMDg1OEVGQUQ)
info_description: The northern of the two main islands of New Zealand, centred around NZTM 1865000E, 5674000N. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BH36 650740
info_note: For information about the alternative official Māori name for this island, Te Ika-a-Māui, see the alternative name record in this Gazetteer.

name: Northland
info_origin: The term Northland appeared to be in popular usage for many years before the date of gazettal, and was considered to be the district North of Auckland City, probably as an abbreviation of North Auckland. Moves to have the name officially recognised began around 1935, as the region was looking forward to the centenary of the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi. A proposal was formulated by H W Crawford and E L Whimp, and put before the first conference of the Northland Associated Chambers of Commerce, in 1936. The first attempt to have the name formalised was rejected by the Honorary Geographic Board in 1941. In 1948 further submissions were made to the Geographic Board led by the Whangarei Chamber of Commerce, and backed by all of the Chambers of Commerce and Local Authorities in the region. Rodney and Warkworth Councils objected to their inclusion in the region, citing that they had no community of interest with the North, and that their interests lay with Auckland. The Geographic Board approved the name Northland as covering a non administrative area, North of Rodney County, in 1949.
info_description: All that land area being that portion of the North Auckland Land District lying to the north of the northern boundary of the County of Rodney as existing at the 13th day of January, 1949.

info_origin: In 1891 the Lands Department exchanged three blocks of land near Waimate with the Education Department and subdivided these into small farms which were initially taken up as leases-in-perpetuity. One of these blocks, 3km north of Waimate, was initially called Wainono after an adjacent coastal lagoon of the same name. Because of its position in relation to Waimate it became known as Norton – a contraction of ‘north town.’ Hon William J Steward (1841-1912) proposed this name. UK born Steward came to New Zealand in 1862 and had a lengthy career as a newspaper editor (from 1879 in Waimate) and as a politician. He was MP for Waitaki (1871-75) and for Waimate (1881-1912). Steward was speaker of the House of Representatives from 1891-93 and was knighted in 1902. He played an important role in proposing amendments to the Land Act, opening the way for the Crown to repurchase 1000acre (404 ha) blocks for resettlement and for transferring education reserves to the Lands Department for this purpose. In his own electorate he persuaded the government to establish village settlements at Nukuroa (known as Hannaton), Waitaki and Norton. Wainono was used in Lands Department reports, with both Wainono and Norton being used as alternative names locally in the early 1900s. As early as 1895 Stewart had unsuccessfully pressed the Department of Internal Affairs, which had naming responsibilities under the Designation of Districts Act, 1894 to adopt Norton. Undetered, Steward presented a petition from 22 Wainono settlers to the Waimate County Council seeking the name be changed to Norton in 1908. The Council supported the request. This alteration became official by a Governor’s proclamation in the Gazette.

info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche August 2023: Objective ID: A5568126 {Dollimore, Edward. 1952. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand: Wises.; [Oakura Bay History](https://oakuranorthland.org.nz/oakura-bay-whangaruru-northland-history/#:~:text=Oakura%20is%20said%20to%20be,with%2Dthe%20red%20sky%E2%80%9D); [Northland Beaches even more Popular. 1949. Northern Advocate, 23 December, Page 4.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NA19491223.2.31); NZGB XXVIII/235}
info_origin: An original Māori name, Ōakura is said to be named after ‘ao-a-kura’ translatable as ‘the light-that comes with-the red sky’. The locality was long settled by Māori and contains many sites of cultural significance. By the 1930s, along with the sale of seaside sections the area now informally referred to as Oakura Beach, was gaining in popularity for bathing and fishing. The name Oakura Bay came into use in the 1940s to distinguish it from Oakura Beach in Taranaki. In turn this was replaced by Ōakura in the 1950s when a new 1:250000 topographical map series was being prepared. The Chief Cartographer of Lands and Survey identified 18 names that were duplicated and sought resolution from the New Zealand Geographic Board.

info_origin: Named after Oamaru, Otago, New Zealand, the port the Terra Nova first visited on 10 February 1913, after the death of Captain Robert F. Scott. Newspaper articles on the day noted the vessel was a month earlier than expected, and initially 'supposed' the two men that briefly disembarked to be 'Captain Scott and one of his officers'. It was actually Lieutenant Pennell and Dr. Atkinson under orders to 'say nothing', who wired a telegram to London with news of the expedition's fate. The vessel departed for Lyttelton, and news of the death of Scott and the others returning from the South Pole broke in New Zealand later on the 11th, once wired back from London.

name: Oates Land
info_origin: Discovered in February, 1911, by Lieut. H.L.L. Pennell, RN, in the Terra Nova, expedition ship of the British National Antarctic Expedition (1910-13). Named after Capt. L.E.G. Oates of the 6th Inniskilling Dragoons, who with Captain Scott and three companions, lost his life on the return journey from the South Pole in 1912. The coastal region of Oates Land was photographed or explored by USN Operation Highjump (1946-47), the Soviet Antarctic Expedition (1958), ANARE (1959, 1961 and 1962), US Navy (1960-62), US Geological Survey (19622 Expedition (163-64). (See Handbook and Index that accompanies the 1939 Map of Antarctica by Bayliss and Cumpston for the extent of Oates Land). When the names of Coasts and Lands were under consideration in the 1960's the name Oates Coast was considered redundant as Oates Land and Oates Coast were essentially the same feature. Oates Land was retained being the original name given by Pennell.
info_description: The sector of Antarctica between 155 degrees E and 164 degrees E (partly in the Ross Dependency), approximately between Cape Andreev and Cape Williams.

name: Ōhaupō
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2023: Objective ID: A5238764 {[Attack on a Native Pah. 1864. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1k16/krippner-martin) (accessed 21 February 2023)}
info_origin: An original Māori name literally translated as 'where the wind blows at night', although historian-journalist James Cowan (1870-1943) writing in 1935 under the pseudonym of 'Tohunga' favoured 'The place or home of Haupo'. Ōhaupō was a fortified pā and large village. Both were abandoned by March 1864 with the invasion of the Waikato. Troops then demolished the pā and village and established a military post. General Duncan Cameron's ADC, Major McNeill, won a Victoria Cross for rescuing one of his orderlies, Private Vosper, during a skirmish near Ōhaupō on 30 March 1864. A company of the Forest Rangers under Major Gustavus Von Tempsky (1828-68) was based at Ōhaupō in September 1864. In the aftermath of fighting a ring of redoubts and military settlements were established around the Waikato. A small township was settled at Ōhaupō by 29 members of the Bohemian militia under Captain Martin Krippner (1817-94) with each man being granted town and country sections. Generally referred to as 'Germans' from Puhoi, they had formed a Company of the Waikato Regiment. In June of 1865 the New Zealand Herald reported that, 'in the Ohaupo district there are about 50 allotments of swamp, which at the present time are under water; there is not a square yard (0.8 sq m) on which you could build a house or even sit down ….. if drained it would become some of the best land in the district, but to do so would require an extensive and organized system of drainage beyond the means of the men.' Ōhaupō was connected to Auckland by telegraph in 1864 and the railway arrived by 1878. In 1908 a subdivision plan of 12 sections up to 2 roods (2023 sq m) in area and surveyed by Harry Briggs was submitted by the Chief Surveyor for Auckland, John Strauchon (1848-1934), for the approval of the Chief Surveyor in Wellington. Maytown or Feoraville were suggested as possible names although the actual plan used Teddyville. John Teddy was previously proprietor of the Ōpauhō Hotel and well-known as an owner of trotters. The Surveyor-General, Thomas Humphries (1841-1928), was satisfied with the layout but not the proposed names which he rejected in favour of the original Māori name of Ōhaupō, noting that the old town had never been properly surveyed and the subdivision was near the Ōhaupō Railway Station. A second subdivision plan, prepared by licensed surveyors Sims and Norman for 'Ohaupo Extension No. 1' of 16 sections nearly all of 1 rood (1012 sq m), was submitted in 1910. Final approval was not secured until 1914. A further suburban extension plan was approved in 1952 as being on suitable land and meeting 'the existing demand' under the Land Subdivision in Counties Act, 1946.

name: Ōhau / West Island
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/1017; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Kuri and Te Aupouri history: After spirits leave Te Rerenga Wairua they dive under the water to Manawatawhi and ascend the summit of Ōhau, where they stop to look at their homeland and sing their laments, before moving on their spiritual journey to Te Reinga. The name Ōhau dates back to the ancients of Hawaiki. It also makes reference to the prevalent winds that can stir the seas in this area. Stokes recounts evidence of Waerete Norman before the Waitangi Tribunal regarding a waiata tangi about Te Rerenga Wairua: “Rimui rimu tere tere. E tere ra i te moana. E ahu ana ki ripo. I raro ra e -. Ka kati, ka puare. Mo wairua e -. Te huringa i Muri Motu. Te huringa i Te Reinga. Te moana i kauria. Te wairua e -. Ohau i waho ra. Te puke whakamutunga. Haere whakangaro atu te wairua e.” “Seaweed drifting, drifting. floating out to sea. Flowing with the currents. the whirlpool below e. It opens and closes. for te wariua e. flowing around Murimotu. around Reinga. the seas swum. by te wairua. Behold the summit of Ohau. out yonder. Farewell e” . (Stokes, The Muriwhenua Land Claims Post 1865 Wai 45 and Others, pp. 159-161). Waerete Norman also submitted a transcript of W T H Panga talking about the spiritual pathway, which included the statement: "naa, ka ruku nei ngaa wairua, ka whiti ki ngaa motu. E kiia nei, ko Oohau te mea mutunga, engari he maha aua motu. E kiia ana e etahi ko Tirii Kiingi, ko te puke tino mutunga mai, tenei e kiia ana ko Oohau. Ka tae ki reira, ka tangi mai ngaa wairua" ("now the spirits dive under water and cross to the islands. It is said that Oo-hau is the last one, but there are many islands there. It is said by some that of the Three Kings Islands, the hill closest to here is Oohau. On reaching there the spirits sing their laments"). (Stokes, A Review of the Evidence in the Muriwhenua Lands Claims, Vol 2, pp. 717-718). Stokes also notes that “West Island is known to Māori as Ohau, the place where the spirits who have departed from Te Rerenga Wairua pause for a last look at their homeland”. (Stokes, The Muriwhenua Land Claims Post 1865 Wai 45 and others, p. 159).
info_description: An island approximately 65km north-west of Cape Reinga / Te Rerenga Wairua. It is the most western island of the Manawatāwhi / Three Kings Islands. Feature shown on: NZMS260 L01; NZTopo50-AS21 110168

info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: ‘Birds were snared near the headwaters of the Ōheao Stream. Piupiuterangi is another place near this location. In Heao Falls are mauri stones that have been placed by our tohunga. The most prized delicacy of all, for Hikaia and all of Ngāti Hāua, was the piharau or lamprey, the blind eel that is caught in pā erected in the shallows, facing downstream. Deep in the forested vastness west of the Whanganui is the Haeo (Heao sp) stream, feeding into the Tangarākau: ‘Up in the waterfall of the Haeo (Heao sp) that’s where the lamprey come from’, Hikaia said, referring to a mauri stone placed by tohunga near a magnificent twelve-metre high waterfall with several chutes’.’

name: Ohinemuri River
info_origin: 'The full name is Te Waitangi-o-Hinemuri. Lit. te: the; wai: waters; tangi: weeping; o: of; Hinemuri. Hinemuri was the daughter of the chief Te Onekiteakau of Ngati Te Upokotioa, who forbade her to marry until her two eldest daughters were married. Her suitors eventually left her and she was left alone to weep bitter tears. Another story relates how a chief’s daughter sought refuge with a taniwha in the river when her pa was attacked. The taniwha fell in love with her and was devastated when her people reclaimed her, so he left the area, never to return.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Ohinemutu
info_origin: Not "Ohinenoutu"; 'The chief Ihenga, who discovered Lake Rotorua, was married to Hinetekakara, the daughter of Kahumatamomoe, and they had a daughter who was also called Hinetekakara (Fragrant girl). She was captured and murdered, and her entrails were cast into the lake. Ihenga searched frantically for her, and when he found her intestines caught on a snag at the edge of the lake, he named the place Kakaipuku and set up a memorial stone as a rahui (a mark to warn people against trespassing) that he named Ohinemutu (The place of the only girl, or The girl cut off). The settlement was named after the stone. For many years the presence of the rahui prevented the local people from fishing in the lake.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

Wanganui Herald, 26 February, Page 3.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WH18920226.2.26.6); Best, Elsdon. 1919. Topographical Nomenclature of the Maori. New Zealand Official Year-Book. New Zealand: Government Printer.; Downes, T.W. 1909. Early history of Rangitikei, and notes on the Ngati Apa tribe. Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand, 42, 74-114.; Mair. S.A.R. 1909. Notes upon a find of Kauri-gum in Rangitikei, Wellington Province. Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand, 38, 499-501.; [Opening of Ohingaiti Post Office. 1924. Wanganui Chronicle, 19 July, Page 15.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WC19240719.2.87); Reed, Alfred. 1975. Place names of New Zealand. New Zealand: Reed.}
info_origin: An original Māori name. Ngāti Wahine from Hawke's Bay were defeated by Ngāti Apa near Ōhingaiti in pre-European times. The Otara kāinga was located close by. The first auctioning of 132 sections for 'Ohingatiti Township' took place in 1892 with the arrival of the North Island Main Trunk railway line. The original Post Office was opened that same year but spelled as Ohingaite but changed to Ohingaiti in 1893. When a new Post Office was opened in 1923 it was reported that Ohingaiti meant a 'resting place.' Ohingaite was still used in local newspapers until the 1920s. Publisher and author Alfred Reed offered a literal translation of 'o' place of, 'hinga' childhood and 'iti' small. Ethnographer Elsdon Best was more cautious than Reed in translating place names including Ōhingaiti: 'O may be a prefix, which would leave Hinga-iti, possibly a personal name. Ohinga denotes childhood, youth. Iti- small, unimportant.' In 1948 the New Zealand Geographic Board affirmed Ohingaiti.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 T22 Edition 1 1983 Reprinted 1990; NZTopo50-BL35 316840

name: Ōhura River
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; A7856323; Objective folder ID: fA640497; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: The Ōhura, on right bank, is the largest tributary of the Whanganui River downstream of the Ōngaaruhe River. It enters the river as a fall called Ratakura. There is a much higher fall a hundred yards or so further up this stream called Reinga-kōokiri, which cannot be seen from the river.  A third fall, about half a mile higher, is known as Rerehape. All of these falls were at one time great fishing places for Ngāti Hāua, who used to journey down from Taumarunui and even up from Pipiriki to catch a very small eel called tuna-riki, that in the summer months made its way up the slippery, perpendicular banks in thousands. Today the pool below the lower fall is a rather good hole for Rainbow trout. A number of Ngāti Hāua kāinga and pā, were located on the Ōhura River, including Maraekōwhai, Opatu, Te Kiekie, Rauwhare and Rauponga.’
info_description: A river that flows for approximately 125km from Tangitu (hill) west of Lake Taupō / Taupōmoana generally southwest then southwards into Whanganui River. Feature shown on: NZMS260 R18 Edition 1 1987; NZTopo50-BG33 951203 to BH32 787769

info_origin: 'Okura River: Lit. o: place; kura: red. The land in the locality is predominantly red clay.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. ; An original Māori name, literally place and red, it being comprised of red clay. A nearby colonial settlement was named Redvale. In 1819 missionary Samuel Marsden (1765-1838) visited Ōkura and met local chiefs Waitara, who ‘had got one of the neatest huts I had seen in New Zealand’, and Te Morenga. William Anderson Pye (1837-1915) began to develop a farm at Ōkura in 1892 and from 1895 advertised his Riverview house as providing ‘Good accommodation for visitors’ for ‘Boating, bathing, and fishing’. His son Henry Alston Pye (1871-1952) operated a dairy farm in the vicinity, selling up in 1920 but retaining some land adjacent to Okura River. With better road connections with Takapuna the area became a popular motoring and camping destination by the mid-1920s, which prompted local landowner Pye to subdivide some of his land. In 1924 he developed a small 4½ acre (1.8 ha) 15 lot Ōkura town subdivision facing Okura River on undulating grass-covered land, which was surveyed by CH Jackson and approved by the Minister of Lands, David Guthrie (1856-1927). As part of the development Pye included a 3/4 acre (0.3 ha) plantation reserve and a 1 ¼ acre (0.5 ha) scenic reserve on mānuka covered land along the riverbank. Two years later Pye secured approval for another subdivision of ‘seventeen saleable lots for summer seaside resorts’ on adjoining land, also laid out by Jackson.

info_origin: Extension to the extent to encompass Obelisk Range declined 21/10/99; 'The range takes its name from Old Man Rock, a slender pillar of stone 27 m high and only 8.5 m in thickness. It was supposed to be the petrified form of the giant Kopuwai (Water-swallower) who fled down the Clutha River. Nearby is Te Ana-o-te-karara: lit. te: the; ana: cave; o: of; te: the; karara (ngarara): monster, and between it and the river lies Te Hapua-o-Kaiamio: lit. te: the; hapua: lagoon; o: of; Kaiamio. The pack of two-headed dogs belonging to Kopuwai was out hunting at the time the giant was burned to death. Finding themselves masterless, they wandered about and were turned to stone in various pools where they came to drink.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={4d77ee69-3e52-e311-8212-005056970030}))

name: Oliver Bluffs
info_origin: Named for Dr Robin Langford Oliver (1921-2001), a New Zealand geologist and the first to study the bluffs in 1961. Dr. Oliver’s first Antarctic expedition was in 1959-60 (NZ Alpine Club expedition), where he served as Chief Geologist. Dr Oliver spent most of his career as a Lecturer and then Senior Lecturer of geology at the University of Adelaide and made seven trips to Antarctica. The name was first applied following an Ohio State University 1985/86 expedition under Professor Peter Noel-Webb. The feature is notable due to its fossiliferous deposits, including trees from the Pliocene (5.3 to 2.6 mya), meaning they grew near the South Pole in relatively recent geological time.
info_description: Mostly ice-free bluffs 90-100m high, north of where Rutkowski Glacier joins Beardmore Glacier at the northwest of Dominion Range.

name: Olivine Range
info_origin: 'The name Olivine was originally applied by the surveyor Gerhard Mueller to the mineralised ultrabasic section of the range above Cascade River to the north, but popular usage extended it to the country bounded by the Pyke, Arawhata and Dart rivers. Jack Holloway led parties to explore here in the 1930s, and gave the imaginative names of Blockade, Intervention, Darkness, Gable, Climax, Destiny, Typhoon and Tempest. Olivine is a yellowish-green mineral, magnesium silicate, found in basalt and gabbro. Maori name: Oturu: lit. o: place of; Turu; a Waitaha chief.' name: Omahu
info_origin: 'Hawke’s Bay, 6 km from Hastings. Correctly, Oomahu: o: place of; o: provisions for a travelling party; Mahu; i.e. The place where Mahu ran out of food. The original site was washed away in a flood by the Ngaruroro River, and the name was applied to a locality earlier known as Otupaopao, q.v., The place of knocking (or scratching). Tamateapokai- whenua was carrying a pet lizard in a calabash, and it scratched on the side of calabash to be let out.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

Also named for Quintin McPherson McKinnon (1851-1892) a surveyor, explorer and guide who had a significant association with the area.; ’Previously Mackinnon Pass, the name was officially altered by the NZGB in 2022. On 17 October 1888 Quintin McKinnon and Ernest Mitchell were the first Europeans to discover the route from Lake Te Anau to Milford Sound that became the Milford Track. McKinnon’s surname was also spelt Mackinnon and MacKinnon. In 1887, McKinnon had been the first European to discover the lake that was named after him; he was accompanied by a rabbiter, G. Tucker, whose name lives on in Lake Tucker.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Omoana
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche December 2022: Objective ID: A5113372 {Crown Lands Department. 1891 Appendicies to the Journals of the House of Representatives, C1.; The Annual Sheep Returns 1905. Appendicies to the Journals of the House of Representatives, H23.; NZ Geographic Board correspondence XII/95, XIII/79; [To be let. 1852. Taranaki Herald, 8 September, Page 1.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/TH18520908.2.2.3); [Bruce Biggs. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3w20/williams-herbert-william/sources) (accessed 8 November 2022)}
info_origin: An original Māori name. Taranaki newspapers from the 1850s often used Omona and in the 1890s the Lands Department perpetuated this usage in its Omona Survey District, which was further continued by the Department's land development activities in the Omona Block. However, Patea County Council created an Omoana Special Rating District in 1896 and from 1905 farmers in the official Sheep Returns also favoured Omoana. An Omoana Post Office also dated from 1906. In 1936 the Chief Surveyor for New Plymouth sought the opinion of the Honorary Geographic Board about the correct spelling. Board member the Right Reverend Herbert Williams, a respected Māori language scholar, considered that Omoana was probably correct. The Survey District spelling was adjusted and new Certificates of Title for land were subsequently issued under the corrected spelling.
info_description: Locality near intersection of Rawhitiroa Road and Tahuri Road, approximately 25km east-southeast of Stratford. Omoana Survey District. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BJ31 354367

name: Ōmokoroa Beach
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche May 2023: Objective ID: A5325931 {[Joseph Tice Gellibrand. n.d.](https://westernbay.recollect.co.nz/nodes/view/1078); Melvin, L.W. 1962. Te Waharoa of the Ngati Haua. Journal the Polynesian Society, 71, 361-78.; [Omokoroa. 2000. Abstracted from Peter Rolleston, University of Waikato, Local History Lecture Series 2000, 'Omokoroa' written by Jenny Woods.](https://westernbay.recollect.co.nz/nodes/view/1351); Omokoroa Beach. R10859832. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; Stokes, Evelyn. 1959. Changing Patterns of Settlement in Tauranga County. New Zealand Geographer, 16, 170-188.; Stokes, Evelyn. 1980. A History of Tauranga County. New Zealand: Dunmore.; Te Raupatu O Tauranga Moana. Report on the Tauranga Confiscation Claims. 2004 Wai 215: New Zealand: Waitangi Tribunal.; [Evelyn Stokes. 'Te Waharoa', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1990. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1t81/te-waharoa) (accessed 24 March 2023)}
info_origin: Ōmokoroa is an original Māori descriptive name for the peninsula according to some translatable as 'long point'. The Wai-Huri pā was located at the tip at the peninsula and Rauhuria was a second pā lower down on the peninsula, which was covered in fern and manuka scrub with significant cultivated areas. By the 1700s Ngāti Ranginui occupied Ōmokoroa and the western half of Tauranga Harbour and its hinterland. In the early 1800s Ngāiterangi began to venture into the larger Tauranga district with conflict resulting. During the musket wars of the 1830s Te Waharoa (?-1838), principal leader of Ngāti Hauā was occupied in forming alliances and fighting in Waikato, Hauraki and Tauranga. Although mainly residing in Matamata, Te Waharoa and his people repelled Ngāpuhi in a battle at Mōtītī Island in 1831 and they lived for a time at Ōmokoroa where they harvested sea food, although there were no permanent settlements on the peninsula in 1840. The New Zealand Wars moved from the Waikato to Tauranga in 1864 and the Crown confiscated the entire Tauranga district of 290000 acres (117359 ha) in 1865 and later pressed owners to sell some 90000 acres (36422 ha) known as the Te Puna-Katikati Block which included Ōmokoroa peninsula. Ngāti Hauā were granted 400 acres (162 ha) of reserve at Ōmokoroa. Charles Heaphy (1820-1881), Commissioner of Native Reserves in 1871, listed another 271 acres (110 ha) of reserve at Ōmokoroa for 'Raihi, Hakairiwhi, “and tribe”'. Richard Gill, clerk to the resident magistrate at Tauranga and later Under-Secretary of the Native Land Purchase Department, privately purchased two sections in September 1868 and leased lots 49 (150 acres) and 50 (52 acres) from Te Raihi and Hakiriwihi in 1871. The leases were transferred in 1876 to Tice Gellibrand (1826-1887) a Church of England missionary who arrived in New Zealand via Tasmania in 1874. Increasing tensions amongst Māori and European settlers along the peninsula remained high and were finally resolved by Gellibrand purchasing lots 49 and 50 for £350 in April 1877. Gellibrand named his property Ōmokoroa, -'the place of Mokoroa' in recognition of Mokoroa who first introduced him to the peninsula. Gellibrand's purchase was of supposedly inalienable reserve land. As Henry Tacey Clarke (1825-1902), the Under Secretary for Native Affairs hoped, the arrangement maintained the peace. Ngāti Hauā were removed from the district, pleasing Ngāiterangi leaders while Ngāti Rangiwehiwehi also 'agreed to move from Omokoroa'. Never-the-less Māori protested against the extension of the telegraph wire across Ōmokoroa peninsula in 1872. Recreational users of the beach for fishing and picnicking near the point increased in the early 20th century. Facilities were gradually improved and in 1956, following local requests triggered by the numbers of summer holiday makers, the Post Office set up a small branch designated as 'Omokoroa Beach'. In 1961 Ōmokoroa Beach became a County Town, which had a population of 231 by 1966.

info_origin: This locally used name is in memory of the first European settlers in the bay. O'Neill shown as owner on ML plan 1902B in 1894. 'Auckland, north of Te Henga (Bethells Beach). Maori name: Kauwahaia: a shortened form of Te Awakauwahaia: The channel across which she swam. info_origin: Various efforts to capture the meaning of Onetangi range from ‘murmuring sands’, ‘the singing tide’, ‘sighing sands’, to ‘crying sands’. Historian-journalist James Cowan (1870-1943) instead preferred ‘the sounding shore’ referring to the noise of the surf on the beach, audible even on the other side of the island. He observed that the origin of the name was captured in a chant ‘Whakarongo ake au, Ki te tai o Hauraki, E wawa mai nei’ which he translated as ‘listen to Hauraki’s tide, Crashing yonder on the shore; Roar, oh ye waters, roar!’ Standing on the beach Cowan listening to ‘the sound of the trampling surf on the rocks and the hard sea-sand’ affirmed the effectiveness of the name. A less frequently advanced alternative is ‘weeping sands’ in reference to an 1821 battle during the musket wars when the forces of Hongi Hika (1772-1828) captured and destroyed Putiki o Kahu pā in Putiki Bay. In 1858 Donald McLean (1820-77), the Chief Commissioner of Land Purchase, finalised the sale of 10900 acres (4411 ha), the eastern two thirds of the island, for £800 from Tikaokao and others. A subdivision called Ostend, which was advertised in late 1915, included some sections at Onetangi. Adjacent land at Onetangi was subdivided for sale in 1923 and a lengthy wharf constructed. A post office was established that same year. Horse races on Onetangi Beach have been held intermittently for over a century.

name: One Tree Hill
info_origin: 'Auckland, a hill and suburb of Auckland. Maori name: Maungakiekie, lit. maunga: mountain; kiekie: a climbing plant (Freycinetia banksii). Sir John Logan Campbell was informed of the name by Waipeha, yet he wrote later in Poenamo that ‘as it had one large solitary tree on its crater summit we christened it “One Tree Hill,” which for ever obliterated the Maori name from Pakeha vocabulary, but the grand old tree has passed away, causing later-day arrivals to wonder why the hill bears it name.’ The tree was a totara, and was also acknowledged during European settlement in Totaraiahua (ahua is a form or appearance); the name applied to the summit. James Cowan specified that Te Totaraiahua was only the north-east peak, the south-east peak being Te Tu-po-o-te-tini, lit. te: the; tu: standing; po: night; o: of; te: the; tini: host or myriad. The totara tree originated when Ngati Awa were passing southwards to Taranaki, a child was born and its umbilical cord cut with a twig of totara that was planted and became the great tree atop the hill. The child’s name was Korokino. The hill has at times been known as Mt Prospect and Lofty Hill.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA640497; Objective ID: A7410134, A7454071
info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: ‘Named after the abundance of aruhe (bracken fern) in this area. Located at the confluence of the Taringamotu and Ōngaaruhe Rivers was a pā tuna named Rahoto. Described in 1892 as being an old pā, it was noted that Tapaka was the last tupuna to live in it. Rahoto is also the name of the kāinga located there. Te Hoata II, Tamahina, Whakaneke, Te Oro, Topine Te Mamaku and Pikikotuku were among those recorded as living there. A carved post, which was named Tamahina, was raised there by Ngatai te Mamaku. It was then erected after Matakitaki put the boundary through the Native Land Court to mark the boundary between Ngāti Hāua and Ngāti Maniapoto. Te Horangāpai arose from the phrase 'Horahiangāpai' meaning to put aside all adverse things and to instead bring peace that people might work together and move forward. This peace came about when Pikikotuku met a party of Ngāti Maniapoto that were coming into the district. At Te Koura, he laid down his patu as a token of peace. That is said to be where the true Te Horangāpai is located. The later ceremonies took place at the confluence of the rivers which resulted in the area there also being known as Te Horangāpai. Also, at the at the confluence of the Taringamotu and Ōngaaruhe Rivers was a kāinga named Ngāpuanui where Te Āwhitu is buried. As Hakiaha Tawhiao explained: "Ngāpuanui was not a kāinga tūturu and belonged to Ngāti Hāua as an occasional settlement - none of the settlements on Ongaruhe were permanent places of abode and were only occupied while procuring food". South of the confluence of the Taringamotu and Ōngaaruhe Rivers, was a large kāinga named Kaiwaka. The names originate from Whakaneke and his people moving to Taumarunui from their pā Kaiwhakauka on the Whitianga block. The new pā and kāinga they established was called Kaiwaka after the Whitianga pā. The lands of the Kaiwaka papakāinga extended over what is today the Taumarunui High School, Taumarunui cemetery, the refuse centre, the Taumarunui Golf Course and the Tuhua Domain.’

info_origin: An original Māori name. The literal meaning was cautiously advanced by Edward Dollimore (1904-73), compiler of The New Zealand Guide, as ‘the place of earthworms’ on the basis of Lake Ōnoke in the Wairarapa. In 1870 a newspaper more enigmatically claimed that it ‘is either named after certain stones found there, or the stones are named after the place itself’. Ōnoke was a good point to cross the harbour to Te Karaka and a place where along-harbour journeys might be broken. Dublin born Frederick Maning (1811?- 83), a trader in the Hokianga 1833-37, returned in 1839 and purchased approximately 200 acres (81 ha) of land at Ōnoke, where he built a house and resumed business as a timber trader. Maning’s deed outlined the land boundaries and was signed by 15 Māori chiefs. Maning provided goods to the value of £100 including 220lb (100kg) of tobacco (valued at £22), guns and powder, 14 shirts, 15 pairs of blankets, 6 spades and £4 in cash. He used gunpowder to persuade Māori that he had banished a taniwha from a tapu pool at Ōnoke, an action for which he was never completely forgiven. In 1859 the Old Land Claims Commissioners, investigating pre-1840 land purchases, awarded him 99 acres (40 ha) at Ōnoke. A fluent Māori speaker, Maning served as a judge of the Native Land Court from 1865 to 1876, sometimes sitting at his Ōnoke property. In 1868 a dispute over land at Whirinaki caused Ngāpuhi to build two pā on the beach at Ōnoke and another on the hill beside Maning’s house while Te Rarawa constructed two wooden pā across the harbour at Karaka. James MacKay (1831-1912), the Civil Commissioner, and eight influential chiefs successfully mediated in the dispute. On a tour of Northland in 1870 Governor Sir George Bowen (1821-99) visited Ōnoke. Maning organized a ball and the next day Bowen met with 100 Māori from around Hokianga Harbour.

name: Ōpaoa River
info_origin: Ngati Rarua translates this as Smoking River, which can be described as the mist or fog rising off this particular river giving the appearance of smoke hanging over the water. This awa along with the Wairau was an important food resource and integral part of day to day life for Ngati Rarua. Rangitane notes that Inskull in Place Names of Marlborough (p. 54) translates ‘Paoa’ as smoke – ‘smoky river’. There are several different explanations for the name. This place was very swampy and the river became murky with the appearance of smoke. It is also known as the place of the grey teal. The tupuna Paoa had a pa there and the place was named after him. Place names of Marlborough; Inskull, pp. 53, 54.

info_origin: An original Māori name for the river that had rich oyster beds at its mouth, on a Māori track that connected Kawhia to the Waipā River valley. In 1859 Austrian geologist Dr Ferdinand Hochstetter (1829-84) travelled through the area. He observed 'The country on the Oparau is extremely fertile and well cultivated. The soil consists of decomposed trachytic tuff and conglomerate [i.e. Composed of volcanic ash], extending from the trachyte-stock of the Pirongia as far as the Eastside of Kawhia Harbour. We proceeded a few more miles up-hill, and, when evening had set in, we pitched our tents upon a potatoe-field at the edge of the bush'. By 1878 the Māori population totaled only 45 males (20 over 15 years) and 22 females (14 over 15 years). When the Armed Constabulary constructed a ferry across the river in 1883, they named that place Ōpārau. The first major balloting of farmland at Kawhia took place in 1900 with farms along Ōpārau River being especially sought after. An Ōpārau School was established in 1900 and a post office in 1902. An Ōpārau Co-operative Dairy Company was formed in 1912. In 1913, licensed surveyors Young Booker (1871-1961) and John Jack (1868-1942) of the Kawhia based partnership of Young and Jack prepared a subdivision plan of 14 sections, six of ½ acre [0.2 ha] and eight of 13 roods and 1 perch [1341 sq m]. This required the extension of Rotoiti Road at the approved width of 66 feet [20.1 m] to provide access. The Chief Surveyor for Auckland, Harry Skeet (1857-1943), approved the plan under section 3 of the Land Laws Amendment Act 1912, which required a proper surveyed town plan showing roads and reserves and the proposed name. Surveyor General, James McKenzie (1849-1928), approved the subdivision and deemed the proposed name of Ōpārau to be suitable. Prime Minister William (Bill) Massey, in his capacity as Minister of Lands, then authorized the subdivision which was gazetted in May 1913. The Minister of Māori Affairs, Ernest Corbett, announced a £68500 'Oparau Scheme' encompassing 1410 acres (570 ha) in 1956, which by 1964 was to be subdivided into one dairy and four sheep farms.

name: Opononi
info_origin: ’This name was a household word in New Zealand because of the presence (1955–56) of the frolicsome dolphin Opo. G.G. Hooker found four renditions of the name: Oponui, Opononui, Oponini and Opounoni. The first would mean Place of Ponui, but there is only one record of an ancestor called Ponui at Hokianga, and that long after the name was applied. Opononui means The place of great hospitality, in reference to the hospitality of local resident John Webster, but contemporary maps show the name applied beyond Webster’s property. Oponini was probably no more than a misspelling. The fourth theory, put forward by Wiki Patuawa Nathan, has the name as a corruption of Opounoni, in reference to to a crooked fishing post at the mouth of the Opononi stream, a favoured fishing spot.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Ōpōtiki
info_origin: ’Lit. ō: place of; Pōtiki, the ancestor of the iwi that bears his name. In full it was Pōtiki-maitawhiti (tawhiti signifying that he came from afar, namely Hawaiki). A nearby spring was called Ō-Pōtiki-mai-tawhiti, the name eventually being transferred to the township. There is no clear historical record of Pōtiki, and it is likely he was a very early settler in the area; Ngā Pōtiki, of the central Urewera region, are his descendants. An alternative translation is that here the chief Tarawa released the two fish that had guided him from Hawaiki to Waiotahi, hence Ō-pōtiki-mai-tawhiti would mean The pets from Hawaiki. This rendition of pōtiki would be quite unusual, however. The name Ōpōtiki is said to date from European times, and the locality was earlier Pakowhai: lit. pā: village; kōwhai: tree (Sophora tetraptera or S. microphylla). It was an occupied area where the kōwhai tree grew profusely, as it has later done at the mouth of the Mōtū River.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: A military garrison and commercial settlement dates from 1865 with an Opotiki Town Board being set up in 1877. A plan of the town district was drawn by G Wood under the authority of Surveyor-General Thomas Humphries (1841-1928) in 1908. The town became a borough in 1911. Opotiki Road Board existed by 1875 and was dissolved in 1900 when Opotiki County was formed. The borough and county merged to form a District Council in 1973 after the first negotiations had begun a decade earlier. Chairman of the Local Government Commission [Sir] Brian Elwood, meeting with Opotiki District Council in 1988 just prior to a major restructuring of local governments, praised the borough and county for its earlier voluntary amalgamation.
info_description: The district that is administered by the Ōpōtiki District Council.

name: Ōraumoa / Fighting Bay
info_origin: Ngāti Toa history: Fighting Bay, located on the Eastern Coast of Te Tau Ihu was a very important Ngati Toa tauranga waka. It was located in close proximity to the concentrated Ngati Toa settlement at Port Underwood, and provided a site from which Ngati Toa could travel directly across Te Moana o Raukawa to the South Coast of Wellington. It was the site of a battle with Ngai Tahu and hence its name. Rangitane history: Raumoa was the name of a Rangitane ancestor who lived in the Wairau and travelled to this place for special seafood hence the name O-Raumoa, - the place of Raumoa.

name: Ōrere Point
info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche June 2023: Objective ID: A5446617 {Best, A. D. W. 1966. The Journal of Ensign Best, 1837-1843. (Ed. N. M. Taylor). New Zealand: Government Printer.; [Land Sales. 1900. New Zealand Herald, 15 June, Page 3.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH19000615.2.15.1); [Selwyn, George. 1847. Annals of the Diocese of New Zealand.](https://kura.aucklandlibraries.govt.nz/digital/collection/manukau/id/4379/); [Shipping. 1873. New Zealand Herald, 5 August, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH18730805.2.3); [Warren E. Limbrick. 'Selwyn, George Augustus', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1990. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1s5/selwyn-george-augustus) (accessed 23 May 2023)}
info_origin: Named for the adjacent point, also known as Rangipākihi, and associated locality and river. An old pā site was at the northern end of the beach, the site of intertribal conflicts. Captain Abel Dottin William Best (1816-45) described the area in 1842 as ‘creeping along with the tide in our favour until we reached the Maori Settlement Orere the distance being about twelve miles [from Maraetai]. The situation of Orere is exceedingly romantic and strong the little Pa's being on either side of a deep Gulley beautifully wooded with Pohutikaua [pōhutukawa] through the bottom runs a rapid stream into which we brought our Boat. Amused ourselves wandering about 'til dark when we took up our abode in a clean hut without fleas. The People were generally employed building new houses of a description far superior to their old dens a symptom of improvement’. Bishop George Selwyn (1809-78) had selected the coastal site he referred to just as Ōrere for a mission station in 1843, Māori having set apart a place for an ultimately never constructed residence. It was a strategic location. Selwyn was ‘pleased’ for it ‘commands on one side the whole Firth, from Coromandel harbour to Auckland, and on the other, the mouths of the Thames and Piako [rivers]’. By the 1870s the Auckland firm of Henderson and Spraggon was purchasing pōhutukawa from Ōrere Point forests for shipbuilding. Lands sales in the area were advertised from 1900 and a sea borne mail service commenced in 1914. From 1918 local farmers used Ōrere Point as an address in the annual Sheep Returns. There was a named polling station in the 1919 election. A named primary school opened in 1926.

name: Orewa
info_origin: 'Orewa originally referred to the river rather than the beachfront, writes Robin Grover. Other possible origins are the Maori transliteration of olive, and the river mouth’s use as an end point for canoe portage to the Kaipara Harbour, hence o: place of; rewa: to float, to get underway. Grover considers the most likely, however, to be a contraction of Te Wai-o-Rewa: lit. The water of Rewa, an early Te Kawerau-a-Maki rangatira. In 1856 Captain Isaac Rhodes Cooper of the 58th Regiment took up land and called his home Orewa House.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Oringi
info_origin: 'The inhabitants of a besieged pa included a young woman who was admired by one of the aggressors, Takaringi (or Takarangi). When he heard that the defenders were short of water he walked boldly up to the palisades with a calabash and gave it to the young woman. This action brought an end to the conflict. A sign at the spring where he filled his calabash once read: Ko te Puna Ringi (The spring of Ringi). A pun may be involved, for Oringi has the same meaning as Orini, q.v.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Ōrongotea Stream
info_origin: Whanganui Iwi statement: 'Orongotea Stream is the eastern boundary of the Ngārākauwhakarārā land block. The 1913 Annual Report of the Wanganui River Trust, refers to ‘Orongatea’ as one of the Whanganui River rapids. Furthermore, maps of the Ngārākauwhakarārā block that were drawn in the 1920s refer to the name of the stream as ‘Orongatea’. However, the succession paper to Kihirangi in 1886 refers to the Ngārākauwhakarārā block, situated at ‘Orongotea’ on the Whanganui River. Furthermore, evidence presented by Haami Te Kee in 1909 refers to workings (or mahinga kai) that his tūpuna had along the Orongotea Stream, and that “the karaka trees at the old kāinga belonged to my tūpuna” (56 Whanganui MB, p. 47). Arama Tinirau states that “we had a number of pā tuna in the river Orongotea” (56 Whanganui MB, p. 87). The name of the stream, as spelt throughout the Whanganui Minute Books at that time, is clearly ‘Orongotea’. The name Rongotea features in the oral traditions of the Aotea people, to whom the Whanganui people share genealogical connections. Ngāti Rongotea is noted as the iwi of Turi Ariki, captain of the Aotea canoe. Whilst in Hawaiki, Turi’s wife Rongorongo overheard the following lines being chanted by Uenuku, which outlines his intent to enact revenge on Turi and his people, Ngāti Rongotea, for the death of his son: Tikina atu rā. Te Tini o Ngāti Rongotea. Kumea mai, tākina mai. Kia huna, kia tineia … '. Sole, T. (2005). Ngāti Ruanui: A history. Wellington: Huia Publishers, pp 12-13.

name: Orowaiti River
info_origin: 'The name remembers Reuben Waite, who chartered the steamer Jane to take supplies to the first gold-diggers on the West Coast. On arrival at the mouth of the Buller River he was greeted by Maori with cries of ‘Ora, Waiti!’, which is an unusual but not inconceivable greeting translatable as ‘Come on, Waite!’. Another explanation is that the name was Oro Waiti (Old Waite), or simply a corruption of Ora iti, which means Escaping with difficulty.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: 'Auckland, south of Manukau Heads. A tohunga koko rangi (astronomy expert) of the local tribe named the bay after hearing a mystic sound coming out of the night, as described in Eric Coulthard’s Orua Saga. name: Otago Harbour
info_origin: 'Otago originates from the Māori name Ōtākou, which was the traditional name for the channel that runs down the eastern (southern) side of the Otago Harbour from the mouth to Harwood Point. Today the name Ōtākou specifically refers to the small Ngāi Tahu kāika situated on Otago peninsula near the harbour’s entrance. When the British Weller Brothers’ settlement was established on the peninsula it became known to the whalers as Ōtākou, which was then later adopted by the wider region as Otago, owing in part to difficulties of the settlers with pronouncing te reo Māori. For a time the harbour was known as Port Daniel, later changed to Port Oxley in honour of John Oxley, surveyor-general of New South Wales. About 1832 it was known to whalers and sealers as the Otago River.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Ōtahatekapua
info_ref: Objective ID: A2406188. Shown on NZMS 273 1975 Map 4 as Tahatekapua.
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: Ō-taha-te-kapua is an historic hunting and occupation site of Ngāti Rangi situated adjacent to the Rangataua Forest on the western boundary of Karioi Forest. Both the historic site and the ridge (with the trig point) are named Ō-taha-te-kapua. The name Ō-taha-te-kapua means belonging to Te Kāhui Kapua (the Cloud People) or otherwise, belonging to the tupuna Kapua Te Ariki. Hence this refers to the nearby waterway also – Te Unuunu a Kapua Te Ariki. The Kāhui Kapua are descendants of Ruatipua and descend to Uenukumahoenui, husband of Taiwiri. There are 11 generations from Te Kāhui Kapua down to Uenukumahoenui. Ō-taha-te-kapua is a large area that encompasses the trig point, a ridge and the historic hunting and occupation site beside the Unuunuakapuateariki (Te Unuunu a Kapua Te Ariki) stream. The fern ridge above the occupation site is also referred to as Ō-taha-te-kapua. Sometimes it is also referred to in its’ extended less known form, Te Kurae a Tatekapua.
info_description: A ridge on the southern slopes of Mount Ruapehu, on the western edge of Karioi Forest, approximately 11km northwest of Waiouru. NZTopo50-BJ34 204324.
treaty_legislation: Section 56 and 57 Ngāti Rangi Claims Settlement Act 2019

name: Ōtāhuhu
info_origin: ’The most popular explanation is lit. ō: place of; tāhuhu: ridgepole of a house. The portage of the Tainui canoe from the Tāmaki River to the western seaboard crossed a low ridge, which was likened to the ridgepole of a house. The name was probably first given to one of the hills, one tradition stating that this was Mount Richmond. A literal version of the name is ota: raw or uncooked; huhu: a grub found in decayed timber, the larva of the beetle Prionoplus reticularis. It is regarded as a delicacy by Māori. Both explanations may be correct, for during the portage of the Tainui canoe the crew was sustained by a meal of grubs. Another division of the name yields ō: place of; Tāhuhu; according to Ngāti Whātua this is Tāhuhunui-o-te-rangi, captain of Moekakara canoe and founding ancestor of Ngāi Tāhuhu.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Ōtaki Forks
info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5111558 {Adkin, Leslie. 1948. Horowhenua. New Zealand: Internal Affairs; Crawford, James Coutts. 1880. Recollections of Travel in New Zealand. Great Britain: Trubner & Co.; Maclean, Chris. 1991. Otaki Forks Gate way to the Tararua mountains. Otaki Historical Society Journal, 9-18.}
info_origin: A locality at the confluence of the Ōtaki River and Waiotauru River. Māori crossed from Ōtaki Forks to the Wairarapa as well as using another track linking Ōtaki Forks to Ōhau River. In 1863 Wellington Provincial geologist JC Crawford was one of the first Europeans to visit the Ōtaki Forks area having been instructed to look for signs of gold. Crawford was accompanied by Manahi, an Ōtaki ferryman who acted as guide. Crawford’s description of the journey up Ōtaki River noted that ‘The river winds between vertical cliffs about seventy feet [21m] high, composed of vertical slates and sandstones, capped by drift-gravel terraces, the latter formation being of various thicknesses, from 6 to 30 feet [1.8m to 9.1m]. Mamaku and other tree-ferns abound in the forest. The stream is rapid, and as deep as could be waded; indeed, it was sometimes difficult to keep one's feet. The mode of progress was wading the river, then crossing a shingle bed, then wading again, and so on alternately. Had the river risen, it would have been difficult, or impossible in most places, to ascend the cliffs for safety, they were so steep. We passed the mouth of the Waitatapia falling into the right bank; up this stream lies the track to the Ohau river. A short distance higher up, and we may say at the base of the central range, the Otaki forks, the northern branch retaining the name of the Otaki, while the southern branch is called the Waiotauheru [Waiotauru]’. The larger Tararua area was surveyed and mapped from 1866-73. Sawmills were working in the Ōtaki Forks area by the early 1900s. In 1907 Ōtaki MP, WH Field, urged the preservation of the forest of the Otaki catchment and from 1909-11 was involved in leading tramping trips from Ōtaki Forks up Mount Hector and across to the Wairarapa. Track development and building of permanent huts followed in the 1920s. The name was sometimes reduced to ‘The Forks’ in the 1920s and 1930s. Sawmilling ceased in the late 1930s.

name: Ōtamakotinga
info_ref: Objective ID: A2409052; NZMS260 S21 Edition 1 1987; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: Ōtamakotinga, located at Karioi approximately 1 km east of the sacred peak Te Turi o Murimotu (on the Murimotu Plains between Ohākune and Waiouru) was the name of a kainga and the ridge upon which it stood. There were lakes and swamps, (refer to Ō-Te-Mataraha) at the base of Ōtamakotinga where the local people fished for eels, caught birds, and grew kai. The name Ōtamakotinga means “the place where the ceremony was held for the burying of the pito (navel cord)’ and commemorates the place at which Paerangi, the eponymous ancestor of Ngāti Rangi, had his navel cord cut. ‘Koti’ is a reference to the words of the karakia used in this ceremony. Along with names such as Tuhirangi and Te Whakatara o Paerangi, Ōtamakotinga is one of a set of names that were intentionally branded upon the landscape. This tikanga was used to establish and affirm mana whenua of Ngāti Rangi. For the descendants of Paerangi today this place helps tell the history of their ancestor.
info_description: A hill at 892m with a beaconed geodetic mark A6QT at the summit, approximately 10km west-southwest of Waiouru. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BJ34 199251

name: Otamatea
info_origin: 'Otamatea River: Northland, Kaipara Harbour. Lit. o: place of; Tamatea. The name refers to Tamatea-pokai-whenua, for he visited both districts. For his sojourn at Wanganui, see Putiki. The Northland Otamatea (also known as Batley, q.v.), in Kaipara District, was in full: Te Toka-turanga-o-Tamatea (q.v.): lit. te: the; toka: rock; turanga: circumstance of standing; o: of; Tamatea. It referred to an occasion when Tamatea was hard pressed by warriors of Ngati Whatua. His only chance of escape was to swim across a river, but other enemies may have been lying in wait for him there. He begged for help from his atua Raiera, who came swiftly in the form of a large rock, which bore Tamatea safely to the middle of the stream. Ngati Whatua then welcomed him to their pa. Before returning to Hawke's Bay, Tamatea thanked them for their kindness and left this manifestation of his atua as a bridge for their descendants, thus naming the river and the district.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Otangiwao Point
info_origin: The site was of one of four Ngāti Tamateatūtahi pā at Lake Rotomā. The palisades were said to still be evident in 1893. Tradition states the feature becomes an island when lake levels were high. Ngāti Tamateatūtahi/Ngāti Kawiti advise a commonly cited story for the origin of the name is not correct as it is not one passed down from their tūpuna, being that the name refers to waka travelling from the point to urupā in the forest on the opposite side of the lake, hence 'Otangi' [to cry] 'wao' [forest].
info_description: A small point on the southwest shore of Lake Rotomā. Feature shown on: NZMS260 V15; NZTopo50-BE38 137819
info_note: There are a number of local use names for the feature. the most common being Letterbox or Mailbox Island/Point, referring to a feature that was once used for jumping off into the lake. Divers Point is also used as the surrounding waters are a popular site for recreational diving. Tourist Point has been noted, and 'Ngātangiwao' is another name for the point advised by the proposers.

name: Ōtewā
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA378423; NZMS260 S16 Edition 1 1987; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Maniapoto statement: Pera MacDonald (nee Rangitaawa, of Ngāti Urunumia) quoted (c.2004) “Ō te wā o te hokinga mai o te Arikinui ki Te Nehenehenui” in reference to “the return of [King Tāwhiao] to Te Nehenehenui”. The late Rua Anderson (revered elder of Ngāti Maniapoto in his time) also claimed “Te hokinga mai o Te Wherowhero ki Te Nehenehenui”, c.1990’s. . King Tawhiao born in Maniapoto around 1822, and the name ‘Ōtewā’ comes from this, referring to that time. Ōtewā is within the traditional rohe of Maniapoto hapū, Ngāti Matakore and Ngāti Parewaeono. Before the Waitangi Tribunal, Harold Maniapoto spoke of the Amiowhenua war party, Te Wherowhero’s war party who, on their return home to Waipā, to Kakepuku and Pirongia, found Ngapuhi had besieged Mātakitaki, and that pā, Mātakitaki, fell to Ngāpuhi. The survivors fled to Orongokokoia and Ōtewā with Ngāpuhi in pursuit, all the way to Huiputea. (Wai 898, #4.1.001 Transcript of Kōrero Tuku Iho Hearing Week #5, p 44 (Harold Maniapoto).)

name: Ōtorohanga District
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-18/739; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche February 2024: Objective ID: A6141746 {[Agreement at Last. 1921. King Country Chronicle, 3 March, Page 5.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/KCC19210303.2.21); Local Government Commission – District Council. R1145195. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; Otorohanga District Council. R18147989. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; Local govt Commission -District Council - Otorohanga District Council. R1145195. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; [Otorohanga Town District. 1916. Waipa Post, 28 April, Page 3.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WAIPO19160428.2.23)}
info_origin: An Otorohanga District was first formed in 1979 when Otorohanga County applied under the Local Government Amendment Act of 1978 to become a ‘District’ to better describe the local authority which included rural and urban communities. In 1971 Otorohanga County and Otorohanga Borough had amalgamated to form a new enlarged Otorohanga County – at that time ‘district’ was not an officially available designation. This was one of the first such borough-county mergers in the country. In 1955 Otorohanga Borough had succeeded the earlier Otorohanga Town District, which had been created in 1916 under the Municipal Corporations Act, which in turn had replaced Otorohanga Native Town proclaimed in 1903 and in which 236 leasehold sections were advertised for sale in 1904. Otorohanga County dated from 1922 when it was formed out of the former Wharepapa and Mangaorongo Road Districts, to which was added the northern half of Kawhia County in 1956. The Local Government Commission reviewed the performance of Otorohanga District as part of a national review of local government areas in 1985-86 and considered that it met their performance criteria. In 1988 the Commission considered merging Otorohanga District and Waitomo District as part of a countrywide exercise in local government restructuring, but the outcome was that the Local Government (Waikato Region) Reorganisation Order 1989 established the current Ōtorohanga District with very similar boundaries to the prior one. The macron was added in 2019.
info_description: The district that is administered by the Ōtorohanga District Council.

name: Ōtukopiri
info_origin: Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui history: 'The pā Ōtukopiri was built in the 1840’s to ease the over-population of Ngāti Pāmoana that had developed at Operiki Pā (located approximately half a mile north of Ōtukopiri). The name Ōtukopiri also traditionally refers to the high point of the ridge on the hills on the western side of the River above the Ōtukopiri Stream. That ridge – between the Ōtukopiri Stream and a smaller stream called Te Hapu which falls into the Ahuahu Stream – was said to be the pā of the taniwha, Te Maru. Ōtukopiri was a tupuna of the Awa (o Whanganui) before Pāmoana arrived and was connected to Ngāti Tauira, Ngā Poutama (Ngā Poutamanui-ā-Awa), Ngāti Hineoneone, and Ngaa Rauru Kiitahi. This was also the name attached to the land blocks on both sides of the river near Te Waiherehere. Around 1848, Richard Taylor (a missionary who regularly travelled to Māori settlements of the Whanganui River) had dubbed a biblical name ‘Corinth’ upon this area during one of his visits. This was then translated in Māori and became known as Koriniti (sometimes incorrectly spelt Koroniti). NZGB’s 1995 map labels this locality ‘O Tū Kopiri’ – “pinched with cold”. The correct spelling is a single word – Ōtukopiri.' [Note: Ōtukopiri Stream is recorded on topographic maps as Otuporiki Stream]

name: Otūwairoa Stream
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: ‘Ngāti Tamaoho have strong cultural, traditional and historic links with the waters of their awa. The rivers are the life-blood of their rohe. From them come the means for survival by way of lamprey, tuna and other kaimoana. They also provide the main means of travel and trade to many otherwise inaccessible parts of the rohe during ancient times. They also provided the main sources of fresh water, essential for survival. Thus, they were the connecting tissue between the many kainga, pa and cultivation throughout the rohe. Moreover, they were a source of great mana for Ngāti Tamaoho. Their use for travel, resources and kai was closely governed by complex principle of tikanga. Sometimes their use was shared and at other times it was used by other tribes on a reciprocal basis. Otuwairoa (Slippery Creek) is particularly important to Ngāti Tamaoho because of its traditional use and its location. The stream is a confluence of many other important awa of the area including the Waipokapu (Hays Stream) and the Mangapu (Symonds Stream). It carries the mauri of these awa with its waters as it drains into the Manukau Harbour. The outlet of the Outwairoa is also significant because of the Opaheke kainga site along its northern bank. Prior to deforestation of its catchment and other contributing factors, Otuwairoa would have been far wider, deeper and faster flowing. Traditional evidence recalls that the rivers in this area were navigable for several miles inland. Stories tell of waka from the Manukau making their way up streams to very near the base of Pukekiwiriki. Ngāti Tamaoho often built settlements at the mouths of rivers to benefit from their great wealth of kaimoana. Tuna were harvested with nets or weirs built across strategic parts of the rivers. Ngāti Tamaoho were experts at the sustainable use of the resources of these awa. The lives of the people were closely intertwined with the quantity and quality of the freshwater that was available to them. It provide habitat and spawning grounds for native plants, bird and fish, building and weaving materials such as raupo and flax, and precious medicines and dyes. Modifications to waterways and their catchment areas have significantly altered the relationship of Ngāti Tamaoho with these resources. The protection of freshwater resources remains one of most important parts of the responsibilities of Ngāti Tamaoho as kaitiaki of the environment and their rohe. Values (both tangible and intangible) that are assigned to specific water bodies include: Ngāti Tamaoho believe that each waterway carries its own mauri. A water body with a healthy mauri will sustain healthy ecosystems, support cultural uses and mahinga kai, and be a source of pride and identity to the tangata whenua.'
info_description: A stream that flows generally south for approximately 3km from east of Coulthard Terrace, off Great South Road, to the inner reaches of Manukau Harbour just north of Drury. NZTopo50 BB32 729942 to BB32 727928.

name: Owen River
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Haast, HF von 1948. The Life & times of Sir Julius von Haast. New Zealand: Wellington; Haast, Ferdinand. 1860. Topographical Map of the Central and Western part of the Province of Nelson [reproduction in endpapers of Haast (1948)]; Hochstetter, Ferdinand and Haast, Julius. 1860. [Geological Map of the Province of Nelson](https://teara.govt.nz/en/zoomify/8137/geological-map-of-nelson-province)}
info_origin: Owen River was named by geologist Julius (von) Haast for Sir Richard Owen the British palaeontologist who was first to identify moa bones formally and scientifically. The river was associated with Mount Owen which was also named by Haast. Owen River was depicted on Hochstetter and Haast’s (1860) ‘Geological Map of Nelson Province’ and Haast’s ‘Topographical Map of the Central and Western part of the Province of Nelson’ also from 1860, although it was not published until much later. Haast and Hochstetter believed science transcended political boundaries and named topographical features in New Zealand after leading scientists from many nations. In addition, Haast significantly underestimated the number of features that possessed original Māori names in southwest Nelson and the Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana. The actual position and labelling of Mount Owen on various maps and to a lesser extent Owen River was also the subject of an official inquiry in 1869 as it had implications for the boundary and administration of the Wangapeka goldfield.

name: Owens Creek
info_origin: Named after Richard David Owens, a Welsh pioneer who lived in the area in the late 1800s. He was a ferryman at the Morven Ferry from 1867 to 1879 (and possibly until 1881), which crossed the Kawerau River mouth at its entrance into Lake Wakatipu. He was also the proprietor of the Gibbston coal pit from 1877 to 1887, during which time he was also the licensee of several hotels in Arrowtown, Cromwell and Gibbston. However he was bankrupted in 1887 and little was known of him after that time. Spelling correction from Owen Creek

info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; A7856323; Objective folder ID: fA640497
info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: ‘The Ōwhango district was an occupation area for several uri of Ngāti Hāua including Hauaroa, Hekeāwai, Reremai, Hinewai, Tū and Matakaha. Among the kāinga here was one of Topine Te Mamaku that overlooked the Whakapapa River near the present-day township of Ōwhango. Where Otapouri Road joins the State Highway, a significant marae was located. This acted as a meeting place for Whanganui and Tuwharetoa. Each iwi built a wharepuni here to signify that they had reached an agreement to resist the railway and colonial encroachment on their lands. Te Kere directed Ngarangi Te Uhu to erect the whare. The wharepuni were named Whatika and Rumatiki and they both faced the sacred Maunga.  The area of land given to Turaki I called Tutumai is in the environs of Ōwhango, as is Kauwautahi.’

feat_note: Parts of Ōwhango Domain Recreation Reserve subject to the Reserves Act 1977 are revoked under sections 104 and 138 of the Ngāti Hāua Claims Settlement Act 2026 (‘Settlement Act 2026’) and the official Crown protected area name no longer applies to those parts, in accordance with section 140 of the Settlement Act 2026. info_origin: An original Māori name carried over from land blocks Ōwhata A and Ōwhata B on a small peninsula jutting into Herekino Harbour and the site of the Ōwhata Marae, kāinga of the hapū Ngāti Torotoroa. Ōwhata is connected ancestrally to the maunga Rawhitiroa, the awa Puhata Wairere and the moana Nga-Tai-o-e-Uru. Ōwhata grew in 1906 when the Mitchelson Timber Company set up a new sawmill employing 16 hands, cutting increasingly scarce kauri (Agathis australis) off Māori and European land. Thereafter in quick succession a named telephone office was opened in 1906 and a mail service commenced in 1907 along with the construction of a school that same year. Milling had ceased by 1912 and mill worker houses were sold off, families moved away, and the school closed. By 1920 Ōwhata attracted renewed attention as a seaside resort ‘Though it is little known, it possesses charms and advantages of a high order. The harbour has acres of safe, sandy-bottomed bathing places where the water has a uniform depth of three or four feet (0.9m to 1.2m). It has boating facilities and good fishing’. By this time Ōwhata (43 acres) [17ha] was also one of only two small blocks on the southern shore of Herekino Harbour remaining in Māori ownership as places to live. A contested dispute over a road line on the Ōwhata block in the 1930s led to an arrest and imprisonment. The Ōwhata reserves were further reduced by the creation of an esplanade reserve bordering the water in 1976. The Waitangi Tribunal visited Ōwhata in December 1990. In its assessment, the Crown had failed to properly survey the reserves and preserve access to the wāhi tapu. The peninsula itself has been considerably eroded on the western side since the 1890s.
