info_origin: An original Māori name associated with the stream of the same name. The meaning of Ōwhiro has proven challenging for various compilers of New Zealand place names. Wise’s Index from 1946 offered the unlikely ‘big willow’, Edward Dollimore (1904-73) in The New Zealand Guide ‘the place of an evil spirit’, and publisher Alexander Reed (1908-79) in contrast to his usual confidence suggests literally the place of Whiro, ‘possibly the god of evil and darkness’. His caution likely stems from drawing on historian-journalist James Cowan’s (1870-1943) translation of the meaning of the South Island railway station of the same name. An Owhiro Post Office and Telegraph opened in 1916 and closed in 1955. Ōwhiro was the site of a Public Works Camp in the 1930s. The 1946 edition of Wises Index of New Zealand listed Ōwhiro as a locality.

Although the New Zealand Company used ‘Ohiro’, around 1844 ‘Happy Valley’ became an alternative appellation for the area and continued in use until after WWII. Ethnologist Elsdon Best, a member of the Honorary Geographic Board, was behind the correction of the spelling from Ohiro to Owhiro in 1930. The orthography was updated to Ōwhiro when the New Zealand Geographic Board Ngā Pou Taunaha o Aotearoa gazetted the suburb name as official in 2019.

info_origin: Packard Peak (2066m) was one of a number of feature names in Craigieburn Forest Park put forward by the New Zealand Forest Service in 1973 and approved by the New Zealand Geographic Board that same year. It was named after William Percival (Bill) Packard (1925-2009). Packard joined the Canterbury University Tramping Club and the New Zealand Alpine Club as an undergraduate. He completed an MA thesis on land use problems caused by overgrazing in the Lake Coleridge catchment, the basis of a separate report for the North Canterbury Catchment Board. Packard’s study area included some of Craigieburn Range and lay behind the Forest Service’s advancing of his name. His excellent thesis, in conjunction with his representative cross country running, mountaineering and leadership enabled him to become the first New Zealand Rhodes Scholar in geography in 1948. The thesis made quite a mark in its day pointing out the dangers of overgrazing from deer and sheep in a low rainfall, loose substructured land. In 1950 while in the UK, he was invited to join HW (Bill) Timan’s expedition to Nepal to attempt the ascent of Annapurna IV. Packard contracted poliomyelitis on the descent. While a lecturer at University College London, he assisted with preparation for the 1953 Everest expedition. Returning to a geography lectureship at Canterbury University in 1955, he became a foundation member of the Mount Cook National Park Board and member of the New Zealand Alpine Club committee. He also became warden of Rolleston House and in 1961 moved to Canberra as Warden of Bruce Hall at the Australian National University. In 1987 he was awarded the Order of Australia Medal.

name: Paekākāriki Hill
info_origin: The meaning of Paekākāriki according to Reeds¹ ‘Place Names of New Zealand’, 2010 is: “Lit. pae: perch or snare; kakariki: parakeet (Cyanoramphus novaezelandiae). There is a legend to the effect that Haupipi, pursuing his wife, came to a rock barrier at the end of the beach. This gave the name to the locality. He drove his taiaha into the cliff, made a hole through it and came out the other side, where he found his wife.” The name Paekākāriki Hill has been historically and traditionally associated with this cliff type hill. Another Māori name, Pai-a-te-Rangi, exists, but Ngāti Toa support Paekākāriki Hill (for the hill feature), and consider it to be an older name than Pai-a-te-Rangi. ¹ Reed, A.W. (2010). Place Names of New Zealand. (Revised: P Dowling). Penguin Group: North Shore.
info_description: Located along the northern boundary of Paekākāriki Hill locality, height 274m. NZTopo50 BP32-Paraparaumu GR 628 587. Geodetic mark, coded A2FP, named “Paekakariki”, beaconed, is located at the summit. Assigning a new name for an unnamed feature.
info_note: Paekākāriki Hill was originally notified as a proposal between 19 July 2012 and 26 October 2012, but was later found to have been attached to the wrong feature - the highest point of the hill network through which the Paekakariki Hill Road winds, rather than the cliff face hill overlooking the sea and the township of Paekakariki. After reconsideration by the NZGB on 31 July 2013, the name was re-notified and publicly consulted at its correct location. No objecting submissions were received and one supporting submission was received.

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/71208; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Statement of Association provided by Ngāti Manuhiri: Paepae-o-Tū. The standing place of Tū, is the traditional name for the coastal promontory more commonly known today as Bream Tail. The name is of major spiritual significance as it is associated with Tūmatauenga – the deity associated with man and war. Paepae-o-Tū is also significant as it marks the northern boundary of the Ngāti Manuhiri Rohe. The name Bream Tail was introduced by Captain James Cook. The place name Paepae-o-Tū is shown on the plan of the Mangawhai Purchase, 1854. (H.H. Turton Maori Deeds of Land Purchases in the North Island of New Zealand, Vol.1, Deed 98, pp. 133-136). Reed's Place Names of New Zealand records the following information: Bream Bay: Northland, the bay from which Whangarei Harbour opens. Bream Head: Bream Islands: Bream Tail: The bay was named on 25 November 1769 by Captain Cook, who wrote: ‘We caught between 90 and 100 Bream (a fish so called). This occasioned my giving this place the name of Bream Bay.’ The north and south heads of the bay are named respectively Bream Head and Bream Tail. The ‘bream’ were probably snapper."; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMERDQkIwQjZGRjEwMDgzNDI1MkI)"

name: Pāhangahanga
info_origin: 'The full name was Pa-hangahanga-noa-iho, which signifies an uncompleted fortified village. A beautiful girl named Te Ripo was sent from Hokianga to Kaipara on a goodwill mission. She was warmly welcomed by Ngati Whatua at Poutu. After a short stay there, she disappeared with an unknown man in a canoe in the direction of Oruawharo. An intensive search was made of the Oruawharo and Otamatea rivers, without result. Ngati Whatua then feared an attack by Hokianga people to find and rescue Te Ripo, and they built a number of pas. Five were built near the Oruawharo — Pokapu, Nga-ringa-o-matariki, Puatewhero, Huruhuru, Matawhero, and Pahangahanga (near Nuhaka). The last named was never completed, hence the name. In fact Te Ripo had fallen in love with a stranger to Ngati Whatua. They evaded the Poutu people, then returned to live on the West Coast as man and wife. As the man was not Ngati Whatua, they could not be blamed, and were not attacked.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: In one version of the Kupe tradition, Pāhaoa is the location where Rere-whakaaitu, one of Kupe’s children, was left behind. In historic times Ngāti Rongomāiaia, the hapū descended from Tūmapuhia-ā-Rangi, lived at Pāhaoa, as did Ngāti Hikawera descendants. Barton’s Run (Mataōperu) was purchased in October 1853, followed by four adjacent acquisitions in the Āwhea-Pāhaoa area. This included two separate purchases in October 1853 and January 1854 of land known as ‘Pahaoa’. A Native Reserve including the Pāhaoa pā and kāinga was set aside on the coast. The correct spelling of Pāhaoa came before the Honorary New Zealand Geographic Board in 1939. This was prompted by a request from Alan Mulgan, then writing ‘The City of the Strait’ who had been informed that the run was actually known as ‘Pahaua’. This spelling did exist on an 1861 plan but alongside the ‘Pahaoa River’ and ‘Pahaoa Native Reserve’. Board member, Sir Āpirana Ngata, was clear in his view ‘As a place name Pahaoa is not uncommon meaning the pa surrounded or besieged. Pahaua does not carry any intelligible meaning’. This spelling was confirmed for the river and block by the Board in 1940.

name: Paines Ford Scenic Reserve
info_origin: The Paine family was associated with the ford across Takaka River adjacent to the Scenic Reserve hence the naming of the reserve in 1976. Unfortunately the name was spelled incorrectly in the 1976 NZ Gazette notice. Nathaniel Paine came to NZ on the 'Queen Bee' in the 1850s. He was from a family with a piano making company called Paine and Jackson. He settled at the junction of Takaka River and Waingaro River on the true left bank of Takaka River around 1868. He mined coal, established an orchard and ran sheep on both sides of the river (and used the tramway). Nathaniel died in 1881. Herbert (Barty) Paine was a son of Nathaniel, and took over land at Paine’s Ford (an important crossing place on the route up Takaka Valley). Barty was part of the Takaka Brass Band. In later life Barty lived at Waitapu and drowned in 1938 as a result of a boat accident at Waitapu. Barty’s house site is marked today by a line of Lombardy poplar trees.

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-05/888; Feature shown on: NZMS260 U18
info_origin: Ngāti Tūwharetoa history: Ngātoro-i-rangi is a principal ancestor of Tūwharetoa. He was the priest navigator of the Te Arawa waka, and upon his arrival in Aotearoa he journeyed inland, seeking land for his people. Eventually, he arrived in the Taupo area. He climbed Tauhara mountain and then travelled eastwards around the lake. He arrived at the area [later] known as ‘Halletts Bay’, about 27km south-east of Taupo township. He found a tuahu (altar) already constructed by Tia (an important tupuna for Tūwharetoa) that included green leaves, indicating it was of recent construction. Ngātoro-i-rangi used old, scorched materials to build his own tuahu, which he used to conduct certain sacred rites and to establish his claim to the lands. He showed Tia his tuahu who, seeing the older materials, agreed that Ngātoro-i-rangi had a prior claim to the land. Accepting Ngātoro-i-rangi’s claim, Tia left for Titiraupenga on the western shores of Lake Taupo (Taupomoana). The name ‘Pākā’ means ‘to be burnt’. It refers to Ngātoro-i-rangi scorching branches of leaves. Missionaries renamed Pākā “Hamaria” in the mid 1800s (transliteration of Samaria). Later, it was renamed again “Halletts Bay”.

name: Pākawau
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; Objective ID: A3379678; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412 {Andersen, Johannes. 1942. Maori Place Names. Report of a Topographical and Geological Exploration of the Western Districts of the Nelson Province, New Zealand](http://api.digitalnz.org/records/37333922/source); Mitchell, H. and Mitchell, J. 2004. Te Tau Ihu O Te waka. A History of Maori of Nelson and Marlborough Volume 1. Huia, Wellington; [Notes of an expedition to Kawatiri and Araura, on the western coast of the middle Island, performed by Messrs. Heaphy and Brunner.1846. Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle, 5 September, Page 105](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NENZC18460905.2.4); [Mitchell, H. and J. (1996). Kehu (Hone Mokehakeha): biographical notes. Nelson Historical Journal 6(1), 3-19](https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-NHSJ06_01-t1-body1-d1.html)}
info_origin: An original Māori name for a pā by the river of the same name. Thomas Brunner, Charles Heaphy and Kehu (Hone Mokehakeha) stayed overnight at the kāinga (village) in March 1846 while exploring the coastal route to Westland and hired Hemi Kuku as a porter. In 1851 Major Matthew Richmond (1801-87), Superintendent of the Southern Division, on Governor Grey’s urgent instructions commenced the Pākawau purchase. Grey, with Richmond’s concurrence, intended to acquire lands that were potentially mineral bearing before the Māori owners appreciated their extra value. The deed was signed in 1852. There were long term complaints over the designation and location of reserves leading ultimately to a Te Atiawa Waitangi Tribunal claim in 2002 as well as hearing of other Ngāti Tama grievances. In 1861 Julius Haast returned from his topographical and geological expedition to Western Nelson ‘after a very muddy walk of three hours’ via Pākawau River. In ‘Lore and History of the South Island Maori’ William Taylor offers as a translation ‘Pa kawau - the pa of the shag’. In ‘Maori Place Names’ ethnologist Johannes Andersen offers pa – ‘a flock’ and kawau ‘a bird, shag, or cormorant’.

info_origin: Whakatōhea history (extract): The harbour entrance has, since the earliest arrivals of people to Aotearoa been a major entranceway to Ōpōtiki and the surrounding districts. The name Pakihikura is derived from one of the earliest waka to arrive in this area, the Pakihikura. The ancestors that arrived on the Pakihikura travelled inland and settled at a place that is now known as Whakapaupakihi, another reference to the earliest arrivals. Its legacy continues to the naming of the Pakihi Valley to the south of Ōpōtiki. The Ngariki people were some of Whakatōhea’s earliest inhabitants, and provide important whakapapa lineage to Whakatōhea. They believed “that they were a people from Hawaiki. Their canoe was Pakihikura – allegedly a Fleet canoe – which landed at Ōpōtiki, the bar at the river entrance being named Pakihi after the canoe.” The full name Pakihikura was also used for the whole stream from the Confluence of the Otara and Waioweka rivers, to the sea, where the river mouth was given the shortened name, Pakihi.

name: Pakipaki Stream
info_origin: Pakipaki Stream is a freshwater stream that is fed by an underwater spring located on the upper reaches of Rangiuru. The name Pakipaki was given to this stream after the killing of Marukukere. Pakipaki Stream was one of the most sacred waterways of Tapuika and treated with the utmost caution as it was home to the colony of taniwha who were not disposed towards the presence of humans in their territory. There were many stories related to the taniwha that reinforced the need to exercise care when within the vicinity of the stream. At the source of this stream is a spring called Te Waitohi o Tumatauenga. It was the place where the toa would go to undertake the tohi rites both prior to and after battle to cleanse them from the influences of the battle. Toa could not return to their villages and families until the completion of the tohi rites. The battle site of Omaropoporo is also located beside the lower reaches of the Pakipaki Stream. This was one of the pakanga between Tapuika and the tribes known as Haeremaire and Waiohua in revenge for the killing of Marukukere.

info_origin: Named in association with a reef in the area where green-lipped mussels (Perna canaliculus), kuku, were gathered. The Ngāti Kahungunu associated Rongomaraeroa Marae consider the name of significant ancestral importance. A kāinga or pā also known as Pākuku was on the hills above the stream and reef, and was visited by both William Colenso in the 1840's and missionary William Williams in 1848. A colloquialism 'Pakuk' has sometimes led to mistaken beliefs of an association with Lt. James Cook, ie 'Pā Cook'.

name: Pakuranga
info_origin: 'Auckland, a suburb of Auckland. Lit. paku: small in numbers; ranga: company of people, or a shoal of fish. Sometimes translated as Small hill or ridge on the plain. Pakuranga may have been the original name of Pigeon Mountain, but this may have been Oroke, and Pakuranga that of the stream. It has also been claimed as a contraction of Pakurangarahihi, said to mean Battle of the sun’s rays, lit. pakura: red glow in the sky; ra: sun; hihi: which means rays of the sun. There is a local legend of a battle among the early Turehu or people of the mist. Near Pigeon Mountain a war party from Hunua fought a party from Waitakere; the cause is said to have been a woman. The battle was cut short when a tohunga from Hunua invoked an early sunrise (the Turehu could not stand sunlight).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Pākuratahi Stream
info_ref: Te Hata Kani II, Statement of evidence, 11-15 November 1996, Wai 201, Doc # J40, p. 2; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-12/95
info_origin: Pākuratahi was a land block to which Ngāti Tū, Ngāti Tauira and Ngai Te Ruruku had rights and became grantees. Ngāti Tū had the strongest association being descended from the original occupant groups. The pa site Ngamoerangi, located on the Pākuratahi block was used by Marangatūhetaua during a conflict between his people of Ngāti Tū and neighbouring tribes. The neighbouring tribes had been raiding the fishing grounds at Tangoio which led Marangatūhetaua to seek support from the rangatira Te Ruruku who was offered fishing rights at Arapawanui in return. Marangatūhetaua placed a number of his warriors at Ngamoerangi under the leadership of Te Ruruku, who was a skilled fighting chief. The neighbouring tribe were repulsed and Te Ruruku gained rights to land within the Ngāti Tū and Ngai Tatara rohe.In his statement of evidence,Te Hata Kani II referred to the abundance of ducks and fish at Pākuratahi when he was young.

name: Palliser Bay
info_origin: 'Named by Captain James Cook after his mentor Captain Pallisser, afterwards Sir Hugh, comptroller of the British navy. Until 1773 he signed his name Pallisser. Jules Dumont d’Urville named it Useless Bay in 1827, when he was unable to go ashore on account of heavy seas, despite the comments he made at the time: ‘Instead of the names Tera-Witi and Palliser given by Cook, they [the Māori] gave me Poli-Wero and Kawa-Kawa, which on our map I restored to the capes which should bear them, convinced that it would be absurd not to designate these points by the names used, for centuries perhaps, by tribes as numerous and intelligent as those of New Zealand.’ Māori name: Te Kawakawa: lit. te: the; kawakawa: a shrub (Macropiper excelsum). Kupe went ashore near Cape Palliser and named it Te Kawakawa because it was here that one of his daughters wove a headband of kawakawa leaves. Cape Palliser / Mātakitaki-a-Kupe also recalls Kupe’s stay here. Standing on a rock, Kupe recited karakia to attract fish such as hāpuku, and in the distance observed snow-covered Tapuae-o-Uenuku. He explained this to his daughter Hine-a-uira, who bestowed the name meaning ‘The outlook of Kupe’.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: ’As with Palmerston in Otago, and at least two other localities assigned Palmerston in the nineteenth century, it was named in honour of Lord Palmerston, the British prime minister. Because of confusion with the Otago place, a public meeting was held on 6 March 1873 at which it was decided to append ‘North’ to the name. Thereafter the name was challenged sporadically, with the best alternative, Manawatu, failing to change the status quo. Māori name: Te Papaioea. Two alternatives are available depending on hyphenation: lit. te: the; papai: good, beauties; oea: indeed; Beauties indeed; or a reference to the beauty of water when dead bodies are soaked in it.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Pānia Rock
info_ref: NZ 56, NZ 561; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836; Objective ID: A3379678
info_origin: Reed (2010:302) records [abridged]: Pania was a half-human, half sea-maiden who lived in the sea by day and on land at night. Pania breached tapu and was driven back to sea, where she became a rock formation.; 'This is the legendary rock that is commemorated by the well-known statue on Napier’s Marine Parade. Pania was a half-human, half-sea maiden who lived in the sea by day and on land by night. She fell in love with the handsome young Karitoki, and they had a son, Moremore. Tiring of Pania’s absence during the daytime, Karitoki took a tohunga’s advice and placed cooked food on their bodies. This breach of tapu drove Pania back to the sea, where she became a rock formation that can be seen below the water at ebb-tide. Moremore metamorphosed into a taniwha, which appears as a shark.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

The stream was the original boundary of the tribe from the mouth of the Waiapu River in Rangitukia to the Stream of Paoa o ruku. It was at the stream where many notable battles were fought, and lands belonging to the Wahine Iti subtribe of Ngati Porou, passed into the hands of the chief Tinatoka under claim of Raupatu (conquest). Replaces Pauoruku Stream 1941 Hon p. 25. Information obtained by A T Mahuika, Senior Lecturer, Social Anthropology and Māori Studies Department, Massey University. See Correspondence volumes (esp. 43) for further details.

info_origin: Papamoa is an original Māori name for a pā approximately 3km inland, which overlooked the fertile coastal dune plains and coastal fisheries and gave its name to the associated locality. Historian-journalist James Cowan translated Papamoa as 'level cultivation ground with beds or raised plots.' Papamoa Beach was named for its proximity to the locality of Papamoa. A Māori track ran close to the beach from Maunganui to Maketū. In 1879 the original Papamoa Block of 12655 acres (5121 ha) was 'awarded to 60 owners under the Tauranga District Lands Act'. However, from the mid-1880s Tauranga Borough Council pressured the government to purchase Papamoa coastal lands for small farm settlement. This land passed through the Native Land Court in 1893 and was split into two blocks one of which was purchased by the Crown. The other, Papamoa No. 2 Block, was divided into smaller sections of 100 to 700 acres (40 to 283 ha) each allocated to groups of owners. It included 'burial reserves' along the coast. The northern coastal block was of poor quality with sand dunes and swamp. A road along the coast was known as Papamoa Beach Road by the early 1900s and was extended south through swampy ground in the 1920s. In 1922, residents requested that the Minister of Lands create a recreation reserve on the northern end of Papamoa Beach Road to cater for the increased number of fishers and picnickers. In 1938 a Papamoa Beach Rifle Range was constructed. The beach settlement proper began in 1952 when Mr Taylor formed a subdivision around Papamoa Beach Road, Motiti Road, and Karewa Parade. This involved levelling dunes to fill lagoons that ran parallel to the coast. In 1973 residents of Papamoa Beach voted to become a County Town. Mount Maunganui Borough had made an earlier offer for Papamoa to join the Borough, but this had been robustly rejected by Tauranga County Council. In 1989 as part of nationwide restructuring of local government Papamoa became part of a new Tauranga District Council, later enlarged to form the Western Bay of Plenty District Council.

info_origin: An original Māori name which an ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member translated as an area 'more or less flat covered with a particular growth, in this case toetoe' (Rubus australis). The area was on the Waokauri-Pūkaka portage route, which enabled waka to be transported across land from Manukau Harbour to Tamaki River and remained in use into the 1860s. The flat landscape did not favour pā construction although one known as Te Pā-o-te-tū-tahi-atu was located on today's Hillside South Park. Missionary William Thomas Fairburn (1795-1859) claimed to have purchased some 83000 acres (33589 ha) stretching from Ōtāhuhu to Papakura in 1836. The purchase was not upheld by the Land Claims Commission with Fairburn being granted only 5500 acres (2226 ha) in 1848 when European settlement of land in the area commenced. This increased with the construction of the Great South Road in 1851.The spellings Papatoitoi and Papatoetoe were used in the 1850s, the former persisted into the 1940s. A Papatoitoi Highway District was defined in 1865 and the newly formed Road Board in 1883 also adopted Papatoitoi. However, as early as 1902 Judge Henry Dunbar-Johnson (1844-1924) of the Native Land Court and a licensed interpreter wrote to Sir Joseph Ward (1856-1930), Minister of Railways, informing him that Papatoetoe was the correct spelling. The railway had reached Papatoetoe by 1875 but it was not until 1907 that Railways formally adopted this spelling for its station. A Papatoitoi Post Office opened in 1863 although this was at Wiri and was renamed Woodside in 1867. In the late 1920s some locals still defended Papatoitoi in the press as the original Māori spelling. In 1928 pioneer town planner EV (Ted) Blake AMTPI (London) (1890-1964) produced one of the first town plans showing existing and proposed land uses for the Papatoetoe Town Board under the Town-planning Act, 1926. In 1975 Papatoetoe became a city.

name: Papawhero / Mount Moturoa
info_origin: Te Atiawa statement: The original name of this site is Papawhero – red earth – and was named after a battle between Taranaki and Te Atiawa because the earth ran red with blood. It is therefore wahi tapu. The pā was established by Taranaki Iwi and later occupied by Te Atiawa. It was located on the boundary between Taranaki and Te Atiawa and mana whenua moved from one to the other depending on the victor. In the 1840’s, it was occupied by Te Atiawa. The current name of Mount Moturoa was given by the New Plymouth District Council, probably as it is located in the suburb of Moturoa.

name: Papawhitu Pā
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA258815; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki history: The name, Papawhitu, means “The Place of Gathered Forces”, referring to its importance as a defensive pā. It is a small but prominent headland pā, commonly referred to as Pah Point, Maraetai Pā and Waiomanu Pā. It is part of the Waiomanu Reserve currently owned by Council and co-governed by the Council and Ngai Tai. The name Waiomaru (or Waiomanu) is more correctly applied to the stream immediately southeast of the headland. The pā is believed to have been built during the sixteenth century, and to have supported a population of around 200 people. Ngāi Tai occupied Papawhitu pā and the adjoining coastal settlement of Pōhaturoa until shortly after the Land Wars of the 1860s.

name: Parahaki
info_origin: The island was a seasonal kāinga, mahinga kai site and urupā for Rangitāne with a sacred karaka grove opposite the island on the southern side. Only the island was reserved from the Ahuaturanga Crown purchase. The name may refer to strategic signalling fires once maintained in the area. Early 19th century surveys recorded 'Motuere' for the island, and some early 20th century newspapers named the feature Rabbit Island. In 1907-11 the Crown acquired part of the island in payment for outstanding surveying costs from 1879, unbeknownst to the owners. This was petitioned against for nearly 20 years until reversed by Section 57(1) of the Native Land Amendment and Native Land Claims Adjustment Act 1929. However, under 57(2) of that Act the Commissioner of Crown Lands ordered a new survey due to the notable accretion and erosion to the island. The new survey costs were charged to the owners of the island and took several years to pay by leasing the island for grazing.
info_description: An island approximately 15ha at the confluence of Pohaninga River with Manawatū River, just southeast of Ashhurst. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BM35 351348

name: Paraiti River
info_origin: Paraiti River is a spring fed river that commences in the Mangorewa – Kaharoa at Te Taita where the Ohaupara Stream meets the Mangorewa River. In traditional times Paraiti River was considered a very tapu river due to the number of urupa and burial caves along it. Otangikura was the principal burial cave on Paraiti River for the hapu living at Maungarangi while Okaha was an urupa where the dead of Ngati Tupare were buried; Piako was also a burial cave on Paraiti River. Te Pehu and Te Weta are pa on the river with man-made limestone caves that were used as an elaborate system of defence. Other settlements and pa abound Paraiti River are; Pukeroa and Otangikura urupa. Mid way along the river is a bend in the river called Kopuapatiki which is directly below the pa site Oteranginui, and was the place where a particular founder was caught. Places associated to Oteranginui on the river are; Mokai ate koko, Oreriwaho, Tunaroa, Tangatarua, Te Kawakawa, Te kauri. Another site on Paraiti River is a large cultivation called Taraoneone which was used in former times to feed those that went eeling during the tunaheke. These eelers would live in this area for the duration of the tuna run and these were prepared at this place. Further along are the pa sites Te Kawakawa, Te Kauri, Mahanganui, Te Puketapu, Upokopatuiwi, Te Hoho. At the confluence of Paraiti River and Kaituna River is the pa Kaiwaka and urupa Otamamarere.
info_description: A river flowing generally northeast from the confluence of Mangorewa River and Ohaupara Stream near SH 36 on Mamaku Plateau, approximately 10km northwest of Lake Rotorua/Te Rotorua nui ā Kahumatamomoe, to its confluence with Kaituna River. Paraiti River replaces Mangorewa River for the lower section of the river. NZTopo50-BE37 787938 (source) to NZTopo50-BD37 984077 (mouth)

info_origin: Parawhenuamea Stream is a marsh stream named after the Goddess of Freshwater and carved by the taniwha Mapu as he left his lair on the Kaituna River and made his way up the Pakipaki to join the colony of taniwha there. In the waiata Tenei Te Aroha the Parawhenuamea was referred to as ‘te pukaitanga o nga taniwha’. Along the mid- section of this stream a series of eight hollows can be viewed which are the lair of the taniwha that reside there and is held in great respect/tapu by Tapuika. It was stated in tribal lore that Parawhenuamea was the domain of the taniwha Pareawheawhe whose physical form is that of the manta ray. It is Pareawheawhe who carries the wairua of our deceased, north to Te Reinga. Te Ahikoauau is a subterranean warm water spring connected to the Parawhenuamea from which Pareawheawhe would sometimes emerge on her journeys across her domain. The area around Parawhenuamea Stream support a number of settlements at Paetawa, Maheatataka, Otahurihuri and Waitangi.
info_description: A stream flowing generally northeast from a location along Te Matai Road halfway between Reeves Road and Waimea Drive, into Kaituna River at the same location that Wairi Stream flows into Kaituna River, approximately 3km northeast of Te Puke. NZTopo50-BD37 913054 (source) to 946148 (mouth). Parawhenuamea Stream was assigned to another stream but was replaced by Pakipaki Stream in the Tapuika Treaty Settlement 2014.

info_origin: An original Māori name that also occurs in Wellington and Northland. Here it describes a sizable land block inland from Tolaga Bay and alongside Mangaheia River including a Māori settlement. Joseph Rhodes and Samuel Locke leased Māori land at Paremata in 1867-68, to be followed by Edward Murphy. Individual titles to portions of the block were awarded to Māori owners by the Native Land Court in the late 1870s. Local boosters soon identified the land as being suitable for settlement. A 7974 acres (3227 ha) Paremata Block was vested in Wiremu (Wi) Pere (1837-1915) and William Rees (1836-1912) with the New Zealand Native Land Settlement Company taking over this and other lands in return for company scrip. The intention was that land would remain in trust for the Māori owners, investors would provide capital, and migrant farmers would be brought out from the UK. Wi Pere was Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki and Rongowhakaata and MP for Eastern Māori and William Rees was a lawyer and politician. The Paremata Block exemplified the many problems faced by the company. Matters remained unsettled as late as 1889 when MP James Carroll (1857-1926) presented a parliamentary petition on behalf of 36 Māori owners of the Paremata Block. By 1891 the company had over £240000 of liabilities and was eventually liquidated in 1905. Pere and Carroll were installed as Trustees. In 1919 the Government purchased 1000 acres (405 ha) from George M Reynolds at £17 per acre (payable half in cash half in war bonds) for a discharged soldier settlement. Subdivided into 14 farms totalling 790 acres (320 ha) some 115 applicants balloted for the first six farms in 1921. DG Robertson, the Crown Lands Ranger for Gisborne, proposed Paremata as the name of the soldier settlement. In 1950 the Crown held a ballot for Paremata Station described as a ‘pleasantly situated fat lamb farm of 426 acres’ (172 ha) which attracted the large number of 85 applicants.

info_origin: Ethnologist-Geologist Leslie Adkin (1888-1964) offered a literal translation for Pārengarenga Harbour as being a kind of legging made of flax leaves. Artist and writer Augustus Earle (1793-1838) spent eight months in the Bay of Islands and Hokianga in 1827-28. Sailing from England in 1831, he became an official artist on the HMS Beagle. In 1832 Earle published A Narrative of Nine Months Residence in New Zealand. This included a passage about his visit to Pārengarenga Harbour and pā: 'visited Parengarenga, a village lying round the base of a large conical hill, about three hundred feet [91m] high, with a fortification on the top, which gives it its name, pa signifying in their language a fortified place. Behind it lies a swamp, which is covered at high water, and which adds greatly to its security'. In 1895 government surveyor Thomas Kirkpatrick (1862-1936), who from 1892-95 was engaged in 100 miles (160 km) of triangulation surveys between Waipu and Cape Maria van Diemen, produced a topographical plan of Pārengarenga that included pā sites. In 1958 the New Zealand Geographic Board confirmed Pārengarenga Pā as a feature in a review of names shown on existing of topographic maps.

name: Pariroa Marae
info_origin: 'Taranaki, near Patea River. Lit. pari: cliff; roa: long. There is a tradition that in the mid-nineteenth century the chief Tupito boasted that if he were as long as the ‘long cliff’, he would be able to stride across the river and deal effectively with his enemies. Another attribution is to Tutangi Waionui and his wife Ngati, who in 1894 crossed from the Hukatere pa where they lived to the west side of the river, to show they were not afraid of the encroaching Pakeha. Their new home was hidden from the old one by the long ridge or cliff — the pari roa.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Passchendaele Ice Fall
info_ref: Evening Post, 14 November 1924, p. 2.; Heathcote, Tony, The British Admirals of the Fleet, 1734-1995: A Biographical Dictionary, Barnsley: Leo Cooper, 2002.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Correspondence, vol. 59, pp. 169-226.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 2011 (81).; Reed, A.W., Place Names of New Zealand, Rosedale: Penguin, 2010.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: Situated between Passchendaele Peak and Mount Destiny, this glacier is named after one of the First World War’s bloodiest confrontations. Fought between July and November 1917, the Passchendaele Campaign around the Belgian city of Ypres has come to symbolise the dreadful conditions that soldiers faced. In heavy rains that reduced the ground to mud, both sides carried out a series of offensives where gains were usually measured in yards rather than miles. British Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig has been criticised by many historians for continuing the battle even after all hope of a breakthrough had passed. Total Allied casualties numbered between 200,000 and 400,000; with the German forces sustaining similar loses. Passchendaele proved particularly costly for the New Zealand Division, which suffered more than 18,000 casualties. Although it did carry out some successful actions, such as the capture of Gravenstafel Spur, the Division also endured the bloodiest day in New Zealand’s military history. On 12 October 1917, at Bellevue Spur, 845 of its men were killed and over 2,700 wounded in an attack lasting only a few hours. name: Passchendaele Peak
info_ref: Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 14, p. 51.; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Minutes, 1938 (75).; New Zealand Geographic Board: Correspondence, vol. 24, p. 7.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: This feature is named after one of the bloodiest confrontations of the First World War. Fought between July and November 1917, the Passchendaele Campaign around the Belgian city of Ypres has come to symbolise the dreadful conditions that soldiers faced. In heavy rains that reduced the ground to mud, both sides carried out a series of offensives where gains were usually measured in yards rather than miles. British Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig has been criticised by many historians for continuing the battle even after all hope of a breakthrough had passed. Total Allied casualties numbered between 200,000 and 400,000; with the German forces sustaining similar loses. Passchendaele proved particularly costly for the New Zealand Division, which suffered more than 18,000 casualties. Although it did carry out some successful actions, such as the capture of Gravenstafel Spur, the Division also endured the bloodiest day in New Zealand’s military history. On 12 October 1917, at Bellevue Spur, 845 of its men were killed and over 2,700 wounded in an attack lasting only a few hours. Climbers originally referred to this feature as ‘Mount Passchendaele’. However, it was believed that confusion might arise with the feature of the same name (which later became known as Passchendaele Cliff) in the Cook District. After an investigation by the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand, the official name was assigned as Passchendaele Peak in 1938. The New Zealand Geographic Board then confirmed this decision in 1948.

name: Pātapu Spit
info_origin: Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui history: 'Pātapu was a seasonal fishing ground that local hapū of Pūtiki stayed at to gather kai. A flood breached the wall through Pātapu in the early 1900s. A steel girder and rock wall was built to close the breech which is still evident today. The locality in which Pātapu is located has always been known to local hapū and iwi as Wāhipuna. The Pātapu fishing kainga derived its name after the residential tupuna that lived in this area, his name was Koroheke Pātapu. His descendants, Epiha Pātapu (son) and Kurumate Pātapu (grandson), later occupied the land and utilised its plentiful resources. However, amongst travel across the Pūtikiwharanui-ā-Tamatea-pōkai-whenua and Whanganui region resulted in this area becoming land lost to the Whanganui Purchase 1840.'

name: Pātea
info_origin: ’Turi, captain of the Aotea canoe, who was one of the great name-givers among the early migrants from the Pacific Islands, reached the parara ki te uru (river facing the west). As he and his followers threw down their burdens (pātea) he named the place, in full, Pāteanui-a-Turi, lit. patea: burden or pack; nui: great; a: of; Turi. There are variations on this story, in one of which it was Turi’s men who exclaimed ‘Kua pātea tātau’ or ‘We’re relieved of our loads’. The ancient name of the river was Te Awa-nui-a-Taikehu, lit. te: the; awa: river; nui: great; a: of; Taikehu, who was a chief who lived nearby. The township was first named Carlyle after an early surveyor, but was changed to Patea in 1881.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Pati Tapu Bush Scenic Reserve
info_origin: The reserve was created after the areas were purchased from the McKenzie family by the Nature Heritage Fund in 2012. Pati Tapu Bush was part of Seventy Mile Bush, an historic forest that once stretched from Wairarapa to Hawke’s Bay. The area is made up of dense podocarp forest – tōtara, mataī and kahikatea, which reveal the density of that original huge forest tract. Pati Tapu Bush was the name always used locally and by the Department of Conservation who used it throughout the entire Nature Heritage Fund process. The reserve protects more than 100 native plant species, including dactylanthus – a rare botanic treasure that dwells on the forest floor. It is also important habitat for forest birds, such as kereu, tui and tomtit, and long-tailed bats.

info_origin: Locality by the river mouth and initially the residence of Niho, a significant Poutini Ngāi Tahu figure in the mid-1830s, until it was taken over by Ngāti Tama chief Te Pūoho who was leading a raid against Ngāi Tahu by travelling down the West Coast and across Haast Pass/Tioripatea to the eastern side of the island. Te Pūoho constructed a stockade at Pāturau River supposedly for prisoners he intended to capture. Brunner, Heaphy and Kehu crossed Pāturau River without incident in 1846, but when geologist Haast and his party reached the river in 1860 he recalled that 'Paturau, it was swollen, and gave us more trouble than any river we had previously crossed'. In 1897 the river was listed amongst those in which mining tailings could be discharged. The next year goldmining company Taitapu Estates moved its headquarters from Parkeston to Pāturau River. Never-the-less within three years it was selling its land. The area along the river was described as 'flat alluvial land' with a good deal of 'heavy timber suitable for milling. In affirming Haast's care in recording Māori names along the coast and lamenting Collingwood County Council's inexactness over spellings, in 1904 one newspaper correspondent asserted that Pāturau meant 'club - a hundred' or 'a hundred clubbed' and alluded to a battle or ambush in which many perished. Publisher Alexander Reed offers patu 'to strike' and rau 'many' as a literal translation.

name: Pearl Island

The name Chase Island had by this stage become unused, and in the interests of consistancy and safety, Pearl Island was approved as the name in 1969. name: Pēhiakura
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA270725; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: 'Pehiakura is a traditional Ngati Tamaoho village of long-standing, located between the bountiful dune lakes of Pokorua and Pehiakura on the high Tasman Sea coast of the Awhitu Peninsula, west of the Manukau Harbour. It was a strategic site with a strong defensive and lookout position at the adjacent Pakakina Pa, abundant food sources, and easily cultivatable soils. From this location, Pehiakura became a trading centre in north south and east-west trade in goods and ideas, and a place of innovation. The settlement was incapable of defence against the Ngapuhi musket raids of the 1820s, and along with other Waiohua hapu of the Manukau Harbour, the people moved south to the safety and peace of central Waikato for a decade. In 1835/36, Ngati Tamaoho returned to these lands and others on the peninsula, under the protective leadership of Te Wherowhero. Epiha Putini, (Te Rangitaahua Ngamuka, or Jabez Bunting) a young leader of Ngati Tamaoho, and adopted son of Wiremu Wetere Te Kauae, led a group of the hapu to re-establish the Pehiakura village putting into effect new learnings gleaned from contact with Wesleyan Missionaries around Whaingaroa, Kawhia and Waipa. Ligar reported in 1842 that an eight-foot high palisade, encircled the village, within which individual whare were fenced off for further protection and livestock control. Within the village, Ngati Tamaoho kept goats, pigs, horses, geese and fowl, as well as commercial cultivations of potatoes, pumpkins, maize, kumara and wheat. The Village had an impressive gate, a church measuring 20x40 ft and 25 ft high, with American-made chairs. Governor Hobson, himself donated ornate doors and windows. The school had a roll of about 100 students. Culturally, this historic record is an important measure of Ngati Tamaoho innovation, adoption of new ways and successful participation in the new society and economy. The adjacent lakes and West Coast surf beaches provided abundant fisheries, and were famous throughout Tamaki and Waikato, especially for their seasonal kahawai fishery. Exercising mana over access to these resources resulted in reciprocal rights from other hapu, such as to shark fisheries in the Waitemata/Hauraki Gulf, and to birding rights in the southern Waitakere Ranges; as well as to political and cultural alliances. Internecine skirmishes with neighbours, declining soil fertility, and a desire to be close to the educational, social, political and economic opportunities of the emerging Auckland caused Putini and his followers to abandon Pehiakura between 1846 and 1849, and move to a new marae on Ngati Tamaoho traditional land at Ihumatao, near Mangere. Captain Lloyd’s British forces destroyed the almost deserted remains of the village in 1863. After the Wars, the Crown confiscated all of Pehiakura. While some land was returned as compensation, that land was individualised by the courts, and never effectively came into the hands of Ngati Tamaoho owners. Ngati Tamaoho never returned to Pehiakura, but urupa and memories remain.'. 'Pehiakura is one of the most important Ngati Tamaoho sites, perhaps the most important during the period 1835-1849. During this time Pehiakura was a model settlement replete with a church and school as well pigs, fowl, wheat, maize, potatoes, kumara and fish from the numerous lakes in the area. The settlement was overseen by Ngati Tamaoho rangatira Te Rangitahua Ngamuka (baptised as Epiha Putini or Jabez Bunting), a chief of Ngati Tamaoho, respected by both his Maori and Pakeha. Though Ngati Tamaoho have not been able to return to this sacred land it remains one of the most significant sites in their history. Pehiakura is a testament to the peaceful resilience of the Tamaoho people and to their imagination and ingenuity in creating one of the finest settlements of its time. It is a symbol of the spirit of persistence and determination, the strength to overcome, which is inherent in the Tamaoho people to this day.' Information source: B Leonard, Ngati Tamaoho Sites of Significance, 74-88; D Armstrong, Ngati Tamaoho: Land and Politics 1840-1970, 165-175; D Armstrong, Ngati Tamaoho Environmental History DRAFT, 114-115.
info_description: The site of a traditional Ngāti Tamaoho village and kāinga, approximately 400m southeast of Pēhiakura Lake. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BB31 437834

name: Pelorus Bridge
info_origin: 'Pelorus River: Pelorus Sound: The brig HMS Pelorus, commanded by Lieutenant Chetwode, anchored at Oyster Cove, Port Underwood, on 22 August 1838 owing to the captain’s illness. Piloted by John Guard, the vessel entered Pelorus Sound on 1 September, and left New Zealand nine days later from Admiralty Bay. Maori name of the river and sound: Hoiere, or Te Hoiere, the name of a canoe in which early Maori arrived from the North Island. The whalers pronounced it Hosiery, a named which lingered on for some years. Te Hoiere may have been an alternative form of Te Hoihere: lit. te: the; hoihere: lacebark tree (Hoheria populnea). Another name was possibly Wakamarino, see Wakamarina River.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Pelorus Sound / Te Hoiere
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Ko Matua Hautere te Tangata, Ko Kaikai-a-waro te taniwha, Ko Te Hoiere te Waka, Ko Ngati Kuia te Iwi. Ngāti Kuia notes that Inskull in Place Names of Marlborough (p. 55) translates this name as a type of tree, and it was the name of the waka, captained by Matua Hautere, which brought Ngati Kuia to the area. It was guided here by their two kaitiaki, Kaikaiawaro and Ruamano. It forms a substantial part of Ngati Kuia identity, history and place of occupation. Ngāti Toa history: Te Hoire is the traditional name given to Pelorus Sound by Ngati Toa; the sound was renamed by Lieutenant P. Chetwode after the ship he commanded: the HMS Pelorus. Pelorus Sound was an area of concentrated Ngati Toa occupation and control; the iwi were considered to be the ‘direct owners’ of the Sound, as well as the connected valley and river, in the 1830s and 1840s. Ngati Toa first came into possession of the region following their conquest during 1829 and 1830. According to historian W.J. Elvy, at the time of Te Rauparaha’s raids, Ngati Kuia held the Pelorus Sounds and the valley. The invaders, however, “cleaned up the districts pretty thoroughly, reducing the survivors to slaves, or forcing them to hide in the mountainous fastness of the hinterland.” Hopai Pa located in Crail Bay, is one famous battle site at which Ngati Toa were victorious. Two Ngati Toa pa, the Canon point pa, and Te Akaroa pa, are located at Port Ligar. Another site of significance was the stream mouth at Clova Bay, which was given the name Totaranui. This was a landing site for waka that crossed from Omere on the Wellington South Coast, and was used extensively during the invasion and conquest of Te Tau Ihu.
info_description: A sound extending generally north-east, north, north-east from the mouth of Te Hoiere / Pelorus River approximately 2km north of Havelock, and including Hikapu Reach, Tawhitinui Reach and Waitata Reach, to Cook Strait. name: Peterman Glacier
info_origin: Named by the Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Kenneth Peterman of the National Geospatial-intelligence Agency (NGA). Mr. Peterman was instrumental in facilitating access to, and distribution of sub-meter commercial satellite imagery to the US Antarctic and Arctic science communities. Prior to Peterman's work, the principal sources of land-surface imagery were historical air photography and coarse resolution satellite imagery (typically at a resolution of 15m). Mr. Peterman developed paths for the near-real-time access to commercial high-resolution satellite imagery acquired for US Government use by NGA so that the Polar Geospatial Center (PGC) could exploit the data for emergency and safety purposes. His work also made it possible to collect repeat imagery of biological hotspots, areas of change in glaciers, ice sheets, and permafrost phenomena, as well as geologic outcrops, sea ice, and other areas of scientific interest. This imagery has provided new insight into time-dependent processes that were poorly understood or never before seen. The sub-meter imagery mosaic made from imagery provided by this program is used by PGC to improve the geographic coordinates in the ACAN place names database for the Antarctic. It has also been made available to international geographic naming authorities to for coordinate improvements. Mr. Peterman spent the 2012-2013 season at McMurdo Station, the Dry Valleys, and around the area of McMurdo Sound.

info_origin: The name's origin is with Pito One Pā near the foreshore. Mana whenua advise that the name refers to the pito [umbilical cord] being ceremonially buried in the one [sand/earth] as an expression of their ahi kā [occupation] and mana whenua status, it being a ‘symbolic tethering of a newborn to the land and their tūrangawaewae’. In early 19th century documentary references following the arrival of New Zealand Company settlers and colonisation the spellings 'Pitone' and 'Petoni' predominated, although there was also use of Pitoone, until the spelling 'Petone' stabilised in the late 1870s. This followed the suburb's origin in the 1877/78 ‘Town of Petone’ subdivisions, accompanied by the opening of 'Petone' railway station, post office and schools.

name: Picton
info_origin: ’Named by Governor Sir Thomas Gore Browne in October 1859, ten years after the town site had been surveyed, after Sir Thomas Picton. A commander under the Duke of Wellington in the Peninsular War, Picton achieved fame as the hero of Badajoz; he was killed in the Battle of Waterloo. Māori name: Waitohi. It may have been a stream where the waitohi baptismal rite was performed. It may be, in full, Te Wera-o-Waitohi: lit. te: the; wera: burning; o: of; Waitohi. Waitohi, the sister of Te Rauparaha, is reputed to have been burned to death in a scrub fire. Or it may have been the clearing burnt by Waitohi to make a plantation. An early name was also Urukakea: lit. uru: head; kakea: festered; subsequently Te Rauparaha changed the name to Waitohi. Picton had a succession of European names as well. In 1832 Captain William Steine of the barque William IV named it Horne Bay, after the ship’s owners. In 1847 the name became Newton Bay; Cromwell and Beaconsfield were other early appellations. In searching for a definitive name, Francis Dillon Bell proposed Raleigh after Sir Walter Raleigh, while William Fox supported Wakefield after Captain Arthur Wakefield, until Gore Browne settled the matter.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Pigeon Bay
info_origin: 'Canterbury, Banks Peninsula, 22 km from Little River. So named by whalers because the forest at the bay was alive with kereru or wood pigeons. Several other names such as Pigeon Bush (near Featherston), Pigeon Flat and Pigeon Hill (near Dunedin), Pigeon Island (Lake Wakatipu), and Pigeon Valley (near Wakefield) were all given for similar reasons. Maori name: Whakaroa, lit. long bay. Dr Edward Shortland gave it as Wakaoroi, which if correct would be the South Island equivalent of Whanga-o-roi, meaning Bay of fern-root, or of a person named Roi.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Named for the abundance of kererū (Hemiphaga novaeseelandiae) – native pigeons in the vicinity, Pigeon Bush Station, a property of 903 acres (365 ha), was taken up by Thomas Roberts in 1858. Roberts sold out unexpectedly in 1859 and returned to Great Britain. The farm included 20 acres (8 ha) of tōtara and beech forest. The property subsequently passed to William Lancaster Lucena. name: Pigroot Hill
info_origin: The state highway and creek in close proximity to the hill are also named Pigroot. 'Otago, the old goldfields route from Palmerston to the diggings. According to local historians the name originated on an occasion when two wagons were stuck on the road. One wagoner said to the other, ‘What does this remind you of?’, the reply being, ‘A bloody pigroot.’ Another explanation was that the name was given because of the many wild pigs on the Kakanui Range. Diana and Jeremy Pope suggest that the name derives from Pigroot Hill, a prominence surveyed in 1857 by J.T. Thomson and named for a huge boar that rubbed noses with his horse. Maori name of the saddle: Ohinemaru.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Pirinoa
info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5104718 {Return of Native Reserves. 1862. Appendicies to the Journals of the House of Representatives, E10; Scholefield, Guy H. 1940. A Dictionary of New Zealand Biography. New Zealand: Department of Internal Affairs; [Local and General. 1876. Wairarapa Standard, 12 September, Page 2](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WAIST18760912.2.8); Wairarapa ki Tararua Report (2010) Wai 863. Waitangi Tribunal, Wellington; NZGB Correspondence XXXIII/88}
info_origin: An original Māori name translated as meaning ‘cliffs with clinging creeper’. This kāinga or village was adjacent to local natural resources, including forest land but particularly tuna (eels). The land was part of Chief Land Purchase Commissioner Donald McLean’s much larger East Side of Lake Block 1 Tūranganui purchase of 1853. Pirinoa at 485 acres (196 ha) was to be one of eight reserves set aside as part of the purchase, but this was not ratified until a decade later. Richard Barton (1790-1866), formerly estate manager for the Duke of Sunderland, arrived in Wellington on the Oriental in 1840 and initially farmed in the Hutt Valley. In 1843 he accompanied New Zealand Company surveyor Samuel Brees, Hugh and John Cameron, Taringa Kuri (Te Kāeaea) and four unnamed Māori guides plus Edward Cheltham into the Wairarapa. Barton then took up land known as the Pirinoa Run, selling the 2617 acre (1059 ha) property in 1876r to move to the Fernside Estate. One of the largest Māori sheep runs was Whatarangi station at Pirinoa which ran over 20000 sheep and 500 cattle between 1894 and 1919.

name: Piwhane / Spirits Bay
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/1017; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Te Hiku Forum history: This has great significance as it is where Tōhē’s spirit was caught at the end of the spiritual pathway. Mutu Kapa (kaumatua of Whanau Pani hapu of Aupouri) stated, in evidence to the Maori Land Court in the 1957 Ninety Mile Beach case, the ancestor Tōhē and his servant came from Kapowairua to look for Tōhē’s daughter Raninikura. Tōhē’s grandfather, Ngaruru, advised him not to go lest Tōhē met his death. Tōhē replied “if I die you are to catch my spirit”. Thus, Tōhē gave that place the name Kapo Wairua (extract from Northern Minute Book Volume 85, p. 718, 12 November 1957). Stokes also tells the story of Tōhē saying “te mea ma koutou he kapo mai taku wairua (if I should die, catch my spirit and stop it getting to Te Rerenga Wairua)” this giving the place name Kapowairua (Stokes, pp. 23-24). Kapowairua is noted as papakainga in the evidence of Reverend Marsden, Wai 45, Document A7, “Te Mana O Te Hiku O Te Ika”, December 1986, p.3. According to the Bateman New Zealand Historical Atlas Ko Papatuanuku e Takoto Nei, Malcolm Mckinnon (ed), Auckland, 1997, plate 18, when Tōhē decided to journey to see Ranini-kura, his people did not wish him to go. His response was: Whakarua e te hau, e tae ate karo. Whakarua I taku tamahine, e kore a taea to karo. Taea Hokianga, a hea, a hea. Ko ta koukou e kapo ake ai, Ko taku wairua. I can shelter from the wind. But not from the longing for my daughter. I shall venture as far as Hokianga and beyond. All that you shall possess, Is my spirit. Richard Taylor drew sketches labelled Kapowairua when he visited the area in 1841. These are held in the Alexander Turnbull Library. Tuinui Sylva gave evidence at the Waitangi Tribunal hearings the Reweri Hongi was the paramount chief at Kapowairua. After Rewiei, Murupaenga became the chief at Kapowairua. Kapowairua was a kainga into the 1940s. Te Paraha Ratahi (who had been in Rewiri Hongi’s army), had told Tuinui Sylva that Ngāti Kuri would bring their captured enemies back to a tree at Kapowairua to hang them. The name referred to what they would say in battle ‘kapohia mai tena, grabbing the spirits of their enemies and taking them to that tree’. (submission of Tuini Sylva, Wai 45, F33). Wiremu Paraone told the Waitangi Tribunal that ‘on return from a trip to North Cape to his pā at Maunga piko, Tōhē was told that his daughter Raninikura had been stolen. Concerned, Tōhē decided to go and find her. The tribe’s kaumatua feared for his safety as he was getting on in age. To this he replied “Te mea ma koutou he kap mai taku wairua” hence Kapowairua is formerly Piwhane’ (evidence of Wiremu Paraone, Wai 45, Doc C13, p.2). Dorothy Urlich Clother (The Tribes of Muriwhenua:Their Origins and Stories, Auckland University Press, 2002, p. 24.) states that “The name Kapwairua [Tōhē] gave to the place between Te Reinga and Murimotu Island, and area now commonly referred to as Spirits Bay and of great spiritual significance.” Kapowairua is also noted in a map in The Muriwhenua Report (Figure 6, p. 31 and figure 9, p .37).
info_description: A coastal bay located at the northern extremity of New Zealand between Cape Reinga / Te Rerenga Wairua and Ngataea / Hooper Point. Feature shown on: NZMS260 M02 N02 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-AT24 837894
info_note: Ngāti Kuri, Te Aupouri, NgāiTakoto and Te Rarawa are four of the iwi which make up Te Hiku Forum. These four iwi have shared Treaty settlement redress including this geographic name. Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "where Tōhē told his grandfather "If I should die, catch my spirit and stop it getting to Te Rerenga Wairua""

info_origin: Plimmerton was named after Mr John Plimmer (1812 – 1905) a Director and principal shareholder of the Wellington Manawatu Railway Company and a Wellington businessman. name: Poor Knights Islands
info_origin: ’Named by Captain James Cook on 25 November 1769, possibly in reference to a popular English dish at the time of Cook’s voyages. Poor Knights pudding consisted of hunks of bread dipped in egg and fried — and Cook, in one of his rare moments of imagination, may have used it for these islands, ‘brown, upstanding and rocky’. Māori name: Tawhiti Rahi, also the name for the largest island; the other ‘Knights’ in order of size are Aorangi, Motukapiti, Aorangaia and Archway.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEU0REZDMERCNjBGRUFBNjU1ODU)

name: Poor Knights Islands Marine Reserve
info_description: The Poor Knights Islands are the remains of a group of ancient volcanoes. Beneath the waves these volcanoes have been hollowed and shaped by the ocean into a web of caves, tunnels and cliffs which Jacques Cousteau rated as one of the top ten dives in the world. Because of their incredible form and biodiversity, the sea surrounding the islands has been a marine reserve since 1981. It extends to 800 m around the islands. The Poor Knights Islands are located 22 km off the east coast of Northland.

name: Pōrangahau
info_origin: Pōrangahau was a fierce warrior who was known for his unique style of carrying and attacking with his taiaha. He wielded it behind his body, which was an identifying factor when he was killed. Pōrangahau had killed the husband of Tuteihunga and came here for refuge after. Kahukuranui asked to marry Tuteihunga, and her condition to marry was that he avenge her husband's murder by killing Pōrangahau, and so he did. His taiaha stance was the confirming factor that Pōrangahau had been killed.
info_description: Area around Pōrangahau (locality). Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BM38 033344

info_origin: The inlets of Porirua Harbour have been inhabited since about 1450 CE. The name Porirua, considered a corruption of Pari-rua, has been translated as 'the tide sweeping up both reaches' or pari 'flowing of the tide' and rua meaning 'two'. The harbour was an important source of kai moana. Various people have resided here across the centuries including Ngāi Tara, Ngāti Kahungunu, then Ngāti Ira who, in turn, were displaced in the 1820s by Ngāti Toa. In 1846 Governor George Grey considered this area of strategic significance since it was the junction of roads leading into the Wellington district. Grey was concerned about a rumoured attack on Wellington, so seized Ngāti Toa leader Te Rauparaha from his pā near Porirua and held him captive for two years. From the 1860s Porirua was a parliamentary electorate. After 1877 it was part of Hutt County. By 1945 Porirua was identified as a site for urban expansion with available and reasonably priced land, rail links, and a projected motorway connection to Wellington City. Porirua became a borough in 1962 and attained city status in 1965 when it reached 20000 inhabitants.

info_origin: Altering an existing recorded name. Replacing Porirua City (recorded name). According to Best Hone Wairere of Whanganui informed him that Porirua Harbour was so named from the fact that it possesses two arms or channels quoting the following: “ko Porirua mo te ruanga o nga moana te take, koia a Porirua”. The harbour is one of the earliest permanent settlements of the region by the Ngāi Tara peoples. Adkin p68 cites Henry Stowell (Hare Hongi) as alluding to the correct form of the name being Pari-rua. Literal descriptions include "pori" as a fold in the skin or people dependants, "rua" meaning two.

name: Porters Pass
info_origin: 'Porter Heights skifield: Porters Valley: Named after the three Porter brothers who owned the Castle Hill station. The name was given in 1858. name: Possession Islands
info_origin: The group was named by Ross in commemoration of the planting of the British flag and taking possession in the name of the British Sovereign on 12 January 1841. He landed on a small rocky beach on Possession Island. Other landings have been made by Borchgrevink in 1895 and 1899, and by Colbeck in 1903. Bull named the individual islands in 1895. Note, Henryk Bull tentatively applied the name Svend Foyn to Ross' Possession Island, noting he was unsure which it was, resulting in longstanding confusion and the two names being swapped in many records, including the Provisional Gazetteer of the Ross Dependency, 1958. The nomenclature of the Possession Islands was resolved in official records in correspondence between the Board and US-ACAN in 1962.
info_description: A group of nine islands and islets lying in the western part of the Ross Sea, about 8-9km off the northeastern coast of Victoria Land, southeast of Cape McCormick. The group extends north to south a distance of about 12km and they vary in size from 2.5km in length to mere pillars of rock. The northwestern island, Possession Island, is approximately 2.4km long, and is low and bare. Foyn Island, the middle large island is 2km long with high with vertical sides, rising to ~175m at St Marie Peak at its north, and the southernmost island is Heftye Island. name: Pouākai
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA383591. Feature shown on: NZMS260 P20 Edition 1 1984
info_origin: Taranaki Tūpuna written and oral history: 'Pouākai preceded the arrival of Taranaki Maunga and stood as a mountain range alongside other prominent features of the time. The range was also known as Ruatawhito (Pouākai). The original inhabitants were the Kāhui Pou. The Kāhui Pou established the Pou (embedded knowledge systems) associated with harvesting, preparation and cultivation of food on the slopes of both the Kaitake and Pouākai ranges. They held mana over the lands and gave meaning to the names Pouākai (the pillar or source of food) and Kaitake (the source or abundance of food able to be grown on its slopes) known today.'
info_description: A peak at 1400m being the highest peak in Pouākai Range on the northwestern slopes of Taranaki Maunga. NZTopo50-BJ29 875563.

name: Pouhōkio Stream
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA221999; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Heretaunga Tamatea history: ‘The Pouhōkio stream flows north through the Te Āpiti Valley, and reaches the sea at its mouth where it was called was Kaiwhakatōrea (the place of the oyster catcher bird). It has had many causes across the Waimārama flats, at one stage joining the Waingōngoro. Variant spellings on maps for Pouhōkio are Puhoia and Puhokio and sometimes this stream has been confused for the Waingōngoro Stream. Pouhōkio was named after a woman who was extremely skilled with weaponry and after an experience where she had to fight (naked) for her and her siblings lives, she was ritually blessed in this river taking her from the life of a prized high born woman destined for a cloistered life and a political marriage to that of a seasoned warrior of her Rangitāne people.’
info_description: A stream that flows for approximately 11.5km from its source south of Waimarama into the sea approximately 18km southeast of Havelock North. NZTopo50-BL39 382778 to 419856
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "for a skilled warrior woman who was ritually blessed in this stream after having to fight naked"

name: Poukawa
info_origin: 'Poukawa, Lake: lit. pou: post or pole; kawa: lean. Two chiefs lived by the lake. The lesser chief, Te Rangihirawea, asked to agree that fishing boundaries be defined; the other chief, Te Rangikawhiua, felt insulted and refused. The lesser chief erected a pole to indicate his portion of the lake, placing it in command of the more favourable part of the fishing ground, thus leaving the tuna kawa (lean eels) to his opponent. From this incident, which led to severe fighting, the lake gained its name.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Poutākoro Head
info_origin: The name was consistently misspelled on records throughout history as 'Putakolo Head' and following a commissioned research report and the support of Te Rūnanga o Koukourārata and Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu, the Minister for Land Information confirmed the NZGB's decision to assign the name. Putakoto could have many meanings. Literally (from Williams) Puta means an opening, hole or perforation; move from one place to another; pass through; come; escape, survive; appear, come into sight; be born. Literally (from Williams) Koto means loathing, averse; small, of no account; pull up; sob or make low sound. ‘Place-names of Banks Peninsula: A Topographical History’ by Johannes Carl Andersen, published in 1927, records this name as Putakolo Head describing: 'It is spelt Puta-Kolo on the F.C.B.P. [French chart of Banks Peninsula, prepared in 1844-45 by officers of Le Rhin], and Poutokoro on M.M. [Mantel, on map numbered 140 (red) in Christchurch Land Office]. It is an instance of the confusion of spelling caused by the ‘r’ sound in Māori, which at times approached the sound of ‘l’.'

name: Pouto
info_origin: 'Northland, 64 km from Dargaville. Lit. To cut off. The locality is known as Kaipara Heads, and Pouto was the name of the Kaipara North Head, Okaoka the South Head. The story goes that Rongomai died and his children left the settlement of Taporapora on the Mahuhu waka. Those left at Taporapora felt resentment at the abandonment and by magic raised a storm that battered the canoe. But the effects were most severe for the perpetrators, as the waves cut off the peninsula and formed an island that then slipped into the sea, taking everything with it. The disaster was known as Taraitanga (Shaving off).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: 'Captain James Cook was not enamoured of the district. Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Powder Flask Peak
info_origin: Mr McGahan, N P Ranger Makarora, suggested a change in the position of Mt Cameron based on the finding of Charles Cameron's powder flask found at this position by T N Brodrick in 1881. Change of position rejected by Geographic Board and above name substituted. Refer "Māori and Pakeha in North Otago" (Stevenson) p51 for further info.; 'Charles Cameron’s powder flask was found at this position west of Haast Pass in 1881; Cameron had buried his flask here, inscribed with the date, to mark his purported crossing of the pass in January 1863. In February 1863 Cameron wrote to an Otago newspaper that he had crossed to the coast in the previous month, using an old Māori route. Julius von Haast reached the coast nine days after the newspaper report, and his party hotly and publicly disputed who had been first to the pass. ‘All Mr. Cameron has done has been to crawl about the ranges between Lake Wanaka and Hawea’, claimed one of von Haast’s men. The pass was named in von Haast’s honour; later research suggests that Cameron did indeed get there first.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki history: Pōhaturoa (also known by the dialectic variant of Pōwhaturoa) refers to the coastal settlements of Ngāi Tai extending between the Waipārā Creek and the Ōhinerangi stone, known today as ‘Maraetai Beach’. Pōhaturoa is also identified among the lands gifted by Te Uri-o-Te-Ao hapū of Ngāti Tai/Te Wai-o-Hua to the descendants of Te Raukohekohe and Te Whataatao. The name, Pōhaturoa (or Pōwhaturoa), refers to the large stones that are a feature of the beach, including the boulder called Ōhinerangi. Ngāi Tai occupied this important coastal settlement until the 1860s.

name: Prince of Wales

Two mining companies, the Prince of Wales Company and the Alexandra Quartz Mining Company (cf Princess Alexandra of Denmark 1901-1910, Princess of Wales) worked the reef. Survey plan SO 1531 (1866) also shows a Prince of Wales Creek and Alexandra Creek flowing down from this peak.

name: Puetou
info_origin: Puetou is the name of the pā nohonga which is situated at the source of the Puetou Stream today known as Hururu Stream. It is an important feature strongly related to Tapuika hapu Ngati Pahiko and Ngati More, as a nohonga used for the procurement of stone termed pue. In earlier days this area was used as a rua keri kōhatu a stone quarry for the manufacturing of stone implements. During this process the stone quarried would be shaped roughly then grounded smooth using sandstone [hoanga kōhatu]. The action of dripping the stone into water is termed tou. These tools were predominately used in the construction of caves for the purpose of storing crops during the winter periods. In latter times these caves were made larger to provide a safe haven for women and children during times of inter tribal warfare. During the Native Land Court hearings ref: Ngati Pahiko, Tapuika chiefs spoke of Puetou being a southern eastern boundary that was occupied by Tapuika whanau up to the turn of the 19th century and as being located on the old walking track from Te Kaharoa o Ruangutu to Te Waerenga to Kaikaitahuna, therefore providing access to Lake Rotorua.

name: Puhi Kai Iti / Cook Landing National Historic Reserve
info_origin: Puhi Kai Iti was one the puhi (feathered streamers) from the taurapa (sternpost) of the great ocean waka Te Ikaroa-ā-Rauru. Its navigator Māia Poroaki laid the puhi to rest on the shore and built a whare wānanga school on top of it to teach knowledge brought from Hawaiki. The reserve is just north of the site where Lieutenant James Cook came ashore in 1769 with crew from HMB Endeavour. This was the first onshore contact between Europeans and Māori.

name: Puhinui
info_origin: 'Puhinui: Auckland, near Papatoetoe. Puhinui Creek: Lit. puhi: plume at the bow of a war canoe; nui: large. In a tale recounted in a number of local histories, the canoe Puhinui was concealed in a creek by a Hauraki party, which was avenging an ambush attack by their ostensible hosts, the Waiohua. The latter discovered the canoe because of the conspicuous plumes on its prow. But the discoverers were so occupied by their find that they were surprised by the owners of the canoe and defeated at a battle known as Waipuhinui. A.E. Tonson’s Old Manukau tells the full story. Tonson also refers to another theory that puhi was a large variety of eel, with nui having its usual meaning of big. He adds that English immigrants were astounded at the size of the eels in the creek. When a railway station was placed between Papatoetoe and Wiri, it was suggested that it be named Cambria, but this was rejected in favour of Puhinui.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Pukaha / Mount Bruce
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-13/839; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Rangitāne o Wairarapa and Rangitāne o Tamaki Nui-ā-Rua history: The name Pukaha was gained via Rangitāne Matekite (Barbara Kopua) and tohunga (Jim Rimene) who conversed with the matua tipuna of this area on site. It was the old people that informed us of this name back in the mid-1990’s. Consequently, this name was suggested to DOC and the National Wildlife Trust and formally adopted to the Visitor Centre. The name refers to the strong winds that are persistent in this area. There is a misconception that the name is Pukahu which refers to the Hawk (Kahu) and its’ nest (Pu). This area was a dense podocarp forest with an impenetrable canopy. As such Hawk are not endemic to this type of terrain preferring to hunt in more open grassy plains where they can sight their pray. Before her death, Aunty Barbara was asked if it would be appropriate for us to alter the name of one of the maunga to reflect the original name Pukaha. She said that this would be a great gesture to the old people. Given the choice she choose [sic] that we alter the name Mt Bruce No 2 [Bruces Hill] which is within the Scenic Reserve. ; 'Pukaha refers to the strong winds that are persistent in this area. The English name is most likely after Alexander Bruce, a settler who came here from the Kopuarangi area.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Pūkākā / Marsland Hill
info_ref: Objective ID: A1263678; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Te Atiawa statement: The hill was a pā site known as Pukaka. It was named Pukaka because the trees were inhabited by parrots. As a pā site, it was established by Taranaki Iwi but finished and occupied by Te Atiawa. It was a defensive pā, and many other smaller pā sites surrounded Pukaka. Te Atiawa would move to Pukaka in times of trouble. Pukaka was abandoned during the Waikato raids of the late 1820s when Te Atiawa moved to Otaki. In the 1830s, many Te Atiawa migrated to Waikanae, Wellington and Te Tau Ihu. In the early 1850s, the top 12 metres was taken off the hill and the site was leveled. It became a military barracks and stockade for the British army and was used during the 1860s Land Wars. Pukaka pā is of cultural and historical significance given that it was an ancient Te Atiawa pā site. Its use as a military barrack and stockade during the land wars is a significant source of grievance that continues today given that its traditional name has been replaced.

info_origin: Ngati Rarua records that this was the first landing place of the Ngati Rarua taua in the fight for Wairau. name: Pukeahurangi / Jumbo
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-13/839; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Rangitāne o Wairarapa and Rangitāne o Tamaki nui a Rua history: 'Pukeamoamo and Pukeahurangi are said to have been named by the Rangitāne ancestor Hinetearorangi. The landmarks linked her to her ancestors, as she would gaze from Tirohanga pa (north of Masterton) and use the twin peaks Pukeamohau and Pukeahurangi to guide her line of sight towards Kapiti Island. These are the traditional names of the twin peaks that provide the basis of the name ‘Tararua’. Pukeahurangi means ‘high up’ or ‘elevated’ and Pukeamoamo refers to the pou of the wharenui on which the ancestors are carved.' Origin of the name Jumbo: A working manuscript found in LINZ file system refers to the origin of the name Jumbo in a letter from FC Brockett to the Surveyor-General, dated 26 July 1926: “We use it because from the Blue Range, which is traversed by the track to the foot of the Mitre, this peak [Jumbo] bears a strong resemblance to the head and ears of an elephant seen from behind”.
