name: Pukeamoamo / Mitre
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-13/839; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Rangitāne o Wairarapa and Rangitāne o Tamaki nui a Rua history: 'Pukeamoamo and Pukeahurangi are said to have been named by the Rangitāne ancestor Hinetearorangi. The landmarks linked her to her ancestors, as she would gaze from Tirohanga pa (north of Masterton) and use the twin peaks Pukeamohau and Pukeahurangi to guide her line of sight towards Kapiti Island. These are the traditional names of the twin peaks that provide the basis of the name ‘Tararua’. Pukeahurangi means ‘high up’ or ‘elevated’ and Pukeamoamo refers to the pou of the wharenui on which the ancestors are carved.' Origin of the name Mitre: In describing the history of Tararua Forest Park, the Department of Conservation states that ‘Mitre’ was named by Europeans “because its shape resembled that of a bishop’s mitre”.

name: Pukehiki
info_origin: 'Known to early European settlers as Sandymount from at least as early as 1876, when the first post office was opened. Robin Startup records that in May 1904 another post office called Sandymount opened at the local school, so a new name had to be found for the old Sandymount. After considering The Camp (the then name of nearby Larnach Castle), the postal authorities in Dunedin proposed Pukehiwi: lit. puke: hill; hiwi: ridge, which was approved in Wellington but in the form Pukehiki. It is not known whether this was a misreading of the handwritten name sent from Dunedin, or a recognition that Pukehiki was in fact the Maori version of Sandymount. Pukehiki itself, on the slopes of Peggy’s Hill, is not sandy.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Translates literally as puke: hill and kohe an abbreviation of Kokekohe, a native tree (Dysoxylum spectabile). The name was adopted by European settlers in this heavily forested area on their arrival in 1856. A temporary Presbyterian church was constructed here in 1861 and replaced by a permanent structure in 1863, one of the first in South Auckland. Surrounded by a hastily erected associated stockade, notable for the logs being laid horizontally rather than vertically, this was the scene of fighting on 14 September 1863 in the New Zealand Wars. Ten military settlers from the locally raised Forest Rifle Volunteers and nine special constables under the command of Sergeant Perry garrisoned the stockade with reinforcements arriving during the day. They were attacked by a war party mainly comprising Ngāti Maniapoto and some Upper Waikato Māori and Ngāti Pou with some 40 perishing during the engagement. In 1920 Edith Statham (1853-1951), Inspector of Old Soldiers' Graves for the Department of Internal Affairs unsuccessfully sought a memorial to the six Māori buried in the churchyard. It wasn't until 1929, a year after her retirement, that a memorial boulder was unveiled along with another plaque to the defenders which was located inside the church. In later accounts the fighting is typically referred to as being at Pukekohe East, however, until 1865 the settlement was known simply as Pukekohe. At this point, the now expanding Pukekohe West became known as Pukekohe with the former Pukekohe becoming Pukekohe East. This was further entrenched by the creation of a Pukekohe East Highway Board in 1865. A Pukekohe East postmaster was appointed in January 1870 with twice weekly mail services. The original Highway Board boundaries were a source of local dispute and were redrawn in 1872.

name: Pukeone / Mount Campbell
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Te Atiawa notes that Pukeone (meaning sandy hill) is where Te Atiawa carried the sand to the top of the hill to signal to whanau. The brown area today marks where the fires used to be. Pukeone is highly significant to Te Atiawa. Ngati Rarua history: there is korero regarding the origins of the name Pukeone and one theory advances that it is a tupuna name from early times perhaps belonging to one of Rakaihautu’s party. The translation of Sand Hill however can be related to the practice of carrying sand to the summit of the maunga where signal fires were lit to tell of special occasions. The fires burning on top of Pukeone could be seen as far as away as Whakapuaka. A fire was lit on Pukeone following Wakefield’s acceptance of Nelson as a settlement site.

name: Puketapu
info_origin: 'Otago, a hill near Palmerston. Named after a female slave. On one account she was a slave of Rakaihautu of the Araiteuru canoe, who failed to return to the canoe before dawn and was turned into a hall. On another account, Puketapu was the wife of Pakihiwitahi (see Pakihiwitahi Range). She collected firewood, probably without propitiating the atua, going as far south as Owaka bush and gathering two bundles of firewood, one of which she bound with flax and the other with toetoe leaves. Being insecurely fastened, portions of the load fell off at Kaitangata, Henley, Dunedin, Waitati, Puketiraki, and the remainder at Goodwood. Puketapu was then changed into the hill that bears her name. On it can be seen the straps of her bundles in two gullies, one of flax and the other of toetoe. The sticks she dropped during her return journey took root and formed patches of bush, the one at Dunedin being the origin of the trees in the Town Belt. See also Puketapu, Te Urewera National Park.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={2dd8d314-f6b6-e411-a1da-0050569755f4})

info_origin: Named in association with a nearby pā. Literally translated as ‘sacred hill’, the name recalls an occasion in the aftermath of a battle at the hill-top pā when Tūtaekurī River ran red with blood. Puketapu was the site of fighting between Ngāti Raukawa and Ngāti Kahungunu for regional dominance in the early 19th century. European farmer Alexander Alexander (? - 1873) initially took up 170 acres (69 ha) of fern covered land at Puketapu in 1859, although the initial town was a military encampment intended to protect the settler population. A post office was opened in 1860. The Armed Constabulary also worked on road construction. In 1866 approximately 100 Hauhau gathered opposite Puketapu prior to their clashing with Napier militia and their Māori allies at Omarunui. Puketapu locality was settled by Ngāti Hinepare who had earlier resided at Moteo particularly after the sale of the Omaranui Block in 1869. Puketapu on the Napier to inland coach road by Tutaekuri River was a convenient stopping place for watering stock, with local settler John Heslop (1812?-94) advertising private accommodation from 1860. He later sold the land for the first school established in 1864.

info_origin: Pūkio is the name of the name of the original Māori land block. name: Pūkorokoro / Miranda
info_origin: Pūkorokoro is locally translated as “the long throated purse net”, which describes the entrance to Pukorokoro Stream and regular fishing that occurred in the area. In mid 1863 the Crown sent HMS Miranda as part of a naval blockade to suppress rebel forces. HMS Miranda tried to land soliders at the well-populated village of Pūkorokoro based on information that Kīngitanga forces might be there. Waka, whare and surrounding bush were destroyed and a large number of Ngāti Pāoa people were killed. Crown forces later constructed a redoubt which was named Miranda after the ship. This name was subsequently used for the town and surrounding area.
info_description: A populated place on the south-western shore of the Firth of Thames approximately 20km west south-west of Thames. Alteration from Miranda (recorded name). Feature shown on: NZMS260 S12 Edition 2 1994; Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BB34 054820

name: Pupu Springs
info_origin: Recognised as correct name for springs instead of "Waikoropupu". A W Reids Place names of New Zealand gives the name "Wai-ngaro-pupu" meaning "up gushing hidden waters". W A Taylor's "Lore and History of the S I Māori" gives the name"Wai-gnuru-pu Springs", meaning "the place of the rumbling water"; 'The full name is Waingaropupu: Lit. up-gushing hidden water. It seems most likely that the original Maori name was Waikaremumu, which can be translated as Boisterous wind ruffling the water. It was shortened by Pakeha to Mumu and then distorted to Bubu. For this reason an attempt to retransliterate produced Pupu, with Waikoropupu as an attempt to get back to the full name.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_ref: Corres III pp 139, LXVI, LXVII; File 222605 3 v/18 pp 78, 79, 81, 82, GS-N15-07-32
info_origin: Mr Tama Parata was quoted as saying "the word should be spelt Purakaunui, 'pu' meaning heap of anything, 'rakau', wood, and 'nui', plenty. A tribal fight took place on the peninsula at Bluecliffs close by. Many of the combatants were drowned or slain. Next morning the bodies were piled up like a heap of wood, and so the spot was named.". Spelling alteration from Purakaunui (28/05/1992 78:1514). Quoted from The Evening Star, 22 May 1902. Also mentioned in "Place Names and Early History of Otago and Southland", by W H Sherwood Roberts and "Māori Place Names of Otago", by H Beattie, which refers to "Purakaunui (great heap of wood)".; 'Purakaunui Bay: Purakaunui River: Pūrākaunui: Lit. purakau: myth; nui: big. Otago, 20 km from Dunedin. Pūrākaunui Bay: Pūrākaunui River: lit. pū: heap; rakāu: firewood; nui: large. After the capture of a pa on Goat Island/Rakiriri, the inhabitants were slaughtered and the bodies piled up like logs of firewood.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: The site of a coastal pā with good natural defenses situated on a small plateau. In archeological terms this was a 'a late occupation' pā of the early 19th century. With associated pā sites it comprises the 'important earthwork site' in Golden Bay. The name Purāmahoi was adopted by farmers further inland in the 1850s and coastal steamers in the 1860s that plied from Collingwood to Motueka, Tōtaranui, Motupipi and Puramāhoi. Quartz reefs were discovered in 1891 with the Hidden Treasure Mine, a largely Auckland syndicate, starting its first crushing in 1904. A supposed platinum discovery was announced in 1898. Tests undertaken by the Government Analyst, William Skey (1835-1900), found no platinum in the samples provided. Miss Jeannie Walker operated the Purāmahoi Post Office when it opened in 1897, one of the early group of women post office staff. Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen considered Purāmahoi to be an instance of a 'doubtful spelling' and believed the correct spelling should be Puremāhaia after the river of this name that flows through the area.

info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: 'Purapura was a large Ngati Tamaoho settlement south of Waiuku. The village was at the northern most navigable point along the Awaroa River, forming part of the Awaroa portage, an important route of travel between the Waikato and the Manukau. During the late 18th and early 19th century the village was overseen by Ngati Tamaoho rangatira Te Tuhi, the father of Epiha Putini. It was home to the Maungaunga hapu of Ngati Tamaoho, a group closely associated with the Waikato iwi. After Te Tuhi’s death (likely to have been in the late 1810s or early 1820s), his brother and Putini’s adoptive father Wiremu Wetere Te Kauae took control of the settlement until it was eventually sold. With the departure of Putini from the Awhitu Peninsula and his early death, his plans for the redevelopment of Purapura lapsed.'. Information Source - B Leonard, Ngati Tamaoho Sites of Significance, 90-91; D Armstrong, Ngati Tamaoho: Land and Politics 1840-1970, 386-403.

info_origin: Pureora takes its name from Pureora State Forest which in turn was taken from the 1275m hill with the original Māori name of Te Pureora-o-Kahu. The State Forest Service (New Zealand Forest Service 1949-87) managed the forest area as Pureora State Forest No. 96. In 1945 the Forest Service announced that it planned to construct 12 staff dwellings and community amenities in indigenous forest as it opened the area to logging. In organising construction of the village, Director of Forests Alex Entrican (1898-1966) referred to it as Pureora State Forest Village. The government architects at the Ministry of Works, who designed the buildings, tended to favour Pureora Forest, while Work’s engineers called it Pureora Logging Village and later settled on Pureora Village. By late 1947 the State Forest Service in-house correspondence also used Pureora Village. When the New Zealand Post Office opened a branch in 1945 the village was known as Pureora Forest. By 1957 Edward Dollimore (1903-73) who compiled The New Zealand Guide noted that Pureora was now favoured over Pureora Forest. Containing unlogged podocarp forests, Pureora was the site of a successful environmentalist tree sitting protest in January 1978 in support of the Native Forest Action Council’s demands that the government end logging of Pureora and other indigenous forests.

info_origin: Reed: Lit. a sacred rite performed for the recovery of the sick. Rakataura of Tainui had claimed land in what is now the King Country. Leaving Kawhia with his wife Kahurere, he descended to the Waipa River valley. At Wharepuhanga Kahurere gave birth to a son, Hape-ki-te-tua-raki, but failed to recover from the birth. Rakataura agonisingly besought the atua to restore his young wife to health. His pleading was commemorated in the name Pureora-a-Kahu (Health-restoring karakia of Kahurere). After a while Kahurere seemed much better, but her recovery was short-lived. She died while climbing the mountain, which her husband named in her memory Pukeokahu, q.v.

info_origin: An original Māori name and old pā site. Publisher-writer Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) suggested a sacred rite and two as a literal translation. The name was carried over to 416 acres (168 ha) which Thomas Hansen (1762-1837) occupied in 1832. Hansen, as captain of the brig 'Active', brought missionary Samuel Marsden (1765-1838) to the Bay of Islands in 1814. Returning as a non-missionary settler at Rangihoua Bay, Hansen worked as a carpenter, farmer and trader before moving to more fertile land at Purerua in 1832. In 1855 Hansen purchased 24 acres (9.7ha) at Purerua from Kingi Hori Kira and others in exchange for a stallion for which he submitted a declaration to the Old Land Claims Commissioners in 1858. On occasions from the 1870s-90s the name was incorrectly spelled in the press as Purirua. In 1880 visitor Dr RH Bakewell (1831-1908), a former army surgeon, was captivated by the attractiveness of the area: ‘These little bays are the most beautiful and picturesque places in the world. There are no tall trees in them, but plenty of nice ferns and trees of various kinds (including the beautiful Christmas tree [Pōhutukawa]), forming a low dense scrub. Here and there are found patches of smooth green sward, as closely grown as an English lawn, the remnants of former Maori cultivation. These are composed of a deep black soil, mixed with shells, to the presence of which they owe their continual fertility’. A primary school was opened by 1903. Ethnologist Johannes Andersen, a member of the Honorary Geographic Board, who undertook a sheet-by-sheet review of names on the provisional 1:63360 topographical map series in 1943, confirmed the existence of a post office at Purerua.

info_origin: 'The name originates in the love of Pūtauaki for Whakaari / White Island. Iwi including Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Te Arawa and Tuhoe tell different versions of this tragic affair, involving Pūtauaki’s separation from his troublesome wife Tarawera, his passage across the land with his young son trailing behind, and Whakaari’s location out at sea. Captain James Cook named it Mount Edgecumbe on 2 November 1769, perhaps after John Edgecumbe, sergeant of the marines on the Endeavour. Two other possible sources were Mount Edgcumbe at Plymouth or, more probably, George Edgcumbe, a noted naval officer (later Lord Edgcumbe).’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Putiki
info_origin: 'The full name of the Maori pa was Putiki-waranui-a-Tamatea-pokai-whenua: lit. where Tamatea who travelled all over the land tied his hair in a topknot with the species of flax waranui. Tamatea, commander of the Takitimu canoe, travelled up the Whanganui River, at the mouth of which the he tied up his hair. Another account is that it was a slave of Kahungunu, the son of Tamatea and ancestor of Ngati Kahungunu, who sought to tie up his putiki (topknot) here. An early missionary, thinking of a massacre that had taken place not long before, interpreted it as meaning ‘great shaving off of scalps’ and described it as a Golgotha; one of the hills behind Putiki is called Korokata, q.v., the Maori pronunciation of Golgotha. At one time Putiki was referred to as Williamstown after the chief Hoani Wiremu Hipango, known to the settlers as John Williams.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Pyramus Peak
info_ref: Auckland Museum, ‘James Robert Dennistoun’, Online Cenotaph, http://www.aucklandmuseum.com/war-memorial/online-cenotaph/record/C33709; Colledge, J.J. and Barlow, Ben, Ships of the Royal Navy: The Complete Record of All Fighting Ships of the Royal Navy from the 15th Century to the Present, Newbury: Casemate, 2010.; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 9, pp. 35, 56-57.; Reed, A.W., Place Names of New Zealand, Rosedale: Penguin, 2010.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: The name of this feature came about from a family connection. Amongst the party who first scaled it in 1914 was Jim Dennistoun, a prolific New Zealand climber who had already achieved the first ascent of Mount D’Archiac and Mitre Peak. On this occasion, Dennistoun decided to use the title of the Royal Navy ship to which his younger brother George had been posted. The HMS Pyramus was a Pelorus-Class protected cruiser. Being lightly gunned and armoured, it tended to be used for ‘police’ duties and did not sail with the main battle fleet. Pyramus formed part of the escort for the New Zealand force that occupied German Samoa in 1914, before taking part in the Rufiji Delta action in German East Africa. George Dennistoun served throughout the First World War. In addition to his time on the Pyramus, he was a transport officer for one of the ships that carried the Main Body of the New Zealand Expeditionary Force to Egypt, and was Senior Naval Officer in the Lake Nyasa Gunboat Flotilla. George received the Distinguished Service Order after showing conspicuous bravery during an engagement with a German vessel. Jim Dennistoun was to prove less fortunate. After making his way to England on a steamer, he managed to obtain a commission in the North Irish Horse. By 1916 he had transferred to 23 Squadron of the Royal Flying Corps. Jim was shot down over Germany and underwent several operations as a prisoner of war. Complications arising from the last of these procedures resulted in his death on 9 August 1916.; 'Jim Dennistoun named the peak in 1914 after HMS Pyramus, the ship to which his brother George was posted at the time.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Queen Charlotte Sound (Totaranui)
info_origin: See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDY1MThCMkUyNDBGRjg1RThFMUI); 'After a stay of just over a fortnight in the sound, on 1 February 1770 Captain James Cook recorded the setting out of two inscribed posts on the top of Motuara Island, q.v. In his journal he wrote: ‘After I had thus prepared the way for setting up the post, we took it up to the highest part of the Island, and after fixing it fast in the ground, hoisted thereon the Union flag, and I dignified this Inlet with the name of Queen Charlotte’s Sound, and took formal possession of it and the Adjacent lands in the Name and for the use of his Majesty.’ Queen Charlotte Sophia was the consort of George III. Maori name: Totaranui: totara: tree (Podocarpus totara); nui: big.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Te Atiawa and Ngati Tama state that: Totaranui waterways are the veins of Te Atiawa, each and every bay is highly significant to Te Atiawa. Totaranui is the original Te Reo name. Totaranui was bountiful of Totara. Following a series of taua between 1827 – 1830, Ngati Toa established themselves at a number of locations in the Marlborough sounds, including Queen Charlotte Sound. There were a number of Ngati Toa pa site in Totaranui, including Te Rei o Karaka pa at Karaka Point, and Ngakuta Point Pa. Ana-o-koha, located in the Dieffenbach point area is the site of an historic battle, at which Ngati Toa successfully repelled and defeated an attempted ambush . Another site of significance is Ship Cove, an important tapu area where the daughter of Te Pehi Kupe is buried. Colonel Wakefield, while collecting signatures for the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, encountered a large Ngati Toa. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDY1MThCMkUyNDBGRjg1RThFMUI)

name: Queenstown
info_origin: ’The popular belief is that both Kingston and Queenstown on Lake Wakatipu were named after places in Ireland. The site of Queenstown was earlier known as The Camp and then Canvastown; the latter was a name frequently used during the gold rushes when ‘canvas towns’ sprang up virtually overnight (see Canvastown). The most plausible account is that the miners, particularly those of Irish origin, had followed with interest news that Queen Victoria had bestowed the name Queenstown on The Cove, which was a small settlement in County Cork, Ireland. W.G. Rees had a hotel here called the Queen’s Arms, which may have been another influence. The Māori name of Queenstown flat and bay areas is Tāhuna, meaning ‘shallow bay’ or ‘sandbank’.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: ’After Lord Raglan, commander-in-chief during the Crimean War in 1844 and 1845, at the time of the Charge of the Light Brigade. The little township was established in 1854, and named in 1858. Māori name of the harbour: Whāingaroa: lit. whai: stingray; nga: the; roa: long or large. Alternatively: whāinga: possessed or occupied; roa: long. The name may commemorate Te Aowhaingaroa, the tohunga of Manaia’s canoe Tokomaru, which called here after the battle with Nuku off Pukerua, near Wellington. Another explanation is that Whaingaroa was named by Rakataura of the Tainui canoe, as there is traditional evidence that the name was originally Whangaroa. When Rakataura ascended Karioi mountain, it is said that he looked down at the harbour and named it Whangaroa (Long harbour). It was subsequently changed to Whaingaroa to distinguish it from the harbour of the same name in Northland.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Rainbow Mountain
info_origin: Also known as Maunga Kākaramea, Rainbow Mountain is an iconic feature in the geothermal region of the central North Island. The name refers to the colourful strata of volcanic soils - a similar meaning to Maunga Kākaramea. While 'Kakaramea' appears on maps as early as 1866, the use of 'Rainbow Mountain' appears in print and on maps following the Tarawera Eruption in 1886. The 1880's had seen a marked increase in tourist activity targeting the 'geothermal wonderland'. Stripped of most vegetation by the nearby eruption, most of the feature is covered in regenerated forest or plants adapted to the volcanic environment.; 'So named on account of the vari-coloured rocks on the sides of the mountain. Maori name: Maungakaramea: lit. maunga: mountain; karamea: red ochre. The Maori name has much the same significance as the Pakeha one, for karamea can be loosely translated as coloured earth. The summit was Tihi-o-ruru: lit. tihi: summit; o: of; ruru: owl or morepork (Ninox novaeseelandiae).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: A 743m hill feature located at the intersection of State Highway 5 and State Highway 38, approximately 25 km southeast of Rotorua. Beaconed geodetic mark 3081 and a transmission mast are located at the summit. The hill is part of the ‘Rainbow Mountain Scenic Reserve’. Feature shown on: NZMS260 U16 Edition 1 1982; NZTopo50-BF37 962533.

name: Rakaia
info_origin: 'The name Rakaia specifically refers to the section of the river from the mouth to the junction of the Wilberforce and Mathias rivers. For some time the Rakaia River was known as the Cholmondeley. Māori names for the upper tributaries of the Rakaia include Rakaia-wai-pākihi for the Mathias River, Rakaia-wai-ki for the southern branch and Waitāwhiri for the Wilberforce River. There is dispute as to the validity of the meaning sometimes attributed to Rakaia, that it may be the South Island form of rangaia, referring to the practice of strong men standing in line to break the force of the water when crossing a river.' info_origin: Rakitchu is a reference to a celestial body. The islands were often used by Moriori for birding. Karaka Kahukura claimed the island group for Moriori in a letter to the Native Ministers (1879) but the Land Court awarded the islands to Māori in 1885 (WN26b/563) determining that the islands had already been decided on by the 1870 court, which in fact had not occurred. name: Rangatauaiti
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: The names of these two lakes derive from the word ‘Rangataua’ meaning war party. Rangataua was also the name of a demi-god who lived in the clouds. He was a famous warrior and his weapons were rain, hail, snow and lightening. Te Mokai o Rangataua (a cloud formation) was his waka which would transport him. Ngāti Rangi would often call upon Rangataua to fight for the tribe. Rangatauanui is the name of the larger of the two lakes, while Rangatauaiti is the name for the smaller lake. Rangatauanui was also the name of the hill between the two lakes.
info_description: The smaller of two small lakes covering approximately 1 ha, within Ngā Roto-o-Rangataua Scenic Reserve, approximately 3km southwest of Ohakune. NZTopo50-BJ34 052319.

name: Rangiāwhiao
info_ref: Corres LXXII pp 78-163; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Johannes Anderson knew the name Rangiawhia and had seen it used for the peninsula but suggested Rangaunu. Rangiawhia was the name of a pa above Parakerake Bay but no trace of it was found in 1943. The ancestors Te Parata and (his wife) Kahutianui (from whom Ngati Kahu are named) came from Tauroa (near Ahipara) and having come via Murimotu (Nth Cape area) on the Mamaru, landed beneath the mountain (Pūwheke) at the entrance to Rangaunu Harbour. They stayed there a while before moving across Karikari moana (bay) to Maroewhiti (where they established the main dwelling place of Te Whanau Moana hapu). They then sailed around Whakapouaka and down to Merita where Te Rorohuri hapu were set down to establish their turangawaewae. Te Mamaru (waka) continued on round to Parakerake then up the waterway Waimango (now only a swamp) and came out again at Pūwheke. Thus at this time the area was an island and the island was named Rangiāwhio from Te Rangi i Taiāwhiotia mai e Te Mamaru. 'The area circumnavigated by Mamaru (canoe)' N.B. The rest of what is now known as Karikari Peninsula is actually Tokerau (which is known only as the name of the beach to Pakeha).
info_description: Area between Whatuwhiwhi and Merita (localities) mostly consisting of Toupiroroa Range, traditionally described as an 'island' as waka could almost be paddled straight through the adjoining swamps. NZTopo50-AU27 379421
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "the area circumnavigated"

name: Rangiawhiao Pa
info_origin: The ancestors Te Parata and his wife Kahutianui sailed from Tauroa, via Murimotu, landed beneath Puwheke mountain, sailed across Karikari Moana, establishing a dwelling place of Te Whanau Moana hapu. They sailed around Whakapouka and down to Merita where Te Rorohuri hapu were set down. Te Mamaru (waka) continued round to Parakerake then up the waterway Waimango (now only a swamp) and came out again at Puwheke. Thus the area at the time was an island and was named Rangiawhiao from 'Te Rangi i Taiawhiotia mai e Te Mamaru', "The area circumnavigated by Mamaru (Canoe)". Correction of spelling from Rangiahwiao Pa (8/12/1994 133:4349). For further details refer to correspondence.

info_origin: An original Māori name which is duplicated in various places across the country. Ethnologist Percy Smith (1840-1922) noted that in one of the traditions of voyaging of Kupe, he left an anchor stone at Rangiora. A pā known as Te Rangiora occupied this strategic site, a bottle neck overlooking movements along the harbour. The Customs Officer was initially based at Rangiora before relocating to Rawere. Former Royal Navy Lieutenant Robert St Aubyn’s home ‘Rangiora House’ was built was here after he was appointed a magistrate in 1843. The next year he also became Hokianga Harbourmaster. St Aubyn is considered to have introduced both oak trees and gorse to the area. In 1846 he left the area, having been appointed as Sub-Inspector of Police for the District of Auckland. Timber trader John Webster (1806-95) next occupied the house. In 1862 Rev. William Gittos (1829-1916) relocated the Wesleyan mission from Oruawharo to Rangiora. Judge John Rogan (1823-99) of the Native Land Court adjudicated on 233 acres (94 ha) at Rangiora in 1867. Soon afterwards, kauri sawmilling commenced here spreading to other locations in the Hokianga in the 1870s. The site was commercially valuable as the deepwater of the Rangiora Narrows enabled larger draught ships to moor for loading. In 1885 the Lands Board accepted seven tenders for sawmilling rights on the Rangiora Block ranging from 7d to 3/3d per acre. The medium sized Rangiora Timber Company was established on the foreshore by 1905. It cut 4000000 superficial feet in 1907 or 80% of its annual capacity and exported almost all its kauri and rimu, along with some kahikatea to Australia. The mill’s lengthy tramline ran back into the hills. A serious landslip in 1907 necessitated the relocation of the mill. In 1912 Umutahi hapū leaders complained that the company tramline crossed their land without permission or payment. After WWI the mill again concentrated on kauri for export to Australia.

info_origin: Te Rarawa history: The Narrows is a name that has been used to describe the narrowing of Hokianga Harbour as it turns towards Kohukohu. The original name of this area is Te Rangiora which is the name of a pā site prominent above the harbour at this point. Te Rangiora pā was an important strategic point in the defence of the Ngai Tupoto hapū of Te Rarawa. It provided good surveillance of the Harbour up river to Kohukohu, Utakura and beyond; across the Waima River; and downstream to Rawene, the Omanaia River, and down towards the Harbour mouth. The pā is mentioned in stories relating to the earliest altercations and battles that took place on this land nearly 20 generations ago. More recently there was a mill and settlement called Rangiora within a few hundred metres of the pā site. Little remains of this settlement area except a reference on an odd old map. This site derived its name from the Pā. The Department of Conservation has a reserve called Rangiora about half a kilometre from this area. Again the name is derived from the pā site at “The Narrows”.

name: Rangipo Desert
info_origin: 'Lit. rangi: sky; po: night or darkness; i.e. Place where the sky is dark. Some time after his arrival in the Arawa canoe, Ngatoroirangi explored the volcanic plateau in search of land he proposed to claim for his people (descendants who were later named Ngati Tuwharetoa). After nearly perishing with cold on the summit of Tongariro (q.v.) he saw a party of explorers from the Takitimu canoe crossing the eastern plain. To protect the land he had claimed, Ngatoro appealed to Ruaumoko, the god of volcanoes and subterranean forces, for help. Smoke and ashes poured out of Ngauruhoe and enveloped the strangers in darkness, to which was added a heavy snowstorm, thus giving rise to the name. Also called Onetapu Desert, q.v. Originally Rangipo applied only to the region between the volcanoes and the Kaimanawa Range. The Desert Road which traverses the area is named for the desert.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: A desert within the central plateau, between Mount Ruapehu and State Highway 1. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BJ35 306452

info_origin: An original Māori name. Edward Dollimore (1904-73), complier of The New Zealand Guide, described the locality as ‘In vicinity of eminence of same name’ referring to the 861m hill 14km distant in Rangitoto Range. Journalist-historian James Cowan recounted a legend of Te Aroha in which the ‘fairy people’ of Colville Range seized a Ngāti Matakore woman from far away ‘Rangitoto country’ before another ‘fairy chief’ from the Rangitoto Ranges using ‘powerful hypnotic charms’ freed her and returned her home. In 1882 there were short lived rumours of gold discoveries in the Rangitoto Ranges. From April to May 1883 James Kerry-Nicholls (?-1888) denied permission to travel through the King Country by Tāwhiao (?-1894), entered instead via Tauranga and the central North Island producing a travelogue and one of the first maps of the region which included Rangitoto as a 2500 feet (762m) – actually 758m – hill. Laurence Cussens (1843-1903), District Surveyor for Auckland, commenced the triangulation survey of the King Country later that same year. In 1884 he was warned to expect resistance to the survey work in the Rangitoto Ranges, but this did not eventuate. In 1907 Sir Robert Stout and (Sir) Āpirana Ngata were appointed as commissioners to report on Māori land in the Rohe-Potae or King Country. Their investigation revealed that of 69 Rangitoto land blocks, 5000 acres (2023 ha) were for sale, 10277 acres (4159 ha) for lease and 4806 acres (1945 ha) for ‘Native occupation’, with another 8359 acres (3383 ha) still to be dealt with. In 1910 Herbert Horatio Spencer Westmacott (1885-1960), leased and later purchased the bush covered Rangitoto 28 block. In 1914 Westmacott joined the New Zealand Expeditionary Force as an officer and was wounded during the Gallipoli campaign. He was depicted as one of the 2.4 times life sized figurines created as part of the Galipolli: the scale of our war exhibition held at Te Papa.

name: Rangitoto Island
info_origin: ‘Occupation by different iwi has led to alternative names for the island. In Te Arawa tradition it was named after Tamatekapua of the Arawa canoe came to blows with Hoturoa of the Tainui canoe because he was devoting too much attention to Hoturoa’s wife. Tamatekapua had the worst of the conflict, and took some time to recover from his wounds. The beach where he rested was therefore named Te Rangi-i-totongia-a-Tamatekapua: lit. The day Tamatekapua had a bloody nose. In another version, Tamatekapua, accompanied by his sons Tuhoro and Kahumatamomoe, landed on the shore of the island at Islington Bay and fought with the earlier inhabitants, who were known as Kahu-a-marama, with the same result as in the conflict with Hoturoa. A popular translation of Rangitoto, alluding to the volcanic eruption of the island, is ‘bloody sky’. In the tradition of Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki, the island is known as Ngā Tuaitara-a-Taikehu: lit. The dorsal fins of Taikehu, the founding ancestor of Ngāi Tai. The ‘fins’ refer to the three summits on the island, as does another: Ngā Pona-toru-a-Peretū: lit. ngā: the; pona: knuckles; toru: three; a: of; Peretū, once the chiefly owner of the island. The channel was Awanui-o-Peretū (Big channel of Peretū).’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Rangitoto ki te Tonga (D'Urville Island)
info_origin: [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Jules Sébastien César Dumont d'Urville](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1d19/dumont-durville-jules-sebastien-cesar); 'Lit. Rangitoto to the south. It is believed to have been conferred by the chief Nukutamarore, who explored here before settlement began, and saw smoke from a fire on the western side of the island, reminding him of a volcano in Hawaiki. It was also named after the French navigator Dumont d’Urville, who took the Astrolabe through French Pass in January 1827. D’Urville recorded: ’The officers of the Astrolabe, eager to perpetuate the memory of their commander, wished his name to be attached to this portion of the discoveries of the voyage, and he did not think it right to refuse this mark of esteem on the part of his brave companions. The name D’Urville Island can therefore remain attached to this part of the land until such time as the name given to it by its inhabitants be discovered.’ ' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: Rangituhi was the early Māori name for this peak located south-west of Porirua. The name, which translates as ‘sky glow’, was given because of the red ‘glowing’ appearance of the hill at sunset when viewed from Te Awarua o Porirua. Ngati Toa have a long and extensive association with the Porirua region. The pa and kainga of the iwi were in their greatest concentration along the coastline parallel to Mana Island and Kapiti Island. Their most important pa in Porirua was initially Taupo, but after the arrest of Te Rauparaha and exile of Te Rangihaeata, the concentration of Ngati Toa settlement shifted to Takapuwahia. From these settlements, Ngati Toa controlled the Porirua region via the harbour, which according to Governor Grey, was “the key to the Wellington district” in the 1840s. Ngati Toa have continued their occupation of Porirua up until the present day and Takapuwahia Marae, the marae matua, remains the centre of tribal activity. It is the location of Toa Rangatira the Whare Tupuna and Parehounuku the Wharekai.

info_origin: The Wellington suburb of Redwood is named for Francis William Redwood (1839-1935), Archbishop of Wellington from 1887 until his death aged 95. In 1852 Governor-in-Chief Sir George Grey granted the land on which the suburb would later develop to Bishop Viard, Wellington’s first Roman Catholic bishop. Grey granted the land (Section 38, Porirua District) for the purpose of building a Catholic school. The Catholic Church held the land in reserve for more than a century, leasing it to local farmers. In 1958 the Catholic Church sold most of the land to the Tawa Development Corporation for a housing development, the largest of its kind in Tawa. By this time, improved road and rail access combined with a shortage of housing stock and suitable development land in Wellington central meant that Tawa had become an attractive area for new housing developments. The Catholic Church retained 8 acres on which it founded the parochial school St Francis Xavier School (1960), at last fulfilling the intent of Grey’s original land grant. The new housing development was named ‘Redwood’ in honour of the former Archbishop of Wellington, being ‘part concession’ of the Catholic Church’s sale. The subdivision comprised over 300 sections in 27 streets and initially developed around its main thoroughfare Redwood Avenue. The remaining streets were completed in the 1960s-1978. Redwood Avenue and three other street names reflect the suburb’s Catholic origins, being named for Roman Catholic clergymen, as do Redwood Railway Station (1963) and Redwood School (1966). The other streets were named for English university colleges, primarily in Oxford and Cambridge. [See entry in the Dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Francis William Redwood] (https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2r6/redwood-francis-william)

info_origin: A suburb of Blenheim named after Thomas Redwood (1833-1918). In 1842 Redwood arrived in Nelson with his parents on the George Fyfe. His father Henry Redwood farmed Stafford Place station in Nelson and was a pioneer runholder in Marlborough. In 1848 Thomas Redwood first took sheep to the Wairau valley. He returned in 1852 as manager of Bank House Station held by his father Henry on lease from Dr David Monro (1813-77). From 1855-76 Redwood was also manager of his father’s Vernon Run. Redwood and his wife were converts to Catholicism. He was elected to the Marlborough Provincial Council serving from 1865-68. With his brother Henry, he was involved the horse racing industry. In the early 1870s he purchased Burleigh run from James Wemyss the Provincial Secretary. He sold out in the 1890s to farm at Woodbourne and retired to Blenheim in 1900.

info_origin: ’The extensive gold-bearing quartz reefs were discovered in 1870. Shortly after the township was founded, two names were in circulation — Rest Town and Quartzopolis. (It was a time of colourful naming: the locality of Broadway was named after the West Coast magistrate and warden, Charles Broad, and the nearby Wealth of Nations mine received its name because it was discovered by a man named Adam Smith.) The township was originally spelt Reef Town. An earlier settlement had been established by Donald Ross on the opposite bank of the Inangahua River in about 1870, but the business premises, known then as Ross Town, were shifted to the present site in 1871. Reefton’s longest-lasting gold reef led to the establishment of the satellite town of Waiuta, with its Prohibition and Blackwater mines; Waiuta died after the mine closed in 1951.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Remuera
info_origin: 'A contraction of Remuwera: lit. remu: buttocks, otherwise edge or hem; wera: burnt. It is said to commemorate an incident in which a chieftainess of Hauraki was killed and put in an umu (earth oven) still wearing her piupiu. The name was applied by Māori to Ōhinerau / Mount Hobson. Remuera has also been related to the burnt edge of the volcanic cone, or the burnt hem of a skirt. Earlier known as Ōhinerau, the place of Hinerau (goddess of whirlwinds), or Ōhinerangi, the place of Hinerangi (goddess of the sky).' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Remuera Settlement
info_ref: Corres LII, pp 153-156, 161; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche May 2023: Objective ID: A5383945 {Lake Omapere R3950859. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; NZGB Correspondence Vol 52, 1985; Remuera Settlement [plan] R675884. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; Remuera Settlement R18648334. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; [Remuera Estate Romney Marsh Stud. 1910. Northland Age, 31 January, Page 5.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NORAG19100131.2.44.4)}
info_origin: The World War I Discharged Soldiers' Settlement legislation enabled demobilized aspiring farmers to ballot for farms on Crown land. The Remuera Settlement, a farm settlement under the Discharged Soldiers' Settlement Act, which comprised 3553 acres (1438 ha) and 31 farms of 76 to 373 acres (31 to 151 ha) was advertised in 1919 and ultimately adopted as the name for the wider locality. The name Remuera Settlement was approved by the Minister of Lands, David Guthrie (1856-1927) in 1919 prior to the land being balloted. In this instance Guthrie was approving the perpetuation of the name of the larger estate that Henry Dickeson (1857-1924) and Arthur Thayer Close (1880-1919) had purchased in 1910, which had functioned mainly as a Romney Marsh stud farm. Close died before the 1919 sale was finalised, with his transactions for some small areas of Māori land still incomplete. Previously a portion of the estate had been part of the Lake Ompaere Estate owned by Messrs Wright, Laing and Pitcaithly, itself on a portion of the Tautahanga block. The government purchased the land comprising the settlement from Dickeson with another portion being acquired from William Henry Wright (1872-1944) and his business partner George Pitcaithly. In 1918, Pitcaithly was residing in the Auckland suburb of Remuera. The name Remuera Settlement may include a word of Māori, but it does not appear to be an original Māori name for the locality. In updating names for inclusion on New Zealand topographic maps in 1985 the New Zealand Geographic Board recognised the area as a locality being on the then 'new national place name index'. In so doing it seemed not to have appreciated the earlier history of the area as a discharged soldier settlement.
info_description: Locality NE of Kaikohe and just east of Lake Omapere

info_origin: An original Māori name, which literally translates as 'long or wide swamp'. Ngātoroirangi, the powerful high priest who arrived from Hawaiki on the Te Arawa canoe journeyed down the Tarawera River to Tongariro via Reporoa. The larger area went through the Native Land Court in the 1860s. Some land was leased to European settlers, but 1000 acres (405 ha) around Reporoa to the west of Waiotapu Stream remained as Māori Land into the 1920s. In 1899 Henry Robert Butcher (1840-1933) purchased 48000 acres (19425 ha) from John Smellie Grahame (1846-1902) which became known as Strathmore Estate occupying part of the Waiotapu valley and a portion of the Kaingaroa Plains. In the process he became one of the first European settlers in the Waiotapu district. In 1911 Butcher retaining 20000 acres (8094 ha) and the Strathmore name sold the other 28000 acres (1131 ha), including the homestead, to Wilfred Gatenby Stead (1879-1933) and EJ Watt, who renamed it Reporoa. For the new owners 'the chief [task] of which is a huge drain to tap what is known as the long swamp'. In 1919 the Land Settlement Board for £86675 purchased 28082 acres (11364 ha) of freehold land and 1297 acres (525 ha) of 'Native leases' that comprised Reporoa station, now owned by W Richmond, Wilfred Stead, and Mrs Stead. The witness for the vendors was (Edward) Earle Vaile (1869-1956), a prominent Auckland real estate agent and promoter of settlement in the 'pumice lands' where he successfully developed the adjacent 53000 acres (21448 ha) Broadlands Estate, despite some of the land being 'bush sick' because of a cobalt deficiency. The Lands Department transferred 15000 acres (6070 ha) of Reporoa over to its Forestry Branch while appreciating that some swamp land, which gave the area its name, remained to be drained. The Department also set about purchasing the title to the remaining Māori leasehold land. A detailed plan for Reporoa Township was prepared by Lands Department staff surveyor Percy Wilkinson (c.1880-1954) in late 1919. Wilkinson had earlier been sent to Maungapōhatu by the police to gather evidence against Rua Kēnana (1868/69-1937). In December 1919 the Commissioner for Crown Lands for Auckland, Harry Skeet (1857-1943), indicating there was 'no township near' forwarded Wilkinson's plan to the Under Secretary of Lands, (Thomas) Noel Brodrick (1855-1931). The town plan provided for 61 sections including reserves for a police station, a pound, a post office, an education reserve, metal reserves, cemetery and recreation. An area was specifically marked as 'Maori ground cultivations.' On 24 May 1920, 11 farms of some 90 (36 ha) to 300 acres (121 ha) on a 2071 acres (838 ha) block were advertised at Reporoa under the Discharged Soldier Settlement Act. Three of the sections contained sizable areas of swamp land. Over time some 17 relinquished their sections leading it to be considered something of a failure as a soldier settlement.

info_origin: An original Māori name shared with the lake. Te Arawa Lakes Trust translates it as 'the lake of wandering spirits'. Sir Apirana Ngata (1874-1950) affirmed the 'aa' in the spelling for the Honorary Geographic Board in 1938. At the time Rerewhakaitu was being used in the newspapers and for the Survey District. An old Māori trail led from Rerewhakaaitu through to the Rangitaiki Valley. Rerewhakaaitu was the site of a battle between Arawa and Tuhoe in pre-European times. In 1870 during the New Zealand Wars there was a running fight from Ohinemutu to Lake Rerewhakaaitu between an Arawa contingent under Lieutenant Gilbert Mair (1843-1923) and Te Kooti (? -1893). Government land purchases in the Rerewhakaaitu Block commenced in the 1870s with remaining areas passing through the Native Land Court in the 1880s. As early as 1867 Gilbert Mair and his brother William leased an 8000 acre (3237ha) property from Māori at Rerewhakaaitu. In the early 20th century newspaper commentators called for greater efforts at Rerewhakaaitu 'in order to lift these vast areas of light lands from desolate wastes to productive use'. As early as 1908 MP Thomas Wilford (1870-1939) considered tourism rather than farming was the future of the area and urged 'the erection of an accommodation house at Rerewhakaaiu — a lake of 30 acres [12 ha] in extent, about eight miles [12.8km] from Waiotapu, for this would supply a fishing ground for scores of tourists, the fish being in first-class condition, and of good size'. Allied to this, in 1922 Sambur deer captured at Himatangi were released at Rerewhakaaitu for future game hunting. During WWII the American forces had a training ground at Rerewhakaaitu. Live ammunition was found here as late as 1959. The Lands & Survey Department continued with land development after WWII. In 1961 the Chief Surveyor for Auckland 'to cater for future demand' submitted a plan prepared by registered surveyor William Boyes for a 5 acre (2 ha) 'town of Rerewhakaaitu' subdivision on Crown Land near the shore of Lake Rerewhakaaitu under the Town and Country Planning Act, 1953. This included 11 residential and six commercial sections. Ministerial approval was given by Richard Geoffrey Gerard (1904-97) under the Land Subdivisions in Counties Act, 1946.

Earlier editions of the Dictionary (eg 1912) stated 'Rhos, a moor, a dry meadow ; Colyn is perhaps allied with Colofn, a column, a pillar. There are a series of pools below the Riuwaka resurgence and each pool has specific cultural purpose for the manawhenua iwi.

name: Roche Pass
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche June 2024: Objective ID: A6399382 {Walshe, Harry (Surveyor-General) to Geographic Board for comments 4/6/32 Correspondance Vol 9 1932 f.45, 52-55 (map), 85; Correspondance Vol 10 1933 JC Andersen to Surveyor-General has gone over list of names asks about dates considered incl Roche Pass; DK [Dave Kennedy] 1959. Obituary Herbert Roche. New Zealand Journal of Forestry 8 (1), 169-70.; New Zealand Gazetteer 1948 p. 939; [Maxwell Gage. 'Speight, Robert', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1996. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3s30/speight-robert)}
info_origin: Named after State Forest Service Ranger Herbert (‘Hub’) Roche (1892-1959). Early in 1932, realizing that some of the topography in the vicinity of Poulter River on sheet 22 of the 4 inch to the mile map series was incorrect, CGS (Charles Gilmour Stead) Ellis (1897-1986) Lands and Survey Chief Draughtsman in Christchurch made a compass survey and checked the heights of the peaks in the doubtful area. In May 1932 his superior William Stewart (1881-1957), Chief Surveyor Christchurch, forwarded a new map to Harry Walshe (1883-1948), Surveyor-General and ex-officio member of the Honorary Geographic Board. This map included a dozen new names which Walshe sent to the Honorary Geographic Board for consideration. The proposed new names included two New Zealand State Forest Service staff, including Herbert Roche. These names Walshe recommended ‘for the favorable consideration of the Geographic Board’. Phlegmatic in his assessment he noted that ‘in the absence of local traditions or history other than the accident of residence or visits to the district I think these suggestions might be adopted failing any more imaginative or outstanding facts for perpetuation or otherwise’. The names were confirmed at the Honorary Geographic Board meeting on 8 July 1932 and in 1948 made official under the New Zealand Geographic Board Act, 1946. Herbert Roche worked on survey and tunnelling projects before joining the State Forest Service on its formation in 1921. He enrolled in the rangers’ course at the Canterbury College Forestry school in 1925 and from 1929-40 was officer-in-charge of Hanmer State Forest where he oversaw thinning of the plantations, later becoming Conservator of Forests for Nelson (1940-46). His colleagues recognized ‘His outstanding characteristics were his humanism, his shrewd commonsense, acquired the hard way, and his ability to lead people’. Field investigations by Canterbury College Geology Professor Robert Speight (1967-1949) revealed that the most seriously disturbed area in the aftermath of the Arthur's Pass earthquake of 9 March 1929 was in the vicinity of Poulter River and Roche Pass. In 1947 the Representation Commission ruled that part of the northern boundary of Malvern County would run through Roche Pass.

info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA417315; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5111558 {Bannister, Charles. 1999. Early history of the Wairarapa. New Zealand: Castonbury, [first published 1940].; [Mount Holdsworth Track. 1906. Wairarapa Age, 22 December, Page 5.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WAG19061222.2.13); [Local and General. 1930. Wairarapa Age, 17 February, Page 4.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WAG19300217.2.11); https://www.rankers.co.nz/experiences/10316-Mount_Holdsworth_Summit_Tararua_Forest_Park}
info_origin: A feature on the ‘Gentle Annie’ section of the Holdsworth Track, the high point of this part being a rock outcrop. A Mount Holdsworth Track Committee was set up in 1906 with the aim of constructing a route to the summit of Mount Holdsworth. Principal figures on the committee were James Ewington (Chair), WM Easthope (Secretary) and Duncan McGregor (Treasurer). Charles Bannister, who had climbed Mount Holdsworth as early as 1881 acted as guide. Support was obtained from the Department of Lands and Survey and the Tourist and Health Resorts Department. By 1910 a thousand visitors a year were walking the Mount Holdsworth tracks. Visiting parties noted that from Rocky Lookout ‘a fine view is obtained over the Wairarapa plains’.

name: Rongotai
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA417315; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Best, E. and McLeod, H.N. 1919. The Land of Tara part VI. Journal of the Polynesian Society, 28, 1-17; [News of the Bay. 1921. New Zealand Times, 1921, 28 October, Page 4](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZTIM19211028.2.33); https://teara.govt.nz/en/photograph/13180/wellington-harbour-before-the-haowhenua-earthquake}
info_origin: An earthquake circa 1430-80 AD known to Māori as Haowhenua, the earth swallower, raised the Te Awa a Tia channel between the then island of Motukairangi, today’s Te Motu Kairangi / Miramar Peninsula and Kilbirnie. The large magnitude 8.2 Wairarapa earthquake of 1855 resulted in further uplift forming an isthmus and completed the turning the island into a peninsula. Elsdon Best, ethnologist at the Dominion Museum, recorded Rongotai as an original Māori name for a ridge line running along the western side of Te Motu Kairangi / Miramar Peninsula. A road, Rongotai Terrace, followed this feature and in 1905 became a dividing line between Miramar Borough and Wellington City. In 1915 residents on the isthmus requested that Wellington City Council name the area Rongotai. The dunes on the southern part of the isthmus were used as a runway by early light aircraft and an aerodrome opened in 1929. The Centennial Exhibition fair venue opened at Rongotai in 1939-40. Construction of a new Wellington airport in 1959 obliterated the old Rongotai Terrace and surrounding houses. The name has been translated literally as ‘rongo’ - sound and ‘tai’ - sea. Rongotai College opened in 1928, marking the beginning of the westward expansion of the boundary of Rongotai.

info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA325625; fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963; A5147295 {[Auctioneers and Land Agents. 1912. Marlborough Express, 21 September, Page 8](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/MEX19120921.2.56.4); Roselands. R21031470, Archives New Zealand, Wellington.}
info_origin: Roselands was described as ‘the most desirable suburb of Blenheim’ and 'the finest locality around Blenheim’ by Griffith & Sons the local auctioneering, real estate and land agent firm that offered sections for sale in September 1912. In May 1912 Griffith & Sons sought approval from the Commissioner of Crown Lands for Marlborough, William Henry Skinner (1857-1946), for the subdivision to proceed under the provisions of the Land Act 1908. The Chief Surveyor of Marlborough in turn wrote to James McKenzie (1849-1928), the Chief Surveyor of the Lands Department at head office in Wellington for approval. There were no objections, since the subdivision was not at a crossroads and there was adequate set back of 33 feet [10 m] from the centre of the road as required under the Public Works Act 1908. Finally, the Under-Secretary of Lands, John Strauchon (1848-1934), advised the Minister of Lands, Hon. Thomas MacKenzie (1853-1930), that Roselands was a suitable name for the subdivision. Griffith & Sons first approached the Commissioner of Crown Lands on 10 May and final approval was granted on 16 May.

info_description: The Ross Dependency comprises the sector of the Antarctic continent between 160°E, and 150°W together with the islands lying between those degrees of longitude and south of latitude 60°S. name: Ross Ice Shelf
info_origin: Discovered on 28 January 1841 by Ross for whom it is named. Ross mapped the ice front eastward to 160°00' W. Not Grosse Eisebene (German), Ross Barrier, Ross Ice Barrier or Ross Shelf Ice.
info_description: A vast ice shelf, to a large extent grounded, between Ross Island and King Edward VII Land, and occupying the entire southern part of the Ross Sea embayment and ending seaward in a cliffed ice front generally along a line of 635km (straight line) from Cape Crozier to Roosevelt Island where it is intended by the Bay of Whales, and a further 150km to its eastern edge, west of Cape Colbeck. A dynamic feature with new ice pushed out to the edge and old ice calving from the front, including the massive Iceberg B-9, 154km long, from the eastern side in 1987, and the colossal Iceberg B-15, 295km long, from just east of Ross Island on the western side, in 2000. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MF16
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Ross Island
info_origin: This area was first discovered by Ross in 1841, but he thought it formed part of the mainland of Victoria Land. First discovered to be an island and named by the British National Antarctic Expedition (BrNAE) (1901-04), in 1902, for Sir James Clark Ross.
info_description: An island on the eastern side of McMurdo Sound and extending for approximately 78km from Cape Bird on the north to Cape Armitage on the south, and approximately 78km from Cape Royds on the west to Cape Crozier on the east. This island is entirely volcanic, Mount Erebus, 3790m high, near the centre, being an active volcano, and Mount Terror, approximately 34km eastward, being an extinct volcano, 3288m high. Mount Bird at the north rises to a height of 1799m. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MD13&14, ME13-16, MF13-16

name: Ross Sea
info_origin: Ross Sea is the most easily accessible area of Antarctica. Every vessel that has attempted to enter this area at the correct season has been successful. The sea is named for Sir James Clark Ross, who discovered it in 1841.
info_description: An extensive bight in the coast of Antarctica almost due south of New Zealand.  It lies between Victoria Land on the west and King Edward VII Land on the east, and is bounded southward by the Ross Ice Shelf. Its northern limit starts at Cape Adare at the west, and extends directly northward to 70 South Latitude, then easterly along 70 South Latitude to 170 West Longitude, then in a straight line running south-easterly to Cape Colbeck. It includes both the Pennell Bank and the Iselin Bank. The depths of this sea are not very great, and there is a central, comparatively shallow, area culminating in the Pennell Bank in about 74°00'S, 179°00'E, with a least depth of 58 fathoms.
info_note: The NZGB endorsed the description of the Ross Sea in the 'feature' heading. The IHO definition is included for reference. The IHO definition of the Ross Sea: On the North: From Cape Adare (71 °18 'S - 170°14 'E) eastward. Along the parallel of 71 °18'S, to position 71 °18'S -157°50'W; On the East: From position 71°18'S -157°50'W southward, along the meridian 157°50'W, to Cape Colbeck (77°06'S -157°50'W); On the South: From Cape Colbeck westward, along the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, to Cape Crozier (77°30'S- 169°20'E), on the eastern coast of Ross Island; thence from Cape Crozier westward and southward, along the northern and western coasts of Ross Island, to Scott Base (77°52'S- 166°40'E), on the southern end of this island; thence from Scott Base southeastward, a line to the northern extremity of White Island (78°00'S -167°30'E); and thence from the northern extremity of White Island, westward, along the northern coasts of White Island and Black Island, and continuing northwesterly, to Brown Peninsula (78°02 'S- 165°32 'E), on the Hillary Coast of the Antarctic mainland; On the West: From Brown Peninsula northward, along the coast of Victoria Land, to Cape Adare (71 °18'S- 170°14'E), the point of commencement.

name: Rotoroa
info_ref: Objective ID: A1738920; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ahuriri Hapū statement (extract): One of the ancient tribes associated with the area was Ngāti Ruapirau who intermarried with the Ngati Mahu people, the people of the Tutaekuri who later married into Ngāti Hinepare. The story about the seven boulders of Mahu provides a fragment of history associated with the twin lakes. There were seven boulders up the Owhakau gorge with the first being at Owhakau, the entrance to the gorge. When the seventh was reached that was the sign to climb out of the gorge and proceed to the twin lakes at the foot of Kaweka Range. The Hapū/kin groups associated with the twin lakes were Ngāti Ruapirau, Ngāti Mahu, Ngāti Hinepare and Ngai Te Upokoiri.
info_description: The smaller of two lakes, approximately 2km east of Kuripapango Hill in Kaweka Forest Park. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BJ37 900375.

name: Rotten Tommy
info_origin: Around the 1860's, when stringent dipping regulations were enforced A Burnett and the Pattersons were out hunting for sheep infected with sheep scab on the then uninhibited country. Rough weather ran them short on "tucker" and they made a form of damper, from grease flour and sugar, baked in hot ashes. This was known in the early days as "rotten tommy" and therefore the block of land was dubbed "Rotten Tommy". Not for peak at NZMS1 S89 855285 as shown. Since the island reported by Balleny has not been found by other explorers in the vicinity, the name was assigned to another island by the personnel of Discovery II in 1936. Not Rowe Island. name: Roxburgh
info_origin: ’After an ancient ruined town on the banks of the Teviot River in Scotland. It was most likely given by the surveyor Johnston, who laid out the new town, but it has also been attributed to Walter Miller of Millers Flat, or J.T. Thomson. Most of the men who arrived at the time of the Dunstan goldrush came from Roxburghshire. At one time the town was known as Teviot, a name which is retained for features in the vicinity. With post office changes the name became Teviot Junction on 18 May 1863, reverted to Teviot on 1 September 1866, and became Roxburgh on 18 April 1877.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. info_origin: Literally translated, the terms ‘rua’ and ‘kākā’ conjoined as they are can mean ‘a place where the kākā parrot hides', as in ‘burrows or secretes itself'. The kaka is a bird that was employed by the ancestors of Patuharakeke as a ‘decoy’ or ‘distracter’ whereby they would attract other birds' attention by their animated actions, and lure them into a trap where they would then be ensnared. The kākā is also a metaphor for chiefs, and their plumage was employed in cloak making and weapons of war for those warriors of the highest rank. This name would certainly apply to Patuharakeke hapu who it is known were the first of the northern tribes to bear the brunt of any marauding war parties from the south and in effect fulfilled the all important function of ‘distracting’ the main onslaught until other tribes could marshal their forces.

info_origin: An original Māori name taken from the associated river which served as a significant route to and from the coast. Writer-historian Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) puzzled over possible literal meanings such as ‘to vomit’, ‘a fence post’, ‘water’ and ‘the place of Turi’. In 1834 missionaries William Williams (1807-78) and William Yate (1802-77) his later disgraced colleague, preached to 500 at Ruakituri. On a return visit William Williams baptised over 200 Māori here in 1841. Printer, missionary, botanist and explorer William Colenso (1811-99) also journeyed through the area in 1841 visiting Ruakituri, which he described as a ‘large native settlement’ where he collected fossil moa bones. Ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Elsdon Best (1856-1931) believed that having found fossils in the area Māori incorporated them into traditional stories about huge teeth. In 1843, with difficulty, missionary James Stack (1801-83) purchased 10 acres (4 ha) at Ruakituri. In 1868 military and Rongowhakaata religious leader Te Kooti (?-1893) defeated Napier militia under the former regular soldier Lieutenant Colonel George Whitmore (1819-1923) at Ruatikuri before establishing a defensive pā at Puketapu. In reporting his losses, Whitmore adopted the misspelling Ruakiture which continued to be used in newspapers until at least 1918. The Native Land Court sat at Wairoa in 1875 where Judge John Rogan (1823-99) investigated the 52000 acres (21044 ha) Ruakituri Block and issued memorials of ownership. Almost immediately the Crown indicated its intention to purchase, and the negotiations were completed by licensed translator Josiah Pratt Hamlin (1841?-98). Once roading was completed, in 1883 the government offered 18 sections for sale (in total 24960 acres – 10101 ha) and five for lease (in total 1865 acres – 755 ha) – described as largely ‘pastoral country’ with ‘fern on the spurs and in the valleys, and of scrub and bush in the steep gullies’. The next year the Sydney based trio of J Aitkin, TF Knox and EH Moore purchased the whole of the freehold of 23960 acres (9696 ha) with Moore acquiring the ten year lease on the remaining lands amounting to 4865 acres (1969 ha). By 1885 the block had passed to the stock and station company Dalgety and Company.

info_origin: Ruakituri River is culturally significant for the people of Te Rohe o Te Wairoa. In Ngāi Kohatu tradition the river was created when two taniwha Ruamano and Hinekorako, hearing the sounds of ocean waves, raced each other to the sea. Ruamano chose what became Ruakituri River while Hinekorako formed Hangaroa River. Writer-historian Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) puzzled over possible literal meanings such as to vomit, a fence post, water, and the place of Turi. The river served as a route way for Tūhoe, Ngāti Kahungunu and Ngāti Ruapani undertaking seasonal food gathering. Traditional settlements on its banks included Te Reinga and Erepeti. Soon after his escape from the Chatham Islands, Te Kooti (? -1893), Rongowhakaata military leader, prophet and religious founder, successfully repulsed a small force commanded by Captain William Richardson (1836-1912), with Lieutenant George Preece (1845-1925) as interpreter, at the junction of Ruakituri River and Hangaroa River in late July 1868. On 8 August there was a larger engagement when Te Kooti’s forces ambushed the Armed Constabulary under Colonel George Whitmore (1829-1903) who were in an exposed position in the riverbed. With some 100 men and 40 Māori allies Whitmore’s force in difficult terrain had to repeatedly cross the swiftly flowing ice-cold river. Of Whitmore’s men Lieutenant Davis Canning and Captain Carr were killed making for the shelter of a rock in the river ‘known as Te Wero-a-Tohe’ while others took cover where Makokomuka Stream joined Ruakituri River. Of the pursuers, four others were killed with five wounded. Te Kooti himself was wounded in the foot, and seven of his men were wounded and two killed, but he regrouped with his followers at Puketapu Pā. Without supplies and in wintery conditions Whitmore broke off the pursuit. Accounts vary, but historian James Belich considered that while Whitmore’s political opponents were too quick to label the encounter ‘a thrashing’, Te Kooti never-the-less narrowly won the tactical contest while achieving strategic success in escaping to Puketapu Pā. Honorary Geographic Board member Sir Āpirana Ngata (1874-1950) confirmed the spelling Ruakituri in 1941 when checking the new provisional inch to the mile topographical maps.

info_origin: An initial portion of the Ruakituri Scenic Reserve was set aside in 1905 on Crown Land under the Scenery Preservation Act 1903 which set up a Commission chaired by retired Surveyor-General Stephenson Percy Smith (1840-1922) to acquire land with scenic or historic interest, or thermal springs as reserves. In 1903 the Cook County Liberal Association advised Liberal party MP James Carroll (1857-1926) that it had resolved to seek ‘the preservation of the scenery on the Ruakituri river’. Carroll offered his assistance. Of Ngāti Kahungunu descent, a farmer and interpreter, and a former MP for Eastern Māori, since 1893 he had held the general seat of Waiapu. After inspection by the Commissioners, 123 acres (50 ha) between the river and Ruakituri Road, part of Small Grazing Run 86, were gazetted in August 1905 although only after land occupied by Alexander Mills was swapped for an area of adjacent forest reserve. The scenic reserve also included some caves with stalactites. In 1911 an additional 555 acres (224 ha) on the opposite side of the river was added by the Scenery Preservation Board, which replaced the Commission in 1906. A further 613 acres (248 ha) were added in 1930. This last acquisition was described in the annual report of the Scenery Preservation Department as comprising ‘precipitous and broken bush country on the Ruakituri River, situated in full view of the main Wairoa Waimana Road’ and quite ‘unsuitable for settlement’. It was noted that the ‘preservation of this bush will add greatly to the beauty of the route, and the land has also a certain amount of historic interest’, as it was from the shelter of the forest that in 1868 Te Kooti (?-1893) and his followers had repulsed pursuing government forces. Casualties included Captain Carr and Lieutenant Canning whose graves were on the opposite side of the river. In 1976 part of the adjoining small Erepati Scenic Reserve, a former Native Reserve set aside as a burial ground, was merged with Ruakituri Scenic Reserve.

info_origin: An original Māori name taken from the associated river. Ethnologist Elsdon Best (1856-1931) later a member of the Honorary Geographic Board described how Ruakōkoputuna was a ‘marker on the eastern boundary of the lands granted to Ngāti Kahungunu in the southern Wairarapa area by the Native Land Court’ in 1890. In 1897 the Ruakokoputuna Block of 8761 acres (3545ha) was surveyed by Percival Richard Earle (1855-1928) into ten grazing runs of 700 to 1400 acres (283 to 567ha). A Forest Reserve was proclaimed on part of the block in 1897. The misspelling Ruakokopatuna was frequently used on official plans and in newspapers, government reports and scientific papers into the 1920s. A Ruakokopatuna Settlers Association Incorporated also existed from 1957 to 1980. A detailed but unsubstantiated explanation of the meaning of the name was published in the Evening Post in 1932 referring to the limestone caves in the vicinity. These were ‘apparently well known to the Maoris, who named the district after them. "Ruakokoputana" (which is no doubt the same, as the above) means "the pit where the species of eel, with the firm flesh like the trout lived." The name was very apt, for to this day the caves are guarded by the tuna family, and one eel was seen a few weeks ago in the black depths of the main cave.’ A more literal interpretation was provided in ‘A Cultural Values for Wairarapa Waterways Report’ produced for the Greater Wellington Regional Council in 2011. Noting that the lower reaches are named Huangarua River, but the upper reaches are Ruakōkoputuna River, the report suggested that the latter river name identified two taonga species kōkopu and tuna and that kōkoputuna was a Wairarapa name for a very large eel.

Gazetteer of New Zealand Place Names. New Zealand: Government Printer.; NZGB Correspondence XLII/248; [NZMS 1 N23 1943 1st edition](https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE13267180); [NZMS 1 N23 1973 edition](https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE13267237 )}
info_origin: An original Māori name. An old pā site on a 267m hill. The name was confirmed by the New Zealand Geographic Board in 1973 as part of a sheet-by-sheet review of trig point names on the topographical NZMS1 map series. Trig points, short for trigonometrical points, are shown on the topographical maps as a specific location with its height. On the ground there is a black and white wooden structure which serves as a physical reference point for surveyors. The Board’s new view was that trig points ‘should not be named unless historically named and it is considered that the naming is not for the trig named but for the feature on which the trig stands’. Ruaroa was included the 1969 Gazetteer of New Zealand Place Names. It was named on the 1964 second edition of the NZMS1 series but not on the 1959 and original 1943 editions which gave only a spot height.
info_description: Pā site in Block VIII, Maungaru Survey District, trig Ruaroa A7AD is at the feature.

info_origin: The name of the Ruatangata Railway Station was changed in 1913 to Ruatangata Springs by the Minister of Railways. This was as a result of representations by the proprietor of the Kamo Springs Hotel. People visiting the springs were often inconvenienced by booking to Kamo instead of Ruatangata. The correct designation of the springs was "Kamo Spa", and the name Ruatangata Springs was considered by the Railways Department as unnecessarily unwieldy. Later changed to Kamo in 1962 without going through the process to alter the official name which remained Ruatangata Railway Station. Closed in 1982.

name: Saddle Hill
info_origin: 'Otago, 16 km from Dunedin. The hill was seen by Captain James Cook on 25 February 1770. He described it as ‘a remarkable saddle hill laying near the Shore’. In the early days it was frequently referred to as Saddleback Hill. Maori names: The pommel of the saddle was Makomako, lit. the tree (Aristotelia serrata) or the bellbird (Anthornis melanura); alternatively Makamaka, lit. To throw about, Cast a glance, or Recite incantations. The other peak was Pikiwaro, lit. piki: to climb; waro: abyss (both words have a variety of meanings). The flat between the peaks was Papakaio, lit. papa: flat; kaio: probably the South Island form of ngaio (Myoporum laetum).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: NZGB Correspondence Vol. 53 p.64 - Notes on D'Urville Island place names: Tower Rocks, Saddle Rocks. A group of tall rocks between Stephens Island and Cape Stephens, referred to on some maps as Saddle Rocks. There is a reef between Tower Rocks and Stephens Island. Seamen used to the area know of a channel through the reef but this is not advisable for outsiders to try and find it. The Saddle Rocks or Flat Rocks are a group of flat saddle like rocks lying on the south side of Stephens Passage and adjacent to Bilhook Bay. On many maps these names are switched around so that Tower Rocks are Saddle Rocks and vice versa. The Captain of the 'Jane Douglas' which was wrecked in Stephens Passage said that he had a problem recognising which rocks were where as the map contradicted the actual shape of both groups of rocks.

name: Sandfly Point
info_origin: ’In Milford Sound / Piopiotahi. Māori name: Te Namu-a-Hinenuitepō, the sandfly of Hinenuitepō. The English name copies that given in Māori tradition. After carving the sounds, the atua Tūterakiwhānoa showed his handiwork to Hinenuitepō, the goddess of death. Concerned that future generations would be entranced by the natural beauty and forget to work, she released a giant sandfly to remind them of the need to keep moving. To this day the descendants of that first namu (sandfly) faithfully carry out her orders.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

Cabbage Tree Swamp bore the Māori name Ngāanawai: lit. ngā: the; ana: caves; wai: water; The place where water ran into underground lava caves.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Scott Island
info_origin: Edward Evans, navigator on the SY Morning under Captain William R Colbeck, RNR, first sighted the islands (Haggitt Pillar and Scott Island) on 25 December 1902 during a relief expedition bringing supplies for the British National Antarctic Expedition (1901-04) under Robert Falcon Scott. Colbeck initially intended to name the feature Markham Island, for Sir Clements Markham who organised the British National Antarctic Expedition. On finally joining Scott in McMurdo Sound he was likely advised of the existing Markham Island back up the coast south of Mount Melbourne, already named by the British Antarctic Expedition, 1898-1900. In private letters with Sir Clements Markham, Colbeck discussed and confirmed the revised names he intended to give to the two features, with Markham replying on 20 May 1903 ‘I am glad you have given Scott’s name to your island, and Haggitt is a very good name for the small one’.
info_description: An island approximately 430m long southwest to northeast and half as wide, and approximately 583km northeast of Cape Adare, the northeasterly extremity of Victoria Land. The island is 54m high and is covered with an ice-cap.
feat_note: Scott Island and Haggitt Pillar were found to be 2.4km north of the previously charted position during a NIWA hydrographic and coastline survey (TAN0602) commissioned by LINZ  in 2006. See: https://www.hydro-international.com/content/article/surveying-in-the-ross-sea
