name: Scotts Ferry
info_origin: Named after Thomas Scott, who settled his family on a section/farm near the river mouth in the mid 1800s. Soon after he established a ferry service across the Rangitikei River for settlers in the area, for the port of Rangitikei and for his accommodation house and general store. Not named on previous mapping. This place was originally intended to be called Okanogan (or Okanagan), when first subdivided in the 1920's (DP 8196). The original property developer/planner was Canadian and Okanagon was the Indian name for his home town in Canada. However, locals at the time did not favour this name and preferred to be identified with pioneering icon Thomas Scott. [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Thomas Scott](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1s2/scott-thomas); 'From 1849 until 1897, Thomas Scott operated a ferry across the Rangitikei River, at first using a canoe. He was the father-in-law of James Bull, after whom Bulls was named.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Seaford
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {[A Trip to Taitapu, Nelson. 1909. Colonist, 23 February 1909, Page 4](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/TC19090223.2.38); [Pakawau Coal. 1862. Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle, 18 October 1862, Page 3](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NENZC18621018.2.9.4); [Town of Seaford. 1879. Alexander Turnbull Library](https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE26830798)}
info_origin: On the north side of the Pākawau Inlet. After a town was laid out here, there was an unsuccessful attempt to auction the mainly 5 acres (2 ha) sections in 1857. A further somewhat more successful auction took place the following year. Three Seaford residents appeared on the 1861 electoral roll. The town was still quite isolated up until road making commenced in 1862. Coal from the area was used successfully in Provincial Government trials. Now more accessible, further land sales occurred in 1864. A full town plan published under the authority of JS Browning, the Chief Surveyor for Nelson, was completed in 1879. The handful of streets were given as Miller, Layard, McLure and Livingstone. Another round of land sales occurred in 1904. But by 1909 Seaford had fallen into disuse locally being replaced by Pākawau, an original Māori name for the adjacent area. A Seaford Coal Company operated for 1912 until 1917 when it went into liquidation.

name: Sealey Glacier
info_origin: The original proposal made by John P. Findlay to the Honorary Geographic Board in December 1939 stated that the feature was ’named after E. Sealey [sic], a member of two expeditions into this country in 1936 and 1937.’ Earlier in the 1938/39 summer Findlay and companion Ian Whitehead first documented a ’symmetrical dome between Temple and the top of Jagged Ridge’. They named the dome Holloway Peak and the glacier descending from it Sealey Glacier. Findlay meant to name the glacier to recognise the accomplishments of fellow mountaineer Eldred H. Sealy (1913-1993), who accompanied John T. Holloway on two expeditions in the Olivine Range area in the 1936/37 and 1937/38 summers before moving to the United Kingdom later in 1938. On these expeditions Sealy and Holloway accomplished recorded first ascents of nine peaks in the Olivine Range and surrounding area. Climbing into the Olivine Ice Plateau to access Climax, Destiny and Ark Peaks is notoriously difficult and was a much-prized accomplishment by mountaineers at the time. 1936/37 was not a good climbing season owing to large snowfalls, so it was not until a fourth attempt that Sealy and Holloway made it into the Olivine Ice Plateau. Their 1937/38 expedition was also plagued by weather, both blinding hot temperatures and heavy summer storms. Early on Sealy and Holloway had abandoned plans to climb in the northern ranges but ascended several peaks around the Olivine Ice Plateau and in the Barrier Range.
info_description: A west flowing glacier in Olivine Range at the head of Sealy Stream, a tributary of Pyke River. Feature shown on: NZMS260 E39 Edition 1 1994 Limited Revision 1996; NZTopo50-CA10 335766.

info_origin: ’Named after Seatoun in Lanarkshire (or, less likely, Seaton in Forfarshire), Scotland, the home of the Crawford family, who had associations with both places. Māori name of Seatoun Beach: Te Tūranga-a-Kupe: lit. te: the; tūranga: waiting, wounding; a: of; Kupe. Kupe and Ngahue landed here, the former hurting his knee while bathing. Tūranga may refer to his wounding, his resting, or possibly both. When the beach was raised by earthquakes it was called Kirikiri-tatangi, lit. kirikiri: gravel; tatangi: to rattle, no doubt referring to the swishing of the gravel with the action of the waves. The flat area near the wharf was Te Pou-a-Amukete: The post of Amukete, a Ngāti Awa name.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: 'Abel Tasman National Park, between Golden Bay and Tasman Bay. On 14 January 1827 Dumont d’Urville wrote: ‘As we advanced towards the south, we saw that the vast bay comprised between the land of Cape Farewell on the one part and that of Cape Stephen on the other, and which Cook in his first voyage named “Blind Bay”, is divided into two basins very distinct by a remarkable point which I named “Separation Point”.’ Maori name: Te Matau, lit. te: the; matau: fish-hook.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: A coastal point between Whariwharangi Bay and Mutton Cove extending into Golden Bay / Mohua approximately 18 km northeast of Takaka. Feature shown on: NZMS260 N25; Infomap 346-02 Te Wai Pounamu Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BN25 998854

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Te Matau is an ancestral name and important to Ngati Tama and Te Atiawa as it is one of the boundary markers between Onetahua and Motueka. The name was changed by D’Urville, but iwi still refer to this name and old title deeds support the name Te Matau. Te Atiawa Tribunal evidence also recorded this name (see A Riwaka Nga Hekenga p. 117, Tribunal casebook Northern South Island Inquiry). Ngati Kuia and Ngati Apa note that Peart in Old Tasman Bay translates the name as meaning the fish hook of Maui. It was the western most point of the tukuwhenua and an occupation area. An older name for this place is Te Matau-a-Maui. Peart, Old Tasman Bay, p. 136. Ngati Rarua history: This translates as The Hook and represents the Eastern most point of Golden Bay and the Western tip of Tasman Bay. It was an area surrounded by a number of settlements of the local manawhenua iwi.
info_description: A coastal point between Whariwharangi Bay and Mutton Cove extending into Golden Bay / Mohua approximately 18 km northeast of Takaka. Feature shown on: NZMS260 N25; Infomap 346-02 Te Wai Pounamu Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BN25 998854

name: Sheep Hill Island
info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche February 2023: Objective ID: A5197802 {Claims of Natives to Wairarapa lakes and adjacent lands. 1891. Appendices to the Journals of the House of Representatives, G4; [Return of Occupation licenses. 1859. Wellington Independent, 8 March, Page 5.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WI18590308.2.12.3); Taylor, NM. (ed) 1966. The Journal of Ensign Best 1837-1843. New Zealand: Government Printer.; [Tiffen sketch maps](http://waihinga.ac.nz/chronology.htm); Wildlife Management Reserve (Ponui) R 143029 Archives New Zealand, Wellington.}
info_origin: British Army Lieutenant Abel Dottin William Best (1816-45) travelled from Wellington into the Wairarapa in 1840. He described the land around and to the north of Lake Ōnoke as 'a belt of swamp constantly subject to inundation either from freshers or from irruptions of the sea, next a belt of fine land then a belt of scrub immediately at the bottom and on the side of the hills which are low, broken by little valleys'. He observed that the waters 'now assume the form of a marshy river'. Future run holder Frederick John Tiffen's (1828-1911) impressionistic 1845 sketch maps of Lake Ōnoke and environments suggest small 'toi toi', ie, toetoe (Austroderia spp.) covered islands in the swamp. This area formed the eastern margin of Charles Matthew's Māori leasehold run. Sheep Hill Island was a fragment of the 150000 acres (60702 ha) west side of Lake Block 1 (Tūrakirae) purchase negotiated by Donald MacLean in 1853-54. Into the 20th century Sheep Hill Island remained in Crown ownership, although the immediate environment was altered by land drainage activities and engineering work on Ruamahanga River. In 1973 the Wildlife Division of the Department of Internal Affairs approached the Lands & Survey Department about designating 200 acres (80 ha) of the wetland area as a Wildlife Reserve. An inspection by the Division's Game Management Officer in 1973 indicated 100 acres (40 ha) of tidal swamp, 180 acres (72 ha) of undrained swamp and 370 acres (149 ha) of drained swamp. Lands & Survey accepted Wairarapa Catchment Board's advice that the area was gradually being inundated by sediment from Ponui Stream and declined the proposal. Correspondence was escalated to the Head of Department level, but Lands & Survey were unrelenting and by 1975 the Wildlife Division had abandoned its plans. The exact origins of the name remain obscure but are likely descriptive and date from the 1840-50s with either the white flowery plumes of the toetoe from a distance resembling sheep or the actual flocking of sheep on slightly higher ground.

name: Shiraishi Peak

Shiraishi has had continued involvement with ANSMET and the equivalent Japanese programme. He has also served as the Head of NIPR’s Antarctic Meteorite Research Center. Across his career Dr Shiraishi has collaborated internationally on many significant ventures including a three year term as COMNAP chair 2014-2017.

info_origin: ’The tidal river that flows through Silverdale village was named Te Weiti: lit. te: the; we: water; iti: little, by the Māori who used it as a waterway. An alternative translation is lit. te: the; wei: water; tī: cabbage tree (Cordyline spp.). In the late 1820s or early 1830s the first Europeans in the district corrupted the name to The Wade, but as the area became established by farmers and orchardists the need was felt for a new name. A public meeting in 1911 rejected such names as New Jerusalem and Mud-dale, and selected Silverdale, possibly because of silver poplars in the area, the leaves of which had silvery undersides. A local source proposed that the name originated in the 1860s from a prospector in search of silver, noting that the old poplars in the area are mostly eastern cottonwoods (Populus deltoides), not silver poplars.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Siple Coast

name: Skelton Glacier
info_origin: The name, bestowed by the New Zealand Party of the TAE, 1956-58, derives its origin from the Skelton Inlet. This glacier was chosen in 1957 as the New Zealand Party's route from the Ross Ice Shelf to the polar plateau. The TAE's Skelton Glacier was considered to be that flowing south between Clinker Bluff and Mount Tricouni, with Lower Staircase, The Landing, and Upper Staircase treated as features on the glacier. Over time cartographic use of the name shifted with the name use on the glacial ice flowing more directly southeast from Skelton Névé (eg, refer NZMS 135 (1970)).
info_description: A large glacier flowing from Skelton Névé, Victoria Land and entering the Ross Ice Shelf at Skelton Inlet. Feature shown on: AntTopo50-MH08

info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Skelton Névé
info_origin: Surveyed by New Zealand parties of the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition (CTAE), 1956-58, from January 1957 onwards. It was named by them for the Skelton Glacier.
info_description: The immense névé of the Skelton Glacier, lying on the west side of the Royal Society Range. It is almost circular in outline, 52km east to west, and has an area of over 2000km². It is bounded on the east by the western ridges of the Royal Society Range; on the south by the outlet of the Skelton Glacier, the Worcester Range, Escalade Peak, and the north end of the Boomerang Range, on the west by low nunataks and a continuous low ridge mostly inundated by ice moving east into the névé, and on the north by Mount Feather, the source of the Ferrar Glacier, and Pivot Peak.

name: Snares Islands/Tini Heke
info_origin: 'These ‘seven craggy islands’ were discovered by Europeans almost simultaneously in November 1791, by Captain George Vancouver in the Discovery and Lieutenant William Broughton in the Chatham. Broughton named them Knight’s Islands, after Captain Knight of the Royal Navy. When the two commanders compared notes and it was certain that Vancouver’s discovery took precedence, his choice was confirmed. Captain Raven of the Britannia ‘rediscovered’ them in 1792 and called them Sunday Islands. One larger island in the group was known to Maori as Te Taniwha: lit. te: the; taniwha: water monster.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. ‘Tini-heke translates as ‘descending mist or drifting fog’.’ Source: Beattie, H. Our Southernmost Maoris, 1954. (Beattie assembled the information from Māori informants at Bluff and veteran whalers and sealers.)

info_ref: File BRD-02-02-00-07; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760}
info_origin: 'The Māori name of this major mountain range dates from the explorer Māui’s first visit to Te Waipounamu. As related by Ngāi Tahu’s Kā Huru Manu site: ‘During their remarkable journey down the west coast of the island, the mountainous terrain of the Southern Alps was shrouded in clouds, with the alps a blur in the horizon. A crew member remarked that the line of white in the sky that could be seen in the distance was actually the summit of a range of lofty mountains. Although many others held the same view, Māui replied, “He tiritiri o te moana” — “It is only a mirage of the ocean”. As they arrived closer to shore, the “mirage” turned out to be an unbroken chain of mountains, stretching the length of the land. Upon arriving at Maitahi (Bruce Bay) in South Westland, the crew named this mountain range “Kā Tiritiri-o-te-moana” in memory of Māui’s false impression that the white-tipped mountains were an optical illusion.’ Captain James Cook bestowed the name Southern Alps on 23 March 1770, observing: ‘No country upon Earth can appear with a more ruged (sic) and barren Aspect than this doth.’' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDAzNDkxQjJBMzEwMDM3RTk4QkM); [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={986e9e2c-e8fc-e311-84cb-0050569755f4}))

name: South Island
land_district: Nelson, Marlborough, Westland, Canterbury, Otago, Southland
info_origin: The name South Island has been in long term and common usage for over a century. The island has had other English names historically (Middle Island, New Munster, Island of Victoria). A 1907 Minister of Lands instruction relates to the renaming of Middle Island to South Island. Early naming of the Northern and Southern Islands was recorded by Hobson in the Proclamation of Sovereignty of 21 May 1840. Hobson had intended to use the native names as per Cook’s chart, but Colenso inserted ‘the Nothern Island’ and ‘the Middle Island’. The name for Nothern Island was later corrected by Hobson’s Proclamation of 13 May 1841 to Northern Island. The Royal Charter of 1840 was received in New Zealand in early 1841 and it named the islands New Ulster (for the North Island), New Munster (for the South Island) and New Leinster (for Stewart Island / Rakiura), with Royal sanction and the gazette notice using these names. Since Royal Charters are perpetual, the names New Ulster, New Munster and New Leinster arguably have some legal standing (but not as Geographic names under the current NZGB Act 2008). They have not been used for the island names since 1841, though they did survive as provincial names up until 1853. Assigning South Island as an alternative name made official under the NZGB Act 2008, is an action that effectively overrides the Royal Charter by bringing the name within the statutory place naming framework empowered by Parliament in the NZGB Act 2008. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDRDNTNFOEQxNTEwMDM5MEQyMDM)
info_description: The southern of the two main islands of New Zealand, centred around NZTM 1446000E, 5177000N.
info_note: For information about the alternative official Māori name for this island, Te Waipounamu, see the alternative name record in this Gazetteer.

info_note:
Shown on NZ 250000 map 53. The original feature named Sponsors Peak was the adjacent peak to the southeast. The original proposers published a geological map naming the feature in Formations of the Beacon Group: A. D. Allen (1962) Geological investigations in southern Victoria Land, Antarctica, New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics, 5:2, 278-294,
DOI: 10.1080/00288306.1962.10423116. On the United States Geological Survey (USGS) 1:250k topographic map ST 57-60/5 Taylor Glacier (1965) the name was mispositioned, and in 1977 Nickell Peak approved for the original peak. While some New Zealand publications continued to refer to Sponsors Peak in the original position, over time Sponsors Peak and Nickell Peak became set in common use for the positions as mapped. At its 27 January 2026 hui the Antarctic Names Committee reconfirmed Sponsors Peak in the position as shown on maps since 1965 and Nickell Peak in the position from 1977.

name: St. Arnaud
info_origin: Named after Arnaud Jacques Leroy de Saint-Arnaud (1798-1854), Commander-in-Chief of the French army during the Crimean war (1854-56). William Travers named the St. Arnaud Range to the East of Lake Rotoiti in 1855. The township of St. Arnaud gained its name from the range in 1921, formerly being Rotoiti after the adjoining lake, to avoid confusion with Rotoiti near Rotorua. This being when sections of the township were first offered for sale. Despite protest, the post office name was changed to St. Arnaud in 1951, and an attempt to revert the name to Rotoiti in 2007 failed. Another proposal in 2019 to replace the abbreviation St. with the full word Saint, was also declined.

name: Stephens Bay
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA325625; fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412 {Broad, Lowther. 1892. Jubilee History of Nelson, 1842-1892. New Zealand: Bond Finey; [Statistics of New Zealand. 1860. Colonist, 11 September, Page 2](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/TC18600911.2.9); McAloon, James. 1997. Nelson A Regional History. New Zealand: Cape Catley; Mitchell, Hillary and John. 2004. Te Tau Ihu o te Waka. New Zealand: Huia Publishers; [Pattie, Robert. 1934. Early Riwaka, Mr and Mrs Samuel Stephens. Nelson Evening Mail, 5 May, Page 3](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NEM19340505.2.32); [Pattie, Robert. 1939. Early surveyors – Samuel Stephens founding of Riwaka and Motueka Pioneering day at Riwaka. Nelson Evening Mail, 15 April, Page 9](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NEM19390415.2.117)}
info_origin: Samuel Stephens (c.1803-55) was part of the Nelson Preliminary Expedition which arrived in 1841. Technically well trained, he commenced surveying duties under Chief Surveyor Frederick Tuckett, whose high-handed manner soon alienated Stephens and others. Involved in the initial surveys of Nelson township, Stephens was also in charge of the party that surveyed settlements at Riwaka and Motueka in 1842-43. Local Māori upset over section boundaries disrupted some of the work by removing survey pegs. Stephens’ assurance that their habitations and cultivations would not be included in the 50 acres (20 ha) sections that were to be auctioned placated them and they allowed the survey to continue. However, the New Zealand Company did not honour these commitments. Stephens replaced Tuckett as Chief Surveyor to the New Zealand Company in Nelson Settlement in 1844. He made a detailed assessment of the Aorere and Tākaka areas in 1844. With William Fox, Edward Jollie and others he travelled through Queen Charlotte Sound / Tōtaranui and on to the Wairau plains in 1845. Resigning from the company because of ill-health and being of some means, he purchased a large area of flat land on the north bank of Riuwaka River where his property was known as Dehra Doon. Stephens imported goats for the farm – the source of later large feral populations. In 1850 he took up a sheep run in Wairau. For over a decade he collected local meteorological data. He was the District of Motueka’s member of the Provincial Council in 1854-55 and MP for Nelson in 1854-55. For many years Stephens owned land at what became known as Stephen’s Bay. Samuel Stephens, his wife and her maid camped there for several weeks during summer. The 1892 ‘Jubilee History of Nelson’ observed that ‘from his many estimable qualities [he] was much, respected’. A more recent regional history paints him as unlucky in having his house burnt down several times and being ‘snobbish.’

(Page 12 Rickard); NZGB Correspondence Vol. 53 p.64 - Notes on D'Urville Island place names: Takapou=Matipou tree. Rewa=float. Stephen's Island was once covered with Matipou trees, particularly around the lower parts of the island right down to the waters edge. It looked like an island of Matipous floating on the ocean. Thus, Takapou-rewa. Older names were Ti-tapu and Ti-tapua, possibly relating to the tuatara lizards often regarded as a bad omen and best left tapu.

name: Stephens Passage
info_origin: Stephens Island named by Captain Cook in memory of the British Admiralty Secretary. It is said, that in the early days that rum ships were sailed by tradees through the passage on their way to the West Coast goldfields to trade rum for gold. Three ships carrying gold bars were wrecked and are now in Stephens Passage sea floor. A local fisherman was dragging in an extra heavy lump of rock to the waters surface when he was drawing in his fishing line,. The rock was a muddy colour about ten inches long, three inches wide and tapered at each end. A fish hook caught the fisherman's hand and forced him to let the line and rock go, so we will never know if it was gold as he believed it to be.

info_origin: ’It is believed that the island, which Cook thought to be a peninsula, was charted by William Stewart, first officer of the Pegasus, in August 1809. Most of the names applied by Stewart and Chase, captain of the Pegasus, were subsequently removed or replaced during the Acheron survey led by Captain John Lort Stokes. For a brief period the name New Leinster was applied to the island, but was discontinued when New Munster, which had encompassed only the South Island, was applied to the South Island plus Stewart Island and the southern portion of the North Island (then New Ulster). At one time a glowing report on the island by W.H. Pearson, commissioner of crown lands at Invercargill, caused it to be nicknamed Pearsons Paradise. Stewart Island / Rakiura is the site of Rakiura National Park. Māori name: Rakiura, often translated to ‘glowing skies’ in reference to the story of Te Rakitāmau, who was embarrassed when he was declined the hand in marriage of the two daughters of a high-ranking Ngāti Māmoe chief. It is said that the red skies of Rakiura reflect his blushing embarrassment. Alternative names are Te Puka-a-Māui: lit. te: the; puka: Ngāi Tahu pronunciation of punga, anchor stone; o: of; te: the; waka: canoe; a: of; Māui; and Te Puka-a-Aoraki. The South Island was Māui’s canoe, the North Island his fish. The Anglicised name Te Picamoke was used for the whole island at the time of its acquisition.’' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={b7af3198-4052-e311-8212-005056970030})
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS265/2; Infomap 346-02 Te Wai Pounamu Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-CJ09 199826

info_origin: Originally approved for a new post office name in 1940 on request of the Post and Telegraph Department. Gazetted in 1948 for the locality. Johannes Andersen noted in 1940 that the name had been used for at least sixty years but did not know who Stewart or Stewarts was. The name refers to the adjacent gully, in which the main channel of the Waimakariri River now flows. Prior to an overflow flood in the 1880s, the river flowed northward through Kaiapoi as a number of meandering channels, before turning east to the sea.; 'The picnic grounds were in a gully until the Waimakariri River changed its course and flowed through it. The gully was part of a farm owned for a time by John Stewart; in 1924 a son, John Dougall Stewart, regained possession and began sheep farming, retaining the portion by the river as a picnic ground. Maori name: Te Rau-a-kaha: possibly te: the; rau: leaves; a: of; Kaha.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Sticking Up Gully
info_origin: The name commemorates an historical event which took place in 1861, when Henry Garrett, with a gang of 7 others, held up a group of 15 men travelling back to Dunedin via this route from their gold diggings at Gabriels Gully. Only about £400 was taken from the victims because they had already sent their gold to Dunedin via the gold escort. The victims were tied to trees and treated well, then left with the promise that someone would return to release them. However, the victims were able to get loose and subsequently Garrett and another of the gang members were caught, tried and imprisoned in Dunedin for the crime. The area is well known for this piece of history, with the trees used to tie up the victims being able to be identified for many years after the event.

name: Sturdee Peak
info_ref: Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 1, pp. 65-71; vol. 7, pp. 134-146.; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Minutes, 1930; New Zealand Geographic Board: Correspondence, vol. 23, pp. 65-66.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 1948 (42).; Otago Daily Times, 5 May 1915, p. 3.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: The naming of this feature proved to be a rather fraught process. In August 1919, the Survey Department tried to label it ‘Beatty Peak’ to commemorate the recent visit of HMS New Zealand. The New Zealand was an Indefatigable-Class battlecruiser whose construction had been financed by the Dominion’s Government as a gift to Britain. She had served under Admiral David Beatty’s command as part of his Battlecruiser Fleet during the largest seaborne action of the First World War at Jutland. However, unbeknown to the Survey Department, the peak had already been climbed by Hugh Chambers and Hugh Wright who had conferred on it the name Sturdee Peak. By a remarkable coincidence, Doveton Sturdee, like Beatty, was a prominent British naval officer. He led the British forces at the 1914 Battle of the Falkland Islands, during which a German cruiser force was almost completely destroyed, and commanded the 4th Battle Squadron at Jutland. Chambers and Wright had chosen Sturdee Peak to complement the surrounding features, all of which were all named after famous ‘navigators’. After an investigation by the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand, the name Sturdee Peak was assigned in 1930. The New Zealand Geographic Board then confirmed this decision in 1948.

info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412 {[Angela Ballara. 'Mahupuku, Hāmuera Tamahau', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1993. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2m27/mahupuku-hamuera-tamahau) (accessed 7 September 2022); [Angela Ballara. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2n15/niniwa-i-te-rangi) (accessed 7 September 2022); [Wairarapa News 1902. Evening Post, 17 February, Page 6](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19020217.2.48)}
info_origin: Land on higher ground east of Martinborough owned by Tamahau Mahupuku (c.1840-1904). He sold the 26000 acres (10521 ha) Tablelands Estate as well as his Longbush Estate to the Land Settlement Board for closer settlement in 1902. Māori owners referred to Tablelands as Kehemane, a transliteration of [garden of] Gethsemane, and it was part of the larger Ngā-waka-a-Kupe block. A large portion of the block was controlled by two of the leading Ngāti Hikawera families, Tamahau and Hikawera, parts of which they leased while on another portion they developed a sheep station. Tamahau Mahupuku’s brother Wi Hikawera Mahupuku commissioned the carving of meeting house, Takitimu, which was sited at Kehmane in 1890. It was gifted to the nation in 1901 and destroyed by fire in 1911. Ownership of the Ngā-waka-a-Kupe block was not without dispute coming before the Native Land court in 1890 and 1892. As part of this decision a 1053 acres (426 ha) Ngāti Hikawera Reserve was set aside at Tablelands.

name: Tahoraiti
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5104718 {Colenso, William 1882? On matters relating to the Maori Tongue. Pamphlet Collection of Sir Robert Stout, Vol 65; Cowan, James. 1940. Sir Donald McLean. New Zealand: Reed; NZ Geographic Board, Correspondence 1939, Minutes 1939; Wilson, JG. 1939. History of Hawkes Bay. Hawkes Bay Centennial Committee, New Zealand: Reed.}
info_origin: A clearing in the 70 Mile Bush. Donald Mclean, subsequently the Chief Land Purchase Commissioner, found in 1850 that Te Hiriwanui and Karaitiana had claimed the clearing. McLean provided a description of the area ‘passed through a totara bush, across the Manawatu and Tamaki rivers, through a second bush; then through Tahoraiti, a grassy plain, well-suited for sheep, watered by the Makirikiri stream, surrounded by heavy forest timber, containing about 700 acres (283 ha)’. William Colenso observed that the name was ‘a highly significant one, meaning, the little open wilderness’. Tahoraiti was one of the three original stations in the area leased from Māori. A railway station opened in 1883 as Tahoraite. Historian JG Wilson considered that the name was originally written as Tahora-iti, which he more prosaically translated as ‘little clearing’, a much larger forest clearing being at Oringi, and that ‘Tahoraite’ was a ‘European corruption’. By 1907 the railway station had adopted Tahoraiti. The correct Tahoraiti spelling was confirmed by the Honorary New Zealand Geographic Board in 1939.

name: Tāhuahua-Paopao-Karoro Island
info_origin: NgāiTakoto history: Tahuahua Paopao Karoro (Walker Island) is located in the mouth of the Rangaunu Harbour and was, in earlier years, occupied by NgaiTakoto whanau. According to traditional korero, the traditional name given by Ngai Takoto is Tahuahua Paopao Karoro. Tahuahua (land mass) Paopao (the sound a baby chick makes as it emerges from an egg) Karoro (seagull). This is an ancient Ngai Takoto name that derives from the use of the island as a habitat and food gathering area. This name is supported by a Kaimaumau korero relating to (Kura) who apparently while still a near new born baby, yet to be named, as a girl child, had been taken to the Island with her parents (her father being Kiritipa Te Awa and her mother Ngapeka (nee) Ngauma) and other whanau to collect kai such as kuaka, seagull eggs, and other food. Inadvertently the child was left behind when the whanau packed up and left. On realising what had occurred and with the retrieval of her from the island, the elders of the time decided that because of the incident, the child should be named after the island, so that in the first instance the near loss of a child would be remembered and no other parent would do the same, and secondly, the island’s name would be recalled by this incident and remembered. The child was therefore named Tahuahua Paopao Karoro Te Awa (Paopao for short), after the island. Though the name refers to the abundant availability of seagull eggs on the island it also gives reference to its abandonment by its one time inhabitants. After suffering a calamitous storm that saw the island stripped of both vegetation and fertile soils, an accompanying sea surge that, coupled with the storm, removed possibly more than 9 tenths of its land mass. At one time the land area once stretched from what we see today, to opposite and past Kaimaumau point with an opposing shoreline on the Awanui channel. Today we see only a minute portion of what once was the island, now abandoned by its inhabitants, leaving only a habitat for the migratory kuaka and the seagulls to lay their eggs in prolific abundance.
info_description: A small estuarine island up to 1km in length at low tide, near the entrance to Rangaunu Harbour and west of Karikari Peninsula. Feature shown on: NZMS260 O04 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-AU26 265372.

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; Objective ID: A3379678
info_origin: Reed - 'Tahunanui: Nelson, 5 km from Nelson. Lit. tahuna: shoal or sandbank; nui: large.'. Tahunanui Beach was commonly known as ‘The Sands' until a competition was run in 1902 to suggest a name, with a prize of one guinea. 442 suggestions were made and the Māori name Tahuna was selected, meaning ‘sea beach' or ‘sand hill'. This caused a problem for the post office, however, as there was an existing Tahuna Post Office in Morrinsville, so the name Tatahi was suggested, and was in use from 1908. Tatahi was not popular, however, so the name Tahunanui was coined, referring to the locality, and was officially granted in 1911. Refer www.theprow.org.nz/places/tahunanui/

name: Taieri Lake Recreation Reserve
info_origin: 'The name may properly have been Taiari, the term used for the tide on the eleventh day of the lunar month. Other interpretations are that it means Shining river, or To smash (or pulp), or derives from Makotaieri, lit. an edible fish, a dogfish or young shark, which occurs locally. The original Maori name of Lake Taieri was Tunaheketaha, said to mean Dangling the eels, although other meanings are possible for heke and taha. Taieri Mouth was originally named Hull in 1863 and a street plan drawn up with names of Yorkshire towns. Maori place names in the vicinty include Motupara Pa on the south side of the river mouth; Otuarae, the cave at the first rocky headland; and Te Aokakume, a fishing camp on the beach, named after a wife of the founder of Ngati Mamoe.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Taipā
info_origin: 'Taipa River: Various accounts exist. According to one, after a period of fighting two chiefs erected a fence between their respective pa, calling the place Taiapa (dividing fence or boundary), eventually shortened to Taipa. In another version one of the same chiefs, Kauri, coveted lands close to the sea front and called the place where seafood was so plentiful Taipa: lit. tai: tide or sea water; pa: to touch. Again, Taipa may originally have been the name of a boulder placed in the river to stop a neighbouring iwi plundering pipi beds: lit. tai: sea water; pa: to obstruct. Finally, it has been said that the village by the sea was overwhelmed by a tidal wave, therefore tai meant the water of that wave, and pa their fortified village.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Taitā
info_ref: Objective ID: A3808636; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Best, E. 1921. Old Redoubts, Blockhouses and Stockades of the Wellington district. Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute 53, 14-28; McDonnell, H. 2021. Publicans of the Port Nicholson district on the Colony of New Zealand. Vera, Wellington; NZGB Correspondence XX/154; XXXIII/54, 128-131; [Untitled. 1846. Wellington Independent, 27 May, Page 2](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WI18460527.2.7)}
info_origin: A suburb of Lower Hutt City. Variously translated as driftwood in a riverbed or a snag in a river, Taitā was the site of an established Māori settlement and surrounding gardens. A Native Reserve was laid out after the arrival of New Zealand Company settlers in 1840. For a time in 1846 local militia and some Māori allies occupied a stockade at Taitā. An early settler was George Buck (1817-94), owner of the Traveller’s Rest Hotel at Taitā from 1850 to 1864. With European settlement, the area developed as an important market gardening area until the mid-20th century. Post WWII, Taitā was one of the sites of largescale state housing developments. The Honorary Geographic Board approved the naming of the new Taitā Railway Station in 1945. The spelling ‘Taitai’ was used in the press and by some businesses from the late 1840s until the early 1900s. Ethnologist Elson Best agreed with George Buck’s son, surveyor William Buck, that the correct spelling was ‘Taitai’, which would offer some alternative meanings, but Taitā became the established name.

name: Takanini
info_origin: The name comes from that of a local rangatira, Īhaka Wirihana Takaanini Te Tihi, of Te Ākitai Waiohua. In 1863 Īhaka Takaanini received a Crown grant of 1120 acres, but died the following year imprisoned on Rākino Island. The Crown took some of the land of 'Takaanini's Grant' for the route of the North Island Main Trunk railway in 1878 and in 1885 Takaanini's son Te Wirihana Takaanini sold the remainder of the grant to Auckland solicitor Samuel Jackson. In 1913 the Crown acquired additional land to build a railway station which opened in the same year. In 1914 the Maru Land Company subdivided the ‘Town of Takanini’ (sic) around the railway station. Services for Takanini followed such as Takanini Post Office in 1914 and Takanini School in 1923, perpetuating the misspelling of Takanini over Takaanini. In 1930 the spelling was corrected by the Honorary Geographic Board following a request from the Ākarana Māori Association. This decision was gazetted as official in 1948 (for just Takaanini Railway Station) under the New Zealand Geographic Board Act 1946. The matter was revisited again 1949 when the Board began checking the spelling of the Post Office and Railway Station names. The recently gazetted Honorary Board decisions now held statutory weight and required compliance. In discussions with New Zealand Railways and New Zealand Post Office the Board agreed to backtrack and gazetted the names officially as Takanini to accord with ‘established use’. The reversion to Takanini was also in part supported by orthographic advice from Sir Āpirana Ngata, who considered that the dropping of the double a was appropriate at this time for long vowels. However, this advice was incorrect as the name is personal name and compound word of 'Taka' and 'ānini'. Board member Johannes Andersen pointed out the error in 1951, but while the Board acknowledged it, the decision to alter to 'Takanini' to 'accord with common use' was not rescinded.
info_description: A locality between Manurewa to the north and Papakura to the south. Feature shown on: NZMS260 Q12 R12 Edition 2 1995; NZTopo50-BB32 707988

info_origin: An original Māori name which writer-historian Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) noted referred to the people of the Tainui waka laying down their flax mats and sleeping there, figuratively meaning that they resided there for some time. In 1875 Native Land Court Judge John Rogan (1823-99) ruled on some 30 land blocks including Takapau of 7182 acres (2906 ha) which was awarded to Hepetai Matai and 18 others. That same year, Richard Noble (1842-97), a former sergeant in the Armed Constabulary and later the Hawkes Bay Militia, purchased the Takapau Block of 7,344 acres (2972ha) for £1,436. At the time this was the largest private land purchase north of Gisborne. Noble called the property Broadlands. He sold it in 1883, still partly covered in heavy bush, along with 4500 acres (1821 ha) of leasehold land to James MacFarlane (1851-1931). MacFarlane later became heavily involved in local body affairs. In 1903 the Liberal Government acquired the station, now of 10400 acres (4209ha), as part of its closer land settlement policy and subdivided it into 17 farms renamed Wigan Settlement by Lands and Survey. Takapau school opened in 1895. In 1920 the remaining Takapau Station leases terminated and the land reverted to Māori management.

info_origin: Located on plains at the northern edge of the 40 Mile Bush. A visiting chief bestowed the name Takapau on the area in recognition of the great hospitality he received from Rakaihikuroa and his wife Papauma and named it after their first son Kahukura Takapau. The locality has been occupied since the 16th century and the Horeore pā adjacent to present day Takapau was constructed towards the end of the 17th century. One of the first Europeans to pass through the area was Bishop George Selwyn in 1842. On emerging from the bush Selwyn recorded that, ‘to our great joy we came in a few minutes upon a noble plain, stretching as far as the eye could reach, with the exception of two kahikatea clumps – the small remains of an ancient forest, which had formerly occupied the ground’. Much of the plain was quickly taken up in pastoral runs. In 1876, Sydney Johnston (1841-1917), the son of John Johnston, owner of the large Orua Wharo estate which he ultimately inherited, employed surveyor James Rochfort (1840-1924) to lay out a town on part of the estate. Rochfort, originally an architect in New Zealand, retrained as an engineer and surveyor. He was employed in government service in the Hawke’s Bay Region before moving to private practice as a surveyor and engineer in 1874. The town was named Takapau and in 1877 the sections were offered for sale. The name has been translated literally as ‘a sleeping mat’.

name: Takapaukura / Tom Bowling Bay
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/1017; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Kuri and Te Aupouri history: Takapaukura means reed mat and is named for the mats used to repair the Kurahaupo waka on its journey to New Zealand. Takapaukura is noted as a papakainga by Reverend Marsden in his evidence to the Waitangi Tribunal, 'Te Mana O Te Hiku O Te Ika' (Wai 45, Document A7 December 1986, p.2). He also notes on pp. 4-5 that the Kurahaupo waka made landfall at Takapaukura, which he states is 'a name given to commemorate the use of the mats as repair materials.' Marsden stated that this referred to the tradition that when the migration waka arrived at the Kermadec Islands, the Kurahaupo was holed while crossing into the lagoon. The waka was repaired using woven mats which were held in place by timber placed over them and lashed with the sling-line of their seine net. Stokes notes that Tom Bowling Bay was also referred to as Takapaukura. (Stokes, A Review of the Evidence in the Muriwhenua Lands Claims p. 47). Dorothy Urlich Cloher states that ‘Pohurihanga and his companions continued on to arrive at the northern tip of New Zealand, passed Murimoto Island and landed at Te Wakura or Oakura in Takapaukura (now called Tom Bowling Bay)’ (The Tribes of Muriwhenua: Their Origins and Stories Auckland University Press, 2002, p. 16).
info_description: A coastal bay at the northern extremity of New Zealand, extending south-west from Ngā Atua Tātā / Kerr Point for approximately 5km to Taurere Bay. Feature shown on: NZMS260 M02 N02 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-AT25 955916

info_origin: The name is an historical link for Ngāti Toa to Kawhia, the Waikato and Maniapoto tribes and notes a time during the escapdes and reign of Te Rauparaha. The link between Ngati Toa and Takapūwāhia to Kawhia stems from the history related to the Waikato and Maniapoto tribes. Te Rauparaha, a well known figure in the history of the Wellington area. He quarrelled constantly with his tribal counterparts, causing division and upheavel to the point where Ngāti Mahanga commenced to migrate south and in the course of that event took the lives of a number of Ngāti Toa. Te Rauparaha reacted quickly claiming victory over his adversaries. This resulted in further retaliation by Waikato eventuating in Te Rauparaha journeying southward. Following many a battle, Te Rauparaha finally settled Ngāti Toa in the Wellington area and upper south island. The name Takapūwāhia was the former village where Ngāti Toa resided in the Kawhia rohe.

Standing Rock, is the correct spelling, as advised by Māori elders and the point being named in association with rock at the end of the point. While local histories did record 'Takatu', it was also noted D'Urville in 1827 recorded 'Tokatau Wenoua’ [Tokatu Whenua] for the feature. Locals advised that when settlers arrived in the 1830's the area had been depopulated of its Māori population by the musket wars with only a few families having escaped to Titirangi and who did not return for forty-fifty years. Taking these events into account along with dialectal differences in spoken Māori, locals considered it was unlikely 'Tokatu' could be proven to be correct.

info_origin: An original Māori name associated with Tākou River. The Mahuhu or Māhuhu-ki-te-rangi canoe, in one tradition captained by Rongomai, landed at Whangaroa, Tākou and Whangaruru. In one of several versions of the story, on its return the canoe was turned to stone on the shore at Tākou Bay. In 1831 Archdeacon Henry Williams recorded that 500-600 Māori resided here; by 1870 this number had fallen to 50. This was five years after Land Purchase Commissioner, Henry Tacy Kemp (1818-1901), had secured the 2500 acres (1012 ha) Takou Block for £217/10/- or about 2/- per acre. Hori Kemara was the first of the 10 signatories on the deed. By 1891 1660 acres (672 ha) at Tākou Bay remained as Māori land and was regarded by officials as ‘unproductive’. In 1904 the Takou Bay Native School was established by the Auckland Education Board after discussions dating back to 1901.

name: Tāmaki
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA325625; A3968704; A3955095
info_origin: ’This well-known Auckland suburb takes its name from the Māori name for the Auckland isthmus, Tāmaki Makaurau: Tāmaki; makau: lovers; rau: a hundred, many; also known as Tāmaki-whenua: Contested land. Both names are appropriate, for this fertile region in a strategic position was much valued and many battles were fought for possession of it. Also associated with these names are Tāmaki-kai-ngā-ika-me-ngā-wheua-katoa (Tāmaki where the fish were so succulent they could be eaten bone and all), and Tāmaki-herenga-waka (Tāmaki where waka were moored). In these cases, Tāmaki referred only to the isthmus area (the narrow neck of land between the Waitematā and Manukau harbours). Herenga has the meaning of ‘bound’, which also refers to the binding together of different descent (waka) groups in Tāmaki. Among other accounts are a link to Kiwi Tāmaki, the eighteenth-century leader of Te Wai-o-Hua; to a son of Maruiwi of Taranaki; and to the chief Maki who lived at Manurewa. The original name for the Tāmaki River was Te Wai-o-Taiki, lit. te: the; wai: stream; o: of; Taiki: a chief of Ngāi Tai.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Tapu
info_origin: 'This word, as part or the whole of a name, was given for a particular meaning, relating to sacred prohibitions, connected either with religion or with reservation of land. Tapu on the Coromandel Peninsula preserves a memory of a raid on Taraia’s pa by a war party from Katikati; many local people were killed and buried near the mouth of the river, making the land tapu. As diggers arrived to try their luck at this rich goldfield, notices were erected warning against trespass on the tapu site, and in the course of time the locality was called Tapu by the diggers. It was once known as Hastings, after Warren Hastings, governor general of Bengal, and before that as Rauwhitiora, after a chief who was drowned while gathering shellfish.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Tapuae Marine Reserve
info_description: The Taranaki coast is well known for its ruggedness and spectacular landforms, and the 1,404 ha Tapuae Marine Reserve covers a classic part of this scenery. The remains of an ancient volcano sit at the northern end of Tapuae Marine Reserve, visible as a series of islands and rocks (their steep sides continue deep down beneath the water). The southern part of the reserve is typical of the wild Taranaki coast – reef, mud and sand below, and black sand beaches above. Tapuae Marine Reserve adjoins the Ngā Motu/Sugar Loaf Island Marine Protected Area, south of New Plymouth.

info_ref: Corres XIV pp 187, XXVII pp 75, LVI pp 156-165, LXI pp 102-107; File 14/50-52, 43; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Previously identified as Tapuaenuku on maps, this means to shuffle feet", which was insulting to the Māori people. The Māori translation is "the sacred footprints of the Rainbow God". Commonly referred to as "Tappy". Sometimes stated that Lieutenant James Cook named the feature Mount Odin, but there is no evidence of this name until the mid 19th century (eg, appearing in newspapers 1859 along with Mount Thor and Mount Freya). Published charts from hydrographic surveys of Capt. Stokes (published 1856-57) only name Tapauenuku with 'Mount Odin' appearing later with revisions 1870. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDQ3NzVCNUFBMzEwMDMzQjY2NzE); [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={54bc5ee2-3f52-e311-8212-005056970030})); 'Tapuae-o-Uenuku is the ancestral mountain for the local Ngāi Tahu hapū (subtribe) of Ngāti Kurī. The name refers to the sacred footsteps of the ancestor Uenuku. Tapuae-o-Uenuku was also one of the crew on the Āraiteuru waka.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: A significant hill in close proximity to Te Kawa-o-Tāwhaki. Tāpui means to bespeak or reserve, usually by way of marking. Uira means lightning. Hence, the name Tāpui-o-te-uira means ‘marked by lighting.’ This name is also directly associated with the ancestor Tāwhaki - who in Ngāti Rangi traditions is asociated with lightening and thunder. These hills are the guardians of the local kaitiaki, resident in the Ararawa area, located in the Parapara Ranges.

name: Taputeranga Marine Reserve
info_description: This reserve spans the coast along some of Wellington’s southern suburbs, and is easy to reach by city bus. No two days are the same at Taputeranga - the weather is changeable and the water churns through Cook Strait, creating a moody and complex undersea environment. It lies at the meeting place of two oceanic currents and is home to a richly varied mixture of animals and plants. It is particularly popular with crabs, lobsters, starfish and octopus. Kelp plants up to 20 m tall grow in sheltered places. Sinclair Head and Red Rocks Scientific Reserves can be found 1 km west of Taputeranga. Sinclair Head/Te Rimurapa is a winter haul-out for the New Zealand fur seal. Taputeranga Marine Reserve is located on the Wellington south coast, approximately 6 km from the city centre.

name: Tarakena Bay
info_origin: The name was apparently a "leftover" from previous Māori tribes, beaten in battle and driven out of the area. The occupying tribe, and their descendants have no direct translation of the bay name. The bay was associated with the great Ngai Tara Chief Tuteremoana, as it was the landing area for his twin-pa complex, Rangitatau, on the hills immediately above. Previously identified on maps as "Taraki Bay". Tarakena Bay was the site of Wellington's first Pilot Station. After the 1855 earthquake raised the level of a lot of the land around Wellington and shoaled the bay, the pilot station was relocated to Worser Bay. Refer Correspondence for extensive references for Tarakena Bay mentions in text.

name: Taranaki Maunga
info_origin: Taranaki Tūpuna written and oral history: 'The name of the mountain is memorialised by the deeds of the Kāhui Maunga ancestors Maruwhakatare, Ruataranaki and Tahurangi. As they became a permanent part of the geography, Ruataranaki travelled high up to the source of the Hangatahua River where he ceremonially anchored the mountain. He climbed to its base and dug a rua (cave) where he settled for a period of time. When the time came for the naming ceremony, Maruwhakatare (Ruataranaki’s father in-law) consecrated the ceremony with karakia. After a while Tahurangi then climbed the peak and lit a ceremonial fire to fix the name of Ruataranaki and to place his authority over the whole mountain. The rua that Ruataranaki excavated became a famous burial cave named ‘Te Ana-a-Tahatiti’ which was used up until the end of the 19th century for the interment of bones. This is near the source of the Hangatahua River.' 'In April 2025 the Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act replaced the official names Mount Taranaki or Mount Egmont with Taranaki Maunga; ‘maunga’ means ‘mountain’. In the same ruling, Egmont National Park became Te Papa-Kura-o-Taranaki. The Māori name of the cone-shaped maunga means lit. tara: peak; a: of; naki: possibly a corruption of ngaki, meaning shining, or clear of vegetation. Captain James Cook gave the English name after the Earl of Egmont, John Perceval, the former first lord of the Admiralty. The name Taranaki memorialises the Kāhui Maunga ancestors Maruwhakatare, Ruataranaki and Tahurangi. The chief, Tahurangi, renamed the mountain from Pukeonaki to Taranaki to honour Ruataranaki, founding ancestor of Taranaki iwi. Tahurangi climbed the peak and lit a ceremonial fire to affix Ruataranaki’s name to the mountain. For the contentious history of names for this defining feature of the Taranaki region, see appendix 2.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: The distinctive conical maunga rising to 2518m on the western cape of the North Island. NZTopo50-BJ29 917498.
treaty_legislation: Section 23 and 24 and 25 Te Ture Whakatupua mō Te Kāhui Tupua 2025/Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act 2025

info_origin: An original Māori name, which literally translates as taringa - ear and motu - cut off. A Māori track named Tekowhatungawha 'the cracked stone road' ran from Taringamotu to Wakatumutumu at the headwaters of Mōkau River. Austrian geologist Ferdinand Hochstetter travelled through Taringamotu Valley in 1858, 'We had no difficulty in wading through the [Taringamotu] river, as it rippled along over its broad shingle-bed and proceeded up the valley along the left river-bank; crossed the river a second time and were in Petania (Bethany). Such is the Christian name of a Maori village formerly called Teterenga, and known also by the general designation Tuhua Settlement.' In 1869 the Minister of Defence, Theodore Minet Haultain (1817-1902), possibly inaccurately, was advised that military leader and prophet Riwha Titokowaru (1823?-88) was now somewhere in the vicinity of Taringamotu. Te Kooti also paused near Taringamotu placing pou in the ground and seeking divine inspiration before his meeting with Rewi Maniopoto at Taumaranui. Government Surveyor John Rochfort (1832-93), after examining a possible 'central route' for the North Island Main Trunk railway, appeared before a Parliamentary Select Committee stating that, 'There is some good land and Native settlements up the Taringamotu, and a large amount of totara'. In 1887 a newspaper reporter, when few European had ventured into this area recorded the scene, 'As we approached the Taringamotu settlement I found that distance certainly lent enchantment to the view, for it was situated on a piece of land that in Waikato would be looked upon as very inferior; there was some poor swamp, and on the dry land stunted rushes, and a small patch of oats by the side of the road was struggling for existence against some equally poor-looking sorrel. Here we forded the Taringamotu creek, another tributary of the Ongarue. Along the right bank was a narrow strip of bush, perhaps five hundred yards (457 m) long, the timber being principally matai and rimu'. Whanganui and Maniapoto chiefs had agreed on the boundary of Pukeweka Block when it went before the Native Land Court in 1888. This involved placing pou at the junction of Ongarue River and Taringamotu River and at Whakapapa. After some disagreements the issue came before the Native Land Court again in 1890 and was not resolved until 1908. For a railway station dating from 1903, along with the post office, the spelling was Taringamutu. Both Taringamotu and Taringamutu were recorded on various survey plans. As early as 1910 one newspaper asked, 'How is it that the spelling of the Railway Department is so abominable?' providing several examples including 'Taringamutu [which] should be Taringamotu' and concluded by saying, 'Surely a Maori scholar should have been consulted before the names were painted.' In 1939 the editors of the Historical Atlas of New Zealand (a centennial project that eventually lapsed) asked the Honorary Geographic Board for confirmation of the correct spelling. Sir Apirana Ngata was unequivocal answering with 'Taringamotu' as was Pei Te Hurinui Jones in noting it was Taringamotu 'among all Maoris in the district'.

info_origin: In 1975 Gisborne City Council informed the Ministry of Works and Development that it was naming the area west of Lytton Road to the then city boundary Taruheru. An old pā named Taruheru was located on the northern bank of Taruheru River. CMS Missionary William Williams (1800-78) preached and held church services for Māori in the area from 1844-47. Various Taruheru land blocks passed through the Native Land Court in the 1890s with small areas being leased and ownership contested into the early 1900s. A Taruheru Road Board existed from 1877 to 1917. Nelson Brothers erected a freezing works at Taruheru in 1899, one of several plants managed primarily by William Nelson (1843-1939). It was initially known as the Taruheru Works. The plant was sold to UK family multinational meat company Vesteys in 1920 although it continued to trade as Nelson Brothers before being closed and dismantled in 1923. The 1911 census recorded 671 people residing in Taruheru Road District. The Poverty Bay Cricket Club played an annual match at its Taruheru ground in the first decade of the 20th century.

name: Tasman Bay
info_origin: 'Tasman, between Golden Bay and Rangitoto ki te Tonga (D’Urville Island). Abel Tasman fi rst named the bay Zeehaen’s Bocht (Bay) after one of his vessels. On 31 March 1770, just before leaving New Zealand, Captain James Cook wrote: ‘a Bay there is, and is known on the Chart by the Name of Blind Bay, but I have reason to believe it to be Tasman’s Murderers’ Bay’. The name Blind Bay was in use for many years; Murderers’ Bay is now Golden Bay, q.v. Although Cook did not specifi cally name the bay after Tasman, his reference to Tasman in its relation led Dumont d’Urville, who sailed into the bay on 14 January 1827, to note that he had ‘conserved the name of “Tasman Bay” following Cook in his second voyage’. Since the 1890s Tasman Bay has been the offi cial name. It was once familiarly known as Hobsons Choice, because Colonel William Wakefield’s hope of establishing a settlement at Port Cooper was disapproved by Governor Hobson. Maori name: Te Taitapu.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010. [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Abel Janszoon Tasman](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1t17/tasman-abel-janszoon)

name: Tasman Glacier
info_origin: [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Abel Janszoon Tasman](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1t17/tasman-abel-janszoon); 'Tasman, Lake: Tasman, Mount: Tasman River: Julius von Haast gave the names in honour of the Dutch navigator Abel Tasman. Maori name of the glacier: Haupapa: lit. hau: wind; papa: flat. Maori name of Mt Tasman: Horokoau: lit. horo: to swallow; koau: shag (Phalocrocorax varius). It has been said that the name was given because of a resemblance to the swelling in the neck of a shag when it is swallowing a fish. name: Tasman Sea
info_origin: [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for Abel Janszoon Tasman](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1t17/tasman-abel-janszoon). In 1891 the Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science noted that the sea between New Zealand and the islands to its northwest on the one hand, and Australia and Tasmania on the other, had no definite name. Agreeing to a motion from Justice Chapman, it recommended to the Lords of the Admiralty that they adopt the name Tasman Sea and enter it on their charts. The Admiralty accepted the recommendation and decided to call the ocean that separates New Zealand and Australia the Tasman Sea (Evening Star, Issue 8421, 23 January 1891, Page 2), (Taranaki Herald, Volume XL, Issue 9125, 4 July 1891, Page 2).; 'Use’Use of the name Tasman was proposed first by the Australian Association for the Advancement of Science in honour of Abel Janszoon Tasman. Jules Dumont d’Urville’s journal of 16 January 1827 refers to ‘the channel of New Zealand’. At the end of the First World War an abortive attempt was made to call it Anzac Sea. Māori name: Te Tai-o-Rehua: lit. te: the; tai: sea; o: of; Rehua: a powerful god, one of the sons of Rangi and Papa.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: 'Waikato, near Lake Taupo. Lit. alone, or isolated. Standing apart from other mountains in the surrounding countryside, Mt Tauhara is regarded as the geographical centre of the North Island. According to legend, Tauhara and Putauaki once stood on the present site of Lake Rotoaira. When the battle of the mountains began, they fled towards the east coast. Putauaki went swiftly and reached the sea, but Tauhara tarried, often looking back towards Mt Pihanga. When daylight came he was close to the shore of Taupomoana, and there he still stands, looking at his lost love, Pihanga.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: An original Māori name. Publisher-writer Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) offers the literal translation as ‘to befriend’, which Mabbett in the Rodney County history renders as ‘the bond of friendship’. However, ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) suggests ‘stranger’. In 1864 Governor George Grey (1812-98) under the Native lands Act, 1862 proclaimed the Native Land District of Kaipara South which included Tauhoa. John Rogan (1823-99), Land Purchase Commissioner for Kaipara, began negotiations for the purchase of the Hoteo Block, which included the Tauhoa Block in 1859. The discussions were incomplete when Rogan became Resident Magistrate and Native Land Court judge in 1864 and 1865 respectively. An ambitious proposal from the Auckland Provincial Council in 1866 was to dig a canal from the headwaters of Waitematā Harbour to Kaipara Harbour to open up the Tauhoa and Hoteo blocks. The scheme lapsed because of opposition to the granting of monopoly development rights and the cost. A lack of agreement between all owners over selling the land further delayed the purchase until March 1867 when the Tauhoa Block comprising 41400 acres (16800 ha) was purchased from Te Keene Tangaroa and others for £4000. Initially scheduled for sale in May 1867 as Waste Land of the Province of Auckland, the area was withdrawn in June 1867. In September of that same year the Chalmerston Land Association was formed, and under the homestead system by the end of the year its members occupied 7000-8000 acres (2833 ha-3237 ha) straddling the Tauhoa Block. Te Kiri who had an interest in the Tauhoa lands briefly disrupted surveying over the sale arrangements which fuelled his later opposition to the Pakiri North purchase. A school was opened in 1879.

info_origin: An original Māori name that was carried across to a Māori land block. In 1931 Sir Āpirana Ngata (1874-1950) implemented a Māori land development scheme. This included approximately 100 acres (40 ha) at Taumataroa, one of 149 units assisted in 1931-32 to the sum of £10085. In 1932, as the Great Depression deepened Ngata faced criticism over the management of the scheme and Prime Minister Geroge Forbes (1869-1947) established a Commission of Inquiry chaired by Justice (Sir) David Smith (1888-1982). The Tokerau Native Land Board was commended for its financial management of land development in its rohe, but Ngata resigned after the Commission’s report was released in 1934 because of irregularities in some other districts’ financial accounts. Ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1873-1962), in a 1943 review of names on the new provisional NZMS1 topographical map sheet N15 that appeared that same year, questioned whether Taumataroa was actually a mis-recording of Taumata-Karamu a hill near Lake Ōmāpere. Andersen referred to a specific section of James Cowan’s (1870-1943) The New Zealand Wars first published in 1922. Lands Department staff reported that old plans of the district did not include any names for the area, so Taumataroa was retained.

name: Taumatawhakatangihangakōauauotamateapōkaiwhenuakitānatahu
info_origin: Altered by the Honorary Board as an example of original Māori naming. Supplied to Sir Apirana Ngata by Bishop H W Williams. Translated as "The hill whereon was played the flute of Tamatea, circumnavigator of lands, for his lady love". The Honorary Board noted the original long form names for other hills particularly on the east coast of the North Island followed a similar pattern, but swapping the name of the flute player player, eg: Taumatawhakatangihangakoauauotanenuiarangikitanatahu, substituting 'Tane, the great son of the Sky father'. ; 'No list of New Zealand place names would be complete without this marathon effort, which is often shortened to Taumata. The translation provided to the NZGB by Bishop H.W. Williams is: lit. taumata: brow of a hill; whakatangihanga: place of sounding or playing; koauau: nose flute; o: of; Tamatea-pokai-whenua; ki: to; tana: his; tahu: beloved; that is, The brow of the hill where Tamatea who travelled all over the land played his flute to his loved one. Tamatea was the father of Kahungunu, ancestor of Ngāti Kahungunu. When travelling near Pōrangahau a battle developed with Ngāti Hine, during which his brother was killed. Heartbroken, Tamatea stayed at the site and played a lament each morning on his koauau. Tamatea had acquired the nickname Turipukaka-piki-maunga-pokai-whenua, application of which can further lengthen the name: Te Taumata-whakatangihanga-kōauau-o-Tamatea-turi-pūkākā-pikimaunga-horonuku-pōkai-whenua-ki-tāna-tahu. Ngāti Kere at Pōrangahau give the translation as The peak where Tamatea the great traveller ascended fiercely up the mountainside, slipping and falling about so that he could play laments for his brother on his kōauau.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Taupō
info_origin: ’The name in full, Taupō-nui-a-Tia, derives from a volcanic cliff on the east coast of Lake Taupō / Taupōmoana. Tia was a chief of the Arawa canoe who explored and claimed features of the region for his people. As he passed the cliff he observed that its texture resembled that of his flax cape, which was termed a taupō. He established a tuahu, a place where incantations are repeated, at the foot of the cliff and gave it the name that means The large shoulder cape of Tia. The name was later applied in an abbreviated form to the whole lake: Te Moana-nui-a-Tia: lit. te: the; moana: sea or lake; nui: large; a: of; Tia. Tia slept by the lakeside, and it has also been thought that the name may refer to his long sleep at night: tau: to come to rest; pō: night. The lake is alternatively known as Te Pito-o-te-ika-a-Māui: lit. The navel of Māui’s fish.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Taupō was the name given to a Māori village in the bay attacked with great loss of life in 1826 during the musket wars. The Taupō Land Block gave its name to this locality although the bay was named West Bay in the Admiralty sailing instructions published in 1858. The local stream Taupō Creek was used as a locality name in the 1880s. In checking names on the new provisional NZMS1 1:63360 topographical series in 1942, ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) advocated for the unnamed creek flowing into Taupō Bay / West Bay depicted on the map sheet to be shown as Taupō Creek. The Board agreed to this in 1943. In making his case Andersen referred to his comprehensive ‘card index’ which contained ‘a good deal of interesting historical information which should be preserved’. The 1942 topographical map listed Taupō Bay for the coastal feature with West Bay in brackets. This convention indicated that West Bay was the alternative name, a recent change as West Bay was the only name shown on the 1921 and 1951 cadastral maps of the area. Taupō Bay was used in newspapers in the 1940s for the coastal locality. In 1971 PJ O’Connell drew a detailed 170 section plan for the Taupō Bay subdivision. Taupō marae is a meeting place for the Ngāpuhi and Ngāti Kahu ki Whaingaroa hapū of Ngāti Rua.

name: Taupō Point
info_origin: The locality which comprises Taupō is largely the land which made up the former block, Taupo No. 2. This block comprises various sites of importance to Ngati Toa including Taupō Pa, which, prior to the arrest of Te Rauparaha, was Ngati Toa’s principal pa. The site of the Taupō domestic pa is the location at which Te Rauparaha and four other Ngati Toa chiefs were kidnapped in 1846. This was one of the most significant events in Ngati Toa’s history and makes the site of particular cultural importance. The Taupō fighting pa was a fortified pa which served as a refuge for the inhabitants of the domestic pa. Between the two pa was the outlet of the Taupo Stream which served both settlements. An important and frequently used tauranga waka was located near the outlet of Taupo Stream. Another important site was a cabbage tree which served as a lookout. This site is now marked by a plaque which refers to the capture of Te Rauparaha. Unfortunately, in 1911 the Taupo No. 2 block cemetery was subdivided by the Public Trustee into 45 sections, The Crown had already taken other lands for educational and recreational purposes. Koiwi were disinterred from the subdivided areas and placed in a common grave. Ongoing discovery of human bones in the area is not uncommon. Only a small parcel of burial ground remains. In 1926 on the recommendation of the Ikaroa District Maori Land Board lots 1 to 44 were transferred from the Public Trustee to the Crown so that the lessees could acquire freehold title. Throughout this period, members of Ngati Toa had been requesting for this urupa to be returned to the tribe. When the Crown had no further use of these lands they were transferred to the Porirua City Council and also a local pre-school. Ngati Toa continue to maintain the urupa a task originally given to the Public Trustee who solved his issues by selling the land. An important area, located outside of the former Taupo No. 2 block, is the Taupo Swamp, a wetland of both cultural and spiritual value. The area was a mahinga kai and mahinga raranga for the settlement at Taupo pa.

name: Tauranga
info_origin: ’Lit. Sheltered anchorage, or Landing place for canoes. The word tauranga enters into a number of Māori place names, some of which have been replaced by European names, for example, Taurangamango, Landing place for sharks, which has been superseded by Shelly Beach. In pre-European times, Tauranga was a village located beneath Hikurangi, north of present-day Katikati. Downtown Tauranga was known as Te Papa: lit. The ground, while the harbour was known as Te Awanui: lit. The big channel, or The big landing place. The early arrival, Tamatea-arikinui, chose a place called Kawhainui as a home for his people; it was later changed to Tauranga. Taurangamoana is the grouping of iwi in the area, consisting of Ngāti Ranginui, Ngāiterangi and Ngāti Pūkenga.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: An original Māori name for the locality also applied to the stream, valley and ocean bay. Numerous pā sites along both sides of Tauranga Valley point to lengthy occupation. In 1836 Wesleyan missionary James Shepherd purchased about 2000 acres (809ha) of ‘land called Tauranga’. The boundaries are difficult to trace exactly, but the eastern limit was at Te Anina Point running inland along a ridgeline to the southern boundary at Tutu, a 169m hill at the southwestern corner, then running back to the coast. Shepherd paid James Kemp Tupe/Hemi Kepa Tupe in goods and cash – 50 half crowns (£12/10), the goods included two cows, 25 blankets, 10 iron pots, 5 adzes, 10 axes, various other tools, and one 200lb (91kg) cask of tobacco. Shepherd settled permanently in New Zealand in 1821 and translated various religious texts into te reo Māori. Tupe, a Whangaroa chief, was a signatory of the 1835 Declaration of Independence. Tauranga Bay appears as a locality in newspapers from 1912. Tauranga Stream and the bay, Tauranga Bay, were named on maps from the early 1920s but Tauranga Bay for the locality did not appear on topographical and cadastral maps until 1959 and 1966 respectively.

info_origin: The origins of the City of Tauranga can be traced back to the establishment of a Church Missionary Society mission in the 1830s. The town sited on Te Papa peninsula, grew in the 1870s with a Tauranga North Highway District established in 1871. The southern boundary was today's 11th Avenue, although the district extended to today's 17th Avenue. The Borough was created in 1882. The town expanded along the peninsula over time. By the 1920s residents of its southern margins began to describe themselves as living in Tauranga South. A Tauranga South Bowling and Tennis Club was established in 1924. Four years later a Tauranga South Post Office was opened in a local store. Some residents felt marginalized as one explained in 1934 'the money provided by ratepayers and residents is for the upkeep of the Borough as a whole and not solely for the purpose of making nearby streets attractive. It is not possible for everyone to reside on Devonport Road, and we ratepayers who live in the outer wilderness of Tauranga expect to receive some attention'. A Tauranga South Progress League was formed in 1936, focusing its efforts on the area southwards from 6th Avenue. One of the League's early efforts was seeking a full Post and Telegraph Office and public telephone to be located on 11th Avenue. A Tauranga South public hall was constructed in 1941. Tauranga South is listed in Wises NZ Index for 1946. A decade long campaign to have a Tauranga South school was finally realized in 1949. The 1945 census revealed 121 houses and a population of 536 in Tauranga South and in 1948 through a boundary realignment 377 acres (152 ha) of the urban area and open land for future expansion in Tauranga County was incorporated into Tauranga Borough. Tauranga South initially referred to the area between 6th and 11th Avenues but has 'moved' southwards as the urban area has expanded and as a suburb it lays between Tauranga CBD and Gate Pā.

info_origin: An original Māori name for the locality also shared by the stream, valley and ocean bay. Numerous pā sites along both sides of Tauranga Stream point to lengthy Māori occupation. In 1836 Wesleyan missionary James Shepherd purchased about 2000 acres (809ha) of ‘land called Tauranga’ stretching inland from today’s Tauranga Bay. Shepherd settled permanently in New Zealand in 1821, initially at Waimate North and in 1833 at Kerikeri before purchasing land at Tauranga three years later. Tauranga Valley was in local use by the 1920s although absent from Wises New Zealand Index as late as 1946 but it was included in Edward Dollimore’s (1904-73) The New Zealand Guide by 1952. The 1:63360 topographical map from 1942 uses Tauranga although by 1959 on NM Dudley’s 1:25000 map it had been replaced by Tauranga Valley presumably to avoid confusion with other places named Tauranga. The 1966 1:63360 cadastral map of the area drawn by Jan E Bradbourne included Tauranga Valley.

name: Tauwhare Papauma
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-12/95; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: According to Buddy Mikaere, a significant incident occurred during the migration of the Takitimu waka; when the high-priest Tūpai spotted the Maungaharuru range and threw a spear (staff/dart) called Papaumu towards it. The place where the staff landed became known as Te Whare o Papaumu [Tauwhare Papaumu]. When the mountain was struck it began to rumble, hence the name Maungaharuru which translates as, the mountain that rumbled and roared. Additionally, “Papaumu, contained the mauri or life force for birds and it is because of this that the range was known for its prolific birdlife.” Te Whare o Papaumu [Tauwhare Papaumu] later became a pā site.
info_description: An historic site at spot height 762 m on Te Waka Range. NZTopo50-BJ38 182532

name: Taylors Mistake
info_origin: 'Canterbury, between Sumner Head and Godley Head. Maori name, lit. te: the; one: beach; poto: short. Who Taylor was and when he made his mistake remains unclear. The name was current from at least 1853, and is commonly held to refer to a ship’s captain who mistook the bay for Lyttelton Harbour/Whakaraupö. The prime candidate is the Gwalior, which was shepherded to Lyttelton in 1853 by the first mate Mr Taylor after Captain Davidson had thrown himself overboard in an alcoholic fit; the Volga, piloted by a Captain Taylor, was in the area in 1858, probably too late to have been the Taylor in question. The bay was briefly known as Vincent’s Bay after a logging vessel under the command of Captain John Vincent was wrecked here in 1857.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
