name: Te Ahi-a-Tamatea
info_origin: 'Where the ashes of Tamatea’s fire lay (the South Island form of ngarehu being karehu). Tamatea-pokai-whenua had lost the fire stick he usually carried with him, and was caught in a southerly gale on the Port Hills. By means of karakia he appealed to his relative Ngatoroirangi, and the old tohunga sent flames from the volcanic mountains of the North Island. The fire rolled across the land, down the course of the Whanganui River, touching down at Nelson, Hanmer Springs and Motunau Island off the Canterbury coast, and burst forth on the ridge where Tamatea was lying, saving the chief and his friends from death. The fire blackened the cliffs at Quail Island, and finally flared up above Waiaki Bay, where the ashes can be seen below Mt Herbert/Te Ahu Patiki.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={c30b9400-4052-e311-8212-005056970030})

info_origin: Hineuru history: A site of significance where Te Kohipipi ate the hearts of those slain in the revenge of his daughter’s murder. Te Kohipipi's daughter Te Ahimatutunu was murdered while he and Turangiapa were away from their pa Pukenui on an eeling expedition. The Ngati Maruahine raiding party, which had come from across the Mohaka river, left parts of Te Ahimatutunu's body on a rock near the pa for Te Kohipipi to find. Following this incident Te Kohipipi sought to obtain utu for his daughter’s death so he attacked the Nga Maruahine pa near Te Ngaru. Kohipipi was victorious and once all the Nga Maruahine occupants had been killed he began to collect the hearts of the dead. He gathered them into a kite and at the ascent to the Titiokura summit he rested and cooked and ate some of the hearts. From that point on the area became known as 'Te Ahimanawa a Kohipipi' (the fire of the hearts of Te Kohipipi).

info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2023: Objective ID: A5238764 {Report of the Royal Commission on the Te Akau Block. 1904. Appendices to the journals of the House of Representatives, G1.; [The History the Te Akau Case. 1910. Kawhia Settler and Raglan Advertiser, 23 December, Page 3](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/KSRA19101223.2.21); [Raglan County Council. 1892. New Zealand: Fergusson and Mitchell.; [Te Akau Case. 1904. Waikato Argus, 21 April, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WAIGUS19040421.2.12); [Through Waikato. 1893. Waikato Times, 22 November, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WT19231122.2.74.3); Wises New Zealand Directory. 1952. New Zealand: Wises.}
info_origin: Te Ākau is an original Māori name for the larger area of coastal land stretching from Whāingaroa Harbour to Port Waikato. Beyond the coastal dunes and cliffs was a zone of grass and fern land and further inland an area of bush. Colonial administrator, doctor and linguist Edward Shortland recorded how the Tainui canoe sailed from Manukau Harbour 'along the coast to the southward, till it arrived off the river Waikato. On seeing that river flowing into the sea, the priest exclaimed, "Waikato, Waikato-kau." This jest of his gave the name to that river. As they coasted along the beach now called Te akau, he exclaimed, "Ko te akau-kau" - it's nothing but beach'. Named with reference to the more northerly district of Te Ākau, a Te Ākau South school dated from 1923, although Te Ākau South was not listed in Wises New Zealand Directory until 1952. A Māori trail ran across the larger Te Ākau block from Raglan to Port Waikato. Concurrent with the invasion of the Waikato under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, the Te Ākau block was deemed to be part of the Waikato district and confiscated. In 1866, after a sitting of a Compensation Court, some 91360 acres (36972 ha) were returned to 77 (later 87) 'friendly natives' with the Crown appropriating 62000 acres (25090 ha) from 47 owners deemed to be 'rebels'. In 1874 a Crown grant for 91000 acres (36826 ha) was issued to 88 individual Ngatitahinga Tainui, and Ngāti Mahuta owners. The Māori census of 1874 recorded 32 males and 22 females of all ages residing at Te Ākau, rising to a total of 231 in 1881. In 1886 the block had earlier been leased for 27 years at £800 p.a. by HC Young. In 1875 it was leased again for 30 years at £600 p.a. to Russell and Studholme, the latter John (Jack) Studholme being owner of the Coldstream Estate in mid-Canterbury. In 1892 the leases were transferred to the New Zealand Land Association. The Association increased sheep numbers and immediately converted 4000 acres (1619 ha) of bush and some hundreds of acres of fern land to pasture. The 1866 allocation of land and 1874 land grants was controversial with boundaries, ownership and authority remaining contested. In 1891 the Native Land Court, under Judge Robert Trimble (1824-99), divided the land into 19 blocks. A Court of Inquiry was held in 1893 which led to a rehearing of the 1891 decision, with the land now being divided into three blocks Te Akau Nos. 1, 2 and 3. In 1895 Mita Karaka and others unsuccessfully petitioned Parliament over the division. However, in 1897 a further decision of the Native Land Court divided Te Akau 3 into 2 blocks. Another parliamentary petition forwarded by Honana Maioha (1830-1905) and Tuaiwa Ngatipare (?-1909) followed in 1902, resulting in Native Minister James Carroll (1857-1926) appointing Henry Munro and James Mackay to a Royal Commission of Inquiry in 1904. Situated in Te Akau No. 2 block, Te Ākau South was a designated polling station in the 1943 elections.

name: Te Aparangi
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA275889; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: ‘Te Aparangi was an ancient Ngāti Tamaoho kainga situated on the bank of the Kirikiri Stream about 2km east of Papakura. The settlement has been occupied since ancient times because of the fertile soils that surround it, its proximity to the Pukekiwiriki pa, its proximity to the Manukau harbour and the Mangapikopiko wetland and its strategic location along an important travel route. Te Aparangi was part of a much wider network of pa and occupation sites, being connected by pathways to the Hunua ranges, the Wairoa River, Pukerewa (the Bombay Hills) and the Waikato, as well as more directly connected to nearby kainga and the food sources of the bush on the Papakura flats and the kaimoana of the Manukau harbour. The waterways around Hingaia were frequently used to gain access to Pukekiwiriki and the neighbouring settlement of Te Aparangi as well as the pa at Slippery Creek and the Opaheke settlement. Te Aparangi was also important to Ngāti Tamaoho for its proximity to the forested margins of the Hunua Ranges. Around the forest margins Ngāti Tamaoho harvested a wide variety of foods, rongoa and building materials. Resource use was concentrated on the lower slopes of the ranges, close to the main communication routes and settlement areas. Their main settlements were on the western and southern margins of the ranges, such as those at Papakura and Te Aparangi (near Pukekiwiriki, or Red Hill), as well as at Tuhimata and the mighty Te Maketu pa (Peach Hill). By the 1850s the inhabitants of had established extensive commercial cultivations and orchards on the plains north of Waipokapu. From these Ngāti Tamaoho supplied Papakura and the developing town of Auckland with vegetables and fruit from their gardens and orchards. Te Aparangi became an important place of Maori solidarity after the proclamation of war by George Grey July 11 1863. Members of Ngai Tai, Te Akitai, and other iwi from the surrounding area joined Ngāti Tamaoho at Te Aparangi to escape the advance of General Cameron’s troops and the encroachment of European settlers on their ancestral lands. It was at Te Aparangi that Ngāti Tamaoho were visited by Native Minister Dillon-Bell and the Upper Waikato Resident Magistrate John Gorst. The Minister gave Mohi the choice of either, making a declaration of allegiance to the Queen and handing over their arms, or leaving to the Waikato to join their relatives. He noted that the “Government had no wish to drive them from their land” which was somewhat undermined in the minds of the Maori present given that his official purpose in South Auckland was to evict ‘rebel’ Maori from their lands. Mohi expressed his thanks and appreciation that the Minister should come to Te Aparangi unarmed and stated that if they had come earlier a deal may have been struck between themselves and the Crown. However, General Cameron’s troops intended to cross the Mangatawhiri and Ngāti Tamaoho, who had previously opposed Rewi and his taua, would join their Waikato cousins in battle. Shortly after this meeting took place, a Pakeha settler and his son were found dead on their farm near Ramarama. Ihaka some of the men at Te Aparangi were blamed for the incident which was in fact the work of a band of young men eager to strike the first blow of the war. Nixon’s cavalry (around 30 men from Otahuhu) and the 65th Regiment (around 300 men) invaded Te Aparangi and arrested Ihaka and many others, including women and children. Ihaka and some of his followers were then imprisoned on Rakino Island where Ihaka (who had been ill at the time of his arrest) died shortly thereafter. Ngāti Tamaoho rangatira Pepene Te Tihi (Ihaka’s father) died in Otahuhu military camp along with two of Ihaka’s children. The Ngāti Tamaoho chief Paora Te Iwi was present at Te Aparangi in the days leading up to Nixon's arrest of Ihaka. The events at Te Aparangi were to have deep and long lasting effects on the tribe and this is a key feature of its cultural and historic importance. While Ngāti Tamaoho had, along with other south Auckland iwi, bent over backwards to maintain cooperative and peaceful relations with the Crown and settlers, and at the same time honour their connections and commitments to Waikato, the outbreak of open hostilities - and an imminent assault on the Kingitanga - presented them with little choice. The bonds of whakapapa and their strong connections with Waikato left them with no other real option than to join the King. The importance of Te Aparangi is reflected by the waka-taua of the same name. This vessel was used by Ngāti Tamaoho during the Waikato Wars and is one of the most famous waka-taua of its time. This name tied the Ngāti Tamaoho warriors who used it back to the land of their ancestors and gave them their sense of identity and immense mana. On 22 June 1863 a battle between Ngāti Tamaoho and British infantry in the bush at Pukekiwiriki left seven Ngāti Tamaoho dead and many more injured. Following this battle most of the Ngāti Tamaoho in the Pukekiwiriki, Te Aparangi, and wider Papakura area withdrew to the security of their land in the Hunua ranges, one of their most important traditional defensive strongholds. Though the invasion of the Waikato and subsequent confiscations meant Ngāti Tamaoho were unable to return to their ancestral homes their deep connection with them did not cease. They continue to be tangata whenua and kaitiaki of these places which remain an integral part of their tribal identity and a vital part of their story as a people.'
info_description: The site of a former Ngāti Tamaoho settlement, located on the bank of Waipokapū Stream approximately 3km southeast of the centre of Papakura. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BB32 760952

name: Teapot Valley Stream
info_origin: Journal of the Nelson and Marlborough Historical Societies, Volume 1, Issue 4, October 1984: Named for a Māori known to settlers as 'Teapot'. 'Teapot' and another man 'Tommy' fled up into the Waimea Valleys from Te Rauparaha's raid of Ngaitara Pā, and stayed there for 15 years until English Settlers found them. The original name however applied to 'Garden Valley', Wairoa Gorge, on the opposite side of the river. According to the article, this name was changed on maps by request of the landowner Mr. H. Murcott in 1939. The name reappears in its current location c.1955 (NZMS 15 Waimea 2 ed 2). According to local knowledge the entrance to the valley resembles a “Tea Kettle spout” - the south west wind which blows down the Waimeas from Belgrove. Spring Grove is known as the “spout” or “spouter” "

name: Te Aroha
info_origin: ’Properly Te Aroha-a-uta: lit. te: the; aroha: love or affection; a: preposition; uta: inland; Love flowing inland. While it has been taken to symbolise the longing felt by the early explorers for their homeland, there are a number of variations. In one, Īhenga of Te Arawa and Rakataura of Tainui climbed the mountain and named the two peaks Arohakitai (Love seaward) and Arohakiuta (Love landward). Again, Kahumatamomoe, the uncle of Īhenga, sat on the summit of Mount Te Aroha, his heart filled with affection for the land and the people of Te Paeroa-o-Tai: The long range of Tai. A local legend indicates the name-giver was Te Mamoe, the son of a Bay of Plenty chief who had become lost while travelling. He and his two slaves climbed Whakapipi (see Bald Spur), and making out their pā at Maketu, Te Mamoe declared, ‘This mountain shall be called Te Aroha — and here for ever shall repose the love of Te Mamoe.’ Later the wairua (soul) of Te Mamoe remained on the mountain and created the mineral springs for which the town is famous. One was so deep and clear that it was called The mirror of Te Mamoe. Earlier the northern part of the town was called Morgantown, after the Māori chief Morgan or Mokena Hou, while the southern part was Lipseytown, after Ema Lipsey, his daughter.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

A Te Aroha West Creamery opened by Reynolds and Company in 1895, but by 1911 had passed from proprietary to co-operative ownership as part of the Te Aroha Co-operative Dairy Company. name: Te Atatū Peninsula
info_ref: Corres LXXII pp 273-302; File 222605 3 v/19 pp 209; Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche February 2024: Objective ID: A6141746 {[Gill, J. & J. n.d. Auckland Public Library George Church Map Collection 995.1172TeA (digital).; [Houses and Land for Sale.1929. New Zealand Herald, 17 December, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH19291217.2.4.8); https://nzhistory.govt.nz/keyword/te-atatu; [Wymer, Paul. n.d. Early Te Atatu c1870 – 1920.](https://markboyd.co.nz/a-short-history-of-te-atatu-peninsula/)}
info_origin: A Māori name but not an original Māori name. Archaeological remains indicate sizable Māori settlements on the peninsula which has been variously known as Orukuwai – the place of Rurkuwai an ancestor of Te Kawerau-a-Maki, and Orangihina – the place of Rangihina a female ancestor of Te Kawaerau-a-Maki. Timber miller, flour miller and trader Thomas Hendersen and his business partner John McFarlane purchased the peninsula and much of present day Hendersen from the Crown in 1855 for £2377. The peninsula was subdivided and sold off as Henderson Mill Estate in 1894. In the early 1900s it was known as Henderson Point and sometimes 5 Mile Point. Te Atatu was coined about 1907-09 by Reverend Jackson Bennett (1839-1925) who had recently shifted to the peninsula. Meaning literally ‘dawn of the day’, Bennett’s choice of name was inspired by the spectacular sun rises reflecting off the waters of Waitematā Harbour although Henderson Point lingered in some newspaper notices until 1929. The North-West Motorway (now known as the Auckland-Kumeu Motorway), which was completed in 1956, cut across the peninsula introducing the gradual use of the names Te Atatu North and Te Atatu South for the areas on each side of the motorway. Local residents voted to change the name Te Atatu North to Te Atatu Peninsula. This change was gazetted in 1994.
info_description: Suburb on the peninsula of land on the northern side of the Auckland-Kumeu Motorway. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BA31 471220

'Semple, Robert', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1996. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3s11/semple-robert)}
info_origin: Te Atatū South is a descriptive name for the suburb south of the Auckland-Kumeu Motorway. Te Atatū is a Māori name but not an original Māori name for the larger Te Atatū Peninsula. It was coined about 1907-09 by Reverend Jackson Bennett (1839-1925) a recent arrival to the area. Literally meaning ‘dawn of the day’, Bennett’s choice of name was inspired by spectacular sun rises reflecting off the waters of Waitematā Harbour. In 1944 the Minister of Works, Robert ‘Bob’ Semple (1873-1955), announced plans for a new northern route linking Auckland and Helensville. By 1946 it was decided that the ‘new northern outlet would cross the shoal water near Pollen Island, traverse the Te Atatu Peninsula, and then run northward past Hobsonville and Whenuapai to Dairy Flat’. Construction was authorised in 1949, began in the early 1950s and completed in 1956. The motorway cut across Te Atatu and the area to the south of it became known as Te Atatu South. A Te Atatu South Post office was opened in 1961, which the Post Office briefly considered calling Edmonton, the name of one of the roads at the junction where the Post Office was to be located and the name of a local school. The recently formed Residents & Ratepayers Association, Te Atatu South Branch, favoured Te Atatu South, as did Waitemata County Council. Behind the scenes Post Office Head Office pointed to departures from its naming policy: adding compass directions to an existing name was not favoured because of delivery difficulties stemming from poor handwriting and local authorities were to be involved early in the process. Head Office even went so far as to suggest that the Chief Post-Master for Auckland revisit the matter to obtain ‘a more suitable name’. However, Te Atatu South remained and newspapers referred to the suburb as Te Atatu South from at least 1964.

name: Te Aumiti / French Pass
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; Objective folder ID: fA325625; Infomap 346-02 Te Wai Pounamu Edition 1 1995; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Ngāti Kōata states that Te Aumiti is of significance to Ngati Koata, who have many cultural historical stories and korero associated with Te Aumiti. Ngāti Kuia translates Te Aumiti as “The current that is swallowed.” This was the place where the Shag guardian of Kupe drowned. The story of the naming sets up part of the oral map for navigating the waters and the customs behind it. The full name is “Te Aumiro o te Kawau a Toru”. ;  'Lit. te: the; au: current; miti: to lick. A reef in the pass was believed to be one of the wings of a shag that Kupe had sent from the North Island to find safe harbours and calm waters as his daughter’s kaitiaki or protector. In trying to stem the current its wings were broken and the bird drowned. There is another tradition that Nukutamaroro, who left Hawaiki in pursuit of Manaia, named the pass Te Au-miro-o-te-kawau-a-Toru: The swishing current of the shag of Toru. The European name derives from when French navigator Jules Dumont d’Urville sailed the Astrolabe through the narrow pass between D’Urville Island and the mainland in 1827. The vessel was taken from Croisilles Bay on the west to Admiralty Bay, striking the rocks twice and losing her false keel. ‘To preserve the recollection of the Astrolabe,’ d’Urville wrote, ‘I named that dangerous strait “Passe des Français”.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Te Awa is derived from Te Awa Avenue, the area's principle road is primary link between the suburb and the city. Te Awa is a shortened form of Te Awatoto which means "a stream where the canoes are hauled". Te Awatoto was the sight of the pā of Tareha, the paramount chief of Ahuriri c1850 and M.P. for northern Māori from 1868 to 1870. Prior to flood events, drainage works and the Napier earthquake the route between Napier and Awatoto was characterised by a number of waterways giving access to the common mouth of the Ngāruroro and Tukituki rivers. The naming of Te Awa Avenue acknowledges the destination of the previous route as well as the previous mode of transport and the areas low land river surrounds.

name: Te Awaatu Channel (The Gut) Marine Reserve
info_origin: Te Awaatu or Te Awa-O-Tu translates as ‘the channel of Tu’. In Maori legend the mythical ancestor Tu-Te-Raki-whanoa carved out the fiords and lakes with his giant digging stick or ko, with one foot on Secretary Island (Ka-Tu-Waewae-O-Tu) at the entrance to Doubtful Sound and the other foot on Resolution Island (Mauikatau) at the entrance to Dusky Sound
info_description: At 93 hectares, this is the smallest marine reserve in Fiordland. It is sandwiched between Bauza and Secretary Islands and has a high tidal flow. The reserve is much shallower than the surrounding deep-water basin habitats, which are the deepest in Fiordland, reaching depths of about 420 metres. There are significant rock wall and deep reef habitats, and the reserve is known for its sea pens and other suspension feeders, including the red and black corals, zooanthids and lampshells. Monitoring has shown more and larger rock lobsters exist in the reserve than outside it.

info_origin: The name 'River Hutt' was given by Captain Edward Main Chaffers and Colonel William Wakefield whilst charting 'Port Nicholson' in the barque, Tory, over a two week period from 20 September 1839. [Reference: 'Put Him in a Longboat' by Doug Edwards (1989), page 48]. Te Awa Kairangi is an original name from the earliest settlers, the Ngāi Tara peoples. The meaning for ‘Kairangi’ is told by Adkin as ‘esteemed’ or ‘precious’. The name of the river changed over a period of time when Ranginui of Ngāti Kahunungu visited the brothers. During his stay he saw nothing but hills and forest on either side of the river. He remarked about how appalling it was to have to live in such a place after having left the plenteous Heretaunga.; 'After Sir William Hutt, MP, a director of the New Zealand Company. Māori name of the Hutt River: Heretaunga, or Awa-kairangi: lit. awa: river; kairangi: something treasured, wandering, rainbow, a variety of greenstone, or a chief of high rank. Māori name of Hutt Valley: Awakairangi: lit. River of food from the sky. The name refers to the plentiful birdlife once found here.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: ‘This river was renowned as a mahinga kai, particularly for freshwater kōura (crayfish). The tāruke is a woven crayfish trap and thus the traditional name refers to the abundance of kōura and kōura traps in the flowing waters. Within the Retaruke were kāinga such as Upokotouiri, which in the early days held a large population and supported over 3000 people. There was also a Niu pou here. The Crown took a substantial proportion (17320 acres) of this whenua and left four reserves for the Ngāti Hāua owners, 500 acres of Ngamoturiki, 185 acres of Mangapuwhero, 100 acres for Te Ropita and minors and 2480 acres for Terekau and others.’

name: Te Awarua-o-Porirua Harbour
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: The name Porirua originated from Parirua – Pari meaning ‘flowing of the tide’ and rua meaning ‘two’. The two tides are the tides to Pauatahanui and Porirua harbours. Te Awarua o Parirua is also the name of the taniwha who is said to live in the Porirua harbour. Te Awarua o Parirua resides near Mana and created the distinctive shape of Te Mana o Kupe ki Aotearoa (Mana Island). There can be little doubt that Ngati Toa were the dominant iwi in the Porirua region, maintaining unparalleled control over the Porirua harbour from the time of their conquest in 1820 until the mid nineteenth-century. Countless Ngati Toa settlements and sites of significance are located in the wider Porirua region as the iwi exercised a polity over the land, the coastline and the inner Porirua harbour. Te Awarua o Porirua was a particularly valuable political asset, being, the key entry point into Wellington from the north . Governor Grey himself saw the necessity of commanding the harbour, stating, “Porirua is the key to the Wellington district, being the point through which all roads from all other settlements pass to that place, I determined to take possession of Porirua, and to hold it by a strong military force.” The harbour was not only important politically, it was an important source of food. Shellfish was of great importance as a food resource for the Ngati Toa communities located around Porirua Harbour. Pipis could be gathered from the uncovered mud flats. References used by Ngati Toa: Mitchell, James, An evaluation of the Crown’s actions in relation to the Kapiti Island Public Reserves Act (1897), p. 7; McClean, R.A., Te Whanganui-a-Tara Foreshore Reclamations Report, Vol. 1 & 2, Wai 145, #A9, p. 123 (Grey quote: Grey to Lord Stanley, 7.5.1846, G.B.P.P.); Boast, Richard, Ngati Toa in the Wellington Region, 1997, Wai 145 H8, 118
info_description: A harbour that extends towards Porirua City and Pāuatahanui. Te Awarua-o-Porirua Harbour replaces both Porirua Harbour and Porirua Harbour (Pauatahanui Arm). Feature shown on: NZMS260 R26 Pt R25 Edition 2 1993: Reprinted 1996; NZTopo50-BP32 565489

info_origin: An original Māori name connected to Hāpara Stream, which runs into Taruheru River from the north bank, but is now more narrowly demarcated as a suburb of Gisborne on the south side of the river. Writer-publisher Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) literally translated the name as meaning the dawn, a spade or a shovel. Edward Dollimore (1904-73) who compiled The New Zealand Guide was more cautious suggesting it ‘may mean the spade’. Te Hāpara initially referred to the land on both sides of the river opposite the mouth of the stream. In 1880 Allan McDonald advertised his intention to purchase 1000 acres (405 ha) on the southern bank of Taruheru River, part of the Whataupoko Block known as Te Hapara. The incorrect spelling Te Hapera also regularly appeared in the local newspapers from 1875 until as late as 1949. There were various newspaper mentions of Te Hapara during the 1880s and 1890s referring to land on the southern bank of Taruheru River. These include from 1882 when a Te Hapara cricket team was organised by William Rees (1836-1912), who had represented NSW in his youth, to play on his specially laid out ground. The Poverty Bay Agriculture and Pastoral Association held its 1884 show in Rees’ paddock at Te Hāpara. In 1887 a local consortium purchased 100 acres (40 ha) at Te Hāpara for a racecourse. A lawyer and politician, Rees was associated with Wī Pere in a trust scheme to prevent the further alienation of Māori land. After Rees’ bankruptcy, in 1883 William Common acquired the title to the former’s 54 acres (22 ha) property abutting Lytton Road on the boundary of Gisborne township and named the property Te Hapera. The land passed eventually to sheep farmer James MacFarlane in 1893, who subdivided and sold the 25 mainly 1 acre (0.4 ha) and 2 acre (0.8 ha) sections in 1903. These are shown again as Te Hapera on Lands and Survey Departmental draughtsman W Paltridge’s 1915 map of the borough and suburbs of Gisborne dating from 1910. After MacFarlane’s subdivision, in 1905 the Hawke’s Bay Education Board gave approval to build a primary school on the eastern side of Lytton Road. Initially this was called Milltown School (being on Mill Road) and not within the bounds of MacFarlane’s land, but by 1911 it was known as Te Hapara School, briefly as Gisborne West from 1917, but reverting back to Te Hapara in 1921. Newspapers referred to the suburb of Te Hapara as early as 1912. On the original national 1:63360 topographical map series sheet for Gisborne published in 1944, drawn by Lands and Survey draughtman WH Burton (1908-85), Te Hapara stretches westward from the old town boundary of Lytton Road to the racecourse and north to south form Gladstone Road to Waikanae Creek. In 2021 Te Hāpara was formally gazetted and the name standardised with a macron.

info_origin: Te Hapū is an original Māori place name. Farmer and explorer James MacKay described the location of Te Hapū stream in 1857. The London registered Taitapu Gold Estates Ltd established in 1895 acquired 89000 acres (36000 ha) of freehold land in the vicinity of the Whanganui Inlet. Gold returns never matched expectations with some of the land passing to other mining companies. From 1908 Taitapu Gold Estates released some coastal land between Whanganui Inlet and Sandhills Creek for selection, although this failed to prevent the company's eventual liquidation. Sometime after 1912, 784 acres (317 ha) at the south end of the inlet was taken up by William John Addison who adopted the original Māori name for the property.

name: Te Haupa Island
info_origin: Named for Te Haupa, an important Ngāti Pāoa rangatira. Te Haupa was born in the mid-1700s at Waitakaruru during a great easterly gale (marangai) that tore and ripped away (haupa) at both the land and sea. Te Haupa led Ngāti Pāoa through the unsettled years of the late 1700s and early 1800s. Te Haupa died of influenza and was laid to rest at Karaka Taupō, Kawakawa Bay. Te Haupa and his people regularly occupied the island and other nearby islands during the fishing seasons. The waters here were highly prized for shark fishing and contested too, with other iwi also gathering during shark season.

name: Te Hauturu-o-Toi / Little Barrier Island
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/71208; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Statement of Association provided by Ngāti Manuhiri: Te Hauturu-o-Toi, is the traditional name for Little Barrier Island. The name, meaning “the windswept post of Toi”, applies to the whole island and to its highest peak, though the peak name is officially Mount Hauturu by NZ Gazette 2004 (33) p.751. The island is visible from almost all parts of the traditional rohe or tribal domain of Ngāti Manuhiri. The physical presence of Te Hauturu-o-Toi, its mauri or spiritual essence, and its traditional history are central to the mana, identity, unity, and tribal affiliations of Ngāti Manuhiri, extending over many generations down to the present. Te Hauturu-o-Toi features in whakataukī, pepeha and waiata, and is a reminder of the earliest period of human settlement. (see Little Barrier Island Hauturu, complied by W.M.Hamilton, DSIR, pp. 18-23). The name stems from the arrival of the renowned ancestor and voyager Toi Te Huatahi within Te-Moana-Nui-o-Toi (the Hauraki Gulf) and his brief occupation of the island. Ngāti Manuhiri are his direct decendants. Te Hauturu-o-Toi is not only seen as a place associated with, and occupied by, the ancestors of Ngāti Manuhiri. It is also seen as being a tupuna or ancestor in its own right. Te Haututu-o-Toi was occupied by Ngāti Manuhiri as a permanent home for many generations until 1896. The name of Hauturu is widely recognised, however its correct name is Te Hauturu-o-Toi, which is not widely known. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEU4Njk5RDAxODEwMENGNEE2MEI).

info_origin: "Statement of Association provided by Ngāti Manuhiri: Motu-Hāwere-a-Maki, generally referred to as Motu Hāwere, is a name of particular significance to Ngāti Manuhiri. In Ngāti Manuhiri oral tradition this place name stems from the fact that the island was likened to the shape of an ear pendant, or hāwere, worn by Makinui, the father of the eponymous ancestor Manuhiri. Motu-Hāwere-a-Maki was later occupied by Te Maeaea a great grandson of Manuhiri, and by a close relative who was named Te Hāwere a Maki. Title to the island was awarded to Ngāti Manuhiri in 1901. (Native Land Court, Auckland Minute Book 7, May 1901, pp. 190 – 191). name: Te Henga / Bethells Beach
info_origin: According to Mr John Bethell the name was made up by members of the Bethells family and the name given to the guest house, being a combination of two names meaning "eating place" and "meeting place". On old surveys, Te Henga is named on one plan, ML 1902/A1 (1891) for a small lake (Lake Waiataru on current maps). John T.Diamond however stated in 'Once the Wilderness' (1953) that 'in Maori times there was, along the foreshore, a high sand dune curving upwards from high water mark behind which were cultivations interspersed with clumps of trees. This high fore dune sheltered the cultivations from the cold west wind so it was likened to the boards (Te Henga) which were fitted along the gunwale of a canoe to give more freeboard and protection when journeying in rough seas." To be more precise, the henga (singular) was the batten that covered the joint between the side of the canoe and the fitted topstrake (rauawa).' Bethells Beach was named after the family who has owned land in the area since the 1860's.
info_description: Locality at the mouth of Waitākere River on the west coast of Auckland. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BA30 295171
info_note: Te Henga was could also mean "place from which the food comes".

name: Te Hēnui Stream
info_origin: Taranaki Tūpuna written and oral history: ‘Te Hēnui can be translated as a big mistake or error. A verbal account explains that Te Hēnui takes its name from an event that occurred during the time of the battles between Waikato and Te Atiawa. Knowing that the war party was nearing their boundaries, Te Atiawa sent messengers to Taranaki Iwi for an alliance. Taranaki of course agreed to this alliance and began their journey from around the coast to Ngāmotu or New Plymouth. It is not known the direction taken but we do know that they eventually arrived in Ngāmotu at night time and headed up to what is now known as Te Hēnui river. It was at this time that scouts from Te Atiawa saw the war party coming through but as it was night time it was difficult for them to know who they were. So they sent word back to Te Atiawa who, before long, gathered with their war party on the other side of the river. Seeing this war party stretched out on the other side of the river, Taranaki Iwi felt a need to prepare themselves; as they were also unaware of who the war party on the other side was. A confrontation ensued and there were losses experienced on both sides. It wasn’t until the sun had begun to rise that each iwi realised that they were fighting their own allies. This was ‘the big mistake’; family fighting family, friends fighting friends, and allies fighting allies. In recognition of those who had fallen and the event that should not have occurred, the people called this river – Te Hēnui.’

info_origin: An original Māori name which translates as ‘the paddle’. Shore whaling commenced on Māhia Peninsula in the late 1830s after whale fishing was exhausted in other parts of New Zealand. Māhia was a popular whaling spot as pods of southern right whales would migrate from Antarctica to birth their calves in the larger bays on the peninsula. Te Hoe was established around 1840 and Joseph Carroll (grandfather of Ngāti Kahungunu leader and politician James Carroll), Captain Mansfield and John Smith were all known whale masters at the station, supported by a crew of Māori and Pākehā whalers. Samuel Harrington (of Australian Aboriginal descent) is also said to have worked for Carroll. John Smith was born in Prussia as Johann Hacken Schmidt but Anglicised his name. He married Tauarai Paraparakurekure in Nūhaka and they had 13 children. The Smith family became renowned as whalers and boat builders. By the early 1860s the Māhia Peninsula whaling industry had mostly died out and Smith was one of ‘three old whalers’ left, the other two being Englishman William Bartlett and Frenchman John (Jean) Morrell. Smith had been at Te Hoe for more than 20 years, although the exact nature of the arrangements that enabled him to run the station are unclear. When the Crown purchased the Mahia Block in 1864, Land Purchase Commissioner Donald McLean wanted to ensure that the holdings of whalers and traders in the area were acknowledged. The subsequent Hawke’s Bay Crown Land Sales Act 1870 authorised the sale of the 50-acre ‘Agricultural Section 1’ to John Smith for £50 and he was issued a Crown Grant for this land (encompassing Te Hoe) in 1878. Newspaper accounts indicate that the Smiths were still whaling at Te Hoe in both the winter and summer seasons in the mid-1880s. The station was likely abandoned by the end of the 19th century. A 2005 archaeological excavation revealed evidence of earlier Māori occupation beneath the whaling station. Artefacts from the whaling station such as a copper fish hook and whale bone patu provided strong evidence of Māori-Pākehā interaction.
info_description: 3km south of Māhia Beach on the west coast of Māhia Peninsula.

info_origin: Ko Matua Hautere te Tangata, Ko Kaikai-a-waro te taniwha, Ko Te Hoiere te Waka, Ko Ngati Kuia te Iwi. Ngāti Kuia notes that Inskull in Place Names of Marlborough (p. 55) translates this name as a type of tree, and it was the name of the waka, captained by Matua Hautere, which brought Ngati Kuia to the area. It was guided here by their two kaitiaki, Kaikaiawaro and Ruamano. It forms a substantial part of Ngati Kuia identity, history and place of occupation. References: Supplement to the New Zealand Gazette, 16-08-1883, pg 1185 and 1191 no 36; Maori Nomenclature, WH Sherwood Roberts, pp. 35 & 41; Place names of Marlborough, Inskull, p. 55. Ngāti Toa history: Te Hoire is the traditional name given to Pelorus Sound by Ngati Toa; the sound was renamed by Lieutenant P. Chetwode after the ship he commanded: the HMS Pelorus. Pelorus Sound was an area of concentrated Ngati Toa occupation and control; the iwi were considered to be the ‘direct owners’ of the Sound, as well as the connected valley and river, in the 1830s and 1840s. Ngati Toa first came into possession of the region following their conquest during 1829 and 1830. According to historian W.J. Elvy, at the time of Te Rauparaha’s raids, Ngati Kuia held the Pelorus Sounds and the valley. The invaders, however, “cleaned up the districts pretty thoroughly, reducing the survivors to slaves, or forcing them to hide in the mountainous fastness of the hinterland.” Hopai Pa located in Crail Bay, is one famous battle site at which Ngati Toa were victorious. Two Ngati Toa pa, the Canon point pa, and Te Akaroa pa, are located at Port Ligar. Another site of significance was the stream mouth at Clova Bay, which was given the name Totaranui. This was a landing site for waka that crossed from Omere on the Wellington south coast, and was used extensively during the invasion and conquest of Te Tau Ihu.

info_origin: A beach settlement on the coast by the mouth of Mangaone Stream named with respect to its location to the township of Te Horo, from 1945-51 the work initially of local farmer and developer Edward (Ted) Kitchener Gawler (1914-94). Fish traps and moorings found when dunes were levelled for the development were evidence of lengthy Māori occupation and the area was part of the Ngakaroa Block. The land was acquired by the Crown in the 1870s. Some 1000 acres (404 ha) was later owned by James Gear (1839-1911) a Wellington butcher who expanded into farming and frozen meat processing. This land was subdivided in to 50 sections and auctioned on Gear’s death in 1911. Sections 47 – 107 acres (43 ha), 48 - 111 acres (44 ha) and 49 – 112 acres (45 ha) ultimately formed the basis of Te Horo Beach. Herbert Hodge purchased sections 47 and 48 but there were no bids for section 49. Sections 46, 48, 49 and 50 passed to Percy Gillies in 1916, and were in part repurchased by the Crown in 1918 and subdivided to be administered as part of the adjoining Pukenamu Soldier Settlement. One of the Pukenamu farms was purchased by local dairy farmer Ted Galwer in 1933. Section 47 passed through several hands before Gawler also acquired it in 1941. In 1945 his first subdivision plan for 27 ‘seaside residential sections’ was approved by the Minister of Lands under section 16 of the Land Act, 1924. Extensions to the subdivision were approved in 1946 (twice), 1950 and 1959, the latter for additional land purchased in 1953.

info_origin: Horohoro was named by Kahumatamomoe, a son of Tama-te-Kapua. He and his party were returning from Moehau after depositing the bones of his father in a cave high on that mountain in the Coromandel. They were travelling to Rotorua via the Kaimai and Mamaku ranges and they emerged from the bush just to the north of Horohoro mountain. Before leaving the bush, Kahumatamomoe washed his hands in a small stream to remove the tapu on him; that stream is called Waikarakia. Consequently, the mountain became known as Te Horohoroinga o ngā ringa o Kahumatamomoe – the washing of the hands of Kahumatamomoe. Today the mountain is commonly refered to as just Horohoro and the stream is still known as Waikarakia.

name: Te Huruhuru
info_origin: The South Canterbury Regional Committee of the New Zealand Historic Places Trust submitted an appropriate Māori name for one of the highest peaks in the Hunters Hill in South Canterbury. It is believed that the Hunters Hills derive their name from the Māori chief Te Huruhuru, a South Island chief who belonged to the Ngai Tahu tribe, and who was described by Torlesse, the early surveyor, as "The Old Hunter". name: Teichelmann Creek
info_origin: Named for Dr Ebeneezer Teichelmann (1859-1938). Teichelmann emigrated from Australia in 1897 to assume the role of Surgeon-Superintendent for the Westland Hospital and soon developed a keen interest in mountaineering. Between 1899 and 1924 Teichelmann made numerous expeditions, especially up Fox Glacier / Te Moeka o Tuawe and Franz Josef Glacier / Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere. He accompanied mountaineers Alexander (Alex) Graham and Henry Newton on a number of first recorded ascents from the West Coast.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I35 Edition 1 1993 Limited Revision 1996

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-05/875; See https://www.linz.govt.nz/our-work/new-zealand-geographic-board/recent-place-name-decisions/north-island-and-south-island-nzgb-decisions-17-october-2013; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Te Ika-a-Māui means the fish of Māui. This name has been most commonly and consistently used in oral tradition by Māori living on the island, sourced from traditional Māui mythology, as well as its consistent depiction on earlier maps and charts up until the 1950s. Other traditional Māori names are known for the island: Te Ahi no Māui (the fire of Māui, recorded as Aeheinomouwe by Cook c.1770) and Aotearoa (land of the long white cloud), which is sometimes used by South Island iwi for describing the North Island. Cook's Aeheinomouwe spelling might be He Ahi No Māui (a fire of Māui) or He Hi No Māui (a thing of Māui). See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDA1MDZGQUY4MjEwMDg1OEVGQUQ); ’The Māori name for the North Island: lit. The fish of Māui. This name has been consistently used in oral tradition by Māori, sourced from traditional Māui mythology, and depicted on maps and charts up until the 1950s. Other traditional Māori names are known for the island: Te Ahi no Māui: The fire of Māui, recorded as Aeheinomouwe by Cook around 1770, and Aotearoa: Land of the long white cloud, which is sometimes used by South Island iwi for describing the North Island. Cook’s Aeheinomouwe spelling might be He Ahi no Māui: A fire of Māui or He Hī no Māui: A thing of Māui. See appendix 2.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: The northern of the two main islands of New Zealand, centred around NZTM 1865000E, 5674000N. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BH36 650740
info_note: For information about the alternative official English name for this island, North Island, see the alternative name record in this Gazetteer. Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "the fish caught by Māui"

info_origin: Te Kawerau ā Maki history: “The northern foothills of the [Waitakere] Ranges were named Nga Rau Pou Ta Maki, ‘the many posts of Maki’, in honour of the eponymous ancestor of Te Kawerau a Maki. In time all of the hills in Te Wao nui a Tiriwa were accorded names, many of which reflected the ecology found on and around them, as referred to throughout this account.”

name: Te Kainga
info_ref: H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5111558; A6399382 {[Advertisements. 1900. Evening Post, 15 December, Page 8.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19001215.2.63.4); [Late Commercial. 1901. Evening Post, 20 May, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19010520.2.70); NZGB Correspondence, Vol 16}
info_origin: Land known as the Te Kainga Estate, then part of the Onslow Borough, was subdivided in 1900. Sections in Te Kainga were advertised for sale as a new ‘suburb’ of Khandallah. The promoter was Lewis Henry Balfour Wilson (1849-1926) a well-known auctioneer and valuer. Te Kainga is not shown in authoritative listings and maps of Māori place names of the Wellington area. So, although a Māori name, it may not be an original Māori name for this area. The Superintendent of the Road Services section of Railways Department queried the spelling of Te Kainga in 1941. Inquiries by then Assistant Surveyor-General, Russell Dick (1898-1966) and passed to Surveyor-General Harry Walshe (1883-1948) indicated that the house of Roy Cecil Temple (1891-1953), publisher of The Dominion and other newspapers, who lived at 80 Jubilee Road was named Te Kaianga. Temple believed that the house stood at a resting point and food stop on an old Māori track across the hill from Johnsonville. The Road Services Superintendent in follow up correspondence indicated he had mistakenly written Te Kainga for Te Kaianga. This letter was dated a week before the Honorary Geographic Board met in 1941 and it is unclear if they received it. In any case Te Kainga was confirmed as the name.
info_description: In the vicinity of Khandallah

name: Te Kamo
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-21/895; NZMS260 Q06 Pt R06 Edition 1 1988
info_origin: The oral tradions of Ngāti Kahu-o-Torongare recall Te Kamo as a tupuna who occupied this area and beyond. He was considered an introvert working behind the scenes to ensure the productivity of the land for the benefit of his people. Having wider tribal connections he also organised trade with coastal hapū. An alternative kōrero held by some whanau and hapū consider the name Te Kamo to refer to an historic event rather than a person. The name Te Kamo was recorded in 1858 as the name of the block on the original Crown purchase deed, but quickly shortened to Kamo on subsequent maps and survey plans.
info_description: A suburb of Whangārei, approximately 5km north-northwest of the CBD. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-AX30 177504

name: Te Kauwhata
info_origin: In 1930 a request from Māori in Auckland, through the Akarana Māori Association, to the Railways Department was made to have the spelling of Te Kauwhata changed to Takauwhata, a burial ground on the borders of Lake Waikare where was buried Takauwhata, an ancestor. Much debate ensued, the Honorary Board, and Māori scholars being unable to agree that the name submitted could be accepted. The Honorary Board's decision was Kauwhata. Further representation by the Akarana Māori Association resulted in the Board reviewing that decision and recommending Takauwhata. The Railways Department declined to act on this recommendation. No name was gazetted. The matter was revisited in 1949, during checking of spelling of Post Office and Railway Station names. The spelling was reverted to Te Kauwhata, to retain the well established form of the name. Instead of Kauwhata; 'Lit. te: the; kau: empty; whata: storehouse. It is likely that the name commemorates a time when the local iwi was visited by another hapū and caught without provisions.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Locality on the Northern shore of Lake Waikare, 2.5km from Rangiriri.  Rangiriri Survey District.

name: Te Kawa-o-Tāwhaki
info_ref: Objective ID: A2408675; NZMS260 S21 Edition 1 1987; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: Name of key hill near Whangaehu River near Karioi, immediately downstream of Te Pā station, where a whare wānanga (school of learning) was located. The name Te Kawa-o-Tāwhaki means “the Sacred Order of Tāwhaki” and is recorded in old maps. Refers to the whare wananga teachings of Ngāti Rangi that align with the teachings of the ancient Tāwhaki Whare Wānanga. There are other significant sacred sites nearby that attest to the potentcy of the area. E.g The sacred toka at the junction of the Ararawa and Mangawhero Rivers, where entry to the Ngāti Rangi rohe was by means of ‘uruuruwhenua’ ritual. Te Kawa-o-Tāwhaki was also referred to in Native Land Court evidence as the site of a significant feast.
info_description: A hill at 778m with a beaconed geodetic mark B1XD at the summit, approximately 15km south of Ohakune. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BK34 045190
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "the sacred order of Tāwhaki, a whare wānanga"

‘Te Kerikeri means meeting pool, this maunga was a maunga for bird snaring but also a number of Ngāti Hāua urupā are at its base such as Pokoera and Oruatapu. Therefore, it holds great significance to Ngāti Hāua.

name: Te Kōhanga / Shipwreck Bay
info_origin: Te Rarawa history: Te Kohanga is one of the oldest settlements of the Far North. The area was first referenced by Tāwhaki ā Hema in his archaic karakia concerning his seafaring adventures. The name Te Kōhanga is a metaphorical reference to the establishment of a safe haven or sanctuary within which the early Maori explorers could retire to retain sustenance and consolidate their strength. The bay was named Te Kōhanga by Kupe some generations after Tawhaki, in association with the adjoining area name Te Angaanga, a burial area held sacred for its antiquity and status as a place of interment for people of high rank. Te Kōhanga was set aside for the living and Te Angaanga for the dead and this has remained the case until the present day. Several generations after Kupe, new decendents arriving on the waka Ngātokimatawhaorua and Māmari also began to populate the area. However, it was the arrival of the Tinana waka captained by Tūmoana that immortalized the name Te Kōhanga and the genealogical basis upon which the Iwi of Te Rarawa is founded. Te Kōhanga became the haven of the descendants of Tumoana reaffirming the name and function of the bay as the safest place from adverse weather along the entire north western tip of the tail of the fish. Toakai, descendant of Tūmoana, also established Te Kōhanga as his tūrangawaewae. Taurtaru the eponymous ancestor of Te Rarawa further consolidated the mana of Te Rarawa though Poroa and later Panakareao. Even today Te Kōhanga is used as a safe haven from storms by all manner of ships and waka. Māori communities of the Far North continue to refer to the bay as Te Kōhanga in spite of the fact that Pākēha people have come generally to refer to it as Shipwreck Bay after the grounding of a trade steamer at the turn of the 18th Century. Whilst the Pākēha name has attained common usage the ‘mana’ and antiquity of the name Te Kōhanga is of deep historical and national significance symbolising the burning fires of occupation for over fifteen hundred years. Te Rarawa descendants remain a tangible manifestation of the ahi kaa and reserves the right as tangata whenua to insist upon our indigenous nomenclature. Consequently Te Rarawa seeks the instatement of the name Te Kōhanga over the bay while retaining the English name as that is commonly used by non-Māori of the area.

info_origin: "Statement of Association provided by Ngāti Manuhiri: Te Kohuroa is the traditional name for Mathesons Bay. It takes its name from the sea mist which sometimes hangs in the bay. The bay was the site of a Ngāti Manuhiri settlement, and fortified pā, and has particular importance as the birthplace of the nineteenth century Ngāti Manuhiri leader Te Kiri Kaiparaoa. (Native Land Count, Kaipara Minute Book 2, May 1869, P. 142). In the early nineteenth century Te Kohuroa was also the site of a major battle involving Ngāti Manuhiri after a sacred place there was despoiled by a visiting party. (Native Land Court, Kaipara Minute Book 4, February 1884, p. 188). The bay received its present name from the Matheson family who arrived there from Nova Scotia in 1859".

name: Te Koko-o-Kupe / Cloudy Bay
info_origin: Ngati Rarua history: The scoop of Kupe. The place that was scooped out or formed by legendary explorer Kupe. Rangitane translates this name as the scoop of Kupe. Kupe’s waka went aground at Wairau (Vernon) Lagoons. Ngāti Toa history: The wider Cloudy Bay region, encompassing both the Wairau and Port Underwood, was an extremely significant area to Ngati Toa. Ngati Toa was acknowledged to have possession of this Bay and it was a location of concentrated occupation. Ngati Toa had both residences and cultivated lands in Cloudy Bay. Cloudy Bay was also an important centre of the thriving whale industry. The population did decrease in the late 1840s, however Ngati Toa did maintain their occupation of Cloudy Bay. Ngati Rarua history: This name originates from the time of Kupe and his infamous pursuit of the octopus Te Wheke o Muturangi. The name literally translates as the Scoop of Kupe meaning the place or area that was scooped out or formed by Kupe. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEJGODNCNjQ2RTEwMDMxMEU3RTc)

name: Te Komanga Bay
info_origin: Ngatikahu ki Whangaroa statement: Kainga noho of the Ngati Kaitangata and where they met their demise during the battle of Okahumoko in 1826. Also the location of the urupa where the Tupuna Hone Tua is interred. Te Komanga means to store or the storage of food. It was deemed as ideal for the preparation of seasonal foods to support the nearby Pa of Okahumoko. Kahu being a distant Tupuna of Kahukura ariki and moko to mean mokomoko (lizard) kaitiaki. 'The moko moko of Kahu', which is also the kaitiaki of the pa and the ana Ko Iwi within the whenua of Kowhairoa Peninsular. The hapu of Kaitangata also used bay to whakatau their waka, hence the application of the name 'Te Komanga Bay.’ All the information has been orally provided by our Kaumatua Wake Tua whom is 90 years of age, and states that he received this information from his grandfather Motukiwi Hone Tua, and ably supported by Kaumatua Rawiri Timoti whose great great grandmother Maungaroa was an elder sister to Motukiwi as well as Kaumatua Rawiri Henare and Kaumatua Pita Pangari. He has in his possession minutes (papatupu books) of the Land Commissioner’s hearings in Kaeo during their investigations of land ownership during the late 1800s and early 1900s, but will not allow transcribing or copying for fear of losing this long held information. Information also provided orally by Matua Rawiri Henare Kaumatua Mangatowai Marae.

info_origin: Publisher-writer Alexander Wyclif Reed (1908-79) literally translated kōpuru as heavy cloud while believing it was ‘more likely’ a type of moss. Wises New Zealand Index claimed the area was named after ‘an aromatic shrub growing on cliff shores’ used by Māori as an additive to kererū fat and ochre and subsequently identified as the southern crestwort (Lophocolea semiteres). Both interpretations are traceable to ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Elsdon Best (1856-1931), who identified kōpuru as one of several mosses used for making a scented oil for people or for making dwellings fragrant but didn’t specifically associate the term with the locality. In 1842 the 6000 to 8000 acres (2428 to 3237 ha) Te Kōpuru block was ceded to the Crown after a muru or the retaliatory destruction of Thomas Forsaith’s trading store at Mangawhare, it being believed that Forsaith had desecrated an urupā. Surveyor General Charles Whybrow Ligar (1811-81) sketched the block bounded by Wairoa River and Tasman Sea to the east and west and Te Aratapu Stream and Te Makaka Stream to the north and south. Forsaith accepted compensation in scrip and Te Kōpuru was retained by the Crown. In 1860 some 400 Ngāti Whātua and 200 Ngāpuhi gathered at Te Kōpuru to arrange a peace. In 1861 the ceding was contested without success before Judge Rogan at the Native Land Court and again in 1867 resulting in an out of court settlement. Protest over Te Kōpuru continued, including a parliamentary petition in 1881 and an application to the Native Land Court in 1891. A sawmill was erected at Te Kōpuru in 1871 after protracted delays, including ownership changes. It began felling kauri (Agathis australis) the following year, although not before a dispute over land boundaries between Winiata Tomairangi and the mill owners was resolved through intervention by Henry Tacey Kemp (1818?-1901), formerly Native Secretary, and Ngāti Whātua leader Pāora Tūhaere (1825?-92). This plant was the third sawmill in the district and the largest in the colony ‘a large two storey wooden building, 130 ft. (39m) long by 100 ft (30m) wide, roofed with galvanised iron, the light being admitted through numerous skylights,’ capable of cutting logs from 7 ft 6’’ (2.3m) diameter and 40 ft (12m) in length and employing 120 men, with company and Māori leased forest, estimated at containing over 100,000,000 feet (@ 236000cu m) of timber. A town developed around the mill, including a hall by 1872, school, churches and a post office in 1877. The Melbourne based Kauri Timber Company purchased the Kopuru Saw Mill Company in 1888 in an attempt to dominate production of valuable and already scarce kauri. In 2000 Garry Hooker and Alex Nathan on behalf of the Ngāti Whiu and Ngāti Kawa hapū of Te Rōroa laid a claim before the Waitangi Tribunal over the cession to the Crown of land at Te Kōpuru in 1842.

name: Te Kūiti
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA378424. Feature shown on: NZMS260 S16 Edition 1 1987.
info_origin: Ngāti Maniapoto statement [extract]: Te Kūiti is of both cultural and historical significance to the Ngāti Maniapoto and in particular the hapū, Ngāti Rora. The Te Kūiti name is taken after one of the main settlements which lay in the Mangaokewa Gorge near the modern day township. Its full name was Te Kūititanga-o-te-whakaaro-o-ngā-iwi which may be translated as the convergence or the narrowing of the thoughts of the people. It was here that Maniapoto the ancestor lived with his wife Paparauwhare. To them was born Rora, the eponymous ancestor of Ngāti Rora. Te Kūiti is surrounded by numerous landmarks and wāhi tapu of Ngāti Rōrā, including Mōtakiora, the ancestral mountain which overlooks Te Kūiti and the scene of Rora’s death. The Te Kūiti area was a place of refuge for many migrations of the Ngāti Maniapoto people. It was also a refuge for King Tāwhiao and his Waikato followers who took up residence around the Tokangamutu settlement higher up the valley than the present town following the confiscation of their Waikato lands.

name: Te Kuti Stream
info_origin: Ngāi Tai Ki Tāmaki history: . Te Kuti refers to the narrow stream running behind Umupuia Marae before turning to discharge into the small cove between North Road and the Whakakaiwhara Peninsula. Kuti means ‘Drawn Tightly Together’ or ‘Pinched’, referring to the narrowing of the creek at its neck. Te Kuti was also the name given to a coastal settlement surrounding the mouth of the creek at Umupuia Beach, and is noted in traditions dating from about the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century, when the land was gifted to relatives from Tōrere as a place “to hang up their nets”. Ngāi Tai occupation of Te Kuti of Umupuia continued throughout the early-mid twentieth century, and is still remembered by kaumātua as a large papa kāinga supporting both freshwater fishing in the stream, and seafood gathering from the beach. From about the 1930s, the name began to appear in maps by the corrupted form “Te Kuiti”.
info_description: A stream that flows for approximately 3km from an unnamed hill, with geodetic mark B2GL at the summit, into Tamaki Strait at the northern end of Umupuia Beach. NZTopo50-BA33 849136 to 828123.

info_origin: An original Māori name. This locality was not connected by road to Portage until about 1898. There were optimistic but unrealized proposals for a road tunnel to connect Te Māhia to Ōnahau in the early 1900s which resurfaced again in the late 1930s. Early settler, Joseph F. Foster (1855-1918) acquired 347 acres (140 ha) of freehold and 1519 acres (615 ha) of lease-in-perpetuity land to which he carried across the name Te Mahia. Foster sold off this farm in three blocks in about 1910 and became manager at Welds Hill Station. Te Māhia became more of a holiday destination, described in promotional material as 'New Zealand's finest bathing beach' and 'only five hours from Nelson by launch'.

info_origin: In 1913 the 'Mangaroa (Main Road) School Committee' asked the Education Board to change the school's name to Te Marua which came into effect the following year. Te Marua was variously translated as 'the pit,' a 'little hollow', or 'valley' seemingly relating to a depression at the head of Hutt Valley. Te Marua was then used locally for a housing estate in the 1920s with Te Marua golf course being opened in 1932. One notable local resident was Dame Elizabeth Knox Gilmer (1880-1960) a daughter of New Zealand Premier Richard Seddon (1845-1907). She was heavily involved in civic affairs having an enduring interest in horticulture and conservation, being awarded the Loder Cup in 1938. Another resident was (Sir) Alistair McIntosh (1906-78) for many years head of the Prime Minister's Department and Secretary of External Affairs. In 1983 the Upper Hutt City Council, Wellington Regional Council and the Hutt District Historical Society were involved in preliminary discussions over the naming of what eventually became Stuart Macaskill Lakes. A search by the Chief Surveyor of Wellington suggested that the original Māori name for the wider valley and stream was Pākuratahi with Te Mārua being in established use for the locality.

name: Te Māunu a Tū Bluff
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: ‘Te Maunu a Tū is one of Ngāti Tamaoho’s most ancient and revered places, located in the heartland of our rohe. In former times it was a pa taua of great strength, protecting our people’s lands. The rocky bluff is located on a crucial travel route from the pā and papakāinga of Te Maketu and Tuhimata in the East to Patumahoe and Puhitahi in the west. It also controlled movement along the north south route from Pukekohekohe to Opaheke and Hingaia. It protected some of the most important parts of our people’s lands and the routes that connect them. It was also a place of defence and refuge. Its name refers to the great atua Tūmatauenga, and it is his mana that still embraces this place. The pā taua that sat atop the bluff was one of our peoples most important defensive postions and crucial in the time before Pākehā. The blood that has been spilled on this land makes this entire area a wāhi tapu of great significance.’
info_description: A small bluff near the east bank of Oira Creek, approximately 2km northeast of Paerata. From end to end the bluff is less than 500m, jutting out at its midsection forming a narrow point. NZTopo50 BB32 697862 to 698861.

name: Te Mōrere Pā
info_ref: Objective ID: A1370907; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Te Atiawa statement: This was the site of a battle between Pai Marire warriors and British soldiers in 1864. The site was, at that time, a British redoubt named Sentry Hill, although it was originally the site of a Te Atiawa pā know as Te Morere. Te Morere, according to James Cowan, meant “the swing” and referred to “a tall swing-tree” or “giants stride” which stood there – with long ropes attached by which the youth of the pā were accustomed to go flying over a swimming pool in the river.” The pā site was located on top of a large man-made mound, giving it an advantageous strategic position. Although it was not inhabited in the early stages of the war in Taranaki, it was used at that time as a lookout by Te Atiawa. In 1863, however, the Military Settlers occupied the land and built a British redoubt at the top of the mound. At that time, Te Atiawa had a large settlement at Manutahi, located within close proximity to Te Morere. As a consequence, Te Atiawa considered the construction of the redoubt a serious insult and a challenge to their mana. A decision was made by the leaders of Te Atiawa and a number of allied tribes, to attack the garrison. According to Kahu-pukoro, a Ngāruahine warrior and veteran of the battle, the group assembled at Manutahi pā where a number of spiritual and sacred ceremonies were carried out by Pai Marire leader, Hepanaia prior to the battle. Hepanaia led the warriors – numbered up to 300 – into battle chanting Pai Marie hymns: “Hapa, hapa, hap! Hau, hau, hau! Pai-marire, rire, rire – hau!”. Te Morere is of cultural and historical significance given that it was an ancient Te Atiawa pā site. It later became the site of the loss of many of our people, giving it further spiritual significance. Te Atiawa feel a sense of grievance and offense that the loss of our land and tipuna is compounded by the loss of the traditional name, having been replaced by a name associated with the British military history of the site.
info_description: An historic pā site located next to Mountain Road within Sentry Hill locality, approximately 5km southwest of Waitara town centre. Feature shown on: Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BH29 037783

name: Te Motu Kairangi / Miramar Peninsula
info_origin: The current Miramar Peninsula was once an island at the time of the Ngāi Tara settlement. Struthers, concurs that now well over 1,000 years later it has become Miramar Peninsula. A channel named Te Awa-a-Taia separated the island (Te Motu Kairangi) from the mainland. The channel was closed by an earthquake, in 1460 called Hao-whenua, which occurred in the time of Te Ao-haeretahi, a descendant of Tara. Te Motu Kairangi was the largest of the three islands in the harbour of Whanganui-a-Tara. The other two being Matiu / Somes Island and Mākaro / Ward Island, both named after the daughters of Kupe. Struthers referred to them as nieces of Kupe. Whatonga realised the potential of the island as a strategic place to live, so he sent his sons, Tara and Raukawa (Best, page 782 - named him Tautoki) to settle on Te Motu Kairangi. Tara and his people moved there from their temporary residence on Matiu /Somes Island and commenced to build their pā atop the ridge of Te Motu Kairangi. The meaning of Te Motu Kairangi as provided by Adkin, p44 is ‘esteemed’ or ‘precious’ island, implying that it was the most favourable locality for occupying at the time in Te Whanganui-a-Tara. Adkins credits Kupe as the first person to land on the island without settling there. The first settlers being the sons of Whatonga and their people, the Ngāi Tara and Rangitane iwi. Later settlers were Ngāti Mamoe, Ngāi Tahu and Ngāti Ira. Miramar Peninsula: When the original island became a peninsula, its first name fell into disuse and the peninsula and its isthmus became known as Whātaitai then eventually Hātaitai. The first English name applied to the peninsula was Watt’s Peninsula after Mr Jas. Watt and remained as thus until 1872. Mr Watt had no association or connection with the peninsula other than he once landed a cargo of cattle there. James Coutts Crawford purchased 5 land orders for 1300 guineas from the NZ Company in 1839. Each land order authorised the buyer to select 1 town acre and 1 hundred country acres. He has the distinction of being the first genuine Wellington settler. Draining the lagoon Burnham Water (formerly known as Parawai), Crawford settled and farmed the peninsula by constructing a tunnel into Evans Bay. The lagoon comprised of approximately 200 acres and once drained became the first racecourse of the colony.
info_description: A north-south peninsula, extending from Point Halswell in the north to Palmer Head in the south. NZTopo50 BQ31-Wellington, from: GR 529 281 to GR 523 214.  Not Watts Peninsula.

info_origin: Heretaunga Tamatea history: 'Te Motuokoura is the island that sits out from Waimārama. It is an old pā site that was noted early by D’Urville who in 1827 said that it was occupied at that time noting: It is an scarped rock, naked, and a mile or more from land. A pa or fortress of some size occupies the summit, and ought to be an impregnable position. There was also to be seen several houses on the slopes of the isle, and by aid of a glass we easily distinguished the inhabitants moving about their fortress, and occupied in regarding attentively our passing. As at other points of the coast they made some great fires to call our attention". This island was previously known as Bare Island and now Motuokoura. But Motuokoura is more than a spelling mistake. The present Motuokoura implies that it is an island (motu) of crayfish (koura). The Motu-o-Kura is in fact named after the woman Kura who lived on that island and who was able, with assistance from kaitiaki sea creatures, to collect fresh water from the sea at the outlet of the aquifer (known properly as Ngā Puha-ake o te ora) for the people living on the island.' See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEYxQkJCN0Q4RTEwMDJGNDhCMjc)"

name: Temuka
info_origin: ’A corruption of Te Umu Kaha: te: the; umu: earth oven; kaha: strong; There are two possible meanings for the name. The first account refers to the large umu in the area that were used to extract a sweet substance (muka) from the roots of cabbage trees. Another interpretation refers to umu or whirlpools that occur in the river near the crossing. At first the Māori name for the nearby forest, Arowhenua: lit. aro: front; whenua: land, was used for the government township, and Temuka for the area on the north bank of the river as far as the sea. Land to the north and west of the present Main South Road was called Wallingford by Samuel Hewlings after his birthplace in Berkshire, England, and it was here that the present town developed. The name Wallingford was retained until 1866.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Te Ngāherehere-o-Kohukohunui Forest
info_origin: Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki history: The Hūnua Ranges lay within the exclusive core territory of Ngāi Tai ki Tamaki. The Ranges are known as Te Ngaherehere o Kohukohunui: 'The Expansive Forest of Kohunui’. Kohunui is a contraction of Kohukohunui, the “Great Misty Peak” representing the highest point within the ranges. The forest is a very sacred place to Ngāi Tai. It provided food, medicines and timber resources, and also contained numerous wāhi tapu. Te Hūnua properly refers to the volcanic hill country lying between present-day Clevedon and Papakura. Ngāi Tai’s specific interests in Te Ngaherehere o Kohukohunui were alienated by the Crown’s 1854 ‘Hūnua Purchase’, and the confiscation of the East Wairoa block.

name: Te Ngarue Stream
info_origin: Te Ngarue is a stream or river which was traditionally abundant with eel and whitebait. A tipua of the same name resides in the river; it appears as an eel and is carved on the front of the meeting house at Tangoio. Frederick Reti describes a historical event which illustrates the richness of the Te Ngarue as an eeling resource. “Arriving at the fighting Pa, Te Rae o Tangoio, Maranga Tū saw that the mouth of the stream, Te Ngarue, was blocked sending forth his young sons, Te Kouae and Hopu, he ordered them to open up the channel from the mouth of the stream to the sea. As the current of the stream began to flow swiftly to the sea the eels began their run, but, up blind channels that had already been prepared. As the rest of the party arrived, the people of Ngāti Tū squatted over the channels and with legs astride began pulling out the eels beneath them, swiftly killing them. The eels were entering the channels faster than they could be emptied. From the banks the women and children would gather eels thrown out of the channels. As Te Ruruku watched this ritual, he saw why Maranga Tū had boasted, “Ko taku kai uru ake ai i roto i te kotore”.”
info_description: A stream flowing from near Waipunga Road into Hawke Bay at the mouth of Pākuratahi Stream. Feature shown on: NZMS260 V20; NZTopo50-BJ39 314438 to 372373.

name: Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē / Ninety Mile Beach
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/1017; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Te Hiku Forum history: “Tōhē is an eponymous ancestor of the people of the Far North whose ancestry traces to the Kurahaupo waka and to the original inhabitants of the Murimotu on the Far North eastern peninsula. Tōhē was renowned for his exploits which are embodied in the landscape by the many places he named. It is remarkable that so many of the names he gave to various locations have survived in iwi history for more than one thousand years. The name Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē, is not only the name given to the long stretch of coastline more commonly known as Ninety Mile Beach, but also a reference to Tōhē’s endevours which resulted in the naming of every feature of land and at sea along its length. Moreover each name represents a specific event concerning Tōhē and all of these names have survived among Te Rarawa descendents through to today. They are our map of the beach indicating the signs and times for coastal activities from fishing to the gathering of plant life. This is not to say that Tōhē was the only ancestor with [links to] the beach. Kupe established the Ara Wairua, the sacred path for Māori spirits to return to Hawaiki, and the lives of subsequent tupuna are marked by the middens and sacred sites that remain along the length and breadth of Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē. One of the most important taonga along Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē, for Māori generally and not Te Rarawa alone, is the Ara Wairua. As tangata whenua, Te Rarawa has kaitiakitanga for the Ara Wairua from where it appears on the beach at Paripari in Ahipara. It continues northwards down the beach between the high and low tide marks. Besides a source of spiritual sustenance, Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē has also been a critical source of food and plant life, and continues to supplement the diets of Te Rarawa people into the present. Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē is our takutaimoana, a part of our very being. It is the Te Rarawa view that Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē is a name with iconic status for all Iwi of the Far North. Consequently, Te Rarawa seeks the reinstatement of the name with preeminence and the English language name “90 mile Beach” secondary.” Aroha Harris – 10 February 2008.; ’In fact the beach is only about 96 km (60 miles) in length. The English name may have been given because early missionaries could travel 30 miles by horse in a day, and because of the sand it took them three days to travel down the beach. Māori name: Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē: lit. The long beach of Tōhē. Also known as Wharo-one-roa-a-Tōhē: wharo means stretched out and is a reference to Tōhē having his servant stretching out his arms to measure the tide. The Māori name for the stormy western seas off Ninety Mile Beach is Te Tai Hauauru i Whakatūria e Kupe ki te Marowhara: The western seas created by Kupe with his war kilt. Marowhara was also one of the daughters of Kupe.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Te Paepae o Aotea (Volkner Rocks) Marine Reserve
info_description: The Volkner Rocks are three volcanic rock stacks attached to White Island (an active volcano) by a submarine ridge known as the Whakaari High. They rise 112 m above sea level in a stark and forbidding group. Beneath the water they are colourful and prolific. Te Paepae o Aotea (Volkner Rocks) Marine Reserve was created in 2006, and covers 1267 ha in a rough circle around Volkner Rocks. The reserve is located in the Bay of Plenty 55 km north/north east of Whakatane, and 5 km north west of White Island.

name: Te Pounui-o-Peretū
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA258815; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki history: “The Great Carved Post of Peretū”, the island is named for the ancient (pre-Toi) ancestor Peretū, from whom Ngāi Tai, Te Wai-o-Hua, Ngāti Huarere and several other iwi claim mutual descent. In common with several other Ngāi Tai place-names in which the suffix “nui” is interchangeable with “-rahi”, Ngāi Tai ancestors also sometimes identified the island as “Pou-rahi”. During the 1850s, the Crown purchased the island from chiefs of other Hauraki iwi who derived their rights from Ngāi Tai ancestry, and who had no traditional rights to alienate Ngāi Tai interests in the island.
info_description: An island approximately 1770 ha in size, in Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana, southeast of Waiheke Island. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BA33 943178

info_origin: An original Māori name. A headland on high cliffs running between Tapuaekura and Hauparu which marks the boundary between the Tapuaekura and Waione blocks. The Matarehua pā was at Te Puapua on the cliff edge above the lake. The old fortified pā marked the western end of a lake edge settlements that extended northwards to another headland where Tapaniao pā was located. The land was mainly occupied by Ngāti Rongomai. The Waione land block came before the Native Land Court in 1885. In 1927 the Honorary Geographic Board considered various Rotorua district names and spellings and on the advice of board member ethnographer Elsdon Best (1856-1931) and Rev Frederick Hamilton Spencer (1854-1932), a licensed interpreter, endorsed Te Puapua over the earlier Te Pua Pua. The area was listed as locality by Dollimore in his New Zealand Guide in 1951. In 1991 the Rotorua Lakes Council recognised the area with its adjacent former Matarehua pā and associated urupā as a site of cultural significance. ; Named on ML 5620

name: Te Punawaitī
info_origin: Te Punawaitī is a contemporary Māori name. Puna means spring and Waitī is a star within the Matariki cluster representing fresh water, including springs, rivers, and lakes, and the creatures and foods that thrive in these environments. The word Waitī combines wai (water) and tī (sweet), symbolising the essential and life-sustaining nature of fresh water and its connection to all living things. The spring has cultural, spiritual and ecological values for mana whenua. It was an important source of drinking water and was used for baptism rites and market gardens.
