name: Te Puru
info_origin: "Te Puru" meaning "the obstruction" is referred to in "Whitianga" by A L Lee. Historically known as "Puru" the "te" meaning "the" has been embedded in popular usage if only because it euphoniously 'sounds right'. The locality and stream had been referred to as either Te Puru or Puru from the time of the earliest survey records. Te Puru was the name of a large Māori Block near the stream mouth. The form Puru had been the current form for Census listing, directories, and had been in local usage for many years. Puru had been favoured by the Thames County Council, and the Thames-Hauraki Historical Society. Despite the above, the Geographic Board approved the name Te Puru. The decision was revisited in 1981, and the Te Puru was reconfirmed.

info_origin: An original Māori name. In 1852 as part of the ‘Pakawau purchase’ 115 (47ha) at Te Rae was given as a Crown Grant to Wiremu Kingi Te Koihua (?-1865?). This was one of two reserves laid out by magistrate and interpreter John Tinline (1821-1907). Kingi, a noted warrior, was the leading Atiawa chief with a pā at Pakawau. He had shifted from north Taranaki to Kapiti in 1824 and by 1830 had taken part in conquering Te Tau Ihu. He shifted to a pā at Pakawau in the early 1840s. Baptised in 1845, he took the name Wiremu Kingi after King William IV. He was known as ‘Billy go ashore’ by whalers. Te Rae reserve was vested in the Wakatū Incorporation in 1977.

name: Te Rae-o-Tangoio
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-12/95; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Te Rae-o-Tangoio – the forehead of Tangoio – was a pā site originally established by Tangoio, a very ancient chief who named the pā on his deathbed. In later years the pā came to be occupied by Marangatūhetaua of Ngāti Marangatūhetaua (Ngāti Tū) and Tataramoa of Ngāi Tatara / Ngāti Kurumōkihi. On one occasion when the chief Te Ruruku was visiting Te Rae-o-Tangoio, Marangatūhetaua took him to the nearby Te Ngarue Stream where he observed the vast quantities of eels available to the people of Ngati Tū. Following this Te Ruruku agreed to act as a fighting chief for Ngāti Tū and Ngāi Tatara in exchange for fishing rights; together Te Ruruku and Marangatūhetaua ensured the lands of Ngāti Tū were not encroached upon by other hapū. The Ngāi Tatara chief, Tataramoa, also occupied Te Rae-o-Tangoio at one point. He married Kohipipi’s daughter Porangi thus further solidifying the alliance between Ngāti Tū and Ngāi Tatara.
info_description: An historic site adjacent to Te Ngarue Stream approximately 7 km northeast of the mouth of Esk River. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BJ39 374384.
info_note: Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "the forehead of Tangoio, which he named on his deathbed"

The word Rau means "leaf" and Pua means "seed" or "bud". From the highest peak one can look down an expansive valley to the sea in the direction of the setting sun, hence the derivation of the name. Mr John Klaricich advised that the translated meaning could differ from area to area, but the translation given is that accepted by the elders who recalled the name.

info_origin: Named in association with Cape Terāwhiti. The Board's 1935 archives record Elsdon Best's argument that ‘Tarawhiti’ is the correct spelling. name: Te Rekereke Stream
info_origin: Name submitted by the South Auckland Chief Surveyor, December 1971, after research in connection with the revision of NZMS1 N64. Te Rekereke, shown as a place name on South Auckland SO plan 2480 (1882), is a stone with an embedded footprint, located on the spur on the South side of the stream. The property was named Te Rekereke by the original owner, Mr J F Jackson (1860-1948) in 1880, and has been known by this name ever since. The stream was shown as Jackson Stream on a geological map of 1925, however Te Rekereke is local usage, and the then current owner Mr T A Jackson (a grandson of J F Jackson) wanted to see this name officially recognised. Rekereke translates to heel, but origin and true meaning unknown.

name: Te Rere-o-Tahurangi Falls
info_origin: Taranaki Tūpuna written and oral history: 'This waterfall honours Tahurangi. It is near the head of the Hangatahua River where the river flows from the Ahukawakawa swamp, its source, then through a chasm between Te Umu o Tao Manawa on the south bank of the river and Pouakai on its north bank.’ ‘Tahurangi is a founding ancestor of the Taranaki iwi tribe who lived on the slopes of Mount Taranaki in a pā called Karakatonga. It was from here that he ascended to the peak of the mountain, said to be the first man to do so, according to Taranaki iwi traditions. Once he reached the top of the Mountain he lit a fire to fix the name of Ruataranaki upon the mountain and to place his authority over the area. The lighting of the fire by Tahurangi is commemorated in the following statements: 'Ko te ahi a Tahurangi moo te pukeaao,ka tuu tonu te pukeaao kia tiketike, ka whakahinga te pukeaao i ngaa awatea i ngaa ahiahi’. ‘The fire of Tahurangi is like an alpine cloud, that ascends [the peak] and remains suspended, it then falls during the day and in the evening'.' The proverb of Tahurangi for the peak of Taranaki: ‘Ka puta ki waho ko Puketoretore, e whakakaitoa ana mai ki taku taiaha, takahia atu au ko raro ki te whenua, haapai atu ai au i taku taiaha me he kakau toki’. (‘Puketoretore (the water soaked peak) has emerged, my taiaha expresses satisfaction, I tread the land there below, bearing my taiaha like the kakau toki (ceremonial adze)’.
info_description: A waterfall on the upper reaches of Hangatahua River between Te Umu-o-Taomanawa and Pouākai Range on the northwestern slopes of Taranaki Maunga. NZTopo50-BJ29 897538.

The feature's name order and generic feature type were translated to English and adopted by SCUFN in 2012.

Te Ruapekapeka also comprised a grove of trees in the past, which were possible roosting trees for pekapeka (native bats). Pekapeka were a traditional staple part of the diet for Ngāti Rangi. Te Ruapekapeka means “burrow of bats.” Te Ruapekapeka was cited in the Native Land Court by Tohiora: ‘My father and self went on to Hauhungatahi, a hill, in the summer time. This hill is sufficiently elevated to enable one to see a large area of country. We went there from Te Ruapekapeka.’

name: Te Tāhuna-o-Tūtawa
info_origin: Taranaki Tūpuna written and oral history: ‘Known as Warwick Castle, this is a large promontory situated high on the slopes of Mount Taranaki. Given it's prominence it became a key geographic boundary point between iwi. It was also known to have large tawa poles erected as markers, signalling to those crossing the ridge line that they were crossing a boundary point between iwi. Te Tāhuna o Tutawa means a large elevated bank (or beach) associated with Tūtawa. It's importance to iwi in Taranaki is a key boundary marker for iwi who have a footprint up on to the mountain. Iwi currently identify this unique land form as the place where their interests inter-connect.’

name: Te Tapere-nui-o-Whātonga
info_ref: Objective ID: A96528 ; A2685203 ; Williams A Dictionary of the Māori Language 1971: 225
info_origin: From Ngāti Rangitāne ki Wairarapa Deed of Settlement: "Whātonga encountered a vast forest in his travels, covering an area from Takapau in the north to Pukaha and Opaki in the south, and named it Te Tapere-nui-o-Whātonga (‘the great district of Whātonga’). In the nineteenth century, this area became known to Pākehā as the Seventy Mile Bush. Te Tapere-nui-o-Whātonga was a defining feature of Rangitāne’s customary takiwā and tribal identity as it connected and provided sustenance and shelter for the Rangitāne people of Wairarapa and Tamaki nui-ā-Rua. Whātonga eventually settled in Hawke’s Bay. He named his house Heretaunga, which became the accepted name for the wider region. The ancient forest formerly covering the western part of the Tamaki nui-ā-Rua region and the north-western part of the Wairarapa region, and known as ‘Te Tapere-nui-o-Whātonga’, was a taonga of great significance to Rangitāne"
info_description: The former 70 Miles Bush, from Pukaha / Mount Bruce in the south to Takapau in the north

name: Te Teoteo Pā
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA27725; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: 'Te Teoteo pa was part of a line of defensive positions built along the eastern shore of the Waikato River during the early stages of the invasion of the Waikato by government forces in 1863. It was built by Te Huirama and his taua, including Ngati Tamaoho warriors, who sought to prevent the Crown forces’ progress into the deeper Waikato. Ngati Tamaoho men were amongst those who died or were injured in the defence of this site, late in the opening battle of the invasion - the Koheroa ridge battle on July 17 1863. The position was lost by 14 August when General Cameron and his men established the nearby Whangamarino Redoubt to begin attacking Meremere. Te Teoteo pa is now within the Crown owned Whangamarino Redoubt Historic Reserve, managed by the NZ Historic Places Trust, recognising its wahi tapu status and its importance in the history of Maori resistance to colonial domination. It is a place much revered by Ngati Tamaoho as a testament to their tupuna’s steadfast defiance of the unjust attack by the Crown on their lands, people, and mana.'. Information Source - J Cowan, The New Zealand Wars: A History of the Maori Campaigns and the Pioneering Period: Volume I: 1845-1864, (1955), 251-256; N Ritchie, The Waiakto War of 1863-1864: A Guide to the Main Events and Sites (Department of Conservation: 2007), 11.
info_description: An historic Ngāti Tamaoho pā site on the north bank of Whangamarino River’s confluence with Waikato River, next to Whangamarino Redoubt. NZTopo50-BC33 826707

name: Te Tōangaroa
info_origin: Means ‘the long dragging’ of canoes. Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei advise that, as part of their seasonal fishing cycle, the area was commonly used when waka would be dragged up to where Beach Road runs now, and on the low tide they would have the arduous task of dragging the waka back, hence ‘the long dragging of canoes’ given as the name for the bay Te Tōangaroa. The modern area of Te Tōangaroa is land reclaimed from the original bay. Ngāti Paoa advise that in 1851 Ngāti Paoa, Ngāti Whanaunga, Ngāti Maru, Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki and others, arrived in force by waka taua at Waipapa (Mechanics Bay) with demands to address an insult given by a Māori policeman to a Ngāti Paoa chief, Hoera. Colonial military showed up in strength, demanding that they leave immediately. As the tide had receded the waka party were forced to drag their heavy waka taua a long distance to the water, hence the name.
info_description: An area of approximately 30ha on the south side of Waitematā Harbour, Auckland. NZTopo50-BA32 584205

name: Te Toka-a-Kōraria
info_origin: Ngāti Rangi history: A rock in Karioi Forest named for Kōraria, who was killed in battle by Ngāti Rangi and whose head was put up on this rock. Koraria and Hiakai, of Ngāti Upokoiri and Ngāti Kahungunu were killed at the same time. There is an inference from sources that Koraria was not from here and that the people of Hioi were responsible for his death. Hioi was a son of Rangiteauria. The name means “the rock of Kōraria’ but is also referred to as Te Upoko o Kōraria,”the head of Kōraria”. The rock is more commonly referred to as “Te Toka.”
info_description: An historic site on the southern slopes of Mount Ruapehu and at the southern end of Karioi Forest, approximately 9km northwest of Waiouru. NZTopo50-BJ34 227318.

name: Te Toka-a-Tia
info_origin: Ngāti Tūwharetoa history: Tia was an important tupuna for Tūwharetoa. He arrived on the Te Arawa waka and journeyed inland seeking land for his people. Whilst travelling south down the Waikato River seeking its source he named several landmarks, including Te Toka-a-Tia. It is a large rock that Tia and his followers came to rest on after accidentally going over Huka Falls. The island marks the boundary of Tūwharetoa ownership of the bed of Lake Tāupo (Taupomoana), certain tributaries and the Waikato River. The literal translation is ‘The Rock of Tia’.
info_description: A rock in Waikato River, approximately 200m north of Huka Falls on the western side of the river (often submerged), locally known as the Rock of Tia. NZTopo50-BG36 689178.

name: Te Umu-o-Taomanawa
info_origin: Taranaki Tūpuna written and oral history: 'The great dome shaped rock crammed between the Ahukawakawa, Pouakai and Taranaki. The meaning of its name is derived from ‘the oven that cooked the heart of Tamaheia’ after he was killed by Te Ati Awa at Karakatonga. Te Umu o Taomanawa has particular importance to iwi as it records a tumultuous event from one of the major conflicts between Te Atiawa and Taranaki Iwi. This particular conflict took place up in the headwaters of the Waiwhakaiho River course and was spurred on by competition over local natural resources called Kōkōwai. Tamaheia, a Taranaki Iwi ancestor, was captured and killed by Te Atiawa and his body parts separated and eaten. His feet and heart were cooked and eaten at Te Marua and Kaiauahi, on the lower flanks of the north eastern side of the mountain. Tamaheia was a significant Taranaki iwi ancestor who descended from Te Kāhuirua and Kahukura-roa and Tamatahara, of the mountain clans (Te Kāhui Maunga). Tamaheia's father Kahukura-roa was one of the main Taranaki Leaders during his time. Te Umu o Taomanawa provides a direct physical and whakapapa link to Taranaki and Te Atiawa's past and acts as a trigger to wider iwi narratives of settlement on the Mountain. The landform is a natural lava dome formed from the moderate viscous lava flows. Our people continue to visit the site as it is situated within a wider area occupied at different times by Taranaki iwi ancestors prior to confiscation in the 1860's.'
info_description: A hill at 1052m on the northwestern slopes of Taranaki Maunga. NZTopo50-BJ29 899536.

name: Te Urewera National Park
info_origin: 'Lit: te: the; ure: penis; wera: burnt. According to the Urewera hapū of Ngāi Tūhoe, the rangatira Murakareke, son of Tūhoe-pōtiki, discovered that his wife was having an affair with his younger brother, Muraanini. Murakareke then killed Muraanini and cut off his penis, which he first plaited in to the topknot in his wife’s hair before throwing it into the cooking fire and commanding his wife to either eat it or die. Murakareke then killed her. A different and possibly sanitised version has Murakareke as an elderly rangatira who had a disagreement with his sons near the Whakatāne River while fleeing from a battle. Murakareke suffered a fit and fell onto their cooking fire, where his penis was badly burnt. On some accounts, he died from his burns.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Changed from Urewera National Park by Order in Council 3 April 2000 (Gazette 2000 (59) p.1281)

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-09/304; GES-N15-08-07/331; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Waikoropupū River was notified as a proposal 9 September 2010 and considered at the NZGB meeting 3 August 2010 and published as an official name 16 December 2010. The river is an associative name with Waikoropupū Springs. The Māori name for Springs is 'Puna' and "koropupū" means to bubble up or well up. Spelling alteration from Waikoropupu River (“Te” and macron added to a recorded name). Te Atiawa and Ngati Tama state that the river is in the sacred valley for Te Atiawa outlined in evidence in Te Atiawa Tribunal hearing Motueka. Ngati Rarua translates this name as “Bubbling Waters” and notes that this is the home of the kaitiaki Huriawa who was responsible for keeping the waterways of Mohua clear and pristine. The waters have been utilized for many sacred occasions such as blessings, cleansing and revitalization of the unwell. Manawhenua iwi always offer karakia before entering this sacred place.
info_description: A stream flowing from the northern end of Walker Ridge generally northeast into Tākaka River approximately 1 km northwest of Tākaka. Feature shown on: NZMS260 M26 Edition 1 1986; NZTopo50-BN24 826791 - BP24 734772

name: Te Wai o Tūranga
info_ref: Objective ID: A2704995; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairarapa Tāmaki nui-a-Rua statement: ‘According to Robin Potangaroa of Te Hika a Pāpāuma hapū of Ngāti Kahungunu, “Te Wai ō Tūranga is a spring and the water from the spring runs down a cliff face to the north of the road across from Wharepōuri’s mark. The significance of the water that trickles down is where the tohunga Heperi used to perform his rites and that is where my grandmother was allowed to bathe for who she was, a rangatira. That place was called Te Wai ō Tūranga. It is also an ancient burial site and a place of peace, a wahi tapu.” The spring and its location has significance to Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairarapa Tamaki Nui a Rua because a peace had been established at this place by Pakuia and Tūranga for Kahungunu; and Te Hina-Ariki and Matangiuru for Rangitāne (c1700). Ngāti Kahungunu defeated Rangitāne at the Mātaikona river, at Taheremaro Pā, and further at Awapiripiri at a place called Pākōwhai. Robin says that “It was because of those defeats that Rangitāne accepted that they had to live in peace with us and we had to live in peace with them. Out of the peace came numerous inter-marriages between Kahungunu and Hāmua people who came to be regarded by 1840 as Ngāti Kahungunu.”'
info_description: A small spring on an unnamed stream at the eastern foot of Coast Hill and across the road from Te Wharepouri Mark, approximately 5km north-northeast of Castlepoint. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BP36 731720

land_district: Nelson, Marlborough, Westland, Canterbury, Otago, Southland
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-07-05/875, see: [North Island and South Island NZGB decisions - 17 October 2013](https://www.linz.govt.nz/our-work/new-zealand-geographic-board/recent-place-name-decisions/north-island-and-south-island-nzgb-decisions-17-october-2013); 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Te Waipounamu means the waters of greenstone. This name has been most commonly and consistently used in more recent centuries as the name applied by Ngāi Tahu and iwi from the top of the South Island. It was also recorded by Cook c.1770 (spelt Tovypoenammu). Te Wai-Pounamu (sic) has also been consistently depicted on earlier maps and charts up until the 1950s. There are several other traditional Māori names, particularly Te Waka-a-Māui (the canoe of Māui) which is sometimes used by North Island iwi for the South Island. Other Māori names known for the South Island are: Te Tumuki – the oldest recorded name; Te Arapaoa; Tovypoenammu – Cook’s spelling of Te Waipounamu; Tavai Poenammoo – Arrowsmith's spelling of Te Waipounamu; Te Wāhi Pounamu; Te Waka-a-Māui; Te Waka o Aoraki; Tau Ihu o te Waka. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDRDNTNFOEQxNTEwMDM5MEQyMDM); ’The Māori name for the South Island: lit. The waters of greenstone. Ngāi Tahu and iwi from the top of the South Island used this name, which Captain James Cook recorded as Tovypoenammu. The original form may have been Te Wāhipounamu: lit. te: the; wāhi: place; pounamu: greenstone. Among other traditional Māori names is Te Waka-o-Aoraki (the canoe of Aoraki) and Te Waka-a-Māui (the canoe of Māui).’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: The southern of the two main islands of New Zealand, centred around NZTM 1446000E, 5177000N.
info_note: For information about the alternative official English name for this island, South Island, see the alternative name record in this Gazetteer. name: Te Waka-o-Ngārangikataka Ridge
info_origin: The chief Tauira, husband of Mateawha of the Turehu people, and the great grandson of Tunui, the famous Tohunga and chief of Heipipi pa was a man of great mana. It is also said that he traced his descent from the sea god Tangaroa, Oruaamano, the whale that guided the Takitimu waka, also Pania and her son Moremore. Te Waka-o-Ngārangikataka is the location of Tauira Mateawha, the site where Mateawha leapt to her death. At the base of the cliff there is also located a carving of a lizard. These sites, amongst many others, make the Te Waka Range a site of great historical, cultural and spiritual significance.

The Whakahūhi flows near a kainga of the same name. In Native Land Court minutes there is talk of a Whakahūhi – a bush – with lots of bird snaring trees within it. The land north of the Kaimatawi stream up to Tuhirangi, where the Raketapauma conservation areas are located, was also known as Te Whakahūhi.

info_origin: An original Māori name. The larger area formed part of the 13000 acres (5260 ha) Tupurupuru Estate purchased by brothers (Sir) Walter and Donald Buchanan in 1871. Donald Buchanan (1831-1910) left to farm in Hāwera in 1878. Walter Buchanan (1838-1924) subdivided the estate in the early 1900s and transferred half to his three nephews. Of these Donald Buchanan purchased approximately 4000 acres (1618 ha) named Te Whanga after the locality. Literally translates as ‘harbour, bay, or large valley’, the latter meaning describing the topography. TH Smith further observed that Te Whanga has associated meanings such as ‘open’ and ‘space,’ as at the mouth of a river or a bay and as ‘a way out’ in relation to present surroundings and to ‘wait or watch for someone or something.’

info_origin: Ngati Rarua: Te Whanganui means the large harbour. Ngati Toa: This was the largest and most concentrated area of Ngati Toa settlement in Te Tau Ihu; their interests in Port Underwood were based upon both conquest and effective occupation. According to Dieffenbach there were approximately 400 Ngati Toa living in the ‘Cloudy Bay’ area. This community was led by Nohorua, Te Kanae and Rawiri Puaha and was centred on the mission and whaling industry. A pa and urupa were located on Horahora Kakahu Island in Te Whanganui. This is a very important historical and cultural site as this was the location at which a number of Ngati Toa chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi.

name: The Bluff
info_description: A long, narrow bold peninsula 49km long from Minna Saddle in the west to the end of Minna Hook to the east and up to 7.7km wide, projecting southeast from Mount Discovery into the northwest portion of the Ross Ice Shelf. Like Brown Island, it is connected with Mount Discovery only by a low isthmus, but itself rises in many peaks over 900m high, with a highest point of c.1081m at Minna Hook. On its northern face it is very free from snow, but its southern side, which receives the full force of all the southerly weather and the pressure of the Ross Ice Shelf, is ice-covered except where the cliffs are too steep to hold the snow.

Captain Edward Catlin (sometimes spelt Cattlin), who ran a supply ship to a whaling station in the area, made a land ‘claim’ for which he paid Tuhawaiki, Karetai and other Māori £92 5s in cash and goods prior to New Zealand being annexed by the Crown. 'Otago, South of Balclutha. ’Named after the whaling captain Edward Cattlin (or Catlin). On 15 February 1840 he purchased an extensive block of land from Tūhawaiki and Karetai for £30 and a few muskets and gunpowder; most of the purchase was later disallowed by the land commissioners. The NZGB recognised The Catlins as the official name for the area in February 2010.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: South-eastern extremity of the South Island. Defined generally as being bounded by the coastline from Clutha River/Mata-Au in the north to Mataura River at Fortrose in the south. info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche June 2023: Objective ID: A5446617 {Bell, J. M. assisted by Webb, E.J.H. and Clarke, E de C. 1907. New Zealand: Lands and Survey.; [Harris, G. E. 1907. Geological map of Aorere Survey District. New Zealand: New Zealand Geological Survey.](https://ndhadeliver.natlib.govt.nz/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE1271054); [Obituary. Mr K. M. Graham.1958. Press, 19 June, Page 7.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/CHP19580619.2.52); Report of the Geological Survey Department. 1907. AJHR, C9.; Report of the Geological Survey Department. 1908. AJHR, C9.; Roche, M. 2021. ‘Dr. J. M. Bell, FRGS: A Canadian Auxiliary Geographer in New Zealand’. Journal of New Zealand Studies. NS32, 108-122.; Webb, Ernest John Herbert - WW1 10/1021 – Army. info_origin: A descriptive name applied to a point where the ridge sloped steeply downward possibly bestowed by Ernest Webb and Reginald Greville. The newly reformed New Zealand Geological Survey under Dr James Mackintosh Bell completed field work in the Parapara district in 1906-07. Bell directed the work aided by Assistant Geologist Edward de Courcy Clarke (1880-1956) MA and Ernest JH Webb (1881-1914) BE Assistant Mining Geologist, with Kenneth Montrose Graham (1880-1953) AOSM and Reginald Palmer Greville (1862-1923) the latter two being responsible for the topographical mapping. Their collective endeavours were published in 1907 in New Zealand Geological Survey Bulletin No. 3, The Geology of the Parapara Subdivision, Karamea Division, Nelson Land District. George Edward Harris drafted the associated ‘Geological map of Aorere Survey District’. Bell married Vera Beauchamp in 1909 to become Katherine Mansfield’s brother-in-law. He left New Zealand in 1911 to work as a consultant mining geologist in various parts of the world. Clarke departed for the Geological Survey of Western Australia in 1912 before joining the University of Western Australia retiring as Professor of Geology in 1948. Webb studied at the Otago School of mines but had qualified as a medical practitioner when he enlisted in 1914. Commissioned as a Lieutenant in the New Zealand Medical Corps he died in an accident at Colombo. Greville was Commissioner of Crown Lands for North Auckland (1919-23) and Graham trained at the Otago and Thames School of Mines, qualified as a surveyor and was later topographer in the survey section of the Defence Department and rose to be Commissioner of Crown Lands for Southland (1923-25) and Auckland (1925-46). The Gazetteer of New Zealand Place Names published in 1968 mistakenly listed The Drop Off as a peak.

info_description: A prominent bare rock scar of football shape on the north side of the ridge separating Edisto Inlet and Edisto Glacier from Tucker Glacier, at the base of Hallett Peninsula, Victoria Land. It is said to be always visible, though occasionally lightly covered by snow for short periods. At the base of The Football there is a prominent rock knob and a small lake, with a train of medial moraine running from it down the centre of Edisto Glacier.

info_origin: This is a descriptive name for the point where Top Valley Stream divides into two branches. The name appears at the time gold miners were prospecting in the vicinity in 1865. A named post service to The Forks commenced the same year. The population quickly rose to 400-600, but by 1866 had fallen to 14 with little gold being recovered. By 1872 the Marlborough Press reported that 'The Forks are nearly deserted, and men are too poor to prospect for new ground'. There was renewed interest in the 1880s which saw the setting up of The Forks Sluicing Company in 1882, but mining never proved particularly successful. The Wellington Mine ran an equally short-lived quartz mining operation nearby in the early 20th century.

Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/4h12/hammond-reginald-bedford) (accessed 12 January 2023)}
info_origin: Seemingly named for the raised flat mānuka scrub covered area where the subdivision was located and approved in 1926 by Reginald Hammond, the newly appointed Director of Town Planning, under the Town-planning, Act 1926. The subdivision was promoted by Messrs Goodwin, Chichester and Pavitt. Geoffrey Denzil Mallaby Goodwin (1894-1981) and English-born Francis Chichester (1901-72), who migrated to New Zealand as an 18-year-old, were a firm of Lower Hutt land agents involved with other subdivisions in Lower Hutt at this time. They formed the private company of Goodwin and Chichester in 1928. Surveyor and engineer Henry Hastings Pavitt (c.1878-1948) was a partner of Seaton Sladden and Pavitt, registered engineers of Masterton and Wellington established in 1912. Goodwin and Chichester had an early involvement with commercial aviation in New Zealand via the Goodwin Chichester Aircraft Company formed in 1927. Having returned to the UK in 1929, Chichester then unsuccessfully attempted to beat the record for a flight from the UK to Australia. In 1931 he flew single handed from New Zealand to Australia via Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island. Chichester returned to the UK and in 1966-67 he completed the first single handed circumnavigation of the globe in his 16m yacht Gypsy Moth IV and was knighted in 1967. Chichester Drive and Goodwin Place in Upper Hutt are named after them. The Plateau subdivision with its 50 sections and recreation reserve was intended for 'weekend cottage sites' and approved by the Surveyor-General under the Land Act, 1924. Section sales were slow – three in 1926 to a maximum of seven in 1930 with only 28 of the sites being sold by 1937. In 1936 Plateau No 1 Extension was created by registered surveyor AK Hounsell and further extensions to the subdivision took place in 1950 and 1962.

name: The Sisters
info_ref: See map of Robertson Bay, South Victoria Land at end of Carsten E. Borchgrevink (1901) First on the Antarctic Continent, London: George Newnes; During the hydrographic survey by LINZ of January - March 2004, the following was recorded in the Report of the Survey, dated April 2004: "The survey launch Pelorus investigated the “Sisters” and Gertrude was not found. A 17m depth was found at the charted position of “Gertrude”. “Rose” was found to be much smaller than charted and a new position was surveyed." The new edition of chart NZ 14906, dated August 2006, therefore shows 'The Sisters' and 'Rose Rock', but not 'Gertrude Rock'. Topographic map SR 59-60/13 Cape Adare. The Sisters officially removed by New Zealand Gazette 2007 page 1514.
info_origin: One of the two rocks was named Gertrude Rock which no longer exists, and the other remains Rose Rock. First charted and named in 1899 by the British Antarctic Expedition, 1898-1900, then individually named at the suggestion of Levick during the British Antarctica Expedition (Terra Nova expedition, BrAE), 1910-13. In 2004 New Zealand's RV Tangaroa and its launch Pelorus discovered Gertrude Rock no longer existed, with depths of 17m at the last reported position. Rose Rock still existed in a much reduced state. It was initially theorised Gertrude Rock had been obliterated by Iceberg B-15A, however research found the feature had disappeared earlier, perhaps victim to an earlier iceberg or perhaps just the forces of erosion. The collective name was officially discontinued given there were no longer two rocks.
info_description: Formerly two stacks, or pillar rocks, lying close to the north tip of Cape Adare in northern Victoria Land.

info_origin: A descriptive name where two loops in Hikuwai River are spanned in close proximity by three bridges. Tenders for four bridges over Hikuwai River – one more distant – were called by Waiapu County Council in 1900. Duplicate specifications were for ‘a central span of 80 feet [24 m] on concrete piers, with smaller side spans, the average length of the bridges being about 190 feet [58 m]’ and designed by Waiapu County Council engineer William O'Ryan. The work was undertaken by Gisborne’s McLaughlin and Company and completed by 1902, the bridges having concrete piers with tōtara timbers and trusses, stringers and decking of kauri. The original line of the road was vulnerable to land slips and flooding. A government subsidy enabled Waiapu County Council to construct a new dray road and bridges over the river flats linking Tolago [Tolaga] Bay to Tokomaru Bay at a cost of £8000. The road did not prove as resistant to slips as hoped but by the time this damage occurred in 1936, The Three Bridges name was in well-established in local use.
info_description: Where three bridges cross two loops of Hikuwai River, approximately 1.5km north-northwest of Tolaga Bay. Feature shown on: NZMS260 Y16 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-BF44 594532

info_origin: Named by US-ACAN in association with Thwaites Glacier.
info_description: A glacier tongue which is the seaward extension of Thwaites Glacier into the Amundsen Sea. It enters the sea about 100km east of Mount Murphy in Marie Byrd Land. At the time of naming the feature projected approximately 100km from the grounding line, with the Thwaites Iceberg Tongue projecting off at 45° for a further 150km (the Iceberg Tongue no longer exists). As of 2020 the feature has drastically reduced in size, the tongue having a significant calving in 2012 (Iceberg B-22) followed by extensive disintegration.

info_description: A former large and rather compact iceberg tongue described as 'about 70 mi long and 20 mi wide.' In January 1966 its south end was only 3 mi north of Thwaites Glacier Tongue, from whence it had broken off.' In 1986 the feature ungrounded and began heading out to sea, rotating a full 90° by 1990. After grounding briefly again at the Bakutis Coast in 1995 it drifted north and broke up.

info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche December 2022: Objective ID: A5139262 {Prickett, Nigel. J. 1996: British Army and colonial fortifications in north Taranaki, 1863–64. Records of the Auckland Institute & Museum 33: 1–51.; [Danny Keenan, 'New Zealand wars - Pai Mārire, South Taranaki and Whanganui, 1864–1866', Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](http://www.TeAra.govt.nz/en/new-zealand-wars/page-8) (accessed 8 November 2022)}
info_origin: This redoubt, a small temporary defensive fortification, took its name from the adjacent Tīmaru Stream. The Redoubt was a classic design with square bastions at opposite corners allowing all the walls to be defended. It was constructed in late 1864 by military settlers during the Taranaki Wars. The Redoubt's purpose was to protect communication lines. It was abandoned in 1865.

info_ref: H/O/M entry with acknowledgement of the contributing and research of Patrick Fotheringham {Objective folder ID: fA810284, Archives New Zealand: [R18832503]( https://collections.archives.govt.nz/en/web/arena/search#/entity/aims-archive/R18832503/accommodation-timpanys?q=R18832503&source=aims-archive); [R2674596]( https://collections.archives.govt.nz/en/web/arena/search#/entity/aims-archive/R2674596/timpanys---station-and-yard?q=R2674596&source=aims-archive); [R2674624]( https://collections.archives.govt.nz/en/web/arena/search#/entity/aims-archive/R2674624/seaward-bush---messrs-timpany-bros.---private-siding-at-15-miles?q=R2674624&source=aims-archive); [R7261682]( https://collections.archives.govt.nz/en/web/arena/search#/entity/aims-archive/R7261682/seaward-bush---private-siding---timpany-bros---8-miles-30-chains?q=R7261682&source=aims-archive); [R1832859](https://collections.archives.govt.nz/en/web/arena/search#/entity/aims-archive/R1832859/timpanys-general-file?q=R1832859&source=aims-archive)}
info_origin: Timpanys comes from the name of a historic railway siding associated with the Timpany Brothers company that established several sawmills in the area. Timpany Bros. was comprised of three entrepreneurial European settlers, brothers William, Robert and Thomas Timpany. From 1896 to 1906 it operated a private siding on the Seaward Bush Line 15 miles from the Invercargill intersection. When milling ceased, the siding was closed and the rails pulled up. In 1907 the District Engineer approached the Timpany Bros. about a new siding at 8 miles 30 chains, for a sum of £215. The Timpany Bros. were unwilling to fully finance it, citing a large initial outlay to re-establish milling operations. A bush fire in January 1906 had destroyed its nearby Waimatua mill along with ‘100,000ft² of sawn timber’ and its logging tramways. Instead, Timpany Bros. suggested NZR open it as a public siding given the area was coming under settlement. They offered a £50 upfront contribution for four years rent-free, or a yearly rent of £15. After much back and forth between NZR and Timpany Bros. over the cost and whether it would be public or private, NZR’s final offer was a new public siding at 8 miles 40 chains, for a £100 contribution as Timpany Bros. would effectively have exclusive use for several years. After further argument, in November 1907 Timpany Bros relented and sent their ‘first payment’ of £50, the balance to be paid on 1 May 1908. Meanwhile, the District Engineer incorrectly drafted plans and a Deed of Agreement for a private siding and construction pre-emptively began, reusing construction material from the original ‘Timpany’s Siding’ at 15 miles. Perhaps with the apparent decrease in cost from the originally quoted £215 for a private siding (or just seizing on the error), Timpany Bros. quickly signed the deed on 16 December 1907, paying the £1 registration fee without complaint. The new ‘Timpany’s Siding’ opened 23 December 1907 - and public timetables were notified. Confusion ensued in subsequent correspondence between Timpany Bros., the District Engineer, Chief Engineer and General Manager of NZR given the siding was meant to be public, with the District Engineer apologising for his error. NZR unilaterally cancelled the contract and refunded the £1 fee but reiterated its demand for a further £50. Ultimately with much back and forth, including threats to entirely pull up the brand new siding, demands for the remaining £50 were withdrawn in January 1909. Timpany Bros. continued to operate the siding as if it were private and apparently encouraged this misapprehension. There was no public access to the siding, so passengers had to skip the line or trespass Timpany’s yard. However, in 1911/12 the first ‘settlers of Timpany’ (the name now coming into use) successfully petitioned NZR for a level crossing and right of way. A ‘Timpanys’ post office also opened in 1912. In 1913/14 ‘Timpany’s Siding’ was upgraded to have a shelter, platform, and loading bank, and in 1920 the platform was elongated further. After the sawmills wound down again and the predicted settlement had developed, the now resident population of ‘Timpanys’ made petitions and counter-petitions to the Minister for Railways in 1919/20 over whether the station should be moved half a mile west. The station was never moved. As it became a populated place the apostrophe in the name dropped out, including on official maps by the 1940s. While the last train on the Seaward Bush Line ran on 5 April 1966 and the line was ripped up in 1969, ‘Timpanys’ remained the name for the locality.

name: Tinakori Road
info_origin: 'Wellington, immediately to the west of the city area. Correctly Tinakore: tina: dinner; kore: none; No dinner. The story is that Maori at work on roadmaking forgot to take their dinner with them on one occasion, or had to finish their job before lunch, with the name arising as a jocular response. Another version is that the horse and cart bringing their dinner was upset in a ditch and failed to arrive. The hill was probably named after Tinakori was accepted for the road. The original Maori name of the hill was Otari; for a short time it was called Mt McCleverty.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Tītahi Bay
info_origin: Described as one lonely cabbage tree. Kupe was known to have landed nearby. Occupied by original settlers Ngāi Tara and Ngāti Ira until their displacement by Te Rauparaha during the early 1800's. Altering an existing recorded name (macron added). Kupe is known to have landed at Kōmanga Point 3 kilometres west of Tītahi Bay where he left his anchor stone. It is now a notable taonga in the National Museum. Early Māori inhabitants from the time of Whātonga and his sons arrived and settled in the area. A whaling station was established in the Bay during the early 1800’s. The Wises NZ Guide concurs with the submitters descriptive meaning of Tītahi as one, single cabbage tree. Dollimore (1962) concurs with Wise’s historical account of Māori settlement.

info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA270725; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: 'Titi is a small but prominent hill in the Manukau low-lands, north of Whakaupoko and the revered Tongaroawhata pa. The name is said to have originated from the titi trees which grew along the slopes of the hill. Traditionally, Titi was a Ngati Tamaoho pa surrounded with the cultivations extending from the base of Whakaupoko and proved a useful vantage point to survey the surrounding landscape. Titi is particularly significant for Ngati Tamaoho because of the battle which took place there during the early stages of the invasion of the Waikato in October 1863. Reports from the incident vary but it is generally accepted that a small taua, including Ngati Tamaoho warriors, were engaged by a group of the settler militia leading to several deaths on both sides. Thus, Titi is a wahi tapu and a symbol of Ngati Tamaoho resistance to the invasion of the Waikato and the sacrifice of those brave men.'. Information source: D Armstrong, Ngati Tamaoho Environmental History DRAFT,190-196 & 203-204.

name: Tītī / Muttonbird Islands
info_ref: Mins v/11 20/02/2001 pp 8; Corres XXXV pp 36-43, 110, 129, 180, XLIII pp 108, 110, 124, 138, 139, 159, 160; File BRD-02-01-00-22; Dual name standardisation: Objective IDs: A4405369, A4507521
info_origin: These islands are the breeding places of the tītī, or muttonbirds (sooty shearwater, Ardenna grisea). The birds visit these islands in October and after mating leave for the sea. They return again at the end of November for the females to lay their eggs in burrows. The islands are divided among the local Māori families for harvesting before the colonies depart at the end of May. These sea birds were described in an 18th century account of the harvesting on Norfolk Island as having meat that tasted like mutton hence the name muttonbirds.

info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche January 2023: Objective ID: A5144656 {Tokaanu. Andersen Card Index ATL; [The Baths at Tokaanu. 1887. New Zealand Herald, 19 November, Page 1 (Supplement)](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH18871119.2.55.5); [Obituary Mr Henry Biggs. 1934. Waikato Times, Volume 115, Issue 19222, 5 April, Page 7.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WT19340405.2.40); [Untitled 1886. Hawke's Bay Herald, 20 October, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/HBH18861020.2.6); [Plan of Toka-anu township, situated in Block VI, Pukawa Survey District [cartographic material] / H.J. info_origin: Literally 'cold rock' and relating to the name given to a stream that rises from the base of a rock and was also applied to the nearby village. Ethnologist Johannes Andersen recorded that the circumstances behind the naming related to an incident when a group of Māori were sitting on the rock when water suddenly burst forth from beneath it, stranding them on it. The water was intensely cold, chilling the rock and providing the origin of the name. A Tokaanu Post Office was opened in 1886 and the Tokaanu Native School in 1887. The thermal pools and springs in the area were praised in 1887 – 'some 20 feet deep [6m], and 20 or 30 feet [6 or 9.1m] across, and being surrounded by an incrustation resembling marble pavement, as clean as a table, the hand of man could scarcely construct more perfect bathing places. Moreover, the waters have been proved to be remarkably good in cases of rheumatism, liver complaint, etc., In addition to the baths there are one or two geysers worth inspecting, also a pretty little petrifying spring. Several cold water creeks flow down from the hills at the back'. The town was surveyed by Henry Biggs (1862-1934) in 1898.

name: Tokomaru
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5111558 {Adkin, Leslie. 1948. Horowhenua. New Zealand: Department of Internal Affairs.; [Editorial. 1884. Manawatu Times, 5 March, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/MT18840305.2.4); [Manawatu Railway Company. 1894. Manawatu Herald, 31 March, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/MH18940331.2.12)}
info_origin: A town on the Wellington and Manawatu Railway Company line. Unlike other towns laid out by the company, such as Shannon, Tokomaru did not bear the name of one of the company directors. Instead, it was named after the nearby Tokomaru River. Tokomaru River was an important part of the channel system draining the Makerua swamp. The river is said to be named for the Tokomaru waka or canoe of the Great Fleet tradition by local Māori ancestrally link to those on the waka.

name: Tokomaru Bay
info_origin: ‘The local hapū recognise several derivations of the name Tokomaru Bay, including Toka-a-namu, or Sandfly rock, and Toka Maru meaning Sheltering rock. The name is sometimes mistakenly attributed to the Tokomaru canoe of the Taranaki people. A post office was opened on 1 October 1876 with the name Te Mawhai, which is the southern peninsula of the bay, altered to Tokomaru on 1 December 1887, and on 24 November 1890 this changed to Tokomaru Bay to avoid confusion with Tokomaru in Manawatū. The bay is increasingly known locally as Tokomaru Ākau (‘ākau’ means ‘bay’). This also recalls the historical name of the resident hapū Whānau a Te Ākau, and the succesful takutai moana (foreshore and seabed) claimant group Ngā Hapū o Tokomaru Ākau.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Tonga Quarry
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-07/1670; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5103412 {NZGS Card Index Tonga Roadstead; Nelson Historical Society 1976. Glossary of coastal Names. Nelson Historical Society Journal 3 (2), 22-27; Field, L. W. 1968. Place-Names. Nelson Historical Society Journal 2(3), 24-30; [Nelson City Council. 1913 Nelson Evening Mail, 11 January, Page 3](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NEM19130111.2.10)}
info_origin: Named for the Tonga Stone Works quarry owned by the Tonga Bay Granite Company. This was a locally owned concern established in 1904. Having been sold to a Wellington contractor in 1906, the quarry provided stone for the Wellington General Post Office and Public Trust Office as well as granite for the Cawthron Institute steps and the cathedral steps in Nelson after which it was closed in 1913. The granite was shipped from the quarry by scow. The quarry and other assets were taken over by the New Zealand Marble Company in 1920. The quarry’s name was derived from the adjacent Tonga Island. Charles Heaphy in 1847 had recorded this island as both Tonga Island and Tagui Island. French explorer Jules Dumont d’Urville in endeavouring to reproduce the original Māori name recorded Tagui Island on his 1827 chart.

name: Tongariro River
info_origin: Tongariro River is named after the Mountain, it means "seized by the cold south wind" it is named after the journey of the ancestor Ngātoroitangi, who climbed the mountain in a bitter southerly. Freezing, he called to his sisters in Hawaiki to send fire. The fire came to him by way of White Island and Rotorua, leaving tokens of their visit for all time. This river is world famous for trout fishing and there was much debate about the possibility of naming of the river Upper Waikato River Tongariro Branch.
info_description: The Tongariro River flows from the junction of Upper Waikato Stream and Waipakihi River through Turangi to meet Lake Taupo at the township of Tokaanu.
info_note: Defining the limits of the Tongariro River: [Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand](http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/volcanic-plateau-region/4). There was much debate about the limits of the Tongariro River and the Waikato/Upper Waikato Rivers. Some Māori people referred to the whole portion of the river as Waikato, and some referred to the limit between the lake and the upper reaches as Tongariro. Refer also "The Reed Dictionary of New Zealand Place names", p525

name: Tory Channel
info_origin: 'The channel was surveyed and named by Captain E.M. Chaffers, commander of the New Zealand Company’s survey vessel Tory, on arrival on 31 August 1839. In 1832 the William the Fourth under Captain William Steine passed through the channel, and Steine named it William the Fourth River; the ‘river’ was of course the channel. Steine’s name was not recognised, and until the arrival of the Tory it was not distinguished from Queen Charlotte Sound. Maori name: Kurateau: lit. kura: red; te: the; au: current. Kupe gave the name to describe the red colour in the water, which was made by krill. Another Maori name from Kupe’s voyage here was Whekenui (Great octopus), after the octopus of Muturangi that the great explorer killed in the channel.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Te Atiawa and Ngati Tama note that this was an important mahinga kai and settlement site for Te Atiawa, was the Te Atiawa main highway, Te Atiawa continually monitor and defend this waterway today in Environment courts. Kura Te Au separates Arapaoa Island from the mainland in the Marlborough Sounds. Kura Te Au so named because of the red colour of the sea imparted by a variety of plankton and the by multitude of the crustacean krill. Kura Te Au is place where Kupe killed the giant wheke and the blood ran through the channel. Kurahaupo and Rangitane note that this means “the red current”. When Kupe killed Te Wheke o Muturangi, the octopus bled into the current there, turning it red. The name also denotes the red krill found all around the outer Sounds which is eaten by octopus and whales (hence the whaling presence) and is part of the Kupe oral map.; 'The channel was surveyed and named by Captain E.M. Chaffers, commander of the New Zealand Company’s survey vessel Tory, on arrival on 31 August 1839. Kura Te Au is so named because of the red colour imparted by a variety of plankton and the multitudes of the crustacean krill. It is where Kupe killed the giant wheke/octopus and its blood ran through the channel, turning it red.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: 'In the early days mail was brought here by sea from Kerikeri, and the captain was accustomed to tie his vessel to a large totara tree by the Iwitawa bridge. Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: An original Māori name for the area which included a large village, occupied until at least the 1820s, by the mouth of Tōtaranui Stream. It was a recognised safe landing place for waka (canoes) crossing Cook Strait. Charles Heaphy and Thomas Brunner recorded this name in 1846 in the course of their expedition. Donald McLean (1820-77), as Chief Land Purchase Commissioner, concluded the sale of various lands in Marlborough and Nelson including Tōtaranui in 1854. Two years later in 1856 William Gibbs purchased 272 acres (110 ha) including the beach at Tōtaranui. Over the next decade he bought over 1000 acres (404 ha) and leased another 6000 acres (2428 ha) stretching from Separation Point / Te Matau to the Awaroa River. He built a lavish home at Tōtaranui in 1878, which he called after the locale. Literally translates as 'many tōtara trees'. Ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1873-1963) was emphatic that the name meant 'many' rather than 'big' tōtara trees.; 'Lit. tōtara: trees; nui: many. The name was given by Ngāti Apa iwi. Tōtaranui is also the Māori name for Queen Charlotte Sound.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_ref:
Objective ID: A4635550; A7175936; [ALTERATION OF BOUNDARIES](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBH19200715.2.81).
Poverty Bay Herald, Volume XLVI, Issue 14963, 16 July 1919, Page 4
info_origin: Named in relation to Arthur Trafford, a sheep farmer. His run (Section 5 Block I Motu West SD) and the Trafford family homestead were just to the north at the border between Opotiki County and Waikohu County, on the Ōpōtiki side. While Ōpōtiki was closer as the crow flies, the railroad to Gisborne at Mātāwai was just a few miles to the southeast, so all Trafford's business was conducted in Gisborne. In 1919 he and others in the area initially attempted to have the country boundaries altered to move them to Waikohu County, and then in 1920, to form their own county, both unsuccessfully. Construction to upgrade the track from Mātāwai to Waioweka to a road that could be used by motor vehicles began in 1923, opening in late 1929. By at least 1935 the section from the Trafford homestead up and over to Te Kapu had become known as Traffords Hill.

info_origin: Tuapeka Mouth is the name of the locality where Tuapeka River joins Clutha River/Mata-au. It was a Ngāi Tahu food gathering area and a kāinga mahinga kai, particularly for tuna (eels) and pora (‘Māori turnip’ - Brassica rapa). The Tuapeka area was also the locality of the first major goldrush in Otago in 1861. Miners worked their way down Tuapeka River towards its junction with the Clutha River/Mata-Au. This area was known as Tuapeka Mouth. In 1863 a town site was laid out by Otago surveyor James Moran on the north bank of Tuapeka River where it entered Clutha River/Mata-au. Moran gave it the name of Dalhousie after the former Vice-Roy of India who had died in 1860 and for a time the town served as an inland port. Local inhabitants resisted jokes about being described as ‘down at the mouth’, but Tuapeka Mouth retained favour and from the 1870s increasingly replaced Dalhousie. Herries Beattie, a collector of Māori place names, suggested that Tuapeka means to cut down the branch of a tree for firewood, elsewhere it was thought to be a corruption of ‘the fruitful branch’.

info_origin: Unsuccessful applications to the Tuapeka goldfield Mining Warden for leases of agricultural land in Tuapeka West dated from 1868. Tenders were called for a 4500 acre (1821 ha) survey of the area in 1869. The first sawmillers began work there that same year. Previously the area was known as ‘scrubby run’ and served as a source of firewood for the town of Lawrence and surrounding areas prior to the arrival of the railway in 1877. Sections in the area were proclaimed as open for selection by the Commissioner of Crown Lands in Dunedin in 1874. The first settlers were miners from the neighbouring goldfields.

info_origin: Tui Lake was named by Thomas Bell (1839-1929) who with his family settled on Raoul Island in 1878, remaining there until 1914. The name was bestowed because of the large number of tūī (Prosthemadera novaseelandiae) observed catching insects in the pōhutukawa trees (Metrosideros kermadecensis) that surrounded the lake. Surveyor and ethnologist, Stephenson Percy Smith (1840-1922) who was sent to the Kermadec Islands by the New Zealand government to oversee its annexation, included the lake on his 1887 map of Raoul Island but did not record any name for it. However, naturalist WRB Oliver (1883-1957), who spent 12 months on Raoul Island in 1907-08, recorded Tui Lake on the map included in his 1909 article on the vegetation of the Kermadec Islands. The name was also shown on government surveyor J Allan Henderson’s topographical survey map of the island completed in 1939 and based on fieldwork in 1937-38.
info_description: A small lake just south of Dry Crater and west of Green Lake, near the centre of Raoul Island, Kermadec Islands. Feature shown on: NZOITopo25-KI01

name: Tungongo
info_ref: Objective folder ID: fA490228; A4405895; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche November 2022: Objective ID: A5098963 {Raukawa's old canoe routes - heading south. 1985, Tu Tangata, 27, 1, Page 42; Waikawaiti - heading north (Old South Island terminal). 1985. Tu Tangata, 27, Page 43}
info_origin: On canoe journeys from Te Waipounamu the South Island to Te Ika-a-Māui the North Island, the vessels hugged the east coast of Arapaoa Island. If weather conditions deteriorated the party would come ashore at Tungongo and wait until the weather improved. As this was an inhospitable location the crew would climb over an old trail, now gone through erosion, and descend to the sheltered East Bay at Ruapara. Tungongo has been literally translated as a chrysalis. There is some confusion over the name, for in traditional chants the place of departure is given as Omere which is the prominent background range of coastal hills on the island.

info_origin: Tūranganui-a-Kiwa describes the long standing or waiting place of Kiwa of the Horouta or Tākitimu waka. There are a number of stories behind the name, originally applied to a place beside Turanganui River. Kiwa is an important tupuna of many iwi, with mana whenua Ngai Tāmanuhiri, Rongowhakaata, and Te Aitanga a Māhaki also describing themselves as Tūrunga iwi. Poverty Bay was given by Cook. In October 1769 the HMB Endeavour sailed into the bay, captained by Lieutenant James Cook. Following altercations with local Māori, Cook was unable to resupply his ship. After six days the Endeavour moved on, Cook writing that the bay 'afforded us no one thing we wanted'. He originally intended to name the feature 'Endeavour Bay'. The dual name Tūranganui-a-Kiwa / Poverty Bay recognises the important heritage of both place names. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMEREQzM3NzEwMDBGRjg3ODI3MEM)
info_description: A large bay on the east coast of the North Island, south of Gisborne (town), bounded on its seaward side between Tuaheni Point (NZTopo50-BG43 409034) to Young Nicks Head (Te Kuri) (NZTopo50-BG43 322985). Feature shown on: NZMS260 Y18 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-BG43 343033

info_origin: Named by Dunedin mountaineers Hugh Francis Wright (1866-1938), John Robertson (1870-1946) and Harry Dodgshun Bedford (1877-1918) who climbed on the western flanks of Mount Earnslaw/Pikirakatahi in 1912-13. They first scaled what was then known as Black Peak in 1912 and ‘rechristened’ it ‘Turret Peak’ because there was another Black Peak ‘on the Rees side’ of Mount Earnslaw/Pikirakatahi and the 2350m peak’s ‘resemblance to the turret of an ancient castle’. Free of snow, the party spent the night on the summit sheltered amongst the boulders. The Honorary Geographic Board confirmed Turret Head in 1938. The adjustment was plausibly chosen to avoid confusion with Turret Peaks, which face Lake Te Anau and had been named by Otago surveyor James McKerrow in the 1860s.

info_ref: Min 2, 81/41, Min 3, 6/70; Corres XVII pp 32, 62-3, 68, XLI pp 111-2, 136; Review of Trig names - Objective folder ID: fA521344
info_origin: A 1941 Geographic Board ruling was based on the Sir Apirana Ngata's evidence that although it had always been spelt Tutamoe, older Māori had always pronounced the name Tutamoi. However in a submission by the Chief Surveyor, Gisborne, evidence was produced that there had been no record of the spelling Tutamoi before the Board's decision of 1941, on any record found anywhere, and that the translation of Tutamoe, Tu meaning to stand, and Tamoe, meaning to press flat, seemed to have some significance. The hill on which the Trig. Tutamoe stands is a flat topped hill, and it appears that the name was derived from this feature. Instead of "Tutamoi". (1941 Hon p. 38)

name: Tyrwhitt Peak
info_ref: Evening Post, 14 November 1924, p. 2.; Heathcote, Tony, The British Admirals of the Fleet, 1734-1995: A Biographical Dictionary, Barnsley: Leo Cooper, 2002.; Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand: Correspondence, vol. 2, p. 19.; New Zealand Geographic Board: Minutes, 1948 (42).; Reed, A.W., Place Names of New Zealand, Rosedale: Penguin, 2010.; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-06-14/2013
info_origin: In 1924, Sir Frederick Chapman, a former Supreme Court judge and member of the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand, suggested new names for two features on Lake Wanaka. He proposed that the body of water on ‘Pigeon Island’ should become Arethusa Pool and that the Island’s highest point should be titled Tyrwhitt Peak. When the time came to seek official approval for these changes, the Governor-General, Admiral John Jellicoe, further moved that ‘Pigeon Island’ be renamed ‘Harwich Island’. At the outbreak of the First World War, Commodore Reginald Tyrwhitt was placed in command of the Royal Navy’s Harwich Force. This squadron was largely composed of destroyers, together with some light cruisers and flotilla leaders. Harwich Force had three main objectives: to protect the approaches to the English Channel; to monitor German activities in the North Sea; and to escort ships between Britain and the Netherlands. Tyrwhitt and his men successfully carried out these tasks. Although it was absent from the largest naval engagement of the War at Jutland, Harwich Force played an important role at the Battles of Heligoland Blight, Texel, and Dogger Bank. It also captured or sank 24 enemy merchant vessels, and escorted 520 eastbound and 511 westbound ships between British and Dutch ports. The name Tyrwhitt Peak was first Gazetted by the Honorary Geographic Board of New Zealand in 1924, and was officially confirmed by the New Zealand Geographic Board in 1948.

info_origin: Mrs Margaret McCulloch of Howick made a submission to the Minister of Lands and to the Geographic Board in June 1970 to have the name Umupuia restored as the name for the beach 3km South-west of Maraetai. The beach area was the site of the ancient Māori Pa site of Umupuia, and the pa site forms the background of the portrait of Tara-Te-Irirangi, painted in 1844 by George French Angas. Tara's descendants still farmed the area at the time of submission. The Duder family who farmed a portion at the South end of the beach had no objection to a name change from Duders Beach. There was a Duders Beach in Devonport, which was associated with the family, that had prior claim to the name. Instead of "Duders Beach"

name: Upper Ātiamuri
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2023: Objective ID: A5238764 {NZGB IV/95; Upper Atiamuri. R10858748, Archives New Zealand, Wellington; [Sidney Takimoana Anaru. 'Ānaru, Karauria Tiweka', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 2000. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/5a11/anaru-karauria-tiweka) (accessed 16 March 2023)}
info_origin: A branch Post Office known as Atiamuri was opened in the Atiamuri Hotel in 1890 where it remained until 1916 when, after staff resignations, it was transferred to Thomas Vivian Humphrey who ran it from his home some '8 miles' [12.8 Km] from the original location. The branch office retained the name Atiamuri. In 1924, on account of demand for a telephone from the increasing users of the Putaruru – Taupo highway, the Post Office reopened a telephone office at the initial site which it renamed Atiamuri Bridge. In March 1926 Auckland Weekly News journalist (Fredrick) Carr Rollett (1861-1931), author of Angling in New Zealand (1924), wrote to the Postmaster General complaining that letters addressed to him at Atiamuri had been delivered 'to eight miles way at a farmhouse with no claim whatever to the name'. Rollett pointed to the difficulty of collecting his mail and claimed that the Māori name was specific to the area where the bridge was sited. While contesting some of Rollet's arguments the Postmaster General did agree to investigate his assertion that the Atiamuri name was now displaced. The views of the Honorary Geographic Board and the Under Secretary for Native Affairs were sought. The Surveyor-General, replying on behalf of the Board, indicated that Atimauri was linked to a local Māori woman, an ancestor of the tribe, who was turned into a large rock called Pohaturoa visible in the river. Moreover, survey plans dating back to 1882 pinpointed Atiamuri to the junction of the road, bridge and river. Separately the Board had been approached by the Department of Agriculture requesting that Atiamuri Bridge be renamed Atiamuri, a change which it supported. The Under Secretary's inquiries reached a similar conclusion, both the Head office translator and the knowledgeable Karauria Tiweka Ānaru (1901-77), Registrar of the Native Land Court at Rotorua, confirmed that Atiamuri was linked only to the area where the bridge now stood. Furthermore, Ānaru's informants stated that the new post office site was known as Te Papa-a-Hinemaru and the nearby stream Waipaheke. The Surveyor-General recommended that Atiamuri replace Atiamuri Bridge and a new name be found for the office on Humphrey's farm. Before this could take place, local residents wrote to the Post Office objecting to the proposed name change. A meeting of 'settlers and residents' unanimously opposed the change citing the 'annoyance and delay' that would arise from the misdirection of 'eighty telegraph and telephone communications per week'. They claimed that Atiamuri adequately described the area where the post office had been relocated. In addition, they demanded 'We would like to know what practical bearing the geographical and historical reports relating to the specific point which has given the name by which the district has become known can have on the alteration of the name of the office'. In June 1926 the Chief Postmaster in Rotorua approached Humphrey for suggestions about alternative names but without success. Writing to Head Office he explained, 'No reply has been received. Evidently a policy of passive resistance is being followed'. In October that year Head Office officially changed the name of the Post Office to Upper Atiamuri which was subsequently adopted by the surrounding area.

info_origin: A descriptive name seemingly applied to distinguish it from another junction 2km downstream (later known as Lower Junction). In 1867 [James] Roger Dutton a Nelson farmer, JP, and one-time Resident Magistrate at Cobden and Warden of the Nelson South West Goldfields organised the completion of a track beginning from the junction of Graham River and Motueka River, linking Nelson to the Karamea goldfields and which passed along Flora Stream and Balloon Creek. It was one of four such tracks to the goldfields. Nelson Provincial Assistant Engineer Arthur Dobson (1841-1934) inspected the track late in 1867. In 1887 a later traveller wrote of how he descended 600 ft (180m) ‘to the junction of the Flora creek and River Takaka, then followed the track up the Takaka River till we reached the Table-Land’. Notes for and reports by recreational users from the inter-war period consistently use the descriptive term ‘junction of the Flora and Takaka Rivers’. At some point post World War II this was cemented as the ‘Junction’ and then modified to Upper Junction to avoid confusion with what became the Lower Junction 2 km away where the Upper Tākaka, Bullock, and Asbestos tracks converged. Upper Junction was not listed in the 1968 Gazetteer of New Zealand Place Names but was included on the metric 1977 1:50000 map series.

info_origin: Kawhātau is an original Māori name given to the river which fleetingly attracted European attention in 1869 when small quantities of gold were found in the it. Kawhātau was used in the 1890s by European settlers to name the valley and newly constructed road that ran along it. The area around the junction of the Kawhātua River and Rangitīkei River was taken up by the Kawhatau Improved Small Farms Settlement in 1895. The settlement spread up the valley and by 1897 the locality was known as Upper Kawhātau to distinguish it from Kawhātau which in turn became Lower Kawhātau by 1902. In 1910 a party of men organised by John Stevens (1845-1916), a former auctioneer, a licensed translator and later MP for Rangitikei (1881-84, 1893-96) and Manawatu (1896-1902, 1905-08), and under the charge of Alexander [Alick] Cameron (1867-1941), a Turakina based shepherd with good bush skills, ventured up the Kawhātau valley through Upper Kawhātau into the Ruahine Ranges on one of the last unsuccessful expeditions initiated by Dominion Museum director Augustus Hamilton to search for huia for transferring to the Kapiti Flora and Fauna Sanctuary

info_origin: An original Māori name for the Mātakitaki valley and river which was used to describe an area further along the valley from Mātakitaki. William Fox, Charles Heaphy and Thomas Brunner all journeyed through the Mātakitaki valley in 1846 and noted the original Māori name in their reports. In the aftermath of gold discoveries in southwest Nelson, by 1863 Upper Mātakitaki was used to designate its position on Mātakitaki River with respect to Mātakitaki. In 1864 Nelson Provincial Engineer John Blackett, in searching for transport routes between Nelson and Westland, uses Upper Mātakitaki as a location. By 1877 there was a Post Office of the same name at Upper Mātakitaki which gave the locality official standing. Mātakitaki has been translated as meaning 'an open view'.

info_description: A range 26km long that includes Escalade Peak (2035m), Tate Peak (1885m) and Mount Marvel (1540m), located at the south margin of Skelton Névé between Boomerang Range and Worcester Range.
info_note: The New Zealand Geographic Board and Antarctica NZ accepted Van Allen Range on 4/11/1999.

name: Vance Bluff
info_origin: Mapped from air photographs taken by the US Navy. Named by US-ACAN after USS Vance, ocean station ship between New Zealand and McMurdo Sound during USN Operation Deepfreeze 1962.
info_description: A small ice-covered eminence, approximately 2400m above sea level, 34km southeast of Wilhoite Nunataks. The flat summit of the feature merges with the ice sheet to the north and west but there is a steep cliff on the southern side.

name: Vancouver Arm
info_origin: 'Vancouver, Mount: Southern Alps. After Captain George Vancouver. Charted as Nobody Knows What by Captain James Cook in 1773 because it had not been possible to penetrate the full length of the arm. George Vancouver — who had served under Cook as midshipman on the Resolution — returned to New Zealand in 1791 in command of the ships Discovery and Chatham and renamed it Somebody Knows What. See Broughton Arm. The name Mt Vancouver was adopted by the New Zealand Geographic Board in November 1953, continuing the practice of naming the peaks after famous navigators.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 B43

name: Vancouver Mountain
info_origin: George Vancouver served as a midshipman under James Cook on the Resolution in 1773. In 1791 he returned as commander of an expidition comprising the Discovery and the Chatham, on his way to explore the Pacific coast of North America. Name originally suggested by D O W Hall of Dunedin around 1938. Also Gazetted in Canterbury Land District
info_description: On Main Divide immediately north of Mount Dampier and South of Malaspina.   Block XI Mount Cook Survey District (Westland LD) and Block III Mueller Survey District (Canterbury LD).

name: Vancouver Rock
info_ref: Mins v/2 27/52; Corres XXIV pp 253, XXVI pp 246, 256, 269
info_origin: Named after the discoverer of the Snares Islands, Captain George Vancouver of the HMS Discovery.
info_description: Rock breaking the surface between the main island and the Western Chain islets in Snares Islands/Tini Heke. Feature shown on: NZOITopo25-SI01

name: Vandament Glacier
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Charles H. Vandament, US Antarctic Research Program (USARP) ionospheric physicist at South Pole Station, 1962.
info_description: An east-flowing glacier draining the central portion of the Dominion Range icecap. The glacier lies parallel to and south of Koski Glacier, flowing for approximately 12km before merging with the later, to the northwest of Safety Spur.

name: Vanda Station
info_origin: Vanda Station was a New Zealand summer season research facility that operated from 1969 to 1991. It supported a contingent of 12 staff with some overwintering events in 1969, 1970, 1974. The station was administered by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) and scientific programmes principally included meteorology, hydrology, seismology, earth currents, and magnetics. The station was originally constructed 200m and 15m above the shore of Lake Vanda. From the mid 1980s the level of Lake Vanda and other lakes in the McMurdo Dry Valleys began to rise rapidly. The base was dismantled and removed in 1993 and the local environment remediated including the removal of tonnes of contaminated soils and groundwater. As of 2025 nearly the entire footprint of the station is under water. As lake levels continue to rise, impermanent replacement facilities to the north known as 'Vanda Huts' are now themselves under threat of inundation.
info_description: The site of New Zealand's Vanda Station, occupied 1969-1991. Now almost fully submerged in Lake Vanda. Feature shown on: AntTopo50-ME08

name: Van der Veen Ice Stream
info_origin: Named by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) after Cornelis J. "Kees" van der Veen, Byrd Polar Research Center and Departments of Geological Sciences and Geography, Ohio State University, Columbus, OH
info_description: A large southeast tributary to Whillans Ice Stream in Marie Byrd Land.
