name: Van Leeuwen Landing
info_ref: Min 3, 63/68; Corres XXXIX pp 270-2, XL pp 18, 118
info_origin: Name submitted by the Chief Surveyor Invercargill for revision of NZMS219 Stewart Island. Name supplied by Mr Roy Traill. Named after Dutchman John Van Leeuwen, who in 1963, became the first and only person to swim across Foveaux Strait, regarded by many to be a much more difficult task than swimming Cook Strait. The point on which the landing was made did not warrant a name, hence the somewhat facetious use of the word "landing".
info_description: Small point located halfway between Trig. 18651 (Geodetic Code A02C) at Garden Point,and Rollers Beach, 500m North by North-west of the Trig.  Stewart Island.  Block 11 Anglem Survey District.

name: Van Loon Glacier
info_origin: Mapped by United States Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and US Navy aerial photography, 1960-62. Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for meteorologist Harry van Loon, a member of the Antarctic Weather Central team at Little America on the Ross Ice Shelf 1957-58, who has written numerous scientific papers dealing with Antarctic and southern hemisphere atmospheric research.
info_description: A tributary glacier, approximately 17.5km long, draining the eastern slopes of the Bowers Mountains between Rastorguev Glacier and Montigny Glacier. It merges into the larger Graveson Glacier at the east margin of the mountains.

name: Vantage Hill
info_origin: The feature was the most southerly point reached by the Darwin Glacier Party of the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition (CTAE) (1957-58), who gave it this name because of the splendid view it afforded.
info_description: A flat-topped hill, c.2080 m above sea level and 300 m above the surrounding plateau, standing 18km southwest of Mount Henderson in the western part of Britannia Range. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MP04

name: Vantage Hills
info_origin: Named from their position of vantage by the Northern Party of the NZGSAE, 1962-63.
info_description: Escarpment like hills overlooking Campbell-Rennick saddle from south.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Vapour Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I34 Edition 1 1994

name: Varcoe Headland
info_origin: Named by NZGB after Technical Services Officer Garth Edwin Varcoe, helicopter pilot, who worked in the NZ Antarctic Programme over a period of 15 years until his accidental death in a helipcopter crash near this headland in October 1992. His expertise was in the mechanical and electrical areas and he played a leading role in the reconstruction of Scott Base. The feature had been unofficially named Varcoe Headland since the accident. Note that Varcoe Headland is not the same feature as Rocky Point. Refer to an email from the US of 2/12/1999 which confirms that ACAN accepts this name.
info_description: A low headland, 34m, that marks the north entrance point to Horseshoe Bay in west Ross Island. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME13

name: Varleys Hill
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I44 J44 Edition 2 1987

name: Varney Nunatak
info_origin: Mapped by U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and U.S. Navy air photos, 1957-62. Named by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Kenneth L. Varney, U.S. Navy (USN), Equipment Operator at McMurdo Station during the 1965-66 and 1966-67 summer seasons.
info_description: An ice-free nunatak on the south side of the mouth of Harbord Glacier, where Harbour Glacier Tongue projects out into the Ross Sea, in Victoria Land. 4.4km south-southwest of Starr Nunatak, opposite across the glacier.

name: Vashka Crag
info_origin: Named by VUWAE, 1959-60, for nearby Lake Vashka.
info_description: A prominence at the eastern end of a flat-topped divide capped by Beacon Sandstone overlooking Lake Vashka. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME08
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Vaughan Bank
info_ref: SCAR #16784; Balleny Chart©, Sturge Island Chart©; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836
info_origin: Source: SCAR Altered to Vaughan Seamount. NIWA advises that the feature was named for VJ Vaughan, Commanding Officer, USS Glacier, which was used in the United States/New Zealand Balleny Island Expedition in 1965. Vaughan Promontory, which overlooks the Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica, was also named after Commander VJ Vaughan of the United States Navy.
info_description: A seamount in the Southern Ocean, west of Sturge Island, Balleny Islands.

name: Vaughan Glacier
info_origin: Mapped by United States Geological Survey (USGS) from surveys and US Navy (USN) air photos, 1960-64. Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) in association with Mount Vaughan.
info_description: A tributary glacier, draining eastward from Mount Vaughan for approximately 23km to enter Scott Glacier just south of Taylor Ridge, in the Hays Mountains of the Queen Maud Mountains.

name: Vaughan Promontory
info_origin: Named by the United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) for Commander Vie J. Vaughan, US Navy (USN), commanding officer of USS Glacier during Operation Deep Freeze (OpDFrz) 1964 and 1965.
info_description: A high, rugged ice-covered promontory which extends approximately 34km eastward from Holland Range between Ekblad Glacier to the north and Morton Glacier to the south, terminating at Cape Maude which overlooks Ross Ice Shelf.

name: Vaughan Seamount
info_ref: Balleny Chart©, Sturge Island Chart©; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836
info_origin: Altered from Vaughan Bank. NIWA advises that the feature was named for VJ Vaughan, Commanding Officer, USS Glacier, which was used in the United States/New Zealand Balleny Island Expedition in 1965. Vaughan Promontory, which overlooks the Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica, was also named after Commander VJ Vaughan of the United States Navy.
info_description: A seamount in the Southern Ocean, west of Sturge Island, Balleny Islands.

name: Vauxhall
info_origin: ’Pleasure gardens were established here in 1862 by Shadrach Edward Robert Jones MD, who had come to Dunedin from Bendigo in 1861. He named them Vauxhall after the well-known gardens in London; there is a similar origin for the suburb on Auckland’s North Shore, between Cheltenham and Narrow Neck.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I44 J44 Edition 2 1987

name: Vauxhall
info_origin: 'Auckland, North Shore, between Cheltenham and Narrow Neck. The district takes its name from the Vauxhall Gardens, the pleasure gardens on the south bank of the River Thames in London that closed in 1859.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 R11 Edition 2 1994

name: V Cliffs
info_description: Steep, mainly ice-covered cliffs, extending for approximately 7.2km between Aurora Glacier and Terror Glacier on the south shore of Ross Island. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MF14

name: Vee Cliffs
info_origin: The name is suggested by two prominent V-shape wedges which protrude from the cliff wall. The name was first used by Dr. Edward A. Wilson who, with Thomas V. Hodgson of BrNAE, 1901-04, visited the cliffs in November 1903.
info_description: Steep, mainly ice-covered cliffs, extending for approximately 7.2km between Aurora Glacier and Terror Glacier on the south shore of Ross Island. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MF14
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Vee Spur
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E40 Edition 1 1993 Limited Revision 1996

name: Vee Stream
info_origin: Name submitted by Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, New Zealand Geological Survey after recent geological mapping of part sheet N158 and N159 had necessitated the naming of some of the watercourses. Name in local use, and used in geological literature. Origin and meaning unknown.
info_description: Left bank tributary of Makirikiri Stream rising South of Trig. Manawa (Geodetic Code A408), flowing southward and joining Makirikiri Stream 3km West of Burton Fields Homestead.  Block VII Mangapakeha Survey District.

name: Vegetation Island
info_origin: Discovered by the Northern Party, led by Victor Lindsay Arbuthnot Campbell, of the British Antarctic (Terra Nova) Expedition, 1910-13. Explored by Priestley and Dickason of this party on 5 February 1912, and named by Priestley because the rocks were densely covered with all sorts of lichens. Not Lichen Island.
info_description: A narrow island about 3.6km long north to south, lying 4.6km north of Inexpressible Island and west of the Northern Foothills, at Terra Nova Bay, along the coast of Victoria Land.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Veil Col
info_origin: Named from the Veil Stream below and to the West of the col. Name suggested by J C Pattle and submitted by D L Parr, Canterbury Mountaineering Club, April 1953.
info_description: At head of Veil Stream leading into unnamed tributary of Frances River.  Ramsay Survey District.

name: Veil Peak
info_origin: The peak supports a permanent veil of snow falling from the higher southern slopes. The name is in line with a first impression and is readily recognised from such a description. Name suggested by J C Pattle and submitted by D L Parr, Canterbury Mountaineering Club, April 1953.
info_description: At end of south-western ridge of Trireme Peak.  Tyndall Survey District.

name: Veil Stream
info_origin: Named from Veil Peak, which dominates this streams's outlet to the Havelock River. Name suggested by J C Pattle and submitted by D L Parr, Canterbury Mountaineering Club, April 1953.
info_description: In deep valley flowing from Cloudy Peak Range into Havelock River at point one and a half miles above Eric Hut.  Tyndall Survey District.

name: Vela Stream
info_origin: Replaced by Vella Stream 22/06/2006 63:1515
info_description: Stream flowing north-easterly into the Opanuku Stream in West Auckland, Topographic Map 260-R11 Auckland, GR 525 768

name: Veli Peak
info_origin: The name, originally supplied by the Superintendent of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR), was stated to be from 'Norse Mythology', so was likely meant to be 'Vali', a son of Odin and the giantess Rindr.
info_description: A peak at 2085m just east of Idun Peak and 1.8km south of Brunhilde Peak in Asgard Range of Victoria Land. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MF08

name: Vella Flat
info_origin: Named by United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) (1999) after Prof Paul Vella, Department of Geology, Victoria University of Wellington, who made a reconnaissance survey of Brown Peninsula and Black Island stratigraphy with the Victoria University of Wellington Antarctic Expedition (VUWAE), 1964-65.
info_description: A coastal flat to the south of Lake Cole in the northwest part of Black Island, Ross Archipelago.

name: Vella Stream
info_origin: Named after John Vella (c1863 – 1935), an immigrant Dalmatian pioneer vine grower and wine maker, who established a vineyard at Waikumete (now known as Oratia) in 1903. Spelling alteration from Vela Stream (13/07/1989 120:3005).; 'Formerly known as Vela Stream, and thought to be after the Vela family, orchardists and winemakers of Dalmatian origin. The New Zealand Geographic Board corrected the spelling in 2006 because this was the name of a family of settlers here in the nineteenth century.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Stream flowing north-easterly into the Opanuku Stream in West Auckland, Topographic Map 260-R11 Auckland, GR 525 768

name: Vening Meinesz Fracture Zone
info_ref: Daniel E Karig (1970) Kermadec arc—New Zealand tectonic confluence, New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics, 13:1, 21-29; https://doi.org/10.1080/00288306.1970.10428203; PF Ballance & KB Spörli (1979) Northland Allochthon, Journal of the Royal; Society of New Zealand, 9:2, 259-275, https://doi.org/10.1080/03036758.1979.10419416; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836
info_origin: Probably named for Felix Andries Vening Meinesz (1887-1966), a Dutch geophysicist and geodesist who invented a precise method for measuring gravity.
info_description: The scarp-like northwest trending rectilinear northern boundary of the New Zealand  microcontinent. It separates Lord Howe Rise, Norfolk Ridge and Rēinga Basin from Three Kings Ridge and Colville Ridge.

name: Venison Top

name: Ventifact Knobs
info_origin: Although the knobs were noted by British geologists in early expeditions they were first studied and described in scientific papers by Professor T L Péwé of the US Deep Freeze III, 1957-58. He gave them this descriptive name.
info_description: Knobs composed of lake clay covered by glacial drift. Ranging up to 12m high, the glacial drift has cobbles which are well wind-polished and cut into ventifacts. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-MF09
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Venture Creek

The Hadfield family, then residing at Awaroa, owned a boat of that name, which was abandoned in this creek in the 1930s, remains of the hull were still in evidence there at the time of submission.
info_description: Stream rising 500m North of Stony Hill [Trig. N (Geodetic Code A73A), flowing Northward into the eastern arm of Awaroa Inlet, North-east of Mount Rollinson.  Abel Tasman National Park.  Blocks VI and VII, Totaranui Survey District.

name: Venus Bay
info_origin: 'The English form of Anse Venus, the name given by the 1874 French expedition to observe the transit of Venus.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.
info_description: Bay in Perseverance Harbour, Campbell Island/Motu Ihupuku. Feature shown on: NZOITopo50-CM01

name: Venus Creek
info_ref: Min 3, 257/65; Corres XXXVIII pp 84, 87, 104, File 11/67 f/299-300
info_origin: One of a series of names proposed in the North-west Nelson district, to facilitate Search and Rescue operations in the area. Name suggested by Lands and Survey Department, Nelson, in keeping with the cosmic naming theme in the area.
info_description: A left bank tributary of the Karamea River, rising from the Herbert Range, North-east of Twenty Four Tarn Basin and entering the Karamea River approximately 1.5km north of Mercury Creek.  Tasman Survey District.

name: Venus Valley
info_description: Valley north of Terror Cove, along the coastal margin around Seeliger Creek, and around the site of the place marked as “German expedition”. Feature shown on: NZOITopo50-AK03

name: Vereyken Glacier
info_origin: Named by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) (1994) after Jill Vereyken, ASA manager of Field Support Services, McMurdo Station, who was active in coordination and planning of science support in Antarctica from 1984.
info_description: A glacier which, together with Morning Glacier, drains the northeast slopes of Mount Morning, Victoria Land. Vereyken Glacier flows north between Riviera Ridge and Hurricane Ridge into Koettlitz Glacier. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MH10

name: Vernier Valley
info_origin: The name is one of a group in the area associated with surveying applied in 1993 by NZGB. A vernier is a graduated scale used on measuring instruments to allow the reading of finer subdivisions.
info_description: An ice free valley on the eat side of Mount Blackwelder in the northeast part of Wilkniss Mountains, Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MG08
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map No available map; Shown on US 250000 Not shown on Taylor Glacier (USA) map, ST 57-60/5.

info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 Q05 Edition 1 1983

name: Veronica Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 J33 Edition 1 1991 Reprinted 1994

name: Ver-Sur-Mer Inlet
info_ref: See Map of the Bay of Whales published in Richard Byrd (1930) Little America, New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, p.416
info_origin: Named by Admiral Byrd on 1 January 1929 for the village in France where he landed and was most hospitably treated at the end of his Trans-Atlantic flight in 1927.
info_description: A former small inlet in the eastern portion of the original Bay of Whales, indenting the Ross Ice Shelf. Little America, the base for the Byrd Antarctic Expedition, 1928-30 and 1933-35, was located at the head of this inlet. No longer exists because of the changes in configuration in the Ross Ice Shelf.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Vertebrae Col
info_origin: Name submitted by the Canterbury Chief Surveyor, September 1969, after research in connection with the revision of NZMS1 S72. Originally submitted by David Parr of the Canterbury Mountaineering Club in July 1953, and resubmitted by Alwyn Chin in June 1963, the name was disallowed on both occasions. It has been mentioned in Canterbury Mountaineer, and was now a well established name. Origin and meaning unknown, but name in keeping with those in the area.
info_description: Pass 1km South-east of Mount Barlow, the lowest point on the Devils Backbone ridge.  Block II Tyndall Survey District.

name: Verter Burn
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 H44 Edition 1 1987

name: Vertigo Bluff
info_origin: Rock samples were collected at the bluff by John Gunner and Henry Brecher of the Ohio State University Geological Expedition, 1969-70. The name suggested by Gunner reflects the precipitous nature of the bluff face.
info_description: A prominent rock bluff at the south of Holland Range, its domed icecap rising to 1998m, on the west side of Lennox-King Glacier opposite Ressler Peak, and 8km south of Asquith Bluff.

name: Veryan Bank
info_ref: GEBCO 5.10; NZ 224F; NZ 14600; Brodie, 1958a, 1964a; Brodie & Pantin, 1960 (South Is Chart); Krause & Cullen, 1970 (Bounty Chart); LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836
info_origin: Named after HMS Veryan Bay from which soundings in this area were taken in 1950.
info_description: South Chatham Slope. At the western end of the South Chatham Slope, that lies between the Chatham Rise and the Bounty Trough. Centred about 250 km ESE of Banks Peninsula. Rises from surrounding depths of between 500 m and 700 m to a flat top at about 150 m deep.

name: Veryan Channels
info_ref: Krause, 1966; Bounty Chart©, Krause & Cullen, 1970; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-01-05/836
info_origin: Named after HMS Veryan Bay, which took soundings in the area in 1950.
info_description: An undersea valley at the southwestern end of South Chatham Slope, extending from -45.1917 latitude, 176.5209 longitude, to -45.1490 latitude, 177.5968 longitude.

name: Veryan Valley
info_origin: Named after HMS Veryan Bay, which took soundings in the area in 1950.
info_description: An undersea valley at the southwestern end of South Chatham Slope, extending from -45.1917 latitude, 176.5209 longitude, to -45.1490 latitude, 177.5968 longitude.

name: Vesta Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 L25 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-BN22 GR 385 803

name: Vestal Ridge
info_origin: Named by Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) in 1993 after J. Robie Vestal (1942-92), microbiologist at the University of Cincinnati, 1983-92, chairman of the advisory committee to the Division of Polar Programs, National Science Foundation, 1990-91. His research in Antarctica focused on adaptations of microbial ecosystems to the extreme environments.
info_description: A steep rock ridge in southeast Beacon Valley, trending south-north for approximately 3.5km and rising to 2275m, forming the divide between Mullins Valley and Farnell Valley, in the Quartermain Mountains, Victoria Land. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-MF07

name: Veto Gap
info_origin: Named "Veto" by the Northern Party of the NZGSAE, 1962-63, because it was decided that Pinnacle Gap to the north offered the best route from the Rennick into the Aviator Glacier.
info_description: A gap between Tobin and Gair Mesas and connecting the Rennick and Aeronaut Glaciers.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

info_description: A basin in Auckland Harbour on the south coast Waitematā Harbour. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BA32 569212

info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 R09 Edition 1 1981

info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 I34 Edition 1 1994

name: Vickers Nunatak
info_origin: Named by the Southern Party of the NZGSAE, 1961-62, for E Vickers, radio operator at Scott Base 1961-62, who was in contact with the Southern Party almost every day during the three months they were in the field.
info_description: A prominent nunatak in the Shackleton Glacier about 12 miles south-east of Mt Black.
info_note: Shown on NZ 250000 map 53.

name: Vic Mountain
info_origin: Named by Kate Gardiner after Vic Williams, guide and later Chief Guide at the Hermitage, in the 1920s and 1930s. Williams along with Gardiner and another guide Frank Alack made the first ascent of this peak on January 31st 1934.
info_description: On Main Divide between Mounts Meeson and Goldsmith, 9,196 ft.  Waitangitaona & Cook Survey Districts.

name: Victor Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 E39 Edition 1 1994 Limited Revision 1996

name: Victoria Channel
info_ref: LINZ Hydrographic Chart NZ 6612 Approaches to Otago Harbour S
info_description: The main navigable channel in Otago Harbour. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-CE17 131214

name: Victoria Creek
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 M25 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-BN23 GR 625 915

name: Victoria Dunes

info_origin: The US-ACAN advised that it was named for the purposes of scientific investigation and use in scientific literature. The name was reported to be in local use. All of the ‘Victoria’ names in Antarctica are named after Queen Victoria, with Victoria Land named in the first instance by Capt James Clark Ross in the 1840s.
info_description: A clearly defined and continuous tract of sand dunes trending east west for approximately 8km from the northern shores of Lake Vida towards Lower Victoria Glacier. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME09

info_description: Found to the west of Marion Plateau next to Mt Victoria (2055m).

name: Victoria Glacier
info_origin: 'West Coast. Leonard Harper gave this name to what became the Franz Josef Glacier in 1857, but it was transferred to the present glacier after von Haast’s visit in 1865. See also Franz Josef Glacier/Ka Roimata o Hine.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Victoria Gully
info_origin: 'So named because of the many gold-diggers who came from the state of Victoria in Australia.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Victoria Hill
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 J41 Edition 1 1984

name: Victoria Lake
info_description: Feature depicted on: NZMS 17 Christchurch (1974); NZTopo50-BX24 695805

name: Victoria Land
info_origin: Discovered by Sir James Clark Ross in February 1841 and named by him for Queen Victoria (1819-1901). The name was evidently intended to apply to the whole of the Antarctic Continent, not just to the area now designated Victoria Land. Not South Victoria Land or Syd Victoria Land.

Ethnologist Johannes Andersen (1873-1962), member of the Honorary Geographic Board and its successor the New Zealand Geographic Board from 1924-58, considered Waerenga-a-hika was a descriptive name that carried ‘meaning clearly in its form’ – ‘Hika’s clearing’. Thomas Lambert’s East Coast regional history of 1925 preferred ‘the clearing of Hiku’. 593 acres (240 ha) were offered to the Anglican church and finally ceded in 1857. By this time the mission buildings had been shifted from Whakato and re-erected at Waerengaahika some 200m from the pā and in 1856 some 160 acres (65 ha) of land was cleared. In 1860 Governor Gore Brown paid a tense visit to the region and stayed at Waerengaahika. With the Hauhau rising the mission school and buildings were closed and the missionaries departed. Hauhau fighters strengthened the pā adding three lines of defence, including an outer stockade or wītā, a main fence or tūwatawata, and an earth breast work or parepare. After a seven day siege, late in 1865 they surrendered to a 600 strong force of colonial troops and Māori allies under Major James Fraser (1841-70). Historian James Belich considered ‘the surrender of a strong and well-manned’ pā ‘remains to be explained’. Eru Peka Makarini (?-1870), later an important fighter for Te Kooti was among the captured. Also among those arrested was Te Kooti (? -1893), later a Rongowhakaata leader, military leader, prophet and religious founder who had been educated at the mission station school and at the time was actually a member of the government forces. He was dispatched without trial to the Chatham Islands along with other prisoners. The old mission buildings were used as a native school from 1890-1937. The pā was finally destroyed by ploughing in the 1950s. Waerenga-a-hika remained as a variant spelling in newspapers from 1867 to the 1980s.

info_origin: Wai-au and Wai-aua are original Māori names for Coromandel Harbour. The literal translations are 'swirling current' and 'waters containing herring'. The name recalls an event when Kahuatamomoe, son of Tamatekapua, captain of the Arawa waka and his followers were moving along the shoreline when an enormous school of fish being herded by other predatory fish in panic stranded themselves on the shore in huge numbers. This provided food for Kahumatamomoe and his followers. The Waiau name was carried over to the river entering the bay and to the associated locality where it was recorded by Europeans as early as the 1820s. In 1835 Patene Puhata, the Ngāti Paoa chief of Waiau extended his protection over Gordon Browne who was in charge of Randulph Dacre's (1797-1884) spar gathering station and sawmill at Mercury Bay. In 1836 American William Webster (1815-1897) secured cutting rights to kauri trees at Waiau from Te Horeta Te Taniwha (?-1853) and at nearby Matawai from Patene Puhata. In 1837 Webster purchased some blocks of land at Waiau. After initial gold discoveries at Coromandel Harbour in 1852, Lieutenant Governor Robert Wynyard (1802-64) secured the opening for mining of a 10000 acres (4046 ha) block of Māori land stretching from Waiau to the lower Kapanga Stream and Matawai Stream. The larger Coromandel area was purchased by Donald McLean (1820-77) in 1872. Gold mining was taking place at Waiau by 1874. By 1878 there was a bush licence hotel, initially trading as the Half-Way House Hotel, but by 1881 as the Waiau Hotel. A Waiau survey camp was operating in 1883. The New Zealand Index for 1946 still listed only the Waiau River, but Edward Dollimore's New Zealand Guide identified Waiau as a named separate locality by 1951.

info_origin: Named in association with nearby Waiau Pā. The coastal bays were covered with Māori kāinga and gardens, and Waitete Pā. The latter was a seasonal fishing headland pā established by Ngāti Whātua and fortified in 1835, which lay on a main trade and communication route along the Waiuku River inlet and portage to Waikato River. There were also large artificially propagated karaka (Corynocarpus laevigatus) groves around the bay, the fruit of which required detoxification before being eaten. In 1939 an old resident recalled the 1870s with ‘the Karaka, and very delightful they looked in the autumn when their glossy dark-green foliage was flecked with masses of their golden fruit’. Large numbers of pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa) trees also lined the coastline. In 1852 the Crown purchased the land known as the Kahaware Block. The pōhutukawa were felled for ships timbers in the 1860s and 1870s. European settlers cut down karaka groves for winter cattle food in the 1870s, and stock raised locally for the Auckland market.

info_origin: 'Canterbury. Also known as Waiau-ua River, Waiau-uha River, and formerly the Dillon River, q.v. In Maori tradition this river,Waiau-uha, is the female lover of the male Waiau-toa (the Clarence River). At first they are close together, but their paths separate. When Waiau-uha grieves for her lover, her tears melt the snow at the source of the river and cause floods, which are called the lament of Waiau-uha. The sources of these rivers in the Spenser Mountains are not far apart.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Waihāhā
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche March 2023: Objective ID: A5238764 {Cowan, James. 1935. Hero Stories of New Zealand. New Zealand: Whitcombe and Tombs.; Grace, J. Te H. 2002. Tuwharetoa, a history of the Maori People of the Taupo district. New Zealand: Reed. [1st published 1959]; Kerry-Nicholl, James. H. 1884. The King Country or Exploration in New Zealand: Great Britain: Sampson Low Marsden.; Meade, Herbert. A. 1870. Ride through the Disturbed Districts of New Zealand. UK: Murray.; Taylor, N.M. 1959. Early Travellers in New Zealand. Great Britain: Clarendon Press.; Waihaha No. 1 R232859699. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; Waihaha 3A R23384476. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; Waihaha 3D R23909157. Archives New Zealand, Wellington.; Whirinaki and Erua forests. 1978. These must be saved. Salient, Vo. 41 7 April.}
info_origin: 'Noisy water' is the translation offered by the New Zealand Ministry for Culture and Heritage. James H Kerry Nicholls (?-1888), one of the first Europeans to travel through the King Country in 1884, recorded a different meaning for the name, 'The tableland fell to 1700 feet (518m), as we gained the Waihaha River, the name of which literally means "still waters”. There was a very steep descent to it. and looking from the top of this down upon the stream, there was not a ripple upon its surface'. Ngāti Toa settled on the western shores of Lake Taupō at Opurukete, Maraekowai, Waihora and Waihāhā. Three high ranking brothers, Rongohaua, Rongohape and Te Atuareretahi built three pā at Waihāhā which they named Opurukete, Keritane and Hikurangi. Lieutenant the Hon. Herbert Meade (1842-68) RN of HMS Curacoa, and well-travelled Englishman Julius Brenchley (1816-1873), at Governor George Grey's (1812-98) instigation accompanied Gilbert Mair (1843-1923) and a party of Māori on 'a semi-official flag showing' journey to Taupō late in 1864. The New Zealand Wars were temporarily paused but tensions remained high. Near Oruanui, Meade was saved from possible assault by Hauhau supporters by the high born Ahumai Te Paerata (c.1836-1908) who in 1864 had rejected Gilbert Mair's offer to send out and spare the women and children from the final assault at Orakau, and although badly wounded had managed to escape in the aftermath of the battle. Meade described Waihāhā as 'a village built on a small alluvial flat at the mouth of a river of the same name, and completely shut in, except on the side of the lake, by lofty columnar cliffs of basalt'. As well as the river and village Waitaha was also used as the name for several adjacent land blocks that were passed through the Native Land Court and into Crown ownership from the 1890s to 1930s, for example, the 16430 acres (6613 ha) Waitaha No 1 block sold for £16400 in 1894. By the 1970s environmental groups were calling for the preservation of the unlogged mixed podocarp forests around Waihāhā as well as the larger Pureora Forest, Whirinaki Forest and Erua Forest.

name: Waihoehoe Stream
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: ‘Ngāti Tamaoho have strong cultural, traditional and historic links with the waters of their rohe. The rivers are the life-blood of their rohe. From them come the means for survival by way of lamprey, tuna and other kaimoana. They also provide the main means of travel and trade to many otherwise inaccessible parts of the rohe during ancient times. They also provided the main sources of fresh water, essential for survival. Thus, they were the connecting tissue between the many kainga, pa and cultivation throughout the rohe. Moreover, they were a source of great mana for Ngāti Tamaoho. Their use for travel, resources and kai was closely governed by complex principle of tikanga. Sometimes their use was shared and at other times it was used by other tribes on a reciprocal basis. The Waihoehoe Stream flows from the foot hills of the Hunua Ranges north of Te Maketu. From here it continues north-west until it joins with the Otuwairoa (Slippery Creek) and drains into the Drury Creek. Prior to deforestation of its catchment and other contributing factors, Waihoehoe Stream would have been far wider, deeper and faster flowing. Traditional evidence recalls that the rivers in this area were navigable for several miles inland. Waihoehoe Stream is the correct and traditional name for the stream known today is Waihoihoi. Ngāti Tamaoho often built settlements at the mouths of rivers to benefit from their great wealth of kaimoana. Tuna were harvested with nets or weirs built across strategic parts of the rivers. Ngāti Tamaoho were experts at the sustainable use of the resources of these awa. The lives of the people were closely intertwined with the quantity and quality of the freshwater that was available to them. It provide habitat and spawning grounds for native plants, bird and fish, building and weaving materials such as raupo and flax, and precious medicines and dyes. Modifications to waterways and their catchment areas have significantly altered the relationship of Ngāti Tamaoho with these resources. The protection of freshwater resources remains one of most important parts of the responsibilities of Ngāti Tamaoho as kaitiaki of the environment and their rohe. Values (both tangible and intangible) are assigned to specific water bodies. Ngāti Tamaoho believe that each waterway carries its own mauri. A water body with a healthy mauri will sustain healthy ecosystems, support cultural uses and mahinga kai, and be a source of pride and identity to the tangata whenua. Waihoehoe Stream is the correct and traditional name for the stream known today is Waihoihoi. Ngāti Tamaoho is not certain of the meaning of the name.’

info_origin: Named the Thames River by Captain James Cook, who in November 1769 explored 14 miles up river from the mouth, on account of it's bearing some resemblance to that river in England. The Māori name for the river was Wai Kahou Rounga, this was shortened to Waihou. Survey plans of the 1800s showed either Thames or Waihou as the river name, or on a few occasions both. Early maps showed both names. Some confusion was inevitable until 1947, when an enquiry was made from a member of the public. The NZGB ruled that the official name of the entire length of the river be the Waihou. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDY1RUJFQjQwMzBGRUFCQjNDRjI)

name: Waikaiā / Rabbit Island
info_origin: Ngāti Hei history: 'Ngāti Hei has a long association with the island. The proposed name, Waikaia [sic], is the name that has been passed down for generations from tupuna. This island is seen as one of the many floats of the great fishing net that stretches across the rohe moana of Ngāti Hei. Ngāti Hei speak of huge physical nets that were strung between islands in the rohe moana and caught massive amounts of kaimoana which was then distributed between the whanau for the islands involved. The net at Waikaia would have stretched to Kuranui (Penguin Island). Similar nets would have existed in the area included on the islands around Whakahou.'
info_description: An island approximately 4km northeast of Opoutere Beach on Coromandel Peninsula. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BB36 602933

name: Waikanae
info_origin: Established by Ngāti Mutunga under its chief Ngātata (or Wiremu Piti) Pomare following arrival in November 1835. The surrounds of the harbour were planted out with potato cultivatations. info_origin: An original Māori name. Seemingly initially applied to the semi-enclosed tidal inlet and mudflats flanked by Taimatea Point on the seaward side and some 80 acres (32 ha) in extent when geologists Montague Ongley (1888-1976) and Eric Macpherson (1892-1948) were working in the vicinity in 1919-20. Members of the Harvey family purchased coastal sections here in the 1880s. The New Zealand Geological Survey recorded the area as Harvey Bay on their 1922 geological map of the wider district. By 1967 the topographic map included Waikato as a coastal feature as on earlier maps, and Waikato as a locality on the southward side of the entrance to the mudflats. The name has subsequently migrated to the built-up area on Taimatea Point.

info_origin: ’Lit. wai: river; kato: to flow. The river was often referred to as Waikato-taniwha-rau: lit. flowing river of a hundred taniwha. In this case taniwha was a symbolic term for a chief, the expression being one of admiration for a river where there were so many chiefs. Another translation is Gathered waters, referring to the backing up of water in the Taupō basin at the time of the river’s formation. On another version Hoturoa, the commander of the Tainui canoe, was surprised at the size and strength of the current and exclaimed playfully, ‘Waikato! Waikato kau!’: ‘Flowing water! Nothing but flowing water!’ The river has lent its name to the region and former province.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: A pā was established here in 1826. Tidal flows up the stream from the nearby bay made the water brackish. Alfred Reed favoured 'bitter waters' as a translation, but according to ethnologist Johannes Andersen, the name is figurative and alludes to a well-trodden floor mat. The New Zealand Company's William Fox (1812-92) journeyed through the district in 1848 and noted that local Māori were prepared to sell the area. A town site and Native Reserve was laid out in 1849. Erection of a 'native chapel' commenced the same year. New Governor Thomas Gore Browne (1807-87) visited the township in 1859.

name: Waikawau
info_ref: Objective ID: A3495892; A3572612; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche February 2024: Objective ID: A6141746 {Graham, George. 1921. A legend of Te Tatua Pa, Three Kings, Auckland Isthmus. Journal of the Polynesian Society, 30; 164-67.; [Lawn, C.A. 2005. Part IV. The Pioneer Land Surveyors of New Zealand.](https://www.surveyspatialnz.org/Attachment?Action=Download&Attachment_id=2674); Report by Mr Commissioner McKay relative to the Thames goldfields. 1869. New Zealand: Waitangi Tribunal.](https://forms.justice.govt.nz/search/Documents/WT/wt_DOC_68330839/Hauraki%20Vol%201.pdf); Turton, H.H. 1883. An Epitome of Official Documents Relative to Native Affairs and Land Purchases in the North Island of New Zealand. New Zealand: Government Printer.; Waikawau No. 1 & 2. R25284805. Archives New Zealand, Wellington [map]; Waikawau – Hauraki R12153280. Archives New Zealand, Wellington [map]; Waikawau No. 3. R25284773. Archives New Zealand, Wellington [map]}
info_origin: An original Māori name which Honorary Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) literally translated as ‘’water shag”, while noting there was another Waikawau Stream on the opposite coast of the Coromandel Peninsula. Te Whao-roa was buried at Waikawau. The Waikawau Block was estimated at 39144 acres (15841 ha). In 1867 James MacKay (1831-1912), Civil Commissioner for Hauraki, was particularly interested in securing the block for gold mining, Māori owners having closed the gold bearing lands further south around Ohinemuri to miners. A larger area stretching from north of Te Mata to Omaha Stream in the south was proclaimed a goldfield in April 1868. Separate titles for Waikawau North, Waikawau No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3 were issued for small areas around the mouth and along the banks of Waikawau River in 1870-72. Waikawau No. 1 and No. 2 were surveyed by Horatio Nelson Warner (1819-1906) the Official Government Agent on the Thames and Coromandel Goldfields. Chief Judge of the Native Land Court, Francis Dart Fenton (1820/25?-98) confirmed the title of Waikawau No. 3 of 3 acres (1.2 ha) to Karoraina Wairakau and Karauria Tairoa in 1872. In March 1872 MacKay advised John Williamson (1815-75), Superintendent of Auckland Province, that the ‘surveys and negotiations for the Waikawau and Cape Colville Blocks are in a forward state, and I anticipate being able to acquire these at a price not exceeding 2s. per acre’. He believed ‘£5,000 would probably accomplish this now’. Auckland Government Surveyor Oliver Creagh (?-1922), who accompanied MacKay, estimated the entire Waikawau Block at about 100000 acres (40469 ha). MacKay’s practice of advancing tangi expenses and raihana, the acceptance and charging of storekeeping purchases against the land prior to eventual purchase, meant the debt ultimately exceeded the freehold value of Waikawau and was used as a lever to open Ohinemuri to gold mining and later acquisition. In 1993 Rikiriki Rakena registered claim Wai 418 before the Waitangi Tribunal alleging that the Crown failed to establish reserves as agreed under the sales agreement. The Waitangi Tribunal summary report on Hauraki was critical of MacKay’s officially sanctioned purchasing strategies.

name: Waikutakuta / Robin Hood Bay
info_origin: Ngati Rarua describes this as the place of the water rushes. It was a former site of large Maori settlement, and an extensive cultivation site. This was the name used by Ngati Rarua for Robin Hood Bay. However, the original name may only relate to a feature or natural marker within the Bay. The name Waikutakuta is recorded in a waiata tawhito of Ngati Rarua titled “Ka kati i te karaka”. Ngati Toa history: Robin Hood Bay, located in the south of Port Underwood was an area of concentrated Ngati Toa occupation. The settlements of Cloudy Bay and Port Underwood were predominantly coastal, at locations such as Robin Hood Bay, however inland areas were heavily utilised for various resources. In the 1830s Te Rauparaha had a home in Robin Hood Bay, which he visited and occupied during the whaling season each year. Te Rongo, wife of Te Rangihaeata, is said to be buried at Robin Hood Bay. She was killed at Wairau during the 1843 incident.
info_description: A bay southwest of the entrance to Te Whanganui / Port Underwood approximately 10 km southeast of Picton. Feature shown on: NZMS260 P27 Edition 2 1995; NZTopo50-BQ29 902207.

name: Waimarino
info_origin: Waimarino or the Waimarino Plains is an original Māori name for a wide area at the northwest of Mount Ruapehu and Hauhungatahi. The name refers to the 'calm waters' pooling in the plains. In the mid-1880s the expansive ‘Waimarino Block’, greater in size than just the Waimarino Plains, was surveyed by the Crown with purchases beginning in 1886. One of the 'non-sellers' blocks, Waimarino 4 was reserved in the vicinity of Ngātokoerua pā at the southern edge of the Waimarino Plains. The final route of the North Island Main Trunk railroad was then surveyed through the Waimarino 4 Block and in 1908 Waimarino Railway Station was established just outside the northern boundary. In 1910 a 'Town of Waimarino' was surveyed around the railway station. This remained mostly a town on paper and was sparsely populated until the Marton Sash & Door sawmill opened in 1925. In 1924-1925, in response to local petitions, the Railway Department agreed to change the name of Waimarino Railway Station to 'National Park' based mainly on issues with misdirected mail. Use of National Park for the village followed as it developed as a gateway to Tongariro National Park, with official maps naming the ‘Town of Waimarino’ eventually transitioning to just ‘National Park’. In 1957 the National Parks Authority requested to change the name of the railway station back to Waimarino. This time, there were mail and freight issues with deliveries for other national parks around New Zealand arriving at National Park. In 1958 the Federated Mountain Clubs also submitted a proposal to alter the name of the village back to Waimarino. However, the Board declined the proposals as 'National Park' had become well established. Once more in 1967-68 the National Parks Authority informed the Board it intended to alter the names of the railway station and village back to Waimarino. Mail and freight were still being misdirected to 'National Park' after further national parks had been created. The residents of National Park objected under a petition and based on the objections, the Board again declined the change. In 1969 the Board considered a further proposal from Taumarunui County Council to conversely, alter Waimarino to National Park, likely prompted by confusion with the cadastral property parcel appellations, many remaining 'Town of Waimarino' from the 1910 survey. In 2023 Uenuku hapū/Te Korowai o Wainuiārua, an iwi collective representing hapū affiliated with Uenuku, Tamakana and Tamahaki, proposed altering the name back to Waimarino. The proposal was widely supported. Objections included another petition from the residents of the village. The Minister for Land Information agreed to alter the village name back to Waimarino in December 2024, but did not change the railway station name.

info_origin: A descriptive name for the valley containing Waimā River. Waimā literally translates as clear water but according to Sir Āpriana Ngata (1874-1950) the full name was Waima-tuhi-rangi after a village and valley in Tahiti. In 1828 a gathering of chiefs met in the valley in the aftermath of the death of Hongi Hika (1772-1828) and after one of the sons of Patuone (?-1872) had been killed, to reach a peace agreement. In 1836 timber trader and Additional British Resident Thomas McDonnell (1788-1864), a controversial figure, claimed to have purchased sizable areas along Waimā River. By the 1860s Wesleyan missionaries thought the ‘spiritual condition’ of the Māori in the valley was low, but they applauded their industry and efforts at improvement in ‘fencing all their lands and building timber houses’. A scene from a decade later was recalled by a one time resident in 1925, ‘Nearly the whole country in those days was under heavy bush, the valley being a picture of beauty; forest-clad hills on either hand, the alluvial flats verdantly green with the cultivations of the many Māori farmers’. Plentiful peaches were fed to pigs with kūmara, taro, rīwai (Māori potatoes) and Indian corn being the staple foods in addition to pork and fish. In 1898 Waimā Valley was the location of the ‘dog tax rebellion’ – a refusal to pay an annual 2/6d license fee resisted by being little involved in the cash economy and using their dogs for hunting. Armed Māori visited Rawene to voice their opposition to this and other taxes and a closed season on pigeons and ducks, a formal declaration of war having been sent by telegram to the Resident Magistrate in Russell. Premier Richard Seddon sent troops under Lieutenant Colonel Stewart Newall, who marched on the valley heading towards an ambush. Only the intervention of MP Hōne Heke Ngāpua (1869-1909) persuaded one of the leaders of the ‘rebellion’ Hōne Tōia (1858?-1933) to surrender and call off the planned ambush.

name: Waiotahi Stream
info_origin: 'Originally and correctly Waiotahe: lit. wai: water; o: of; tahe: menstruation; The waters in which the menses were cleansed. The stream used to flow through Te Koronaeiti pa. When young women of Ngati Maru had their first menstruation, they were placed under strict tapu and housed in a special whare where they washed in stream water.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Waioweka River
info_ref: Objective ID: A3169985; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Whakatōhea history: The local hapū that was prominent in this area, Ngāti Ira, do not recognise the word “eka”, and it is loosely translated from the English word “acre”. Evidence shows that the original name stretches much further back than the arrival of the European. However, the area is known to thrive with the native Weka, and the following comment is also made: "Waioeka" is a natural elision of "Wai-o-weka", lit. "wai": stream; "o": of; "weka": flightless woodhen. Ngāti Ira’s history recounts one of the earlier tipuna that settled here, Tamatea Matangi, who eventually married Muriwai from the Mataatua waka. In traveling through the Waioweka Gorge Tamatea named sites in and alongside as he went, which are still recognised today. Other hapū talk of this historical association to the River. Upokorehe have a connection through Kahuki, a son of Rongopopoia, who was the son of a chief at Gisborne at the time, Rongowhakaata. Rongowhakaata pursued his wife Uetupuke who was pregnant but was traveling back to her home land in Whakatōhea. Rongowhakaata said to her while standing on the banks of the Waioweka River, that if the baby is to be a girl then name her after the waters of Waioweka. If it is to be a boy, then name him Rongopopoia. When Kahuki was born and came of age he settled at a pa at the mouth of the Waioweka.
info_description: A river flowing generally northwards from the confluence of Kahunui Stream and Koranga River in Kahikatea Range, for approximately 50km into Bay of Plenty at Ōpōtiki. NZTopo50-BF41 745415 to BE41 758853

name: Waipaparoa / Howick Beach
info_origin: Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki history: The little-known name of Waipaparoa refers to the ‘Expansive Waterfront’ of present-day Howick Beach, and is one of several names applied broadly to what is now Howick. The contractions of Waipapa and/or Paparoa are also sometimes used, whilst Ōwairoa refers to the swampy inland areas reclaimed for what is now the Howick Domain. Another name used by Māori for the colonial settlement of Howick during the nineteenth century was Hāwaki – a simple transliteration of the Pākehā name. Thus, Waipaparoa (sometimes shortened to Waipapa, or Paparoa) is the correct name for Howick Beach, and Ōwairoa is the traditional name of Howick Domain.
info_description: A small beach that stretches for approximately 400m on the coast east of Howick in Tamaki Strait. NZTopo50-BA32 729153 to 732151.

name: Waipātiki Beach
info_ref: Te Hata Kani II, Statement of evidence, 11-15 November 1996, Wai 201, Doc # J40, p. 4; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-12/95
info_origin: Waipātiki is a beach at Tangitū and also the name of a river and valley which flows from the interior to the Coast. During the time of Marangatūhetaua, Ngāti Tū were facing repeated raids upon their lands by neighbouring tribes. In order to protect their lands they made an alliance with the fighting chief Te Ruruku who agreed to command a party of Ngāti Tū warriors from a base at Ngamoerangi. In exchange for his skills and leadership, Te Ruruku gained fishing rights and land interests at Arapawanui and Waipātiki, land which was under the control of Ngāti Tū and Ngai Tatara. There is archaeological evidence indicating occupation within the Waipātiki valley. The land at Waipātiki which is located within the Tangoio North block was confiscated by the Crown in 1867 and although other land was returned to Māori owners in 1882, Tangoio North was retained. Parsons states, “. In February, 1910 it was partitioned into 12 farms by the Government and advertised for lease and later for purchase. The Waipātiki forest sits on the 983 acre block bordering the Waipātiki stream to the south and the coast to the east. It was originally balloted by Mrs C.E. Lowe.” Although the land was confiscated and those resources lost to Ngāti Tū and Ngai Tatara, they were still able to access the kaimoana. until the mid twentieth century these resources which included kina, pāua, kūkū and kouia, were still plentiful and collected regularly.
info_description: A beach adjacent to Waipatiki Beach (locality). Locally known as Waipatiki Beach, but not currently named on mapping. NZTopo50-BJ39 427420 to 431424.

info_origin: ’Several meanings can be applied, the most popular being Smoky water: wai: water; pawa (or paoa): smoky. Paoa is also a term for a bird snare. It may be a corruption of Waiopawa: Pawa’s stream, or a contraction of Waipawamate: Dead water or Water with a strong smell. An unfounded local belief is that it means Meeting of the waters, as the town is on the confluence of the Waipawa and Tukituki rivers. The township was first known as Abbotsford, after Frederick Sedgwick Abbot, who subdivided his run for this purpose in 1860. The prior claim of Abbotsford near Dunedin necessitated a change of name. Two outlying areas were to be named Sedgwick and Hadley, the latter being preserved in the name of the Hadley cemetery.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Waipokapū Stream
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: ‘Ngāti Tamaoho have strong cultural, traditional and historic links with the waters of their awa. The rivers are the life-blood of their rohe. From them come the means for survival by way of lamprey, tuna and other kaimoana. They also provide the main means of travel and trade to many otherwise inaccessible parts of the rohe during ancient times. They also provided the main sources of fresh water, essential for survival. Thus, they were the connecting tissue between the many kainga, pa and cultivation throughout the rohe. Moreover, they were a source of great mana for Ngāti Tamaoho. Their use for travel, resources and kai was closely governed by complex principle of tikanga. Sometimes their use was shared and at other times it was used by other tribes on a reciprocal basis. Waipokapu (Hays Stream) is particularly important to Ngāti Tamaoho because of its traditional use and its location. The stream flows west from the lower Hunua Ranges toward the Manukau Harbour, recalling the connection between these two important Ngāti Tamaoho places. The stream flows from a small catchment at the top of today’s Hay’s Creek Road. From here it flows westward toward Papakura. It passes just below the ancient Ngāti Tamaoho pa of Pukekiwiriki and so is intimately tied to the tapu of this revered site. From there it flows south to join Otuwairoa (Slippery Creek) before meeting the Manukau by site of the Opaheke kainga. Prior to deforestation of its catchment and other contributing factors, Waipokapu would have been far wider, deeper and faster flowing. Traditional evidence recalls that the rivers in this area were navigable for several miles inland. Stories tell of waka from the Manukau making their way up streams to very near the base of Pukekiwiriki. Archaeological evidence also shows terraces and pits along the upper reaches of the Waipokapu. Ngāti Tamaoho often built settlements at the mouths of rivers to benefit from their great wealth of kaimoana. Tuna were harvested with nets or weirs built across strategic parts of the rivers. Ngāti Tamaoho were experts at the sustainable use of the resources of these awa. The lives of the people were closely intertwined with the quantity and quality of the freshwater that was available to them. It provide habitat and spawning grounds for native plants, bird and fish, building and weaving materials such as raupo and flax, and precious medicines and dyes. Modifications to waterways and their catchment areas have significantly altered the relationship of Ngāti Tamaoho with these resources. The protection of freshwater resources remains one of most important parts of the responsibilities of Ngāti Tamaoho as kaitiaki of the environment and their rohe. Values (both tangible and intangible) that are assigned to specific water bodies include: Ngāti Tamaoho believe that each waterway carries its own mauri. A water body with a healthy mauri will sustain healthy ecosystems, support cultural uses and mahinga kai, and be a source of pride and identity to the tangata whenua. Ngāti Tamaoho is not certain of the meaning of the name.’
info_description: A stream that flows generally west for approximately 8km from the dam at the top of Hays Creek Road into Otūwairoa Stream less than 2km north of Drury. NZTopo50 BB32 793951 to 733938.

name: Wairarapa Moana
info_origin: Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairarapa Tāmaki nui-a-Rua statement: Wairarapa Moana comprises Lake Wairarapa and Lake Ōnoke as well as the Narrows ie the Ruamahanga River connecting the two lakes. All three names are highly significant to Ngati Kahungunu.’; 'Wairarapa Moana is the traditional name for Lake Wairarapa. The early rangatira Haunui-a-Nanaia named the lake Wai: water; rarapa: glistening eyes; not only of the beauty of the lake, but of the glistening of his eyes on finding his wife Wairaka (or Hinerakahanga). Different accounts ascribe the naming to Tara, or to Kupe, whose daughter suggested, ‘Me waiho tō moana ko te rarapatanga o ou whatu’: ‘Let us remain here at this lake you have descried, your anchor stone’. Kupe replied, ‘E pai ana. Me waiho ko Wairarapa’: ‘Good. Let it remain Wairarapa’.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: A moana (collection of connected waterways) east of Remutaka Range, extending from near Featherston in the north to Palliser Bay in the south. The moana consists of Lake Wairarapa, Lake Ōnoke and part of Ruamahanga River, which joins the two lakes. NZTopo50-BQ33 827267.
info_note: Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairarapa Tāmaki nui-a-Rua Treaty Claim Settlement.

name: Wairarapa Moana Wetland
info_origin: Wairarapa Moana is the traditional name for the area that includes the wetland as confirmed in the Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairarapa Tāmaki nui-a-Rua Deed of Settlement. An early rangatira, Haunui-a-nanaia, named the lake Wai (water) rarapa (glistening eyes). Moana refers to the size of the water body.
info_description: A wetland complex of 10,547 hectares, located approximately 5km southwest of Featherston, containing a number of connected freshwater and coastal water bodies. It comprises the full extents of Lake Wairarapa and Lake Ōnoke. The southern limit is the coastal shingle spit. The eastern and northern boundaries include the freshwater wetlands that are within the conservation areas adjacent to Lake Wairarapa. The wetland complex also includes several rivers and streams, including Ruamahanga River, which connects the two lakes.

name: Wairoa
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche June 2023: Objective ID: A5446617 {Cowan, James. 1983. The New Zealand Wars. Volume II. New Zealand: Government Printer. [first published 1922].; Stokes, Evelyn. 1980. A History of Tauranga County. New Zealand: Dunmore.; [Tauranga. 1866. Daily Southern Cross, 22 December, Page 5](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/DSC18661222.2.26); [Tauranga. 1867. New Zealand Herald, 11 February, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH18670211.2.29); [The War at Tauranga. 1867. Daily Southern Cross, 1 March, Page 7.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/DSC18670301.2.37)}
info_origin: An original Māori name, translatable as ‘long stream’. The locality’s name is derived from the river of the same name, and is one that occurs in several places across the country. In 1866, in the aftermath of the 1864 Tauranga campaign of the New Zealand wars, surveyors at work on lands on the upper part of Wairoa River and Waimapu River south of Te Puna were intimidated and raided by Hauhau. In December 1866 some 100 men of the 1st Waikato Regiment were stationed at Wairoa for three weeks to protect the survey party still working in the area and the transport vessels on the river. In February 1867 some 500 militia and 250 Arawa camped at Captain Tovey’s farm at Wairoa heading for Ihiranga and an engagement with Hauhau fighters.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260 U14 Edition 1 1980; NZTopo50-BD36 724213

name: Wairoa
info_origin: ’Lit. wai: river or stream; roa: long. This is among the most common place names in the country — recorded as the name for a borough, beaches, trigs, towns, bays, localities, channels, pā, points, streams, rivers, hills and valleys — but the Hawke’s Bay town and river are the most widely known. During the period when names related to the Indian Rebellion of 1857 were popular there was an attempt to call the town Clyde, after Lord Clyde (Sir Colin Campbell). At Ardmore, Clevedon and Waverley, however, the name Wairoa has been superseded.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Waitaangata
info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: 'Waitaangata was the original name of the stream and a Ngāti Hāua kāinga, which was turned into a mining village just as most Māori kāinga were. Waitaangata has spiritual connotations, which is more than just water and people, for example the water falls Rerepahupahu in the Waitaangata was used as a tūāhu for tohunga from Ngāti Hāua.   Not just about the joining of two kupu it is about this concept "ko te wai te mana o te tangata," or as koro Titi Tihu states, "the mana of the Māori is by water." If our tohunga did healing of the land or people or communed with our atua it was by the wai or the water which is why this place was called this. It is now also used as a name for the area of land that is now known as the Waitaanga Conservation Area. This kōrero is provided by Hakiaha in his evidence to the Māori Land Court.’

name: Waitakere or Nile River
info_origin: 'West Coast. The explorer John Rochfort reputedly named the river after observing three small pyramid-shaped hills on the right bank in 1859; he then chose Atbara and Sirdar as names for its tributaries. However, the naming of the tributaries has been attributed to Thomas Hughes (see Atbara River, Sirdar River). On another account, the first steamer to enter this difficult channel was the SS Nile in 1866. It was also known as the Browning River in 1869, after the fi rst chief surveyor of Westland. Maori name Waitakere, originally Ngawaitakerei, lit. nga: the; wai: waters; Takerei. Takerei was a leader of the invasion of the south-east coast under Te Puoho in 1833.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={0562e61a-3e52-e311-8212-005056970030}))

name: Waitākere River
info_origin: 'Ancient name of the Waitakere River: Te Awakotuku, lit. te: the; awa: river; kotuku: white heron (Egretta alba modesta). Graeme Murdoch notes the name should be River of the white heron's plume, which refers to the Waitakere Falls, standing out like a plume against the river and bush. In West Auckland Remembers (1990) Murdoch sets out that the top end of the river was Waikirikiri (Stream with the stony bed), descending to Waitipu (The stream that floods quickly) then Waitoru (Stream of the toru tree, Toronia toru) before reaching Te Awa Mutu (The end of the river, being the point beyond which canoes could not venture. Then it becomes Hukerewai (Where the river meanders), descending to Pu Harakeke (Clump of flax), and then Turingoi (Where the river flows slowly). The river mouth was Turanga Kawau (Shag's roost).' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

'Beattie, James Herries', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1998. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/4b16/beattie-james-herries)}
info_origin: Waitaki River was a principal travel route to the interior and part of a ‘food gathering highway’ for Ngāi Tahu stretching from the coast to the lakes. Journalist-historian Herries Beattie (1881-1972) noted that ‘the hollow at the north end of the bridge’ was called Punakawa which he translated as bitter spring’. Construction of the Waitaki to Moeraki railway line began in 1874. The same year tenders were let for construction of a road and rail bridge over Waitaki River, which was completed in 1876, replacing the existing ferry service. A settlement developed on a site adjacent to the river on the south bank. Town sections were sold in 1876 and a railway station was built. The bridge connected the Otago and Canterbury provincial railway systems.

name: Waitangi
info_origin: ’Lit. wai: waters; tangi: noisy or weeping. The famous ancestress Maikuku, who lived in a cave beneath what are now the Waitangi Treaty Grounds, had a taniwha that was said to have been wailing, which attracted a leader from Whangaroa Huatakaroa. The noise is sometimes taken to refer to the Haruru Falls on the river. The name is to be found in many parts of New Zealand, including in the South Island form Waitaki, and the Moriori form Waiteki on the Chatham Islands.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Waitangirua
info_origin: Porirua City Council describes the name to mean "music made by two waters that flow" - this is in reference to the nearby streams, Waitangi and Cameron. Waitangirua was established during the 1960s almost exclusively as a Government housing development for New Zealand's burgeoing working class immigrant population. The ethnic demographic of Waitangirua at the time of establishment comprised primarily of Pacific Island, Scottish, Indian, Irish, English and Chinese as well as Māori. Until the late 1990s the hilly suburb was almost semi-rural surrounded by farmland with Whitby to the northeast, Pāuatahanui inlet and estuary further to the north and the Belmont hills and Hutt Valley to the east. Waitangirua has a diverse and colourful multi-racial community.

name: Waitara
info_origin: ‘Lit. wai: river; tara (short for taranga): long steps. One origin of the name is that Turi crossed the river with long strides. Another is Te Whai-tara-nui-a-Ngārue: lit. follow the dart of Ngārue. Whare Matangi threw a magic dart (tara) that would locate the house of his father Ngārue. After a number of throws, the tara struck Ngārue’s house at the mouth of the river, thereafter known as Te Whai-tara-nui-a-Ngārue. As one word, waitara means hail. Other explanations are that the name in full was Waitarangia, a place where the water was so cold that Turi’s skin was wrinkled. In 1880 the Rev. James Buller gave the name of the township as Raleigh.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: Wises New Zealand Guide from 1945 suggested the name meant majestic waters. Writer-publisher Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) was more literal suggesting ‘rough or storm water’, seemingly influenced by ethnographer and Honorary Geographic Board Member, Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) who favoured: toa, male of animals and rough boisterous, stormy or strong water. A description of Waitoa River from 1846-7 observed that it ‘runs in the centre of a deep bed or holm, about twenty feet (6 m) below the level of the plain … in some places is several hundred yards wide and filled with kahikatea, rimu, totara, and tawa: this bed is covered in flood to a considerable depth, and the river is then impassable’. The river provided the name for the surrounding district. Until the 1870s Waitoa referred to the larger area stretching from Waitoa River to Morrinsville, access to the district at this time being via Waihou River. The original post office at Morrinsville was known as Waitoa before being renamed Morrinsville in 1878. Purchase of land between Piako River and Waitoa River began in 1858. After the invasion of the Waikato by colonial forces, Major George Frederick Nelson (1842-1914) and other former officers and men of the 3rd Waikato Regiment took up land at Waitoa. In November 1872 the 8000 acres (3237ha) Waitoa Block was purchased for £750. The purchase of a further 3000 acres (1214ha) of ‘undrained swamp land’ at Waitoa was arranged in 1875 by William Moon (1848-1924). A Parliamentary committee, known as the Waitoa Land Transactions Inquiry Committee, which was comprised of MPs John Ballance (1839-93), Sir George Grey (1812-98), Edward Wakefield (1845-1924), Edward Stafford (1819-1901), William Reynolds (1822-99) and William Murray (1832-1900) was appointed in 1877 to investigate the purchase of lands in the Waitoa district by Frederick Whitaker (1812-91) and James Mackay (1831-1912). By 1882 only one Waitoa Block remained in Māori ownership - Waikehau 4 (leased to William Moon). In 1887 Charles Gould (1857-90) subdivided land from his 2000 acres (809 ha) Te Kahia Estate for farm workers and gifted two acres (0.8ha) for a school site. These became the nucleus of the town of Waitoa. The school’s centennial volume observed that Gould ‘could be called father of Waitoa’. The first of some 11 subdivision extensions to the town from 1910 to 1942 was approved under section 16 of the Land Act, 1908.

info_origin: Ngāti Hei history: 'Waitoko is a name that has been passed down for generations by Ngāti Hei tupuna whose name is difficult to translate without wider context but refers to the origin and specific features along the stream. Waitoko was the major water source for the inhabitants of the pā in this location. The pā was located near the existing one-way bridge. info_origin: An original Māori name for some of the nearby cave systems had extended to include the valley by the late 19th century. Thomas Humphries (1841-1928), the Chief Surveyor for Auckland Land District, included Waitomo Stream but didn’t label the valley on his 1898 map of the Waitomo Caves area. Travel writers such as JR Large writing in 1898 used it as a descriptive name noting that the ‘limestone hill in which the Waitomo Caves are situated blocks up the Waitomo Valley like a huge dam’. Waitomo Valley was also used by settlers in the area at this time. The Public Works Department funded making roads in the valley from 1902. Discussion about establishing a Waitomo Valley School commenced in 1914 with it opening in 1917 before closing in 1925. Farmers used it as a location in the annual sheep returns from 1917. A Waitomo Valley Land Drainage District was formed in 1921. Edward Dollimore (1904-73) included Waitomo Valley as a locality in the 1962 edition of the New Zealand Guide.

info_origin: An original Māori name, which literally translates as water and tōtara (Podocarpus totara). A belt of submerged tōtara stumps which were part of an old forest that prevented navigation up the river appears to have inspired the name. A kāinga shared its name with the associated river. There were several pā in the vicinity of the kāinga, a notable one being Wereroa pā on higher ground above the river. In 1840 Edward Jerningham Wakefield described Waitōtara, 'The valley is here broad and fertile, but intersected on the south bank by some nasty swamps, which might be easily drained, however, the banks of the river, being high. There are some groves of fine timber on the sides of the valley; the hills which bound it are high, but on their tops lies a table land only partially wooded'. The Waitōtara-Ōkehu block was purchased from Ngā Rauru by the Crown in 1863. In 1865 Governor George Grey, believing that Pai Māirie supporters posed a threat to Whanganui, dispatched General Cameron and a force of 2000 men to recapture the Waitōtara Block. Having condemned Cameron as a 'lame duck' in a propaganda move, Grey then led a force of Māori allies, volunteer cavalry and forest rangers to occupy the now abandoned Wereroa pā. The private township was surveyed in 1874-77 by Whanganui surveyor and architect George Frederick Allen (1837-1929) and the government town in 1878 by de Gennes Fraser (1852-1933). Allen had become Wellington Provincial Council Surveyor in 1856 and later worked in private practice. He was a foundation member of the New Zealand Institute of Surveyors. UK born Fraser, a trained civil engineer, arrived in New Zealand in 1870 and briefly taught in Māori schools in Northland before joining the Lands Department in 1872 and completing his surveying examinations the following year. He was based at Patea, where he was involved in surveying confiscated land. Fraser later returned to civil engineering and was a long time county engineer at Cook County. Fraser was also a foundation member of the New Zealand Institute of Surveyors.

New Zealand: Department of Internal Affairs; Tenquist, John. D. 1990. Wallaceville Veterinary Laboratory, an Anecdotal History. New Zealand: MAF.}
info_origin: On 4 January 1868 approximately 56 one acre [4046 sq m] lots in the Mangaroa valley were advertised for sale at public auction by JH (John Howard) Wallace, at what in a second advertisement on 15 January 1868 was now described as the township of Wallaceville. Liverpool born John Howard Wallace (1816-91) arrived in Wellington on the Aurora in January 1840. He worked as a general merchant, auctioneer and commission agent. Wallace was active in civic affairs encompassing church, school and library, and a member of the Wellington Town Board (1863-70) and Provincial Council (1861). In 1864 Wallace was elected first chairman of the Mangaroa Board of Highway Wardens. He also supported the development of a Wellington to Wairarapa railway. Wallace published an early 'Manual of New Zealand History' in 1886 and in 1890 collaborated with Richard Sherrin to produce the substantial 'Brett's Early History of New Zealand'. A Wallaceville Railway Station was established in 1876. By the early 20th century many of the sections had reverted to farmland. The Department of Agriculture's Wallaceville Veterinary Laboratory was established by 1905 and eventually expanded to become the DSIR Animal Research Station.

In 1855 the township was christened Pembroke after the British colonial secretary. Residents were dissatisfied with the name, and succeeded in having it formally changed to Wanaka on 1 September 1940. To celebrate the demise of the name, a coffin was paraded around the Wanaka Golf Club hall late that same night, and at midnight (as the Otago Daily Times reported): ‘Mrs A.M. Douglas entered the hall, with the “newly born Wanaka”, Miss Joan Scaife.’ The NZGB added the macron to make the official name Wānaka in 2021.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; Note, Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu consider that 'Oanaka' its variant spellings are a simple orthography error where the ‘W’ has been misheard and spelt with an ‘O’. Therefore, any purported meanings are entirely speculative, and unsupported in their traditional knowledge or by any documentary records.

info_origin: The town/city takes its name from Whanganui River. The word ‘Whanganui’ is a compound word made of ‘whanga’ and ‘nui’. ‘Wanga’ is not a word in the Māori lexicon. Whanganui means the long wait and relates to traditional oral histories of (i) Kupe's people waiting for his return from a journey up the Whanganui River, or (ii) when the ancestor Hau (Te Ati Hau-nui-a-Paparangi) stood at the mouth of the river, waiting for the tide to change before he could cross safely. During planning of the city (c.1850) the New Zealand Company proposed that it be named Petre (pronounced Peter). ; 'Lit. wanga (whanga): wait; nui: great. The name relates to traditional oral histories of Kupe’s people waiting for his return from a journey up the Whanganui River, or when the ancestor Haunui-a-Nanaia (of Te Ati Haunui-a-Paparangi iwi) stood at the mouth of the river, waiting for the tide to change before he could cross safely. When the city was being planned the named of Petre (pronounced ‘Peter’) was proposed, after William Henry Francis Petre, Baron Petre, a wealthy director of the New Zealand Company; the name was not popular. In December 2009, Minister for Land Information Maurice Williamson announced that the city would have alternatives, Whanganui or Wanganui, but that Crown agencies would move to the name Whanganui over time. The decision capped a period of intense public debate about the issue.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: City at the mouth of Whanganui River. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BL32 732777.

name: Watanuki Pond
info_origin: Named by United States Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names (US-ACAN) (2004) after Kunihiko Watanuki, Department of Chemistry, University of Tokyo, Japan. Participant in the McMurdo Dry Valleys Drilling Project during the 1973-74 field season, Labyrinth pond studies, 1985-86.
info_description: A pond in the northwest part of the Labyrinth of Wright Valley lying 3.5km south-southwest of Minotaur Pass at Apollo Peak. The pond is 600m east-northeast of the larger Kurasawa Pond and 1.2km east of the Upper Wright Glacier terminus. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-ME07
info_note: The NZGB committee on place naming in the Ross Sea Region in Antarctica at its meeting on 7 July 2004 accepted this name, but had an issue with the feature. The issue with the ponds is not just their permanence but also whether they are geomorphologically less significant than surrounding unnamed features. However, at its meeting of 8 November 2006, the NZGB agreed to accept this name.

name: Watson Bay
info_origin: Named for Nigel Watson for his extensive and significant contributions to the conservation of Antarctic historic sites. In his 23 years as Executive Director of Antarctic Heritage Trust (2000-2023). Watson galvanised global support for the Ross Sea Heritage Restoration Project and represented New Zealand through the Antarctic Treaty to ensure continued protection of the historic sites. Three of the historic huts were listed as Historic Sites and Monuments under the Antarctic Treaty in 1972, including Shackleton's 1908 'Nimrod' Hut, 5km south-southwest of Watson Bay at Cape Royds. This was followed by Hillary’s TAE/IGY ‘Hut A’ at Pram Point in 2001. Watson is also recognised for his science communications skills, publicising archaeological findings and promoting the work of the Antarctic Heritage Trust. In 2023 Watson was awarded the New Zealand Antarctic Medal for his life’s work in Antarctic conservation.
info_description: A 1km wide bay at the east side of Lichen Promontory and at the south of Maumee Bight, on the west coast of Ross Island, Antarctica. Feature shown on: NZ AntTopo50-ME13

In the early 1900s the local school was called Maruimata, apparently in an attempt to translate the area name into te reo Māori. ‘The members of the board got a Maori dictionary, and turned up the words — white “ma”; a deep valley, “mato”; s-o-w “rui” — and, thinking only of sow the female pig, it never struck them that “rui” was the verb “to sow seeds”’, reported the Otago Witness in January 1909.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Wellington
info_origin: ’When it was decided to transfer the New Zealand Company’s settlement from Petone to Port Nicholson in April 1840, the name Britannia was also transferred. But in late May of that year the company’s directors wrote to their principal agent at Port Nicholson, Colonel William Wakefield, stating: ‘Considering the probability of that settlement becoming at no distant period the centre of British power and influence in those distant regions, it is the opinion of the Court of Directors that the name of “Wellington” is peculiarly appropriate.’ Company founder Edward Gibbon Wakefield had enlisted the Duke of Wellington’s support for South Australian settlement in 1834 and promised that, in return, the capital of that proposed colony would be called Wellington. King William IV, however, requested the honour for his consort, Queen Adelaide. The name of Wellington, Britain’s pre-eminent soldier, was therefore available for the settlement at Port Nicholson.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
