name: Wellington City
info_origin: The city that is administered by the Wellington City Council. Constituted by Local Government (Wellington Region) Reorganisation Order 1989, Gazette 1989, p2491 Shown on SO 35959 | 'Wellington, city and region. When it was decided to transfer the New Zealand Company’s settlement from Petone to the present site in April 1840, the name Britannia was also transferred. But in November 1840 a communication was received from the directors of the Company saying it was their desire that their chief settlement at Port Nicholson be named in honour of the Duke of Wellington. An extract from a letter that the secretary of the New Zealand Company had sent to Colonel William Wakefield on 29 May 1840: Considering the probability of that settlement becoming at no distant period the centre of British power and influence in those distant regions, it is the opinion of the Court of Directors that the name of ‘Wellington’ is peculiarly appropriate, and will connect the most honorable national association of the Mother Country with the future Town. It is therefore the wish of the Directors that the First Town should be called ‘Wellington’ accordingly. The New Zealand Gazette and Wellington Spectator of 28 November 1840 said: The directors of the New Zealand Company always contemplated calling the town of their principal settlement after the illustrious warrior of modern times. This intention was entertained in gratitude for his having given life to the great principle of colonisation, which they are extending to the best of their abilities, by advocating the enactment of the South Australian Bill. Had a proper spirit animated those in power, Adelaide would have enjoyed a name which must live through all the ages, but they sought profit by pleasing the King rather than honour by paying an honest debt. Wakefi eld had first considered naming the new settlement Adelaide. As a footnote to this statement it should be mentioned that Adelaide was named after Queen Adelaide, consort of William IV. See also Wellington Harbour.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Wellington Harbour / Port Nicholson
info_ref: Corres XXX, L, LII, pp 75, 76; 82-97, 135-138; 164, 226-232; Dual name standardisation: Objective IDs: A4405369, A4507521; Notes on early use of 'Poneke': Objective ID: A7035313
info_origin: The name Port Nicholson was given in 1826 by Captain James Herd of the barque "Rosanna". He was said to be the first European to sail into the "Harbour" and named it after his friend Nicholson who was the Sydney Harbour master. The name Wellington Harbour was given in 1839 by the crew of the vessel Tory after their ship's figurehead which depicted the Duke of Wellington. Local and published usage has favoured "Wellington Harbour" but the historical name Port Nicholson is still in use and has been recognised accordingly. General definitions:- Harbour - topographical feature; Port - those man made facilities with a harbour area. Captain Herd wrote in his log "The navies of all the nations of the world could lie at anchor here.”. The ancient name is Te Whanganui-a-Tara, meaning "the great bay of Tara". The Māori name adopted in Colonial times is Poneke, said to be a rendition of Port Nick. (refer Wises Guide 7th Ed, 1976). ; 'The name Port Nicholson was given in 1826 by Captain James Herd of the barque Rosanna after his friend John Nicholson, master-attendant and harbourmaster at Port Jackson (Sydney). The name Wellington Harbour was given in 1839 by the crew of the vessel Tory after their ship’s figurehead, which depicted the Duke of Wellington. The Māori name, now applied to Wellington City as well, is Te Whanganui-a-Tara, meaning The great bay of Tara, in full Taranohu, the son of Whatonga. On another account the name means Long waiting of Tara, and is connected with an involved story of his journey from Hawke’s Bay, the theft of his dog, which was eaten by the local iwi, Tara’s long waiting to discover what had happened to it, hearing it barking in the stomachs of the eaters, and his subsequent revenge. An earlier name may have been Te Whekenui: The great octopus, not on account of the mythical octopus chased by Kupe, but because the arms of the harbour were fancifully like those of an octopus. The name Pōneke, used colloquially and for cultural purposes, is a transliteration of ‘Port Nick’, although in recent times it has been explained as a shortened form of pō nekeneke, meaning Journey into the night, relating to the exodus of Te Āti Awa to Waiwhetū in the 1860s as European settlers moved in. It is possible the name took on this additional meaning later, given that Pōneke was already long in use as a transliteration — by at least 1841 if not earlier.' Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: In 1908 Noel Lee Buchanan (1848-1925), New Zealand attorney for Taitapu Gold Estates Company, an elected member of the Collingwood County Council 1905-1914 and its chair in 1909-10, approached the local MHR for Motueka, Roderick McKenzie (1852-1934) at the time a leading supporter of ‘county’ interests in the Liberal party, with a proposal to rename West Wanganui as New Haven on the grounds of the confusion caused by duplication of the name Wanganui, believing it was detrimental to the economic development of the area. McKenzie approached the Minister of Marine, John Andrew Millar (1855-1915), but was informed that this was a matter for the Minister of Internal Affairs, David Buddo (1853-1937), under the Designation of Districts Act, 1908 which provided for the assigning and alteration of place names as well as avoiding their duplication. A resolution from the Collingwood County Council was necessary for the Minister to make a recommendation to the Governor, William Lee 5th Baron Plunket (1865-1920). At this point Buchanan advised McKenzie that he considered West Haven more euphonic than New Haven. On the motion of Councillors’ Buchanan and John Charles Fish (1871-1931), the necessary resolution was passed on 9 September 1909 and forwarded to the Department of Internal Affairs. The Governor’s proclamation published in the Gazette on 17 September 1909 declared the new name for the locality and the inlet to be effective from 1 April 1910. The existing Post Office at West Wanganui was named Mangarākau, but the Department had no objection to renaming this West Haven. The Nelson Education Board opened West Haven School late in 1911. In 1948 Whanganui Inlet replaced West Haven Inlet.

info_origin: In 1960 Westland National Park was established under the National Parks Act, 1952, becoming New Zealand’s ninth national park and fourth largest. The beginnings of Westland National Park/Tai Poutini National Park lay in the designation in 1911 of two scenic reserves under the Scenery Preservation Act, 1908, at Mapourika of 1266 (512 ha) and 5481 acres (2218 ha) and another at Wahapo of 1420 acres (575ha). In 1914 another very large 48478 acres (19618 ha) scenic reserve was set aside at Franz Josef Glacier/Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere and through the advocacy of Arthur Harper (1865-1955), a leading figure in the New Zealand Alpine Club and Honorary Geographic Board member (1934-55), another 75220 acres (30440ha) was set aside at Fox Glacier/Te Moeka o Tuawe and 64000 acres (25900ha) at Copland. Some 16 adjacent areas were set aside as scenic reserves to 1958. From 1930 Harper advocated for the creation of a ‘South Westland National Park’. In 1959 a meeting of 56 representatives of West Coast local bodies and organisations resolved on the motion of Thomas McNee (1909-73), Chairman of the Westland District Progress League, to have the ‘Glacier and Lakes areas of South Westland’ declared a National Park. After discussion, Westland National Park was chosen as the preferred name. Another 8072 acres (3267ha) of Karangarua State Forest and 523 acres (212ha) of scenic reserve and Crown land were added to the park in 1969. Importantly and after considerable controversy, parts of Ōkārito and Waikūkūpa State Forests comprising lowland forest were included in the park. UNESCO World Heritage status was secured for the park and adjacent land in 1986. As part of the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act, 1998, the park was given the dual name Westland National Park/Tai Poutini National Park. Other Ōkārito State Forest and Saltwater State Forest lands were added to the park in 2002.

info_origin: The name Westmere was derived from the Westmere block farmed by early pastoralists such as Angus McMaster (1800-88) and later the Beethams as part of the much larger Brancepeth Estate. In 1870 Thomas Coldham Williams (1825-1912), an in-law of the Beethams purchased the Westmere block for £7930. Extension of roading in the form of Westmere Road helped cement the name. In 1905 the Beethams’ and William’ reorganised the working division of the larger Brancepeth estate with the ‘Williams blocks’ being Westmere (3288 acres [1330 ha]), Te Parae, Mamaku, Rawhiti, Poroporo, and Longridge. Part of the Westmere estate was sold to form the Westmere soldier settlement in 1919.

info_origin: The lagoon has been formerly known locally as Frank Kitts Lagoon, Frank Kitts Park Lagoon and The Lagoon. The name Whairepo Lagoon was suggested by mana whenua (Mark Te One) - referring to the abundance of eagle ray attracted to the food source within the lagoon and also using it as a haven from their predator orca. The Whairepo are considered to be kaitaiki or guardians of the lagoon, looking after the waka activities associated with the Wharewaka. Whai means Ray and Repo means Swamp, but together Whairepo refers to the eagle ray.
info_description: The lagoon is an open public area, centrally located along the Wellington Waterfront.  It is a small man-made sea water filled lagoon connected to Wellington Harbour (Port Nicholson) through a narrow channel and adjacent to Frank Kitts Park. name: Whakaari
info_ref: Laddie Anaru, Harata Taurima, Mere Kingi Ratima and Violet Koko, oral account, in Taylor, Bevan, Mohaka- Waikare Confiscated Lands: Customary usage Report, 1993, Wai 201, Doc #J5, p. 24; LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-12/95
info_origin: Whakaari was a Ngāti Kurumōkihi pā which was occupied by them continuously until the land was confiscated by the Crown in 1866. Following this Whakaari remained a mahinga kai from which women would gather kaimoana. According to Harata Taurima, “The women folk would go to the beach at Whakaari to gather pāua and kina, putting them into a kete. When filled, this was taken ashore and emptied into a sack that was split on one side, so that the kaimoana would be evenly spread when loading onto the horses back, for the journey home. It was customary not to eat any kaimoana on the beach. We would return home with the kaimoana, put the kina in fresh water, then cleaning and preparing the pāua and kūkū, leaving them overnight, not eating the kaimoana until the next day. This was another custom we observed, much the same as when killing a sheep. The old people use to-say “haere ki te wai, haere ki te moana, karakia ai”, when entering the water, or entering the sea, say a prayer.”. “The women folk would go to Whakaari to gather pāua, kina, kūkū, crayfish and pūpū”
info_description: A coastal point between Flat Rock and Tangoio Bluff. NZTopo50-BJ39 391382.

info_origin: Whakaari means to make visible". When Ngātoroirangi was freezing to death on Mount Tongariro he called upon his sisters Kuiwai and Haungaroa in Hawaiiki for help. They dispatched two fire taniwha which travelled swiftly under the sea and ground. The spirits surfaced several times to to check where they were going, one spot being offshore, forming Whakaari/White Island. The name White Island was given by Lieutenant Cook on account of the dense clouds of white steam emitted. The feature is named Isle of Wight and Isle of White on some manuscript charts, giving the name a double meaning by reference to the island off the south coast of England. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDc1NkI1MTJFNjBGRjk5NTA2RDg)"

name: Whakahīrangi Scenic Reserve
info_origin: Ngāti Hāua kōrero: ‘Whakahīrangi was a Ngāti Rangitengaue/Ngāti Hāua tupuna associated with this whenua. Whakahīrangi the tupuna was the Chief/leader of the taua of Ngāti Rangi/Rangitengaue that came from their pā Otapoia on Maraekowhai who then joined up with Whakaneke who came from his pā Makakoti to fight the lower Whanganui taua, at Kirikiriroa, Te Hautapu fighting for 3 days hid in the cave Tuwhakairiao. It is here that Ngāti Hāua tupuna Porotihi died, Tamahaki also according to the Minute Book 17. Whakaneke escaped making his way through Te Awa o Rere Tāruke, he had the covering of a hāngī thrown over him so his pursuers wouldn’t catch him. Whakahīrangi fled to the Taranaki Coast to Te Kawau Pā, to find Tutemahurangi who was at that time gathering seafood to bring back inland.  Whakahīrangi told him about the defeat and that the only thing left was the rippling waters, meaning men had died or were scattered. Tutemahurangi with his men and also his Ngāti Tama relations numbering 240 came to defend the lands. Totoro the sister of Kimihia had married Tinirauariki of Ngāti Tama, also Tarapohe had also married into Ngāti Tama, this is why Ngāti Tama came to assist.  The lower Whanganui were turned back seeing a large taua waiting for them.’
info_description: A scenic reserve just north-northwest of Maraekowhai and approximately 21.5km southwest of Taumarunui. Centred on NZTopo50-BH32 781803.

name: Whakakaiwhara Peninsula
info_origin: Ngāi Tai ki Tamaki history: Whakakaiwhara refers to the “Feast made with Whara”, referring to the edible flowers of the kiekie vine. This refers to an event when the waka Tainui was forced by an easterly gale to take shelter under the lee of the peninsula, and certain tūpuna of Ngāi Tai came ashore and made the said feast. Several other acts of tapatapa-whenua and uruuru-whenua were also carried out at this time. Ngāi Tai/Ngāti Tai maintained occupation of the peninsula from that time forward, down to the time of Thomas Duder’s purchase of the Whakakaiwhara block from Hōri Te Whētuki of Ngāi Tai in 1866. The peninsula includes pā sites, urupā, wāhi tapu and numerous other places of cultural, historical and spiritual significance to Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki.
info_description: A coastal peninsula that extends for approximately 2km from the southern end of Umupuia Beach into Tamaki Strait. NZTopo50-BA33 870141
treaty_legislation: Section 94 and 95 Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki Claims Settlement Act 2018

name: Whakapoungakau
info_origin: 'Lit. whakapou: to fix, or firmly establish; ngakau: also whakangakau: to long for, or desire. It has been translated Hills of heart’s desire. The sisters Kuiwai and Haungaroa and their brother Tanewhakarara came from Hawaiki and, following in the footsteps of Ngatoroirangi, camped in the Tikitere Valley, which had no hot springs at that time. Tanewhakarara left on a bird hunting expedition, but never returned. The sisters named the range Whakapoungakau because of the great longing Tanewhakarara had for them and they for him. Finally the sisters resolved to return to Hawaiki, but first they prayed to Ruwaimoko, god of volcanoes and earthquakes, who caused the hot springs to gush forth. The sisters left happy in the belief that if Tanewhakarara ever did return, he would have these hot springs in which to rest his tired limbs.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

name: Whakatāne
info_origin: ’Lit. To play the man. When the Mataatua canoe arrived at the mouth of the river, the commander, Toroa, took his men ashore to inspect a cave. Presently the canoe began to drift away on the outgoing tide. Seeing the danger Toroa’s daughter, the great chieftainness Wairaka, cried, ‘Me whakatāne au i au’: ‘I shall act like a man’, and the women managed to save the canoe. There are several versions of the famous event. An early Māori name was Kakahoroa, lit. long stems of toetoe (Austroderia sp.). The river was first called Tamāhine-a-Hinemataroa: Daughter (or Daughters) of Hinemataroa, the mother of Wairaka.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Whakatete Bay
info_origin: 'Lit. disputed territory, quarrel, or dispute. The name goes back to the time when James Mackay negotiated with Maori for prospecting to be undertaken on their tribal lands in the Coromandel area. The bay was the boundary between Ngati Maru and Ngati Naunau, and therefore the negotiations were involved. After precautions had been taken to protect the wahi tapu (sacred places), agreement was reached, and prospectors were permitted to look for gold in the disputed territory. The place was previously called Otoi, lit. Place of Toitehuatahi, the early explorer.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

info_origin: An original Māori name that John White considered meant a waka tiwa, the simplest form of dugout canoe but with added sideboards. WP Wydle writing in the Hauraki Plains Gazette in 1929 offered a different interpretation asserting it was ‘another descriptive name, showing, it to be a pleasant landing place where fish and shellfish were found to be plentiful, so it a good place to camp’. Whakatīwai was where Marutuahu, ancestor of the Hauraki peoples, lived with his father’s adopted people. It was also the site of Te Tikiore Pā and on a coastal track leading to Pukekaroro and further northwards. Early missionaries sailing southward down Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana stopped at Whakatīwai before using Whakatīwai Stream to venture into the Waikato. In 1836 missionaries met with warring factions at Whakatīwai to broker peace. Canoe races were held at Whakatīwai from the mid-late 19th century, the organisation of which the government contributed to financially in 1868. By June 1874 the Māori population of Whakatīwai comprised 18 males under 15 years and 53 over, 16 females under and 42 over 15 years – 129 people in total. That same year James MacKay (1831-1912) arrived at Whakatīwai where some 400 Māori had congregated and commenced purchasing land for the government. He then continued onto Parawai, Thames and Ohinemuri district prior to the opening of the Thames goldfields. MacKay’s Whakatīwai purchases were not settled until the 1880-90s.

name: Whakaupoko
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: 'Whakaupoko is a prominent hill between Mauku and Pukeoware. The name is considered traditionally to have originated in the time of the great Chief, Kokako. “Upoko” refers to the head, as its unforested summit appeared before the time of European pastoral development in the second half of the 19th century. The site of the ancient Ngati Tamaoho Pa of Tongaroawhata. Because of its long history, Whakaupoko is regarded as a sacred place by all Tainui and is traditionally acknowledged by the Kingitanga, notably at the annual Poukai at Reretewhioi. It was one of Te Wherowhero’s homes when he escorted Waiohua tribes, including Ngati Tamaoho, back to Tamaki in 1835/6. Ngati Tamaoho Chiefs were party to the sale of Whakaupoko in 1854.'. 'Whakaupoko is an ancient and extremely important site for Ngati Tamaoho. The hill lay on the main route between Pukekohe/Mauku and Waiuku, the trail eventually being converted into the road used today. The Whakaupoko area has been a centre for Maori since the first settlement of Tamaki Makaurau, representing an important link between the people of the Waikato and those of the isthmus. Consequently, the area is of inter-regional significance to Ngati Tamaoho. The titi of Whakaupoko was crowned with the Tongaroawhata pa, a large pa taua with extensive living areas and cultivations extending around the base of the hill. The annual Poukai at Waipipi Pa Reretewhioi, established by King Tawhiao, illustrates the significance of the Whakaupoko. During the reign of King Koroki, Te Puea and the King would travel to the Pokai via Whakaupoko, pausing at its summit to recognise this taonga tuku iho.'. Information source: B Leonard, Ngati Tamaoho Sites of Significance, 58, 68; D Armstrong, Ngati Tamaoho Environmental History DRAFT, 190-196.
info_description: A hill at 147m with geodetic mark code A8UH at its summit. Located beside Bald Hill Road approximately 7km north-east of Waiuku and 9km south-west of Pukekohe. NZTopo50 BB32 598778.

name: Whakawhitirā
info_ref: Objective ID: A4635550; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche April 2024: Objective ID: A6258696 {Colenso, William. 1888. Fifty Years ago in New Zealand. New Zealand: Hawke's Bay Philosophical Institute.; [Correspondence. 1897. Poverty Bay Herald, , 2 July, Page 3.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBH18970702.2.28); [David Mackay. 'Colenso, William', Dictionary of New Zealand Biography, first published in 1990. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1c23/colenso-william); Reed, A. W. & Dowling, P. 2010. Place Names of New Zealand. New Zealand: Reed.; Williams, William. 1867. Christianity among the New Zealanders. London: Jackson, and Halliday.}
info_origin: An original Māori name. Writer-historian Alexander Wycliff Reed (1908-79) suggested as a literal translation ‘to be conveyed across a river’. In 1834 printer, missionary, botanist and explorer William Colenso (1811-99) regarded the pā at Whakawhitirā to be the largest that he had ever seen. It was surrounded by fields of taro and tobacco. Colenso paced the length of the fence along one side of the pā at ‘nearly a mile’ (1600m). The pā had three defensive fences; ‘the massy [massive] and combined outer one being twenty-five [7.6m] to thirty feet [9.1 m] high; its main posts consisting of entire and straight trees denuded of their bark, with large carved full-length human figures painted red on their tops - of these figures there were above a hundred’. When missionary William Williams (1800-78) visited in 1838 the occupants of the pā had built a chapel ‘one of the best buildings of the kind in the country’ and 500 attended the service. The Treaty of Waitangi was brought to the East Coast for signing, but the majority who gathered at Whakawhitirā were ‘suspicious and declined to sign’.

info_origin: An original Māori name. From the New Zealand Company and Crown's perspective this land was illegally leased by Māori to pastoralists Robert Russell and (Richard?) Wilson in about 1844 who adopted Whangaimoana as the name for their run. In 1847 the run was occupied by three men, each with a horse as well as two cattle, 1000 sheep and two acres (0.8ha) of cultivations for a £12 annual rent payable to the Māori owners. In 1856 the larger district was part of a government land purchase from Ngāti Kahungunu chiefs that was conducted by Donald McLean. Robert Russell and his brother (John) Purvis Russell (1830-1906) who arrived in New Zealand in 1852, freeholded the station and retained the locality name. The Russells expanded their land holdings to some 9256 acres (3746 ha) by 1870 by purchasing the reserve of Rāniera te Iho and part of Whakatomomo, after which JP Russell assumed sole control of the property. In 1891 Russell gave evidence before the 'Claims of Natives to the Wairarapa Lakes and Adjacent Lands Commission' supporting Māori over land boundaries. After Russell's death in Scotland in 1906, his trustees unsuccessfully offered the estate to the government's Land Purchase Board. Arapata Te Maari (1862-1936) on behalf of others then took the opportunity to seek the restoration of 400 acres (161 ha) considered to have been inaccurately included in Russell's acquisition of Rāniera te Iho's reserve. Ngāti Kahungunu and Rangitāne leader Hoani Parāone Tuniārangi (c.1843/44-1933) also unsuccessfully approached the Crown to directly purchase approximately 700 acres (283 ha) to the east of Omoikau Stream. Instead, William Boyce Chennells, the Masterton Public Trustee representative, as Russell's executor had Masterton surveyors and engineers Seaton and Sladden subdivide the estate into 25 farms ranging from 117 (47 ha) to 776 acres (324 ha), with the exception of the 2545 acres (1029 ha) homestead block and a small 11 section township of one-acre sections (0.4 ha). Abraham and Williams Ltd sold all the land at public auction in 1907. Whāngaimoana was the recorded spelling in the 1850s, but Whangamoana was also used in the newspapers from the 1870s until the 1910s. The New Zealand Geographic Board affirmed Whāngimoana on the advice of Board member (1952-67) Sir John Te Herekiekie Grace (1905-85).

name: Whangamarino Redoubt
info_ref: Objective ID: A3968704; A3955095; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche May 2023: Objective ID: A5383945 {[Auckland. 1863. Otago Witness, 7 November, Page 6.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/OW18631107.2.19.4); [A Fresh Post is Established. 1863. Auckland-Waikato Historical Journal 63. Special Issue.; Prickett, Nigel. 2016. Fortifications of the New Zealand Wars. New Zealand: Department of Conservation.; [The War in Auckland. 1863. info_origin: A relict of the New Zealand Wars and the invasion of the Waikato, this redoubt was constructed close to an old abandoned pā site that had been temporarily occupied by Māori forces while stronger positions were constructed to the north along Koheroa Ridge. The redoubt was occupied by 474 men of the 14th Regiment on 14 August 1863. It took the form of a 26m x 26m square with bastions at opposite corners. Earthworks faced south although it had only a wooden stockade of split logs on the northern side which was not completed until September 1863. A contemporary newspaper report recorded 'The bush has been well cleared from the main spur and the gullies surrounding the position. The tall fern has been cut and burnt off, as well as the green bows; and the outer trench of the redoubt and stockade has been dug. A new road, about a furlong [200m] in length, from the main camp to the Waikato, below the old Maori landing, and concealed by the bush, winds along the side of the hill'. Initially it was called Pickard's Redoubt after its commander Royal Artillery Lieutenant Arthur Frederick Pickard (1841/44?-1880), who later won a VC at Rangiriri. By September 1863 it was known as Whangamarino Redoubt. The fortification was intended to hold the southern part of Koheroa Ridge with Suffolk Redoubt commanding the northeast. It overlooked Waikato River and Māori positions at Meremere, as well as being intended to deny them use of Whangamarino River thus preventing resupply of Meremere by canoe from Paparata. Ensign Gustavus Von Tempsky (1828-68) of the Forest Rangers and Sub-Inspector McDonnell (1831/33?-99) of the Colonial Defence Corps scouted from the redoubt for Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron (1808-88). The redoubt's two 40lb Armstrong guns shelled Māori fortifications at Meremere some 3 km away on the 29th and 30th October. Captain Phelps, the commanding officer, was the first to send word to Cameron that Meremere pā complex was being abandoned on 1st November. That same day militia replaced British regular troops in the redoubt. Governor George Grey (1812-1898) paid a flying visit in Mid-October 1863 and the Whangamarino Redoubt was abandoned in October 1864.

info_origin: The town/city takes its name from Whanganui River. The word ‘Whanganui’ is a compound word made of ‘whanga’ and ‘nui’. ‘Wanga’ is not a word in the Māori lexicon. Whanganui means the long wait and relates to traditional oral histories of (i) Kupe's people waiting for his return from a journey up the Whanganui River, or (ii) when the ancestor Hau (Te Ati Hau-nui-a-Paparangi) stood at the mouth of the river, waiting for the tide to change before he could cross safely. During planning of the city (c.1850) the New Zealand Company proposed that it be named Petre (pronounced Peter). ; 'Lit. wanga (whanga): wait; nui: great. The name relates to traditional oral histories of Kupe’s people waiting for his return from a journey up the Whanganui River, or when the ancestor Haunui-a-Nanaia (of Te Ati Haunui-a-Paparangi iwi) stood at the mouth of the river, waiting for the tide to change before he could cross safely. When the city was being planned the named of Petre (pronounced ‘Peter’) was proposed, after William Henry Francis Petre, Baron Petre, a wealthy director of the New Zealand Company; the name was not popular. In December 2009, Minister for Land Information Maurice Williamson announced that the city would have alternatives, Whanganui or Wanganui, but that Crown agencies would move to the name Whanganui over time. name: Whanganui River
info_origin: 'Manawatu-Wanganui, Wanganui District, 192 km from Wellington. Lit. wanga (whanga): harbour; nui: great. First named Petre (pronounced ‘Peter’), after William Henry Francis Petre, Baron Petre, a wealthy director of the New Zealand Company. See also Thorndon. The name was conferred by his fellow directors as noted in the New Zealand Company fifth annual report. His son, Henry William Petre, held a number of offices, being appointed colonial treasurer in 1851 and postmaster general in 1853. Never popular, the name was used only on special occasions. On 3 May 1844 a petition signed by thirty-five of the foremost residents was forwarded to Wellington, and is worthy of reproduction: We have the honour to submit to you, that the name given to our town — ‘Petre’ — is so universally disliked, that we believe there is not one in the entire community who uses, or acknowledges, the designation. But this arises from no factious motive, nor from any undue feeling of personality to the noble lord whose name it bears — though we can make out no private, public, local or general claim that entitles him to that distinction — but simply because the name is not appropriate either in sound or sense; and because by its non-adoption by people generally, it is likely to be productive of confusion and mistake. We have therefore to solicit your Honor, that you will be pleased to represent to His Excellency the Governor, the anxious desire of the Inhabitants to have reinstated the former and now well-known name, ‘Wanganui’, or if His Excellency should prefer an English appellation, the Patronymic be of someone entitled by public beneficial acts to such commemoration. Official assent was delayed until 26 January 1854. The city’s coat of arms is still that of the Petre family. It will be noted that the petition gave the name as Wanganui, not Whanganui. The dropping of the ‘h’ is said to have been begun by the tohunga Haupipi, who named the river and its environs, although the lullaby of Hau for Wharaurangi, reproduced in Place Names of the Ancestors, gives the name as Whanganui, meaning Great river, which Hau ‘won great renown’ for crossing. The Maori Language Commission states that the name is correctly spelt with an ‘h’, and Bishop H.W. Williams wrote : ‘Here we have the example of the natives dropping an “h”: it is no more correct to write and say “Wanganui” for “Whanganui” than it would be to write and say “’Ampstead ’Eath” and plead the example there of the natives.’ But both spellings were used in the nineteenth century. On 18 December 2009, Minister for Land Information Maurice Williamson announced that the official name for the city of Wanganui would be the alternatives, Whanganui or Wanganui, but that Crown agencies would move to the name Whanganui over time. The decision capped a period of intense public debate about the issue, following the submission by Te Runanga-o-Tupoho to the New Zealand Geographic Board on 11 February 2009, seeking to change the city name to Whanganui. In the present book, the spelling Wanganui has been retained for the city and Whanganui for the river; see also Whanganui River. An earlier Maori name was Kaihau-o-Kupe (Wind eating of Kupe), q.v. When Kupe’s canoe Matahourua reached the mouth of the river, the rough water at the bar obliged Kupe to anchor the canoe off the river mouth for several days while Kupe and a number of his people went ashore. During their stay their provisions ran short, obliging them to ‘eat the wind’.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.; 'Place Names of the Ancestors, A Maori Oral History Atlas suggests that the name describes cloudy waters. The relative claims of the spelling of the name are briefly discussed under Wanganui, q.v. Regarding the vexed question of how to pronounce the name, the late Professor Bruce Biggs observed: ‘Apparently Wanganui is one of our few conventional spellings that gives evidence of the fact that there is a very substantial difference between the initial sound of the word and the initial sound of such words from other dialects as Whangarei. However a Wanganui Maori would say Whangarei as if were W’angarei, a sound which is again very different from the English w as in water.’ From this it might be said that the perfectionist would write W’anganui, which would not be accepted by the average reader. An ancient name for the river was Wainui-a-Tarawera: lit. wai: river; nui: great; a: of; Tarawera. During European colonisation the river was known as the Knowsley River. According to Chapple and Veitch’s centennial history of Wanganui, ‘the only reason that can be advanced is that Knowsley Hall was the ancestral seat of one of England’s statesmen at that time, the Earl of Derby, who held opinions favourable to overseas colonisation, and who was later interested in the New Zealand Company. This Hall is situated about eight miles from Liverpool.’ See also Whangaehu.' Source: Reed, A.W. & Peter Dowling, Place Names of New Zealand, 2010.

Wises New Zealand Index. New Zealand: Wises.}
info_origin: Publisher-historian Alexander Wyclif Reed (1908-79) offered the literal translation of whanga – harbour and parapara – sediment, while ethnologist and Honorary Geographic Board member, Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) suggested that for the associated harbour, parapara referred to the two tree species - Parapara (Pisonia brunoniana), known as the bird catcher tree because its sticky seed pods could trap insects and in turn birds, and Houpara (Pseudophanax lessoni). Wises New Zealand Index without explanation offered ‘end for end’ as the meaning. In 1844 the entrepreneurial Frederick Whitaker (1812-91), politician and later Premier, and John (Jean) Du Moulin (1817-1901), a French surveyor, purchased the 3500 acres (1416 ha) Whangaparapara and Okupe blocks from Tomati Waka and others for goods including a sailing cutter complete with a dinghy, two casks of gun powder, a double barrelled gun, oars, clothing, tobacco, two cows and £10. In 1846 Whitaker took the northern portion dividing a line from Te Ahumata to just south of Awana and Du Moulin the southern 1000 acres (404ha). Whangaparapara was shown as the harbour name just inside Whitaker’s boundary. The Kauri Timber company erected a large mill at Whangaparapara in 1909 which operated until 1927. In 1915 newspaper proprietor and politician Henry Brett (1843-1927), who had expended large sums on goldmining on the island, now subdivided his land at Whangaparapara into eight mainly one acre (0.4 ha) sections. The plan was prepared by Peter Cheal (1846-1931), a licensed surveyor. A further extension of the subdivision in 1929 was signed off by the Director of Town-Planning, John Mawson, under section 16 of the Land Act, 1924 and a third followed in 1956. In 1938, when preparing for a proposed historical atlas to be part of the Centennial of 1940, the Honorary Geographic Board was asked to consider the spelling and recommended Whangaparapara. In 1948 with the planned reopening of the Post Office, the question of spelling came before the New Zealand Geographic Board. The Board considered that Whangapara, which had been used by the Post Office that closed in 1943, was only an abbreviation and that Whangaparapara was the correct name. The Barrier Whaling Company operated here from 1956-62.

info_origin: An original Māori name. Where Tōhē found people harvesting karaka berries and an ancient pā of Ue Oneone. Ethnologist and Honorary New Zealand Geographic Board member Johannes Andersen (1873-1962) believed this was an ‘imported name’ following ethnologist Elsdon Best (1856-1931), another Honorary New Zealand Geographic Board member, who considered Fa’a referred to a valley on Tahaa Island in Tahiti and that whanga was used to denote an expanse of space of water, land or air. Whangapē along with Hokianga were landing places of the Māmari waka captained by Ruanui. Numbers of pā were at various times built along the length of the harbour. Timber trader and controversial Additional British Resident Thomas McDonnell (1788-1864) recorded the harbour as ‘false Hokianga’ on his 1834 chart because of the similarity of the headlands, although after the loss of HMS Osprey in 1846 this informal name was reapplied to Herekino Harbour. An account from 1837 noted that Māori had cleared and enclosed gardens which extended up to near the tops of the hillsides. In 1874 Edwin Torrens Brissenden (1837-1907), Land Purchase Commissioner at Hokianga, purchased Te Ana Tuturu Block at Whangapē and began negotiations for another 21000 acres (8498 ha). That same year John Fairchild (1835-98), captain of the government steamer Luna, surveyed the entrance of Whangapē Harbour, which he repeated in 1889 finding all the soundings 3ft (90cm) shallower. A Whangapē export kauri (Agathis australis) timber industry commenced in the late 1870s. By 1905 the Mitchelson Timber Company, controlled by (Sir) Edwin Mitchelson (1846-1934), was operating from Whangapē with an estimated supply of four to five years. The mill employed 16 hands, had a cutting capacity of 5,000,000 superficial feet p.a. and in 1907 had cut 4,000,000 superficial feet. This was the largest firm independent of the Kauri Timber Company operating in North Auckland.

name: Whangara
info_origin: ’In full Whangarā-mai-tawhiti: lit. whanga: bay; rā: sun; mai: from; tawhiti: far away. The ancestor Paikea arrived at Ahuahu (Great Mercury Island) from Hawaiki, riding on the back of a whale. He came on to Mercury Bay and, thinking one day that he was still in Hawaiki, he set out to find his home Whangarā. From the top of a hill he pointed to the south and exclaimed, ‘There, in the distance, Whangarā juts out into the sea!’ But when he reached it at last, Paikea realised that it was not his old home. Turning to a companion, he said, ‘This is not my kāinga, this is Whangarā-mai-tawhiti.’ Nevertheless, he settled here at a place called Te Ana-a-Paikea: lit. te: the; ana: cave; a: of; Paikea, and named many places that reminded him of Hawaiki. Another tradition says the bay was named by Tahu and others of the Takitimu canoe.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

name: Whangārei
info_origin: ’The origin and meaning of the name have at least seven interpretations, most of which are subject to local variation. One narrative has the name as lit. whanga: waiting; rei: short for Reipae. Reipae was a young woman of rank from Waikato. Her sister Reitū was sought after by northern (Whangapē) chief Ue-oneone. Both sisters travelled north on a large bird sent by Ue-oneone. Reipae stayed in Whangārei, marrying another leader in the area (Tāhuhu-Pōtiki, although some stories have the chief as Manaia), while Reitū went to be with Ue-oneone. This story emphasises the importance of the genealogical link created between Tainui and Ngāpuhi through these marriages. A variation to this narrative is that it could mean whanga: to wait; rei: birds or treasure, and derive from the story of the chief Manaia who intercepted a beautiful bird that was flying over the harbour, and discovered it to be the woman Reitū, whom he married. An alternative is Bountiful harbour; or as a contraction of Whangarei-te-rerenga-parāoa: lit. whanga: harbour; rei: to leap, rush, or run; te: the; rerenga: place of swimming or floating; parāoa: whale; which could be rendered: Bay frequented by swimming, leaping whales. A famous tohunga visiting the local tribespeople rebuked a man for asking him so many questions, asking: ‘E aha tau e whanga nei i te rei o te tohorā?’: ‘Why are you waiting for an opportunity to extract the breastbone of the whale?’ The whale was to be interpreted as the visiting tohunga, the breastbone the treasured knowledge he possessed. Another posited origin is that of a group of warriors who were waiting to ambush some attackers in a swamp, hence, lit. whanga: to wait; rei: swamp. There is a small island in the harbour known now as Castle Rock that was used as a sentry point in times gone by, therefore Whangārei might mean: To wait and watch; possibly derived from the northern tribes lying in wait for those coming from the south. Other possibilities are: Waiting in anticipation, or the battle-order ‘Steady — charge!’, or a contraction of Whanga-i-Ahurei, on the hypothesis that the Tainui canoe may have made a landing here and planted kūmara before proceeding south. Pronunciation would obviously vary based on which interpretation is adopted. The accepted pronunciation at the time that Sir Alfred H. Reed lived there, in the late nineteenth century, was ‘wangaree’, and the final ‘ray’ sound used nowadays was unknown. Bruce Biggs, who lent his weight to the Reipae version of the name’s origin, stated the modern position: ‘Well-informed elders from the north use, in my experience, the pronunciation Whar-ngar-ray, both a’s long and the wh varying from English f to an aspirated or affricated bilabial.’’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.

info_origin: A descriptive term for land that flanks the entrance to Whangārei Harbour. In 1827 French navigator Jules Sébastien César Dumont d’Urville (1790-1842) captaining the Astrolabe, charted the harbour. Lieutenant Victor Charles Lottin (1795-1858) sent to survey the head of the bay reported an ‘excellent anchorage’ and a ‘splendid channel’. Lottin and Dumont d’Urville later climbed the bluff to overlook the harbour and ocean. Captain John Lort Stokes (1811?-85) of the Acheron made the first Admiralty survey of the harbour in 1849. In the 1850s ‘Wangarei Heads’ referred to both sides of the harbour entrance prior to the name Marsden being attached to the southern side. The spelling Wangarei Heads continued to be used in newspapers until 1891. Timber, flax and kauri gum trader Gilbert Mair (1799-1857) made large land purchases in the area in 1839. The Old Land Claims Commission accepted only the southernmost – 5577 acres (2257 ha) Wharau portion of these, all but 414 acres (168 ha) later being taken over by William Brown (1809/10?-98) and his business partner John Logan Campbell (1817-1912). Meanwhile in 1855 John Grant Johnson (1824-73), Land Purchase Commissioner, purchased the 5365 acres (2171 ha) Manaia Block for £200 from Wiremu Eru Pohe, Tipene Hari, Hirini Taiwhariga and Hinewaru. Officials anticipated the main settlement would be at Whangarei Heads rather than the town of Whangarei at the head of the inlet. In 1848 Harcourt Richard Aubrey (1818-96) became Sub-Collector of Customs and postmaster at Hokianga before shifting to Whangarei Heads. In 1856 Aubrey was appointed Collector of Customs and Resident Magistrate at Whangarei Heads, remaining there until his retirement in 1880. Some of Norman Mcleod’s religious community from Nova Scotia who settled at Waipu later took up land at Whangarei Heads.

info_origin: A name borrowed from the harbour of the same name, with Whakaruru Pā historic site on the headland. The ocean-going waka Māhuhu or more fully Mahuhu-ki-e-rangi captained in one tradition by Rongomai, reached New Zealand near North Cape then sailed south to Whangaroa, to Whangaruru, and eventually on to East Cape. Missionary Samuel Marsden (1765-1838) visited the harbour in 1820, which he phonetically rendered as ‘Wangadoodoo’. J Macquarie Palmer, in making a pre-Treaty of Waitangi land purchase in January 1840, used the spelling ‘Wangaruru’. In 1859 Archdeacon Henry Willliams (1792-1867) recorded how his party ‘reached the next settlement, called Whangadudu’ where friendly Māori provided food and shelter for which Williams’ ‘gave them some fishhooks’. A native school was opened in what was then just Whangaruru in 1891. The New Zealand Geological Survey Geological map of Bay of Islands, Russell and Whangaruru Survey Districts drawn by George Edward Harris (1874-1932) and published in 1922 also labels the settlement Whangaruru. Lands and Survey published a cadastral map of the Whangaururu Survey District in 1926, the work of chief draughtsman Harry Edward Walshe (1883-1948), later Surveyor General and member of the Honorary Geographic Board. This map depicted the wāhi tapu and Native School Reserve all labelled as Whangaruru. Almost opposite across the harbour was another Whangaruru, where a post office was located on Tokitoki Point, but this was not shown on the first 1:63360 topographical map NZMS1 in 1942. In 1939 the New Zealand Herald first referred to Whangaruru North. This use was continued on the earliest 1942 NZMS1 topographical maps. Edward Dollimore (1904-73) noted in his 1952 New Zealand Guide that Whangaruru was ‘sometimes’ called Whangaruru North, hinting at an alternative use. However, by 1962 he had further adjusted his stance to list the settlement as Whangaruru Beach ‘formerly Whangaruru North’. However, the 1964 cadastral map used Whangaruru North and also located Whangaruru South. By 1970 the area opposite Whangaruru North, on inland from Tamateatai Point and flanking Punaruku Estuary, was now labelled Whangaruru.

info_origin: Named for the harbour and in association with Whangaruru North. As a locality, the name appears in newspapers from 1922. The locality was unnamed on both the New Zealand Geological Survey map of 1922 and Lands and Survey’s cadastral map published in 1926 A named post office was established in 1910 and a telegraph office added in 1926 the same year in which local farmers gave Whangaruru South as their address for the Sheep Returns. In 1936 the Whangaruru South Native School, its name suggesting that ‘Whangaruru South’ included the southern portion of Whangaruru North peninsula as well as the western side of the harbour, was shifted across the water to a new site at present day Whangaruru South. In 1940 the area gained fleeting national attention when a ticket inscribed ‘Mac’ won the first prize of £2000 in the Art Union raffle. Whangaruru South was recorded on Sheet 16 of the first national topographical series NZMS1 in 1942 although shown north of Ōkiore Point / Rugged Point to the headland separating Ōakura Bay and Ohawini Bay. Whangaruru South again featured in the newspapers in 1947 when two yellow bellied sea snakes washed up on the beach. The 1964 cadastral series show Whangaruru South was at its current position in the northern part of Ōakura Bay.

name: Wharekākā
info_ref: Objective ID: A4635550; H/O/M entry from Mike Roche April 2024: Objective ID: A6258696 {[Death of Mr Andrew Reeves. 1903. Poverty Bay Herald, 5 November, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBH19031105.2.14); Dollimore, E. S. 1952. The New Zealand Guide. New Zealand: Wises.; [Long Delay in Settlement of Wharekaka Block. 1949. Gisborne Herald, 20 August, Page 4.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/GISH19490820.2.21); Makay, J.A. 1949. Historic Poverty Bay and the East Coast, N.I. N.Z. New Zealand: Mackay.; [Our District and our Settlers No. 14. 1884. Poverty Bay Standard, 23 February, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBS18840223.2.16); [Our District and our Settlers No. 15. 1884. Poverty Bay Standard, 23 February, Page 2.](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBS18840223.2.16); R21490125 Lands for settlement, Wharekaka Settlement, archives New Zealand, Auckland.; Reed, A.W. & Dowling, P. 2010. Place Names of New Zealand. New Zealand: Reed.; [Settling the Back Blocks. 1924. Poverty Bay Herald,5 January, Page 4 (Supplement).](https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/PBH19240105.2.131.25)}
info_origin: Edward Dollimore (1904-72) compiler of the New Zealand Guide offered a literal translation of Wharekākā as the house of the kākā parrot (Nestor meridionalis). Writer-historian Alexander Wyclif Reed (1908-79) was less literal, suggesting nesting place of the kākā. Andrew Reeves (1832-1903) who arrived in New Zealand from Scotland in 1857 and formerly managed sheep stations in the Hawke’s Bay Region, leased Wharekākā land in 1865-66. By 1878 merchants John Kinross and Andrew Graham of the partnership of Messers Graham and Kinross were also leasing Wharekākā from Māori owners, although the property was managed by W Walter McClive (1856-89). Graham and Kinross eventually secured the freehold of 6000 acres (2428ha) although initially there was uncertainty over the title to the land. Mānuka, flax and scrub were gradually replaced with pasture. In 1919 The government purchased 780 acres (316 ha) from the estate of the late Andrew Reeves at £33 per acre, paying half in cash and half in war bonds. The land was subdivided to become a discharged soldier settlement. Initially officials suggested Uawa Settlement as the appropriate name, but Wharekaka prevailed. The land was subdivided into 14 sections of 37 (15 ha) to 92 acres (37 ha), some with drainage problems. Balloted for in 1921, the seven good sections each attracted 17 to 21 applications with only single figures for the remaining six. In 1950 a further 690 acres (279 ha) was developed as five rehabilitation farms for WWII veterans.

name: Wharekāpu / Paxton Point
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-09/1017; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Ngāti Kuri and Te Aupouri history: This site has great significance as part of Te Ara Wairua (the spiritual pathway). Piri Paraone mentioned Wharekāpu in a korero about the spiritual pathway: "I timata mai i tera taha, ko o tatou matua i heke mai i tenei tahataha, ahu atu ki Ngāti Kahu, Ngai Takoto, Ngāti Rehia. Kia rere mai i Rangaunu, Houhora ki Wharekaapu, i Rangiora, tatu ki Murimotu, kia huri kia ahu anooo ki Te Reinga. Ki tera taha ko te Oneroa a Tōhē. Tona ingoa tuatahi ko te Ara Wairua". "It begins on the east side ascending from this side onwards to Ngāti Kahu, Ngāti Takoto, and Ngāti Rehia. The flight begins at Rangaunu (Doubtless Bay), Houhora to Wharekaapu to Rangiora, setting down at Murimotu and turning in the direction of Te Reinga. On the other side is Te Oneroa a Tōhē. The original name for this coast being Te Ara Wairua, the spiritual pathway' (submitted in the evidence of Waerete Norman to the Waitangi Tribunal and cited in Stokes, 'A Review of the Evidence of the Muriwhenua Lands Claims, Vol 2, p. 718). Reverend Māori Marsden noted in his evidence to the Waitangi Tribunal that Wharekaapu was a pā of the Ngāti Awa people on the southern side of Parengarenga. The Ngāti Awa people occupied the foreshore of Rarawa between Parengarenga and Houhora for a time. Reverend Marsden recounts fighting between Ngāti Kaha (the people of Pohurihanga of the Kurahaupo waka), who were assisted by Ihutara, and Ngāti Awa. Ihutara was slain at Wharekaapu pā and his body taken by his son Taihaupapa to an island in the Parengarenga Harbour where three dogs were slain for the 'whangai-hau' ceremony of the funeral rites (Te Mana o Te Hiku o Te Ika', Wai 45, Doc A7,p.5 and 6). This name has its origins in the word wharekaapunipuni - a gathering place and an assembly point after battles or skirmishes. However, it was better known as a training place for young Te Aupouri warriors. They lived, cultivated and harvested rawa whenua and preserved kaimoana. Urupa are often exposed by the elements here.
info_description: A coastal point within Great Exhibition Bay, located at the northern end of Rarawa Beach. Feature shown on: NZMS260 N03; NZTopo50-AU25 064592

info_origin: This is an original Māori name for a stream and the adjacent area. The area was the scene of some confrontations pre-1840. Wharekauhau was part of the 150000 acre [60702 ha] West Side of Lake Tūrakirae block purchase in 1853. In 1864 Henry Eglinton (1837-1904), who arrived in Wellington on the Slain's Castle in 1849 and initially settled in the Hutt Valley, took up 416 acres (168 ha) at Wharekauhau and expanded his land holdings over the next 25 years. By 1900, and known as Wharekauhau Station, the property amounted to 2200 acres (890 ha). The station remained in family ownership until its sale in 1979. The current owners of the property consider that Wharekauhau means 'place of knowledge'. Although Wharekauhau was used in official documents from the 1880s, the locality and station was sometimes rendered in local newspapers as Wharekaukau. Questioned by the NZ Automobile Association about the correct spelling, in 1966 the New Zealand Geographic Board confirmed it was Wharekauhau.

name: Wharemoa
info_origin: The name is derived from the railway station, altered from Karoro to Wharemoa in 1963. The Honorary Geographic Board first approved Wharemoa for an area in the vicinity of Watson Creek to the south. The name Wharemoa was not original, coined and proposed by the 'South Beach Ratepayers Association', its literal meaning 'hollow' in reference to the dredging that used to take place in the area, though technically the word in te reo Māori applies only to a hollow in a tree. In 1963 it was determined this southern area was better known as Karoro, though Karoro Railway Station and Lake Karoro were 1.5km-2km north. Despite the small distance the localites were on either side of the boundary between Greymouth Borough and Grey County, causing some confusion and communication issues. The NZGB discontinued Wharemoa (in the south) and altered Karoro Railway Station to Wharemoa Railway Staton (in the north), though attracted objection from Greymouth Borough Council who believed Karoro remained the more appropriate name in the north, and that Wharemoa "had no local significance and would not gain ready acceptance." Over time Wharemoa did come into use as the name of the suburb adjacent to the railway station. Effectively, Karoro and Wharemoa swapped places.
info_description: Suburb of Greymouth. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BU19 519972

name: Wharepapa / Arthur Range
info_ref: LINZ file reference: GES-N15-08-07/331; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760};
info_origin: Ngati Tama notes that Wharepapa is a sacred ancestor, providing a historical and spiritual link to the natural world. Wharepapa is the highest maunga in the takiwa and a vital link to the spirits. Ngati Rarua history: the highest peak of these ranges is Tu Ao Wharepapa and is one of the two sacred maunga for the manawhenua of Motueka. Its significance is embodied in the pepeha “Ko Tu Ao Wharepapa te maunga, ko Ngati Rarua te iwi….”. Important source of the plant Nei Nei which was used to manufacture the wet weather capes worn by our tupuna. Also a number of sacred caves or tomo are situated within this maunga.

name: Whatapaka Creek
info_origin: Ngāti Tamaoho history: 'Ngati Tamaoho have lived along the shores of Whatapaka Creek for generations. They have relied on the awa for their daily food, their clothing, housing, transport and trade, and the other necessities of life. This made the estuarine waters and seabed of the Creek a highly valued taonga. The water body was also valued for spiritual and cultural reasons, as a source of mauri and mana, and holds a central place in the tribal identity. The contemporary Ngati Tamaoho Marae is located on the waterfront of Whatapaka Creek, just inside the entrance from the Manukau Harbour. The Meeting House has a carving of Papaka as its koruru or head figure. The image of Papaka and the Wharenui carvings record and recall the strong and long connections and ancestral relationships between the people and the adjacent Creek and the Manukau Harbour, and its creatures, and the special role of this marae in exercising kaitiaki and mana over the Creek and Harbour - relationships that bind people and place together. Tradition suggests that the name may relate ti a string of drying fish. Above the Marae and overlooking the Creek and Harbour is the Ngati Tamaoho urupa, containing many forebears. Tradition holds that a previous ancient Ngati Tamaoho Marae, also named “Whatapaka” was located at the very head of the Creek at Puhitahi. The banks of the Creek, and indeed parts of the Creek bed are studded with records of Ngati Tamaoho occupation and burials, extending back to the earliest settlement of this area by humans. In 1867 the Native Land Court investigated claims to land in the Whatapaka area and held that some land around the Creek was a Native Reserve, and granted title that included areas of seabed, including shell-banks used for birding near the mouth of Whatapaka Creek (Deeds Registry 37987NC). This title to the seabed (the only seabed title issued in the Manukau Harbour) appears to have been extinguished unintentionally by the Manukau Harbour Control Act 1911. Following an exploration of customary and legal rights to Whatapaka Creek by the Waitangi Tribunal in 1984 (WAI-8, Recommendation 6) the Whatapaka Marae Committee applied to the Maori Land Court to have the Creek set aside as a Maori Reservation. In 1990 the Maori Land Court stated that “it was left in no doubt as to the historical, traditional and spiritual importance of Whatapaka Creek to Ngati Tamaoho”. A year later the whole of Whatapaka Creek was gazetted as a Maori Reservation under Sections 439 and 439A of the Maori Affairs Act 1953.' Information source: David Armstrong Ngati Tamaoho Land and Politics March 2012. Ben Leonard Ngati Tamaoho Sites of Significance Feb 2012. Waitangi Tribunal Report of the Waitangi Tribunal on the Manukau Claim (WAI-8), July 1985. Survey plans in 1884 (SO Pan 3119) and 1970 (SO Plan 11114) and newspaper reports of 1927 refer to this feature as “Whatapaka inlet). 'Whatapaka Creek (Clarks) is a tidal inlet on the southern shore of the Manukau Harbour. At the mouth of the Whatapaka Creek, on the eastern bank, lies the Whatapaka marae, one of three current Ngati Tamaoho marae. The banks of the Whatapaka creek were once densely occupied with pa and small fishing settlements stretching to Puhitahi in the south. On the western bank the Paraheka area was also the site of several pa and cultivations. Prior to European settlement the Whatapaka creek was plentiful in Tuna, Kahawai, snapper, mullet, shark, stingray and yellow-bellied flounder with the shellfish banks providing piaro, pupu, cockles and oysters. Aside from its use as a fishing and shellfish gathering ground, the Whatapaka creek also has significant spiritual and ceremonial associations for Ngati Tamaoho.' Information source: B Leonard, Ngati Tamaoho Sites of Significance, 93-98. D Armstrong, Ngati Tamaoho: Land and Politics 1840-1970, 303-305 & 380-386. Waitangi Tribunal, Manukau Report: WAI 8, 10, & 41-42.
info_description: A tidal inlet extending north for approximately 4km from near Kingseat to it's mouth at Manukau Harbour. Karaka Creek and Puhitahi Creek are two main tributaries flowing into the creek from the south. Te Hihi Creek is the third main tributary flowing into the stream 1.5km south of it's mouth. NZTopo50 BB32 587891 to 596933.
treaty_legislation: Section 43 and 44 Ngāti Tamaoho Claims Settlement Act 2018

name: Whātaumā Stream
info_origin: Whanganui Iwi (Whanganui River) statement: 'The stream is the boundary between the Rānana and Ngārākauwhakarārā land blocks, which extends to the Oruawharo Stream (59 Whanganui MB, p. 92), though Haami Te Kee noted that this boundary was fixed by Pākehā (59 Whanganui MB, p. 58). The name of the stream, as spelt throughout the Whanganui Minute Books at that time, is clearly ‘Whātauma’. We have added the macron to the first vowel in Whātauma, as this vowel is stressed or lengthened when the name ‘Whātauma’ is articulated by our kuia and koroheke, who were born and raised in Rānana, and know the Whātauma Stream and associated lands well. They fondly remember gathering koura (fresh water crayfish) from the Whātauma Stream as children, and moa bones have also been found in the Whātauma. The stream is also a source of tuna (eel) for our people.'

info_origin: A Māori name meaning ‘suspended heads’, relating to intertribal fighting about 1740 when two young men were taken prisoner and killed, and their heads hung from a rail before later being taken away and preserved. Originally limited to the area between the junction of Taruheru River and Waimata River, it eventually described a total of nine land blocks over 20000 acres (8094 ha) extending to the west on the northern bank of Taruheru River. In 1864 William Parker Snr (1823-?) leased the Whataupoko Block from Henare Ruru, Otene Pitau and Tom Jones for 21 years. A Crown grant for the 19200 acres (7770 ha) Whataupoko Block was issued to Raharuhi Rukupo and 47 others in 1871 as joint tenants under the Poverty Bay Grants Act, 1869, but not before trader and mariner George Edward Read (1814/5?-87) had acquired interests in the block. A long and complicated history of leasing, land sales and litigation followed involving notably Parker, lawyer politician William Lee Rees (1836-1912), politician and runholder Wiremu (Wi) Pere (1837-1915), the New Zealand Native Land Settlement Company and Kate Wylie (?-1913) who was Pere’s half-brother and a formidable figure at Native Land Court hearings. From 1881 attempts were made to sell 12500 acres (5059 ha) of the Whataupoko Block. Bridging of Taruheru River the same year enabled Whatauporo to overtake Waikanae ‘as the favorite Sunday afternoon resort. There is a long stretch of country to ramble over, the scenery is diversified, and health-giving recreation may be found in clambering up the hill tops. To those of a meditative turn of mind there are many secluded and shady retreats along the riverbank’. Administratively, the area was organized as Whataupoko Road Board (1883-1917). In 1905 in part Whataupoko became a suburb of Gisborne Borough. Rees’ obituary claimed that ‘It was largely through his instrumentality that the Whataupoko was converted from a sheep run and scrub-covered area: into a smiling suburb of Gisborne’.
info_description: A northern suburb of Gisborne, on the left bank of Taruheru River. Feature shown on: NZMS260 Y18 Edition 1 1984; NZTopo50-BG43 375097

name: Whatawhata
info_origin: According to Ngā Iwi o Tainui, in about 1525 Māhina-a-rangi, heavily pregnant, travelled from the Kahotea district, near present day Te Aute College through to her husband’s homeland at Rangiātea. Her husband was Tūrongo. When Maahina-a-rangi was due to give birth she came by way of Te Wairoa, detouring by way of Waikaremoana and reaching Rotorua. According to the stories it was a very large party and they were entertained by the local people people wherever they went. After leaving Rotorua, and a little this side of Tiirau, Maahina-a-rangi felt her pains. There was a hot spring there and Maahina-a-rangi remained there to give birth. Her child was a boy, who was named Raukawa in memory of the perfume she used when she and Tuurongo were courting. Her child Raukawa is the eponymous ancestor of the iwi of Raukawa in the south Waikato. As Māhina-a-rangi and her entourage made their way down the Kaimai Ranges with the new born baby, in order to orientate themselves in the lower Kaimai region they crossed the Māhina-a-rangi Stream at Whatawhata climbing to higher ground from which they were able to see the prominent mountain, Maungatautari. The Māhina-a-rangi Stream runs through Whatawhata to the Waiomu Stream.
info_description: An historic site at the confluence of Māhina-a-rangi Stream and Waiomou Stream, approximately 10km south-east of Matamata near the intersection of Stopford Road with State Highway 24. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BD35 519064

Whenua ā-kura, according to Ngāti Kirihika sources, was dominated by a peak at the top of the Kaimai Range. Its history for Raukawa stems from the apical ancestress Māhina-a-rangi [of the Takitimu waka] and her journeys to her husband Tūrongo [of the Tainui waka]. Thomas Smith, of Ngāti Kirihika and others, states that Raukawa was born at Whenua-Thomas Smith, of Ngāti Kirihika and others, supports this as he states that following the birth of Raukawa at Whenua ā-kura.

name: Whillans Ice Stream
info_origin: The feature is identified as Ice Stream B in reports by the SPRI-NSF-TUD airborne radio echo sounding program (1967-79) and USAP from 1984. The name was changed by US-ACAN in 2001 to honor Ian M. Whillans (1944-2001) glaciologist, Byrd Polar Research Center and Department of Geological Sciences, Ohio State University, whose work in Antarctica spanned the years from 1967 until his death. Whillans was a major figure in the study of West Antarctic ice streams, particularly this one, and he had a central role in recognizing from the earliest years that these ice streams hold the key to determining the stability of the West Antarctic ice sheet.

info_origin: Named after the village where Captain James Cook was born. Name given during the development of the housing estate. Named in honour of the 200th annivesary of Captain Cook’s historic voyage to New Zealand. The basis of the honour states that Whitby is where Captain James Cook served his apprenticeship and where his vessel the ‘Endeavour’ was built. The proposal to build the village and name it in honour of Captain James Cook’s 200th anniversary was supported and approved by the Hutt County Council.; 'This subdivision on the eastern arm of the Porirua Estuary was named after the English town of Whitby, Yorkshire, where Captain James Cook worked as an apprentice to a shipping firm. The name was given by the developers, Huapai Properties, in 1969, the bicentennial year of Cook’s first visit to New Zealand. Many of the street names also have a nautical flavour.' name: Whitehall Glacier
info_origin: The name was applied partly because of its literal meaning, and partly because of proximity of the glacier to the Admiralty Range, the Admiralty Office in London being situated in Whitehall. Its terminal face abuts against the lower part of Tucker Glacier but does not contribute ice to it, being stagnant and probably afloat . It has a low gradient and could probably be used as a sledging route between the Lady Newnes Ice Shelf and the Tucker Glacier-Hallett Station district, but for the fact that extremely broken area near its terminal face is a maze of melt pools and ice ridges. Sledging in that area would be almost impossible, especially in January and February. Named by the NZGSAE, 1957-58.

name: Wigley Glacier
info_origin: Named after the Wigley family who were early pioneers at the Hermitage. They pioneered motor transport and ski plane development. Sir Henry Rudolf of Timaru was long associated with alpine flying in New Zealand. He pioneered the use of ski-equipped planes for rescue, mountaineering, and tourist purposes in this country. Gaz notice says "Totare" Range not "Tatare" Range. There was debate about getting another glacier in which Sir Harry Wigley apparently "discovered" from the air named after the Wigley's but this did not eventuate. His son Rudolpf introduced skiing to South Island and was the first to climb Aoraki/Mount Cook in winter.

info_note: The NZGB committee on place naming in the Ross Sea Region in Antarctica at its meeting on 7 July 2004 accepted this name, but had an issue with the feature. The issue with the ponds is not just their permanence but also whether they are geomorphologically less significant than surrounding unnamed features. 22 features in Antarctica with the name ‘Williams’ or ‘Williamson’, with 6 being in the Ross Sea Region (Cape Williams, Williams Air Operating Facility, Williams Bluff, Williams Cliff, Williams Peak, Williamson Rock). However, at its meeting of 8 November 2006, the NZGB agreed to accept this name.

info_origin: Original description: The highest and most snow-free of all the nunataks on the Polar Plateau between the Otway Massif and Roberts Massif. Frank Wong (1950-1992) led the New Zealand initiative to establish a comprehensive and internationally legally binding regime to protect the Antarctic environment, and tabled the first draft of that Treaty at the ATCM XV in Paris in 1989. He led New Zealand delegations to the programme of subsequent negotiations of the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty, culminating in its conclusion in 1991. He had previously been involved in representing New Zealand at other Antarctic negotiations and was part of an official visit to Antarctica in 1983.
info_description: A peak 3km northeast of the summit of Mount Bird in northwest Ross Island. The feature rises to over 1698m. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME13
info_note: Feature # 7 in ACAN minutes of 19/06/2000. The name is included with proposals # 4, 6 and 8 for "prominent statesmen and administrators." The feature was requested to be named by the US on 12/01/2000. A new name was recommended by the NZ Antarctic Place Names Committee at its meeting of 31/03/2000 which was ratified by the NZGB at its meeting of 20/02/2001 and Antarctica NZ were consulted on 23/03/2001.

info_origin: NZGB Correspondence Vol. 27 f.147: Marlborough Express 29 Nov 1951: The late MR Tosswill, of Yncyca Bay, told me his elder brother was the first to take up and clear this area, and that the name was given by his wife, who was of Indian extraction, the name meaning "My Home" in her language. The picturesque Maori name of the bay is Pirau-Ngaehe, and a tale attached to the bay relates how a Maori hapu living there were warned by the crackling of dry wood of their enemies' approach and so were able to combat or evade them. Hence the name pirau, "dry or brittle wood," ngaehe, 'a crackling or rustling sound."; ’An Indigenous American name meaning ‘My home’, given by Mrs Tosswill, the wife of the first European settler, who was of American Indian extraction. Māori name: Pirau-Ngaehe: lit. pirau: dry wood; ngaehe: to crackle or rustle. The crackling of twigs and dry wood underfoot gave warning of would-be attackers.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. name: Young Nicks Head / Te Kurī
info_ref: Dual name standardisation: Objective IDs: A4405369, A4507521, A4537063; A4635550
info_origin: ’The first person on the Endeavour to sight New Zealand, on 7 October 1769, was the surgeon’s boy, Nicholas Young. Captain James Cook named ‘Young Nick’s Head’ after him, perhaps with one of those rare touches of humour that enliven his place names. In the log compiled by Robert Molyneux, master of the Endeavour, the boy’s name is given as Nicholas Young, and he appears on the Nominal Index, but it has been stated that no such name appears in official lists of the ship’s company. Māori name: Te Kurī: lit: te: the; kurī: dog; or Te Ūpoko-o-te-kurī-a-Paoa, The head of Paoa’s dog. The final destination of the Horouta canoe was at Muriwai to the south of Tūranganui-a-Kiwa (Gisborne). Not far from here Paoa’s dog Whakao was killed by mākutu (magic spell) and transformed into the white cliff.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.; See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDNCNkQ3QTZGMjBGRjg3QjA0N0I)
